We open our tale with young Harry Warrington crossing the Atlantic for the first time, bound for the old Esmond family estates in England, little guessing the steep, unexpected price he will pay for his very first supper on foreign soil. We shall first introduce you to the sprawling, sun-dappled Tidewater plantation of Castlewood in Virginia, where the ancient, storied Esmond line has taken deep root across two generations, before Harry stumbles on a long-lost kinsman he never knew existed, touching off the small, sharp family frictions that no great landed clan ever escapes.

The two Warrington boys, George and Harry, will soon leave their Virginia home to see the wider world, just as the drums of the French and Indian War begin to beat across the colonies. George will first fall victim to the universal young man’s ailment of head-over-heels, all-consuming infatuation, before the pair are welcomed into the warm, generous hospitality of neighbours and strangers alike on a sweltering mid-summer Virginia afternoon. Soon two men both named George — our hero George Warrington, and the young up-and-coming colonial colonel George Washington — will gird their swords to march against the French, and dispatches back from the front will lead Harry on a foolish, fruitless quest across hundreds of miles of wilderness, until he at last takes ship for England.

He will find himself a welcome guest at the ancient English Castlewood manor on a soft, quiet 1750s Sunday, where his faithful valet Gumbo will astonish the stuffy local gentry with his unexpected skill at the ancient English sport of archery. The scent of half-forgotten secrets will hang thick in the halls of the old house, and a long-buried old family romance will come spilling out, tangled up both in unlooked-for good fortune and the giddy, heedless pull of reckless young love. The path of ease and indulgence is all too easy for a young colonial heir to slip down, but he will soon find kind Samaritans to catch him when he stumbles, and a stretch of gentle convalescence in a quiet country inn, followed by bright, giddy holidays that carry him from the sleepy village of Oakhurst all the way to the fashionable spa at Tunbridge Wells, where he will make a host of new acquaintances that carry him far, far away from the quiet plantation life he once knew.

Chance will pile on top of chance as he gambles his way through the London pleasure districts, treading all the familiar crooked paths of the 18th century metropolis, whiling away days in idle, unhonoured ease before he pens a long, fond letter back home to his kin in Virginia. Soon he will find himself caught between a fiery political agitator and a surly, quarrelsome bear of a man, a gilded family coach will be ordered to carry the party cross-country, and sharp-tongued old Hester will deliver a long, bitter soliloquy over the state of the household. Mr. George Warrington will host a lavish tea party and a grand ball for his new London acquaintances, but the festivities will quickly tangle the pair up in messy romantic and financial entrapments that all but spell ruin. A string of duels will be fought over petty slights and contested honour, the blustering parson Sampson will face down his own personal Philistines, and Harry will step in to save the day more than once, paying off a decades-old family debt even as he racks up crushing new ones of his own, falling into the heedless, reckless life of a rake that carries him to dizzying social heights before the fate everyone expected finally arrives to bring him low.

Harry will stumble across two uncles he never knew he had, find himself tangled in the chains of a loveless engagement, welcome troubled visitors to his London lodgings, and start at an apparition that appears out of the London fog one night to prove an unexpected friend in need. We shall lay out pages of the finest, most earnest moralising over the follies of young men, then fall quiet as a grave at the climax of a long-awaited revelation, every eye fixed and every mouth stilled, before we settle into the glittering, gilded Court end of London society. Harry will spend many quiet nights smoking his pipe by his fireside, the two brothers will have long, earnest talks that mend old rifts, and one young woman left pining will find herself abandoned like Ariadne on her empty island. Harry will time and again find himself pushed out of favour, left to watch from the sidelines as others take the limelight, before the pair attend a raucous night at the play, where a performance of *Macbeth*, a midnight supper, and a very messy misunderstanding leaves everyone in a fine kettle of fish. The young pretender to the crown will march his troops up the hill and down again, and swords will be drawn as the two men head off to war, following the tragic muse Melpomene through battlefields that Harry will survive to tell the tale, coming home at last to the warm welcome of a soldier long returned.

He will soon set off to court the lady of his heart, only for a private domestic tragedy to play out, followed by two new romances just beginning. Harry will head west across the Atlantic to return to his Virginia home, where a sweet, sheltered young innocent catches his eye, and Cupid will weave his mischief through half the households of the Tidewater, handing out favours and breaking promises in equal measure. We draw on the old Warrington family manuscript to tell you how our lady of the manor climbed to the very top of the social ladder, and how the whole clan gathered to keep Christmas at Castlewood in the frosty winter of 1759. News will come sailing across the ocean of Britain’s great victory over France in Canada, the course of true love will run all its expected bumpy paths, before Mr. Warrington makes a wild, impulsive leap into a waiting Landau coach that somehow sees every last passenger clamber out safe and sound. The pair of star-crossed lovers separated by family secrets will play out their own Pyramus and Thisbe farce, mixing bright comedy and sharp tragedy in equal measure, before a bright young mixed-race girl known to all as Pocahontas changes the whole shape of the family’s fate. Hard times will fall on the household, the last of old Miley’s precious gold moidore will be spent through a run of bad luck, and the family will find troubles and small, quiet consolations to carry them through. Harry will meet the same fate that all men must, but at last he will find his safe harbour, to settle at home under his own vine and fig tree, long after the old royalist anthem *God Save the King* has faded to be replaced by the sprightly new tune of Yankee Doodle marching through the towns of a new nation. He will find himself a colonel with no regiment to lead, fight a battle and run away with honour, satisfied that he has fought enough fights for one lifetime, at last to rest in peace — and this is the full tale of *The Virginians*.

On the library wall of one of America’s most revered writers hang two crossed swords, once worn by his kinsmen in the great War of Independence. One was drawn gallantly in the service of the British Crown, the other wielded by a brave, honoured republican soldier. The man who keeps these harmless, precious trophies has earned a name equally honoured in his ancestors’ old country and his own, where genius of his calibre is always welcomed with peace and respect.

This story brings those paired swords to mind. In the Revolutionary War, the two men at its heart—native sons of Virginia, the Old Dominion—found themselves fighting on opposite sides of the conflict. When the war ended, they returned to each other as brothers should: the anger of the strife had divided them, but never truly lessened the love between them. The colonel in scarlet and the general in blue and buff hang side by side now, their portraits framed in the wainscoted parlour of the Warrington family estate in England, where a descendant of one of the brothers once showed me those likenesses, stacked piles of their surviving letters, and the tattered books and papers they once owned. The family has long called these two men “the Virginians” to distinguish them from other lines of their respected house, and that is the name these memoirs bear.

Both spent large stretches of their lives in Europe, living right on the cusp of that old, vivid world we are drifting away from so swiftly. They knew all sorts of people, rose and fell through many turns of fortune, and brushed shoulders with historical figures we only read about in books. As I read their yellowed, centuries-old letters—some blotted with the boyish tears of disappointed young passion, some scribbled hastily after famous royal balls and court ceremonies, others scrawled by campfires or smuggled out of prison, even one pierced clean through by a bullet, most of its text smudged away with the blood of the man carrying it—it feels like those figures are alive, like I can almost hear their voices. None of these letters would have survived at all if not for the tender thrift of the woman they all wrote to without fail: their mother. Madam Esmond Warrington kept every single one, starting with the very first note from younger twin Harry, sending his love to brother George, laid up with a sprain at their grandfather’s Castlewood home in Virginia, and thanking his grandpapa for a new horse he rode alongside his tutor. She kept them all right down to the final note marked “from my beloved son,” that reached her only hours before she drew her last breath. The venerable lady had only visited Europe once, as a girl with her parents in the reign of George II. When Castlewood House burned down mid-war, she fled to Richmond, and everyone called her Madam Esmond from that day on, holding the Warrington family name in far lower esteem than her own Esmond lineage.

As you will soon see from the excerpts shared here, the Virginians’ letters are never full, detailed accounts. They are hints, outlines, little clues rather than dense descriptions. I may have guessed wrong at the shapes of their days, filled in the colours of their scenes incorrectly—but poring over those fragile documents, I have tried to imagine where each writer sat as they scribbled, who stood around them, what they saw and smelled and felt. I have drawn their figures as I picture they were, written down conversations I could almost fancy overhearing, and done my best to breathe life back into those long-gone times and people. Whether I have succeeded, and whether this tale brings you profit or simple amusement, I leave to your kind judgement, dear reader.

It was a bright summer morning in 1756, in the reign of King George II, when the *Young Rachel*, a Virginian trading ship under master Edward Franks, sailed up the Avon River on her happy return from her annual voyage to the Potomac. She rode the tide all the way to Bristol, mooring in the stream as close as possible to Trail’s Wharf, her assigned consignment port. Mr. Trail, the ship’s part-owner, who could watch his vessel bob in the water straight from his counting house window, immediately called a boat and rowed out to meet her. A large, grave man who wore his own hair unpowdered, with a prim, demure look about him, he shook Captain Franks’ hand on the deck to welcome him, and congratulated him on his fast, uneventful, fortunate voyage. After piously remarking that they all owed thanks to Heaven for its mercies, he promptly turned to business, asking for full details on the cargo and any passengers aboard.

Franks was a jolly, good-natured man who loved a good joke. “We’ve got nothing but that lanky young enslaved negro boy over there hauling trunks out, and one passenger who’s got the whole state cabin all to himself,” he said.

Mr. Trail scowled like he would have preferred a few more mercies from Heaven. “Confound you, Franks, and your rotten luck! The Duke William came in last week with fourteen passengers, and she’s not even half our tonnage.”

“And this passenger who’s got the whole cabin? He doesn’t pay a single farthing,” Franks went on, grinning. “Go on, swear now, it’ll do you good, Mr. Trail, truly it will. I’ve tried the medicine myself.”

“A passenger taking the whole cabin and not paying? Good gracious mercy, are you a fool, Captain Franks?”

“Ask the man himself, here he comes now.” As Franks spoke, a young man of nineteen climbed up out of the hatchway. He had a cloak and a sheathed sword tucked under one arm, and was dressed head to toe in deep mourning. “Gumbo, you idiot,” he called over his shoulder, “stop dawdling and get the baggage out of the cabin. Well, shipmate, our journey’s done. You’ll get to see all the folks you’ve been chattering about for months tonight—give my love to Polly, Betty, and little Tommy, and send my respects to Mrs. Franks. I swore yesterday the voyage would never end, and now I’m half sorry it’s over. That tiny little bunk in my cabin looks almost cozy now I’m about to leave it.”

Mr. Trail glowered at the penniless passenger, barely nodding at him, when Captain Franks cut in. “This here gentleman is Mr. Trail, sir. You’ve heard the name, I expect.”

“It’s well known all over Bristol, sir,” Mr. Trail huffed, drawing himself up pompously.

“And this is Mr. Warrington, Madam Esmond Warrington’s son of Castlewood,” Franks finished.

The British merchant’s hat flew off his head instantly, and he bowed so low he nearly tipped over, as if he stood before a crown prince. “Good gracious powers, Mr. Warrington! What a delight this is! What a crowning mercy that your voyage was so prosperous! You must take my private boat to go ashore. Let me welcome you to England with all cordial respect, let me shake your hand as the son of my benefactress and patroness, Mrs. Esmond Warrington, whose name is known and honoured all across Bristol ‘Change, I promise you. Isn’t that right, Franks?”

“There’s no sweeter tobacco coming out of Virginia, and no better brand than the Three Castles,” Franks agreed, pulling a great brass tobacco box from his pocket and tucking a quid into his mouth. “You don’t know what a comfort it is, sir! You’ll take to it, bless you, once you get a bit older. Won’t he, Mr. Trail? I wish you had ten shiploads of that tobacco instead of one. I’ve told Madam Esmond that myself. I’ve ridden all over her plantation, and she treats me like a visiting lord when I come to the house—never stints on the best wine, never keeps me cooling my heels in the counting house like some folks I could name,” he added, throwing a pointed look at Mr. Trail. “She’s a true born lady, that one. She could grow a thousand hogsheads as easy as her hundreds, if only there were enough hands to tend them.”

“I’ve recently gone into the Guinea trade, and I could supply her ladyship with any number of healthy young negroes before next fall,” Mr. Trail said, obsequious.

“We do not buy enslaved people fresh from Africa,” the young gentleman said, coldly. “My grandfather and my mother have always objected to it, and I cannot bear the thought of selling or buying those poor wretches.”

“It is for their own good, my dear young sir! For their temporal and spiritual salvation!” Mr. Trail cried. “We only purchase those poor creatures for their own benefit! Let me talk this matter over with you at my own house. I can show you a happy Christian home, a British merchant’s honest, warm fare. Can’t I, Captain Franks?”

“Can’t say,” Franks growled. “You never asked me to take a bite or sup at your table. Only invited me once to go psalm-singing and hear Mr. Ward preach. Don’t care much for that sort of entertainment.”

Mr. Trail ignored the jab, continuing in his soft, oily tone. “Business is business, my dear young sir, and I know it is my duty—the duty of all of us—to cultivate the fruits of the earth in their season. As the heir of Lady Esmond’s great estate—for I speak, I believe, to the heir of that vast property?”

The young man gave a short, sharp bow.

“—I must urge upon you, at the very earliest moment, the propriety, the duty of increasing the ample means Heaven has blessed you with. As an honest factor, I could do no less; as a prudent man, would I scruple to speak of what will profit both you and me? No, my dear Mr. George—”

“My name is not George. It is Henry.” The young man turned his head away, his eyes filling with sudden tears.

“Good gracious powers—what do you mean, sir? Did you not say you were my lady’s heir? Is not George Esmond Warrington, Esq.—”

“Shut your mouth, you fool!” Franks thumped the merchant hard on his sleek, rounded side, as the young man turned away to hide his face. “Can’t you see the poor lad swabbing his eyes, and notice his black mourning clothes?”

“What do you mean, Captain Franks, striking your own business partner? I know the late Colonel’s will perfectly well—Mr. George is the heir.”

“Mr. George is there,” Franks said, jabbing his thumb up towards the top of the mast.

“Where?” the factor cried, bewildered.

“Mr. George is there!” Franks repeated, pointing up at the pale sky beyond the rigging. “He’s dead a year, come next 9th of July. He went out with General Braddock on that terrible expedition to the Belle Riviere, and him and a thousand more never came back. They were all cut down where they fell, you know the Indian way, Mr. Trail?” He passed his hand rapidly in a circle around his own head, mimicking the slash of a scalping knife. “Horrible, isn’t it? Horrible. He was a fine young man, the very spit of this one, only his hair was black, and now it’s hanging in some bloody Indian wigwam. He was often on board the *Young Rachel* with his brother, and he’d have his chests of books pried open on deck before we even docked, just to see what new volumes he’d ordered. Shy, quiet lad, unlike this one here, who was the merriest, wildest young rascal you ever saw, full of songs and silly pranks. He took the news terrible, went straight to bed, came down with that swamp fever that lays so many Virginian lads low along the Potomac. He got better on the voyage though—being at sea heals everyone. Ever since we sighted Ireland he’s been cheerful enough, but even when he’s at his merriest, he’ll stop short and say ‘I wish my dearest Georgy could see this with me.’ And as you saw just now, he can’t bear to hear his brother’s name spoken out of nowhere.” The honest captain’s own eyes filled with tears as he turned to look at the grieving young man.

Mr. Trail immediately pulled on a suitably lugubrious face, ready to heap condolences on Harry, but the young Virginian answered him very curtly, turned down all his offers of hospitality, and only stayed at Trail’s house long enough to drink a single glass of wine and withdraw the sum of money he needed for his journey. He parted from Captain Franks on the very warmest of terms, and the whole crew of the *Young Rachel* cheered loudly from the deck as he stepped into his boat to go ashore.

Harry Warrington and his twin had pored over their maps of England a hundred times, mapping out their exact route the day they finally arrived at “Home.” Every gently-raised Anglo-American who loved the old country (and who among them did not?) had rehearsed that imaginary English journey long before they ever stepped foot on its shores, visiting in fancy all the spots their parents had told them stories about, that had wrapped themselves up in all their hopes and fondest daydreams. There are few things more touching in the history of the conflict that later split the two great nations apart than that single, loaded word “Home,” which the young American colonists used without hesitation to refer to the mother country across the sea.

Harry had his whole pilgrimage laid out. Before he went to London to gawk at St. Paul’s Cathedral and the grim old Tower where so many brave loyal men had shed their blood, from Wallace down to the recently condemned Balmerino and Kilmarnock that all gentle hearts pitied; before he stood beneath the Whitehall window where the martyr King Charles had stepped out to his execution; before he visited the playhouses, parks, and palaces that were famous across the world for their wit, pleasure, and splendor; before he visited Shakespeare’s grave beneath the tall spire rising from the banks of the Avon amidst the soft Warwickshire pastures; before he walked the battlefields of Derby, Falkirk, and Culloden, where the cause of Jacobite loyalty had fallen, perhaps never to rise again—before every one of those sacred stops, the twins had agreed they would visit the one place that mattered most to them: Castlewood, their family’s old home in Hampshire, that their grandfather had talked of so fondly all their lives. From Bristol to Bath, from Bath to Salisbury, to Winchester, to Hexton, and then Home—they knew the route by heart, had traced it over the map so many times they could have walked the roads blind.

We can picture the young American traveller: a strikingly handsome nineteen-year-old, his suit of sable mourning only making him look more romantic and interesting. The plump inn landlady, standing behind her bar lined with china punch bowls, gilded bottles of strong spirits, and gleaming rows of silver flagons, looked after him kindly as he walked through the hall to his waiting post-chaise. The obsequious chamberlain bowed him up the stairs to the Rose room, the trim chambermaid dropped her deepest curtsy for his generous tip, and his servant Gumbo bragged to a crowd of townsfolk drinking ale by the inn kitchen fire about his young master’s grand estate in Virginia, and the enormous fortune he was heir to.

The post-chaise whirled Harry through the loveliest countryside his eyes had ever lit upon. English landscape charms the American traveller even today, who contrasts its rich woodlands, glowing pastures, and ancient sunlit villages with the wilder, rougher look of the still-new colonies. But Harry had spent all his prior journeys tramping through Virginian swamps and endless forest solitudes, travelling from one rough roadside ordinary to a log cabin at the end of the day, so this bright, bustling, splendid English summer scene felt like a fairy tale to him. The 1756 highway was nothing like the grass-grown, quiet country roads of today: it was alive with constant traffic and travel. Heavy waggons strung with bells and drawn by plodding teams rumbled past, light post-coaches raced from Salisbury’s White Hart inn to London’s Swan with Two Necks in just two days, long lines of packhorses still trundled along the ruts. He saw lord’s gilded post-chaises drawn by six horses with outriders galloping ahead, country squires’ heavy coaches pulled by shaggy Flanders mares, farmers trotting to market, and the local parson jolting towards the cathedral town on his old plough horse Dumpling, his wife riding pillion behind him. The farmer’s boy Hodge took off his hat as he passed, milkmaid Polly bobbed a curtsy, and the white-headed little children playing on the village green lifted their chubby faces and cheered. Church spires glinted gold in the sun, cottage gables blazed in bright light, and the great old elm trees murmured in the summer breeze, casting deep purple shadows across the grass. Harry never had a happier day in his life. To be nineteen, in perfect health, full of high spirits, with a fat purse in his pocket, rolling through the countryside in a post-chaise moving at nine miles an hour—what happier youth could there ever be?

Harry was far too eager to spare more than a passing glance for Bath Abbey, or pause longer than a minute to gawk at the mighty soaring spire of Salisbury Minster. Until he saw Castlewood, it felt like he had no eyes for any other sight.

At last his post-chaise drew up at the little rustic inn on Castlewood Green, the very one his grandfather had told him a hundred stories about, its sign swinging from an old elm by the porch emblazoned with the Three Castles of the Esmond family. Over the main gateway to Castlewood House hung a matching crest: the hatchment of Francis, late Lord Castlewood, who lay buried in the chapel just a short walk away, his son Frank now reigning in his place.

Harry had heard all the old stories about Francis, Lord Castlewood. It was for Frank’s sake, and out of the great love he bore his young stepson, that Colonel Esmond (the twins’ grandfather) had given up all claim to the English Esmond estates and title, choosing to move out to Virginia instead. Frank had lived a wild youth, fought bravely under Marlborough’s command, married a foreign lady, and foolishly converted to her Catholic faith. For a time he had been a Jacobite, for loyalty to the rightful Stuart sovereign ran deep in the Esmond blood, until he was slighted and wronged by the Pret

Fresh off his transatlantic crossing, Harry Esmond Warrington stood ringing the knocker of Castlewood, his grandfather’s rightful ancestral home, for long minutes before any soul inside bothered to answer. The footman who finally wrenched open the oak door couldn’t have cared less that the visitor was a blood relation to the family inside: the master and mistress were still away, and John the footman was in a tearing hurry to get back to his card game with Thomas in the window seat. The housekeeper, harried and breathless as she prepped for the lord and lady’s arrival that very evening, only let Harry beg his way into the lady’s parlour and the portrait gallery after much pleading. There, exactly as he’d known he would find them, hung the familiar faces: his grandfather in periwig and polished breastplate, the perfect twin to the portrait above the mantel at their Virginia plantation, and his grandmother as the young Lady Castlewood, dressed in the loose, low-necked finery of Charles II’s court, her golden hair cascading over her shoulders in soft ringlets Harry still remembered as snow-white from his childhood. The scowling housekeeper chased him off before he could linger, reeling off the names of the party due to arrive: the Countess, Lord Castlewood and his younger brother, the two young ladies, and the Baroness Bernstein, the girls’ aunt, who was to be given the grand state bedroom. Harry scribbled his full name on a scrap of paper from his pocketbook and left it on the hall table: *Henry Esmond Warrington, of Castlewood, in Virginia, arrived in England yesterday--staying at the Three Castles in the village*. The lackeys scrambled up from their card game to hold the door for him, grinning expectantly for tips, and his own servant Gumbo trundled over from the gate bench where he’d been chatting with old porter Lockwood, who accepted Harry’s guinea half confused what the gift even meant. The only unselfish, kind face Harry saw during his entire visit was that of little scullery maid Polly, and he walked away refusing to admit how deeply disappointed he was. Back home in Virginia, any traveller who rode up to their door would be welcomed even if the master was miles away out hunting—but here, at the gates of his ancestors’ hall, he was forced to trudge to a roadside alehouse to beg a plate of bacon and eggs for his dinner.

After he finished his meal, Harry wandered down to the stone bridge over the brook and sat perched on its parapet, staring back at the great house as the sun dipped behind its gables, rooks cawing home to their nests in the ancient elms. His young imagination ran wild, conjuring the ancestors his mother and grandfather had told him tales of: knights fording the stream, Cavalier gentlemen of King Charles’s court, the old Lord Castlewood, his grandmother’s first husband, riding out with hawk and hound. The memory of his lost twin brother hit him then, sharp with tender grief, and he hung his head, the old familiar sorrow welling back up for the companion he had shared every joy and hardship with since birth. Lost in his own thoughts, half listening to the distant clink of the blacksmith’s forge, the chatter of rooks and evening birdsong, two young men on horseback came thundering over the bridge. One snarled a foul oath, called Harry a fool and shouted for him to get out of the way. The other nearly jostled him straight over the parapet into the water, kicked his horse into a gallop on the far side, and yelled for his companion to keep up. Before Harry could even react to their rudeness, the pair were halfway up the drive to the great house. Two liveried grooms on horseback rode past next, snorting the very British welcome of “Curse you, who are you?” at the lone traveller. Then a great, heavy coach and six rumbled over the bridge, stuffed with three ladies, two maids, and an armed footman perched on the rear seat. Three pale, pretty faces peeked out at Harry, and when he tipped his hat in greeting—recognizing the Castlewood coat of arms blazoned on the coach door—not one of them acknowledged him. The armed footman on the back glared at him as if he were a wandering vagrant. Harry suddenly felt overwhelmingly, terribly alone. The tiny, tossing cabin of the ship *Rachel* he had sailed over on felt warmer and more welcoming than the spot he was standing on. The inn staff told him later that the ladies in the coach were the Countess, her stepdaughter Lady Maria, and her own daughter Lady Fanny; the young man in the grey frock coat who nearly rode him down was Mr. William Esmond, and the man who had yelled the loudest oath was Lord Castlewood himself.

The landlord of the Three Castles had shown Harry a bedroom earlier that day, but he had refused to let his trunks be unpacked, fully certain the great house would send an invitation at any moment. One hour passed, two, three—no note arrived. Finally, he gave in, let the host unpack his bags, and called for his slippers and dressing gown. Just before dark, a second chariot and four rumbled over the bridge, and a stout, sharp-eyed lady with very dark eyes stared hard at Harry from the window. That was the Baroness Bernstein, the landlady explained, my lord’s German-born aunt. By then, the entire party had vanished behind Castlewood’s great iron gates, and Harry trundled off to bed heavy with the sting of neglect and raw loneliness. He could not sleep, and soon he heard raucous shouts, curses, giggles and screams coming from the inn’s taproom, loud enough to rouse even the heaviest sleeper.

Presently he heard Gumbo’s voice outside his door, protesting, “You cannot go in, sar--my master asleep, sar!” before a shrill, swear-laced voice Harry now recognized cursed Gumbo for a stupid woolly-headed negro, shoved him aside, and burst into the room. It was Will Esmond, blind drunk. “Beg your pardon, Cousin Warrington!” he slurred, weaving unsteadily across the room. “Are you asleep? Beg your pardon for riding you over on the bridge. Didn’t know it was you—thought you was a lawyer come with a writ, all dressed in black! Gad, I thought Nathan the bailiff was here to nab me, I was gonna heave you straight in the river. But I ask your pardon. I was over at the Bell at Hexton, their punch is the best in three counties. Hullo, Davis! Bring a bowl of punch up here, now!” Harry sat bolt upright in bed, tall nightcap on his head, every inch the dignified Virginian. “You do me great honour to mistake me for a sheriff’s officer, cousin,” he said coolly. “I have had more than enough drink tonight, and I should think you have too.” Will pouted, rambling incoherently and lurching from side to side across the room. “You want me gone, don’t you? They made me come! I said I’d be hanged before I traipsed down here to look after some fellow I don’t care a pin about. That’s exactly what Castlewood said too! Why the devil should we bother? But the Baroness insisted—if she says a thing, it gets done, so you have to get up and come back to the house with me right now.” Harry’s temper snapped. “I tell you what, cousin, I won’t move an inch for the Countess, or the Baroness, or any of the rest of the Castlewood cousins.” When the landlord trundled in carrying the bowl of punch Will had ordered, Harry shouted at him to throw that sot out of his room. Will went ballistic, screaming, “Sot, you little tobacco-selling colonial! Sot, you Cherokee savage! Jump out of bed and I’ll run my sword right through you! Why didn’t I do it today when I thought you were a pettifogging bailiff!” He carried on screeching oaths and nonsense until the landlord, the taproom drawer, the hostler and half the kitchen staff all piled into the room to drag him away. Harry yanked his bed curtains shut, fuming, and eventually fell asleep.

The next morning, the landlord greeted Harry with obsequious bows and scrapes, now fully aware of his guest’s name and status. Other servants had come down to the inn late the night before to fetch Will home, it turned out, and they’d had to wheel him back to Castlewood in a wheelbarrow—a mode of transport he was hardly unaccustomed to. “He never remembers a thing the next day, poor Mr. William,” the landlord swore. “He’s got a real good, kind heart, sober. The stable boys earn crowns off him just by saying he thrashed them the night before when he was drunk. He’s the devil when he’s in his cups, but the sweetest of young fellows when he’s himself.”

While Harry had waited outside the house the day before, the Castlewood family had held a hasty, quiet council after finding his scrap of paper on the hall table. Lord Castlewood admitted the lanky lad they had seen loitering on the bridge must have been the young Virginian, and since they hadn’t actually drowned him, they supposed they ought to send a servant with an invite. Young Lady Fanny thought it would be far more polite to send one of the brothers, especially after how rudely they had treated him on the bridge. Lord Castlewood agreed Will could go, and Will immediately swore he’d be hanged before he traipsed down to the inn after some colonial stranger. Lady Maria thought the young man on the bridge was quite handsome, and Castlewood was so dreadfully dull, it would be fun to have a new novelty to amuse them, even if he was vulgar. The Countess, her stepmother, insisted they wait for the Baroness to arrive, to see what she thought before extending any welcome—no use making a fuss before consulting the woman whose vast fortune the whole family was angling to inherit. So their hospitality to Harry hung completely in limbo.

When the Baroness Bernstein’s coach finally pulled up, the entire household fawned over her like royalty. The state bedroom had been prepped for days, the cook had spent all the previous day making her favourite dishes, the oak dining table glinted with old silver plate, set beneath walls lined with family portraits: the late Viscount, his father, his mother, his sister, the old Vandyck of an earlier Earl, his Viscountess, and the portrait of Colonel Henry Esmond—Harry’s grandfather, the very man whose grandson they had treated like a stray vagrant. The Baroness tucked into her supper with gusto, and the whole family hovered over her, pouring her champagne, laughing at every one of her famously wicked anecdotes about the scandals of European courts, even the strait-laced, propriety-obsessed Countess snickering at her most outrageous stories. “That was my father’s place,” she said, pointing to the Countess’s seat at the head of the table. “All the old silver that used to sit here was melted down to pay his gambling debts. I do hope you boys don’t play cards for money, eh?” “Never, on my word,” Lord Castlewood said solemnly. “Never, pon honour,” Will echoed, winking at his brother behind her back. She pointed a plump, still elegant arm at the portrait of Colonel Esmond in his red coat and cuirass. “That man there was the only real man this whole Esmond family ever produced. Every other male Esmond before or since has had no more sense than a silly goose, except him. The world was too wicked for him, so he did the sensible thing and went off to live in Virginia. Where would your father have ended up, if not for him?” “Was he that kind to our papa?” Lady Maria asked. The Countess sniffed. “Old stories, my dear! I’m sure the Earl was very kind to him in return, giving him that great big Virginia estate.” “Since his twin brother died,” the Baroness said, “that boy who was here today is heir to all that land. Peste, I don’t know why my father ever gave such a property away.” “Who was here today?” the Baroness asked, sitting up sharp. “Harry Esmond Warrington, from Virginia,” Lord Castlewood replied. “The boy Will nearly rode into the river. I tried to get my lady to invite him to stay.” “You mean a grandson of Henry Esmond, the rightful master of this house, showed up here yesterday, and none of you asked him to come inside?” the Baroness thundered, slamming her hand on the table so all the glasses rattled. The whole family hung their heads. “Call a servant! Get me my hood! I’ll go get that boy myself, right this instant. Come on, Castlewood.” Lord Castlewood stood up, red-faced and angry. “Your ladyship can do as you please, but I won’t. I won’t have you calling my conduct shameful. I’m not going crawling after this American boy just to curry favour with you for your money. You all want her fortune more than I do—you can cringe for it, I won’t.” He flopped back into his chair. The Baroness looked at him, and laughed a little, muttering in German: “I was wrong to say Colonel Esmond was the only man in the family. You have it in you, Eugene, if you choose to show it.” She turned back to the rest. “Fine. If his lordship won’t go, Will will. You boys go fetch him.” Will, already half drunk, jumped up. “Great! And we’ll have another bowl of punch when he gets here!” And that was how he ended up bursting into Harry’s bedroom at the Three Castles, as Harry had already experienced.

The Baroness knew perfectly well why the Countess had refused to welcome Harry: no wealthy aristocrat mother is eager to host a handsome nineteen year old bachelor with a big estate across the ocean, when there are unmarried young ladies in the house, and Harry’s Virginia lands don’t seem nearly as real or desirable as Norfolk acres would. She understood the whole family’s greedy little games, how they all fawned over her for her money, and she found their petty humiliations and greed quite amusing. But by then, warmed by punch and champagne, a good old-fashioned generous fit came over her, furious that the grandson of the man she had loved like a father was stuck sleeping in an inn outside the gates of his own ancestral home.

Long before the languid Castlewood girls had dragged themselves out of their feather beds after a long season of London routs, and long before Will had slept off his night of punch, the Baroness was up, pacing the dewy green terraces, watching the sun rise over the trim flower beds, the fountains splashing, the rooks cawing in the great wood. She sent a note down to the Three Castles by young Lockwood, the porter’s son, summoning Harry up to the house. Soon Harry came trundling up the drive, through the old Gothic arch, hat in hand, his fair hair blowing in the morning breeze, his slim figure dressed in black mourning for his brother. He gave her a deep, elegant bow that would have done credit to Versailles. She held out her hand to him, and he took it, blushing bright pink. “I knew your grandfather very well, Harry,” she said gently. “You came yesterday to see his picture, and they turned you away, even though this house was his of right, wasn’t it?” Harry blushed. “The servants didn’t know who I was. The young gentleman who came to my room last night was very drunk, and I spoke rudely to him. I should like to apologize to my cousin. In Virginia, we welcome every stranger who comes to our door. I confess I expected a different kind of welcome here.” “That was me who sent Will to fetch you last night,” the Baroness said, smiling. “You’ll find all your cousins far more friendly today. You’re going to stay here, in this house. Lord Castlewood would have come to meet you himself this morning, but I was far too eager to see you first. Breakfast will be ready in an hour. Send someone down to the inn to get your servant Gumbo and your trunks. Give me your arm—my cane fell over there, and you shall be my cane to lean on.” Harry grinned. “My grandfather used to call us boys his crutches, when he was old.” “You look just like him,” she said softly, “even with that fair hair.”

Colonel Henry Esmond, a veteran who had earned his rank fighting for Queen Anne through all her continental wars, found himself caught up in the final, failed Jacobite plots to restore the Stuart line to the British throne when the queen died. The nation had set its heart on the new Hanoverian dynasty, and those few loyalists who opposed King George were forced to flee the three kingdoms for safety. Among them, Esmond’s friends soon counselled him to go abroad, though his sincere regret for his part in the uprising, paired with the new king’s famously forgiving nature, meant it was not long before they secured him a full pardon.

As has long been documented, Esmond belonged to the noble house that took its title from Castlewood in Hampshire. It was common knowledge that James II and his exiled son had twice offered him and his father the rank of Marquis, and that he could have claimed the hereditary Irish peerage of his line had he bothered to correct a trivial legal informality in the family papers. Tired to the bone of decades of political strife, and worn thin by messy, lingering family disputes back in Europe, he chose to settle far across the Atlantic, where he took possession of a vast plantation granted to one of his ancestors by King Charles I nearly a century prior. Here, he built his new home, which he named Castlewood, after the old Hampshire patrimony he would never see again. His daughter was born here, and his two grandsons; it was also here that his wife died. The lady who shared his Virginia home had been, in her first marriage, the widow of his kinsman, the ill-fated Viscount Castlewood, killed in a notorious duel with Lord Mohun in the final years of King William’s reign.

Every custom of Virginia in that era was modelled lovingly after the old English ways. It was a fiercely loyal colony, so proud of its early support of the exiled Charles II that it boasted it had been a kingdom of the Stuarts years before the Restoration brought him back to the English throne. The Anglican church and the Crown were honoured side by side, without question. The planter gentry were connected by blood or marriage to some of the finest old English families, and held their heads high above the sharp Dutch traders of New York, and the thrifty, money-obsessed Roundhead descendants of Pennsylvania and New England. No people on the entire continent were less republican than this great province, which would soon step to the forefront of the historic revolt against the British Crown a generation later.

The great Virginia estates ran on a rhythm almost patriarchal in its simplicity. For the rough, fertile work of the tobacco fields, every plantation had scores of hands: indentured assigned servants shipped over from Europe, and generations of enslaved African people, all bound to obey the master of the house. The land gave them all their food, their livestock, their game. The wide rivers teemed with fish for the taking, and the private wharves jutting out into the James or Potomac saw ships come right up to the plantation banks to take on tobacco, the only cash crop the gentry deigned to cultivate, bound for London or Bristol. Those same ships brought back every fine manufactured good, every bolt of English cloth, every luxury trinket the family could want, in direct exchange for their harvest.

Their hospitality was boundless. No stranger who knocked at their gates was ever turned away empty-handed, or sent to find lodging elsewhere. The gentry travelled between each other’s estates for weeks at a time, in a state of ease that verged on the feudal. The great moral conflict over chattel slavery had not yet been born in the era we recount: no Virginia gentleman felt the least moral shock at owning black servants, and the system, for all its inherent cruelty, was rarely administered with deliberate brutality. Food was plentiful on the great plantations; the enslaved people were by and large easygoing, and lived lives far more comfortable than the poorest labourers back in the British Isles. You might as soon have tried to convince Madam Esmond of Castlewood to let all her prize horses run loose, unfed and unbroken, as to argue for negro emancipation. She was fully convinced that the whip and the corn bag were equally good for both her stable stock and her black household.

Her father, for all his quiet scepticism about most established pieties, never pushed the point. His doubts never broke out into open rebellion; he was disaffected with much of the world, but never angry at it. A great old grief in his past had left a faint, permanent tinge of melancholy over every part of his later life. He was not unhappy: he was the kindest, most affectionate of men to everyone around him, gentle and even yielding to the women of his family, whom he almost never contradicted. But some old bankruptcy of the heart had left his spirit too tired to fight for joy, and he submitted to life far more than he ever revelled in it. He was never in better, lighter spirits than in his final hours, when he knew he would soon lay his burdens down.

When his wife died, his daughter took over the full management of his affairs, and he handed them over to her without a single complaint. So long as he had his books and his quiet afternoons, he wanted nothing more. When guests arrived at Castlewood he played the gracious, generous host, with a dry, pleasant, sarcastic wit that charmed every visitor. He was never the least bit sorry when they rode away.
“My dear, I shan’t be sorry to go myself,” he told his daughter once, “and you, for all the love you bear me, will console yourself after a while. Why should a man my age be romantic? You still are young enough for that, after all.” He spoke more lightly than he meant, for the lady he addressed was a thoroughly practical, matter-of-fact little woman, with barely a spark of romance in her entire nature.

Fifteen years after they first settled at Castlewood, the plantation’s profits had grown so large that Esmond easily agreed to his daughter’s plan to build a grand, permanent new stone mansion to replace the plain little wooden house he had been perfectly content to live in, a home worthy of the noble name their heirs would inherit. Several of her neighbouring planters had already built great handsome houses of their own, and Madam Warrington – as she was then known – was determined to take her rightful place at the very top of colonial society. Colonel Esmond cared not a fig for fine lodgings or aristocratic quarterings, but his daughter held the antiquity and merit of the Esmond line in the highest possible regard. In his serene, gentle old age, he humoured all her little peculiarities with easy, teasing good nature, using his own considerable skill as a painter and his deep stores of antiquarian knowledge to help her.

A hundred years ago, a working knowledge of heraldry was a standard part of the education of every noble gentleman and lady. On a long tour of Europe in her youth, Miss Esmond had pored eagerly over every scrap of family history and pedigree she could find, returning to Virginia with a hoard of old documents about the Esmond line that she accepted as unassailable fact, plus all the grand new heraldry volumes just published in France and England. These, to her complete satisfaction, proved the Esmonds were descended not just from the Norman warriors who sailed to England with William the Conqueror, but from ancient English royalty itself. Two magnificent hand-painted heraldic trees, executed by the Colonel’s own brush, showed the family springing in one line from the Emperor Charlemagne, painted in full gilded plate armour, imperial mantle and jewelled diadem, and in the other from Queen Boadicea, whom the Colonel insisted on rendering in the light, furlined costume of an ancient British warrior queen, with a massive gilded crown, a tiny fur mantle, and a handsome, symmetrical figure tastefully tattooed all over in bright woad blue. These two illustrious lines merged somewhere in the 13th century, on the person of the fortunate Esmond ancestor who could claim descent from both.

Good Madam Rachel thought very little of the Warrington family she had married into. She wrote her name Esmond Warrington, but after her father’s death, when she took full rule of the Castlewood estate, everyone in the colony called her Madam Esmond of Castlewood. She did not scruple to get into petty quarrels over precedence at the Governor’s assemblies in Jamestown, so determined was she to assert her rank. Even though her father had burned and disowned the Jacobite patent that would have made him a Marquis, she acted at all times as if that document was still fully in force. She considered the English branch of the Esmond family to be of far lower dignity than her own Virginian line, and openly asserted her superiority over every other member of the colonial aristocracy.

What use is recalling those old trivial squabbles? The people who fought them are long beyond the reach of petty disputes, and the new republic that would rise after Independence would sweep all those old social inequalities away. Before the Revolution, though, there was no more fiercely aristocratic society in the whole world than Virginia. Which means that the two little boys whose story we tell – the Esmond twins of Castlewood – were raised to honour every old English tradition, and were two of the most loyal, devoted little subjects the rightful British king ever had.

When the twins’ grandfather died, their mother proclaimed the elder, George, her formal successor and heir to the entire estate, in great state. Harry, his younger brother by exactly half an hour, was instructed by everyone in the household to honour and defer to his senior. The entire household followed suit: the large, happy extended family of enslaved people, the indentured servants from Europe, every soul on the plantation was taught to treat George as their future master. The only dissenters in the whole household were Madam Mountain, Madam Esmond’s oldest friend and companion, and Harry’s negro foster mother, who could never, for the life of her, understand why her boy should not be the heir – she swore constantly that Harry was handsomer, stronger, and far cleverer than George, though in truth the two boys were so nearly identical in height, strength, and beauty that no one but their mother could reliably tell them apart, save for the faint difference in the shade of their hair. When they were tucked into bed under those enormous, ribbon-trimmed nightcaps all children of the era wore, not even the most sharp-eyed visitor could distinguish one from the other.

For all their identical faces, their temperaments were wildly different. The elder twin was quiet, peaceful, studious, and reserved. The younger was loud, boisterous, and born with an unmistakable martial streak. Harry could learn anything very quickly once he set his mind to it, but he would drag his heels for days before he settled to his lessons. No threat of the ferule could ever make Harry study when he was in an idle mood, and no amount of scolding could stop George from sneaking time to help his brother catch up on his work. Harry loved nothing more than to drill the little enslaved boys on the plantation like a corporal, cane them for misbehaviour, and challenge them to boxing matches – he never bore a grudge for a second if he lost the fight. George, meanwhile, almost never struck anyone, and was gentle to every creature on the estate.

As was the custom, each of the boys was assigned a special little personal servant of their own. It became famous around the plantation that once, George found his small black assigned servant fast asleep on his own bed, and instead of waking him, sat down beside him and fanned the flies off the child with a feather fan. Old Gumbo, the boy’s father, was horrified when he stumbled on the scene, and Madam Esmond was furious, ordering the young negro off to the overseer to be whipped. George begged, pleaded, burst into passionate tears, and implored her to reverse the sentence, but she was inflexible. A fierce, blazing quarrel between mother and son followed. George refused to be pacified. He said the punishment was a shame – that he was the boy’s master, and no one, not even his own mother, had any right to touch him without his say so. He swore, so fiercely it shocked his usually gentle mother, that the very day he came of age, he would set young Gumbo free. Then he ran off to the slave quarters to visit the boy mid-punishment, and gave him his own favourite wooden toy.

The old Colonel had laughed when Madam Esmond told him of the incident, and only shrugged when George turned on him and said, “You let mamma rule you in everything, grandpapa.”
“Why, so I do,” the old man smiled. “Rachel, my love, it’s so plain even this baby has noticed I’m thoroughly petticoat-ridden.”
“Then why don’t you stand up like a man?” little Harry put in, always ready to back his brother.
Grandpapa looked at him, his eyes crinkling with amusement.
“Because I like sitting down best, my dear. I’m an old gentleman, and standing up fatigues me.”

Harry was the grandfather’s favourite, for his sharp, impish drollery and his love of many of the old man’s own pastimes. He would chatter and laugh away the whole of an afternoon with the old Colonel, while quiet George rarely said more than a few words to him. George, for his part, came alive in the library, where his brother would fidget and grow gloomy after ten minutes. He could recognise every book on the shelves before he was even big enough to carry one, and spent hours poring over their pages long before he could properly read or understand the words. Harry, by contrast, was never happier than when he was out in the stables or the woods, desperate to join every hunt or fishing trip, and showing all the signs of becoming an expert sportsman from toddlerhood.

When the boys were still small, their grandfather’s ship was preparing to sail for England, and Captain Franks asked them what presents he ought to bring back for them. George hesitated between a set of new books and a fiddle. Harry, without a second’s pause, declared he wanted a real little working gun. Madam Warrington was upset that her elder son could want something so trivial and low-bred as a fiddle, and applauded Harry’s choice as far more worthy of his noble name and lineage.
“Books, papa, I will admit are a respectable choice,” she argued to her father, “though I am sure you have nearly every book in the world already. But I never can – I may be wrong, but I never can – bring myself to wish that my son, the grandson of the Marquis of Esmond, should be a fiddler.”
“Should be a fiddlestick, my dear,” the old Colonel chuckled. “Remember that Heaven’s ways are not our own. Every soul born into the world has a little private kingdom of thought all its own, and it is a sin for any of us to invade it. If George loves music, you can no more stop him than you can order a rose not to smell sweet, or a bird not to sing.”
“A bird sings by nature,” she tossed her head. “George did not come into the world with a fiddle tucked in his cradle. I hated the harpsichord when I was a little chit at school in Kensington, and only learned it to please my own mamma. Say what you will, dear sir, I cannot believe that fiddling is proper work for a person of quality.”
“And King David played the harp, my dear?”
“I wish my papa would not speak of him in that tone,” she huffed.
The old man never argued further. As he had written in his own memoir years before, it had always been his nature to be led by the women he loved. After his wife died, he spoiled his daughter, humoured every one of her caprices, laughed at her prejudices, and let her have her own way. He believed that harsh, overbearing authority over children never changed their natures for the better, and only made hypocrites of them.

At last, the time came for Mr. Esmond to lay down all the affairs of this life, and he did so as if he were glad to be rid of their weight. We will not open this young story with tolling bells or a lengthy funeral sermon, though everyone who heard Parson Broadbent of Jamestown deliver his eulogy was astonished by the richness of its rhetoric and the fluency of its Latin. The boys’ Scottish tutor, Mr. Dempster, likely knew the truth of the matter, for he had corrected the proofs of the oration, which was printed by special request of the Governor and dozens of leading gentry, at Mr. Benjamin Franklin’s press in Philadelphia.

No such lavish, grand funeral had ever been seen in the whole colony as the one Madam Esmond Warrington arranged for her father – a ceremony he would have been the first to laugh at, for all its pomp. The two little lads of Castlewood, nearly smothered beneath their heavy black mourning trains and broad hatbands, led the procession. They were followed by no less a personage than Lord Fairfax from Greenway Court, the Governor of Virginia in his fine coach, the Randolphs, the Careys, the Harrisons, the Washingtons, and every leading family in the county. All the neighbourhood had loved the departed Colonel, whose great goodness, quiet high talent, benevolence and unassuming courtesy had earned him the unqualified respect of everyone who knew him.

When news of his death reached England, the family of Colonel Esmond’s stepson, the current Lord Castlewood of Hampshire, volunteered to pay for the fine marble monument to mark his grave. After a proper period of mourning, the monument was erected, carved with the Esmond arms and coronet, supported by a group of plump, weeping cherubs, and inscribed with an epitaph that, for once, did not tell a single falsehood.

All the markers of a supposedly perfect earthly happiness were laid at Madam Esmond Warrington’s feet at Castlewood, her Virginia principality in Westmorland County: an ancient, storied family name, thousands of acres of rich tobacco land, a steady fortune, a comfortable home stacked high with every necessity and dozens of fine luxuries, a whole household of Black enslaved servants and white free hands tripping over themselves to tend to her every bidding. She had good health, two loyal young sons, a cook who never served a bad meal, a cellar full of fine Madeira, and a library lined with leather-bound classics. She reminded herself of every one of these blessings daily in her morning and evening prayers. She was scrupulous in her devotions, generous to the local poor, and never knowingly wronged a soul.

And yet, few who knew her would have traded places with the sharp, imperious little matron her neighbors teasingly called “Princess Pocahontas” behind her back. The husband who died young was far better off gone; had he lived decades longer, the pair would have torn each other apart, or he would have ended up the most thoroughly henpecked man in the colony, no exceptions. The truth was, Madam Esmond never met a man or woman she did not immediately try to bend to her will. Obey her, and she was your staunchest, most loyal friend; resist her, and she would fight tooth and nail for months until one of you broke. She was fond of declaring, in the clearest, firmest voice in the parish, that all mortal souls were miserable sinners, as every man admitted aloud every Sunday—she just very rarely acknowledged the sin might be hers, never to anyone but her late father.

Colonel Esmond, her father, had been the only person alive who could tease her out of her worst tyrannical whims, his quiet good humor something she could never boss or bully past. But once he was buried, there was no one left in the whole colony to rein her in, and I for one am very glad I never resided at Castlewood a hundred years back. Even Paradise had its serpent, after all; no mortal is ever perfectly happy for long.

Madam had seized full control of the estate long before the Colonel drew his last breath. She fired his old London factor, hired a new agent who answered only to her, cleared hundreds of new acres for tobacco, built new outbuildings, appointed a strict new overseer, and imported a tutor for her two boys. She had been a dutiful daughter all her life, obeying every last order her parents gave her, so she reasoned she was fully entitled to run her little dominion exactly as she saw fit, even if it went against her father’s old, easygoing rules. Her sons George and Harry were not equal heirs in her mind: they were merely her first two subjects. Before long she dropped her late husband’s Warrington name entirely, insisting every soul in the county call her Madam Esmond, and loved to drop hints about the old Jacobite Marquis title King James had granted to her Esmond forebears. Her father, for all his enormous magnanimity, had given up the family’s claims and titles to the younger English branch, to my Lord Castlewood and his brood—but she and her sons were the true elder line of the house of Esmond, and everyone was going to treat them as such.

Only Lord Fairfax, the grandest old grandee in Virginia, was permitted to walk ahead of her. She insisted on precedence over every lieutenant-governor’s wife, every judge’s lady, and only stepped aside for the royal governor’s spouse, as the direct representative of the Crown. Family papers and surviving letters are full of accounts of the screaming public fights she got into with colonial official wives over these tiny points of etiquette. As for her husband’s Norfolk Warrington relations? They were nobodies, far beneath her notice. She’d only married the younger son of an English baronet to please her parents, when she was barely out of the boarding school schoolroom, and would have jumped over the side of the ship that brought her to Virginia if her father had ordered it. “That’s the way of all the Esmonds,” she’d say proudly.

Unsurprisingly, the English Warringtons and Castlewood Esmonds took deep offense at her endless snubs. For years she sent a solemn formal letter once a year to each branch of the family, until one judge’s lady she’d quarreled with sailed back to England, ran into Lady Warrington in London where Sir Miles sat in Parliament, and repeated all the unkind things Madam Esmond was fond of saying about her English relatives. Lady Warrington passed the gossip on to Lady Castlewood, and after that, none of Madam’s letters got a single reply. Furious, she soon stopped writing them too, cutting off all contact with the entire side of the family across the Atlantic.

She soon fell out with far closer people. The first major rift with her sons came when she dismissed Mr. Dempster, their old tutor and Colonel Esmond’s long-time secretary. While the Colonel was alive, Madam could barely stand the man, and the feeling was mutual: she distrusted bookish folk, convinced scholars snuck radical, bad ideas into impressionable young heads, and spread the rumor that Dempster was a Jesuit spy in disguise, until the poor fellow was forced to move off to a remote backcountry clearing, build a tiny cabin, and scratch out a living running a little school and practicing rough medicine for the scattered farm families. George, the older boy, had loved his old tutor, swore he’d keep in touch no matter what, and kept that promise. Harry, who always preferred fishing and foxhunting to Greek grammar, had never been close to Dempster, so the rift between Madam and George only grew sharper later.

The next fight was over six thousand pounds, a sum left to George Warrington’s heir (young George, of course) by a dead aunt, with Madam Esmond and a London lawyer named Draper named as co-trustees. Madam simply could not wrap her head around the fact that she was only the trustee, not the full owner, of that money. She flew into a rage when Draper refused to ship the entire sum over to her on her order. “Everything I have belongs to my boys!” she’d shout. “I’d cut myself into pieces to serve them! With that six thousand pounds I could buy Mr. Boulter’s entire estate, all his enslaved workers, pull in a thousand pounds a year extra, and set Harry up properly, for he only gets a tiny pittance as a younger son.” Even her young neighbor George Washington of Mount Vernon could not convince her that Draper was doing his legal duty, that he could not hand over trust money before the heir came of age. Madam fired off a scathing letter to the London lawyer, calling him an insolent pettifogger who dared to doubt the honor of an Esmond and a loving mother.

When she demanded fourteen-year-old George back her play, he sided with Washington and Draper, saying he had no right to take the money before he came of age, and would give every penny of it to her to do with as she wished if he could. But Madam Esmond would hear none of it. Feelings were her only logic. Here was a chance to make Harry’s fortune, her poor dear portionless youngest son, and the wretches in London, and even his own selfish older brother, stood in the way! She called George greedy, unkind, disobedient, burst into tears, hurled endless bitter little digs at him, and the rift stretched on for months. There are still plenty of ladies who argue that same way today, after all; the book of women’s logic is blotted all over with tear stains, and justice in their private courts is almost always run by passion.

So Madam decided she would pinch every penny to save a proper inheritance for Harry. She halted all the grand new building work Colonel Esmond had started at Castlewood: the shipments of Dutch bricks from New York, the carved mantelpieces, the expensive imported glass and upholstery she’d ordered from London, all of it, cancelled. No more new books. No more shipments of fine wine. She even regretted buying the fancy new carriage Hatchett’s of London had made her for 380 guineas, and every Sunday when she rode to church in it, she’d groan out loud to her two boys sitting opposite her, “Harry, Harry! I wish I’d put that money aside for you, my poor child.”

Harry, good-natured as ever, laughed it off. “You’ll give me everything I want while you live, and George will give me plenty when you’re gone, ma’am.”

“Not unless Heaven softens George’s hard heart and teaches him charity, which I pray for night and day,” she’d snap, shooting a grim look at her older son, and turning to her companion, the widow Mrs. Mountain, who took the fourth seat in the coach, “Don’t I, Mountain?”

Mrs. Mountain huffed. “I know you carry on about that legacy far more than there’s any need for.”

“Oh, no need at all!” Madam rustled her silk skirts, indignant. “Of course there’s no need for me to be upset, because my eldest born is a disobedient son, an unkind brother, who gets the whole of my father’s estate and leaves my poor Harry with nothing but a mess of pottage!”

George’s eyes welled up with tears. “Oh mother, I wish you would love me too,” he said, and burst out sobbing.

In a second Harry had his arms wrapped around his brother’s neck, kissing his cheek a dozen times. “Don’t mind her, George. I know what a good brother you are. She doesn’t mean a word of it.”

“I do mean it!” Madam started, and Harry roared out at the top of his voice, “Hold your tongue, ma’am! It’s a damned shame to speak to him that way!”

“And so it is, Harry,” Mrs. Mountain said, squeezing his hand. “You never spoke a truer word.”

“Mrs. Mountain! Do you dare turn my children against me?” Madam shrieked. “From this very day, madam—”

“Turn me and my orphan child out on the road? Go right ahead,” Mrs. Mountain said, unflinching. “That’ll be a fine show, all because that London lawyer won’t hand over the boy’s money. Go find another companion who’ll tell you black is white and flatter you all day long. That’s not my way. I didn’t bring much to Castlewood, and I won’t take much when I leave. When should I start packing?”

But Madam heard the church bells starting to ring, and composed herself. “Hush, Mountain, let us try to be calm. The bells are summoning us to service.” She looked at her two boys then, her eyes softening with real affection. George kept his head down the whole walk to church, and during the whole service, Harry sat right next to him, his arm slung around his brother’s neck.

After that, Harry struck out on a little journey of his own, and found himself sitting by the fireside in an old wainscoted parlour that had seen two hundred years of Esmond family dinners, walls lined with the great family portraits. An old lady named Madam Bernstein, who he’d just met, hung on every word of his long, rambling story about life at Castlewood, dotted with all his boyish exclamations. Her hostess and daughters kept popping in to invite her to ride, walk, take tea, or play cards, but Madam Bernstein waved them all off, saying Harry’s conversation was more entertaining than any of those things. Whenever any of the local Castlewood cousins popped into the room, she’d double down on her fondness for Harry, tug him close to her ear, and call out to the others, “Hush, dears! I can’t hear our cousin speak,” until they left the room, trying hard not to look annoyed.

“Are you my cousin too?” Harry asked her, earnest. “You’re far kinder than all my other English cousins.”

Over her easy chair hung a brilliant Sir Godfrey Kneller portrait, painted in Queen Anne’s reign, of a beautiful young woman in flowing loose robes, auburn hair falling over her pearly fair shoulders. Harry stared up at it.

“That’s Sir Godfrey’s work,” Madam Bernstein said, twirling her knitting needles. “He thought he was the finest painter alive, but he was not half as good as Lely, who painted your grandmother, my Lady Castlewood, Colonel Esmond’s wife. Not as good as Van Dyck, who painted your great-grandfather over there, who looks far finer in his portrait than he ever was in real life. Some of us get painted far blacker than we deserve, and some far finer. Do you recognize any of the face in that portrait, Harry?”

“I thought it looked a little like my mother,” Harry said.

“Does Mrs. Warrington—wait, you call her Madam Esmond now, I hear?”

“That’s what everyone in our colony calls her,” Harry said.

“Did she ever tell you her mother had another daughter, born in England before she married your grandfather, Colonel Esmond?”

“Never,” Harry said. “And my grandfather never mentioned her either. But in all the little sketchbooks he drew for us when we were small children, he drew a head that looked exactly like that portrait over your chair, at least a dozen times, right next to pictures of Viscount Francis and King James the Third.”

Madam Bernstein sighed softly. “And that face up there reminds you of no one else, Harry?”

“No, ma’am, it does not.”

“Ah, then I must tell you something,” she said, reaching out to pat his hand. “Once that was my face, Harry. Once I was Beatrix Esmond. Your mother is my half-sister, child. She has never once even spoken my name to you, all these years.”

As Harry Warrington unfolded the plain, unvarnished story of his life at the Virginian plantation to his newly discovered kinswoman Madam Bernstein, the sharp-witted, world-travelled lady of the court formed her own quiet judgment of the people and events he described. If her opinion was not always entirely favourable, one can scarce blame her: no life, after all, is free of imperfection, and the city-bred woman recoiled a little from the thought of her half-sister Rachel’s rough, unpolished country existence.

But Madam Rachel Warrington knew no other life, and was perfectly content with hers. She was a brisk, sharp little matriarch who ruled every inch of her vast Castlewood estate like a minor queen. No pie was baked in the great house without her oversight, she set the maids to their spinning, checked the kitchen maids’ work, trotted the fields on her pony to monitor overseers and enslaved hands tending the tobacco and corn crops. When a slave fell ill, she would trudge out to their quarters in any weather to tend them, armed with an ancient book of home remedies, a closet full of distilled elixirs, and a medicine chest that was the terror of every neighbour for miles: no one wanted to fall sick and face her bitter, pungent decoctions and unyielding pills.

A hundred years before this story, there were barely any proper towns in Virginia. Every gentry plantation was its own tiny, self-sufficient village, housing the family, their workers, and dependants. The neighbouring squires were mostly cash-poor, free-spending potentates who lived rough, kept ragged liveried servants, threw open their doors to every stranger, and were fiercely proud of their good lineage and addicted to field sports. Many a one of these gentlemen would have been only too happy to take the widowed Madam Warrington as his wife, to claim a share of her estate for his own – but Rachel held her Esmond birth as far too exalted for any of them, and gossiping local ladies joked she was holding out even for the Duke of Cumberland, rumoured to be coming over as Viceroy of the Americas. She would respond with great dignity that men of as high rank as the Duke had already sued for the hand of an Esmond.

Her right-hand companion was Mrs. Mountain, widow of an ensign who had been the late Colonel Warrington’s old regimental friend. The two girls had met at Kensington Academy, where Fanny Parker – later Mountain – had defended the young, haughty little Rachel from teasing English schoolmates. They had both married ensigns in the same regiment, and remained the dearest of friends. When Mr. Mountain died penniless, leaving his wife and infant daughter with nothing, Captain Franks brought her across the ocean on his ship the *Young Rachel* to Castlewood.

There was more than enough room at the big plantation house, and Mrs. Mountain made it far livelier. She played cards with her mistress, gave the boys music lessons, saw to the guest chambers and the household linen presses, and was a kind, jolly widow who turned down every local suitor that asked for her hand. One husband who had squandered both his fortune and hers before dying, she said, was more than enough for a lifetime. The two women quarrelled constantly, but loved each other dearly, making up their spats almost as quickly as they started them, and both had adored the old Colonel, who had prized Mrs. Mountain’s cheerfulness during his final illness.

Rachel was endlessly amused to tease her many suitors, telling half of them she was sure they had really come to court Mrs. Mountain first, and offering to put in a good word for them. If any gentleman insisted his addresses were for her alone, she would drop him her gravest curtsy and inform him that the daughter of the Marquis of Esmond had dedicated herself to her people and her sons, and had no intention of remarrying. She was a little Virginian Queen Elizabeth in her own small domain, lapping up flattery as her due, much to the amusement of local wags: Jack Firebrace of Henrico County won months of free board at Castlewood by reciting stolen verses in her honour, and Tom Humbold of Spotsylvania won a fifty-hogshead bet when he tricked her into declaring a silly, mock order of chivalry for her favourites.

The twin boys reacted very differently to their mother’s foibles. Oldest and quieter George seethed at the sight of these sycophants, and used his sharp juvenile satire to try to expose them, much to his mother’s amusement, who would sigh and say the Esmonds had always had a jealous, proud streak. Easy-going Harry, meanwhile, was only too happy to run off hunting, fishing, and cock-fighting with the lot of them, enjoying every bit of the rough country fun.

One winter, after their first tutor was dismissed, Madam Warrington took the boys to Williamsburg for a proper college education, and there the whole family fell under the sway of the famous travelling preacher Mr. Whitefield. The Anglican church in Virginia was staffed by imported parsons of very poor calibre – mostly disgraced, insolvent men who had fled debts or trouble at home – and none of the sleepy local clergy had ever stirred the colonists half as much as Whitefield’s thundering, fiery sermons. For a while, the twins were so caught up in the excitement they sang hymns day and night, waiting for the famous “holy call” to the ministry that every pious Protestant in England was talking about at the time, and would likely have ended up wearing black clerical coats instead of military epaulettes if Whitefield had stayed. But the preacher soon moved on to carry his mission across the colonies, and promised Madam Warrington he would send her a special tutor from England, one who could teach her sons both secular learning and far more precious spiritual truth.

In due course, the chosen “vessel” arrived. Young Mr. Ward had a voice almost as loud as Whitefield’s, and could preach for hours on end. The great hall of Castlewood echoed night and day with his exhortations, and the enslaved household workers crowded the doors and porches to listen, until they were so deeply moved they sang thunderous hymns that could be heard all the way across the Potomac. The old Colonel, who had always been deeply suspicious of clergymen and said he would only ever argue with a parson over a game of backgammon, would have never stood for such noise in his house.

Ward was a handsome, glib young man, and Madam Warrington soon came to adore his sermons far more than she had even Whitefield’s. She pressed her young favourite, Major George Washington, again and again to come stay at Castlewood and benefit from Ward’s spiritual guidance – but the major always contrived to find urgent business that called him away before the evening sermon hour. The twins, however, quickly saw through Ward’s facade: he was a poor scholar, dull, and ill-bred to boot. George already knew far more Latin and Greek than his supposed tutor, and caught him making constant blunders and false quantities. Harry, meanwhile, took to mimicking Ward’s greedy way of eating and his drawling preaching tone, so well that even Mrs. Mountain and little Fanny Mountain would cackle with laughter, much to their mother’s fury.

Rachel refused to see that the man was a vulgar fraud, determined to take her sons’ open dislike of him as nothing more than the infamous proud Esmond family pride. “What does trivial profane learning matter?” she would scold them. “Ward is our master in the things that truly count. His rough manners are no flaw – Heaven does not choose its elect from the ranks of the wealthy and well-bred. It is your wicked arrogance that makes you refuse to listen.” Ward, meanwhile, preached a whole sermon on Naaman the Syrian, too proud to bathe in the humble Jordan to be healed, and implied that the two stubborn boys would be damned forever if they did not submit to his guidance.

George, who had inherited his grandfather’s sharp, sarcastic tongue, began to pick apart Ward’s pompous speeches for fun, making the tutor choke with rage over his meals and turning the whole house against him. Madam Warrington’s authority was openly defied, she thought, by her stubborn older son, and she decided to restore order through force. The birch cane was a common enough method of discipline in those days, used freely by schoolmasters, sergeants, and overseers alike, and the boys had been caned many times by their old Scottish tutor as children.
