But no one had laid a hand on them since their grandfather’s death, and Rachel was determined to make an example of George.

Mrs. Mountain, the boys’ quiet ally, warned them of the plot being hatched against them. “Ward fawns over your mother more than ever now, it turns my stomach to see him gobble his food and flatter her so shamelessly!” she said. “I heard her talking to Major Washington the other day, and he told her: ‘Discipline is discipline. There can only be one commander in a house, ma’am, and you must be master of yours.’” Harry admitted that Washington had given him the very same warning, telling him his mother was “dangerously angry” and he had best obey Ward. But George only grew more haughty and refractory.

The storm broke the next morning. During lessons, George openly defied Ward, who brought the dispute to Madam Warrington at dinner. Poor Harry was forced to confirm that George had been in the wrong, and even George himself, standing under his grandfather’s portrait by the chimney, admitted the accusation was perfectly true. But his mother would accept no apology.

“Spare the rod and spoil the child,” she declared stamping her little foot, and ordered Ward to punish the disobedient boy immediately.

George went pale, and his eyes fell on the precious china cup perched on the mantel under the Colonel’s portrait – his grandfather’s favourite, which Rachel treasured above almost any other possession in the house. “Mother,” he said slowly, “if I broke this cup, it could never be put back together, could it? No tinker’s rivets would ever make it whole again.” When Rachel scoffed that an Esmond ought to be braver than to cower over a trinket, George let the cup slip from his fingers. It shattered on the marble hearth into a hundred pieces.

Harry lunged to catch it a second too late.

“Now, mother,” George said, white-faced, “I am quite ready. And when next I see Mr. Washington, I will thank him for the advice you have chosen to act on.” He bowed stiffly to Ward, and bade him go first to the study to receive his punishment.

Harry followed close behind, his face dark with rage. A few minutes later, a terrible yell rang out that made Madam Warrington leap in her chair. Ward came staggering out of the study, blood pouring from a deep gash on his scalp, and behind him was Harry, his eyes blazing, brandishing his grandfather’s old hunting hanger torn from the library wall.

“I don’t care, I did it!” Harry roared. “I saw him lift his hand to strike my brother, so I hurled the big oak ruler straight at his head. No man – no man – shall ever raise a hand to hurt George while I am alive. If any try, I will kill them.”

After their disgraced chaplain’s abrupt departure, Madam Esmond and her eldest son George appeared to have settled back into full, easy reconciliation—but the bitter quarrel between them weighed so heavily on the quiet boy’s mind that he fell into a raging, delirious fever soon after. For nights on end, the widow sat watch beside his bed, his thin frame tossing restlessly, his voice cracking out over and over in the dark: “Broken! Broken! It never, never can be mended!” Her usual stores of home remedies and folk nostrums, which she dispensed freely to every servant and tenant across Castlewood, did nothing to slow the fever’s advance.
Humility was forced upon her at last. One snowbound morning, her neighbors spotted her riding her pony through drifts up to the stirrups, arriving unannounced at the tiny cottage of Mr. Dempster, the little tutor she had once cast off in anger, to beg him to save her son. “I shall bury my resentment, madam, just as you have buried your pride,” the old scholar told her. “Please God, I may be in time to help my dear young pupil.” He packed his lancet and his small stock of medicines, called his only enslaved manservant after him, locked the door of his lonely hut, and rode back with her to Castlewood.
For three days, it looked certain that poor Harry would inherit the estate before the week was out—but Dempster’s steady care pulled George through. The fever broke, the intermittent chills faded, and when the boy was well enough to sit up for hours at a time, the doctor strongly prescribed a change of air, even a long sea voyage, to rebuild his shattered strength. The widow had long since quarreled with their Esmond kin in England, and was too contrite over her past hasty temper to write and beg for shelter there, so the party planned a grand journey north through the colonies instead.
The two young gentlemen, under Dempster’s charge, with two personal servants in attendance, boarded a sloop bound for New York, then sailed up the sun-dappled length of the Hudson to Albany, where the foremost gentry of the New York province welcomed them with open arms. From there they traveled north into French Canadian territory, bearing carefully sealed letters of introduction that opened every door of the seigneurial estates. Harry threw himself headlong into wilderness life: he camped for weeks at a time with local Indian bands, traded for furs, and tracked and shot bear deep in the pine forests. George, who cared nothing for rough field sports and still moved with the fragility of a man recovering from near death, became an immediate favorite of the French ladies. Few young English colonists spoke French half so fluently as he, and he perfected his accent until native Parisians at the Quebec court mistook him for one of their own. He carried himself with effortless, easy grace, danced the minuet to perfection, learned the newest Parisian court catches and arias, and played them beautifully on his violin—though he could not sing them, for his voice had just broken from treble to deep bass.
While Harry was away on a three-week bear hunt, George even fought an affair of honor with a hotheaded young ensign of the Auvergne regiment, the Chevalier de la Jabotiere, nicked him cleanly through the shoulder, and the two men swore a lifelong friendship immediately after the duel. Madame de Mouchy, the intendant’s wife, wrote a glowing, complimentary letter to Madam Esmond praising her eldest son’s courage and breeding, and the widow was so elated by the news that she gave no thought to how the pious preacher Whitfield would have frowned on her delight over her boy’s dueling prowess.
Ten months later, the lads rode back up Castlewood’s oak-lined drive, tanned, several inches taller, and so nearly identical that even their oldest servants could scarce tell them apart when their hair was powdered—though back in the rough Virginia countryside, they soon abandoned the fussy custom, George wearing his raven-black hair loose save for a simple ribbon, Harry his fair flaxen locks tied back the same way.
Any reader familiar with the boys’ characters will have marked that George Warrington was of a proud, jealous, slow-to-forgive disposition: generous, truthful, and gentle to a fault, he could never deliberately harm anyone, but he almost never let a slight or injury fade from his mind. He had left home nursing a deep, unspoken dislike for one of his mother’s closest friends, a gentleman whose name would one day become famous across the whole world, and ten months of travel had not softened his opinion an inch.
Mr. Washington, though barely twenty-one years old, looked and carried himself with a gravity that made him seem decades older. He had managed his own family’s tangled financial affairs from boyhood, and every magistrate and planter across the region trusted his judgment more than that of many men twice his age. Mrs. Mountain, Madam Esmond’s sharp-tongued, irrepressible companion, who doted on both boys even as she bickered daily with her mistress and threatened to quit Castlewood a dozen times a week, was an avid and wildly imaginative correspondent who sent the lads a steady stream of gossipy, amusing letters while they traveled. She was a born match-maker, convinced every unmarried man who crossed Castlewood’s threshold harbored designs on its wealthy widowed mistress. She was certain the odious Mr. Ward planned to court Madam Esmond, and doubly certain that the shrewd, ambitious young Major Washington was angling for her hand—never mind that he was fifteen years her junior. “Twas always the family way!” she cackled at George. “Her own mother was years older than Colonel Esmond when they wed, and she was so jealous she’d never let the poor man out of her sight! Great tall men like Mr. Washington, who stands six foot two, always marry tiny little women, and Madam’s scarce five feet tall even in her highest headdress and stacked heels! What could be plainer than that?”
She spilled every one of these absurd theories to George, who begged her for heaven’s sake to hold her tongue. She swore she would never breathe a word to Harry—Harry was his mother’s favorite, after all, and could not keep a secret to save his life. He would run straight to Madam, and there would be a screaming row that would get Mountain dismissed for good. George warned her in his most frigid, dignified tone that if she dared repeat such ridiculous suspicions to anyone else, they would quarrel too. Of course, Mountain could not hold her peace, and pointed out a hundred tiny seeming proofs to confirm her tale: Washington had his own permanent guest chamber at Castlewood, he left his portmanteau and spare riding clothes there for convenience, Madam never tired of singing his praises to her sons, and consulted him on every decision, from buying a new horse to selling a barrel of tobacco.
In response, George adopted a stance of stiff, formal courtesy towards his mother’s favorite, laced with sharp little sarcasms that stung the good-natured Washington, though he never complained, brushing them off as easily as he would brush brambles from his coat on a long hunt. While Harry rode and hunted side by side with Washington nearly every day, George retreated to his book room to pore over Latin, mathematics, and French texts, growing sullen and more isolated by the week.
When Harry was away across the county at a cockfight (to Madam Esmond’s great displeasure, his circle of sporting acquaintances was far from reputable), Washington arrived at Castlewood for a farewell visit. He was uncommonly tender to the mistress of the house, and she received him with such open, warm cordiality that George’s jealousy nearly boiled over into open confrontation—until he learned the major was bound on a long, brutal mission far west, to the very edge of the Virginia frontier and beyond.
For years, the French, holding colonies in Canada and Louisiana, had pushed steadily south and west, building a chain of forts to link their territories and block the British Atlantic colonies from expanding inland to the Mississippi. Though the two crowns had signed a formal peace treaty in 1748, the frontier dispute had never been settled, and by 1753, French troops were actively driving British settlers off their lands on the Ohio River. Virginia’s Lieutenant-Governor Dinwiddie resolved to send a formal envoy to the French commanding officer at Fort Le Boeuf, to demand they desist from all incursions on territory claimed by King George.
Young Washington jumped at the chance for distinction, volunteering for the dangerous post. He set out with a small party of guides, an interpreter, and a handful of attendants, following unmarked Indian trails 500 miles through frozen wilderness, navigating only by compass, camping in the snow through the dead of winter. He reached Fort Le Boeuf safely, only to receive a blunt refusal from the French commander: his orders were to hold every post, and drive every English settler out of the Ohio country by force. Washington made it back alive through every peril, his clothes frozen stiff, his horse dead under him, arriving back in Williamsburg a celebrated hero across the colony.
Harry raged that he had wasted his time at a stupid cockfight instead of getting to join such a noble adventure, and Madam Esmond held Washington up as the perfect example to both her sons, scolding George that all his book learning would never amount to half as much as the major’s service to his country. George retorted that he would be happy to sail for England to seek a royal commission, but he would never consent to serve under Washington in a ragtag provincial regiment, and Madam Esmond agreed hotly: an Esmond only served the king directly, and she would rather beg bread than ask Governor Dinwiddie for a favor.
Washington soon began recruiting a small provincial regiment to march west and drive the French out. But before his little force could reach the forks of the Ohio, a much larger French column overran the tiny half-built fort the advance party of Virginians had thrown up there, chased the 40-man garrison off without bloodshed, renamed the stronghold Fort Duquesne, and set up a permanent garrison. For months, no shot had been fired in open anger, even as the two sides eyed each other across the forest clearings. It was in that uncharted Pennsylvania wilderness that young Colonel Washington, marching west with his handful of raw recruits, stumbled on a small French scouting party and fired the first shot of a conflict that would stretch across three continents, cost France its entire North American empire, and eventually spark the revolution that would birth the great United States of America.
He had no idea then what history held in store for him. Outnumbered five to one by well-armed French regulars, he was forced to retreat to a crude, hastily built stockade he named Fort Necessity, and on July 4th, 1754, he surrendered his position and marched his half-starved, nearly ammunition-less men home in defeat.
Saddened, humbled, and sobered by the failure of his expedition, he soon presented himself at Castlewood. He held out his hand to George, admitting he had been arrogant before he left, had bragged too much of what he would accomplish, and had been hurt by George’s obvious scorn for his provincial regiment. George, his old jealousy melting in the face of the man’s obvious, unfeigned grief, took his hand warmly, telling him no fair person could blame him for the defeat. Then Madam Esmond stepped forward, curtsied deeply to the dejected young soldier, and told him no woman of her acquaintance would ever turn away a man who had done his best for his king and country. That one graceful, deferential curtsy rekindled every spark of George’s old jealous suspicion, burning hotter than ever as the chapter closed.

Surely no man could lay fairer claim to universal sympathy than the young, brave, handsome, and ill-starred Major Washington. Madam Esmond, mistress of Castlewood, might have birthed a full score of sons, and still have had every right to dote on her dashing young protégé. His former chamber in the west wing was now more “Mr. Washington’s room” than ever, kept aired, furnished with his favourite books, and spoken of in every company where she found an audience. She held up his sterling, unpretentious virtues to her own two boys at every turn, contrasting his steady, honourable demeanour with Harry’s reckless devotion to pleasure (the wild, warm-hearted boy!) and George’s brooding, listless hours poring over dusty old tomes.

George cared not a whit for Mr. Washington’s merits, however, thanks to his mother’s ceaseless, overblown praises. He nursed the little jealous demon in his breast until it grew to be a constant, gnawing pest to himself and everyone around him, firing off sarcastic quips so layered and sharp that his simple, adoring mother could not parse their meaning. She would sit bewildered, staring at his sallow, brooding face, quite at a loss what to make of his dark, saturnine moods.

All the while, public events were unfolding that would twist the fortunes of this quiet Virginia household for good. The petty border skirmish between French and British colonists in North America had swelled from a provincial squabble to a full-blown national war. French reinforcements had already landed in Canada, and British regiments were sailing for Virginia’s shores.

“Alas, my dearest friend,” wrote Madame la Presidente de Mouchy from Quebec to her old young correspondent George Warrington, “how cruel is fate to us! I see you tear yourself from your adored mother’s arms to throw yourself into the embrace of Bellona. I see you carried wounded from the field of battle. I scarce dare wish victory to our lilies when I behold you ranged beneath the standard of the British Leopard. There are enmities the heart refuses to recognise, and ours, for certain, remain at peace amid all this tumult. Everyone here sends their greetings to you, and to Monsieur the Bear-Hunter, your brother— that cold Hippolyte who would always rather chase game than sit for soft, idle conversation with our ladies! Your friend and rival the Chevalier de la Jabotiere burns to meet you face to face on the field of Mars. M. Du Quesne spoke of you only last night at supper. My husband and he send their most affectionate remembrances to their young friend, joined ever by those of your sincere Presidente de Mouchy.”

That very “banner of the Leopard” the fair French lady wrote of was now unfurled to the winds, rallying thousands of the King’s soldiers beneath it. The crown had resolved to wrest every inch of French-occupied territory back under British rule. Two regiments were raised and funded by the King on American soil, while a fleet carrying two more fresh regiments sailed from home ports under a veteran commander.

In February of 1755, Commodore Keppel dropped anchor in Hampton Roads aboard the *Centurion*, the famous ship that had carried Anson on his legendary circumnavigation of the globe. His small fleet of warships carried General Braddock, his full staff, and the first half of his expeditionary force. Mr. Braddock had been personally appointed by the Duke of Cumberland, known across England simply as “The Duke” in that era—nearly the great military hero his partisans claimed, but far less of the cruel butcher his enemies would later paint him as. A fleet of transports followed hard on his heels, stuffed to the gunwales with stores, fresh troops, and piles of gold to fund the campaign.

The great general landed his men at Alexandria, on the banks of the Potomac, then travelled to Annapolis in Maryland to summon all thirteen colonial governors to a war council, ordering each provincial assembly to raise men, supplies, and wagons for the common cause.

The arrival of the general and his little army sent a shock of wild excitement rippling across every colony, and nowhere was the fever higher than at Castlewood. Harry was off the instant the news reached them, galloping for Alexandria to see the rows of white tents strung across the green fields. The rousing trill of fifes and rattle of drums thrilled him to his bones, and he made fast friends with the officers of both regiments within a week, a welcome guest at their mess table, begging every man he met for a spot on the coming expedition.

Madam Esmond was delighted that her boys had the chance to mix with polished, well-bred English gentlemen of quality. She was certain their company would be a vast improvement over the local horse-racing, cock-fighting Virginian squires Harry usually ran with, and the flock of fawning lawyers, pettifoggers, and toadies that hung around the lieutenant-governor’s table at Williamsburg. Madam Esmond had a sharp eye for flatterers in other people’s houses, and she mocked the little Williamsburg official set relentlessly for their absurd petty etiquettes and squabbles over who got to sit first at dinner.

If only the good lady knew half what Harry and George saw at the camp! If she could have heard the raucous, off-colour jokes the officers shouted over bowls of spiced punch, seen half of them carried dead drunk back to their lodgings after dinner, watched them swagger through the countryside terrorising peaceful farmwives and even insulting the wives of the native Indian allies who had travelled hundreds of miles to join the British fight against the French. The General raved and stormed at his troops for their disorder, and ranted at the provincial gentry for their “traitorous niggardliness” in holding back supplies, but the men treated the whole countryside like conquered territory, looking down on the colonists as crude hicks. Eventually Braddock was forced to ban all Indian women from his camp, and their humiliated, outraged husbands abandoned the expedition entirely—robbing him of the scouts and warriors he would desperately need just a few months later.

Madam Esmond would hear none of the camp gossip, though. Soldiers would be soldiers, everyone knew that, and the officers her sons invited to Castlewood were unfailingly polite, a fact that was quite true. The widow received them all with great graciousness, laying on the finest hunting feasts, venison, and wine the estate could provide.

Before long, the General himself sent a polite note to the mistress of Castlewood. His own father had served under the great Duke of Marlborough alongside her father, the legendary Colonel Esmond, whose name was still spoken with respect across England. With her permission, he wrote, General Braddock would do her the honour of calling at Castlewood to pay his respects to the daughter of so distinguished a veteran.

Had Madam Esmond known what lay behind Braddock’s sudden politeness, his compliments would not have charmed her half so much. The Commander-in-Chief was holding public levees at Alexandria, and among the provincial gentry who turned out to pay their respects were the two Warrington twins, mounted on their finest thoroughbreds, dressed in their latest London suits, with two liveried negro boys trailing behind them in the family’s smart new livery, riding in state to call on the great man. Braddock was sullen and furious at the provincial gentry by that point, and barely spared the young men a glance, casually asking his aide-de-camp at dinner later who those two “Squire Gawkeys” in blue-and-gold coats and scarlet waistcoats had been.

Mr. Dinwiddie, the Lieutenant-Governor of Virginia, who happened to be dining with his Excellency that night, had suffered a hundred petty pert snipes from Madam Esmond over the years, and jumped at the chance to tease. “Oh,” he laughed, “those are the sons of Princess Pocahontas.”

Braddock swore a tremendous oath and demanded, “Who the deuce is that?”

Dinwiddie proceeded to spin a long, disrespectful, absurd anecdote-filled account of Madam Esmond, making merry of her pomposity and grand pretensions until his Excellency fell fast asleep right at the dinner table.

When he woke, Dinwiddie was gone, but Mr. Franklin of Philadelphia still sat at the table, deep in conversation with the other officers. Braddock picked up the thread of their talk where he’d left off, speaking of Madam Esmond in short, rude, soldierly terms, demanding what the name of that “old fool” Dinwiddie had been rambling about was. He then launched into a tirade of contempt and wrath against all the provincial gentry and the whole American countryside in general.

Mr. Franklin repeated the widow’s full name, and painted a far different portrait of her character than Dinwiddie had. He knew a great deal about her, her father, and her vast estate—indeed he knew a great deal about every man and every subject that ever came up for discussion. He explained to the General that Madam Esmond held thousands of beeves, a stable full of fine horses, and stockpiles of stores large enough to provision half his expedition, and strongly recommended he conciliate her by every means possible. Braddock already thought Franklin the shrewdest, most intelligent man in the colonies, and promptly ordered an aide to invite the two young Warrington gentlemen to dinner the next day.

When the twins arrived, he was all charm and good humour, and his entire personal staff fawned over them. They behaved with the modesty and good breeding befitting their name, and rode home delighted with their reception— nor was their mother any less pleased that his Excellency had shown such civility to her boys. In reply to Braddock’s note, Madam Esmond penned a grand, flowery letter in her finest hand, acknowledging his politeness and begging his Excellency to name the day when he might come to Castlewood as her honoured guest.

Naturally, the coming war and the approaching expedition were the constant subject of conversation at Castlewood in the weeks that followed. To march on the campaign was the dearest wish of Harry’s whole heart. He dreamed of nothing but battles and glory, hung around the officers’ mess in Williamsburg every other day, polished and scoured every gun, sword, and pistol in the house until they shone, and revived his childhood game of drilling all the able-bodied negro men on the estate as if they were his private army. His mother, who had a stout, gallant spirit of her own, knew the time had come when one of her boys must leave her to serve the King. She scarce dared to think which of them it would be. She respected and admired her elder son deeply, but she knew she loved the wilder, warmer younger boy with all the passion of her heart.

Eager as Harry was to be a soldier, he scarcely dared to speak the desire that burned in his breast. Once or twice he ventured to bring it up to George, only to see his elder brother’s face darken into an ominous scowl. Harry felt a feudal, almost religious devotion to George, worshipped him with extravagant affection, and deferred to his every wish as the undisputed head of the family. To his infinite dismay, he soon saw that George too, in his quiet, grave way, was immersing himself in all things military. He dragged the old volumes of Marlborough and Eugene’s campaigns down from the shelves, pulled out all his grandfather’s military textbooks, and pored over the most warlike of Plutarch’s Lives. He and old Dempster, the mysterious Scottish steward, were practising fencing with foils every afternoon, the old man a secret adept at the art of war, though he was never willing to say where he had learned it.

Madam Esmond sent the two boys back to the General’s camp with her formal reply, along with such large, handsome gifts for Braddock’s entire staff and the officers of the two royal regiments, that the General thanked Mr. Franklin more than once for bringing such a welcome, wealthy ally over to his side.

“Would not one of you young gentlemen care to come along and see the campaign?” Braddock asked them casually. “A friend of yours who speaks of you often—Mr. Washington, who had such ill luck with the expedition last year—has already agreed to join me as aide-de-camp. I would be very glad to take another fine young Virginian gentleman onto my personal staff.”

Harry’s eyes blazed, and his face flushed bright red. “I would go with all my heart, sir!” he cried out.

George looked hard at his younger brother, and said gravely, “One of us would be proud to attend your Excellency. It will be the other’s duty, of course, to stay here and care for our mother at home.”

Harry let his elder brother speak, as he always did. His will was still completely obedient to George’s. Much as he ached to go off to war, he would not say a word until George had declared his own intentions. He wanted the campaign so badly the very desire made him timid, and he dared not bring the matter up as they rode the miles home in silence, both of them talking of trivial, unrelated subjects while they knew full well what was weighing on the other’s mind, both afraid to force the awful question to its final answer.

When they arrived home, they told their mother of General Braddock’s offer. “I knew this must happen,” she said, her voice trembling. “At such a crisis for our country, our family must step forward. Have you—have you settled yet which of you will leave me?” She looked anxiously from one son to the other, dreading to hear either of their names spoken.

“The youngest ought to go, mother! Of course I ought to go!” Harry cried, turning scarlet.

“Of course he ought!” put in Mrs. Mountain, who was sitting in the room with them. “There! You see Mountain says so! I told you!” Harry burst out, darting a sidelong look at George.

“The head of the family ought to go, mother,” George said sadly.

“No! No! You still have not fully recovered from that bad fever you had last spring! Ought he to go, Mountain?”

“You would make the better soldier, I know that, dearest Hal. You and George Washington are great friends, and you would travel well together. He does not care for me, nor I for him, however much everyone in this house admires him. But you see, it is the law of honour, my Harry.” He spoke to his brother then in a voice of extraordinary kindness and tenderness. “The greatest grief I have felt over this matter is that I must refuse you. I must go. If fate had given you that extra half-hour of life I hold over you, it would be your lot, and you would claim your right to go first, you know you would.”

“Yes, George,” poor Harry whispered, “I own I should.”

“You will stay home, and take care of Castlewood and our mother. If anything happens to me, you will be here to fill my place. I would give way to you, my dear, as I know you would lay down your life to serve me. But each of us must do his duty. What would our grandfather say, if he were here now?”

Their mother looked at her two boys, her face bright with proud tears. “My papa would say his boys were gentlemen,” she faltered, and turned and left the room, not willing to let them see how much emotion was flooding her heart.

It spread like wildfire through the household before nightfall that Mr. George was going on the campaign. Dinah, George’s old foster-mother, wailed at the top of her voice at the thought of losing him. Phillis, Harry’s childhood nurse, was just as loud complaining that Master George was being preferred over Master Harry, as he always was. Sady, George’s personal servant, packed his bags bragging nonstop of all the glorious deeds he would perform on campaign, while Gumbo, Harry’s boy, pretended to whimper that he was being left behind—though he was secretly overjoyed not to have to go anywhere near a battlefield.

Of all the people in the house, Mrs. Mountain was the most furious at George’s decision to march off. She would not hear a word of it. He had no idea what he was doing, leaving home like that. She begged, implored, stamped her foot, and insisted he change his mind, vowing that nothing but utter mischief would come of his departure.

George was surprised by how stubbornly she opposed him. “I know, Mountain,” he said, “that Harry would make the better soldier. But after all, it is my duty to go.”

“Your duty is to stay!” Mountain snapped. “Why didn’t your own mother say that, just now when we were talking of it?”

“Your mother!” Mrs. Mountain gave a dark, sardonic laugh. “Your mother, my poor foolish boy!”

“What is the meaning of that mournful face, Mountain?”

“It may be that your mother wishes you away, George!” She shook her head grimly. “It may be, my poor deluded child, that you will find yourself with a new step-father when you come home.”

“What in heaven’s name do you mean?” George cried, the blood rushing straight to his face.

“Don’t you think I have eyes to see what is going on under my own nose? I tell you, child, Colonel Washington wants a rich wife. The second you two boys are off to the war, he will ask your mother to marry him, and you will come back to find him master of Castlewood. That is why you ought not to leave, you poor, simple boy! Don’t you see how fond she is of him? How much she fusses over him? How she is always holding him up as a perfect example to you, to Harry, to every single guest that walks through this door?”

“But he is going on the campaign too!” George protested.

“He is going on the courting campaign, child!” Mountain insisted. “It is all an artifice to blind you! You will see, he will get himself ‘wounded’ within a week and come straight back home! I have proof of what I say, proof in his own handwriting—look here!” She pulled a half-sheet of crumpled paper out of her pocket, in Mr. Washington’s well-known bold, clerk-like script.

“Where did you get that paper?” George asked, his face turning ghastly pale.

“I—I found it in the Major’s chamber!” Mountain said, looking shamefaced.

“You read the private papers of a guest staying in our house?” George cried. “For shame! I will not look at it!” He snatched the paper from her hand and flung it straight onto the smouldering log fire on the hearth.

On the day appointed for Madam Esmond’s grand entertainment honoring General Braddock, every corner of Castlewood House sparkled with unaccustomed splendor. Fine linen draped the sideboards, silver candelabra gleamed along the dining table, and the whole air hummed with the scent of spiced cider, roasted venison, and freshly baked pastry. Madam Esmond herself had arrayed herself in a heavy silk brocade gown she had only worn twice in her life, determined to do her guest every possible honor, even though the feast weighed on her spirits like lead. The first arrival was the General’s new aide-de-camp, Mr. Washington. The widow met him in the covered gallery that ran along the front of the house, as he dismounted at the steps—no young gentleman in all the colony was a finer horseman, or kept a better string of mounts, than the tall young militia colonel.

Before he retired to change out of his dust-caked riding boots, the pair paced the gallery for some time, deep in talk. She heard from him full confirmation of his appointment to Braddock’s staff, and they spoke long of her elder son George’s upcoming departure for the campaign. Enslaved servants bearing trays piled high with dishes for the feast passed them in a steady stream as they talked, until they descended the steps to the rough lawn below, and strolled in the shade of the gnarled old oaks. Washington told her the General would be along shortly, riding in his coach with Benjamin Franklin of Pennsylvania. Madam Esmond huffed at the news. She had heard Franklin had started life as a common printer’s apprentice—what was the world coming to, when a tradesman rode in the Commander-in-Chief’s own coach? But Washington protested that no shrewder, more honorable, useful man ever walked on foot or rode in a carriage. The widow thought the Major far too generous to the low-born inventor, but he stood his ground firmly.
“I am glad at the very least,” Madam Esmond said, drawing herself up in her stateliest pose, “that when my boy marches out to campaign, he will not be in the company of tradesmen, but of gentlemen—gentlemen of honor and fashion, bred at court, friends of his Royal Highness the Duke of Cumberland.”

Washington, who had seen too many of those fine court gentlemen roaring drunk in the regimental mess, to say nothing of their careless cruelty to new young recruits, wisely held his tongue. He would not speak ill of his superior officers behind their backs. “Harry and George are coming into the world now,” he said instead. “They must take the good with the bad, and learn to sort the wise counsel from the foolish for themselves.”
Then the widow’s tone softened entirely. “And with you, dear Colonel Washington—my own father trusted you more than any man alive, you know. You do not know how high he held you in his regard. You are only five years older than my George, yet I trust you far more than I do men twice his age. My father told the boys, and I have told them a hundred times since, to look up to Mr. Washington in all things.”
“Madam,” Washington bowed, his manner warm and sincere, “there is nothing I would not have done to win your father’s good opinion. There is no risk I would not run now to merit the favor of his daughter.”
The widow blushed so deep the rouge on her cheeks could scarcely hide it, and dropped a curtsey so low it was famous across every tidewater county in Virginia. “Mr. Washington will always have a mother’s affection in this house, so long as he shows such care for her sons,” she said, and gave him her hand, which he kissed with profound, perfect politeness.

The little lady leaned on his arm as they stepped back into the house, and found George waiting for them there, his hair perfectly powdered, his rich silk suit spotless, bowing low to both his mother and Washington. But there was no good humor in him, not at all. A polite fixed smile played around his mouth, while his dark eyes glowered with wrath and suspicion. What had he seen from the window? The innocent hand kiss, the blush on his mother’s cheek, the soft tone between the two, and his mind was already leaping to wild, jealous conclusions.
Washington tried to smooth things over with light small talk, describing the ridiculous hunt he and Braddock had joined that morning, the General floundering through mud and undergrowth in his massive boots, chasing turkeys with a fowling piece, surrounded by hounds and a crowd of shouting enslaved attendants. Braddock had huffed and puffed the whole time, complaining that Sir Robert Walpole back in Norfolk, England, would have had a fit to see such unsporting behavior, hunting turkey with a shotgun instead of riding proper to hounds. Madam Esmond gave a neat little laugh, but George only grew more glum, making snide, sneering remarks about how he was nothing but a milksop tied to his mother’s apron strings, no hunter, no fighter, no proper man of action like the rest of them.

The widow was already close to tears when Harry burst into the room, dressed in a matching fine suit, gold-corded frock coat, silver-hilted sword and all, ready to greet the General. She flew to him at once, sobbing, and Harry wrapped his arms around her, utterly confused. George kept up his mocking jabs, until Harry finally spoke up, red-faced: “If you hate hunting and fighting so much, George, why not let me go on the campaign in your place? I was born for it! I’d march straight at the French and thrash them all.”
George laughed off the suggestion. “Honor obliges the eldest heir of Esmond to go first,” he said. “We cannot both leave, anyway—someone has to stay here and watch over mother, so we don’t end up both scalped by Indians or fricasseed by French soldiers.” Harry sighed, disappointed he would miss all the glory.
George wandered over to the harpsichord, plopped down, and began trilling through the mocking French war ballad *Malbrouk s’en va-t-en guerre*, over and over, the silly little tune ringing through the parlor. Washington pulled out his watch then, saying the General’s coach would be at the gates any minute, and begged leave to go change into his full dress uniform before the rest of the guests arrived. Madam Esmond, furious at George’s insolent behavior, sailed after him to show him to his chamber, leaving the two brothers alone.

George immediately pulled a crumpled scrap of paper out of his coat pocket, the fragment of letter he had found dropped on the gallery steps that morning, and thrust it at Harry. “Look at that,” he snarled. “Common kindness? Do you call that common kindness?”
Harry read the half-finished lines, written in Washington’s neat hand: *... is older than myself, but I, again, am older than my years; and you know, dear brother, have ever been considered a sober person. All children are better for a father's superintendence, and her two, I trust, will find in me a tender friend and guardian. The flattering offer which General Braddock hath made me, will, of course, oblige me to postpone this matter until after the campaign. When we have given the French a sufficient drubbing, I shall return to repose under my own vine and fig-tree. Under my own vine and fig-tree; where I hope soon to present my dear brother to his new sister-in-law. She has a pretty Scripture name, which is...*
“Rachel!” George shrieked, clenching his fist and shaking it at the ivy climbing the outside of the parlor wall. “Rachel Esmond now, I suppose! This whole house, our lands, our father’s legacy, he thinks he’ll slip right into it, with our mother as his wife, and us two saps calling him Papa! Come on, Hal—let’s go upstairs right now, kneel proper, and welcome our new stepfather home to Castlewood.”

His Excellency the Commander-in-Chief set out to pay his formal call on Madam Esmond in a state and splendour befitting the highest ranking authority across all His Majesty’s North American colonies, plantations, and dominions. Ahead of him out of Williamsburg rode his guard of dragoons, greeted by a roar of cheers from a loyal crowd made up overwhelmingly of the town’s enslaved Black population. The General himself travelled in his own heavy, emblazoned coach, Captain Talmadge, his Master of the Horse, at the carriage door before mounting to ride at its flank for the whole journey to Castlewood. Seated up front with Major Danvers, his aide-de-camp, was the little Philadelphia postmaster Mr. Franklin: once a printer’s boy, he was widely acknowledged by the General and his staff as a man of uncommon shrewdness, brimming with curious, precise knowledge of the colonies, and of England too, where he had travelled more than once.
“‘Tis quite extraordinary how a man of such humble origins could have amassed such breadth of learning, and such natural politeness besides, Mr. Franklin!” his Excellency remarked, tipping his hat graciously to the postmaster.
Franklin bowed low, his wide buckled wig shifting to send a small puff of powder into the air. He replied that he had been fortunate enough to fall into the company of gentlemen of the General’s calibre from time to time, and had done his best to study their manners and adapt his own conduct to match theirs as far as he was able. Of formal education, he could not boast much: his father had been a man of straitened means, and schooling opportunities in his native New England were thin on the ground. He had read and observed everything he could, but insisted he still knew nothing compared to the learned men of England.
Mr. Braddock burst out laughing. “As for education, there are officers in the army, by George, who couldn’t tell you if ‘bull’ was spelled with two b’s or one. I’ve heard the Duke of Marlborough himself was no great hand with a pen. I never had the honour to serve under him, his Grace was a generation before my time, but he thrashed the French soundly all the same, and no one ever called him a poor commander for being no scholar.”
Mr. Franklin said he was well aware of that fact.
“Nor is my own Duke a man of books,” Braddock went on, grinning. “Aha, I see that little wink in your eye, Postmaster, you’ve heard that story too!”
Franklin instantly wiped the satirical spark from his eye, turning a face as guileless as an infant’s up to the General’s ruddy, jolly features. “He is no scholar, true, but he is more than a match for any French general who ever made a joke about serving up Englishmen as frog fricassee. He saved the crown for our most gracious sovereign, King George, his royal father.”
Off went Franklin’s hat in a deep bow, sending a whole cloud of white powder billowing from his wig.
“He is the soldiers’ truest friend, and the unflinching enemy of all those beggarly red-shanked Scottish rebels and scheming Roman Jesuits who would rob us of our liberty and our Protestant faith, by George. His Royal Highness, my gracious master, is no scholar either, but he is one of the finest gentlemen who ever walked the earth.”
“I saw His Royal Highness on horseback once, at a Guards review in Hyde Park,” Franklin said, smiling. “He cuts a very fine figure in the saddle, no denying.”
“You shall drink his health to-day, Postmaster. He is the best of masters, the best of friends, the best of sons to his old royal father; the finest gentleman ever to wear an epaulet.”
“Epaulets are quite out of my line, sir,” Franklin laughed. “You know I live in the Quaker City.”
“Of course they are, my good man. Every man to his own work. You and your sort pore over your books, and you’re welcome to it. We don’t forbid it, we encourage it. Our work is to fight the enemy and govern the country. Hey gentlemen? Lord, but these roads in the colony are something dreadful! This cursed coach is lurching like a ship in a gale. Who have we yonder, riding that fine gelding with two liveried negro boys behind him?”
“That is Mr. Washington,” the aide-de-camp answered.
“I’d take him for a corporal in the Horse Grenadiers any day,” the General pronounced. “He cuts a perfect figure on a horse. And he knows this country inside out, don’t he, Mr. Franklin?”
“Indeed he does.”
“And monstrous genteel, for a provincial. I’d have sworn he had the polish of a man who’d made the grand tour of Europe, by George I would.”
Franklin nodded, his face innocent, as he glanced at the stout chief lurching side to side across the carriage seat, his face as scarlet as his uniform coat, who swore every other breath, knew nothing outside parade ground rules save for the merits of a fine bottle and a pretty woman, was absurdly proud of his own no-distinguished ancestry, brave as a bulldog, savage one minute and generous the next, easy to laugh with, dull of wit, entirely unread, and utterly convinced England was the greatest nation on earth and he himself the equal of any gentleman alive. “Yes, he is mighty well for a provincial, to be sure. He was beaten last year at that Fort What’s-it-called, down by the Thingamy River. What was the name of the place, Talmadge?”
“Lord knows, sir,” said Talmadge. “And I’ll wager the Postmaster knows too, and is laughing at us both for forgetting it.”
“Oh Captain, you do me wrong!”
“He was caught in a perfect trap, that’s what. He only had militia and raw Indian levies with him. Fine day, Mr. Washington. A very pretty nag you’re riding. That was your first action, last year?”
“At Fort Necessity, sir, yes,” the gentleman replied, gravely saluting as he rode up, two sharp, well-dressed negro grooms at his heels in smart livery coats and velvet hunting caps. “I began it very badly, sir. I had never been in action before that unlucky day.”
“You were all raw levies, my good fellow. You should have seen our own militia run from the Highland Scots, and cursed be to them for it. You ought to have had regular troops with you.”
“Your Excellency knows it is my dearest wish to serve alongside them,” Mr. Washington said.
“By George, we shall see that you get that chance, sir,” the General swore with one of his characteristic hearty oaths. The heavy coach rumbled onwards towards Castlewood, while Mr. Washington asked permission to gallop ahead to warn Madam Esmond of their imminent arrival.
The Commander-in-Chief’s progress was so slow that a number of humbler local gentry invited to the gathering soon overtook his carriage. Unwilling to pass the great man on the road, they fell in behind his chariot wheels, forming a long, comical procession through the dust. First came Mr. Dinwiddie, the Lieutenant-Governor of the province, attended by his own negro servants, riding alongside Parson Broadbent, the jolly Williamsburg chaplain. Presently they were joined by little Mr. Dempster, the boys’ schoolmaster, wearing his grand Ramillies wig reserved only for state occasions. Soon after that, Judge Laws and his wife came into view, Madam Laws riding pillion behind him, their negro servant trailing behind on a mule, carrying a locked box that held her ladyship’s best cap. The whole rear guard looked so ludicrous that Major Danvers and Mr. Franklin spied them and laughed outright, quiet enough not to wake the General, who was fast asleep by then. They called out to the party of local gentry to ride ahead, there was more than enough room at Castlewood for everyone when the Commander-in-Chief and his dragoon escort followed at their leisure. There would be meat, drink, and the finest tobacco for His Majesty’s soldiers; laughter and plenty of cheer for the enslaved servants; and a warm, overflowing welcome for all their masters.
The honest General made sure to sample nearly every dish on the table, and reach for second helpings of most, holding out his glass for refills constantly. He declared Nathan’s spiced sangaree to be perfection, and had drunk a large draught of it even before dinner was served. There was cider, ale, brandy, and plenty of good Bordeaux wine, some of it brought back to the colony by Madam Esmond’s late husband Colonel Esmond, fit for pontificum coenis—“a feast fit for priests,” little Mr. Dempster whispered with a wink to Parson Broadbent, the clergyman from the adjoining parish. Broadbent winked back and nodded, drinking the wine without a care for the Latin line, which was no surprise: he had never troubled himself much with dead languages. He was a gambling, guzzling, cock-fighting divine who had spent a good portion of his life in the Fleet Prison, at Newmarket racecourse, and at the rough sporting grounds of Hockley-in-the-Hole. He had run all manner of errands for his old patron Lord Cingbars, son of Lord Ringwood (it was widely rumoured that Broadbent’s mother had been Lady Cingbars’ waiting woman, and modern readers need not pry too closely into the details of his paternity), before he was posted out to a rural Virginia living. He and young George Esmond had fought many a cock fight together, hunted roe side by side, hauled in countless shad and salmon, shot wild geese, swans, pigeons, and plover, and bagged myriads of canvas-backed ducks. The envious whispered that Broadbent had once been caught poaching on Mr. Washington’s land, and that Washington had set his dogs on him and thrashed him soundly on the riverbank at Mount Vernon. The parson had broken free of Washington’s grip and scrambled to his boat in the dark, but he was laid up for two full Sundays afterwards, and when he reappeared in public he still bore the fading mark of a black eye, and wore a brand new coat collar. George Esmond and Parson Broadbent had played every game of cards under the sun together, besides hunting every bird in the air, every beast in the forest, and every fish in the rivers. It was widely suspected that while the twins rode off to their lessons with Mr. Dempster, Harry would often slip away and take lessons from Broadbent in the European arts of hunting, drinking, and sport, while George went his own way reading his books, and of course never told tales on his younger brother.
Every game bird of the Virginia woods, every fish in the season’s catch, was laid out on Madam Esmond’s board to feed the General and the rest of the English and colonial gentlemen. The gumbo was pronounced absolute perfection (young Mr. George’s black servant was even named after the dish: the late Colonel had caught him hiding behind a door with his face buried in a bowl of the rich stew, and named him Gumbo on the spot). The shad were rich and fresh, the stewed terrapins were declared worthy of a London alderman’s table—by George, the General said, he would be proud to serve it up to the Duke himself. The enslaved women of Castlewood’s kitchens had a genius for cookery, trained from childhood under the sharp, exacting eye of both the late Colonel and Madam Esmond herself. Many of the sweets and flans Madam Esmond made with her own neat, dexterous hands, following the old hospitable custom of the time, rolling back the laced lappets of her sleeves to show off her pretty round forearms and small, delicate wrists as she carved the principal roasts and fowls at the head of the table. The unwritten old rule of the Virginia table was that the mistress must press her guests to eat with gracious eagerness, watching to encourage those who might be shy to take more, knowing every culinary secret and every trick of carving fowls, fish, game, and joints, cheering her guests to new helpings, and whispering to the General, “I saved the salmon’s jowl just for your Excellency—there’s no taking no for an answer! Mr. Franklin, you drink only water, sir? But our cellar has wholesome wine that never gives a man a headache—won’t you try just a sip? Mr. Justice, you are fond of woodcock pie, I know.”
“Because I know who makes the pastry,” Judge Laws said, bowing low to her. “I wish my own wife could make a pie crust half as light as yours, madam. I tell her all the time, my dear, I wish you had Madam Esmond’s hands.”
“A very pretty hand it is too, I’m sure more than one gentleman would not mind having it,” the Boston postmaster remarked, and Mr. Esmond looked at him half displeased at the familiar line.
“Such a hand for a light, flaky crust,” the Judge continued, “my very best respects to you, madam.” He thought the widow would surely be flattered by the compliment. She replied simply that she had learned all her cookery and carving skills when she was sent to England for her education as a girl, that her own mother had taught her the family recipes, and her father and two sons had always loved those dishes. She was only too glad if they pleased her guests.
More dishes came out, more compliments, more toasts: ten times as much meat as was strictly needed for the whole company. Mr. Washington did not join much in the light banter, but sat deep in conversation with Talmadge, Danvers, and Mr. Franklin, tracing out lines across the table with bits of bread to mark roads, rivers, supply routes, pack horse stops, and positions for the artillery train. He rested his finger on little bread crumb markers for the forts and camps along the Potomac and Ohio, until a passing negro servant clearing the dishes brushed the Potomac right off the table with his napkin, and swept the marked-up Ohio into a spoon when he cleared away the crumbs.
At the end of the dinner Parson Broadbent got up and walked behind the Lieutenant-Governor’s chair to say a short grace over the meal, before returning to his seat to pick up his knife and fork again. The puddings and sweets came next: a dozen different varieties, all made to Madam Esmond’s exact family recipes, though few young ladies of the present day would care to hear a long list of puddings eaten a hundred years ago. When the table was cleared, Nathan, the chief butler, set a glass down before every guest, then filled Madam Esmond’s. Bowing to the whole company, she said she would only propose one toast, and knew every gentleman there would join her with all their hearts. “His Majesty,” she said, bowing to Mr. Braddock, who, with his aides and all the colonial gentlemen, repeated the name of their beloved sovereign loyally. She drank her glass of wine, curtsied to the whole company, and retired from the dining room between two lines of liveried negro servants, giving one of her finest, most graceful curtsies at the parlour door.
The mistress of Castlewood had presided over the whole entertainment with admirable spirit, looking so gay and handsome, speaking with such cheer to every guest, that the few other ladies at the table had crowded around her to congratulate her on the elegance of the feast, and her poise hosting it. But no sooner had they stepped into her drawing room than the brave mask of composure fell, and she burst into tears on the sofa beside Mrs. Laws, mid-compliment from that lady. “Ah, madam!” she said. “It may be a great honour, as you say, to host the King’s representative under my roof, and the Esmond family has hosted far greater personages than Mr. Braddock in our time. But he has come to take one of my sons away from me. Who knows if my boy will ever come home, or how? I dreamed of him last night, wounded, his face as white as a sheet, blood streaming from a gash in his side. I would never be so ill-mannered as to let my grief show before the gentlemen, but you, Mrs. Justice, who have parted with your own children and carry a mother’s heart, would not think the less of me if mine was heavy this evening.”
The ladies offered her all the gentle comfort they could, and Madam Esmond forced herself to pull back from her melancholy, remembering she still had duties to perform before she could give way to her private grief. “There will be time enough to be sad once they are all gone,” she told Mrs. Laws, her good neighbour. “My boy must not see me watching him leave with a wistful face, and make our parting all the more painful with my weakness. It is right that young men of his rank should step forward to answer their country’s call. That has always been the way of the Esmonds, and the same Providence that watched over my dear father through twenty great battles under Queen Anne, I trust and pray, will keep my son safe now that his turn has come to do his duty.” She did not speak of her sorrow again, but sat down with the other ladies to play cards and sip coffee, while the gentlemen remained in the adjoining parlour, still drinking their wine and calling out toast after toast. When one lady remarked that the gentlemen were lingering over their drinks rather too long, Madam Esmond only smiled and said, “It will do my boys good to spend time in the company of these English gentlemen. Such society is very rarely found in our remote province, and though their conversation may sometimes be a little free, I am sure men of their rank and breeding will respect the youth of my sons, and say nothing in front of them that young people ought not to hear.”
It was very clear that the English gentlemen were making the most of Madam Esmond’s generous hospitality. While the ladies were still at their cards, Nathan slipped in to whisper to Mrs. Mountain, the housekeeper, who at first cried out in protest: “No! I will not bring out any more of that special claret! They are welcome to all the ordinary Bordeaux they could want, but I will not touch the Colonel’s private stock.” It turned out that the entire dozen bottles of the prized late Colonel’s Bordeaux had already been finished by the gentlemen, “not to mention all the ale, cider, Burgundy, Lisbon wine, and Madeira,” Nathan added, ticking them off on his fingers.
But Madam Esmond would not hear of skimping on hospitality that night. Mrs. Mountain had no choice but to bustle off with her keys to the sacred vault

The last of General Braddock’s party had been escorted to their chambers, the candles guttering low in the heavy Virginia summer air that clung like damp linen to Castlewood’s wood panelling, when the two Warrington brothers slipped away to their own garret bedroom to unburden the full weight of their indignation at the day’s shocking revelation. Neither would abide the match their mother was clearly contemplating: the heir to the ancient line of Esmond marquises reduced to marrying a 23-year-old ex-land-surveyor of no great birth, who would step straight into the role of their stepfather, lording it over two nineteen-year-old boys of noble blood? It was monstrous, unthinkable.

Harry’s first rash impulse was to storm directly to his mother’s bedchamber, where her two favourite bondswomen were even then unpinning her lace fichu and unlatching the paste diamond buckles she had worn for the feast, to declare that if she went through with the unnatural union, they would abandon her forever and live off their small inherited tract of upcountry land alone.

George, cooler and sharper, advocated a far more decisive solution, which he laid out for his admiring younger brother. “No lady can possibly marry a man who has crossed swords or exchanged a pistol shot with her own son,” he reasoned, his pale cheeks flushed bright from the stolen sips of their grandfather’s old Bordeaux he had snuck at dinner. “Not if he wounded us, or we wounded him, or either of us fell dead on the field. Harry, we must call him out.”

Harry saw the perfect logic of the plan at once, and gaped at his brother’s immense sagacity. “You are right, George! Mother would never marry her own son’s murderer, would she? If we pink him the whole question is settled, just as old Mr. Dempster used to say in our Latin lessons. Shall I send my boy off this very instant with a challenge to Colonel Washington?”

“My dear Harry,” the elder replied, with quiet complacency over the duel he had already fought and survived at Quebec, “you are not yet accustomed to affairs of honour. We cannot insult a guest under our own roof – the rules of honour forbid such inhospitality. But once we ride out through the park gates? The moment the iron latch clicks shut behind us, we may speak our full minds.”

“That we can, by George!” Harry cried, squeezing his brother’s hand tight. A moment later his face flushed bright crimson, and he leaned in to plead: “This ought to be my turn, brother. You are already bound for the campaign with Braddock, you cannot claim every scrap of glory. I deserve this affair, I do.”

“The head of the house must take the lead, my dear,” George declared with a haughty, regal air. “If I fall, you will have your chance to avenge me. But I must fight George Washington. I hate him the worst, after all – it was he who counselled mother to set that brute Ward on me and lock me up like a common criminal.”

“Ah, George, you ought to forgive and forget,” the more easy-going Harry protested.

“Forgive? I will never, not as long as I can draw breath. You cannot command a man to throw his own memory out the window. A wrong that stung yesterday is still a wrong tomorrow. I never did a man harm intentionally in my life, and I will not suffer one to go unpunished if I can help it. Washington is our enemy, mine above all others. He has already interfered in my life to do me harm, and now he means to steal our mother and our home. We must punish him.”

Harry, who worshipped his brother as a near-perfect hero, bowed to his judgement as ever, and they retired for the night, George giving strict instructions that they must remain perfectly civil to their mother’s guests for the rest of their stay, for decency’s sake.

We shall name no names to say which of Braddock’s staff ended the night carried tipsy to their beds by grinning enslaved grooms – the habit of heavy drinking was universal among 18th century British army officers, and no gentleman of the time thought twice about tipping a dozen bottles of Bordeaux between a dinner party. Even General Braddock, a famously hard drinker, was soon snoring peacefully off the night’s feast. Madam Esmond saw her guests’ inebriated state without the least shock, and was up before dawn brewing spiced, cooling toddy to soothe their throbbing heads, which the servants carried up to their chambers. At breakfast, one young English officer teased Benjamin Franklin (who never touched wine at all) for turning down the morning draught, saying he missed two equal pleasures: the pleasant buzz of drunkenness, and the delicious toddy that cured the hangover.

Braddock’s new Virginian aide-de-camp, Colonel Washington, sat perfectly sober and calm at the table, unruffled and clear-eyed. The British officers laughed and vowed they would soon break him in to the ways of the regular army, but Washington only gravely replied that he had no interest in learning that particular part of British military education.

Madam Esmond, run ragged overseeing the great dinner and then the follow-on breakfast, had barely time to watch her sons closely, and only noted that George was being scrupulously polite to her favourite Colonel Washington, just as he was to all their guests. Before Braddock left, he held a private audience with the widow, formally offering to take George onto his personal staff for the coming campaign. Madam Esmond did not make a fuss over the known hard drinking habits of the British officer corps, saying stoutly to her companion Mrs. Mountain later: “My father never drank, that is true, but half the finest company in England do, and my boy must take his chances with the rest of the world for good and ill.” Braddock clapped George heartily on the back, bade him report to the camp at Frederick three days hence, when the expedition would march.

At last the General’s great coach was pulled around, his cavalry escort pranced into formation, and the other guests mounted their horses. The household stood on the veranda steps to see them off: the trumpeter blew a shrill blast, the enslaved servants cheered “Huzzay! God save the King!” as Braddock’s coach rumbled away down the drive.

As the boys turned back up the steps, Washington was lingering to take one last private farewell of their mother. The widow was tearful, visibly moved, for she would not see him again before he left for the dangerous campaign, and George watched the exchange with a sharp, bitter twinge of angry scorn. He put on a perfectly bright, amiable face, and said: “We will go boot up at once, Colonel, and ride a little ways with you to speed you on your journey.” Their horses were already saddled at the stables, and the three men set off at once, their grooms trailing behind them. Mrs. Mountain watched them ride away, sighing in huge relief that Washington had left the house without an open quarrel with the boys, and without making a formal declaration of love to their mother.

Washington was delighted and confused by George’s sudden friendliness. The long history of kindness between the Esmonds and him, the tender farewell with Madam Esmond, the shared danger of the coming campaign, all made him eager to forget the past months of petty friction between him and the boys. He talked amiably about how certain the expedition’s success was – two thousand crack British regulars would easily crush any force the French and their native allies could muster, he argued, and no loyal subject of King George II had more faith in the power of the regular army’s veteran tactics. Only Harry was quiet and withdrawn, hanging back at his brother’s side instead of pressing eagerly to ride next to Washington as he had always done before, which the Colonel mistook for simple anxiety over George’s coming departure.

They rode through the sweltering, hazy afternoon until they reached Benson’s, a rough log roadhouse that doubled as a recruiting station for Halkett’s regiment, where a handful of officers were already loitering on the porch over a big bowl of Virginian toddy. The boys’ horses were led off to be watered and fed, and they stepped into the taproom for a quick bite. George was unnaturally loud and lively, while Harry’s face was pale and drawn, as if he was the one riding off to war.

“One would think it was you off to fight the French and Indians, Squire Harry,” the tavern keeper Benson joked.

“I may fear for my brother, even if I would bear my own share of danger well enough,” Harry mumbled.

Colonel Washington was quick to leap to his defence. “No one here doubts the courage of any man of the Warrington family.”

“You do us great honour to say so, Colonel,” George bowed low, a thin, cold smile on his face. “I assure you, we can hold our own if need be.”

Harry caught his brother’s eye, and read the intent there, so alarming he whispered: “You are not going to do it here and now? For God’s sake let me take this turn. You are going off to campaign, you cannot risk this. We might be wrong, George.”

“Psha, we are not,” George muttered back, steady as steel. “It must be now. Do not be afraid. I will find an excuse that leaves no trace of our original plan.”

He called over to the two half-drunk officers on the porch, Captain Grace and Captain Waring, and invited them to share the toddy bowl, declaring the drink was on him. George called Washington over to join them, and when the Colonel politely said he was not thirsty, George jeered that he need not fear paying for the drink. “When the King’s health is proposed, no gentleman officer can refuse a sip,” he announced, raising the bowl. The toast was unassailable: Grace, Waring, Harry all drank, and Washington had to take a small sip to avoid looking disloyal. Next Grace proposed a toast to the Duke of Cumberland and the Army, and again Washington was forced to drink.

“You do not seem to stomach the toast very well, Colonel,” George sneered.

“I tell you again I do not wish to drink,” Washington snapped, stamping his foot. “The army would serve the crown far better if we spent less time drinking endless toasts and more time drilling.”

Drunk and indignant, Captain Grace slammed his fist on the table. “A British officer never neglects that duty! Any man who refuses to drink the Duke’s toast ought to be court-martialled!”

“Man, you are completely intoxicated!” Washington roared, jumping to his feet.

“Insult me, you provincial militia captain!” Grace shrieked.

“We all heard it,” George cut in smoothly. “This is my liquor, my invitation, and I am shocked that Colonel Washington would speak so abusively to my guest Captain Grace.”

The last of Washington’s patience snapped. “You insolent young jackanapes! I have put up with your impudence for months now, only out of respect for your mother, your grandfather, and your brother, or I would have – I would have dragged you over my knee and whipped you like the snarling little puppy you are!”

Harry sprang to his feet, face blazing red. “That is an insult to both of us, George Washington! You will apologise, or give us the reparation due to gentlemen.”

For a second, Washington’s rage melted, a deep tenderness filling his breast for the two lads he had watched grow up from boys. He stepped back, bewildered. “My words were hasty, I did not mean – tell me what has been the meaning of George’s behaviour to me for months, and I will make amends.”

But George’s rage was unyielding, his black eyes blazing with pure unforgiving hate. “You dodge every question just as you dodged the toast. I am no small boy to suffer your arrogance. You have publicly insulted me in a public room, and I demand satisfaction.”

Before Washington could reply, the slurring Captain Grace staggered forward, wailing that Washington had insulted him too, and Captain Waring declared he could not stand by while a visiting militia colonel called his comrade a hog. Washington shouted that it was a full conspiracy, all of them drunk and ganging up on him, and he would meet any of them, all of them, drunk or sober, for a duel, one after another.

“Pistols, not small swords,” George said coldly. “We beat you every time at fencing from our old bouts when we were boys. Pistols are fairer.”

“As you wish,” Washington said, his face falling with deep, unfeigned sorrow. “God forgive you, George. God pardon you, Harry, for dragging me into this quarrel.”

“Forgive? I will never forgive that boyhood slight, when you acted as overseer at Castlewood once and threatened to whip me like a negro field hand for climbing that forbidden apple tree!” George snarled, gritting his teeth. “I am no slave, George Washington, and I never will be. That insult is long past due to be settled.”

Washington stared at him, stunned, realising the entire months of friction had stemmed from one petty, forgotten boyhood quarrel. He turned to Harry, heartbroken. “And you bear this malice too?”

“I stand by my brother,” Harry mumbled, turning away from Washington’s sad face, and squeezing George’s hand.

Washington sighed heavily. “Very well. I have my own pistols at my saddle. You did not bring yours, so send your groom back to Castlewood to fetch them. That will give me time to write my last letters. I will not run from this.”

Benson the tavern keeper, an old frontier veteran who owed Madam Esmond his wife’s life after she tended her through a dangerous lying-in years before, nodded. “I’ll stand by to see fair play, Colonel. No cheating here. And I don’t need to tell you those boys are both crack shots – George can hit an ace of spades at a hundred paces, no trouble at all.”

The summer afternoon hung thick and heavy over the clearing, the air still and sweltering, as the three men made their arrangements for the duel, under the haze of Virginia’s hot, angry sun.

A thick, heavy hush hung over the rough log walls of Benson’s tavern that crisp Virginian morning. Shut in one bedchamber, Colonel George Washington, newly appointed aide-de-camp to General Braddock, sat polishing his duel pistols with slow, grim strokes, every line of his strong handsome face pulled tight with unspoken sorrow over the coming useless bloodshed. In the opposite chamber, young George Warrington paced restlessly, equally convinced he would not walk away from the meeting, and insisted on drafting his final farewells before the hour appointed for the ground.

He dictated to his weeping younger brother Harry, acting as his reluctant secretary, a grandiloquent letter to their mother, framed with a sharp, bitter edge. He made no mention of her name tied to the quarrel, he told Harry, recalling their grandfather’s memoir of the old duel between Lord Castlewood and Lord Mohun, where no hint of the lady at the heart of the conflict ever appeared in the formal record. Harry’s eyes overflowed so freely with honest, boyish tears that he blotted half the page, misspelling the final phrase “in view” as “in vew”, and George laughed half-heartedly before insisting the boy could not be trusted to write his last wishes at all.

He pushed Harry aside, took a fresh sheet of paper, and filled it with all the grandest flourishes, Latin quotes, and pointed satire his young scholar’s wit could conjure. His will set free his loyal enslaved boy Sady, left his prized copy of Horace, the rest of his book collection, and a small steady stipend to his gentle, impoverished tutor Mr. Dempster. He bequeathed his silver fruit-knife, his sheet music, and his beloved harpsichord to little Fanny Mountain, and asked Harry to tuck a lock of his hair into a locket and wear it always, in memory of his fond, loyal older brother. He sealed the document with his grandfather’s old heraldic signet, pulled out the heirloom gold watch his ancestor had carried, and realized with a jolt that two and a half hours had already slipped by. Sady should long have returned with the matched duelling pistols he had been sent to fetch.

Harry threw his arms around George’s neck, sobbing that if the Colonel killed him, he would step up next and put a bullet straight through Washington himself. The boy poured out so many wild, impious oaths that the recording angel posted at the celestial chancery was sent darting off half a dozen times, his ledger smudged, to add the transgressions to the public record.

Across the hall, Washington had already penned five crisp, firm letters in his steady, bold hand: one to his mother at Mount Vernon, one to his brother, one signed only to “M.C.”, one addressed to General Braddock, and one, the tavern landlord later revealed, for Madam Esmond herself.

Old Captain Benson, the tavern keeper who wore his faded militia uniform for the occasion, popped his head in to inform them the Colonel was already pacing the kitchen garden waiting for them, and most of the redcoat officers who had been drunk the night before were almost sober at last. The patch of ground was ringed with rough shingle palings, all the enslaved servants crowded along the top to crane over and watch, and a handful of squires and neighbouring farmers had wandered over, drawn by the gossip of a duel. Washington paced the dirt path, hands clasped behind his back, head bowed, hating every moment of the predicament he had landed in. He knew he had spoken sharp, insulting words to the hot-headed young Warrington, and was bound by the strict honour code of the colony to answer the boy’s challenge, no matter how much he regretted that his own hasty temper had sparked the whole mess.

A distant roar of whooping, the wild full-throated yell that enslaved Virginian riders gave when galloping full tilt across country, cut through the quiet. Sady came careening into the yard a minute later on a lathered, foaming horse, fired one pistol in the air, then a second, and was immediately surrounded by a crowd of his hooting, cheering fellow servants. He ignored Harry and George’s shouts to bring the pistols over, grinning, snapped the pistol locks shut, pointed one at a panicking farm pig that darted squealing through the fowls scattered in the yard, and nodded down the road. “Comin’, mas’r,” he called. “Everybody a-comin’.”

A minute later the hooves of other horses thundered into view: scrawny little Mr. Dempster spurring his pony so hard its flanks were streaked with foam, and stout, breathless Mrs. Mountain riding Madam Esmond’s grey mare, her riding habit all askew from her wild gallop. They shoved through the crowd of gawking servants, bolted across the porch where the bleary redcoat officers sat staring in confusion, and burst down the steps into the garden where Washington still paced opposite the two Warrington boys.

Before George could even demand what on earth she was doing there, Mrs. Mountain threw her arms around his neck, sobbing. “It’s all a mistake! All my fault! That paper I picked up out of Colonel Washington’s portfolio, the one that said he meant to marry a widow with two children—we all thought it was your mother! But it’s not! It’s young Widow Custis, Martha Custis, the rich one with two little ones. He told your mother that this very morning, before he left the house! She flew into such a temper I thought she’d explode. When Sady came tearing home to fetch the pistols and blabbed the whole duel plan, I told him to fire those guns off to warn everyone, and I galloped after him as fast as my old bones could carry me.”

George huffed that he had half a mind to give Sady a sound thrashing for blabbing his private plans, but Harry grabbed his arm, crying that he thanked God the boy had run his mouth. Before George could protest further, Harry went bounding over the cabbage rows straight towards Washington, his boots crunching through the loose garden soil, and poured out the whole artless, foolish tale of misplaced jealousy and misunderstood private correspondence.

Washington hauled the boy straight into a tight, warm hug, his usually steady voice cracking with relief. “Thank God,” he said, again and again. “Thank God this bloodshed is spared us.” Harry blurted out that he wished he could ride off to the frontier campaign with him and Braddock, and Washington squeezed both his hands hard in a firm grasp of friendship that would never loosen.

Then he stepped forward to young George Warrington, and held out his hand. “I owe you an apology, sir,” George said, stiff but sincere. “I acted under a terrible misapprehension, and behaved very ill to you because of it.”

“The fault was mine,” Washington replied gravely. “I chose to keep a private secret locked away that needed no one else’s eyes on it. All this pain, all this risk, could have been avoided if I had not been foolish enough to leave my personal papers where other folks might read them without my leave. I will say no more, lest my temper get the better of me again. Take a true friend’s advice, George: do not be so quick to think ill of the people around you. Save your powder, and your will to fight, for the King’s enemies on the frontier, not your countrymen.”

He gave the gaping, half-sober redcoat officers a stately formal bow, turned, and walked to his waiting horse, mounted, and rode off down the road to join Braddock’s expedition, leaving the whole relieved, dishevelled party staring after him, the spectre of completely unnecessary bloodshed banished before it could ever draw a drop.

The parting between the two Warrington brothers is long over: George has settled into his place as part of General Braddock’s personal staff, and Harry has drifted back to Castlewood to see to the estate he was left to tend alone. But his heart rides with the army, and none of his old familiar pastimes at home hold an ounce of joy.
