He will not admit to a soul how deep his disappointment burns, that he was left behind under the quiet, suddenly melancholy roof now that George is gone. He passes his brother’s empty bedroom with his face turned away, takes George’s usual seat at the head of the dinner table, and sighs before he takes a sip from the chipped silver tankard the two boys had carved their initials into as children.

Madam Esmond Warrington calls out the toast to the King with ringing, unshakable stoutness every single day. On Sundays, when Harry leads the household in the service and reaches the line of prayer for all travellers by land and by water, her response of *“We beseech Thee to hear us”* rings out with a weight of solemnity that makes the old footmen hovering in the back hall pause mid-step. She talks of George constantly, but always cheerfully, as if his safe return is a certainty no one could ever question. She marches straight into his vacant room every morning, head held high, no sign of tremor on her face, and sees that his books, linen, and scattered papers are all tended with perfect care. She speaks of him with a special, reverent softness, and constantly reminds the old servants over meals of what they must do “when Mr. George comes home.”

Mrs. Mountain is on the edge of tears the second George’s name is spoken, and Harry’s face settles into a tight, haggard grimace whenever the conversation turns to the camp—though he will never confess to the sharp, cold fear coiled in his chest. His mother, by contrast, is always calm, still. She fumbles at piquet and backgammon far more than her usual sharp self would ever allow, and the servants find her already wide awake and fully dressed, walking the halls by candlelight, no matter how early they rise. She has asked old Mr. Dempster, their long-time Scottish tutor, to come back and take up residence full time at Castlewood. No longer sharp or haughty as her old stubborn temper once made her, she speaks to everyone gently, never presses a point harshly, and spends hours recounting stories of her own father’s old military campaigns, how he came home from every battle with no wound worse than a gash across the sword arm—so she trusts and hopes her eldest son will do just the same.

George sends letters home to his brother as often as he can, and once the army sets out on its march, he scribbles a rough, smudge-stained journal on scrap paper that he forwards at every possible chance. Harry devours every line, reading it over and over until he nearly knows it by heart, and reads whole sections aloud in family gatherings as the long summer evenings stretch out: Madam sits perfectly upright at the tea table (no Esmond would ever stoop to lean against the back of a chair), little Fanny Mountain bends over her sampler, Mr. Dempster and Mrs. Mountain linger over their card game, and the old, quiet servants drift near the parlour door in the gloaming, listening to every word of the young master’s adventures. The yellowed pages, covered in George’s slanted, slim handwriting, are handled so carefully you could almost believe the two boys are still there, alive in that fire-lit room—though now their portraits hang, faint and faded, in tarnished gold frames, as if they had never walked the earth at all. But we can almost hear Harry’s warm, eager voice as he reads:
> “It must be said the provinces are treating King George II’s service shamefully, and his Excellency the General is in a proper fury. Virginia is bad enough, and Maryland little better, but Pennsylvania is the worst of all. We begged them to send word they would supply our troops coming over to fight the French, and promised they would sustain the men once they arrived. Now they not only break that promise and make barely any provision for their defenders, but their people charge absurd, exorbitant prices for cattle and stores, and cheat the very soldiers who have come to fight their battles. No wonder the General swears so fiercely, and the men are sullen. Delays have stretched on for weeks and months, while the French have fortified every fort on our frontier unimpeded.
> “Though I will never admit I love Colonel Washington, your favourite (and I swear I am not jealous, Hal), you cannot deny he is a brave man and a fine officer. The General’s whole staff respects him, and he asks his opinion on every matter. He is almost the only man among us who has seen Indians in full war paint, and I own he was right to fire on Monsieur Jumonville last year.
> “That silly quarrel at Benson’s Tavern never came to a duel, rest assured. Captain Waring came into camp eager to pick it up again, bearing a challenge from Captain Grace, and your hot-headed friend here was ready to take it up, and asked Colonel Wingfield, one of the General’s aides, to be my second. But when Wingfield heard the whole story: that the fight started because Grace was drunk, and Waring was tipsy, and the two 44th Regiment men chose to insult a militia officer for no reason at all, he swore he would never let Colonel Washington meet them on the field. He threatened to bring the whole matter straight to his Excellency, who would court martial both captains for brawling, drunkenness, and indecent conduct. The two men were forced to sheathe their swords and swallow their wrath. When sober they were good-natured enough, and they ate their humble pie over a reconciliation dinner hosted by Colonel Washington, who was as calm and proper as any prince could ever be. Hang him, he has no faults at all—that’s why I still dislike him. When he marries that widow, what a dreary life she will lead!”

“I wonder at the taste of some men, and the effrontery of some women,” Madam Esmond says, setting her teacup down sharply. “I wonder at any woman who has been married once, forgetting herself so far as to marry again! Don’t you, Mountain?”
“Monstrous,” Mrs. Mountain agrees, with a quiet, knowing little smirk.
Mr. Dempster keeps his eyes fixed intently on his glass of spiced punch. Harry looks as if he is half choking on suppressed laughter, or some other secret, unnameable feeling. But his mother taps his arm gently. “Go on, Harry. Continue your brother’s journal. He writes well, but ah, will he ever write half so fine as my papa?”

Harry resumes reading.
> “We keep the strictest order in camp here. The rules against drunkenness and disorderly behaviour are severe. Every company’s roll is called at morning, noon, and night, and the officers submit a list of absent or unruly men to their regimental commander, who ensures they are properly punished. The drummers are almost constantly at work. Oh Harry, it made me sick to my stomach the first time I saw the lash cut across a strong, white soldier’s back, and heard the poor man’s piteous scream.”

“Horrid!” Madam cries. “I think I would have murdered my old schoolmaster Ward if he had ever flogged me. Thank Heaven he only got as far as cracking my knuckles with a ruler! The men are well looked after, I see—but I wish the officers were held to the same standard. The local Indians just broke up their camp and left in a huff, because the young officers were forever drinking with the squaws and… and… well, I will not write the rest of that here.”

Harry pauses, clearly not wanting to read that last part out loud in front of prim little Fanny, still bent over her sampler.
“Skip that part about those odious tipsy creatures,” Madam says, and Harry lifts his voice to a bright, more respectable tone.
> “Every regiment holds full Divine Service at the head of its colours every Sunday. The General does everything mortal man can to stop plundering, and encourage local farmers to bring their provisions to our market. He has declared any soldier who dares molest a market woman or interrupt trade will be shot. He has even ordered the price of provisions raised a penny a pound, and lent money out of his own private purse to buy supplies for the camp. He is a strange, contradictory man, this General Braddock. He flogs his men without mercy, but he gives away his own coin without stint. He swears the most tremendous oaths at dinner, and tells stories that Mountain would be shocked to hear after the third glass of punch—but he never misses a single service. He adores the great Duke of Cumberland, and has his name on his lips constantly. Our two regiments both served in Scotland, so I dare say Mr. Dempster knew the colour of their uniform facings.”

“Aye, we saw the tails of their coats as they ran, as well as their facings,” the old Jacobite tutor growls, a dry little smile tugging at his mouth.
> “Colonel Washington has been laid low with a very sharp fever, and has barely been well enough to keep pace with the march. Ought he not to go home and be nursed by that widow of his? When either of us is laid up, we are almost as good friends as we ever were. But I still feel foolish for hating him all those months. Good powers, Harry, I was in such a fury at that tavern we could have fired a few shots off at each other and cleared the air completely! Even if I don’t love him the way you do, I know he is a good soldier, a good officer, and a brave, honest man. At any rate, I shall never dislike him just for refusing to be our stepfather.”

“A stepfather, indeed!” Madam cries out, half laughing and half indignant. “Jealousy and prejudice have quite turned that poor boy’s head! Does he suppose the Marquis of Esmond’s own daughter and heiress could not find far grander men to be stepfathers for her sons than a mere provincial surveyor? If there are any more of those foolish allusions in George’s journal, skip them Harry, my dear. We have heard quite enough about that silly old quarrel already.”

“‘Tis a pretty sight,” Harry continues, “to see the long line of redcoats winding through the pine forests, or forming up camp after a day’s march. We take every possible precaution against surprise, so no prowling Indian can creep up on us unawares. Our advanced sentries and allied native scouts have fallen in with enemy raiding parties more than once, and taken a scalp or two from them first. Those French and their painted allies are such cruel villains that we do not think of showing them any mercy. Only yesterday we found a little boy, scalped but still alive, in an empty lone cottage, where his parents had been murdered and dragged off by the savages. The General was so furious at the cruelty he has offered a reward of five pounds for every Indian scalp brought into camp.
> “When the day’s march ends, you ought to see our camp, laid out with such perfect care. The baggage, the General’s tents, and his guard are placed right in the very centre. We have outlying sentries posted in pairs, in groups of three, groups of ten, and whole companies strung out for miles. At the first sign of an attack, they are ordered to fall back on the main body and rally around the tents and baggage, which are stacked and arranged to form a strong makeshift fortification. Sady my servant and I are marching on foot now, you must know. The Pennsylvanians sent such rickety, useless horses into camp that they dropped dead almost immediately. Any good horses left were ordered to be turned over to the supply train, so Roxana now carries two heavy packs on her back instead of her young master. She still knows me, of course, whinnies the second she sees me, and I walk beside her, chattering about Castlewood all the way down the trail.
> *July 4.* To guard against surprise, every man in the column has been warned to pay strict attention to the drum beats: halt immediately at the long roll, and advance to the beat of the long march. We are all far more alert to the enemy now. Our advanced pickets are doubled, and two sentries stand at every post. The men on the front picket lines stay under arms, bayonets fixed, all through the night, and are relieved every two hours. The men who come off duty lie down right beside their muskets, and are never allowed to leave their posts. It is very clear we are drawing near to the enemy at last. This packet goes out with the General’s dispatches to Colonel Dunbar’s camp, thirty miles behind us, and will be carried from there to Frederick, and then all the way home to Castlewood, to my honoured mother, to whom I send my dutiful respect, and all kindest remembrances to every friend there. I need not say how much love I send to my dearest brother, from his affectionate

The whole of Virginia lay parched and scorched under the blazing July sun. For ten long days, no news had come back from the column advancing on the Ohio. Their march, slow and toilsome though it was through the tangled forest, was bound to meet the enemy soon. The troops, led by experienced, capable officers, were now accustomed to the wilderness, and no one feared an ambush. Every precaution had been taken. The talk in every small town, every gentleman’s plantation, and every rough roadside tavern across the province was that the French forces would never dare make a stand. Braddock’s two veteran regiments from Britain, plus their Virginian and Pennsylvania allies, were more than a match for any force the French could bring down from Montreal. Madam Esmond swore she would buy George the finest thoroughbred in all Virginia or the Carolinas to replace his beloved Roxana. It was only for the King’s service that no one would part with their good horses for any price, of course.

Though everyone at Castlewood pretended to be cheerful at their meals, never speaking of anything but a certain, triumphant end to the campaign, none of them could rest easy. They rode from neighbour’s house to neighbour’s house constantly, chasing every scrap of news that drifted through the province. The plantation negroes, riding cross-country at midnight to visit friends or sweethearts, spread gossip faster than any post rider could. For three weeks after the army marched out, every report was bright and hopeful. But on July 10, a vast, sudden gloom settled over the whole province. A look of terror and doubt fell on every face. The fiddles fell silent in the slave quarters, the singing and laughter of the usually cheerful black families went quiet. Horsemen crowded every roadside tavern, drinking, yelling, brawling over the bars, all bearing the same terrible story: the army had been ambushed. Cut to pieces almost to a man. All the officers were picked off by hidden French and Indian marksmen. The General had been wounded, carried off the field in his silk sash, and now the word came that Braddock was dead, scalped by a French-allied warrior.

Mrs. Mountain gave a sharp, piercing scream the second Gumbo brought the news back from across the James River, and little Fanny ran crying to her mother’s arms. “Lord God Almighty, watch over us, and defend my boy!” Madam Esmond gasped, sinking straight down on her knees, her rigid hands lifted up to heaven. Harry was as pale as his mother’s fine linen tablecloth. He and old Dempster armed themselves, mounted their horses, and set off north that very hour, with two trusted mounted servants riding behind them. Every mile they travelled along the rough, newly hewn road the expedition had cut through the forest, the terrible scale of the disaster grew clearer. Fugitives from the fatal battle of July 9 had poured into Dunbar’s camp fifty miles back from the field. Every straggler they stopped told the same tale: a thousand men were dead. Two thirds of all the officers were killed. Every last one of Braddock’s aides-de-camp had been hit. Harry’s heart ached so sharp he could barely breathe, recalling every childhood memory he and George shared, every secret vow they had made as boys to ride to war side by side. Wounded men looked up at him and wept at the grief written on his face. Rough backwoodsmen clapped him on the shoulder with tears in their eyes, and even the gruff old Scottish tutor could barely look at him for the tears in his own eyes, grieving far more for the heartbroken boy riding north to find his brother than for the rest of the fallen men.

Every step Harry Warrington took north toward Pennsylvania brought with it grimmer, more confirmed accounts of the British disaster that had shattered the colony’s hopes. The two celebrated veteran regiments, hardened by campaigns across Scotland and continental Europe, had broken and fled before an enemy most of them had barely glimpsed, all their parade-ground discipline and vaunted valour useless against a band of Indigenous raiders and a handful of French regulars dug into the brush. The ill-fated General Braddock had fought with reckless, unbreakable courage: four horses were shot out from under him, he sustained two wounds before the final mortal blow that ended his life three days after the rout.

A dozen different passersby recounted the slaughter to Harry as he rode: the fording of the Monongahela, the long, snaking line of redcoats winding through unbroken wilderness, the first crack of unseen musket fire ahead, the gunnery teams screaming as they scrambled to unlimber cannon to clear the path, then the murderous, unceasing fusillade pouring from every oak thicket and rhododendron patch that cut down at least half the expedition before most men had laid eyes on their attackers.

Then the rumor reached him: one of the General’s Virginian aides-de-camp lay feverish, wracked by exhaustion, at Colonel Dunbar’s fallback camp. It might be his brother George, the man said. Harry spurred his horse until the miles blurred beneath its hooves, and stumbled at last into the tent where the sick officer lay. It was not George. It was George Washington. The young colonel admitted that the pain of seeing Harry arrive empty of news of his brother cut sharper than his fever ever had.

Washington dared not tell Harry the whole truth at first. For three days after the battle he had never left Braddock’s side. On that fatal 9th of July, he had sent George forward with a written order for the vanguard, and the young volunteer had never returned. After Braddock drew his last breath, Washington had ridden back alone to the killing ground, searching for his missing friend. The bodies left unretrieved had all been stripped, hideously mutilated by looting raiders. He had buried one under a cairn of stones that he had believed was George’s, and the anguish of that search was what had laid him low.

“Ah! If you had truly loved him, you would have brought him back, dead or alive!” Harry cried, half-maddened by grief. Nothing would satisfy him but that he too must walk the battlefield. He paid two seasoned frontiersmen to guide him, forded the river where Braddock’s column had crossed, and tramped the full length of that cursed stretch of wilderness. No enemy lingered there now, but scavenger birds gorged on the mangled, festering remains scattered under the trees. Save for the peaceful, soft-smiling face of his grandfather laid out in the great hall of Castlewood years before, Harry had never seen death. The horrific spectacle made him turn away, retching, his whole frame shaking with loathing and dread. The empty woods could give him no answer. He tried to persuade his guides to fly a white flag and accompany him to the distant French fort where the victorious enemy had retreated, but they refused flat. The French might honour a truce, they told him, but their Indigenous allies would not. “Keep your scalp for your mother, young gentleman,” the lead guide said. “She has already lost one son to this campaign, no need for her to lose another.”

When Harry stumbled back to Dunbar’s encampment, the fever took him in full force. He raved in delirium for days, his old loyal servant Dempster tending him through every crisis, fully convinced the widow Esmond would lose both her boys before the week was out. But Harry rallied at last, weak as a newborn lamb, and Washington and Dempster both escorted him home to Castlewood.

A servant had ridden ahead to announce their arrival. Mrs. Mountain the housekeeper ran out first, smothering Harry in tears and embraces, barely sparing Colonel Washington a nod of recognition, until her little daughter Fanny crept up behind the young officer with her hands behind her back, and piped up unthinking: “Why have you not brought George back too?” Luckily, the press of Mrs. Mountain’s sobbing hugs and endearments kept Harry from hearing the cruel question.

Dempster was welcomed warmly by the two ladies, but when Harry insisted that Washington, who had nursed him through his fever and ridden hundreds of miles to bring him home, stay for rest and refreshment, Mrs. Mountain pulled him aside to whisper that Madam Esmond had fled the parlour the second she heard who was accompanying her son, swearing she could not bear to look upon Mr. Washington’s face. Harry was stunned—Washington was almost a member of their household, had been like an elder brother to George for years. He ran up the stairs, past the door he had been deliberately avoiding, the door to George’s bedchamber, when his mother burst out of that very room and folded him to her chest, pulling him inside. Every object in the chamber was exactly as George had left it: his book of psalms laid open on the bedcover, his half-written letter to Harry on the desk, his scuffed riding boots propped by the empty fireplace.

“My poor child, how thin you are, how haggard!” she cooed. “Never mind, a mother’s care will make you well again. You were nobly brave to go searching for your brother through all that danger and sickness. If others had been half as faithful as you, George would be here now. But he is not dead— I know he is not. Two nights running, I saw my own father in a dream, and he told me my boy is a prisoner among the western nations. He will come back to us.” Harry noted, bewildered, that his mother was praising her eldest son more tenderly than he had ever heard her speak of him when George was home under her roof.

But when he begged her to come downstairs and welcome Washington, who had risked his own frail convalescence to escort Harry home, her excitement hardened into sharp, cold anger. She swore she would never touch that man’s hand. He had promised her he would guard George with his own life, and George was gone, while Washington had returned entirely unharmed.

“He gave me his own bed when I was at my sickest, mother,” Harry protested, confused. “He was still half delirious with fever himself, and he thought only of me. How can you blame him for George’s loss?”

A friend? A pretty friend! she sneered. Of all Braddock’s aides, he was the only one to come back without a scratch on him. The brave and noble die, and he walks away home safe.

She did descend the stairs at last, leaning on Harry’s far-too-weak arm, and swept into the parlour where Washington sat with a frigid, ceremonious curtsey. She let one of her small hands rest in his for barely a heartbeat, told him she grieved their meeting had to take place in such unhappy circumstances, thanked him for seeing Harry home, then made it abundantly clear Castlewood was no place for him in her current state of distress. She bade him carry her compliments to his own mother, and to the young widow Martha Custis and her children, then swept away up the stairs again, leaving the colonel standing dumbfounded in the parlour. He mounted his horse and rode off before the hour was out.

A heavy, brooding gloom settled over Castlewood after that. Madam Esmond refused to order formal mourning for George, swearing she would not tempt fate by acting as if he was dead when her father’s dream had promised his return, but every corner of the great plantation house felt draped in shadow. A fortnight after the defeat, George’s personal servant Sady stumbled back to the estate, maimed by a musket ball through the leg, and hid in the slave quarters for days too terrified to face his mistress, for he had no news of his master beyond the moment he saw George ride forward toward the enemy lines on the morning of the battle, and never come back. The neighbours whispered Madam Esmond laboured under a dangerous delusion, but her certainty was so fierce that even Harry and the rest of the household half found themselves believing it. She swore that the honour of the Esmond family would not suffer a man who had broken his sacred promise to protect her son to ever set foot on her land again. She laughed at pleas that Washington’s coat and hat had been riddled with bullet holes: “I could step into my study this instant, take my father’s old duelling pistols, and fire two shots straight through my finest paduasoy gown, and walk away unharmed. That is no proof of any real danger he faced.”

Harry, torn between gratitude to Washington and love for his mother, suffered endlessly. He would sneak out to meet his old friend at county court, horse races, or the taverns of the nearest small town, and every time Madam Esmond found out she flew into a rage, calling him ungrateful, willing to forget his perfect, noble brother for a tall, gawky, fox-hunting colonel who swore too much. The constant strife ate at Harry’s health, and he fell ill over and over again with recurrent fevers no local Peruvian bark could fully cure. The colony’s physicians finally ordered a long sea voyage, to get him far away from the oppressive grief and tension hanging over Castlewood. Madam Esmond at first planned to sail with him, but the two quarrelled sharply over Washington, over George, and it was settled Harry would travel to England alone. He boarded a ship at the James River, landed at Bristol, and only put on his full black mourning suit for his brother exactly one year to the day of Braddock’s defeat, the 9th of July, just as he and his mother had agreed.

He told this whole long, sad story to his newly found English relative, old Madame de Bernstein, hanging his head in shame, and admitted that for all Castlewood’s wealth and comfort, all his mother’s love, he had been glad to run away just to breathe freely. After Harry left, Madam Esmond abandoned the old plantation to an overseer, moved to the fast-growing new town of Richmond, held card assemblies and entertained every prominent preacher in the colony, and set up her small, imperious little court there, leaving the great empty house of Castlewood behind her. We leave her there for a time, while Harry travels across England, chasing his own fortune, and still carrying a faint, stubborn flicker of hope that one day, word would arrive that George had come home at last.

When the wandering Trojan hero Aeneas spun his tales of shipwreck and peril to Queen Dido of Carthage, the old fable tells us the queen hung on every word: so enchanted by his eloquent recounting of misadventure that the ensuing romance left her far more heartbroken than any of the hero’s many escapes had ever done. She rued the day she ever let that smooth-spoken, dangerous refugee cross her threshold, after all.

Harry Warrington had none of pious Aeneas’s silver tongue, and his elderly great-aunt, Madam Bernstein, was hardly the soft, sentimental Carthaginian princess. Even so, the young Virginian’s unvarnished, artless tales of his life across the Atlantic, told in his warm, earnest voice, worked their own quiet magic. More than once as he spoke, Madam Bernstein felt her old, hard heart soften in a way it had not allowed itself to for decades. Hers was a life long desert of loneliness, you see—there had been so few oases, so few cool, sweet resting places in all those years, until this bright, friendly lad’s voice filled her rooms, and woke a strange, tender ache of affection and sympathy she had forgotten she was capable of feeling.

She doted on him, clung to this new, unaccustomed sense of care for another human being. Save for a faint, brief flicker of soft feeling in her very earliest girlhood, she had never loved anyone in all her long life. A woman of her sharp, observant nature watched every flutter of her own pulse, of course, and would smile to herself after he left, when she marked how her normally steady heartbeat had quickened just at his nearness. She found herself blushing with foolish, unlooked-for pleasure when he stepped into the room. Her eyes lit up to greet him, and followed his every movement with quiet fondness. Ah, if only she had had a son just like him! How she would have cherished him!

“Wait,” a dark, mocking voice whispered inside her, “wait, Beatrix Esmond! You know you will tire of this fancy, just as you have tired of every other. When this passing infatuation fades, the boy could waste away and die, and you would not shed a tear for him. He could prattle on about his plantations and his hounds, and you would soon grow weary of his stories. Your fate is to be lonely—lonely forever.” Well? Even if life is a desert, there are shade trees by the trail, and springs of cool water to drink. Why not rest here, and enjoy this day? We all know we will have to strike camp at dawn tomorrow, and trudge onward along the path destiny has laid for us.

She smiled to herself as he talked, recognizing little familiar traits in his accounts of his mother that bore the stamp of old Esmond family blood. Madam Esmond was fiercely jealous? Harry admitted as much, with a sheepish grin. She was very fond of Colonel Washington? Harry insisted she only thought of him as a dear friend, no more—he had heard his mother swear that a hundred times over. He even blushed to own that he, fool that he had been, had once been absurdly jealous of the Colonel himself.

“Well, mark my words, my dear,” Madam Beatrix laughed, “my half-sister will never forgive that man for living. And do not look so surprised, sir, that women take a fancy to younger men—after all, do I not dote on you? You can be sure all the rest of the Castlewood household is positively bursting with jealousy over you.”

For all their hidden resentment of Madam de Bernstein’s new favourite, the rest of the Castlewood family never let a hint of ill will show in their words or behaviour to their young kinsman. After just two days staying in the old ancestral stone house, Harry Warrington was “Cousin Harry” to everyone, from the smallest child to the grey-haired elders. The Countess of Castlewood was especially gracious to him whenever Madam Bernstein was in the room, and seized every private opportunity to gush to the Baroness about what a charming young “Huron” they had as a guest, marvelling aloud at the elegance of his manners, and asking how on earth a boy raised in a far-off American wilderness could ever have learned to be so perfectly polite.

The Baroness took all these seemingly admiring comments in perfect good humour, and here the chronicler must pause a moment to note with great admiration the incomparable skill ladies display with one another: the things they say, the things they carefully do not say, the things they whisper behind each other’s backs. How they smile and curtsey while stabbing one another! How they heap compliments on each other while they seethe with hatred! How they bear every petty slight with endless, unflappable long-suffering, never once giving the satisfaction of being openly offended! With what deft, innocent ease they can slip a single drop of poison into a conversation, then hand the brimming goblet around to the rest of the family with a smile, leaving the entire domestic circle miserable without anyone ever being able to point a finger at who did it.

The two great ladies smiled at each other across their drawing room a hundred years ago now, it is easy to picture, pressing cold cheeks together and calling each other “my dear”, “my dearest creature”, “my dear Countess”, “my dear Baroness”, even “my dear sister” while both were fully ready to tear each other’s throats out the second the other turned their back.

“You wonder that the boy is so well-bred?” Madam de Bernstein replied, cool as a cucumber. “His mother was raised by two of the most perfect gentlefolk the Esmond line ever produced. Colonel Esmond carried a grave, stately courtesy and a grandeur of bearing you will not find among the gentlemen of the present day, I assure you.”

“Ah, my dear, we all praise the days we grew up in!” the Countess trilled back. “My own grandmother used to swear there was no court to compare with Whitehall under King Charles the Second.”

“My mother was only at King James the Second’s court for a little while,” the Baroness said, “and you know she was not raised a court lady at all—her father was a simple country parson. But she was still exquisitely well-bred. Her second husband, Colonel Esmond, was a man who had travelled all over Europe, was learned to boot, and moved in the very finest society the continent had to offer. They could not very well leave all their good manners behind when they retreated to their country home in Virginia, now could they? Our Harry inherited those graces naturally.”

“Nay, my dear, you are far too partial to your half-sister,” Lady Castlewood simpered. “She could never have been that perfect, not when she turned cold on her own daughter, as you yourself have admitted. No woman with a truly good heart could ever be that unkind. Manners are all very well, of course, and for a parson’s daughter, your mamma was very decent. I know plenty of clergymen who are perfectly pleasant—our chaplain Mr Sampson, Dr Young, Mr Dodd, all very nice fellows, but none of them have that true air of high birth, do they? For a complete woman, you see, you must have what I have, thank heaven: a warm, feeling heart. Without affection, all the world is nothing but vanity. I protest I do not live, eat, drink or sleep for anything but my own sweet children! My wicked, wild Willy, my wilful little Fanny, my naughty darlings!” She pressed two miniature bracelets to her lips, each holding a tiny portrait of the two children, then called to the two shivering Italian greyhounds that were napping on the rug, who bounded up into her lap and lapped at her painted hands, careful not to smudge the thick layer of rouge on her cheeks. “Nothing do I thank heaven for more than my great sensibility and tender heart, even though it gives me agonies of distress on a daily basis! I would die if any harm came to my dears, or to you, my dear Baroness!”

“You are famous far and wide for your tender heart, Anna,” Madam Bernstein said dryly. “Do share a little of that great sensibility with our young Virginian cousin, won’t you?”

“Nay, I am only a guest here at Castlewood,” the Countess laughed back. “This house belongs to my lord, not me, and I cannot do more for the boy than we already have. He is perfectly delightful, of course! We are not jealous of him, are we, even if it is so obvious how wildly fond the Baroness has grown of him? My own children could almost be mortified, the way he has won everyone’s favour in a handful of days when it took them years to feel half as welcome, but are they angry? Not at all! Willy has already taken him out hunting and riding every morning. This very morning, I passed the music room and saw Fanny teaching him to dance the minuet, while Maria played for them on the harpsichord. It was such a pretty, tender little scene, it brought tears to my eyes!”

But Madam Bernstein had heard the real story of that scene, from her lady’s maid who had been lingering by the door. Here is what actually happened: Lady Castlewood had walked into the music room with her son Willy, who was still caked in mud from the kennels, and clapped her hands loudly, gushing “Bravi! How perfectly charming!” while she beamed her very best smile on Harry, and shot a sharp, significant look at her daughter Fanny that made the girl freeze. Fanny knew exactly what that look meant, and Maria, who was pounding away at the harpsichord, caught it too, and started playing twice as fast, her curls flying as she nodded over the keys.

“Damned little Choctaw!” Willy had grumbled, glowering at Harry. “Is he teaching Fanny a war dance? Is she going to make a fool of herself over him now?” That was exactly what his mother’s look had said, too.

Fanny dropped Harry’s hand mid-step and curtsied so low she almost fell over, while Harry blushed so bright red he could have put the Countess’s finest carmine cosmetics to shame. Maria rose from the harpsichord and made to leave the room.

“Nay, do not stop on my account!” the Countess trilled, seating herself at the instrument. “Let me play for you, go right on dancing!”

“I don’t know how to dance, ma’am,” Harry mumbled, hanging his head.

“Fanny was teaching you? Go right on, dearest Fanny, finish your lesson!”

“Go on,” Willy growled from the corner, half sneering.

“I—I would rather not make a fool of myself in company,” Harry recovered himself, grinning. “When I can dance a minuet properly, I promise you I will ask cousin Fanny to walk one with me.”

“That will be very soon, I am sure, dear Cousin Warrington,” the Countess said, all honeyed sweetness. “What scheme is she hatching now?” Willy thought to himself, for he never could quite figure out what his mother was up to. She called Fanny over to her side, and they left the room together.

No sooner were they out in the tapestry-hung corridor than the Countess’s soft, smiling mask dropped entirely away. “You little fool!” she hissed, pinching Fanny’s arm hard enough to leave black and blue bruises. “You absolute idiot! What do you think you are doing with that wild Huron? You do not want to marry a creature like that, and go be a squaw living in a log cabin in the middle of a swamp!”

“Mamma, stop!” Fanny whimpered, trying to pull her arm away. “You yourself said he was very nice!”

“Nice, yes! Heir to a few thousand acres of swamp, a handful of negro slaves, a rickety log cabin, and a barn full of tobacco leaves! My Lady Frances Esmond, have you forgotten your rank, your name, who your mother is, that three days after meeting this boy from Virginia you are out there dancing cozily with him like you are a tavern girl?”

“But he is our cousin!” Fanny protested.

“Nobody knows where he came from! How can we even be sure he is related to us? He could be a valet who stole his master’s luggage and ran off in his post-chaise for all we know.”

“But Madame de Bernstein says he is our cousin, and he looks exactly like the old portraits of the Esmond family!”

“Madame de Bernstein picks up new favourites one day and throws them away the next! She is besotted with this boy now, but what makes you think she will still care about him a month from now? In public, and when your aunt the Baroness is around, you will be as polite to him as you have to be. But in private? I forbid you to seek him out or encourage him in any way.”

“I don’t care if you forbid me or not!” Fanny cried, stamping her foot, all her patience gone. “Very well then,” her mother snapped back. “I will speak to your father, and we will go straight back to our house in Kensington. If I cannot make you see reason, your brother will.” The rest of their conversation was lost to Madam Bernstein’s eavesdropper.

Madame de Bernstein never told Harry any part of that scene right away. All the young Virginian saw was that his family received him kindly: Lady Castlewood was perfectly gracious, the two young ladies were pleasant, Lord Castlewood, who was cold and haughty to everyone, was no more distant to Harry than he was to his own children, and Willy was happy to ride with him, drink with him, go to the races and play cards with him. When Harry mentioned he might soon take his leave, every single member of the household pressed him to stay longer. He never guessed that the warm welcome he received was part of a dozen hidden schemes, that he had already stepped into the middle of feuds he knew nothing about, or that some of the very people who pressed his hand at breakfast and shared a glass of wine with him at dinner were secretly his enemies. He thought he was loved simply for being their kinsman, fresh from the old Virginia home they had all heard so much about. It never once crossed his mind that he was walking through a den of plotting vipers, all smiling to his face while they calculated how best to use him for their own ends.

The second day after Harry Warrington’s arrival at his family’s English estate dawned soft and sun-dappled, a quiet 18th-century Sunday at Castlewood. The village church, built flush to the castle’s west wing, doubled as the family chapel: a hidden panelled door from the great house led straight to a grand, curtained state pew reserved exclusively for the Esmonds, where the household filed in one by one at the appointed hour, while the rest of the pews below filled with villagers from the surrounding hamlet.

Tattered, dust-caked old battle banners hung from the rafters, and Harry let his imagination wander as he stared up at them, certain they had been borne by his ancestors’ loyal retainers fighting for the Crown in the Commonwealth wars, a cause he knew the Esmond name had been famous for. At the altar rails, the marble effigy of Sir Francis Esmond, the family patriarch from the reign of James I, knelt for all eternity, square-bearded and clad in his carved red gown, his stone hands resting on a marble prayer book beneath his blazoned coat of arms. Even Madame de Bernstein, the late bishop’s widow, never missed a service, her bearing so gravely devout that it nearly matched the eternal piety of the stone ancestor across the chancel.

The parish clergyman, Mr. Sampson, a tall, ruddy, strikingly handsome young man, read the full liturgy in a lively, musical voice, lending dramatic weight to every passage of Scripture he read. One of the younger Esmond girls played the organ, and the music would have run perfectly smoothly if not for a sudden, rich burst of song from the servants’ gallery that sent half the congregation snickering. Harry’s own personal enslaved attendant from Virginia, Gumbo, had recognized the first note of the psalm, and belted out the tune in a voice so loud and honey-sweet that every head in the church turned to stare at the African “warbler” mid-hymn. Even Parson Sampson clapped his handkerchief to his mouth to smother a laugh, while the liveried footmen newly arrived from London gaped so openly they forgot all proper decorum. Delighted by the attention, Gumbo sang on until the clerk’s thin voice was completely drowned out, for he had no idea how to read a single word of the hymnal he was clutching open beside pretty Molly, the porter’s daughter who had been the first to greet Harry and his party when they arrived at Castlewood.

When the singing ended, Sampson climbed into the pulpit to deliver a sermon that Harry thought far too short, even though it ran more than twenty minutes. He did not drag out the stiff, Calvinistic Scripture cadences Harry had grown used to hearing at his mother’s favourite colonial churches; instead he spoke plainly, as one man of the world to a crowd of fellow sinners, recounting a vivid scene he had witnessed only the week before at the Winton Assizes: the hanging of a local horse-stealer. He described the man’s once good name, his loving wife and small children, his desperate agony clinging to his family’s hands in the moments before he was dragged to the gallows. He painted the chase so vividly Harry could almost see the stolen horse galloping across heath and highway, the shadow of Retribution hot on its heels, the law seizing the thief at a country fair, dragging him before the magistrate, and never striking off his irons until they dropped at the foot of the gallows. He mimed leaning into the condemned man’s ear as the cart drew up, then dropped his handkerchief to mime the drop, and Harry jolted back in his pew as if he had felt the noose tighten at his own throat. It felt to Harry like he had only sat down for five minutes, and he would happily have listened for an hour more. The house servants sat goggle-eyed, Gumbo frozen in absolute terror in his gallery seat, but the village yokels in their smock frocks paid no mind at all, tramping out of church chattering about turnip yields and dairy cows as if they had not heard a single word.

Lord Castlewood nodded at Sampson as the clergyman’s wig popped up over the pulpit cushion. “Sampson has been in fine fettle today,” he said. “He smote the Philistines with full force.” “Magnificent!” Harry burst out, still buzzing. “I’ll wager five to four that was his old Assize sermon,” snickered his cousin Will Esmond. “He rode over to Winton not just to preach, but to gawk at those new racing hounds the squire got last month.”

The organ played the congregation out into the bright Sunday sunshine, leaving old Sir Francis Esmond still kneeling on his stone hassock in the empty church. Sampson emerged from the vestry in his cassock, nodded at the group lingering in the family pew, and followed them back through the connecting gallery into the house. Lord Castlewood formally presented him to Harry, the Virginian cousin, and Sampson bowed low, politely asking if Harry was related to Sir Miles Warrington of Norfolk. The man, Harry learned, was his father’s elder brother. “What a pity he has a son,” Sampson joked. “That’s a fine estate, and you look the very picture of a man who’d make a far better baronet than that drunken old sot and his heir.” Harry immediately begged for every scrap of news about his Norfolk relations, while Will at once demanded to hear about the hounds. Sampson laughed, and admitted he had never met two men more fond of their drink than Sir Miles Warrington and his son, the pair of them able to out-drink every man in the county save a handful of their closest sporting friends. From hounds the conversation drifted easily to horses, and Will leaned in eagerly to ask after the upcoming Six Year Old Plate at Huntingdon. “The odds stand five to four on Brilliant against the field,” Sampson said gravely, “but mark my words, Jason – the Duke of Ancaster’s horse, sired by Cartouche out of Miss Langley – is a very strong contender.”

Harry, who had grown up riding and racing thoroughbreds on his family’s Virginia plantations, admitted he ached to see a proper English race. “Do you ever place a small wager on the tracks, Mr. Warrington?” Sampson asked. Harry smiled and admitted he had, from time to time. “I’ll lay you even odds Brilliant takes the whole field, for a pony a side, cousin!” Will shouted, leaning across the table. “I’ll give three to one against Jason, myself,” added Sampson. Harry, stung when Will taunted him that he ought to write home to his mother for permission to bet, bristled at once. “I manage my own affairs without running them past any lady, thank you,” he said. “And for the honour of Old Virginia, I’ll take that bet – both of them. Done and done.”

Will scowled and trundled off to the stables to smoke his pipe with the grooms, while Sampson headed to the drawing room to pay his respects to the ladies, leaving Lord Castlewood and Harry alone in the gallery. The quiet earl, who had been perfectly polite but almost entirely silent since Harry arrived, asked about the size of his Virginian estate. Harry’s pride flared at the hint that Castlewood thought it worthless, and pointed out that his grandfather had never laid formal claim to his share of the Esmond Virginian lands out of choice, not weakness. He then blurted out his honest frustration: the warm, open-handed hospitality of Virginia, where guests were given the very best of everything and welcomed as family, was nothing like the cool, distant politeness of Castlewood, where he was fed well enough but never made to feel like more than a passing stranger. Lord Castlewood laughed and clapped him on the shoulder. “We do not pretend to cry over every visitor that crosses our threshold, that is true,” he said. “But we do not lie about it, either. Just take my warning: my brother William has been on the turf since he was old enough to ride away from Cambridge, and he will cheat you out of every penny you have if you let him play cards or wager against you.” Harry boasted that he could outride, outshoot, outwrestle any man his age, then immediately blushed bright red and apologized for his rude outburst. The earl laughed and took his arm to lead him in to dinner.

Parson Sampson was the life of the Sunday dinner table, regaling the ladies with all the raciest latest gossip from London high society: the latest scandal out of Mayfair’s clubs, Mr. Selwyn’s newest bon mot, the absurd thousand-pound wager Lord March had laid at White’s, the latest royal domestic squabbles, the last man hanged at Tyburn who had died so bravely the crowd had cheered him. His jokes were racy, lively, and entirely unfit for a modern Sunday congregation, but none of the ladies at Castlewood so much as blinked an eye, laughing merrily at every story. When the chapel bell clanged for the short afternoon service, Sampson darted out for half an hour, and was back before the last echo of the bell had faded, yelling for a fresh bottle of Burgundy.

The rest of the Sabbath drifted by lazily around the card tables. Madame de Bernstein was unbeatable at piquet, and only Sampson was skilled enough to give her even a run for her money. The company voted to ignore the warm golden summer evening outside, declaring a hand full of court cards and three honours far more beautiful than any sunset over the park’s elm trees. The chapel clock tolled hour after hour unheeded, the rooks cawed their way home to their nests in the dusk, the moon rose high, and it was nine o’clock before the groom of chambers came in to announce supper was served.

Halfway through the meal, the sharp twang of the postboy’s horn echoed down the village lane. Lord Castlewood took the newssheet that came with his post, smiled, and passed it over to Will. Will scanned the racing results paragraph the earl had marked, and swore so loud all the ladies jumped in their seats. The Six Year Old Plate at Huntingdon, it reported, had been won handily by Jason, leaving Brilliant trailing far behind the rest of the field. Harry’s bets had both come in. Sampson groaned that he owed Harry half the entire income of his clerical living, while Will cursed his bad luck and swore it was the curse of betting on a Sunday. Harry, ever generous, said he would never dream of taking the money from his own cousin, but Will flared up offended, swearing he was no pauper who would welch on a fair wager. The ladies excused themselves to head up to bed soon after, and the rest of the night dissolved into bowl after bowl of spiced punch, the men drinking deep long after the last star had risen high over Castlewood’s rooftops.

Our young Virginian, Harry Warrington, having won a tidy sum from his cousin Will and the household chaplain, was honour-bound to give them fair chance to win their coin back, a course of conduct that would no doubt have made his stern, moralistic mother Madam Esmond clap her hands in horrified disapproval. He fell into far too much gambling for a virtuous young gentleman’s good: beyond the daily games of whist and quadrille that occupied the household directly after their three o’clock dinner, stretching on well until supper, high-stakes matches involving all the gentlemen (my Lord Castlewood included) unfolded long after the ladies had retired to their chambers. Since their frank Sunday conversation, the Earl had grown far more confidential with his young kinsman, betting with him on every idle diversion, and challenging him endlessly to backgammon and piquet. Will and the pious chaplain both loved a little hazard, though they kept their diversion completely hidden from the ladies of the house, who had exacted repeated promises from Will that he would never lead Harry into mischief, nor stray into it himself. So Will swore as many oaths as his mother and aunt could demand, gave his word he would never touch a dice or a card for money—then the moment the rest of the household was asleep, he would slip over to Harry’s rooms with a dice-box and a bottle of rum, to sit up playing until the grey dawn peeked through the casements.

Harry’s glowing descriptions of the Esmond family estate back in Virginia had never been meant as boasting or deception, for the lad was by nature honest and truth-telling. But his life at home had introduced him to every sort of rough, cheerful company: horse-jockeys, tavern loungers, sporting men and gamblers who abounded in the colony. A landed aristocracy whose fields, tobacco plots, and corn rows were tended entirely by enslaved labour had little other amusement to turn to beyond the hunt, the cards table, and the punch bowl. Virginia hospitality knew no bounds: every man’s home was open to his neighbour, and idle young gentry rode from one mansion to the next, finding the same welcome, the same rough plenty, the same jolly diversions at every stop. The Virginian squire might have a barefoot valet and a cobbled saddle, but behind his cracked windows and tumble-down fences there was always corn for the horses, venison and spiced drink aplenty for the master. Harry had slept on straw mattresses, and sat through all-night bouts of claret and punch in chipped bowls until sunrise, when the hounds were called out. He admitted with no little contrition that his own twin brother George was far more sober of temper; that is just how Nature makes men, after all: some love books and tea, and some love Burgundy and a gallop cross-country. None of his new English friends cared for Puritan strictness, nor thought less of Harry for being no milksop. Manners were far looser a hundred years ago, tongues far freer, and things were named and done that we would be shocked to hear spoken of now—ought we not, indeed, thank the Fates for improving our morals so prodigiously and making us so eminently virtuous?

Harry kept a sharp, wary eye on those around him, correctly guessing his cousins were trying to pump him for details of his family’s fortune, and resolved to keep his own counsel. On every game of chance and field sport, he soon proved a match for all three of the gentlemen in his company. Even at billiards, a game his own grandfather had imported one of the very few existing tables in the whole colony of Virginia for, he quickly held his own. Though Will beat him at the first few rounds, Harry soon became too sharp to give away unfair odds, and Will admitted, no little respect, that the American was his equal in most things, and his better in many. He could soon beat the chaplain soundly, and match Will shot for shot at the table—yet somehow, when he played against the ladies, especially one of them, he almost always came off second best. He was unfailingly courteous to every woman he met, that old traditional Virginian politeness that has never left his country. Every soul in the Castlewood household doted on him: the grim housekeeper softened at his greeting, the fat cook met him with blushing, grinning approval, the French and English ladies’ maids giggled and simpered when he passed by, and the pretty porter’s daughter at the lodge always had a warm word for him. Madame de Bernstein watched every bit of this quiet affection, noting every turn of the boy’s behaviour without ever speaking her thoughts.

No one could say exactly how old Lady Maria Esmond was. Peerage directories were far rarer in those days than in our blessed modern times, and even the sharpest observer could not pin her age down to a few years, let alone a five-year stretch. Will was fond of teasing that she was five and thirty, but he was always prone to wild exaggeration. Maria was Will’s elder half-sister: she and the Earl were children of the late Lord Castlewood’s first wife, a German noblewoman the Earl had married during Queen Anne’s wars, a kinswoman of Baron Bernstein, the Hanoverian nobleman who had wed Beatrix Esmond, Bishop Tusher’s widow. If Lady Maria was born under the reign of George I, and George II had sat on the throne for thirty years, how could she be seven and twenty, as she liked to tell Harry Warrington? “I am old, child,” she would murmur when they were alone. “I am a hundred years old. I am seven and twenty. I might almost be your mother.” Harry would laugh and reply, “Your ladyship might be the mother of all the cupids, I swear it. You do not look a day over twenty, on my honour!”

Lady Maria looked whatever age you chose to see in her. She was a fair beauty, with a dazzling peaches-and-cream complexion, cascading blonde hair that fell over her shoulders, and beautiful round arms that showed to perfect advantage when she leaned across the billiard table to take a shot. Harry would catch a glimpse of a delicate ankle, a patterned clocked stocking, and a tiny black satin slipper with a scarlet heel, a sight that filled him with unutterable rapture and made him swear no woman in the world had so perfect a foot. Foolish Harry! His own mother’s foot was far slimmer, half an inch shorter than Maria’s—but boys never stare at their mamas’ slippers and ankles with that kind of adoration.

Lady Maria would tease him mercilessly in front of her sister, aunt, and stepmother, calling him a simpleton, a raw chit, mimicking the faint Virginian drawl in his speech until he blushed and corrected his intonation. His aunt laughed and declared they would soon polish him into a very fine gentleman.

Lord Castlewood, as we have said, grew daily more friendly and familiar with his young kinsman. There was no hunting to be had until the harvest was brought in, save for occasional cockfights at Winchester and the bull-baiting at Hexton Fair, and Harry and Will rode out to dozens of village fairs and race meets across the countryside. Harry was introduced to all the leading county families: the Henleys of the Grange, the Crawleys of Queen’s Crawley, the Redmaynes of Lionsden, and a dozen more. Neighbours arrived in their heavy, lumbering coaches to spend two or three days in the old country visiting fashion, though far fewer came than would otherwise have done: no one dared risk offending Madame de Bernstein, who loathed rough country company and found all the local gossip tedious. “We shall be far merrier once my aunt leaves us,” the young folks whispered to each other. “We have every cause to be civil to her, you see. She was a great favourite with our father, and got him his earldom back when she was a great power at Court with the King and Queen. She rules the roost here, and we are all afraid of her—even my elder brother stands in awe of her, and my stepmother obeys her far more than she ever obeyed our father, whom she ruled with a rod of iron.” The Earl pressed Harry’s hand warmly after this pretty speech, assured him Castlewood was his home in England, promised to introduce him to London society, present him at Court and at the exclusive White’s club. Harry blushed with pleasure, and kicked himself for that first letter he had sent back to Virginia to Mrs. Mountain and his mother, where he had hinted his welcome at Castlewood had been cold. He wrote a long contrite new dispatch, full of apologies for his hasty judgment, and added in his boyish, not entirely perfect spelling: “My cousin, the Lady Maria, is a perfect Angle.”

Back in Virginia, little Mr. Dempster the tutor read that line and muttered the old Latin verse: Ille praeter omnes angulus ridet — “that corner smiles brighter than all the rest.”
“The child hasn’t gone and fallen in love with his ‘angle’, has he?” cried Mrs. Mountain.
“Pooh, pooh! My niece Maria is forty!” snorted Madam Esmond. “I remember her perfectly when I was a girl at home: a great gawky carroty creature with a foot like a pair of bellows.” Where is truth, indeed, and who can lay hold of it? Is beauty inherent, or do our own eyes paint it for us? Anoint my eyes, good Fairy Puck, so that I may ever see the Beloved Object as a paragon! Above all, anoint my mistress’s eyes with the strongest ointment you have, so that my noddle may ever seem lovely to her, and she may keep strewing fresh roses across my honest ears!

Now Harry was not the only favourite in the household: like master like man, his valet Gumbo was universally admired and adored across the servants’ quarters. Gumbo had a hundred accomplishments. He was a fine fisherman, huntsman, and passable blacksmith. He learned to dress hair beautifully under the Earl’s own Swiss valet, and mastered the art of making all manner of delicious Virginian specialities in the kitchen, while picking up new culinary secrets from the household’s French chef. We have already heard how he sang exquisitely in church; but he sang far more than just hymns, making up his own folk airs and verses after the custom of his people, and played the fiddle so charmingly that he set every lass in the Castlewood hall dancing, and the publican of the village’s Three Castles inn would give him a free mug of ale any day if he only brought his fiddle along. He was good-natured, and loved to play for the village children, so Harry’s negro valet was a universal favourite across the whole Castlewood estate.

The servants’ hall was not long in discovering that Gumbo was a shameless liar, a fact that stood plainly in spite of all his good qualities. They had seen him pretend to read the psalm on Sunday from Molly’s prayer book, when he was singing entirely different words from those printed on the page, not a single letter of which he could decipher. When the Swiss valet teasingly handed him a sheet of written music, he had flipped it completely upside down. These little tall tales cropped up every day for all to see, yet no one thought the worse of him for the habit, and they believed far more of what he said than they had any right to, simply because they enjoyed hearing his stories too much.

Gumbo did not gawk or gape openly at the splendour of Castlewood when he first arrived, but examined the park, the stables, the fine appointments with a cool, critical eye. The horses were very well, he allowed, but back at the Virginia Castlewood they had six times as many, and fourteen or eighteen grooms to tend them all. Madam Esmond’s carriages were far finer than the Earl’s, covered in far more gilding on the panels. Her gardens stretched for acres, and grew every fruit and flower under the sun. Pineapples? Peaches? They were so common in his country that they fed them to the pigs. There were twenty or forty gardeners, not white men, all black gentlemen just like himself. Inside the house there were twenty or forty liveried gentlemen servants, besides the maids—he could never keep count of how many maids there were, tinkers he thought there might be fifty, all Madam Esmond’s property, each worth hundreds of pieces of eight. A piece of eight was bigger than a guinea, he told them. Madam Esmond pulled in twenty to thirty thousand guineas a year, had whole rooms full of gold plate. She owned dozens of ships that Gumbo could not even count, and estates covered in tobacco and enslaved people, stretching a week’s ride across the tidewater. And of course, now that Master George had been killed and scalped by Indians, Master Harry was heir to every penny. Gumbo swore he had fought off a dozen Indians himself trying to save Master George, but he was Master Harry’s boy through and through. Harry’s trunks at Bristol were stuffed full of gold lace, fine clothes, jewels. He could have sixty servants if he wanted, but he chose to travel with only one, and that one, naturally, was Gumbo.

This story was not invented all at once, but grew bit by bit, and by the time Gumbo had told it three or four times in the butler’s pantry, it was perfectly consistent, no contradictions left, and he could recount exactly how many enslaved people Madam Esmond owned, and the exact sum of her annual income. It was all perfectly believable, too—any Virginian plantation of Madam Esmond’s standing would have swarmed with far more enslaved workers than any English country house had servants, since four enslaved people did no more work than one white English labourer.

Gumbo’s tale of his mistress’s vast wealth and splendour was passed up the household chain, from the Earl’s valet to the Earl, from the ladies’ maids to their mistresses, getting more and more exaggerated at every retelling. No young gentleman in England is ever less liked for being reputed heir to a vast fortune, and when Lady Castlewood heard of Harry’s stupendous expectations, she regretted her first cold welcome, and even regretted pinching her daughter Fanny’s arm black and blue for being too friendly to the boy. Was it too late to win him over? Fanny was welcome to try, and she resumed their dancing lessons at once, with her mother playing the piano for her with great enthusiasm. But how provoking, that tiresome sentimental Maria kept insinuating herself into the room, trailing after Fanny every single time she walked out in the park. As for Madame de Bernstein, she laughed at all the tales of the vast Virginian fortune, highly amused. She knew Madam Esmond’s London lawyer, and very likely had a good idea of what the true state of her finances was, but she never contradicted the rumours, and was greatly diverted watching the whole household fawn over their young kinsman.

“Hang him! Is he really that rich, Molly?” the Earl said to his elder sister. “Then we can kiss goodbye to any chance of my aunt’s fortune. The Baroness will leave every penny to him just to spite us, because he doesn’t even need it. Though the lad is a good enough sort, it’s not his fault he’s rich, after all.”

“He is very simple and modest in his habits for a man so wealthy,” Maria remarked softly.

“Rich people often are,” the Earl laughed. “If I were rich, I think I’d turn into the greatest miser alive, live in rags and eat nothing but crusts. There’s no pleasure so enduring as making money, it grows on you as you get older. But since I’m as poor as Lazarus, I dress in purple and fine linen, and fare sumptuously every day.”

Maria went straight to the book room and pulled out R. B. Gent’s *History of Virginia*, read all about the mild, perfect climate, the fertile land growing every sort of crop, the great Potomac and Rappahannock rivers teeming with fish. She wondered if the climate would agree with her, if Madam Esmond would like her. Harry laughed when the household brought up Gumbo’s wildest tales, and said the boy was a great romancer, just boasting for the honour of the family. His humble denials only confirmed everyone’s belief that his fortune was even larger than rumoured, that he was far too modest to brag of his own vast wealth. His plain, simple travelling setup, only one servant, no private horses or carriage, was taken as further proof of how very wealthy he was—such humility only belonged to men who had no need to show off their fortune, they murmured. The chaplain Mr. Sampson, ever the obsequious soul, swore he would be so proud to show his young friend all the ropes of London life, warn off all the sharpers and rogues, keep him safe from all harm. Harry loved the respect that was paid to him, and as Madam Esmond’s son, thought it no more than his due. The whole Castlewood household, then the village, then the whole county, chose to imagine Harry Warrington was heir to an immense fortune and a gentleman of the highest importance, all because his negro valet had spun a web of tall tales in the servants’ hall.

After a few weeks, Madame de Bernstein grew tired of Castlewood and all its inhabitants, as that clever, sharp-witted woman grew tired of most people and places sooner or later. She dozed through the chaplain’s anecdotes, nodded off over her whist games and her dinner, and grew snappish and sarcastic, lashing out at the Earl, Will, and both the Esmond sisters with cutting remarks that made them wince, and bear their irritation as best they could. The cook she had once praised now made no dish that pleased her, the wine was all corked, the house was full of draughts, the doors would not shut, the chimneys all smoked. She declared she needed the Tunbridge spa waters for her health, and ordered the doctor from nearby Hexton to prescribe them for her.

“I wish to heaven she’d go!” the Earl growled, the only independent member of his family. “She can go to Tunbridge, or Bath, or Jericho for all I care.”

“Shall Fanny and I come with you to Tunbridge, dear Baroness?” asked Lady Castlewood.

“Not for worlds, my dear! The doctor has ordered absolute quiet, and if you came the knocker would be going all day long, and Fanny’s lovers would never leave the house,” the Baroness replied, thoroughly tired of Lady Castlewood’s company.

“I wish I could be of some service to my aunt!” the sentimental Lady Maria said demurely.

“My good child, what can you do for me? You cannot play piquet half

Young Harry Warrington’s act of open revolt hit Madame de Bernstein so suddenly that the only response she could muster was the fiery burst of anger we left her in the throes of at the close of the last chapter. As she stormed from the room, she shot two blazing, furious glares at Lady Fanny and her mother, but passed over Lady Maria entirely, who sat bent low over her tambour embroidery frame. Maria scarcely lifted her head to watch her aunt retreat, or to catch the sharp, silent looks the Countess and her daughter exchanged across the parlour.

“So after all our warnings, you dare pursue him, madam?” the Countess’s glare seemed to say.
“Dare what?” Lady Fanny’s wide, confused eyes pleaded back.
Her innocent look did her no good. She was not half so convincing a picture of unknowing purity as Maria, who never moved a stitch. Had Fanny been guilty of encouraging Harry, she would have played the innocent far more artfully, rehearsing and perfecting a demure, unassuming face to suit her alibi long before the moment came. Whatever her eyes claimed, her mother glared at her so fiercely she looked ready to tear the very orbs out of their sockets. But Lady Castlewood had no mind to stage the barbarous eye-gouging from *King Lear* in front of guests; when she did tear her daughter down, she would do it all smiling, with an arm wrapped affectionately around her “dear child’s” waist, and gouge her cruelties out in private.

“So you have no taste for running off to Tunbridge Wells with the old lady, then?” she purred to Cousin Warrington, a perfectly polished, well-bred simper stretched across her face.
“Small blame to the lad, too!” my Lord Castlewood interposed. (The face over the tambour frame flickered upward for a single fleeting instant.) “A young fellow ought not to spend all his days in idling and holiday. Let him mix useful learning with his pleasures, and visit Tunbridge or Bath’s fiddles and pump rooms later on. Mr. Warrington is set to inherit and run a great estate in America: it is only right he sees how our English properties are managed. Will has already shown him the kennels, the stables, and all the popular games of the day—games I must say, cousin, you play nearly as well as your tutors. After harvest, we will take him out for a little English fowling and shooting; come winter, we shall ride out together a-hunting. Though there has been a coolness between our side of the family and our Virginia kinsfolk, we share the same blood. Before we send our cousin back to his mother, let him see what a proper English gentleman’s life at home looks like. I should like to read with him as well as hunt with him, that is why I have been pressing him so hard lately to stay and keep me company.”

My lord spoke with such unfeigned, frank openness that his mother, half-brother, and sister all found themselves staring, wondering what hidden scheme he could possibly be hatching. The three of them often held quiet little conspiracies together, gathering to grumble and plot against the head of the house. When Lord Castlewood adopted that particular frank tone, no one could fathom his designs: more often than not, his true purpose would not come to light for months on end. He did not say “this is the truth,” but rather “this story will be accepted and believed across my household.” And so it became a settled, agreed-upon fiction that my Lord Castlewood felt a laudable urge to nurture family affection, educate, amuse, and improve his young relative, that he had taken a great fancy to the lad, and wished Harry to stay near his estate for months to come.

“What game is Castlewood playing now?” William asked his mother and sister once they had slipped away into the empty corridors. He paused, and snapped his fingers. “By George, I have it!”
“What is it, William?”
“He means to lure him into gambling, and win the Virginia estate right out from under him. That’s the whole of it!”
“But the lad has no actual claim on the Virginia estate right now to pay his losses if he loses,” the Countess pointed out.
“If my brother hasn’t some sly scheme in mind, may I be struck dead—”
“Hush! Of course he has a scheme. But what, exactly?”
“He can’t mean to marry him to Maria. Maria is nearly as old as Harry’s own mother,” William mused.
“Pooh! With her old face, sandy hair, and freckled skin? Impossible!” Lady Fanny exclaimed, heaving a little sigh despite herself.
“Of course your ladyship fancied the Iroquois prince, too!” her mother snapped.
“I trust I know my station and my duty better than that, madam!” Fanny protested. “Even if I did like him, that is no reason I should throw my lot in with him and marry him. Your ladyship has taught me that much a hundred times over.”
“My Lady Fanny!”
“Surely you never loved our papa before you married him! You have told me so a thousand times!”
“And you certainly never fell in love with him afterwards, did you?” William cut in with a laugh. “Fan and I remember all the dreadful rows our honoured parents used to have. Don’t we, Fan? And our brother Esmond was the only one who could keep the peace between them.”
“Don’t drag up those dreadful, vulgar old scenes, William!” his mother cried. “When your father drank too much, he was as mad as a Bedlamite, and his conduct should be a warning to you, sir, who are far too fond of the same horrid habit.”
“I am sure, madam, you were never any happier for marrying a man you did not like, and your ladyship’s title brings barely a penny to it,” Fanny whimpered. “What is the use of a coronet when your jointure is less than a tradesman’s wife? Half the shopkeepers’ wives in town are richer than we are. Only lately a grocer’s widow from London Bridge moved into our Kensington Square, and her daughters have three gowns apiece to my one. Even though they only keep a single man-servant and two maids, I know for a fact they eat and drink a thousand times better than we do, picking at our cold scraps of meat while our great lurching, impudent, lazy footmen loll about doing nothing.”
“Ha! Ha! Thank goodness I dine at the palace, not at home!” William cackled. He owed his little post as Deputy Powder, one of the dozens of tiny court sinecures, to his aunt’s favour with Count Puffendorff, Groom of the Royal (and Serene Electoral) Powder-Closet.
“Why should I not be happy without a title, just as many other people are?” Lady Fanny went on. “I dare say they are even perfectly happy out in America.”
“Happy? With a mother-in-law who is a perfect Turk and Tartar, by all accounts? With Indian war-whoops howling all around you, and the constant risk of losing your scalp, or being eaten by a wild beast every single time you set foot outside to go to church?”
“Then I would not go to church,” Fanny said.
“You’d go with anyone who asked you, Fan!” William roared, “and so would old Maria, and so would any woman, that’s the plain truth!” He laughed loud at his own wit.

“Pray, what is all this merriment about?” Madame de Bernstein asked, peeping in on her relatives from the tapestried door that opened onto the gallery where they had been talking.
William told her his mother and sister had fallen to bickering, which was no novelty to Madame de Bernstein, because Fanny was set on marrying their cousin, the wild “Indian” from the colonies, and the Countess would not hear of it. Fanny protested vehemently against the lie. She said since the very first day her mother had told her not to speak to the young gentleman, she had barely exchanged two words with him. She knew her station far too well to run off to the wilderness to get scalped by savages or eaten by bears.
Madame de Bernstein looked puzzled. “If he is not staying here for you, then who is he staying for? At every house he has been taken to visit, you have all made certain he never meets a woman who is not either a fright or still in the nursery, and I think the boy is far too proud to fall in love with a dairymaid, Will.”
“Humph! That is a matter of taste, ma’am,” William shrugged. “Mr. William Esmond’s taste, maybe—but not that boy’s. The Esmonds raised in his grandfather’s household would never go courting in the kitchen,” she retorted.
“Well, ma’am, every man to his own taste, I say it again. A fellow could go farther and fare worse than my brother’s servants’ hall. Besides Fan, there’s only the maids or old Maria for him to choose from.”
“Maria? Impossible!” The words had barely left her mouth before a sudden sharp thought struck Madame de Bernstein: this aging, quiet Calypso might well have lured her unsuspecting young Telemachus into her web. She recalled half a dozen instances from her own long experience of young men utterly infatuated with far older women. She remembered how often Harry had slipped away unaccountably of late—absences she had always written off as his love of field sports. She remembered how often, when Harry was gone, Maria Esmond had vanished too. Walks down cool, leafy avenues, quiet whispers in garden temples, or behind neatly clipped hedges, casual squeezes of the hand in dim twilight corridors, soft lingering glances stolen on the stairs—her lively fancy, her intimate knowledge of the world, and no small amount of personal romantic history of her own, laid every possible scene out before her, even as she had just declared such a match impossible.

“Impossible, ma’am? I don’t know about that,” William went on. “My mother warned Fan off him, didn’t she?”
“Oh, your mother warned Fanny off, did she?”
“Certainly, my dear Baroness! Didn’t she pinch Fanny’s arm until it was black and blue? Didn’t they fight and scrap about it?”
“Nonsense, William! For shame, William!” both the women caught up in the scandal cried out in unison.
“And now that we have all heard how rich he is, it’s nothing but sour grapes, that’s all. Now that he’s been warned off the young bird, maybe he’s hunting the old one instead. Why impossible? You know old Lady Suffolk, ma’am?”
“William, how dare you speak of Lady Suffolk to your aunt?”
A broad grin spread across the young gentleman’s face. “Only because Lady Suffolk was such a favourite at Court! Well, other ladies have succeeded her, haven’t they?”
“Sir!” Madame de Bernstein cried, looking properly offended.
“So they have, I say! Who else is my Lady Yarmouth now, if not? And didn’t old Lady Suffolk fall madly in love with George Berkeley and marry him when she was well past middle age? Nay, ma’am, if I remember right—and we hear no end of town gossip at our dinner table—Harry Estridge went completely mad for your ladyship when you were barely past twenty, and would have married you a third time if you had only let him.”
