This allusion to a well-known adventure from her own younger days did not anger Madame de Bernstein the way Will’s jabs about court favourites had; instead, it put her in excellent humour. “Au fait,” she murmured, musing as she tapped a neat little hand on the table, no doubt thinking of mad, impulsive Harry Estridge. “It is not impossible, William, for old folks and young folks alike to play the fool.”
“But I still can’t wrap my head around a young fellow being in love with Maria,” William went on, “however he might be smitten with you, ma’am. That’s *autre chose*, as our old French tutor used to say. You remember that Count, ma’am? He! he! Maria remembers him too!”
“William!”
“And I dare say the Count remembers the beating Castlewood had him given, the impudent French dancing-master calling himself a nobleman and daring to fall in love with a daughter of our family! Whenever I want to be particularly annoying to old Maria, I just rattle off a few bits of broken French to her. She knows exactly what I mean.”
“Have you been speaking ill of her to your cousin Harry Warrington?” Madame de Bernstein asked sharply.
“Well, she is always speaking ill of me, isn’t she?” William said defensively. “So I said my piece about her, that’s all.”
“Oh, you absolute idiot!” the old lady cried. “What fool ever speaks ill of a woman to her sweetheart? He will tell her every word, and the pair of them will hate you forever.”
“Exactly the point, ma’am!” William burst out laughing. “I had a little suspicion, you see. Two days ago, when we were out riding together, I told Harry Warrington exactly what I thought of Maria. Why shouldn’t I? She’s always at my throat, isn’t she, Fan? And your favourite cousin turned as red as my plush waistcoat. He stared at me, trembling all over with rage, and said no true Esmond would ever malign his own flesh and blood the way I did.”
“Why did you not chastise him then, sir, as my lord did the dancing-master?” Lady Castlewood demanded.
“Well mother, you see that quarter-staff is a sport that uses two sticks,” William replied. “And it is my firm opinion that Harry Warrington can guard his own head uncommonly well. That is one very good reason I did not offer to cane my cousin. And now you mention it, I know he told Maria every word. She has been looking daggers at me, as if she wants to murder me, ever since. All which shows—” he turned to his aunt, grinning.
“Shows what?”
“That we are well and truly on the right scent. We have tracked down the old fox at last!” The ingenuous young man clapped a hand over his mouth and whooped aloud.

The whole question now was how far this ridiculous little intrigue had already gone. Will said that at her age, Maria would be in no mood to waste time drawing things out—she did not have years to spare to wait for her happy ending. There was no love lost between Will and his half-sister. “Scolding either of them will get us nowhere. Threats only make people twice as stubborn in these sorts of cases. I was only ever in real danger once when I was young,” Madame de Bernstein said, “and that was because my poor mother insisted on contradicting me at every turn. If this boy is anything like the rest of his family, the more we oppose him, the more headstrong and determined he will be. We will never get him out of this scrape that way.”
“Faith, ma’am, why not just leave him in it?” Will grumbled. “Old Maria and I don’t care for each other much, that’s true—but an English earl’s daughter is good enough for an American tobacco planter, at the end of the day.”
His mother and sister both cried out in protest, refusing to hear of such a union. Will laughed back at them: “You are acting like the dog in the manger. You don’t want the man for yourself, Fanny—”
“As if I ever wanted him!” Fanny tossed her head.
“Then why grudge him to Maria? I think Castlewood wants her to have him, anyway.”
“Why grudge him to Maria, sir?” Madame de Bernstein snapped, suddenly fiery with energy. “Do you forget who this poor boy is, and what your entire family owes to his? His grandfather was the dearest, best friend your father ever had. He gave up this estate, this title, this very castle you are all conspiring in, so that you and yours could profit from it. And the reward for all that kindness is that you barely let the child in the door when he knocks, and talk casually of trapping him into marrying a silly elderly creature old enough to be his mother! He shall not marry her.”
“That is exactly what we have been saying all along, my dear Baroness!” Lady Castlewood cut in smoothly. “Our side of the family has no eagerness for such a match, though my lord and Maria may be plotting it between them.”
“You would like him for yourselves, now that you hear he is rich—and may be far richer still, young women, mark my words,” the Baroness said, turning on the two of them.
“Mr. Warrington may be ever so rich, madam,” Lady Castlewood retorted with some spirit, “but there is no need for your ladyship to perpetually remind us all how poor we are. At the very least, there is barely any age gap between Fanny and Mr. Harry. Surely you will not be the one to say that a lady of our name and family is not good enough for any gentleman born in Virginia or anywhere else.”
“Let Fanny marry an English gentleman, Countess, not an American. With her name, my support, and all her good looks and accomplishments, she cannot fail to find a husband worthy of her. But from what I know of the daughters of this house, and what I can guess of our young cousin’s character, no happy match could ever be made between either of you and him.”
“What do you know about me?” Lady Fanny asked, flushing bright red.
“Only your temper, my dear. You do not suppose I believe all the idle tittle-tattle and scandal one cannot help hearing around town? But that temper, and that gilded London upbringing, are enough on their own. Imagine one of you forced to leave St. James’s and the Mall behind, to go and live on a remote plantation surrounded by nothing but wilderness and savages! You would die of ennui within a month, or nag your husband to death with your ill humour. You ladies were born to grace royal courts—not wigwams. Let this lad go back to his wilderness with a wife who is suited to his life there.”
The two other ladies assured her in unison that they wanted nothing better. After a few more trivial words, they took their leave, while Madame de Bernstein pulled the tapestried door closed behind her and retired to her own private chamber.
She saw the whole scheme clearly now. She marvelled at how cleverly the pair had hidden their little romance, recalling a dozen tiny, trivial little incidents that had slipped past her notice, and cursed her own blindness for not seeing the intrigue rising right under her nose over the

The moment Lady Castlewood, her son Will, and daughter Fanny stepped through one saloon door to make their exit, the Earl of Castlewood glided out by the other, leaving only Harry Warrington and Lady Maria alone in the room. The demure eyes that had been fixed so diligently on the tambour frame, pretending to trace every last petal of the innocent violets and jonquils stitched there, lifted at once to find Harry. He stood beneath an ancestral portrait hung over the great stone fireplace, his honest countenance flooded with a blush so deep it spread across his cheeks, his forehead, and even the tips of his youthful ears, as though he had gathered every last bloom of that rare, late-blossoming flower that almost never survives the spring of polite society, and piled them all across his face.

“Why did you refuse to go with our aunt, cousin?” Maria asked.

“Because your ladyship bade me stay,” the lad answered simply.

“La, child! What a fool you are to take idle fun for earnest!” she laughed. “Are all Virginian gentlemen so obsequious that every light word a lady speaks counts as a royal command? Our sex must be worshipped like queens in your Virginia, if that is the case!”

“You said it—two nights ago, when we walked the terrace, O heaven!” Harry’s voice trembled so thick with emotion he could barely get the words out.

“Ah, that sweet night, cousin!” she sighed, feigning soft dreaminess.

“Whe—whe—when you plucked this rose from your own bodice and gave it to me!” Harry burst out, yanking a crumpled, half-dead faded bloom from his waistcoat pocket. “I will never part with it, never, by all that is holy, not as long as this heart beats! You told me then: ‘Harry, if your aunt asks you to go away, you will go, and if you go, you will forget me.’ Did you not say that?”

“All men forget, sooner or later,” the spinster murmured, heaving a melodramatic little sigh.

“Maybe in this cold, selfish old country—but not in ours!” Harry cried, glowing with all the fire of his colonial upbringing. “I almost hated turning that kind old lady down, it went right to my heart to say no to her, when she has been nothing but goodness to me, and it was she who first brought me to meet—to meet—oh heaven!” He gave the spaniel dozing before the fire a sharp kick that sent it yelping, and strode rapidly closer to her tambour frame. “Look here, cousin! If you bade me jump out that yonder window, I’d do it. If you bade me strike down a man, I’d do it.”

“La, there is no need to squeeze my hand so hard, you silly child!” Maria protested, though she did not pull her fingers away.

“I can’t help it! That is how we are in the south. When my heart speaks, my mouth cannot hold its peace—and you know exactly where my heart is! Ever since that night, I have hardly slept a wink. I want to do something great, something to distinguish myself. I wish there were giants like in the storybooks I read as a boy, so I could go and fight them for you. I wish you were in distress, so I could rescue you. I wish you needed my blood, so I could pour every last drop of it out for you. And when you told me not to go away with Madame Bernstein—”

“I never told you that, child!”

“I thought you did! You said I preferred my aunt to my cousin, and I told you then what I say now: incomparable Maria, I prefer you to every woman alive on this earth and every angel in Paradise! I would march straight to the dungeons if you gave the word. And do you think I would ever leave this place when all you wish for is that I stay near you?” He paused, breathless.

“Men always talk that way, or so I have heard,” she corrected herself, tossing her head a little. “A country-bred woman like me has no business knowing the ways of you creatures, after all. They say you are all raptures and flames and grand promises when you are at our sides—but the moment you step over the threshold, you forget every last word.”

“But I never want to go away, not for as long as I live!” Harry groaned. “I have grown tired of all the silly things that used to amuse me as a boy: games, sports, even the soldiering I once ached for so badly I tore my hair in rage when my brother went off on that fatal expedition instead of me. Now there is only one thing I care for in all the world, and you know what that is.”

“You silly child! Do you not realise I am almost old enough to be—”

“I know! I know what they say!” he cut her off. “Some of your family showed me the great family Bible, where every one of your names and all your birth dates are written down.”

“The cowards! Who dared do that?” Lady Maria shrieked, flying into a sudden fury. “Was it that grasping, odious, brazen harpy my stepmother? Do you know how she trapped my father into marrying her when he was deep in his cups, the horrid hussey? The shameless—”

“It was not Lady Castlewood, I promise you,” Harry interposed, bewildered.

“Then it was my aunt, that supposed moralist!” she raged on. “A bishop’s widow, forsooth! I dare say she’d have intrigued with the Pretender, the Hanoverian court, the Court of Rome, and the Sultan of Turkey too if she’d had the means! Do you know who her second husband was? That low creature who—”

“But our aunt never said a single ill word against you,” Harry broke in, more and more amazed at the ferocity of her temper.

She checked herself at once, reading the faint alarm on his innocent, inquisitive face. She did not want him to see her as a shrew. “Well, well, I am a fool,” she said, softening at once. “I only want you to think well of me, Harry.”

Her hand slipped into his of its own accord, and the rapturous youth seized it to press a dozen fervent kisses to it. “Angel!” he cried, gazing into her face with his bright, honest eyes. The old, experienced eyes he looked into glowed warmer than two fish pools lit by starlight, though Harry, for all his fire, never suspected that the calm, shining blue depths he thought held all of heaven were no more than the treacherous surface of a pond, where that silly old fable dog saw his own beef bone reflected, snapped at the water, and lost the very meat he was carrying in his jaws in the first place. What wreckage lies hidden under so many of those quiet, smiling surfaces! What dropped treasures, chased golden goblets, jewels of wasted love, piles of bones and bits of the very sweetest heart’s flesh have sunk there, never to rise again? Beware, ye foolish hounds, how you lap at that water! The mischievous siren nymphs never rest until they have dragged some poor young fellow down under the waves: they sing after him, dance after him, twist their glittering limbs around him, whisper soft secrets in his ear, kiss his feet, leer at him from the rushes, calling “Come, sweet youth! Hither, rosy Hylas!” And pop goes Hylas, pulled under forever. The siren no more remembers him than a Brighton fisherman remembers one individual herring out of a hundred thousand he hauls in his net.

Old Ulysses and his weathered crew would not have cared a fig even if a whole shoal of sirens were singing on the bank, combing their long false hair. But young Telemachus—our Harry Warrington—was ready to leap overboard at once. The song he hears is not stale to him, the voice that sings it is not cracked or out of tune. You and I, brother boatswain, who first heard Mozart’s *Cosi fan tutti* when we were young, may laugh now at how trite the whole old story is—but for the boy standing here, all is new, all is magic.

Any soul with half a penny’s worth of sense or personal experience would know exactly what comes next. The lad pulls out his crumpled dead rose, kisses it a dozen times, and treasures it as the most precious relic on earth. No need to trace every last tedious little step of how that rose came to his waistcoat: the way Maria happened to meet him on the garden path at dawn, the way they whispered behind the old curtain, the way she went to read to sick old Goody Jenkins in the village and let Harry carry her basket of calves’ foot jelly. Love stories are all the same, after all, as old as the lanes that generations of lovers have walked up and down before us. They will play out the same for Miss Fanny with her doll, for the governess, for the baby bawling for his bottle, as they did for Harry and Maria.

Maria had no mind to quarrel with her aunt or let Harry run off and forget her, after all. Harry was not yet the master of his Virginian estates, only the heir apparent, and who knew what might happen? His lordship her brother and she had never spoken a single word about their little scheme—but they understood each other perfectly, no words needed. The Earl knew his sister’s tricks, her faults, every twist of her character, after a lifetime of living under the same roof. He had been quietly nudging Harry to spend all his days riding the estate farms, visiting the sick tenants, sitting in his justice court, keeping him safely occupied and rooted at Castlewood, no chance to run off with the Baroness Bernstein.

Three days later, Harry sat down to write a letter back home:
> MY DEAR MOUNTAIN—At first I did not like Castlewood, nor my cousins here, very much. But now I am used to their ways, and we understand each other much better. Give my duty to my mother, and tell her I hope, given her ladyship’s great kindness to me, Madam Esmond will be reconciled to her half-sister the Baroness de Bernstein. The Baroness, you know, was my Grandmamma’s daughter by her first husband Lord Castlewood… She first married the Reverend Mr. Tusher, a learned and good man who was such a favourite of the King that he was made Bishop. When he died, the King kept his friendship for my aunt, who then married a Hanoverian nobleman at Court who left her very rich. My cousin the Earl of Castlewood told me all this, and I have found nothing but the greatest kindness and affection from them all.
> The Dowager Countess and my cousins Will and Lady Fanny are just as we described them in my last letter that went by the Falmouth packet on the 20th ult. Will and I are very good friends. We have ridden out together many a time, and had some famous cocking matches at Hampton and Winton. He is a sharp blade, but I think I showed him that we Virginians know a trick or two. Reverend Mr. Sampson, the family chaplain, is a most excellent preacher, with no bigotry at all.
> The kindness of my cousin the Earl grows every day, and I hope by next year’s ship my mother will send his lordship some of our best roll tobacco for his tenants, and some fine hams. He is most charitable to the poor, and his sister Lady Maria is every bit as good. She sits for hours reading good books to the sick, and is much beloved in the village. There is a very sick old woman there, Gammer Jenkins, who Madam Esmond would like very much, a most religious good soul. Lady Maria visits her constantly to read to her, which she says gives the old woman great comfort. Though her Ladyship has the sweetest voice, both when speaking and singing (she plays the church organ and sings there most beautifully), I do not think Gammer Jenkins can hear a word of it, for she is very deaf in her great old age. But her memory is perfectly sharp, and she remembers my honoured Grandmother Rachel, Lady Castlewood, living here. She says my grandmother was the best woman in all the world, gave her a cow on her wedding day, and cured her husband Gaffer Jenkins of the terrible winter colds he used to suffer from. I suppose that was with the pills and drops my mother packed in my boxes when I left Virginia. I have not been ill once since arriving, so I never used them, though Gumbo has made great use of them, eating and drinking far too much in the servants’ hall. Gammer Jenkins says the next best soul after my grandmother is Lady Maria, who remembers my grandfather and grandmother when they lived here as children. Their portrait hangs in the very rooms I am staying in, rooms Lord Castlewood says will one day be mine.
> Give my best love and duty to my honoured mother, my respects to Mr. Dempster, a kiss to little Fanny, and my kind remembrances to Old Gumbo, Nathan, Old and Young Dinah, the pointer dog and Slut, and all our friends.
> From your well-wisher,
> P.S. I have written to my Uncle Warrington in Norfolk to give him my respects, but have had no answer yet.

Harry handed the precious manuscript to Maria to read when he was done. “Nonsense!” she laughed, “Why do you flatter me so, cousin?”

“You are beloved in the village, and far outside it too,” Harry said, with a soft, knowing emphasis. “And I have flattered you a little more still, just a little further on.”

“I hope the spelling is all right, cousin?” he asked, when she had finished reading.
“’Tis good enough spelling for any person of fashion,” she answered, not caring to be questioned too closely on her own orthography.
“I know I spelled the word ‘angel’ wrong in my last letter to my mamma,” he said. “But I have learned how to spell it perfectly correctly now.”
“And how is that, sir?” she asked, smiling.
“By looking at you, cousin.” He bowed low before her, his face flooding with that familiar, warm blush, as if he laid a whole bouquet of the finest summer roses at her feet with the gesture.

When the household gathered for their next meal, not a trace of yesterday’s frayed temper lingered on Madame de Bernstein’s face. She was soft, cordial, and gracious to every soul at the table, Harry Warrington included. She lavished praise on the cook that night, declared the rabbit fricassee was perfectly seasoned, and swore no eels in all of England could compare to the plump, tender ones pulled from Castlewood’s own moats. She waved off protests that the wine might be corked, refusing to hear of opening a fresh bottle “for a useless old woman like me,” and when the new vintage was brought round, she raised her glass in toast to Madam Esmond Warrington of far-off Virginia, before leaning across to wink at Harry: “I do hope your mama gave you leave to bring home a proper English wife when you sail back, my dear.”

Had he no memory of his grandmother? Her own beloved mother, of course! The Baroness soon had the whole table laughing at her string of lively anecdotes, recounting her mother’s legendary beauty and gentle goodness, her long blissful marriage to Colonel Esmond despite the great gap in their ages. Everyone for miles round had celebrated the couple’s tender attachment, she said—what did disparity in years or station matter to true love, after all? Lady Castlewood and her two children sat quiet, listening, while Harry hung on every word and Maria blinked in quiet surprise. Lord Castlewood, for his part, turned over the sudden shift in his aunt’s mood in his head, wondering what scheme or whim had sparked this unprecedented display of amiability, but never let a flicker of doubt cross his composed, perfectly satisfied face.

The Baroness’s good humour soon infected the whole room. Not a soul at table escaped a kind word from her. When the sweet, unworldly Will blurted out how shocked and pleased he was to see her so cheerful, she laughed outright. “Complimentary, my dear? Of course I am! I am making amends for being shockingly rude to every single one of you this morning. When I was a little girl of seven, back when my own mother and father lived here at Castlewood, I had exactly the same habit. If I’d been cross and naughty all day, I’d coax and pout and charm them into forgiving me by supper time. Why, this very room, this very table—hundreds and hundreds of years ago, it feels!—I sat right here begging my father, my mother, and your grandfather, Harry, to pardon my tantrums. We had collared eels for supper that night, just as we do now. That’s what brought the memory back! I was as wayward then as I am peevish at seventy today, and so I confess my sins here, and ask you all to forgive me, like a good little girl.”

“I absolve your ladyship!” the household chaplain cried, raising his glass.

“Ah, but you don’t know how abominably cross I was,” she laughed. “I scolded my sister Castlewood. I snapped at her children. I even boxed Harry Warrington’s ears—all because the poor boy would not agree to ride with me to Tunbridge Wells!”

“And I will ride with you now, madam!” Harry burst out at once. “Nothing would give me greater pleasure.”

“There, chaplain, you see how dutiful they all are?” she smiled. “I was the only ill-tempered creature in the house. It was cruel of me to treat you all so. Maria, my dear, I beg your pardon, too.”

“Madam, you have never done me any wrong,” Maria said, bewildered by such a humble plea.

“But I have, a great wrong, child!” the Baroness insisted. “I was so bored with my own bad mood that I told you your company would only weary me. You offered to come to Tunbridge with me, and I turned you away rudely. But it will not weary me now! It was so kind of you to offer. I beg, pray, entreat, nay command you to come along.”

Lord Castlewood sipped his wine, looking utterly unconcerned. So that was the end game of this little performance, he thought. “Anything that brings my aunt pleasure will make me happy too,” Maria said, forcing her face bright with joy.

“You shall stay with me as my guest, my dear, and I promise to keep in a good humour the whole while,” Madame de Bernstein went on. Turning to Lord Castlewood, she added, “You will lend me your sister for the trip, won’t you?”

“Lady Maria Esmond is of full age to make her own choices in such matters,” he replied, with a polite bow. “If any of our household can be of service to you, madam, you have but to command us.” The unspoken subtext was clear enough: plague take the old witch, she is stealing Maria away to separate her from this young Virginian heir.

“Tunbridge Wells will be perfectly delightful!” Maria sighed.

Harry traced idle patterns on the oak table with his finger. All the lovely, secret delights he had been daydreaming of—long walks, slow rides, endless whispered conversations, hidden sun-dappled shrubberies and quiet summer houses, hours poring over music books together, moonlight trysts and soft sweet words—he had been certain he was to be left all alone with his adored Maria, when the rest of the household scattered! To sit at her feet, to brush his lips against the hem of her gown, all that unutterable rapture was his for the taking? The thought made his head spin. And then the crash came. He knew something would spoil it, poor Harry thought. He knew some mischance would take her away from the quiet time he’d imagined.

“Of course you will ride with us to Tunbridge, nephew Warrington,” the Baroness said, turning to him. “You will keep us safe from highwaymen, won’t you?”

Harry could feel the heat rush up to his cheeks, and prayed no one noticed how flustered he was. He steadied his voice as best he could, and promised he would ride at their side, and they need fear no danger. Danger? He would welcome it. He would strike down a dozen highwaymen single-handed if any dared approach Maria’s coach. He would not even need to speak to her for days—only ride beside her carriage, catch glimpses of her face at the window, press her gloved hand warmly at the inn at night, and lead her out to the carriage step at dawn. They would have two full days on the road to Tunbridge, and he could stay a day or two after that. Even a man condemned to hang at Newgate would count himself lucky for two or three extra days of life, wouldn’t he?

We will not dwell at length on the full foolishness of Harry Warrington’s lovesick state. Some young men fall gently in love, while others are struck by the fever so fierce it nearly kills them, and carry the scars of that first wild passion all the way to old age, even to the grave. It is no kindness to mock a young man raving in the delirium of that fever. Even if he is head over heels for a woman twice his age—have we not all read the tale of the young French gentleman who killed himself out of passion for Mademoiselle Ninon de l’Enclos, only to learn she was his own grandmother? If you are never guilty of playing the ass for love, you may kick and jeer at poor Harry now. But all you good, honest fellow sinners who have been that silly, all long-eared donkeys who have brayed over a cruel beauty’s face, recognise a brother!

“You will stay a day or two at the Wells with us,” Madame de Bernstein continued, “see us settled in our lodgings, and then you can ride back to Castlewood for the partridge shooting, and all the studies you and my lord have planned together.” Harry bowed in quiet acquiescence. A whole week of seeing her, near her—life was not all empty, after all. “There will be plenty of company at the Wells, too, and I shall be happy to introduce you to everyone,” she added graciously.

“Company?” Harry sighed, before he could catch himself. “Oh, I shall not need any other company. I shall be perfectly content just with the two of you ladies.” His cousin Will stared, bewildered at Harry’s odd taste in entertainment.

This was, by unspoken agreement, to be Harry’s last night of his current visit to Castlewood. So cousin Will suggested that he, the chaplain, and Harry gather in Harry’s private quarters after the ladies retired, to settle their outstanding wagers from their previous evenings of play. Harry, who had won a tidy sum off both of them at cards, was happy enough to agree. Once the ladies had gone up to their chambers, and Lord Castlewood had retreated to his own private apartments as was his custom, the three men gathered in Harry’s little parlour, where a steaming bowl of punch—Will’s favourite midnight companion—sat waiting on the table.

But Will’s idea of settling accounts was pulling out two fresh packs of cards, and proposing they play to double Harry’s winnings, or wipe the slate entirely. The chaplain had no more ready cash on hand than Will, for that matter. Harry had no desire to win either of their money. How could he cause pain to the brother of his adored Maria? How could he let any of her kinfolk accuse him of being ungenerous, or grasping? He was happy enough to give them their chance to win it all back, as they asked. He agreed to play until midnight, for any stakes they named. Soon the dice box rattled, and cards were shuffled and dealt, over and over.

Harry was not paying the slightest attention to the cards, of course. His mind was far away, wandering: At this very moment, my beloved is sitting at her dressing table, her golden hair spilling loose under her maid’s gentle fingers. What a lucky maid that is! Now she is on her knees, my sainted angel, saying her prayers to the same Heaven that holds all the angels. Now she has climbed into bed, behind her soft damask curtains. Bless her, bless her forever.

“A pair of natural vingt-et-uns!” Will was roaring across the table. “You doubled us, so you owe me—wait no, hang it, you have the ten, then the queen—so I owe you another twenty, blast it.”

Will spat oaths by the dozen, and the chaplain grumbled and cursed right alongside him, astonished at Harry’s impossible luck. He won because he did not care a farthing for the cards. Fortune, that flighty, coquettish jade, had a habit of fawn over men who gave her no mind, especially when their hearts were fixed on another far fairer nymph. Will and the chaplain kept raising the stakes, certain the wealthy Virginian would go easy on them and let them win all their losses back. But Harry knew better than to fling his luck away. He had played hundreds of games just like this back on his Virginia plantation, many of which he had kept carefully hidden from his straitlaced mother. He played fair, and he expected fair play in return.

“The luck does seem to be sticking with me, cousin,” he said, when Will’s grumbling grew too loud to ignore, “and I’ve no wish to press my advantage too hard. But you must not think I’m fool enough to throw all my winnings away. I’ve got a stack of your promissory notes already. If we keep playing, let’s have the value of your wagers on the table, please, in hard cash or goods that are worth the sum named.”

“Typical rich man,” Will growled. “Never bet without security, always win because you’ve got the money to throw around.”

“Faith, cousin, you’ve been harping on my wealth for weeks now,” Harry laughed. “I’ve got enough for my own wants, and enough to pay every creditor I have.”

“Ah, if only we could all say that!” the chaplain moaned. “How happy we would be, and how happy all our creditors would be! What have I got to wager against our conqueror here? My new clerical gown, Mr. Warrington—will you lay me five pieces against it? If I lose I can just preach in the old stuff. Wait! I’ve got a fine Chrysostom, a copy of Foxe’s Martyrs, Baker’s Chronicle, and a cow and her calf out in the pasture. What do you say to that lot against your twenty pounds?”

“I will wager one of Will’s twenty-pound notes,” Harry said, pulling the scrap of paper out of his pocket. “Or I’ll bet my brown mare against both your notes of hand, if you haven’t the ready cash.”

“I’ll stake my bay hunter against you for fifty pounds!” Will bawled.

Harry took both wagers. Ten minutes later, the bay hunter, the brown mare, the chaplain’s gown and his whole stack of precious books were all his. Will swore so loud the rafters rattled. The chaplain tore his wig off and threw it on the floor, cursing as loud as his pupil. Harry, meanwhile, was perfectly calm, not a bit elated by his run of luck. They had asked him to play, and he had played. He knew he would win. My beloved is sleeping safe in her room, he thought, staring out his window. How could I lose, when she is kind to me? His gaze fixed on the lit casement across the courtyard, the one he knew belonged to Maria. He had already forgotten all about his two unlucky friends, their groans and their ill fortune, before they even crossed the courtyard to their own rooms. Behind that faint flickering lamp, beneath that bright star hanging low over the roof, was all his joy, his whole heart, all his treasure.

While the good old Bishop of Cambray, in that long-popular romance of his, wrote at length of Calypso’s disconsolation when Ulysses set sail for home, I do not recall if he spared a thought for her lady’s maid, left equally desolate when Odysseus’s own gentleman took his leave. The masters and mistresses might cling to one another in the grand saloon, breaking their hearts over last embraces, but the menials would be huddled snivelling in the fore-cabin too, their own hearts just as heavy. When the last bell clanged and Ulysses’s mate bawled “All ashore that’s going ashore!” Calypso and her waiting-woman would both step over the same swaying gangplank, hearts thudding, eyes streaming; both would wave handkerchiefs of very different quality and thread from the quay, as the crew crowded the ship’s bows cheering, and the onlookers on shore huzzaed the departing voyage. The point to mark here is simple: if Calypso ne pouvait se consoler, Calypso’s maid ne pouvait se consoler non plus. Their grief was of the exact same measure. One would weep in marble halls on her return, the other in the servants’ attic, but their tears were equally salt, equally plentiful.

Harry Warrington did not quit Castlewood alone a victim to love. His body servant Gumbo left the estate equally smitten, his wit, easy good humour, and skills at dancing, cookery, and fiddle-playing having made him the darling of the entire female domestic circle. The male servants might grumble and eye him jealously, but every woman on the place was on his side. In that age, there was none of the cruel prejudice against Black people that would fester in later years; they were not granted full equality, certainly, but they met with general good-natured tolerance, and from women, a far more generous kindness still. Do not women always lean to tenderness for the most marginal among men? They will dote on moral hunchbacks, cherish figurative “negroes” of low wit, and cuddle the dullest, misshapenest souls no one else will suffer. Gumbo was treated as gently as many a white servant far better placed than he, and only the men in the servants’ hall rejoiced to see the young Virginian and his retinue depart.

One can easily picture those last goodbyes: Molly the housemaid slipping out at grey dawn to cull a wistful posy of jasmine and wild roses for Gumbo, Betty the kitchen maid snipping off a thick lock of her chestnut ringlets to trade for a tuft of his woolly hair, even as he spun tales of being the direct descendant of Ashantee kings. Judging by how many of their descendants claim royal blood now, there must have been a vast number of such potent sovereigns scattered across Caffraria, Connaught, and every other land of hereditary bondsmen in old times.

On the morning fixed for Madame de Bernstein’s departure, every servant at Castlewood crowded the passages and doorways: some to catch one last look at her ladyship’s footmen and the irresistible Gumbo, some to bid farewell to her personal maid, and all to waylay the Baroness and her nephew for the parting gratuities that were customary for wealthy guests to distribute far and wide to household staff. Both Harry and his aunt gave liberally to the liveried footmen, the black-ruffled upper servants, and the swarm of maids and scullions. Castlewood had been the Baroness’s childhood home, and as for honest Harry, who had lived free of charge under its roof and won both money and horses from his cousin and the unlucky chaplain, he was naturally open-handed, and felt certain his mother would wish him to be generous to all the Esmond family’s retainers. He scattered gold coins right and left as freely as Gumbo had boasted he could, no one coming near him left empty-handed: from the major-domo down to the boy who blacked boots, from the grim housekeeper in her still-room to the feeble old porter dozing in his lodge, every soul got a token of his remembrance. It is a well-known truth: when a man is in love with one woman in a family, he grows absurdly fond of every single person connected to her. He ingratiates himself with the maids, is extra bland to the butler, lends money to the college son, pats yapping little dogs he would otherwise kick out of the way, laughs at stale old stories that would make him yawn to hear from anyone but his beloved’s father, and even bears the sharp nagging of the cantankerous old maiden aunt with a smile.

For the days past, Harry had been displaying all those artless little marks of affection to the entire Castlewood household, ever since his love for Lady Maria had been declared and returned. He would have happily given cousin Will back all the money he won, and more, too, if the lad had asked for it – but for all that, Harry was sharp, fond of sport and fair play, and a fine judge of a good horse. He had won not just Will’s cash and a stack of Mr Esmond’s valuable old autographs, but also Will’s prized brown hunter, the very animal that had nearly pushed him into the moat on his first night at the estate. He had seen how fast and sure-footed the beast was, and for all his moon-eyed romance over Maria, he could not help being pleased to own such a sound, swift roadster. When he had spent half the night staring at the stars above her window, watching her candle burn low, he had trundled off to his own bedroom daydreaming of how perfect it would be to ride that horse across the island, his beautiful Maria seated pillion behind him, her white arms wrapped tight around his waist. He fell asleep ruminating on those very plans, counting the blessings of the week more he would spend in her company.

Early that morning, poor Chaplain Sampson sent his little black mare over to the house, led by his groom, footman, and gardener, who all wept over the beast’s white nose and kissed it repeatedly before handing it over to Gumbo. The sight of their emotion made both men tearful too: Gumbo snivelled outright, and Harry pressed a couple of guineas into the chaplain’s boy’s hand to comfort him, stunning the poor fellow into instant joy. The two servants led the mare off to the stables, with orders to bring it round alongside Will’s horse after breakfast, when the Baroness’s carriages were due to depart.

Lord Castlewood himself put in an appearance at the morning meal, so eager to see his aunt off that he spared the company his usual sulk. The ladies and the chaplain were all present; the only missing member of the family was Will, who left a badly-spelled note for his cousin explaining he had been called away to Salisbury Races at dawn, but that the horse Harry had won the night before was already set aside, and his own groom Tom would hand it over to Harry’s servant. His absence did not dampen the party’s good humour over tea, and before long the heavy carriages rumbled into the courtyard, the servants piling them high with the Baroness’s vast collection of luggage – vast as it was, it paled next to the overstuffed baggage trains that follow even a modest lady of fashion in our own day.

A large open landau carried the stout Baroness and her niece, two armed menservants perched on the box with loaded pistols and a blunderbuss ready in case of highwaymen. A second carriage held the ladies’ maids and a guard for the trunks, while Harry’s modest valises were stowed under the maids’ care. Gumbo announced he would ride his new mare alongside the carriages for most of the journey.

Lord Castlewood, his stepmother, and Lady Fanny escorted their kinswoman to the carriage steps, bidding her farewell with many dutiful embraces. Then Lady Maria appeared, clad in a riding dress Harry thought was the most beautiful garment ever stitched. A crowd of servants stood about the courtyard calling down blessings on the travellers, and word of the Baroness’s departure had spread through the village, so scores of villagers waited under the trees outside the gates, waving their hats and huzzaing as the ponderous vehicles rolled away.

Gumbo had gone to fetch Harry’s horses, and Lord Castlewood strolled back and forth across the courtyard with his arm tucked through his young guest’s. “Heard you’re taking a couple of our horses away from Castlewood, cousin Harry?” he said.

Harry blushed. “A gentleman can’t refuse a fair game at cards, my lord. I never wanted to play for money, and wouldn’t have, if cousin Will hadn’t forced the matter. As for the chaplain, it went to my heart to win from him – but he was as eager to bet as Will was.”

“I know, I know, no blame attaches to you. When in Rome, you do as the Romans do. And I’m very glad you’ve given Will a lesson. He’s mad for play – would gamble his own coat off his back, and the family has had to settle his debts a dozen times over. How much did you win off him, may I ask?”

“Some eighteen pounds the first two days, a note for a hundred and twenty more, and the brown horse, which we valued at sixty – that comes nigh to two hundred. But it was all fair, you know, I didn’t want to play at all. Will’s no match for me, my lord, that’s the plain truth.”

“He’s a match for most other folks, though,” said my lord. “The brown horse, you said?”

“Yes! Prince William, sired out of Constitution. You don’t think I’d have set sixty pounds against his bay plough-horse, my lord?”

“I didn’t know the breed, that’s all. I saw Will riding out at dawn this morning – I didn’t pay much mind to what horse he was on. And you won the black mare from the parson?”

“Fourteen pounds’ worth. She’ll carry Gumbo perfectly well. Where the devil is that rascal with the horses?” Harry’s mind was already fixed on lovely Maria, and he ached to trot at her side.

“When you get to Tunbridge Wells, cousin Harry, you’d best keep your wits about you. There are sharper players there than Will and the chaplain. All sorts of queer company haunts the Wells.”

“A Virginian learns pretty well how to take care of himself, my lord,” Harry replied, with a knowing nod.

“So it seems! I commend my sister to your care, Harry. She’s no baby in years, but she’s as innocent as one. You’ll see no harm comes to her?”

“I’ll guard her with my very life, my lord!” Harry cried, his heart thrumming with joy.

“You’re a brave lad. By the way, cousin, unless you’re very fond of Castlewood, I wouldn’t hurry back to this drafty, tumble-down old place. I’m off to my other estate for a while, and won’t be back here till partridge shooting season. You stay and see to the ladies, my sister and the Baroness, will you?”

“Indeed I will!” Harry said, glowing.

“I’ll send you word when it’s time to bring my sister back home. Ah, here come the horses now. Have you bid farewell to the Countess and Lady Fanny? They’re kissing their hands to you from the music room balcony.”

Harry ran up to make his goodbyes, cutting the ceremony as short as he could, for he was desperate to be off to his beloved. He came bounding back down the stairs to mount his new prize steed, which Gumbo was holding by the rein while perched atop the chaplain’s little black mare.

There was Gumbo on the black mare, right enough – but the second horse he held was not a brown one. It was a broken-kneed, aged, worn-out bay nag.

“What in the name of hell is this?” Harry cried.

“Your honour’s new horse,” said Will’s groom, touching his cap.

“This brute?” the young gentleman roared, uttering several unprintable oaths common to the age in England and Virginia. “Go and bring me Prince William, the brown horse my cousin Will won off me last night, right now.”

“Mr Will rode Prince William away to Salisbury Races this very morning,” the groom said, unflappable. “His last orders were, ‘Sam, saddle my bay horse Cato for Mr Warrington. He’s Mr Warrington’s horse now, I sold him last night.’ I know your honour’s generous – I hope you’ll remember the groom for his trouble.”

Lord Castlewood burst out laughing at the speech, while Harry fumed and swore all the more.

“Mr Will said he never could bring himself to part with Prince William for less than a hundred and twenty pounds,” the groom added, staring Harry dead in the eye.

Lord Castlewood laughed harder. “Will has got the better of you, Harry Warrington.”

“Got the better of me? Any rascal with loaded dice can throw sixes and get the better of an honest man. This isn’t betting, this is downright –”

“Mr Warrington! Spare me hard words about my brother, if you please. Rest assured I’ll make sure you get your due. Farewell now – ride quick, or the coaches will be at Farnham before you catch up,” he said, waving Harry off and stepping back into the house, unaware that Harry was far too eager to rejoin Maria and the carriages to notice the utter, besotted adoration Gumbo was casting across to a pretty maid lingering in the porter’s lodge doorway.

Once the two young men were gone, the chaplain and Lord Castlewood sat back down to finish their breakfast in peace. The two ladies had already retreated indoors.

“That was one of Will’s confounded rascally tricks,” Lord Castlewood said. “I wouldn’t be surprised if our cousin breaks Will’s head over it, when he catches up with him.”

“He does deserve it,” the chaplain grinned. “Though when we were playing cards last night, no one ever said a word about what colour the horse was. I couldn’t argue the point – I’ve only got the one mare, and the black lad is riding off with her. To do him justice, the young Virginian plays like a man, never caring if he loses.”

“He wins because he doesn’t care about losing, plain and simple. There’s no doubt he’s rolling in wealth. His mother’s law agents are my lawyers too, and they write that her estate is a perfect principality, growing richer year by year.”

“If it were a kingdom, I know exactly who Mr Warrington would make its queen,” the chaplain said, obsequious.

“Who can account for taste, parson?” Lord Castlewood sneered. “We’re all the same. The first woman I fell in love with was forty, and as jealous as a girl of fifteen. It runs in the family – Colonel Esmond, the one in the scarlet coat yonder, married my grandmother, who was old enough to be his mother. If this lad chooses to carry an elderly princess back to Virginia with him, we’ve no call to balk him.”

“‘Twere a consummation devoutly to be wished!” the chaplain cried. “Had I not best travel to Tunbridge Wells myself, my lord, and wait on hand to perform the sacred marriage ceremony for the young couple at a moment’s notice?”

“You shall have a pair of fine new carriage horses if you do,” Lord Castlewood promised. The two men settled back to smoke their post-breakfast pipe of tobacco, perfectly content.

Harry was in such a hurry to join the carriages he nearly forgot to tip his hat to the cheering Castlewood villagers. They all adored the frank, good-natured lad, whose grandfather Colonel Esmond was still remembered locally for his gallantry in Queen Anne’s wars. The village had heard how the young Virginian had out-ridden, out-shot, and out-played Will at everything, and their respect for him was doubled by the wild tales of his enormous fortune that Gumbo had spread across the county. Rumour had it he owned gold mines, diamond mines, endless furs and tobacco fields, enough wealth to make him a prince in his own country. No wonder the honest villagers cheered him so loudly, for there is no land on earth where good fortune is more warmly celebrated than in Britain.

Harry spurred his sorry old nag into a gallop, Gumbo trailing behind him, until he caught sight of the cloud of dust surrounding the Baroness’s chariot. He rode up to the carriage window, and found Lady Maria sitting all alone on the back seat, the Baroness fast dozing on the cushions beside her. She pressed a finger to her lips, warning him not to wake the old woman, and Harry hung back a little behind the wheels, drinking in the sight of her smiles and her bright eyes. The summer landscape was all very well, but it was nothing next to her face; the hedgerow birds sang no half so sweet as her soft, quiet words.

The Baroness’s fat old horses were used to slow, easy paces and frequent stops for feeding, so even on his broken-down nag, Harry had no trouble keeping up with them. At two o’clock they stopped at an inn to bait the horses and eat a two-hour dinner. Harry tipped the landlord so generously the man could not stop bowing, and he spent the entire meal whispering nonsense sweet nothings to Maria, while the Baroness napped peacefully after her roast. They spoke of the crowds of beautiful young people they would meet at Tunbridge Wells, and timid Maria teased Harry that he would soon fall for some pretty young heiress far more worthy of him than her plain self. Harry swore by every god in the pantheon that not even Venus herself could lure him from her side – no, it was he who had to fear, he protested, that the fine young fops of fashion would crowd around her and forget the rough, untravelled American lad who had nothing but a faithful heart to offer her.

Maria laughed, rolled her eyes, and teased him that it was men, not women, who were the faithless, flighty sex – and in his outrage at hearing his whole gender slandered, Harry stretched across the table to grab her hand, knocking over a full glass of wine in the process. Maria gave a little shocked “Oh!” and glanced over to see if the crash had woken the Baroness – but the old woman still slumbered soundly in her armchair, so she let Harry squeeze her fingers tight, while he swore eternal loyalty to her.

When the horses were harnessed again, Harry was standing demurely by the window, pretending to watch the servants load the carriages, when the landlord walked in with the bill. The Baroness woke up smiling, completely unaware of the furtive romance that had unfolded while

Lest any tender-hearted reader lie awake fretting for Mr. Harry Warrington, and fear his broken-kneed horse has carried him clean out of this story and this world, let me set your mind at ease at once: nothing of the sort has come to pass. What sense would there be in killing off our heroes when they have barely outgrown their teens, and we ourselves are not even halfway through the story we set out to tell? We are already in mourning for one of the two Virginians, who met a cruel fate back in the colonies; we could scarce be so cruel as to dispatch the other before he has even set foot to properly explore England.

No, no. Heroes are not hurried off the stage without a very pressing reason. If every gentleman who took a tumble from a horse went straight to his grave, not just our young hero but the author of this chronicle would long ago have been underground. As it is, Harry is only sprawling just outside it, and will be brought fully back to his senses the moment the kind household he was carried to hears their bell ring for the house call.

To prove to you the youngest of the Virginian cousins is well and truly alive, here is an authentic copy of the letter sent to his mother by the good woman whose home he was brought to after his fall from that brute of a broken-kneed mount belonging to Mr. Will:

> At her House at Richmond, in Virginia
>
> If Mrs. Esmond Warrington of Virginia can call her mind back twenty-three years, to the days when Miss Rachel Esmond boarded at Kensington School, she may perhaps remember Miss Molly Benson, her classmate, who has long forgotten every petty quarrel they ever had (in which, I own, Molly was far more often in the wrong) and only holds in memory the generous, high-spirited, lively Miss Esmond, their very own Princess Pocahontas, adored by every girl in the school.
>
> Dear madam! I cannot forget that once you were my dearest Rachel, as I was your dearest Molly. Though we parted on less than friendly terms the day you sailed home to Virginia, you know how close we once were. I still keep the little gold etui your father gave me when he came to our end-of-term speech day at Kensington, the very day we two performed the quarrel scene between Brutus and Cassius out of Shakespeare. Only yesterday morning I dreamed we were both called up to recite our lesson before the formidable Miss Hardwood, that I had forgotten every word of mine, and that, as always, Rachel Esmond outshone me.
> How bright those old days burn in my memory! The very thought of them makes us feel young again. I can still picture our walks in Kensington Gardens, bowing in a row as King George and Queen Caroline strolled past with their entire court trailing behind. I can tell you exactly what we ate for dinner each day of the week, and point out exactly which patch of garden was yours – always far neater and better tended than mine. Your chest of drawers was a model of perfect order, while mine was a shambles. Do you remember how we told stories in the dormitory long after lights out, until the French governess Madame Hibou would creep out of bed and hush us like a hooting owl? Do you recall the poor dancing master who claimed he was waylaid by assassins, though it later turned out he had been beaten by the footmen of your brother, then Viscount Castlewood?
> My dear, your cousin Lady Maria Esmond was just visiting this house, and I was careful never to bring up those old sad days in her hearing, which I now chatter over so freely to you.
> Her ladyship and another of your relatives, the Baroness de Bernstein, have left us now to travel on to Tunbridge Wells. But another, far dearer kinsman of yours remains under my roof, fast asleep in the very chamber next to mine: Mr. Henry Esmond Warrington. Now do you understand why you hear from an old school friend after all these years? Do not be alarmed, dear madam! I know you are leaping to the worst conclusion, thinking your boy is grievously hurt, that is why an old stranger writes. No, my love: Mr. Warrington was unwell yesterday after his fall, but today he is perfectly comfortable. Our doctor, who is no less a person than my own dear husband Colonel Lambert, has bled him gently, set his dislocated shoulder, and swears that in two days more he will be well enough to take the road again.
> I fear my girls and I are secretly sorry he will be well so soon. Yesterday evening, as we sat at our tea, there came a great clanging ring at our gate – a sound so rare in our quiet corner that we all started, for the bell almost never rings save for beggars stopping for alms. The servants ran out, and came back to say a young gentleman who had fallen from his horse lay lifeless on the high road, surrounded by the party he had been travelling with. At that news, my Colonel – the most Samaritan of men alive! – hurried straight out to see what help he could give the fallen traveller, and presently, with the servants' aid, followed by two distraught ladies, carried into our house the palest, most beautiful young man you can imagine. Ah, my dear, how my heart rejoiced that your child found shelter and succour under my roof! That my husband has spared him pain and fever, and will soon restore him to you whole and well! We will be friends again now, will we not?
> I was gravely ill last year, and all feared I would die. Do you know how often I thought of you then, and how we had parted in anger all those years before? I started writing you a foolish little note I never finished, when I was too weak to hold a pen, just to say that if I was called home, I wanted to leave the world in charity with every soul I had ever known.
> Your cousin the Right Honourable Lady Maria Esmond showed the most tender, maternal concern for her young kinsman after his accident; I am sure hers is a very kind heart. The Baroness de Bernstein, being advanced in years, could not be expected to bear the strain quite as keenly as we younger folk, though she was deeply moved and concerned until Mr. Warrington regained consciousness. The moment he woke, however, she declared she was anxious to push on for Tunbridge, and could not abide staying in a house that did not keep a doctor permanently on hand. My Aesculapius laughed and said he would not dream of imposing his services on a lady of quality, though he would answer fully for his young patient's recovery. The Colonel saw no end to such accidents during his years on campaign, and I swear if we called in every physician for twenty miles around, Mr. Warrington could get no better treatment than he is getting now. So, leaving the young gentleman in my care and our daughters', the Baroness and Lady Maria took their leave of us, though the latter went most reluctantly. When he is well enough, my Colonel will ride part of the way with him on his own horses, as far as Westerham, where an old army comrade of his lives. This letter will not go out on the post to Falmouth until your son is fully recovered, by God's grace, so you need never fear for him while he is under the roof of, dear madam,
> Your affectionate humble servant,
>
> *P.S. Thursday.* I was glad to hear from Mr. Warrington's coloured man that Providence has blessed you with such vast wealth, and an heir who will do it every credit. Our own means are comfortable enough, but will be small indeed when divided between all our children. Ah, dear madam! I heard of your sad loss last year. Though the Colonel and I reared five children, we have buried two, and a mother's heart knows exactly what grief you bore. My own heart ached for your boy today, when, in a way that moved me and Mr. Lambert to tears, he spoke of his dear brother. It is impossible to look on your son and not love him. I am so thankful it was our lot to succour him in his trouble, and that when we opened our doors to a stranger, we were giving shelter to the son of my oldest friend.

Nature wrote a letter of credit on the faces of certain men, a note that is honoured almost wherever they go. Harry Warrington's countenance bore that mark from his youth: his eyes were so bright, his cheeks so ruddy and healthy, his whole bearing so frank and open, that almost every soul who met him trusted him – even the rascals who meant to cheat him out of his purse. For all that, as we have already hinted, the lad was by no means the artless, naive stripling he appeared to be. For all his blushing cheeks and easy smile, he was far shrewd, perhaps even warier and wiser in the ways of the world than he would grow to be in later years. A good, generous man who has led an honest life, with no secret shames to plague his conscience, often grows simpler as he ages: he cuts through false arguments far more quickly, hits the mark of truth without endless fuss or overthinking. It may be only a fond old man's delusion, but I swear many of our petty vanities fall away as we grow older, and we grow far fairer in judging both our own faults and our neighbours'.
Young people, for all their bright eyes and unlined faces, are often just as cunning as their elders. What little masters of deceit your frank-faced schoolboys are! How they hoodwink mamma, how they fool papa, how they trick the housekeeper, how they fawn over the older boy they fag for at school! Their conduct towards Dr. Birch for five whole years is one long unbroken string of lies, flattery, and hypocrisy. And their little sisters? Are they any better, only learning their tricks once they are formally presented to society?

You can see from Mrs. Lambert's letter that she, like all good women – and nearly all bad ones for that matter – was a sentimental soul. As she stood by Harry's bed, watching him slumber sweetly after the Colonel set his shoulder, murmuring faint, half-formed words in his sleep, a faint pink flush quivering on his cheek, she owned he was a very beautiful lad indeed, and confessed with a little twinge of guilt that neither of her two boys – Jack at Oxford, and Charles just back to school after the Bartholomewtide holidays – was half so handsome as the Virginian. What a fine figure he cut! And when papa bled him, his arm was as white and delicate as any lady's.
"Yes," she sighed to her husband, "Jack might have been just as handsome, if he had not been marked by smallpox. And as for Charley –"
"Took after his papa, didn't he, my dear Molly?" said the Colonel, glancing at his own plain, honest face in a little wall mirror with a japanned frame, the same glass generations of guests had used to powder their wigs or trim their beards before taking dinner.
"Did I say that, my love?" Mrs. Lambert asked, looking flustered.
"No, but you were thinking it, Mrs. Lambert."
"How can you read my thoughts so, Martin?"
"Because I am a conjurer, and because your thoughts are written all over your face, my dear," he laughed. "Don't fret, our guest won't wake for hours after the draught I gave him. You cannot see a young fellow without comparing him to your own boys. You cannot hear a word about a single gentleman without immediately wondering which of our girls he will fall in love with and marry."
"Don't be foolish, sir," she said, pressing a soft hand over his lips. By this time they had tiptoed out of Harry's bedchamber into the snug wainscoted dressing closet next door, a room that looked out over the gardens, hung with India cotton curtains, stacked with japanned chests and china cabinets, smelling faintly of dried lavender.
"You cannot deny it," the Colonel went on. "The moment you looked at our sleeping guest you thought to yourself: will it be Theo he marries? Or Hester? Or Lucy, who is still away at boarding school?"
"There is no hiding a thing from you, Martin Lambert," she sighed.
"No, because it is written all over your face. What is this strange hunger all you women have to marry off your daughters? We men never want to let them go. For my part, I would not like that young fellow half so much if I thought he intended to carry one of my darlings off to the colonies with him."
"But Martin, I have been so happy myself," she said, gazing up at him with her softest eyes, "that I must wish my girls to have the same good fortune, the same happiness I have known!"
"Then you think good husbands grow on trees, Mrs. Lambert? That you can step out the front door any morning and find one dropped at the gate like a sack of coal?"
"Was it not providential, sir, that this young man should be thrown over his horse's head exactly outside our gate, and turn out to be the son of my oldest school friend?" she insisted. "There is far more than mere accident in such things, you may depend on that, Mr. Lambert!"
"And this was the stranger you saw in the candle flame three nights running, I suppose?"
"And in the fire too, sir! Twice a coal jumped out right next to Theo's feet! You may sneer all you like, but you cannot dismiss such omens. Did I not see you very clearly coming home from Minorca, and dream of you at the exact hour and day you were wounded in Scotland?"
"How many times did I come home unhurt, my dear, when you swore you saw me bleeding to death on the battlefield?" he teased her. "How many times did you imagine me gravely ill when I had not a scratch? You are forever making prophecies, and it would be a very hard thing if you were not right every once in a while. Come, let us leave our guest to sleep in peace, and go downstairs to give the girls their French lesson."
So saying, the honest gentleman tucked his wife's arm under his own, and they descended the broad oak staircase of their old comfortable hall, where the portraits of generations of former Lamberts hung on the walls: worthy magistrates, brave soldiers, and quiet country gentlemen, just like the Colonel we have come to know.

The Colonel was a man of warm, waggish humour. The French lesson he walked his daughters through that afternoon was a scene from Molière's *Tartuffe*, and he teased young Theo mercilessly, calling her "Madam" and bowing to her with exaggerated, mock respect as they read the play. The girls took their turns reading alongside their father, and even for that more modest age their tongues were quick and sharp, and they laughed freely at their father's antics, especially when he read the lines of Orgon, puffing out his chest and declaring to his daughter Mariane that she ought to fall madly in love with their pious houseguest Tartuffe, and marry him at once.
"Did we not read that scene beautifully, Elmire?" the Colonel laughed, turning to his wife. Elmira – that was Mrs. Lambert's given name, though almost no one called her by it – admired her husband's reading enormously, just as she admired almost every single thing Mr. Lambert ever said or did.
O kind reader, can you count on the loyalty of one or two tender, unspoiled hearts? Do you number the love of faithful, unselfish women among the greatest blessings Heaven has granted you? Purify your own heart, and strive to be worthy of that gift. Fall on your knees, and give thanks for that blessing. All the prizes in the world – ambition, wealth, pleasure – are nothing compared to that one. Men chase them, fight for them, grasp them greedily, and almost always find they are empty and worthless. But love seems to survive life, to reach beyond the grave. I think we carry that love with us when we die. Do we not still give it to those who have left us long ago? May we not hope they feel that love for us still, and that when our own time comes, we will leave a little of that love cherished in one or two fond hearts back here on earth?

And where did that little sermon spring from, you ask? The simple truth is that I know this Lambert family far better than you do, who have never heard of them before now. You might take against them, at first meeting, of course. It is only natural to look at a family I praise so highly and think, "What, that is all? The eldest girl is no beauty, the mother is good-natured but plain, the father is perfectly ordinary."
Granted. But can you deny that there is something sweet, something deeply moving, in the sight of an honest man, with a loving, loyal wife at his side, and children who adore him? If you step into such a home, and see the eager kindness on every face turned towards him, that soft glow of easy, unforced affection that radiates from him, can you say it does not touch you? If you stay in that house long enough to join their household prayers at morning and evening, will you not bow your head humbly and add a quiet Amen to their petitions?

On that first night he stayed at Oakhurst, Harry Warrington, still half foggy with the effects of the sleeping draught and a little feverish, thought he heard the familiar notes of his family's evening hymn, and that it was his brother George singing it, back home at Castlewood in Virginia. He smiled, wrapped himself deeper in the soft blankets, and drifted off to a deep, peaceful sleep.

Lulled by soft, lingering, familiar strains of hymnody drifting through his sickroom, young Harry Warrington sank into a honeyed, unbroken slumber free of fevered delirium, and woke only when golden summer sunlight streamed across his bed curtains at dawn. His kind hosts, Colonel and Mrs. Lambert, were already standing beside his bed, smiling down at him. He was ravenous, and the Colonel—who had tended his wound without fee, and proved a far more skilled surgeon than any of the apothecaries peddling their trade in the nearby market town—gave him immediate leave to tuck into a bowl of tender chicken and rice. Mrs. Lambert told him the meal had been prepared entirely by the hands of one of her two daughters.

One of her daughters? A faint, warm, fuzzy memory stirred in Harry’s groggy mind: two red-cheeked girls with dark wavy locks hovering at his bedside the moment he first regained consciousness, slipping away before he could mumble a word of thanks. Then the mortifying recollection hit him, unbidden: the woman he had foolishly doted on only weeks prior, the one whose “pearls” were nothing but paste and whose gilded “golden locks” were mere pinchbeck, and he writhed so sharply Mrs. Lambert leaned over in alarm. He lied smoothly, saying it was only a small twinge in his bandaged shoulder, and stammered out his gratitude for their kindness.

“We are no strangers at all, Mr. Warrington,” Mrs. Lambert laughed. “My husband knew your father long years ago, and I and your own dear mamma were schoolgirls together at Kensington. Your aunt the Baroness Bernstein and your cousin had no need to beg us to take you in when your accident happened. They rode on to Tunbridge Wells last night, and sent a courier all the way from Reigate the day before just to bring us news of how you fared.”

Harry glanced down at his bandaged arm, and the Colonel chuckled, swearing he had worked a fine cure on the gash already, and that now it was the women of the house’s turn to nurse him back to full strength. Mrs. Lambert teased that it was their eldest daughter Theo who’d made the broth, stitched his coat sleeve to fit comfortably around his wounded shoulder, and cut the whole vase of fresh roses sitting on his toilet table that Harry exclaimed over a moment later. The Colonel, amused his wife kept singing Theo’s praises unprompted, nudged her under the side of the bed to prompt a little more discretion, but Harry had already put the pieces together when he asked if the beautiful evening hymn he had half-dreamt he heard the night before had been sung by the girl. The Colonel laughed and teased that their kitchen maids swore Harry’s black valet Gumbo had been singing that same hymn so loud the whole house shook, as if he was a full church organ all by himself. Harry’s voice softened and dropped as he said that all his family at home in Virginia sang that same hymn, that his grandfather had been a close friend of Bishop Ken who had written it, and that his late twin brother had loved it more than any other tune. Mrs. Lambert’s heart ached so much she nearly leaned down to kiss the poor boy’s cheek.

For six weeks straight, Harry had been trapped in the giddy, selfish, corrupt social whirl of London and the Castlewood household, and now, breathing the pure, kind, unpretentious air of the Lamberts’ quiet home, his hard, guarded young heart softened and opened to all this gentle goodwill. He ate his fill, his mood light and brimming with gratitude, and soon the Colonel settled in a chair beside his bed to chat. Harry was usually taciturn, only ever opening up when he spoke of horses, hounds, and the practical work of running a Virginia plantation, but the honest plain-spoken old veteran, who wore a simple fustian coat and a waistcoat with not a scrap of lace on it, put him completely at ease. Harry soon learned that the Colonel’s own father had fought alongside his grandfather, Colonel Esmond, in Queen Anne’s famous wars, that the whole household were longstanding trusted friends of his family.

The Colonel explained that both his sons were away from home: one was studying to enter the church, and the other was in Italy, working as a travel companion and tutor to Lord Wrotham’s son. That meant the only company Harry would have to amuse him while he recovered was Mrs. Lambert and their two daughters, Theo and Hester. He laughed and said he knew his wife overpraised Theo, but the girl was a bright, cheerful, hardworking sixteen, the best little housekeeper he could ever ask for. Then he apologized for unthinkingly bringing up Harry’s dead brother, and said Gumbo had been chattering nonstop to the household staff, boasting that half of Virginia belonged to his master. Harry laughed out loud, and said Gumbo was a terrible liar who thought making his masters sound ten times richer than they were was a point of honour: his family was well-off by colonial standards, but no grand lords, and the man was such a coward he would have run a mile at the first sight of an Indian on the Braddock expedition, not rescued Harry from a whole war party as he had claimed.

The two men soon fell to discussing battles and loyalties, and Harry’s fierce Tory sympathies spilled out unprompted: he swore that if Bonnie Prince Charlie had not turned back at Derby, the king on the throne now would be James the Third, the rightful Stuart heir. The Colonel laughed and advised him, as an old soldier, to keep those opinions quiet, especially around strangers. Even his own wealthy relative Lord Castlewood, and his aunt the Baroness Bernstein, had abandoned their old Stuart loyalties to side with the reigning Hanoverian court, he warned, and servants’ gossip spread far faster than any gentleman realized—Gumbo had already blabbed the whole embarrassing story about Harry buying that broken-kneed horse from his cousin. Harry turned bright red, and swore he would give Gumbo a sound thrashing if he ever dared gossip about his personal affairs ever again.

When Harry was fully dressed, his wounded shoulder supported by a silk ribboned sling, he made his way down the broad oak staircase with the Colonel. The walls of the entrance hall were lined with ancient arms: pikes from Cromwell’s wars, a tattered French guidon taken at the Battle of Malplaquet, a pair of Highland broadswords abandoned on the field of Culloden, and portraits of stern old Parliamentary generals, one of whom was a distant kinsman of the Lamberts. The Colonel joked that his family had been radical Whigs back in those days, riding out to greet William of Orange at Exeter, but that they were all good Church of England folk now, and every last woman in the house was a staunch Tory at heart, as every good woman worth her salt was.

He flung open the parlour door to reveal the two girls waiting by the window. “Here is Miss Hester,” he said, “and this is Miss Theo, the soup-maker, the seamstress, the harpsichord-player, the songstress that lulled you to sleep last night, and the girl who picked those roses you admired so much in your bedroom. Curtsy to our guest, lassies!” Both girls dropped into deep, stately old-fashioned curtseys, the sort the locals called “cheeses”, and Theo blushed so bright the roses in her cheeks outshone the cut flowers in Harry’s vase. She was no simpering fashionable beauty: she had freckled ruddy cheeks, kind soft eyes, dark brown curling hair falling over a round white neck, sturdy red arms bare from the elbow as was the custom for young ladies of the time, no absurd tiny wasp waist, and feet big enough to be seen without a spyglass. But Harry’s heart softened immediately to her sweet, unfeigned shyness.

The Colonel teased his family about their favourite books, naming Rabelais, Fielding, Swift, and Tom Brown, and when Harry admitted he had never heard of any of them, that his book learning had been neglected back on the Virginia plantation where he’d spent all his time with horses and hounds, the Colonel quickly reassured him that honesty and a good heart were far better than any fancy book learning. When Harry said he was dying to go off to fight in the European wars, to see the Prussian king and ride out on campaign, Mrs. Lambert’s face fell soft and sad, and Theo darted a quick, curious, wistful glance at her mother.

It is a foolish fancy of mine, I think, that no matter how quiet and sheltered a young girl is, tucked away in a small country town like Oakhurst, there is a little fairy tale instinct in her heart, waiting for the knight on the white charger to ride up to the castle gate. More often than not, the rider knocking at the door turns out to be nothing more exciting than a postman with a double letter from Northamptonshire, or a costermonger selling panniers of cabbages. First crushes are as common and unremembered as the day you were christened, and no man is ever the very first person his sweetheart ever fancied, no matter how much she swears she is. But there is no mistaking that soft, hopeful little flutter in the air, the very second that young Harry Warrington stepped across the threshold of that quiet parlour on that bright summer morning.

Mrs. Lambert’s soft little daydream had dissolved like frost on a spring windowpane. She and Theo both knew in their quiet hearts that the dashing hero they’d spun out of thin air the day Harry Warrington stumbled wounded through their gate was no grand otherworldly prince—only a flesh-and-blood young mortal, ordinary enough in his ways. They spoke scarcely a word of the disappointment aloud, but as with all people who love one another dearly, each could read the other’s thoughts plain as print. The mother’s way of consoling her daughter was to wrap her in extra soft caresses, her lips brushing Theo’s cheek to whisper, “Never mind, my sweet. Our supposed hero has turned out no great shakes, and none such is half good enough for my Theo. You shall have a real husband ere long, if there’s a worthy one to be found in all England. Why, I was barely fifteen when your father spotted me at the Bury Assembly, and while I was still at boarding school I swore I’d never take any other man. If Heaven saw fit to bless me with the very best husband in the whole kingdom, surely it will smile on my child just as fairly—you deserve a king, if that’s what your heart fancies!”

Indeed, I would not put it past Mrs. Lambert, who kept close track of the young Prince of Wales’s age and all the tales of his handsome, generous nature, to half-expect that the royal heir himself might come cantering past their little gate any day, take a tumble from his horse right on their threshold, be carried inside to be nursed back to health, prevail on his royal grandfather to give Colonel Martin Lambert a full regiment, and promptly fall head over heels in love with her Theo.

The Colonel and his second daughter Hetty, for their part, took the whole affair as a fine joke, laughing at all the silly sentimental match-making going on under their own roof. Mrs. Lambert, you must know, was exceedingly fond of novels, and would cry her eyes out over their tragic pages with the greatest assiduity. No stagecoach ever rumbled past their gate that she did not lean over the half-door, half-expecting a wealthy, titled husband for one of her girls to step down and ring their bell. As for Hetty, her tongue grew saucier than ever, and she dropped a hundred sly, teasing allusions to their unexpected guest. She dragged Prussia and Persia into every conversation with outrageous pertness, asking if the King of Prussia was properly called the Shaw or the Sophy, and how many miles lay between Ispahan and the Saxony border he was currently invading, the campaign that kept her father poring over maps and newspapers late into every evening. She sneaked the *Persian Tales* down from her mother’s book closet and left it slily on the parlour table where the whole family could see. For her own part, she declared, she would never marry a Persian prince: she vastly preferred a gentleman who was limited to one wife at a time.
