She teased Theo unceasingly about “her Virginian gentleman” and “her prince,” and then asked her mother if she would like Hetty to claim their other visitor, Harry’s dark-skinned servant, for her own “black prince.” She rallied both her mother and sister over their romantic fancies until they were cross, at which point she would burst into tears, kiss them both soundly one after the other, and coax them back into good humour.

Simple, open-hearted Harry Warrington never had the faintest inkling of all the jokes, tears, petty quarrels, reconciliations, and secret wedding plans he had unwittingly sparked. A hundred jabs about Shahs and Sophys were shot at him like Parthian arrows, and not one so much as pricked his skin. A Sophy? Very likely he assumed it was a lady’s name, and thought it the height of absurdity that a man with a great bushy black beard would answer to such a title. We step unawares into the midst of quiet families all the time, dropping like a cool, compact stone into a still pond—little do we know the flutter and commotion we stir up, disturbing the fish, scaring the ducks, sending ripples dancing all across the water’s surface. How could Harry guess the effect his sudden arrival had made in this small, sentimental household? He thought well enough of himself on many scores, but he was still shy around women, at that age when young gentlemen need gentle encouragement to come out of their shells, and raised back home in Virginia with very modest, old-fashioned manners towards the other sex. So Hetty’s teasing buzzed around him like summer gnats, and he paid it no more mind than he would have paid a cloud of midges. He was not stupid, as Hetty insisted he was: he was merely simple, far too occupied with his own honest, straightforward affairs to guess at the secret byplay going on around him. Think of all the tragedies, comedies, intrigues, and farces playing out under our very noses in the drawing rooms we visit every week, and we remain entirely blind, self-satisfied, and ignorant of every bit of it. When the two sisters sat of an evening combing out their long flowing ringlets, or whispered to each other in the great shared bed they slept in as was the custom of the day, how could Harry guess he occupied such a large share of their jokes, their laughter, and their quiet thoughts?

Three days after his arrival, his new hospitable hosts took him wandering the wide, green expanse of my Lord Wrotham’s private park, where the Lamberts had permission to roam at will. By the park’s small lake they came upon a flock of swans, which the young ladies were in the habit of feeding with stale bread. As the great white birds glided closer to the shore, Hetty darted a mischievous glance at her mother and sister, then over at her father, who stood by smiling in his bright red waistcoat. “Mamma’s swans are very like these, are they not, papa?”

“What swans, my dear?” her mother asked, confused.

“Not quite so grand, though. They’ve got shorter necks than these, and scores of them are wandering on our village common,” Hetty went on. “I saw Betty plucking one in the kitchen this morning. We shall have it for dinner, with apple sauce and—”

“Don’t be a silly little goose, Hetty,” Theo interrupted, blushing.

“—and sage and onions,” Hetty finished, unperturbed. “Do you care for roast swan, Mr. Warrington?”

“I shot three of them last winter on our river back home in Virginia,” Harry answered easily. “Ours aren’t half such dazzling white birds as these, but they eat very well for all that.”

The poor simple youth had not the slightest clue he was the subject of Hetty’s fable that very minute, that he was the swan being allegorized for his dinner plate. Some very obscure old Latin text I once read tells me that long before Virginia was ever discovered, plenty of other folks were just as slow to catch on to veiled jokes.

That little tender flutter of Theo’s heart, which we have already noted stirred in her breast the first moment she saw Harry stumble to their gate, handsome, pale, and bleeding? It was a premature sentiment, no great grand passion like the one she knew her heart was capable of holding. Like a foolish lark that wakes at false dawn, it had begun to sing long before the sun was up. Hop back to your perch, little trembling creature, tuck your head under your wing! The real day has not yet broken. Roosting is far better than singing for now. By and by the true dawn will come, the whole sky will flush red and gold, and you shall soar up into the light to salute the rising sun with all your music.

You may have noticed, careful reader, that line a few paragraphs back, noting Harry was walking about freely just three days after his arrival. If his shoulder was fully mended, and he could walk with perfect ease, what possible business had him lingering at Oakhurst? Ought he not to have posted straight off to Tunbridge Wells to meet Lady Maria Esmond on the Pantiles, the lady who was waiting for him? His shoulder was healed, his health was fully restored, he did not even own a change of coats, having borrowed all his present clothes from the Colonel. Every duty, every tie of affection, every bond of relationship should have sent him to Tunbridge without delay—for the sake of the gentle lady pining for him there, even for the sake of the washerwoman who had his linen waiting for her to wash. Why did he tarry, unless he was falling in love with one of the two Lambert girls (and I assure you he was not)? Could it possibly be that he did not want to go?

Hath the gracious reader grasped the meaning of the mystic illustration opening our last chapter, of Sinbad the Sailor bowed down under the weight of that hateful Old Man of the Sea clamped around his neck? What if Harry Warrington was Sinbad, and the old man throttling him was his fate? What if for the past two days he had felt those bony knees digging tight into his throat? What if his venomous old aunt the Baroness’s wicked work was fully done, and his once fond love for Lady Maria was as dead as poor fair Rosamond, poisoned by her royal rival? Is Lady Maria lighting the lamp and laying the supper for her Leander at Tunbridge, while Leander sits comfortably by another hearth, never once thinking of swimming across the water to her?

Since that cowardly, sneaking blow was struck to Lady Maria’s reputation by her own kinswoman, all kind hearts must pity her. I know she has her faults, yes—she wears false hair, and no doubt a dozen other little artificial aids to beauty. But a woman in distress, shall we not pity her? A lady of a certain age, are we to laugh at her merely because of the number of years she has seen? Trapped between her tyrannical old aunt and her own foolish delusion, you may be sure Lady Maria Esmond was having no pleasant time of it at Tunbridge Wells. There was no one there to protect her. Madam Beatrix the Baroness had her entirely to herself. Lady Maria was poor, and depended on her aunt for her allowance. The old woman held more than one secret of hers over her head, brandishing it as a threat whenever Lady Maria dared to rebel. For my own part, my heart softens completely when I think of her: picture that antique Andromeda, with all her rich flowing hair falling loose over her shoulders, chained to a rock on Mount Ephraim, delivered over to the dragon that is Baroness Bernstein. Succour, Perseus! Come quickly on your winged feet, with your flashing falchion! But Perseus is not in the least hurry. The dragon feasts on her day after day, unchallenged.

Harry Warrington, who would not have let his half-healed shoulder stop him from going out hunting, lingered day after day at Oakhurst, and every day he liked the kind souls who welcomed him more and more. He could not remember, since his grandfather died, when he had been in such good company. Back home in Virginia his life had been spent amongst fox-hunting squires, whose society he had enjoyed well enough, riding their horses, sharing their punch bowls, living their rough, hearty lives. The ladies he knew from home were no doubt well-bred, decorous, and pious, but they were narrow-minded for all that. His home was a tiny, insular place, full of stiff little pomposities, petty etiquettes, small flatteries, small conversations, and small scandals. He did not realize until long after he left it how confined and narrow his whole life there had been. He was free enough in his movements, to be sure: he had hounds and horses, and could ride and hunt for scores of miles in every direction around his estate. But his mother reigned supreme over the household, and when he was at home he had to breathe the air she dictated.

Here at the Lamberts’ he found himself in a world that was gayer, brighter, and freer than any he had ever known. The man and woman who owned this quiet home had seen the world, even if they chose to live retired from it. From their earliest youth they had enjoyed access not only to good books, but to good company—the living, breathing books that are such pleasant, profitable reading. Society at its best does this much good: it cures you of your conceit, teaches you how small you are, and introduces you to people better than yourself. If you are a young person reading this, take my word for it: nothing is more wholesome than to associate with those who are your superiors. I would never wish my own son Thomas to be first prize boy in every Greek and Latin class, stroke oar on the rowing team, and cock of the school. It would be far better for his body and soul to take a respectable middle rank, to have a fair set of competitors around him, and to get a good sound thrashing now and then, followed by a hearty shake of the hand of the boy who beat him. What honest man who could choose his lot would choose to be a prince, with everyone walking backwards before him, only obsequious courtiers to talk to, no man daring to speak his mind unless your high mightiness gave him permission?

One of the greatest gifts Harry Warrington got from the family Fate had dropped him amongst was the slow realization that he was a profoundly ignorant young man, and there were hundreds of people in the world far better than he had ever imagined possible. A little arrogant around people he considered his equals, in the company of those wiser and better than himself he was docile, generous, and eager to learn. We have already seen how deeply he admired his own brother back home, and his gallant young friend Colonel Washington at Mount Vernon. Towards the gentleman kinsmen at Castlewood he had always felt he was at least their equal. But in Colonel Lambert he found a man who had read books far beyond Harry’s own small knowledge, who had travelled the world and come through its temptations unscathed, the same way he had come through all the battles and dangers he had faced. Kindness and honesty were written plain on the Colonel’s face, and breathed in every word he spoke—qualities our brave young lad had always loved and instinctively trusted.

As for the women of the house, they were the kindest, merriest, most agreeable Harry had ever met. They were far pleasanter than the parson’s black-eyed daughter back home, whose laugh could be heard half a mile off. They were just as well-bred as the fine ladies of Castlewood, all save Madam Beatrix, who could be as grand as an empress whenever the fancy took her. But after an hour’s conversation with Madam Beatrix, no matter how amusing her stories were, Harry would walk away with a bitter taste in his mouth, feeling as if the whole world was wicked and corrupt. The Lamberts were nothing like that: they laughed over the racier pages of Mr. Fielding, and cried over every volume of Mr. Richardson, even the bits that would make straitlaced Mrs. Grundy’s hair stand on end, yet their merry chatter left no sourness behind it. Their gossip about their neighbours was droll, never malicious. The little curtsies and cheerful greetings the villagers gave them when they walked into town were warm, not formal. Their charity was generous and cordial, never done for show. To be in the company of truly good people is a blessing beyond price, though Harry did not realize it fully at the time, until later experience showed him far less pleasant contrasts, and made him feel gratitude for those quiet days. This was a sunshiny, tranquil little patch of peace in a life that was destined to be full of storm and upheaval—an hour or two of sweet rest he would remember for years. Not much happened in that quiet stretch of time. It was only pleasant waking, friendly welcomes, serene, unhurried afternoons. The old house’s gates seemed to shut all the wickedness of the world outside, and the people who lived within seemed better, purer, kinder than other folk.

Harry was not in love, no—certainly not with saucy Hetty, or gentle generous Theodosia. But when the time came for him to leave, he squeezed both girls’ hands hard, and felt a warm, immense fondness for them both. He thought he would dearly love to meet their two brothers, who must be fine, honest fellows if they were raised in such a home. As for Mrs. Lambert, I swear she was as teary and sentimental at his departure as if he had just been the final volume of *Clarissa Harlowe*.

“He is so kind and honest,” Theo said gravely, as the three of them stood on the terrace watching Harry ride off down the Westerham road with the Colonel and two of the servants.

“I don’t think he’s stupid at all, not anymore,” Hetty admitted. “And mamma? I think he really is very like a swan indeed.”

“It felt just like one of our own boys leaving to go back to school,” Mrs. Lambert said softly.

“Just like it,” Theo echoed, a little sadly.

“I’m so glad papa is riding part of the way with him to Westerham,” Hetty went on. “And that he bought Farmer Briggs’s horse. I don’t like the idea of him going to stay with those Castlewood people. I’m sure that Madame Bernstein is a wicked old woman. I half expected to see her ride away on her crooked walking stick.”

“Hush, Hetty,” Theo chided her.

“Do you think she would float if we tried her in the village pond, the way they tested poor old Mother Hely at Elmhurst?” Hetty went on, ignoring her. “That other older lady looked fond of him, you know—the one with the fair hair. She looked very sad when she left, but Madame Bernstein whisked her off with her crutch, and she had no choice but to go. I don’t care, Theo. I know for a fact that woman is wicked. You think everyone is good, because you’ve never done anything wrong yourself.”

“My Theo is a good, sweet girl,” their mother said, looking fondly from one daughter to the other.

“Then why do we call her a miserable sinner in church?” Hetty demanded.

“We are all sinners, my love,” Mrs. Lambert said.

“What? Even papa too? You know you don’t truly believe that,” Hetty cried, and Mrs. Lambert had to fudge a little, for she could never bring herself to say a single unkind word against her beloved Colonel. “By the way, what was it you told John to give to Mr. Warrington’s black servant?”

Mrs. Lambert blushed a little as she admitted it was a bottle of her own homemade cordial water, and a spiced cake she had ordered Betty to bake the night before

Mrs. Lambert and her girls held their lily-edged linen handkerchiefs aloft in a last wave to the departing travellers, watching the two gentlemen amble leisurely down the first stretch of the lane until a clump of gnarled old lime trees at the drive’s bend swallowed them whole, hidden from the ladies’ view. That very same green screen had marked a hundred tender goodbyes before: Mr. Lambert riding off to face battle and danger, their boys trotting away one after the other for boarding school, each vanishing behind those same boughs, to return only when Heaven saw fit, bearing new joy and affection back to their small, warm household.

The quiet, unrushed rhythm of life at Oakhurst only deepened the soft devotion the women of the house bore their absent loved ones. With the men gone, there was all the day to think of them, and the next, and the one after that, when a letter was sure to come. There was Harry’s guest chamber to peek into, where the indent of his carpetbag still pressed deep into the linen counterpane. His riding whip hung on the hall peg by the door, his fishing basket propped by the boot stand, mute little memorials of the happy, brief days he’d spent there. At dinner, the half-eaten cherry tart he’d picked at even while swearing he was too sad to eat sat cold on the table, recalling the way Hetty had sniffled on one side of him and Theo had blinked back tears on the other. Evening prayers sounded off a note without his deep young voice joining the responses. Midnight came, and Mrs. Lambert lay wakeful, counting the miles the riders had travelled, thinking of one of her brood straying out from the nest for the first time. So those rustling limes formed a quiet barrier between the wider world and the gentle household at Oakhurst. Mrs. Lambert always fell silent and pensive if she and her daughters walked up to the trees while the men were away; she swore she would carve all the names of those she loved deep into their silver-grey bark, tangled in the traditional true-lovers’ knots, and Theo, who had a fine turn for verse, wrote a whole poem about the limes that her proud mother promptly sent off to a popular periodical of the day.

“Now we’re quite out of sight of the ladies,” called Colonel Lambert, tipping his hat in a mock salute as the two trotted past the green grove. “I know my wife is still glued to her attic window watching until we round this corner. I hope we shall have you back to see this house and these trees again soon, Mr. Warrington. When the boys are home for their holidays, there will be far better sport for you than we could offer this visit.”
“I never want to be happier than I have been here, sir,” Harry replied warmly. “I feel as if I am leaving old friends behind, not new acquaintances.”
“The friend we will sup with tonight has a son who is an old friend of our family, too. My wife, who is a relentless matchmaker at heart, spent years scheming to pair him off with one of my girls, but the rogue went and fell head over heels in love with someone else entirely.”
“Ah!” Harry sighed.
“Other men have done the same, you know. Brave fellows lived before Agamemnon.”
“Begging your pardon, sir, is his name Aga—? I did not quite catch it,” the young Virginian asked, meek and confused.
Colonel Lambert laughed aloud. “No, his name is James Wolfe. Barely thirty years old, he is the youngest lieutenant-colonel in the entire British army, save for a handful of noble lads who claim rank over us common fellows.”
“Of course, of course,” Harry nodded, perfectly in line with colonial notions of aristocratic precedence.
“I have seen him command captains who are thirty years his senior, men braver than most, who never grudge his rank for a moment. No one envies him his position, for every man who knows him acknowledges he has earned it a hundred times over. He is adored by every man in his old regiment, and knows the name and story of each private under his command. He is a fine scholar as well as a perfect soldier, and speaks half a dozen languages fluently.”
“Ah, sir,” Harry said, his voice soft with humility, “I fear I have wasted my youth dreadfully. Coming to England, I feel nothing but a fool. If my dear brother George had lived, he would have done our name and our colony far more credit than I ever shall. George was a scholar, George played the harpsichord, he could hold his own in conversation with the most learned men back home, and I have no doubt he would shine here too. I am glad I came to Oakhurst, if for no other reason than to learn just how ignorant I am.”
“To know that is already a great gain,” Lambert said, smiling. “Back home, ever since we lost my brother, I thought myself a fine, grand fellow, and all our neighbours flattered me into believing it. Now I am wiser, I hope—though no doubt I am still bragging half the time. But you see, sir, the gentry in our colony know very little besides hounds, horses, wagers, and games. I wish I knew half as much of books as I do of racing odds.”
“Nay—horses and hounds are fine books in their own right, full of more plain truth than half the musty volumes in a university library. Some men are not made to be scholars, and may be fine, worthy gentlemen regardless. What call have all of us to be learned, or to strive for the highest rank in the world? His Royal Highness is commander of the army, Martin Lambert is a colonel, and Jack Hunt, riding behind us now, was once a private soldier, and now he is the finest, most honest groom in the shire. So long as each of us does his best in the station he is given, it matters little if that station is high or low. Who are we to say what is high and what is low? For all we know, Jack’s currycomb, or my epaulets, or his Royal Highness’s baton, all hold equal weight in the end. When I was young I dreamed of glory and great success; now I only dream of duty, and the women we left behind a few miles back. Come, trot on, or we shall never reach Westerham before nightfall.”

At Westerham, the two riders were welcomed by their hosts: a stately, sharp-tongued matron, an old soldier with forty-five years of campaigns under his belt, and their son, Lieutenant Colonel James Wolfe, home on a brief leave from his regiment stationed at Maidstone. Harry stared at the young officer with great curiosity. There was nothing conventionally handsome in his face: he was very lean, very pale, with bright red hair, sharp high cheekbones and a prominent nose. But he greeted his elders with gentle courtesy, hailed old friends with open warmth, and spoke with such bright, eager animation that all who listened soon forgot his plain looks and began to admire them.
Mr. Warrington was travelling on to Tunbridge? Their James would gladly bear him company, Mrs. Wolfe said, and whispered something to Colonel Lambert over supper that made the older man grin and wink knowingly. He called for a toast of port: “To Miss Lowther!”
“With all my heart!” Wolfe cried enthusiastically, draining his glass to the very last drop. His mother leaned over to tell Harry, gossiping, that the pair were soon to be married, and that the lady came of the famous, ancient Lowther family of the north.
“Even if she were the daughter of Charlemagne himself,” Lambert declared, “she would not be too good for James Wolfe.”
“He would not say that if he knew her,” the young Colonel protested, laughing.
“Of course she is his priceless pearl,” his mother teased, “and we are nothing to him now. That is the way of it, Mr. Warrington. We nurse these boys through fevers, measles, whooping cough, smallpox; we send them off to the army and lie awake half the night worrying they will catch a bullet; we break our hearts at parting with them, and see them only a week or two a year, or sometimes ten years apart. And after all that care, some lass with a pair of bright eyes comes along, and our boy vanishes, and never cares a fig for us anymore!”
“And pray, my dear,” the old Colonel Wolfe rumbled, “did you not do the exact same thing when you ran off to marry me, leaving your own parents behind?”
“Only because your gout was so bad you needed someone to wait on you, not because I liked you at all,” his wife retorted, and the rest of the evening passed in easy, affectionate banter and plenty of good wine.

The next morning, Colonel Lambert turned his horse’s head back for Oakhurst, waving many kind farewells to Harry, while Wolfe and the young Virginian spurred their mounts south towards Tunbridge Wells. Wolfe was in a hurry to reach the town, but Harry lagged a little, his thoughts drifting longingly back to the quiet parlour at Oakhurst, the soft peaceful days he had spent there. Wolfe agreed enthusiastically with every word of Harry’s praise for the Lambert family. “To have such a good name, and to live such a quiet, steady life as Colonel Lambert’s,” Wolfe said, “is the height of all human ambition, as far as I am concerned.”
“What of glory, and honour?” Harry asked. “Are those nothing? Would you give up the chance to win them?”
“They were all I dreamed of once,” Wolfe answered, his tone soft, “but my desires are far quieter now. I have been at arms since I was fourteen years old. I have done almost every duty a soldier can do, marched every garrison road in this country, served wherever there was fighting to be done for the last ten years. I have done almost all a man can do in this profession, save command an entire army—something a man my age can hardly hope for. Now I think I would trade it all for quiet, a shelf of books, a wife who loves me, and a few children to dandle on my knee. I have imagined that little Elysium for myself, Mr. Warrington. True love is better than glory, and a warm fireside with the woman of your heart seated beside it is the greatest gift the gods can send.”
Harry pictured that scene in his head, and nodded, but his face was far from cheerful.
“You say yes as if a quiet fireside and a sweetheart are not the things you crave most,” Wolfe noted.
“Look you, Colonel, you have seen sixteen years of the world, you have campaigned and made a name for yourself. I am barely a few months out from hanging off my mother’s apron strings. When I have seen a campaign or two, or six, like you, when I have distinguished myself and made the world talk of me, then I will think of settling down.”
Wolfe, his head full of nothing but his own Miss Lowther, launched into a long, glowing rhapsody on the joys of marriage, listing every one of his lady’s beauties and virtues in great, loving detail, while Harry’s own thoughts turned more melancholy on the subject of a wife and home. The afternoon wore pleasantly on, no accidents troubling their ride save for one small mishap a few miles outside Tunbridge: two horsemen rode out to meet them, and Harry grabbed his pistol ready to charge, convinced they were highwaymen. Wolfe laughed so hard he nearly fell off his horse, telling Harry to put his weapon away, the men were nothing more than agents from the town inns coming to greet new arrivals, not robbers (though Wolfe admitted they would rob a guest of a few extra shillings on the bill soon enough). Even Harry’s servant Gumbo panicked so badly at the sight of the two horsemen that his horse bolted, and they had to chase him down half a mile down the lane amid a great deal of shouting. Soon the pair rode through the gates of Tunbridge Wells, alighted at their inn, and parted ways, each to find the people they had come to visit.

Harry found his aunt Madame de Bernstein installed in handsome, well-furnished lodgings, with liveried London footmen loitering in the antechamber, ready to carry her chair through the town when she went out. She greeted him with the utmost warm affection. His cousin Lady Maria was out when he arrived, and Harry could not tell if he was disappointed not to see her, or if his aunt took any note of his half-hidden feelings. A foppish young beau in a rich figured silk suit (the first of its kind Harry had ever seen) and two plump dowagers in wide, voluminous hoops dusted with rouge were visiting the Baroness when Harry made his bow. She introduced her nephew to the three as the young Virginian Croesus they had no doubt heard rumours of, whose estate was larger than the entire county of Kent, and far more fertile. She told them his mother, Madam Esmond, was known back in the colonies as the Princess Pocahontas, and sang the praises of mother and son alike so loudly that the modest Harry blushed bright crimson under the stream of compliments. The three visitors shook his hand, curtsied, and departed as soon as they could, eager to spread the news of the wealthy, handsome young Virginian across all Tunbridge society.

“You could not have arrived at a better moment, my dear,” the Baroness said, cackling softly as the door shut behind her guests. “Those three have the busiest tongues in the whole Wells. By sundown every drawing room here will be talking of you. I told all sorts of ridiculous fibs about Virginia geography to describe your estate, you see—filled it full of exotic animals, spice groves, gold mines, I do believe I even mentioned diamonds at one point. I said your mother commands armies of negro servants, a veritable sovereign ruling over a magnificent domain. And you must prepare yourself to be treated as that domain’s heir apparent. Do not let your head turn. You will be flattered as no one has ever flattered you in your life.”
“But to what end, ma’am?” Harry asked, confused. “I see no reason to make people think I am far richer than I am.”
“First of all, you must not contradict your old aunt, and make me look a fool in front of my guests. And besides, that reputation was already waiting for you when we arrived. A London newspaper printed a story not long ago about the immensely wealthy young Virginian gentleman, nephew of Lord Castlewood, who had just landed in England. The golden key opens every door in this world, my boy. To be thought rich is just as good as being rich. You will not even need to spend much money. People will say you are careful with your fortune, and that reputation for prudence will only do you good. Watch how every mother in this town smiles on you, and every daughter curtsies low! Do not look so shocked. When I was a young woman, I did what every other pretty girl did, and tried to better myself with more than one well-placed marriage. Your sainted grandmother, the dear old thing, used to scold me and call me worldly. Worldly? The whole world is worldly, and we must serve it as it serves us, give nothing for nothing. Our family name has little credit these days, entre nous, and even less reputation. You know Castlewood was deeply suspected of treason in the ’45 rising? He gambled away every penny he had left after that, his whole estate is eaten up with mortgages.”
Harry had never heard a word of Lord Castlewood’s ruined reputation.
“He never had much to lose to begin with, but he lost all of it and more. He has chased every ridiculous scheme to raise money under the sun—at one point I was so afraid he would steal my diamonds right off my neck that I travelled back to Castlewood from London without a single piece of my own jewelry. Terrible, is it not, to speak so of my own nephew? But you are my nephew too, and you are still unspoiled by the world, so I must warn you of its wickedness. I heard you were playing cards with Will and the chaplain back at Castlewood, and that you won fairly from them. If you had sat down to play with Castlewood himself, you would not have won a single hand. I warned him to keep his greedy hands off you before you arrived, and he dared not disobey me.”
“Ma’am, you interfered to protect me?”
“I kept his clutches off you! You should be thankful you escaped that ogre’s den with any money left in your purse. That gambling fever is the curse of our whole family. My poor silly brother played every night, both his wives played, especially the last one, who lives on nothing but the proceeds of her London card parties now. I would not trust her alone in a room with you for ten minutes—they are all so hungry to win, they would fleece you clean, then turn on each other fighting over the plunder. Without his post at Court, my poor nephew would have nothing at all, and that is all Will’s fortune, and Maria’s, and his other daughters’ too.”
“And are they all fond of the cards as well?”
“Little Molly, no, to do her justice. But Fanny will bet her own eyes out of her head if you let her. I know the madness, sir—do not look so shocked. I had it as a girl, the same way I had the measles. I have never quite got over it. There is nothing else left for an old woman like me to enjoy. You will see high stakes played at my card tables tonight. Hush, dear! That is what I was craving, back at Castlewood where I moped so dull! I could never win of my nieces or their mother, they would never pay their debts if they lost. It is best I warn you in time, so you will not be too shocked to find out. I cannot live without the cards, there is no use pretending otherwise!”
A few days prior, staying with his Castlewood relatives, Harry—who loved cards, cockfights, wagers, and every other kind of sport—would have laughed at that confession. That household had laughed at far worse: they laughed at faith, at honour, at the idea of a pure, unselfish life. They proclaimed selfishness as a universal fact, sneered at sacred duties, and condoned every vice with a flippant shrug. They were no pharisees, these people; they did not pretend to be better than their neighbours, and they despised all the rest of the world heartily. Of course, there are no people like that anymore, a hundred years later; human nature has changed entirely, and card play is so out of fashion that no lady of quality in London can tell the difference between Spadille and Manille

Cousin Maria made her entrance attended by a pair of grinning gardener’s boys heaping wicker baskets full of early summer blooms, intended to deck Madame de Bernstein’s drawing room in readiness for her ladyship’s evening assembly. Three footmen in livery laced thick with worsted bustled about the space, unfurling six card tables between them. A stately major-domo in black broadcloth and powdered bag wig, his ruffled cuffs edged with fine lace and bearing the proud bearing of a man who ought by rights to wear a sword at his hip, followed after them carrying armfuls of wax tapers, setting two apiece on every card table and tucking pairs into the silver sconces nailed to the wainscot. The slanting golden sun of late afternoon gilded the paneling, and spilled out over the green common beyond the windows: over weathered rocks, clumps of gnarled oak, and distant cottage roofs twinkling in the light. Groups of strollers in hoops, powder, and glinting brocade wandered across the grass, their colored silhouettes dappling the turf. On the other side of the Baroness’s windows stretched the Pantiles, where a perpetual fair hummed with chatter and clattering hooves, a band of musicians playing for the benefit of the Wells’ visitors below.

Madame de Bernstein’s chief sitting room would never have suited a recluse or a scholar, but for anyone fond of bustle, gaiety, and bright cross-light, and a full view of all the cheerful, busy life unfolding outside, no lodging in the whole of Tunbridge Wells could be more pleasant. When the lamps were lit after dark, every passerby on the pavement below knew her ladyship was at home holding a card assembly, and an introduction to the evening’s entertainment was easy enough to come by. It strikes me, thinking on it now, that the night-life of high society a hundred years ago was a comparatively dim affair. There was not one wax candle then for ten that light a modern lady’s drawing room today, to say nothing of gas and the wondrous new club illuminations we now enjoy. Horrible guttering tallow candles smoked and stank in every back passage, and the official candle-snuffer was a notorious, well-loved character in every playhouse. Look at Hogarth’s prints if you doubt it: how dark they are, how his great feasts seem begrimed with tallow smoke! In *Marriage A La Mode*, in Lord Viscount Squanderfield’s grand saloon, where the earl and his wife yawn over the remains of their party while their steward cowers in horror, there are but eight candles total: one on each card table, and half a dozen stuck in a chipped brass chandelier. Jack Briefless, inviting his friends to oysters and beer in his Pump Court chambers, would likely have twice that number. We may comfort ourselves with the thought that even Louis Quatorze in all his glory held his most lavish revels in comparative dimness, and bless Mr. Price and all other luciferous benefactors of mankind for banishing the rank, stinking “mutton tallow” of our youth.

So Maria, fairest bloom of all the flowers she carried, tucked roses and sweet-williams and honeysuckle into every vase and dragon jar, adorning the room as best her artistic taste could manage. She lingered over every arrangement, casting only sly, timid glances at her young cousin Harry, whose own deep blush would have done credit to any modest young woman. You might have thought she meant to linger behind after the others left, for a quiet few moments alone with him—until the Baroness, settled in her great armchair with her crooked tortoiseshell cane in her hand, began ordering the servants about imperiously, rating them one by one soundly: Tom for a darn in his stocking, John for slathering too much hair grease out of the tallow candle box, and so on, keeping a stern, unyielding rule over her whole household. It is worth another note on the poor footmen of a hundred years ago: two shared a bed, four a room, and that room was often a drafty cellar, where they washed in a stone trough such as you would barely find anywhere in modern London outside of Her Majesty’s Foot Guards barracks.

If Maria had hoped for a private interview, her fond heart was disappointed. “Where do you intend to dine, Harry?” Madame de Bernstein asked. “My niece Maria and I will make do with a single chicken in the little back parlor, and I think you ought to make for the best ordinary in town. There is a very good one at the White Horse, whose dinner bell will ring any minute now. You must understand, sir, you ought not to spare expense, but comport yourself like the son of Princess Pocahontas, for all the world to see. Your trunks have already been carried over to the lodgings I’ve taken for you. It’s not good for a strapping young lad to be always hanging around the aprons of two old women, is it, Maria?”

“No,” said Maria, dropping her meek eyes to the floor, while the Baroness’s own glinted in triumph. I do believe poor Andromeda had been left exposed to her cruel dragon for the better part of the past five or six days; if Perseus had cut the creature’s head clean off, it would have been no unjustifiable monstricide. But the young man drew no sword or shield, only stared absently at the footmen in their tawny-and-blue livery creaking across the room.

“And the London mercers and tailors who follow the crowds to the Wells will be happy to wait on you,” the Baroness went on. “You ought to call on them, my dear, for your suit is not quite of the latest fashion—you want a little more lace, a little finer cut—”

“I cannot go out of mourning for my brother, ma’am,” said the young man, looking down at the sober black of his coat.

“Ho, sir!” cried the lady, rustling up from her chair and heaving herself to her feet on her cane. “Wear black for your brother till you are as old as Methuselah, for all I care. I have no wish to stop you. I only want you to dress properly, do as other gentlemen do, and make a figure worthy of the Esmond name.”

“Madam,” said Mr. Warrington, drawing himself up with great dignity, “I have not done a single thing to disgrace that name, so far as I know.”

Why did the old woman stop and give a little sharp start, as if she had been struck? Let bygones be bygones. She and the boy had a dozen little fencing matches of the sort already, crossing swords and parrying thrusts as fast as they could speak, and she liked Harry none the worse for the courage to stand up to her. “Surely a little finer linen than that shirt you have on will not disgrace you, sir,” she said, with a rather forced laugh.

Harry bowed and blushed. That plain linen shirt had been one of the homely, loving gifts from his friends at Oakhurst. He felt a secret pleasure in wearing it, thinking of those good, pure, simple, kind people, and it seemed to him that as long as he wore that garment, no evil could touch him. He said he would return to his lodging at once, and make sure he came back arrayed in the very best linen his trunks held.

“Come back here directly, sir,” said Madame Bernstein, “and if our guests have not arrived, Maria and I will find you some extra ruffles to wear!” And with that, a footman showed the young fellow out, and guided him to his new apartments.

Harry found not only handsome, spacious rooms waiting for him, but a groom standing by ready to enter his service, and a second valet, should he choose to hire one to tend to Mr. Gumbo. Barely minutes after he had settled in his rooms, emissaries from the London tailor and bootmaker were knocking at his door, bearing the compliments and calling cards of Messrs. Regnier and Tull. Gumbo laid out the best pieces in his modest wardrobe, the finest linen his thrifty Virginian mother had packed for him before he set sail. Visions of his snowbound home across the Atlantic rose up before him: crackling log fires, the trim quiet ladies of Castlewood stitching by the hearth. For the first time, a small, strange thought crossed his mind: that his homely country clothes were not quite smart enough, that the home-wrought linen was not as fine as that worn by the young men of quality he saw about him now. That he should ever be ashamed of anything belonging to Castlewood! It felt absurd. The simple folk back home were only too well satisfied with every object made, said, or produced on their estate, and Madam Esmond, when she sent her son off on his travels, had thought no young nobleman in England could be better provided for. The clothes could have fitted better, to be sure, and been of a later cut—but the young man cut a very comely, handsome figure when he finished his toilet and stepped back out onto the street, Gumbo calling for a sedan chair and marching alongside it until they reached the White Horse ordinary.

He had expected to find the dashing acquaintance he had made at his aunt’s lodgings a few hours prior, who had told him the White Horse was the most modest dining spot at the Wells, and he mentioned his friend’s name to the landlord. But the host and his waiters led him into the dining room with endless smiles and bows, assuring his honour that he needed no other introduction than his own good name, helped him hang his coat and sword on a wall peg, asked him whether he would drink Burgundy, Pontac, or champagne with his dinner, and ushered him to a table.

Though the most fashionable eating house in the village, the White Horse was not crowded that day. Monsieur Barbeau, the landlord, told Harry there was a grand fete taking place at Summer Hill that had drawn away most of the town’s guests. Indeed, when Harry stepped into the room there were only four other gentlemen present. Two of them were finishing their wine after their meal, and the other two were younger men halfway through their dinner. The landlord must have whispered Harry’s name as he passed the latter’s table, for they looked over at him with obvious interest, and gave him a slight bow across the table as the smiling host bustled away to bring his dinner. Mr. Warrington returned their salute, and the two young men bade him welcome to Tunbridge, and hoped he would like the place better the more he got to know it. Then they smiled and exchanged waggish, knowing glances, the meaning of which Harry did not understand, nor why they cast the same knowing look over at the other two older guests still drinking their wine.

One of those two was dressed in a tarnished velvet coat, with a huge powdered queue tied in a bag, and voluminous, heavily embroidered ruffles at his wrists. The other was a small, beetle-browed, hook-nosed, high-shouldered man, whom his companion addressed out loud as “milord” in a very loud voice. My lord barely glanced at the new arrival as he sipped his wine, then turned back to his friend.

“And so you know the nephew of that old woman—Croesus the newly arrived heir, they say?”

“You missed your mark there, Jack!” one of the two young diners called across the room.

“Never could get the hang of the lingo,” Jack replied. The two older men had switched to speaking French.

“But assuredly, my dear lord!” said the gentleman with the long queue.

“You have shown wonderful energy, my dear Baron! He has been here but two hours. My own servants only told me of him just as I arrived for dinner.”

“I knew him long before! I met him often in London, with the Baroness and his cousin, the earl,” said the Baron.

A plate of smoking hot soup was set down before Harry just then, borne by the grinning host. “Behold, sir! Behold my own fashion of potage!” Monsieur Barbeau said, leaning down to whisper the celebrated nobleman’s name across the room into Harry’s ear. Harry thanked the man in fluent French, upon which the foreign gentleman turned around, grinned most graciously at him, and said, “Fous bossedez notre langue barfaidement, monsieur.”

Mr. Warrington had never heard French pronounced in that strange, mangled way back in Canada. He bowed politely in return.

“Tell me more of this Croesus, my good Baron,” his lordship went on, speaking rather superciliously to his companion, and taking no notice of Harry at all, which nettled the young Virginian not a little. “What can you tell me? Croesus is a youth like any other youth, tall, a little awkward, with black hair, as all men from the Indies have. They have taken lodgings for him at Mrs. Rose’s toy-shop.”

“I have lodgings there too!” Harry thought to himself. “Who on earth is this Croesus they are talking of? But this soup is excellent.”

“He travels with a huge retinue,” the Baron continued. “Four servants, two post-chaises, a pair of outriders. His chief attendant is a black man who saved his life from savage raiders in America, and who will not hear of being freed on any account. He insists on wearing mourning for his elder brother, from whom he inherits his great principality.”

“Could anything console you for the death of your own brother, Chevalier?” one of the young diners called over.

“Milor! His property could,” said the Chevalier. “Which, as you know, is no small sum.”

“Your brother lives on his great patrimony, which you tell me is immense, while you live by your own industry, my dear Chevalier.”

“Milor!” cried the man addressed as Chevalier.

“By your industry, or your wit—how much more noble! Will you be at the Baroness’s card assembly tonight? She ought to be some relation of yours, is she not, Chevalier?”

“Again I do not follow your lordship,” the other man said, sulkily. “Why, she is a woman of great wit, noble birth, who has undergone the strangest adventures, and has precious little principle (there, you happily have the advantage of her). But what do men of the world care for that? I suppose you intend to go and play cards with the young Creole, and get as much money out of him as you possibly can. By the way, Baron—what if this young Creole is a trap? What if our excellent friend the Baroness invented him back in London, and brought him down to prey on all the innocent, unsuspecting folks here at the Wells?”

“J’y ai souvent pense, milor,” said the little Baron, tapping his nose very knowingly. “That Baroness is capable of anything.”

“A Baron—A Baroness, que voulez-vous, my friend? I mean her late lamented husband. Do you know who he was?”

“Intimately. A more notorious villain never dealt a hand of cards. At Venice, at Brussels, at Spa, at Vienna—he knew the insides of every gaol in every one of those cities. I knew the man well, my lord.”

“I thought you would. I saw him at The Hague, where I first had the honour of meeting you, and a more disreputable rogue never crossed my threshold. A minister must open his doors to all sorts of people, Baron—spies, sharpers, ruffians of every description.”

“Parbleu, milor, you treat them charmingly!” his companion laughed.

“A man of my rank, the rank I held then, of course, must meet all sorts of people, including your acquaintance. What that woman ever saw fit to take the name of such a man for, I cannot imagine.”

“Apparently, it was better than her own name.”

“Effectively! Just as I have heard of my friend Paddy exchanging coats with a scarecrow. I do not know which name is more distinguished, that of the English bishop, or that of the German baron.”

“My lord!” cried the other gentleman, rising and laying his hand on the large star pinned to his coat breast. “You forget that I too am a Baron, and a Chevalier of the Holy Roman—”

“—Order of the Spur! Not in the least, my dear knight and baron! You will take no more wine? We shall meet at Madame de Bernstein’s tonight.”

The knight and baron quit the table, fumbling in his embroidered pockets as if for money to tip the waiter, who held out his great laced hat for him. He waved the menial off with a hand ringed with blazing gemstones, sticking out of a mass of fine lace ruffles, and stalked grandly out of the room. It was only after the man they had called “my lord” began to speak of the late bishop’s widow and the German baron’s wife that Harry Warrington realized he and his aunt had been the entire subject of their conversation. Before the full realization had settled in his mind, one of the speakers had quit the room, and the other turned to the table where the two young diners sat. “What a little sharper that man is! Everything I said about the Bernsteins, mutato nomine, applies fully to him. I knew the fellow to be a spy and a rogue. He has changed his religion half a dozen times, for all I know. I had him kicked out of The Hague myself when I was ambassador, and I know he was publicly caned in Vienna.”

“I wonder my Lord Chesterfield associates with such a villain!” Harry called out sharply from his table. The other two diners looked over at him, and to Harry’s surprise the nobleman he had addressed continued talking without pause. “There cannot be a more confirmed rogue than this Poellnitz. Thank Heaven, he actually left my snuff-box behind! You laugh? The man is quite capable of stealing it.” And my lord thought it was his own witty satire the two young men were laughing at.

“You are quite right, sir,” said one of the two young diners, turning to Mr. Warrington, “though, saving your presence, it is hardly your affair. My lord will play cards with anybody who will sit down to the table with him. Do not be alarmed, though—he is as deaf as a post, and did not hear a single word you said. That is exactly why he will play with anyone who puts a pack of cards before him, and that is the reason he consorts with such a rogue.”

“Faith, I know other noblemen who are not particular about their company,” said Mr. Jack.

“Do you mean to say that because I associate with you? I know perfectly well what sort of company I keep, my good friend

The bowling green tucked beside the White Horse Tavern’s eating-room windows glowed soft and crisp under the late Tunbridge sun, dotted with rough wooden tables where guests sipped punch and tea to work off the weight of their dinners. When the three gentlemen pushed back their chairs as their meal drew to a close, Mr. Jack Morris proposed they adjourn to the turf to tap a cool bottle of Burgundy between them.

“Jack Morris would adjourn all the way to the grave itself just to find an excuse for another drink,” Lord March drawled, earning a snort from his friend.
“Every man has his own preferred path to damnation,” Jack shrugged. “I own mine leads through a bottle, and I’ve no shame for it.”
“Lord Chesterfield’s damnation is deuce-ace,” put in Lord March’s companion, Lord March, grinning. “He can’t keep his hands off cards or dice long enough to catch his breath.”
“And you, March, have not one devil but a whole crowd of them,” Chesterfield laughed back. “You gamble, you race horses, you bet on anything that moves, you drink deep, you eat well, you hoard your coin, and you chase every pretty face that crosses your path. You’ve fallen into terrible company, Mr. Warrington, landing in his lordship’s orbit. He’d play you for every single acre you own back in Virginia, given half the chance.”
“With the greatest pleasure imaginable, Mr. Warrington!” March interposed, leaning across the table with eager glint in his eye.
“For every hogshead of tobacco, every crate of spice, every enslaved man, woman, and child, every ox and ass on your plantations, every last thing that bears your name.”
“Shall we start now?” March tossed a glance at Jack Morris. “You never travel without a dice box or a bottle screw. I’ll stake you any sum you like on the turn of a die.”
“Unfortunately my lord,” young Harry Warrington laughed, shaking his head, “none of that tobacco, those enslaved people, or that land is mine yet. I only just turned of age, and my mother, scarce twenty years older than I, has every prospect of outliving me for decades.”
“I’ll bet you she doesn’t. I’ll pay you a fair sum right now against four times the amount coming to you the day she passes. I’ll stake you a handsome purse right now against the reversion of your Virginia estate when the old lady departs. What do you call the place, by the bye?”
“Castlewood.”
“A principality, by all the gossip I hear,” March said. “Though I wager the quidnuncs in London have exaggerated its value ten times over. How did you come by the name Castlewood? You’re related to the English Castlewood family, aren’t you? Oh, of course—your mother descends from the rightful head of the house, the one who took the losing side in the ’15 rebellion. My old Duchess told me the whole story a dozen times. She knew your grandfather, the friend of Addison, Steele, Pope—all the great literary wits of the day. Pity he didn’t stay home and ship the other, grasping branch of the family out to the plantations instead.”
“I’ve just come from staying at that very Castlewood, with my cousin who holds the estate now,” Harry remarked.
“Hm. Did you gamble with him? He’s infamous for his love of cards and dice.”
“Never for anything more than sixpenny stakes, just a pool of commerce with the ladies after supper.”
“So much the better for both of you. But I’ll lay ten to one you played with Will Esmond while you were there, if he was in residence.”
Harry blushed bright, and admitted that he and his cousin had indeed played a few hands of cards on quiet evenings.
“And Tom Sampson the chaplain was the third at the table, wasn’t he?” Jack Morris crowed. “I’d wager half my income Tom joined in, and may the Lord deliver you from the pair of them working together to empty your purse!”
“Nay, the truth is I won fair and square off both of them,” Harry said, smiling over the rim of his wine glass.
“And they paid you? Well! Miracles never do cease!”
“I never said anything about miracles,” Harry chuckled.
“And you don’t go blabbing all your wins and losses around town, that volto sciolto face of yours hides more than it tells, hey Mr. Warrington?” March teased.
“I beg your pardon,” honest Harry said, apologetic. “French is the only other language besides English I know a scrap of.”
“Lord March learned all his Italian at the Opera, and it cost him a pretty penny in lessons too,” Jack cackled. “We’ll have to drag you to see the shows, won’t we, March?”
“Must we, Morris?” March replied, his tone cold enough to hint he did not care for his friend’s overfamiliarity in front of a stranger.
Both of the two English lords were dressed plainly for the country: unpowdered small scratch wigs, blue frock coats with plate buttons, buckskin breeches and heavy riding boots, narrow-laced little hats, no trace of the silks and embroidery of London drawing rooms.
“I don’t much care for the Opera, my lord,” Harry said, the Burgundy warming his blood. “But I’m wild to see Newmarket, and I’ve longed my whole life to watch a proper English hunt.”
“We’ll show you both Newmarket and the hunting fields, never fear. Can you ride well?”
“I think so. I can shoot straight enough, and jump decently too.”
“What’s your weight? I bet we’re evenly matched, or I tip the scales a little heavier. I bet Jack Morris outshoots you at five and twenty paces, any bird or mark. And I bet I outjump you on flat ground, right here on this very green.”
“I don’t know Mr. Morris’s shooting skill—I’ve never met either of you gentlemen before today—but I’ll take all your bets, my lord, for whatever stakes you name!” Harry cried, the wine rushing to his head, determined not to shame his Virginia home by backing down from a challenge.
“Ponies a side on each!” March yelled.
“Done and done!” Harry and March shouted at the same time. The young Virginian would have rather fought a duel than let anyone think his colonial pride would shrink from a fair contest.
“We can try the long jump right now, if your feet are steady,” March said, springing to his feet, stretching his long limbs as he eyed the dry, crisp turf. He pulled off his heavy riding boots, then his coat and waistcoat, buckling his belt tight around his waist and flinging his clothes in a heap on the grass.
Harry was far more careful with his own garments—it was his best velvet suit, after all. He took off his coat and waistcoat, folded them neatly, and seeing all the nearby tables were sloshed with spilled punch, carried them inside the eating room to set them on a dry table by the open window.
There he found a new guest: Mr. Wolfe, the lean young lieutenant-colonel, eating a plain chicken and salad with a modest pint of small beer, completely sober. Harry was in such high spirits he clapped the man on the shoulder, told him of his bet with Lord March, and asked if Wolfe would back him for half the stake. Wolfe laughed and said he was far too poor a soldier to gamble, but he would happily come out and judge the contest to make sure no cheating happened. He set down his glass and stepped through the open window right after Harry.
“Who is that tallow-faced carrot-haired oddity?” slurred Jack Morris, well in his cups by that point.
Harry explained the man was Lieutenant-Colonel Wolfe of the 20th Regiment.
“Your humble servants, gentlemen,” Wolfe said, giving them all a stiff, formal military bow.
“Never saw such a gawky figure in my life!” Jack blurted. “Did you, March?”
“I beg your pardon—did you say March?” Wolfe asked, looking surprised.
“I am the Earl of March, sir, at your service,” the nobleman said, bowing in return. “My friend Mr. Morris is so familiar with me that after dinner, we behave like brawling brothers, no ceremony at all.”
Jack was so delighted to hear his noble friend admit their closeness he yelled at the top of his lungs, “Two to one on my lord!”
“Done!” Harry called out immediately, and a sheepish Jack had no choice but to huff “Done!” right back.
“Take that bet for yourself, Colonel,” Harry whispered to his friend. But Wolfe shook his head, saying he could not afford to lose money, and so had no right to hope to win any.
“I see you’ve already won one of our bets before we even start,” March said, squinting at Harry. “I’m an inch or two taller than you, but you’ve got an inch more breadth across the shoulders.”
“Pooh, Will! I bet you weigh twice as much as he does!” Jack shouted.
“Done, Jack!” March laughed. “All bets are for ponies. You don’t want in on this one, Mr. Warrington?”
“No, my dear fellow, one bet on him is enough for me,” Jack said, backing down quickly.
“Very good, my dear fellow,” March grinned. “Now let’s settle the long jump wager.”
Harry had on his finest silk stockings, black satin breeches, and neat polished pumps, and saw no reason to take his shoes off, unlike his lordship, whose spurred riding boots were useless for leaping. The stretch of green turf before them was thirty yards long, plenty of room for a running start, bordered by a gravel path, beyond which stood a tavern wall hung with the pub’s sign: the rampant Hanoverian White Horse between two skittles, painted bright blue, bearing the landlord’s name and his tavern’s name.
Jack Morris laid a white handkerchief on the grass to mark the takeoff point, and Wolfe walked to the far end of the green to note exactly where each jumper landed. As Harry later wrote in a surviving letter to Mrs. Mountain back at Castlewood, Virginia:
“My Lord went first, though he offered to let me lead. But I remembered the story my dearest George used to tell of the Battle of Fontenoy, so I said ‘Monseigneur le Comte, tirez le premier, s’il vous plait.’ He took his run barefoot, and for the honour of the Old Dominion, I had the great gratification of beating him by more than two feet: exactly two feet nine inches, to be precise. I jumped twenty-one feet three inches, per the inn drawer’s measured tape, and his lordship only eighteen and six. I had already won the weight bet the second I set eyes on him, before we even stepped on the turf. So he and Mr. Jack both paid up cheerfully. My wallet, which had grown nearly empty from tipping servants at Castlewood and buying a new horse at Oakhurst, was soon stuffed full of their banknotes. I will make sure my mother does not take amiss what I did, for I bet only for the honour of Virginia, and my opponent was a peer of the highest rank, holding two earldoms and heir to a dukedom. Gambling is all the rage over here, and the young bloods and fashionables bet from dawn till dusk.
“I told them, for my mischief, that there is a gentleman back home who can jump a full foot further than me. When they asked who, I said Colonel George Washington of Mount Vernon, which is true—he is the only man in either his county or mine who can do it. Mr. Wolfe then asked me a hundred questions about Colonel Washington, and showed he had heard of him before. He talked over last year’s unhappy expedition against the French as if he knew every inch of the ground, and could name all our Virginia rivers, though he did mispronounce the Potomac as ‘Pottamac,’ and we had a good laugh over it. My Lord of March and Ruglen was not at all ill tempered about losing, and not a cross word passed between us.”
When all the feats of strength were done, the four men strolled out of the tavern garden onto the main public promenade, which was thronged with Tunbridge Wells society by that hour. Jack Morris, loud and unrestrained after his wine, made pointed, often rude remarks about every person that passed, and whenever March made a witty joke, Jack would roar out “Oh ho ho! Good Gad! My dear Earl! You’ll be the death of me!” for all the promenade to hear, as if he was determined every last stranger there knew he was on familiar, brotherly terms with a peer of the realm.
A whole procession of famous faces drifted past them: M. Poellnitz, no better dressed than he had been at dinner, grinned and swept off his plumed, tarnished laced hat in salute. Then came Lord Chesterfield himself, in a pearl-colored suit, his blue Garter ribbon and star glittering on his chest, nodding pleasantly to the young men.
“I’ll back that old man to tip his hat more gracefully than anyone in all of England, France included,” March said. “He hasn’t changed the shape of that hat in twenty years. Look over there—see that great big, awkward, pockmarked man in the snuff-coloured coat, who barely touches his clumsy beaver in reply? Confound his impudence! Do you know who that is?”
“No, curse him, who is it, March?” Jack swore.
“That’s Samuel Johnson, the dictionary maker. Lord Chesterfield wrote a whole series of fine papers patronizing the man when his dictionary was coming out. Horry Walpole says they’re excellent pieces, and he knows all about that sort of literary nonsense. The impudent old schoolmaster!”
“Hang him, he belongs in the pillory!” Jack roared.
“The fat little man he’s walking with is another writer, a printer—his name’s Richardson, he wrote Clarissa, you know.”
“Great heavens! Is that the great Richardson? The man who wrote *Clarissa*?” Colonel Wolfe and Harry Warrington both cried out at exactly the same moment.
Harry ran forward to gawk at the kind, round-faced little old man toddling along the path, surrounded by a crowd of doting admiring ladies.
“Dear, dear sir,” one young lady was gushing, “you are far too good and virtuous for this world—surely you were sent here to teach the rest of us how to be good!”
“Ah, Miss Mulso! Who shall teach the teacher?” Richardson replied, lifting his mild round face to the sky. “Even I have my faults and errors. Even my age and experience cannot stop me from stumbling—oh! Heaven bless my soul, Mr. Johnson! I beg your pardon if I trod on your corn.”
“You have done both: trod on the corn, and earned your own pardon,” Johnson rumbled, then turned away muttering verses, swaying as he walked, eyes fixed on the ground, hands behind his back, swinging his heavy walking stick so recklessly he kept nearly poking his gentle companion-author in the eye.
“His eyes are not strong, dear Miss Mulso,” Richardson apologized to the young lady, “but such as they are, I would not dare cross Mr. Johnson’s cudgel.” He bowed low to Harry, who had drifted up beside them, and Harry blushed to the roots of his hair as he returned the greeting, almost too starstruck to speak. Richardson was adored everywhere he went: spinsters scattered tea leaves around his feet like offerings, matrons sewed fancy slippers for him and kissed the toes, a whole halo of pious respect hung even around his nightcap. All Europe had wept and thrilled over the pages of his immortal little novel, and Harry walked back to his friends glowing with pride, happy just to have exchanged a bow with the great man.
“Seen him! Dammy, you can see him any day in his little print shop, can’t you?” Jack laughed.
“My brother George always said he and Mr. Fielding were the two greatest geniuses in all England,” Harry burst out, earnest as ever when he spoke of his dearest friend. “He said the very first thing he would do when he traveled to Europe was go on pilgrimage to visit Mr. Richardson.”
“Your brother spoke like a man!” Colonel Wolfe cried, his pale face flushing bright. “I would far rather be a man of genius than a peer of the realm.”
“To each his own taste, Colonel,” March said, highly amused. “Your enthusiasm is quite refreshing, on my honour it is.”
“So it is—by Gad, perfectly refreshing!” Jack echoed.
“March, which would you rather be? A fat old printer who wrote a story about a ruined girl, or a peer of Parliament with ten thousand a year?”
“March—my Lord March! Do you take me for a fool?” Jack cried, his voice thick with mock hurt. “Have I done anything to deserve that kind of insult?”
“I would rather win honour than inherit honours. I would rather make my name than be born to it, even if my father’s name, thank God, is already an honest one,” Wolfe said, bowing quickly to the group. “Pardon me, gentlemen.” He darted across the promenade toward a small party of people who had just come into view: a young lady, an older lady, and a gentleman.
“That’s the beautiful Miss Lowther,” March said, nodding. “I remember now. He’s taken her arm—everyone says they’re engaged.”
“You don’t mean to say that gawky half-pay soldier is engaged to a Lowther of the North?” Jack squawked. “Curse me, what is the world coming to, with your printers and schoolmasters and all this infernal nonsense?”
Even gruff Samuel Johnson, who had barely tipped his hat to the great Lord Chesterfield a few minutes prior, was seen to take off his beaver and bow almost all the way to the ground before a florid clerical gentleman in a flowing gown and large round hat: the Bishop of Salisbury, Prelate of the Garter, wearing his blue riband and star with immense complacency. Dr. Gilbert paid endless flattering compliments to Richardson, calling him the great supporter of virtue, the preacher of sound morals, the mainstay of all true religion—praise the honest printer accepted with perfect, unfeigned conviction.
Let no young lady today rush to her grandfather’s bookshelf on the strength of this 18th century praise and yank *Clarissa* off the shelf. She would find little to thrill her in the volumes that made her great-grandmothers weep and swoon a hundred years

“Let me hear about those children, child — the little lasses I saw running about the house where they took you in, poor dear boy, after your dreadful fall?” Lady Maria’s voice softened as they paced the sun-dappled common at Tunbridge Wells, her gloved hand tucked tight through Harry Warrington’s arm. “Oh, that fall, Harry! I thought I should have died on the spot when I saw you pitch from that rearing horse! You needn’t squeeze my arm quite so hard, you know full well you do not care for me half so much as you pretend.”

“The Lamberts are the best, kindest, dearest souls I have ever met in all the world,” Harry cried warmly, his face lighting up at the name. He patted the pocket of his riding coat, stuffed plump and crisp with the banknotes he had just won off March and Morris in their wagers over jumps and weights. “Mrs. Lambert was my own mother’s closest friend when she was sent to Europe for her education, decades ago. Colonel Lambert is the most accomplished gentleman alive, has seen service in Scotland with the Duke, in Flanders, and out at Minorca. No own father and mother could have nursed me more tenderly through my fever and my broken bones than they did. I owe them a debt I can never repay, and I swear I shall make them a gift fit to show it.”

“Pish, you would offend them to offer them payment for tending a wounded friend,” Maria said, a little smile tugging at her painted lips. “We can stop at the toy-shop on the high street later, my dear, and buy a pair of fine new dolls for the little girls.”

“Dolls for Hester and Theo?” Harry laughed loud, his arm jostling hers so hard she gave a faint, nearly imperceptible wince. “Do you think a woman remains a child until she turns forty, cousin? I can tell you Miss Hester does not for one moment consider herself a little girl, and Theo is a full year older than her sister. They speak French, Italian, and Spanish between them, they have read shelves full of history and poetry, they play the harpsichord so fine you could listen for hours, and Theo composes her own songs to sing together. They are no mere children.”

“Indeed? I scarcely spoke to them at all, I thought they looked quite youthful. I had no idea they were such wonders of the world,” Maria sighed, a faint trace of jealousy in her tone. “I am sure I would never find fault with anyone who was kind to you, Mr. Warrington — though you must not be angry if I own I envy them, getting to sit by your bed and nurse you while you were ill, when I — I had to leave you to run errands for my aunt.”

“You dear, good Maria!” Harry said, pressing her hand to his arm.

“No, I am not dear or good,” she protested, drawing back a little. “See there! Your black servant is walking yonder with a whole crowd of other livery wretches, heading for the tea-gardens to fuddle and get as tipsy as their masters. That dreadful Mr. Morris was perfectly drunk when I came to fetch you after your accident, and he frightened you half out of your wits.”

“I had just won three hundred guineas off him and Lord March that very morning,” Harry boasted, his eyes sparkling. “What shall I buy for you, my dear cousin? I swore I would beat them fair at jumping for the honour of Virginia, and I did it. With a week’s practice more I do believe I could leap two full feet farther.”

Maria was charmed by the triumph of her young champion, though she shook her head in warning. “You must beware of play, child. You know it has been the ruin of all our family. My brother Castlewood, Will, our poor father, even my own aunt Lady Castlewood herself — every last one of them fell prey to it. And as for my Lord March, he is the most ruthless, successful gamester in the whole of the British peerage.”

“I am not afraid of him, nor of Jack Morris either,” Harry said, fingering the crisp notes in his pocket again. “What games do they play at Aunt Bernstein’s? Cribbage, all-fours, brag, whist, commerce, piquet, quadrille? I am ready for any of them. Hark — the church bells are striking seven already!”

“And you are eager to run off to the cards at once,” Maria said, her voice turning plaintive. “You do not care to walk with your poor cousin any more. Not long ago, you would have chosen this stroll over any game.”

“Hey, youth is youth, cousin!” Harry laughed, tossing his dark head. “A young fellow must have his fling!” He strutted beside her for a few paces, glowing with confidence, health, and eagerness for every pleasure the evening promised. Only a day prior, he had been perfectly happy to sit and chat with Theo and Hester Lambert and their good mother over tea and cake, but the glitter of life, the temptation to shine and conquer, had wrapped itself around the lad. Like every young man before him, he seized the brimming cup of pleasure without a single thought of the throbbing headache he would wake to find the next morning.

As they talked, the fiddlers on the Parade’s open orchestra struck up a raucous squeak and tune as they tuned their strings for the evening’s public concert. Maria knew her aunt the Baroness was awake and settled for the night, and that her own duties as hostess called her back to the house. Harry never spared a thought for the quiet drudgery of Maria’s life, tending the whims of the sharp-tongued old Baroness day in and day out. He never pitied her. He was not thinking of her at all. Though when his riding accident had befallen him, she had suffered a far sharper pain than any he had borne, and he had scarcely ever been absent from her thoughts, which she had long learned to bury beneath smiling, dutiful hypocrisy, as all women of her station learn to do. I know, my very proper Mrs. Grundy, you are ready to call her a foolish old maid for pining after a boy half her age. But do you suppose fools’ caps only fit heads crowned with jet-black or auburn curls? Be gentle with us elderly sinners, you paragon of good sense! It is no less true that late crops of wild oats sprout thick and tall on grey stalks, than that early harvests ripen in the sun of youth — and from long observation of myself and my neighbours, I can swear that wild oats grow right up to the very last days of the year.

Madame Bernstein and her household had drawn all the heavy curtains across the windows while the sun was still high and light, as if determined to tuck the daylight into bed early so they might give their full attention to their cards, their wax candles, their tea and spiced negus and sugary refreshments. Chair after chair pulled up to the Baroness’s door, depositing ladies more or less thickly painted, patched, and draped in rich brocade. The gentlemen soon followed, in their finest evening raiment: Mr. Poellnitz wore the largest star and the most heavily embroidered coat of any man in the room. When Lord March and Ruglen arrived, he bore no resemblance at all to the rough jockey Harry had befriended at the White Horse tavern. His tight brown scratch wig was gone, replaced by a neatly curled feather-top bag-wig dusted with grey powder, his leather jockey breeches swapped out for an elegant sky-blue French suit stitched with silver thread. Jack Morris wore an almost identical wig and near-matching suit, for the pair styled themselves inseparable. Young Mr. Wolfe arrived in attendance on the celebrated beauty Miss Lowther, and her aunt, who was as devoted to cards as every other soul of quality in Tunbridge Wells that season.

When Lady Maria Esmond made her appearance, it was plain Madame Bernstein’s grousing about her faded looks had been nothing but spite. Her figure was remarkably fine, and her gown was cut to show it off to full advantage. Her complexion was naturally very fair, set off by a dark frilled silk ribbon clasped with a large ruby that made the skin of her neck look like sculpted snow. Her cheeks were no brighter rose than every other lady in the room, who all openly bought their rouge from the perfumer’s shops on the high street. A pair of artfully placed patches only added to the glow of her charms. Her hoop skirt was no wider than the absurd iron crinolines ladies wear in our own day, and while the whole costume seems absurd to modern eyes, it was altogether pleasing to all who beheld it. Suppose our modern ladies took to wearing bangles and nose rings? I have no doubt we would laugh at the novelty, but not dislike the sight of them, and no lover would hesitate to lift that little ring aside to kiss the rosy lips beneath.

As for the Baroness de Bernstein, when she took the trouble to dress for a grand evening, she was still a magnificent, even terrifying sight to behold — handsome still, but heavy with melancholy, every line on her old face bearing the story of a hundred old passions long dead. Some old faces soften into gentle meekness in their final years, but not hers. Many eyes go completely dull in old age, the crow’s feet crinkling around irises that once flashed with scorn, anger, or love, but hers still held a faint flicker of the old fire. My fair young reader, if you are not the peerless Lindamira, queen of every ball, and at the end of the night you return to bed and meekly own you only had two or three partners while Lindamira had a whole crowd at her heels, console yourself: be grateful that when you turn fifty, you will still look as kind and pleasant as you do at eighteen. You will never have to step down from the six-horse coach of your own beauty and watch a younger woman climb into it while you trudge on foot. You will never have to forgo the homage you have always known, never watch your admirers drift away, never find your once brilliant saloons coated in dust and cobwebs, with the windows placarded “To Let” as you sit lonely in the dark. You may never have known grandeur, but you will never know the bitter sting of being abandoned. You may never have had a fortune of millions, but you will never suffer the humiliation of bankruptcy.

“Our hostess,” Lord Chesterfield muttered in a confidential whisper to his friend, unaware how loud his voice carried across the room, “puts me in mind of Covent Garden as I knew it in my youth. Back then it was the very heart of the fashionable west end, home to all the great families. Now? Every nobleman’s old house is a gaming den, and you can walk in with a friend and order a bottle of wine for sixpence.”

“Hey, a bottle and a tavern are very fine things in their way,” Lord March shrugged. “I was not born before the Georges took the throne, though I mean to live to a hundred. I have never known the Bernstein as anything but an old woman, and hang me if I can guess where she spent all her supposed beauty.”

“No, hang me too, how did she spend it?” Jack Morris cackled. “Here is an empty table! Shall we sit down for a game? Keep that tiresome Prussian Poellnitz away, he never pays his debts. Mr. Warrington, will you take a seat for a hand?”

Harry and Lord Chesterfield found themselves partnered against Morris and Lord March. “You are too late to join us, Baron,” Chesterfield said as the elderly Prussian nobleman wandered towards them. “We have already sorted our game. What, have you forgotten Mr. Warrington of Virginia? The young gentleman you met in London last spring?”

“The young man I met at Arthur’s Chocolate House had dark hair, a little crooked nose, and was nowhere near as fine in appearance as this gentleman,” the Baron said with great presence of mind, to avoid reminding anyone of the petty altercation Harry had got into at the club months prior. “Warrington, Dorrington, Harrington? We continentals can never keep track of all your English names. I certify this gentleman is not the man I spoke of at dinner.” He gave Harry a friendly little nod, then sidled off to the far end of the room where Mr. Wolfe and Miss Lowther were deep in quiet conversation in a window embrasure.
