He proceeded to bore the Lieutenant-Colonel for twenty minutes with his opinions on the new Prussian drill manual that had just been introduced into King George II’s army — a subject Wolfe knew perfectly, but could not bring himself to care about in that moment, when he was far more interested in the beautiful young lady at his side.

At the start of the evening the Baroness greeted every guest personally, making small talk and performing the introductory courtesies. But as the rooms filled and every gaming table was occupied, she grew more and more restless, until she finally retreated with three of her oldest, closest friends to her own reserved corner table, where her major-domo was already waiting with a stack of cards and a full tray of negus. She sat down there resolutely, and never moved from her place or quit her game until the first cock crowed at dawn. The duty of tending to the new arrivals fell to Lady Maria, who did not care at all for cards, but dutifully performed the honours of the house, rustling past the whist table where her young cousin sat playing, over and over again, her eyes fixed wistfully on his face.

“Come over and cut the cards for us, Lady Maria,” Lord March called out to her as she drifted past the table. “Cut the pack and bring us luck! We have had none at all tonight, and Mr. Warrington is winning every last penny off us.”

“Harry, you are not playing for very high stakes, are you?” Maria asked timidly, resting her hand lightly on the back of his chair.

“Oh no, only sixpences a hand,” Lord March laughed, as he dealt the cards out.

“Only sixpences,” Jack Morris echoed, though his round, red face was so glum it was clear he had lost far more than a handful of pennies that night. Lord Chesterfield sat opposite Harry, sorting his cards with his usual calm, impassive face, and no man on earth could tell if the luck was running for or against him. A tiny annoyed curse slipped from Morris’s lips, and his partner snapped, “Hang it, Morris, play your cards and hold your tongue!” It was very strange that two grown men should be so agitated over wagers of only sixpence.

Maria, lingering behind Harry’s chair, could see his cards perfectly, and spotted a whole flock of trumps ranged neatly in his hand. She had not taken away his luck. She was glowingly pleased that the pack she had just cut had dealt him that perfect hand. As Lord March began to deal the next round, he said quietly to Harry, “The same bet as before, Mr. Warrington? Or shall we double it?”

“Anything you like, my lord,” Harry said, perfectly cool.

“Then we will say shillings a hand,” March said.

“Shillings it is,” Harry agreed, and the game went on.

The end of that night’s sport, and the run of luck that followed for days afterwards, can be fully gathered from the following letter, which was never delivered to its intended addressee, but later found its way across the Atlantic in the personal papers of Mr. Henry Warrington:

>
>
> Since all the joys your life at White’s amounts to are two bottles of Burgundy and a pack of cards, I take for granted you are roosting in London at this very moment, preferring smoke and faro to fresh air and haystacks out in the country. This note will be handed to you by the young gentleman I speak of below, and you will be charmed to make his acquaintance. He will play you at any game for any stake, at any hour of the night, and drink any reasonable number of bottles during the play. Mr. Warrington is no other than the Fortunate Youth all the newspapers and coffee-house gossips have been gushing about these past weeks. He has an estate in Virginia as big as Yorkshire, encumbered only by a mother who rules the roost there like a reigning sovereign. As the place is notoriously unhealthy, full of malarial fevers, let us hope Mrs. Esmond will take herself off soon, and leave this virtuous lad in undisturbed possession of his fortune. She is aunt to that scoundrel Castlewood, who never pays his play debts, unless he has behaved more honourably to you than he has to me. Mr. W. comes of very good stock, and we must make him a member of our society — if for no other reason than that I might win my own money back from him.
>
> He has had the very devil’s own luck here, and won everything he touched, even while that old card-playing beldam his great-aunt Bernstein lost every night at her own table. A few nights ago, when I first had the misfortune to make his acquaintance, he beat me fair and square at the high jump (he learned the trick out in the woods leaping away from bears, no doubt), won wagers off me and Jack Morris over my own body weight, then sat down to cards with us that very night and cleaned every one of us out. If you would kindly settle our last Epsom race accounts, please hand over 350 pounds to Mr. Warrington, which I still owe him after pretty well emptying my entire pocket-book. Lord Chesterfield has dropped six hundred pounds to him too, but his lordship does not wish word of it to get out, as he has sworn publicly to give up play and live cleanly from now on. Jack Morris, who has not lost quite so heavily as the two of us and can afford his losses far better (the fat churl has no house, no retinue to keep up, all his scoundrel father’s fortune sitting untouched in the bank), roars like a bull of Bashan every time he thinks of his losses. We played a second night in private, and our man Barbeau served us a very good dinner in a closed room. Mr. Warrington holds his tongue like a perfect gentleman, and none of us have breathed a word of our losses to anyone, but the whole town of Tunbridge Wells is gossiping about the Virginian’s winning streak anyway. Yesterday the actress Cattarina was as sulky as thunder, because I would not buy her a diamond necklace, and declared I was refusing her only because I had lost five thousand guineas

Three days after young Harry Warrington arrived at Tunbridge Wells, he was far and away the most talked-of, sought-after person in the whole giddy little watering place. No peer of the realm staying there drew half as much curious staring; even the Bishop of Salisbury himself was greeted with less deference than the 22-year-old colonial heir. Passersby on the high road turned on their heels to watch him walk past, country folk trundling into market gaped as if he was some sort of visiting royal, and matrons clustered by the assembly room doors fussed to draw him into their circles, slipping away to leave him alone with their simpering daughters the moment they could.

Every soul in the Wells knew down to the exact acre how much tobacco and pasture land he owned in Virginia, and to the last shilling his yearly rental income. At every tea table across the resort, people gossiped and tallied his recent winnings at the card tables, marveling at how intimately their neighbors’ affairs were known to strangers. The frenzy extended even to his servant: locals slipped Gumbo mugs of spiced ale and slices of cold venison pasty behind the tavern taproom, plying him for gossip about his master’s fortune. Mr. Gumbo grew round and sleek on the free treats, was elected head of the local Society of Valets, and spun wilder tall tales by the hour, claiming Harry owned whole rivers that flowed straight with rum and herds of wild deer bigger than any stag in all of England. No dinner, ball, or picnic was considered complete unless Mr. Warrington deigned to attend it.

The lad was half amused, half bewildered by this sudden tidal wave of popularity, and bore his new honors far better than most might have. Raised to think highly of himself as the heir to one of Virginia’s grandest estates, the constant admiration certainly stoked his natural self-satisfaction, but he never grew arrogant or bragged about his victories on the racecourse or at the tables. When local gentlemen challenged him to contests of skill, he acted by the odd, honor-bound code he’d brought from the colonies: it seemed to him that as the representative of Old Virginia, he could never back down from a fair contest against the best of the mother country, whether that contest was a horse race, a drinking bout, or a hand of cards. He had a strong head for liquor, a steady hand for games of chance, a perfect seat on horseback, and nerves of unflinching steel, and he won nearly every challenge thrown his way.

Aunt Madame de Bernstein, who gambled every night to make up for the losses she’d suffered the chapter prior, was absolutely delighted by her nephew’s triumphs and his sudden social cachet. He’d beaten Jack Morris at marksmanship, outridden Mr. Scamper in a three-mile match race, and within a few days of picking up a tennis racket for the very first time, he held his own against seasoned player Captain Batts. Even the famed professional gamesters Lords Chesterfield and March sang his praises, testifying to his cool head, good humor, and natural gentle breeding. Harry was no scholar, to be sure, but he wrote a clearer, more elegant hand than half the fops of London high society, and the unselfconscious naivete of his ignorance charmed his worldly old aunt. She had read widely in her day, could discourse brilliantly on Moliere and Mr. Fielding with literary guests, but she loved the glittering, messy, human world far more than any library, and would leave any half-finished novel mid-chapter the moment a card table opened up. She fussed over his wardrobe with fond delight, raiding her private stores of fine Mechlin lace for his ruffs and shirt cuffs, and gifting him a tiny sparkling diamond brooch to pin to his frilled shirt front. Before long, he was her undisputed favorite, outshining every other nephew and cousin in the family. Poor Lady Maria seemed almost glad of his success, pleased to see him outstrip her own unpleasant brothers, who no doubt shook in their boots with fear and envy every time they heard of Harry’s triumphs, and how fast he was winding his way into their wealthy aunt’s good graces.

By the end of his second week at Tunbridge Wells, Harry was a full-fledged celebrity. He knew every last member of the respectable upper class gathered there, and by no fault of his own, he soon found himself acquainted with the far less reputable set that orbited the town too. Was he really so wrong to take the world as he found it, to drink deep of the sparkling, brimming cup of pleasure the whole resort seemed to press into his hands? His old aunt, no rigid moralist and hardly a wholesome chaperone for a young man, only egged him on to enjoy himself. Had the French ballet dancer Cattarina sent him love letters, she would no doubt have told him to accept the invitations. Harry, though, still carried the quiet modesty of his colonial upbringing, the honest homespun decency of a place where large cities and their vices were almost unknown. He blushed like a girl at the daring, ribald jokes his new London friends cracked, and even Aunt Bernstein’s racier quips left him stammering so that she teased him constantly, calling him her little Joseph, her silly colonial simpleton.

But no one at the Wells gave him credit for that innocence. Harry had no idea he was not supposed to associate with the saucy Cattarina: he’d seen Lord March driving her around in his phaeton a dozen times, so he assumed she was a perfectly acceptable acquaintance. Barely anyone in the whole resort spoke a word of French, so he thought it kind to offer her his arm on the public promenade when the doctors ordered her to walk and drink the Tunbridge waters for her bad cough. When she paused at the toy shop window and fussed over a tiny enamel locket, his pockets full of recent winnings, he happily bought it for her. The next day it was a length of fine lace, which he also gave her. When she hinted next that she wanted a pair of expensive diamond drop earrings, he laughed off the request, shrewd enough not to waste his money on a trivial fancy.

No one gave him credit for that restraint, of course. Madame de Bernstein insisted on believing he was playing Don Juan, that he’d stolen Cattarina right out from under Lord March’s nose, and she teased poor Lady Maria about it constantly, just to twist the tender spinster’s heart and revel in her miserable, flustered silence. “Boys will be boys, my dear,” she’d cackle. “I won’t have Harry be the first milksop this family ever produced.” The bread Lady Maria ate at her aunt’s table often choked her, so bitter and indigestible did the old woman’s teasing make it.

Colonel Wolfe, meanwhile, was forever riding over from Westerham to court Lady Maria, so Harry hardly expected to see much of him, though he loved the officer’s quiet, thoughtful company far more than the ribald chatter of the gamesters and fops who surrounded him. Wolfe never babbled about cards, or horse pedigrees, or bragged about his hunting exploits, or gossiped about the latest scandal gripping high society. It was a loose, dissolute age: the open mistresses of the king were treated with deference by the greatest lords of the realm, and much of the nobility chased pleasure with a wild, reckless abandon that shocked quiet colonial sensibilities. Harry had fallen in with some of the wildest of that crowd, chaperoned by an old relative who lived right in the thick of their revels.

Harry did not notice at first how Wolfe began to avoid him, how their casual greetings grew colder and stiffer. He had no idea the stories spreading about him: that he was a drunkard, a habitual gamester, a blasphemer who mocked religion, a rake who kept a notorious ballet dancer in luxury. The tales drifted out of Tunbridge Wells all the way to honest Colonel Lambert’s household at Oakhurst, one bad story piling on top of another until the good man’s kind heart was heavy with grief, so heavy his whole family noticed his distress. He tried to hide it at first, but no anxious wife can be put off forever, and Lambert was forced to confess the awful gossip to his wife. Soon the whole household, Theo and Hester included, were crushed by the news. At first Hester flew into a white-hot rage, clenched her small fists, and swore she would not believe a single word of the wicked lies. But scandal almost always wears good, innocent people down, and before long they were all crying over the thought that the gentle, sweet-natured boy they had welcomed into their home was a hardened, profligate rake. Even the parson, when they took him into their confidence, preached a whole sermon the next Sunday denouncing the human weakness to believe the worst of one’s neighbors — but even he, and the whole kind-hearted household at Oakhurst, could not shake the conviction that Harry Warrington was lost.

Harry himself had no clue any of this was happening, until he walked off the tennis courts after a particularly good match and ran straight into Colonel Wolfe, who was just returning from a visit to Lady Maria. Harry held out his hand, and Wolfe took it, but his greeting was so icy that Harry could not miss it, especially when Captain Batts tipped his hat in salute and Wolfe barely grazed the brim of his own hat with his forefinger. The tennis captain walked away confused, leaving Harry to fall into step beside Wolfe. They walked on for a few minutes, Wolfe stiff, silent, and cold.

“I haven’t seen you these many days,” Harry said, breaking the silence.
“You’ve had other, far wilder companions to keep you occupied,” Wolfe said curtly.
“I’d rather be with you than any of them,” Harry protested.
“Then I ought to be far better company for you than some of the men you’ve been keeping,” Wolfe replied grimly. When Harry asked if he meant Captain Batts, Wolfe went on: “He was drummed out of the army for rascality years ago, and his reputation hasn’t improved a bit since. You could do far, far worse than stop calling him friend.”

Harry, bewildered, asked if he had somehow offended the colonel, if he had done anything to forfeit his regard. Wolfe spoke plainly: “I don’t like some of your friends. They are of rank and fashion far too high for a hardworking, poor soldier like me, and if you keep running with that crowd, all us steady, humdrum folk will have to drop your acquaintance. I am here courting an honorable lady, Mr. Warrington. I saw you yesterday walking openly arm in arm with that French ballet dancer, and you tipped your hat to me. I would rather, frankly, that you did not acknowledge me at all when you are in that sort of company.”

Harry’s face burned bright red. “Do you mean to say I must give up the honor of your acquaintance entirely?”
“I will ask you to, when you are in that woman’s company,” Wolfe snapped, using a sharp unprintable oath Shakespeare once put in Othello’s mouth.
“Great heavens, how dare you speak of any woman like that?” Harry cried. “That poor little thing is unprotected, barely anyone here speaks a word of her language! I speak a little French, so I offered her my arm. How was I to know her reputation was so dreadful?”

Wolfe stared at him, stunned. “You mean to say you do not know the whole town is telling the story that you won her from Lord March at the dice table? Every soul at the Wells has heard it. I heard it not an hour ago in the company of good Mr. Richardson the novelist, and the ladies there were calling you a colonial Lovelace, sent over to corrupt all the virtue in England.”

He laid out every single scandalous story circulating about Harry, every false accusation of drunkenness, gambling debauchery, and blasphemy. “I tell you all this,” Wolfe said, when he was done, “because I realized the moment you reacted to that last charge that you are innocent of nearly all the rest. I have done you a terrible wrong, Mr. Warrington, and I sincerely beg your pardon.” The two men shook hands, firm and sincere, all the hard feelings gone.

Harry easily refuted almost all the charges, though he owned that he enjoyed playing cards. It seemed to him no gentleman could turn down a fair challenge from his peers, especially when he was playing only with the money he had already won, and every last person in England but the Methodists gambled, even his own aunt. Wolfe did not argue with him at length, but he warned the lad plainly that an idle life spent racing horses, playing tennis all day and drinking and gambling all night, could never be a fulfilling one. “Every man is born to work,” he said. “You are a great landowner in Virginia: you ought to study the laws of your country, learn the trades and conditions of the people on your estates, prepare to serve as a magistrate for them. Honour is the aim of any gentleman’s life, and every man can serve his country one way or another. Idle bread is the most dangerous bread a man can eat. Cards and pleasure are fine for pastimes after work is done — not instead of work, all day long. Everyone calls you the Fortunate Youth, but I think you are Warrington the Unlucky, followed by nothing but idleness, flattery, and temptation on every side. May the Lord deliver you safely from all this so-called good fortune.”

Harry walked back to his aunt’s lodging with a heavy heart, telling himself he would not drink that night, would not sit down at the card table. But the jolly fellows at the communal supper passed the bottle round nonstop, and he could not be rude enough to refuse. Then Aunt Bernstein’s card table was missing a fourth player, and how could he turn down his own favorite aunt? He sat down as her partner, won hand after hand by some miracle of luck, and when the sun rose over the hills the next morning, he was still at the table, feasting on cold chicken and drinking sparkling champagne at dawn, the colonel’s warnings already slipping fast from his mind.

As long as there were eager card partners waiting for her at her lodgings and the Tunbridge Wells assembly rooms, Madame de Bernstein settled happily into life at the spa, splitting her days between sharp-tongued lectures for her nephew Harry and notching up steady wins at her regular rubber of whist.
At Harry’s age, nearly every spot feels bright and welcoming, so long as it offers lively company, fresh country air, and your fair share of sport and small diversions. Every pleasure tastes sweeter at twenty. We run out to meet joy at a full sprint, speculate on all the fun it will bring, and once a dance or a picnic or a long-awaited party is scheduled, count the days until it arrives. How coolly, how gently we greet those same delights when we reach the end of life’s long season! Madam, do you not recall your very first ball? Does your memory not wander back to that glowing past sometimes, when you sit resting against the wall watching your own daughters spin across the dance floor? For my own part, I can still remember when I thought it the height of delight to walk three miles out into the country and three miles back just to dine with old Captain Jones. Fancy wanting to tramp six miles now just to sup with Jones and drink his thin half-pay port! No doubt that wine was bought cheap from a tiny village vintner, but it was offered with a full, kind welcome, and youth lent it a richness that no aged bottle or seasoned man could ever match these days. *Viximus nuper* – we lived but recently, and none of us can afford to cast too harsh a eye on young Harry’s stretch of idle pleasure, not even his stern friend the Colonel of the Twentieth Regiment, James Wolfe.
O blessed idleness! Divine, lazy nymph! Hand me a novel as I curl up in my dressing-gown at three o’clock in the afternoon, mix me a sherry-cobbler, and set a cigar at my elbow! Dear, soft-smiling, slatternly enchantress! The world may heap cruel names upon you, swear your character away, and call you the Mother of Evil – but for all that, you are the very best company on earth!
Lord of March soon departed for his northern estates, and Lord Chesterfield found the Tunbridge mineral waters did nothing to ease his worsening deafness, so he retreated back to his quiet solitude at Blackheath. But scores of other fashionable gentlemen stayed behind to make merry, and young Mr. Warrington never lacked for companions at his regular table at the White Horse Inn. He picked up the ways of a man of fashion with remarkable speed: soon he could order an elaborate French dinner every bit as well as the most seasoned dandy out of St. James’s, chatted to innkeeper Monsieur Barbeau far more fluently in the man’s native French than most other spa visitors, and developed a sharp, refined taste for wine that let him tell a Clos Vougeot apart from a Romanee with barely a single sip. He was the uncrowned young king of the Wells, and the easy-going, worldly regulars who frequented the spot were hardly shocked by his growing reputation for gallantry and extravagance – the very reputation that had so alarmed Mr. Wolfe.
Though our Virginian moved full time amongst revellers, swimming in the same pleasure-seeking current as all the other loose, careless visitors, the boy had a natural shrewdness and stubborn core of honesty that kept him clear of the snares and traps so often laid for unwary young men of fortune. He almost never made foolhardy bets with the jolly idle fellows around him, and even the oldest, sharpest card sharps at the spa found they could barely trick him out of a farthing. He joined in every game, indoors and out, because he had a natural knack for athletic and playful contests, and could hold his own against almost any fair competitor. He was scrupulous to only play against men he knew to be honourable, and always settled his own debts on the spot the second a match ended. No, he would have cut a very poor figure at a stuffy university examination – but he possessed prudence, fierce loyalty, sharp common sense, overwhelming generosity, and dauntless personal courage, and he got no shortage of chances to prove what he was made of.
Take for instance the troublesome little opera dancer Cattarina, who had already landed him in so much trouble once before. When her importunate demands for money crossed the line Harry drew for his own generosity, he extricated himself from the opera siren’s advances with perfect coolness and grace, leaving her to cast her nets over some softer, easier mark. The girl’s hysterical mother showed up at his lodgings, swearing that a cruel bailiff had seized all her daughter’s trinkets for unpaid debt, and that her venerable old father was rotting in a London debtor’s prison. Harry told her plainly he had no dealings with bailiffs, that just because he’d enjoyed Cattarina’s company and bought her small trinkets and knick-knacks when she fancied them, he was under no obligation to pay off her family’s longstanding debts. He refused point blank to stand bail for her father in London, or settle her outstanding bills at Tunbridge.
The old woman first screamed at him, calling him a monster and an ungrateful wretch, then leered at him like a veteran of a hundred such scams and asked why he did not demand payment for the little attentions he’d lavished on the girl. At first Harry did not understand what she meant – but when the full, horrifying import of her offer landed, the honest young man rose up in utter revulsion. He told her that in his Virginia homeland even the native Iroquois would recoil from bartering a child’s honour for gold, bowed her ceremoniously to the door, and ordered his servant Gumbo to mark her face well and never let her cross his threshold again. She stormed off swearing vengeance, squawking that no Turk or Persian would ever treat a defenceless lady so, and she and Cattarina fled back to London as soon as their landlord would let them leave.
Harry faced perils of the gaming tables as well, of course. As the old saying goes, any man who plays at bowls has to expect a few rubbers. One evening after dinner at the ordinary, Harry declined to play piquet any longer with Captain Batts, and when the man roughly demanded his reason, Harry told him straight he only played against gentlemen who settled their debts as promptly as he did. He added that he would be more than happy to play any number of matches with Batts the second their outstanding little account was settled. The captain declared himself perfectly satisfied, and snuck out of the Wells the very next day without paying Harry or a single one of his other creditors.
Harry also got the chance to show his mettle when he thrashed a rude sedan chairman who had accosted elderly spinster Miss Whiffler one evening as she made her way to the assembly rooms. And when the malicious gossip about him and Cattarina was repeated by Mr. Hector Buckler, one of the most quarrelsome regulars at the Wells, Harry walked right up to him in the crowded pump room, where Buckler was regaling a whole circle of water-drinkers with the lie, and publicly told him the story was a total falsehood, and he would hold any man who repeated it accountable to him from that day forward.
So even though Harry did as the Romans did, living fully into the pleasure-seeking ways of Tunbridge Wells society, he proved himself a valiant, honourable Roman – running with the wolves, as the French phrase goes, even James Wolfe himself admitted he was as brave and true as the best of the pack. When Wolfe found out his young friend was entirely innocent of the ugly rumours he’d circulated, he lost no time in going to see the Lamberts and retracting every last odious charge he’d made against Harry.
The whole Lambert household burst with joy at Harry’s vindication, that bright, tender pleasure good people feel when a soul they care for is redeemed from unfair slander. Never had that little family been so happy – not even when they got the news that their son Tom had won his university scholarship – as when Colonel Wolfe rode over with the full account of his conversation with Harry Warrington.
“If you’d ridden up here leading a whole new regiment for me, James, I don’t think I could be any more pleased,” Colonel Lambert declared.
Mrs. Lambert called her two daughters in from the garden, kissed them both the second they stepped through the door, and blurted out the good news. Hetty jumped up and down for joy, and that night Theo played a series of dazzling, bright flourishes on the harpsichord that she had never managed to pull off before. When Dr. Boyle dropped in for their usual weekly backgammon game, he could not make heads or tails of the glowing, giddy look on all their faces, until the three women burst into happy chorus telling him how right his recent sermon had been, and how dreadfully they had all wronged that poor, dear, good young Mr. Warrington.
“What say we, my dear?” Colonel Lambert leaned over the table and whispered to his wife. “The hay’s all in, we won’t be cutting the corn for another fortnight, the horses are standing idle in the stables. What if we…”
His wife clapped her hands over his, beaming. “My dearest Martin! That’s the very thing!”
“What’s the very thing, mother?” yelled young Charley, home for his Bartlemytide holidays.
“The very thing is that we’re going in to supper right now,” Mrs. Lambert laughed. “Come along, Doctor! We’re opening a bottle of the best wine tonight, to drink a toast to repentance for every soul that speaks ill of a good young man without proof.”
“Amen to that,” the Doctor smiled, lifting his glass. “With all my heart.”
And so the warm, worthy little family trooped off to their supper, full of joy and bright, unspoken plans.

One fine afternoon, Harry Warrington turned up for his customary dinner at the White Horse ordinary, and was delighted to find the whole common room roaring with laughter at the jolly, rosy countenance of Parson Sampson, who held the table enthralled with a string of racy bons mots. Though he had not ventured up to London for months, the parson carried all the latest town gossip — or what passed for it among the country squires who frequented the tavern: the goings-on at the King’s Kensington palace, the latest scandals out of Pall Mall, how Admiral Byng was passing his days in prison, who called on him, the Newmarket race odds, and the reigning toast of Covent Garden. Sampson’s facts were rarely perfectly accurate: he might misname a nobleman’s mistress, mix up which lady had run off with an actor, or muddle the names of the officers who quarrelled at Marybone Gardens — but none of his audience cared a whit. So long as the stories were lively and charmingly wicked, their correctness was of no moment. A century past, the worldly parson who haunted the tavern, the racecourse, the theatre pit, and the fringes of fashion was no oddity in English society: he could shout loudest in the hunting field, sing the jolliest drinking song after a Covent Garden performance, and handle a hand of cards at the gaming table as deftly as any gentleman present.

Whether from a flush of modesty or the glow of claret, Sampson’s red cheeks burned even brighter when he spotted Harry enter. He whispered a line from Horace to the gouty country squire at his side, stumbled over his own feet in his haste, and seized Harry’s hand with warm enthusiasm. “My dear sir, my very dear sir, my conqueror at spades, clubs, and hearts too — I am overjoyed to see your honour looking so fresh and well!” he cried. Harry returned his greeting gladly, and complimented the parson on his cheerful, ruddy looks. The squire in the drab homespun coat edged with gold lace shifted over to make space for Harry beside him, and called for Sampson to return to his own seat across the table to finish his story about Lord Ogle and the grocer’s wife — only for his sentence to end in a loud oath and yell when the flustered parson trod full force on his aching gouty toe.

Sampson begged his pardon, then turned back to rattle off every bit of Castlewood news to Harry, loud enough for the whole room to hear: Lord Castlewood sent his cousin his warmest affectionate remembrances, and had given him special orders to travel down to Tunbridge Wells to look after Harry’s morals; the Viscountess and Lady Fanny were gone to Harrogate to take the waters; Will had won a handsome sum at Newmarket and was off on a visit to a royal duke; even the Castlewood housemaid Molly had cried her eyes out at the departure of Harry’s valet Gumbo. He assured the gathered guests that all Hampshire was gossiping of Harry’s remarkable string of successes at Tunbridge, casting a knowing, arch little look as he implied his popularity with the ladies, and that the whole Castlewood household only hoped he would not grow too spoiled to enjoy their quiet Hampshire home.

By and by the rest of the diners drifted off to their own pursuits, leaving Harry and the parson alone with their bottles. “I have already had more than my fair share of wine,” Sampson laughed, “but that is no reason I should not have plenty more!” He tossed off toast after toast, bumper after bumper, to Harry’s great amusement, and after a while Harry grew so warm-hearted and generous that he insisted Sampson must not waste his coin on a separate tavern room — there was a perfectly good spare chamber in Harry’s own lodgings, free of charge. He ordered Sampson’s trunk sent up at once, and bade Gumbo make his guest as comfortable as possible, before dragging the parson down to the stables to show off his new horses. There, Sampson spotted the very horse he had lost to Harry at cards months prior; the old beast whinnied happily and nuzzled against his former master’s coat, and Harry swore by Jupiter that the horse was Sampson’s again, a gift no strings attached. The parpson seized Harry’s hand to bless him, then flung his arms around the horse’s neck, weeping tears made half of Bordeaux and half of pure grateful joy.

Arm in arm, the two friends trundled over to Madame Bernstein’s apartments, trailing the mixed scent of stables and claret behind them, their cheeks flushed and eyes bright enough that no one could mistake what had been their afternoon amusement. The old baroness received Harry’s companion pleasantly enough: she found Sampson’s raucous broad jokes and rattling good talk an amusing novelty, like a highly spiced new dish her cook might serve the first two or three times it was prepared. The only amusement she never tired of, she insisted, was cards. “The cards never cheat,” she would say. “A bad hand tells you the truth to your face, and there is no flattery in the world sweeter than a good suite of trumps.” When she was in high spirits about to sit down to a high-stakes game, she would laughingly bid her nephew’s chaplain say grace before the “feast”. Sampson had avoided her table at first, slapping his empty pockets comically and complaining that her play was far too high for a poor clergyman, who had already emptied his purse playing cards against Harry back at Castlewood. But Harry, whose purse was overflowing with guineas and whose heart overflowed with generosity, happily pressed a handful of ready coin on him, and the parson was soon seated at the card table beside her ladyship.

Harry adapted to Tunbridge fashionable life with remarkable speed. His suits were still cut from plain black cloth, but they were of the finest possible make and quality. “Give him a star and ribbon, let his stocking fall down a little, and his hair fall over his shoulder, and he would make a perfect Hamlet,” the gay old Duchess of Queensberry joked. “I have no doubt he has already been the death of a dozen Ophelias, back home among the American Indians.” His lace and linen were as fine as his aunt could have wished. He bought gilded shaving plates from the Pantiles toy vendors, and two magnificent rich brocade morning gowns in which he lolled at ease sipping chocolate each morning. He collected custom swords and carved walking canes, French watches with painted backs and diamond settings, and enamel snuffboxes crafted by the most skilled Parisian artisans. Every day his anteroom was crowded with grooms, jockeys, and tradesmen waiting to see him, all ushered in one by one by Gumbo, who acted as master of his household — and no single negro could possibly have tended all of Harry’s new fine possessions, let alone his stable of horses and the custom postchaise he had just purchased.

Harry also applied himself to mastering all the accomplishments proper for a gentleman of his station. A French fencing master and a French dancing master resided in Tunbridge that season, and Harry attended their lessons diligently, soon growing skilled enough with the foil to hold his own against his instructor, and moving through the steps of a minuet so gracefully that Lady Maria — herself an elegant dancer — sighed and admitted no gentleman at the royal court could move through the dance half so finely. When a riding master offered to teach him to “school” the great war horse, Harry laughed it off. His Virginia riding seat was more than good enough, he said, and he had yet to meet a man in all of the fine company of England who could ride half as well as his friend Colonel George Washington, out at Mount Vernon.

Sampson meanwhile was living better than he had in years. He knew the world, and told far more of it than he knew, and Harry, barely twenty, adored his old college jokes, stale puns, and travel anecdotes sloshed through with the wine of a hundred dinner tables. A hundred years ago — and we may be certain no such people exist today, in our blessed Victorian age — there was a class of grown men in London who loved to attach themselves to fashionable young men new to town: act as their unofficial mentors to Covent Garden, escort them to the gaming tables, drink lemonade while their young charges drank burgundy, and stagger home perfectly sober when the young gentleman reeled off to fight the night watch. Sampson was a perfect specimen of this now-extinct breed of companion, and he thrived on Harry’s generosity as cheerfully as any man could. He soon became Harry’s confidential guide, friend, chaplain, and informal secretary, as the following carefully preserved letter from the Warrington family archives makes plain:

>
> Mrs. Bligh's Lodgings, Pantiles, Tunbridge Wells.
> August 25th, 1756.
>
> HONOURED MADAM -- Your honoured letter of 20 June, per Mr. Trail of Bristol, has been forwarded to me duly, and I have to thank your goodness and kindness for the good advice which you are pleased to give me, as also for the remembrances of dear home, which I shall love never the worse for having been to the home of our ancestors in England.
>
> I writ you a letter by the last monthly packet, informing my honoured mother of the little accident I had on the road hither, and of the kind friends who I found and whom took me in. Since then I have been profiting of the fine weather and the good company here, and have made many friends among our nobility, whose acquaintance I am sure you will not be sorry that I should make. Among their lordships I may mention the famous Earl of Chesterfield, late Ambassador to Holland, and Viceroy of the Kingdom of Ireland; the Earl of March and Ruglen, who will be Duke of Queensberry at the death of his Grace; and her Grace the Duchess, a celebrated beauty of the Queen's time, when she remembers my grandpapa at Court. These and many more persons of the first fashion attend my aunt's assemblies, which are the most crowded at this crowded place. Also on my way hither I stayed at Westerham, at the house of an officer, Lieut.-Gen. Wolfe, who served with my grandfather and General Webb in the famous wars of the Duke of Marlborough. Mr. Wolfe has a son, Lieut.-Col. James Wolfe, engaged to be married to a beautiful lady now in this place, Miss Lowther of the North -- and though but 30 years old he is looked up to as much as any officer in the whole army, and has served with honour under his Royal Highness the Duke wherever our arms have been employed.
>
> I thank my honoured mother for announcing to me that a quarter's allowance of 52l. 10s. will be paid me by Mr. Trail. I am in no present want of cash, and by practising a rigid economy, which will be necessary (as I do not disguise) for the maintenance of horses, Gumbo, and the equipage and apparel requisite for a young gentleman of good family, hope to be able to maintain my credit without unduly trespassing upon yours. The linnen and clothes which I brought with me will with due care last for some years -- as you say. 'Tis not quite so fine as worn here by persons of fashion, and I may have to purchase a few very fine shirts for great days: but those I have are excellent for daily wear.
>
> I am thankful that I have been quite without occasion to use your excellent family pills. Gumbo hath taken them with great benefit, who grows fat and saucy upon English beef, ale, and air. He sends his humble duty to his mistress, and prays Mrs. Mountain to remember him to all his fellow-servants, especially Dinah and Lily, for whom he has bought posey-rings at Tunbridge Fair.
>
> Besides partaking of all the pleasures of the place, I hope my honoured mother will believe that I have not been unmindful of my education. I have had masters in fencing and dancing, and my Lord Castlewood's chaplain, the Reverend Mr. Sampson, having come hither to drink the waters, has been so good as to take a vacant room at my lodging. Mr. S. breakfasts with me, and we read together of a morning -- he saying that I am not quite such a dunce as I used to appear at home. We have read in Mr. Rapin's History, Dr. Barrow's Sermons, and, for amusement, Shakspeare, Mr. Pope's Homer, and (in French) the translation of an Arabian Work of Tales, very diverting. Several men of learning have been staying here besides the persons of fashion; and amongst the former was Mr. Richardson, the author of the famous books which you and Mountain and my dearest brother used to love so. He was pleased when I told him that his works were in your closet in Virginia, and begged me to convey his respectful compliments to my lady-mother. Mr. R. is a short fat man, with little of the fire of genius visible in his eye or person.
>
> My aunt and my cousin, the Lady Maria, desire their affectionate compliments to you, and with best regards for Mountain, to whom I enclose a note, I am, -- Honoured madam, your dutiful son,

Scrawled at the foot of the letter in Madam Esmond's sharp, looping hand was a note:
From my son. Received October 15 at Richmond. Sent 16 jars preserved peaches, 224 lbs. best tobacco, 24 finest hams, per Royal William of Liverpool, 8 jars peaches, 12 hams for my nephew, the Rt. Honourable the Earl of Castlewood. 4 jars, 6 hams for the Baroness Bernstein, ditto ditto for Mrs. Lambert of Oakhurst, Surrey, and 1/2 cwt. tobacco. Packet of Infallible Family Pills for Gumbo. My Papa's large silver-gilt shoe-buckles for H., and red silver-laced saddle-cloth.

Tucked inside the first letter was a second, far messier note, written for Mrs. Mountain:
> For Mrs. Mountain.
> What do you mien, you silly old Mountain, by sending an order for your poor old divadends dew at Xmas? I'd have you to know I don't want your 7l. 10, and have toar your order up into 1000 bitts. I've plenty of money. But I'm obleaged to you all same. A kiss to Fanny from -- Your loving HARRY.

Another note in Madam Esmond's handwriting sat below it:
This note, which I desired M. to show to me, proves that she hath a good heart, and that she wished to show her gratitude to the family, by giving up her half-yearly divd. (on L500 3 per ct.) to my boy. Hence I reprimanded her very slightly for daring to send money to Mr. E. Warrington, unknown to his mother. Note to Mountain not so well spelt as letter to me. -- Mem. to write to Revd. Mr. Sampson desire to know what theolog. books he reads with H. Recommend Law, Baxter, Drelincourt. -- Request H. to say his catechism to Mr. S., which he has never quite been able to master. By next ship peaches (3), tobacco 1/2 cwt. Hams for Mr. S.

The two Warrington sons and their formidable mother have long been dust, now. How then to explain that the formal letter home to Madam Esmond is almost perfectly spelled, save for one tiny grammatical slip, while the playful little note to the old family nurse is dotted with charming misspellings? It takes no great detective to guess: the first letter was rewritten and corrected by Sampson, Harry's informal tutor, for his mother's careful eyes. The little note to Mountain Harry dashed off in a hurry, half distracted by a pretty milliner's girl passing the window, or a dancing bear with a tabor parading across the common, or a jockey trotting under his balcony to show off a new horse. There are days when the best of us misspell a word or fumble a grammar rule, after all.

As for the folk who cry out that Harry was hypocritical to send such a demure, prim letter home to his mother, when he spent his days drinking, gambling, and running about with his friends? No young person alive has never written home with a carefully edited account of their doings, to avoid worrying their parents. No parent alive, if they are honest, ever expected their grown son to be perfectly meek and decorous the moment they step outside their front door. It is the gentle, amiable, virtuous hypocrisy that makes the bond between generations work. The parent is king or queen of their castle, and expects their household to treat them with the deference due their rank; and once the young folk are out of their sight, they can dance, skip, tumble, and eat their fill of cakes and ale, as all young people have always done. No one ever tells their dear grandmamma every last silly, merry prank of their youth — and no grandmamma, for all her loud protests that she was perfectly well-behaved in her own springtime, was ever quite as good as she claims to have been.

Every reader who has followed Harry Warrington’s adventures already knows the full, innocent truth of his brief, awkward entanglement with the luckless little dancer Cattarina—but not a single one of the chattering old ladies clustered around the tea tables of Tunbridge Wells believed it. They were all fully convinced the young Virginian was every bit as wild, dissipated, and reckless as the most hard-living young nobleman of the highest rank, and none was more certain of his guilt than his own great-aunt, Madame de Bernstein.

The wily old baroness had long ago lived life by the Roman rule of “do as the Romans do,” and it suited her perfectly to imagine her handsome young nephew cut from the same libertine cloth as the rest of high society. She ate up every scrap of gossip about his supposed Lovelace-esque exploits with greedy, complacent delight. Harry had already won the whole Wells over with his impromptu musical evenings and his courteous, gallant attentions to all the ladies far more respectable than the forgotten Cattarina, so the old woman soon set aside all her old worries about his silly, fledgling Castlewood love affair, and slackened her tight vigilance over her niece, Lady Maria.

Selfishness settles easy into the bones of the elderly: the Baroness had her card games, her elaborate dinner parties, and the constant throbbing of her rheumatism to occupy her, and those once-lively suspicions of a romance between Maria and Harry dozed off into lazy, careless inattention. Perhaps she assumed the danger had long passed, perhaps she simply no longer cared if it lingered, or perhaps the sharp, sly Lady Maria—far older than most girls who learned the art of dissembling—had completely cajoled, soothed, and misled the aging “dragon” placed in charge of her. Dragons grow soft in their old age, you know: their fangs fall out, their scales thin to the point any halfway competent knight can slip a lance through, their claws can do no more than pat feebly against skin, and their venom stings far less than it once destroys. I have met any number of these former society destroyers of men and women in my time, and watched them drag their languid tails back to their caverns at dusk, far too feeble to ruin a reputation these days, let alone gobble up a fresh victim for breakfast as they did in their fierce, venomous youth.

If the quiet, pious Oakhurst family could not bring themselves to disbelieve the false reports of Harry’s misdeeds, why would Madame Bernstein—who had seen far more of the world’s evil in her one lifetime than all of the Oakhurst clan put together—be any more credulous than they? Every last old lady of her social circle gobbled down every story about Harry’s supposed dissipation, and was ready to swallow a dozen more the second they were whispered in the pump room. When little Cattarina returned to London, everyone said it was because the heartless Virginian had abandoned her for half a dozen different local ladies of rank and repute, all names passed from lip to lip behind closed fans. The wells of a century ago were melting pots: fashionables, respected matrons, women of half-repute, virtuous women, women of no virtue at all all danced to the same fiddles, drank from the same glasses, and chased health, amusement, or pleasure side by side, just as modern crowds do at Homburg or Baden today.

This flattering, wild reputation as a rakish conqueror of women eased the Baroness’s mind completely, chasing away all her old fears that Harry was still infatuated with Lady Maria. So unconcerned was she that when the family chaplain arrived to offer to escort her back to Castlewood, she declined outright, choosing instead to keep Maria close by her side, to chatter on to her about Harry’s wild, foolish extravagances, to smile and murmur that boys will be boys, and to confide that she already had her eye on several perfectly suitable young heiresses of just the right age and fortune to make Harry a proper wife. Poor Maria had to swallow every last one of these little pleasantries as best she could, grinding her teeth under her smile.

It was around this time that a famous French duke and marquis roamed across Europe and North America, leaving behind him a very unseemly volume of memoirs I would urge all gentle readers never to seek out. The man had played Don Juan across half the courts of the continent, listing the names of dozens of noble court beauties who he claimed had fallen to his charms, a fact that must make for extremely awkward reading for the great-grandchildren of those very women today, seeing their ancestresses’ frailties printed plain for all the world to gawk at. On his tour of North America, the great heartbreaker set about his usual siege—and failed to win a single conquest. For all the Europeans who raged about the supposed rudeness and barbarism of colonial manners, the plain truth is that American gentlemen are for the most part modest in speech, and their women far more virtuous than the rakehells of European high society had ever prepared to find.

Harry Warrington had brought all that quiet colonial modesty over to England with him. He heard all the free, coarse talk of the pleasure-seeking men around him, but mostly sat silent through their chatter; he never made a crude double entendre in front of a lady, never bragged of a single romantic conquest, and grew shy and awkward whenever other men recounted theirs. Parson Sampson had noticed that modesty back at Castlewood, when Harry grew visibly uncomfortable while his roguish cousin Will told his lewd, crude stories, and the Earl of Castlewood had curtly snapped at his brother to save his jokes for the Kensington school ushers, so they would not give unnecessary offence to their kinsman. That was the source of the chaplain’s old line *Reverentia pueris*—“respect for the boy”—on Harry’s very first night dining at the public ordinary. Sampson was no saint, he had led a rough, unruly life of his own, but he had enough decency not to needlessly hurt an innocent young man with his cynicism.

He was genuinely fond of Harry, too, after the boy had gifted him that fine thoroughbred horse. “You see, sir,” he told Harry once, “I am a man of the world, and I cannot afford to be any more particular than my neighbours. *Video meliora, deteriora sequor*—I see the better path, but follow the worse, as we used to say at college. I have a little sister Patty off at boarding school not far from here, and if I can manage to watch my tongue around her and expect others to do the same, surely I can extend that same courtesy to you.”

The chaplain sang Harry’s praises nonstop to Madame Bernstein, who was happy to listen: she was as fond of the boy as she was capable of being fond of anything, charmed by his good looks, his fearless bearing, the way a ready blush would rise to his cheek, his deep rich voice, and the amusing mix of shrewdness and simplicity that would have tired her to death if he had been witty or learned or overly clever. “We must find him a good wife, chaplain,” she said to Sampson. “I have two or three young ladies in mind who will suit him perfectly. We shall set him up here in England—he will never bear to go back to his so-called savages in the colonies, or his little Methodist mother, ever again.”

Sampson had his own very personal stake in that plan, of course. He had spoken to the Earl of Castlewood before they left, who had promised him a fine, comfortable living and a generous stipend if he could nudge Harry and Lady Maria into the match the Earl wanted. Sampson had every intention of earning that reward, and set about watching for the perfect moment to turn his influence to use.

The chaplain made for delightful company: full of high spirits, good humour, a hearty appetite for fun, and no pretensions to false sanctimony. He never offended Harry with unnecessary vulgarity, choosing only to introduce the boy to the milder, harmless joys of high society—cockfights, shooting matches, card games, gallops across the common, all the while keeping his conversation decent, far more focused on amusing the boy than leading him astray. Sampson had spent his whole life as a professional “toad-eater,” ever since he first entered university as a poor servitor boy scheming his way up in the world, and he was proud to be seen at Harry’s side as his humble retainer, giving orders to his tradesmen, acting as his unofficial aide-de-camp, and gossiping about his young Virginian patron all across the Wells.

“What a reputation they have saddled you with here, sir!” Sampson laughed as he burst back into Harry’s rooms one afternoon fresh from the coffee house. “The Duc de Richelieu himself never won half so many conquests!”

“Who is this Richelieu you speak of? I never fought at Minorca in my life,” blurted honest Harry, who had never heard of the French duke’s famous military and romantic victories.

Sampson explained the joke, then went on to tell Harry the whole town was gossiping that the pretty newly arrived widow Patcham was desperate for him, that Mrs. Hooper had run off with him so openly her alderman husband had dragged her straight back to London to get her away from him.

Harry’s face flushed bright scarlet with rage. “Who dares say such things? I will meet any man who spreads those lies and confound the villain!” he thundered, pacing back and forth across the carpet.

“I would not dare show him to you,” Sampson cackled. “He would come off far the worse for it.”

“It is a shameful thing to talk away the good name of any man or woman as people do here,” Harry fumed. “Back in Virginia a man’s ears would not be safe for half such slander. Only a few months before I left home, three brothers shot a man dead for speaking ill of their sister.”

“Served the rascal right!” Sampson nodded.

“They already spread that old calumny about me and that poor little French dancing-girl Cattarina,” Harry went on. “Wicked, isn’t it? The very same lies they spread about Lord March, too. What if these stories got back to my mother? It would break her heart, I swear it. What do these people think I am? A seducer? They might as well call me a horse thief or a housebreaker. I vow I will cut the ears off any man I catch saying such things!”

“I have read that the Grand Seignior of Turkey sometimes has bushels of ears sent in to his court,” Sampson laughed. “If you punished every person here who has spread slander against you or anyone else, you would fill whole baskets full of them!”

“And so I will, too, the moment I lay eyes on them!” Harry swore.

They headed off to their usual dining spot shortly after that. That was an age when heavy drinking was far more common than it is in our more polished modern day, and Harry had picked up a taste for claret and toasts from the British army officers he had befriended in the colonies before he came over, who considered it a point of honour never to refuse a glass or a cheer. They drank through bottle after bottle, naming a favourite lady with each toast, the claret warming their blood, loosening their tongues, bringing them to that perfect sweet spot every wine lover knows: the moment wit glows, generosity swells, and every secret you have ever held back fights to come spilling out of your mouth before you pour that one extra glass that spoils the whole state of grace, leaving you with a throbbing head the next morning and no memory of all the grand, brave promises you made.

As the last of the other diners filtered out, Sampson leaned across the table, his eyes bright. “I am glad to know the truth of your conduct with that Cattarina girl, Mr. Warrington, truly glad from my soul. You have shown you can rise above calumny and resist temptation. Ah, my dear sir, not all men are so fortunate. What excellent wine this is! Your toast, if you please?”

“I give you Miss Fanny Mountain, of Virginia,” Harry said, filling his bumper to the brim, his thoughts flying thousands of miles back to his childhood home.

“One of your American conquests, I assume?” Sampson teased.

“Nay, she is only ten years old,” Harry said. “I have never made any conquests at all in Virginia, Sampson.”

“True gentlemen never kiss and tell, sir,” Sampson grinned.

“I neither kiss nor tell. It is not the custom of our country to ruin young girls or keep the company of low women,” Harry said proudly, his face glowing. “We Virginian gentlemen honour women, and never wish to bring them to shame. The little lady I just named has lived in our family since she was an infant, and I would shoot any man who did her the smallest wrong, by Heaven I would!”

“Your sentiments do you nothing but honour! Let me shake your hand!” Sampson cried, squeezing Harry’s palm hard. “This is honest friendship you feel, not a poor retainer fawning on his rich patron! With wine this good, all men are equal, all men are rich while it lasts! Tom Sampson is just as wealthy with his full bottle as you are with all the thousands of acres of your Virginian estate!”

“Then let us have another bottle of riches,” Harry laughed, calling over the waiter for another case of yellow-seal claret.

“Capital! Capital! You speak French beautifully, Mr. Harry!” Sampson cheered.

“I speak it well enough for Monsieur Barbeau the waiter to understand what I want,” Harry said.

“You do everything well, that is why everyone here is so convinced you have won the hearts of half the ladies in the Wells,” Sampson said.

“There you go again with the ladies!” Harry groaned. “I hate these stupid lies, why must everyone blacken a gentleman’s name for no reason?”

“Well, at the very least, there is one lady whose preference for you I saw plain as day,” Sampson said, leaning in.

“Who do you mean?” Harry asked, flushing so red his ears burned.

“I name no names. A poor chaplain has no business prying into his betters’ private affairs, or their secret feelings,” Sampson demurred.

“Feelings? What feelings, Sampson?” the boy pressed.

“I saw a certain respected, lovely lady at Castlewood show you every mark of preference. I saw a certain distinguished young gentleman show a very strong liking for her in return. I may well have been mistaken, and I beg your pardon if I overstep,” Sampson said.

“Oh, Sampson, Sampson!” Harry burst out, his voice cracking. “I have been miserable. I have been dying for someone to confide in, someone to ask for advice. You do know then… there has been something going on, something between me and… and some other lady?”

“I have watched it for a whole month now,” Sampson nodded.

“Confound you, sir—have you been spying on me?” Harry snapped, hot with anger.

“Spying? You two made no effort to hide it! Her ladyship was no better at dissembling than you were. You were always together: in the shrubberies, on the village walks, in the long galleries of the house. Plenty of other eyes besides mine saw you,” Sampson said.

“Gracious powers! What did you see, Sampson?” the lad cried.

“Nay, sir, I never kiss and tell,” the chaplain winked.

Harry’s face burned bright red. “Oh, Sampson,” he stammered. “Can I… can I trust you with all of it?”

“My dearest, most generous young friend!” Sampson exclaimed, squeezing Harry’s hand so tight his knuckles went white, rolling his eyes up toward the ceiling with unfeigned, drunken fervour. “You know I would shed my very heart’s blood for you!”

The long-guarded secret Martin Lambert had whispered into his wife’s ear at the close of the third-to-last chapter, the very news that sent the whole Oakhurst household into peals of delighted laughter, we finally reveal here. The hay was all stacked dry in the barn, the barley and wheat still too green to cut, and the farm work left no use for the plow horses for days on end. So Colonel Lambert, leaning back in his chair over supper, proposed that they harness those very workhorses to the old family coach, load all the children in, and make a jaunt to Tunbridge Wells, stopping only to pick up their good friend James Wolfe at Westerham along the way.

Mamma Lambert embraced the idea at once, and if she snuck a quick, loving kiss to the honest man who suggested it, no one there was fool enough to tease her for it. The children all jumped and cheered. The two girls darted straight up to their bedrooms to rummage through every chest for their finest finery: heavy calamanco gowns, glossy paduasoy overdresses, frilled falbala hems, furbelow trims, wool capes, cardinal cloaks, loose sacque gowns, soft negligees, lace solitaires, ribbons by the handful, full draped mantuas, clocked silk stockings, and glossy high red-heeled shoes, all chattering a mile a minute as they laid out every article of their toilet. Mamma hauled her own rarely-worn best brocades from the deep cedar presses where they only came out for weddings and rare feasts, before going back to rest between sachets of dried lavender. The Colonel pulled out his gold-laced tricorn, hand-embroidered waistcoat, and silver-hilted smallsword he had stowed away for formal occasions, while young Charley was gifted a holiday suit cut from the very wedding coat his father had worn decades before—Mrs. Lambert snipped it apart with a little soft sigh for the old days. The two plow horses, Ball and Dumpling, had their manes and tails tied with blue satin ribbon, and old Chump, the shaggy white cart horse, was rigged out as a unicorn leader to pull the heavy coach up the first five steep miles from Oakhurst to Westerham.

That ancient family carriage was famed across the whole shire: local legend said it had joined the procession that brought King George I across the Thames from Greenwich on his first arrival to claim the British throne. It had belonged to Lambert’s grandfather, and every member of the family had grown up convinced it was one of the grandest coaches in all three kingdoms. Their plowman Brian, an old ex-redcoat, sat on the driver’s box with Charley perched right beside him. All the precious new gowns were stowed in thick leather imperial trunks strapped tight to the roof, the Colonel’s matched pair of flintlock pistols were tucked in the carriage door pockets, and a heavy blunderbuss hung within Brian’s easy reach behind the box. No highwayman dared molested their little convoy, no overcharging innkeeper dared fleece the thrifty large family, for young Colonel Wolfe had already booked them a cheap, cozy lodging right across the road from Madame Bernstein’s usual Tunbridge Wells residence, and he rode ahead on horseback to escort them the last stretch of the journey.

They pulled up at their new lodgings on a soft golden Saturday evening, just as the Baroness was throwing one of her famous card routs. From their second-floor window, they watched sedan chair after sedan chair draw up at her door, setting down powdered beaux in gold-embroidered waistcoats and patched, brocaded ladies in full court dress. The sun had not yet set—our ancestors of that century started their entertainments early, tucking into suppers, punch, and cards any time after three o’clock in the afternoon right through to midnight or later. Hetty and Theo decided the view was almost as delightful as being invited to the party itself: they could spot every guest as they stepped inside, and peek through the Baroness’s open casements to watch the chatter and laughter unfold, with Colonel Wolfe whispering the names and titles of every notable person they recognized.

When the old Duchess of Queensberry passed by, Martin Lambert immediately burst out reciting lines from his favorite Matthew Prior, about “Kitty, beautiful and young.” “Just think, that old woman was once as young and pretty as you two girls!” he exclaimed.

“Like us, papa?” Hetty tossed her little head playfully. “We never pretended to be great beauties, after all!”

“Aye, just like you, you little baggage,” he laughed, teasing her with more lines from the same poem, about the young heroine wild to sneak off to the party, sick of the gentle restraints wise mamma laid on her. Hetty retorted that they had never been invited anyway, and if that was the best beauty the rout had to offer, the wit could not be much to write home about. They bantered back and forth about Prior’s verses until Hetty gasped, pressing her face to the glass and pointing down to the street below.

Theo waved a handkerchief at the figure they saw: it was Harry Warrington, the young Virginian, walking arm in arm with a plump, fine-robed clergyman, and the pair of them headed straight for Madame Bernstein’s door. Wolfe told them the clergyman, Mr. Sampson, had preached a brilliant if slightly theatrical sermon the previous Sunday. The family teased Wolfe that he seemed to spend every single day of the week at Tunbridge Wells, not just Sundays, and Mrs. Lambert said they would not send across the road to fetch Harry that night—he ought to enjoy his party undisturbed by a crowd of uninvited country relations. Theo murmured softly that she was glad Harry kept the company of such an eloquent clergyman, her quiet expression clear: she had never believed the wild rumors that some of the local gossips spread about him.

Then they spotted the Bishop of Salisbury, wearing his blue Garter ribbon, followed by his chaplain, and right behind him a gilded sedan chair topped with no less than five earl’s coronets, carried by porters dressed in heavy gold lace livery, preceded by three footmen in matching splendid livery. The Bishop, just about to step through the Baroness’s door, hurried back, bowing so low his powdered wig nearly slipped off his head, to offer his hand to the lady stepping down from the sedan.

Martin teased his wife and daughters a little with a few silly German phrases before explaining the heraldry they were looking at: the lady stepping down was the Countess of Yarmouth, the long-favored mistress of King George II. When the girls pressed him to know why the highest lords and bishops in the realm were all kowtowing to her, Mrs. Lambert quickly put a finger to his lips, stopping him before he named the line of royal mistresses stretching back centuries, to save her daughters’ cheeks from blushing bright red. The old republican Lambert muttered under his breath that it was a crying, unforgivable shame to see the highest clergy and proudest aristocrats in the land bowing and scraping to a painted foreign favorite.

Suddenly Wolfe jumped up from his chair, grabbed his hat, and ran straight out of the room. He had just spotted the young lady he was courting, Miss Lowther, walking across the Pantiles with her guardian, heading straight for the Baroness’s party. Theo turned away from the window looking quiet and grave, almost awestruck, while Hetty stayed right where she was, her cheeks flushed bright red with anger. “I’m thinking what I would do if I ever saw my own papa bowing and scraping to a woman like that,” she told her mother, when mamma came to lead her away to supper.

The hissing tea kettle boiled over the fire, and the whole family sat down to their simple evening meal, leaving Hetty in charge of the window sill. Charley ran out to the crowd gathered outside the Baroness’s house, spent his sixpence on a warm fresh cheese cake from Mrs. Brown’s tart shop, and came darting back to report that he had spotted the great Samuel Johnson beating the stone pillars of the Pantiles with his walking stick, drinking cup after cup of tea at twopence apiece. The women all jumped up to crowd the window when Charley added that Johnson was sitting with his friend Samuel Richardson, the famous author of *Clarissa*. The sun dipped below the rooftops, stars pricked out overhead, and the Baroness’s footmen lit the candles in the parlor across the way. The Lamberts watched a group of adoring lady readers tuck a wool shawl around Richardson’s neck and walk him home, and Theo sighed that he did not look half as grand as the hero Sir Charles Grandison from his own novels. Mamma said she almost wished they had not gotten a peek at their favorite writer at all.

Hetty called them back to the glass, and they saw Harry Warrington being formally presented to the Countess of Yarmouth, before the countess settled down to a card table with the Bishop, the Earl, and a fourth guest. Harry soon stepped into the window embrasure across the street, deep in conversation with his cousin Lady Maria Esmond, the very lady they had met briefly during her visit to Oakhurst. “Just look at those grand lace frills on his shirt!” Mamma laughed. “My dear, he’s not wearing any of the linen we stitched for him back home!” Colonel Lambert roused from his doze on the parlor sofa, told the girls they had no right to be prying and spying on their friend, and pulled the heavy curtains shut, bringing that quiet evening of peeking to an end.

It is worth noting, for no other reason than to mark the gentle contrast between the two households across the road from each other, that while Madame Bernstein and her guests—bishops, noblemen, dignitaries, and all the rest—gambled at cards, gossiped over champagne and roast chicken, and fawned over the king’s favorite Countess, the Lamberts knelt around their own plain dining table. Old Brian the coachman tiptoed in as quietly as his creaking old boots would let him, and Martin Lambert stood to read the evening prayer aloud, asking Heaven to light their path through the dark, and keep all of them safe through the perils of the night.

The whole household was up before dawn on Sunday morning, dressed in their new finery, Charley at their heels, tramping across the empty common and the quiet Pantiles long before any other guests in town were awake to eat their breakfast. It was Hetty who spotted Harry’s black servant Gumbo leaning out of an open window across the street, his hair still in curl papers, waving a feather duster to dust the furniture inside, flirting with the pretty cherry-cheeked milkmaid lingering under the sill. His hands sparkled with rings, and his coat was loaded down with trinkets gifted to him by the fine ladies of the town who adored him. Harry never showed his face at that window. Neither of the girls spoke of him as they walked, and when Hetty snapped at Charley for pestering everyone nonstop about breakfast, Theo laughed, pulled her little netted purse that her dearest school friend had stitched for her out of her pocket, and used her last sixpence to buy him another cheese cake when the shop opened.

The church was packed full of fine company: the old Duchess of Queensberry, Madame Bernstein, Lady Maria at her side, Wolfe singing the psalms out of the very same book as Miss Lowther, Mr. Richardson surrounded by a flock of adoring lady readers, and Samuel Johnson sitting amongst the charity children, knocking over a pair of small boys in leather breeches when he turned to bow at the altar for the Creed. Martin Lambert noticed Harry was not in his pew, and grumbled that it was a shame the young Virginian had skipped the service. Hetty tossed her head and pretended she had not noticed, but honest Theo admitted she had been sorry to see his empty seat.

When they got back to their lodgings, James Wolfe stormed in the door, his face dark with indignation. He had gone looking for Harry that morning, he told them, and found him still in his nightgown at a quarter before eleven, sitting cross-legged at a table playing piquet cards with Mr. Sampson the parson, finishing the game they had started the night before, while all the church bells were ringing for service. Hetty flared up at once, defending Harry fiercely, saying plenty of fine people played cards on a Sunday, even the King himself with that very Countess of Yarmouth they had watched from the window the day before. Wolfe told them he had taken the liberty of scolding both the parson and Harry for skipping service, and Hetty got so angry she spun around and ran out of the room, bursting into tears on the staircase.

Wolfe was mortified, and Mrs. Lambert comforted him, calling him the old childhood pet name of “Aunt Lambert” as she pressed his hand, while Martin whistled his favorite old folk tune “Over the Hills and Far Away” and Charley teased his father that whistling on a Sunday was rude, and begged to eat the last of Theo’s cheese cake. Theo ran out of the room after Hetty, and found her weeping so hard she could barely breathe. The two girls clung to each other, Hetty sobbing all her frustrations out against Theo’s soft shoulder.

Hetty claimed she had a headache and stayed in bed that afternoon, while the rest of the family walked out to enjoy the Sabbath sunshine on the common. There they found Madame Bernstein resting on a bench under a gnarled oak tree, Harry and Lady Maria sitting at her side. Harry ran straight over to greet them, his face glowing with pure unfeigned joy at seeing his old friends from Oakhurst. Theo thought he looked taller, and handsomer than she ever remembered seeing him, and she called him by his first name like he was her own brother. “Why did you not come find us earlier today, Harry?” she asked, chiding him gently with a raised hand, no rebuke in her kind face at all. “I never even guessed you were here!” he laughed.

Ah, dear friendly reader, wandering the world and stumbling through temptation, may you also be blessed with at least one or two pure, loving hearts to care for you, and pray for you, even when you are fool enough to stray.

The instant Martin Lambert, Colonel in his Majesty’s army, realized the small secret his youngest daughter’s trembling outburst had laid bare, his first surge of feeling was wrath towards the unknown lad who had stolen his Hetty’s heart right out from under his roof and out of the little family circle he had guarded so long. “A murrain on all scapegraces, be they English or heathen Virginian!” he roared to his wife that evening. “I wish this one had dashed his nose against any doorpost in the kingdom but ours.”

His gentle spouse Molly only smiled, laying a soft hand on his arm. “Perhaps it is our calling to cure him of being a scapegrace, my dear. That fall he took on our threshold feels almost providential, does it not? You laughed at me when I said so before, but if Heaven did not send that young gentleman to us, who did? It may well prove a blessing for every last one of us, that he came.”

“Ah, but it’s hard, Molly!” the Colonel groaned. “We cherish them, tend them through every fever, scrape and save every penny patching our own old coats so they might have what they want. We lie awake all night if they so much as complain of a headache, work from dawn till dark to grant every silly little fancy they take, and they call us their dearest pappy, their darling daddy, swear no father in the world is half so good. Then come Tuesday morning, I am king of my own house. By Tuesday evening some Prince Whippersnapper saunters through the door, and my reign is over. A whole lifetime of love and nurture is forgotten in a trice, all for a pair of blue eyes, a pair of lanky shanks, and a head of flaxen hair.”

“Is it not written that a woman shall leave all she knows to follow her husband?” Molly reminded him, her cheeks dimpling. “Our own courtship was scarcely three months long, you will recall, dear Martin.”

“Human nature, the jade, what can you do?” the Colonel sighed. “I do not deny I was over the moon when you left your father for me,” she added softly. “And you did your duty right well, my excellent wench! Perdition catch my soul, but I do love thee still, Molly!” the Colonel laughed, squeezing her hand. “But mark you: your father hated me, and rightly so, for stealing his treasure. And if I ever do get sons-in-law, I shall hate every last one of them, just as your father hated me.”

“Do not be absurd, Martin Lambert! Of course my girls will have husbands one day!” the matron cried, half indignant, half amused.

“Nay, my dear, think of the old rotten tooth in my left jaw,” he reasoned. “It is perfectly natural for that tooth to fall out eventually. But when the dentist yanks it, it is also perfectly natural for me to yell with pain. Do you suppose I love Hetty any less than that tooth, or that this does not hurt ten times worse?”

No woman, of course, ever truly resents the thought of her daughter marrying, no matter how fathers stamp their feet and rage at the son-in-law invading their home. Mothers and grandmothers live their own courtships all over again through their girls: they pull out the old laces and muslins packed in lavender at the back of their wardrobes, see the postillion’s white ribbons fluttering once more, and climb back into the postchaise for their own wedding day all over again.

“It will be a sad thing, parting with her,” Molly sighed.
“So you have already settled that, have you?” the Colonel teased. “Had I better head out to the grocer’s and order raisins and currants for the wedding cake right now?”
“And then I shall have to sail all the way to Virginia to visit her when she goes,” Molly went on. “How many miles is it to Virginia, Martin? Thousands, I should think.”
“A hundred and seventy-three thousand three hundred and ninety-one and three quarters by the nearest route, my love,” he replied gravely. “The one that cuts straight through Prester John’s kingdom. The other way takes you all around Persia—”
“Then give me the route with the least sea possible, I beg you! I cannot abide those horrid pitching ships!” Molly protested. “I only hope Rachel Esmond Warrington and I shall be better friends than we were at school. She had a very high spirit, that girl, back then.”
“Had we not best start stitching the baby-linen already, Mrs. Lambert?” her husband interjected, wide with mock wonder. Molly, for her part, saw no cause for wonder at all—she had already spied the prettiest lace caps and bibs in Mrs. Bobbinit’s toy shop down the high street.

That same Sunday afternoon, when Hetty lay on her pillow with flushed feverish cheeks and eyes puffed from crying, her mother looked down at her with perfect calm, even a quiet pleasure, at the girl’s woe.
