Hetty was not only heartsick, she was furious at herself for letting her secret slip. She had not even named the feeling to herself before that sudden outburst laid it bare, and now she burned with shame as if she had committed some terrible crime and been caught red-handed. She raged at her own weakness, swore she would never forgive herself for such a humiliation. Like a young panther struck by the hunter’s dart, she snapped and snarled at everyone around her, lashing out at her sister, her parents, anyone who dared come near.

“What business has any young woman indulging in this silly nonsense?” she cried, voice cracking. “Mamma, I ought to be whipped and sent straight to bed. I know perfectly well Mr. Warrington does not care a fig for me. I dare say he far prefers French actresses, or the little milliner girl at the toy shop, and he is right to. They are far better than me. What a fool I am, to burst out crying like a ninny over nothing, just because Mr. Wolfe mentioned that Harry played cards of a Sunday! I know he is not half so clever as papa—he is stupid, I am certain he is stupid—but he is not half so stupid as I am. Of course I can never marry him. How could I leave you and Theo and go all the way to America? Of course he has some sweetheart back in Virginia, or Tunbridge, or Jericho, somewhere. He is a great estate heir in his own country, he would never look twice at a poor half-pay officer’s daughter with not twopence to her name. You used to tell me I cried as a baby wanting the moon. I am still that silly baby. Do not talk to me, Mrs. Lambert, I am. And the best part is, he does not know a single thing about this, and I would rather cut my tongue clean out of my head than tell him.”

She threatened poor Theo with all sorts of dire punishments if her sister dared betray her secret. Little Charley, meanwhile, was entirely preoccupied with cheese-cakes and had not even noticed her outburst, and of course her parents and Theo all swore they would not breathe a word of it.

“I almost wish we had never come to Tunbridge Wells at all,” Molly sighed to her husband later that night.
“Nonsense, my dear,” the Colonel said. “Human nature will be human nature. Hetty’s own mother told me she had a little fancy for a young curate long before she fell head over heels in love with me. I myself had my heart pricked a dozen different ways before you took possession of it entirely. Our children must follow the same path we walked, I suppose. And to do the girl credit, she is disguising her feelings far better than you might expect. I defy Mr. Warrington to guess the state of her heart from the way she behaves to him.”
“A daughter of ours would never fling herself at any gentleman’s head!” Molly declared with great dignity.
“Nor fling a teacup at him either, my dear,” the Colonel laughed. “That girl treats Harry Warrington like a little vixen. Every time he calls, she boxes his ears one way or another. She is barely civil to him. And knowing what I know, I would never dream of scolding her for it.”
“She has no need to be rude at all,” Molly huffed. “Our Hetty is good enough for any gentleman in England or America. If their ages suit, why should they not marry after all?”
“Why should he not ask her himself, if he wants her?” the Colonel shrugged. “Half of me wants to hitch the horses to the carriage right now and drive us all home this very night.”
“Depend upon it, Martin, these things are wisely ordered for us,” Molly said softly. “Harry Warrington did not turn up at our gate half-drowned for no reason. If that marriage is decreed in Heaven, a marriage it shall be.”

The Colonel only shook his head, smiling at his wife’s eternal matchmaking. “Well,” he said, “you know full well if any of our children wanted our ears served up in a fricassee, we would cut them off and hand them over.” Molly laughed at the absurd image, and he leaned over to tweak her soft little ear, streaked now with just a few silver threads from decades of shared joy and sorrow.

That evening, Harry Warrington arrived not just for tea, but to invite the entire Lambert family to a special dance he was hosting at the Assembly Rooms, in their exclusive honor.
“A dance, for us?” Theo cried, clapping her hands. “Oh Harry, how delightful! I wish we could start this very minute!”
“For a wild Virginian, you are the most civilised young man I ever met,” the Colonel teased. “My dear, shall we dance a minuet together ourselves?”
“We have done exactly that before, Martin Lambert!” his wife laughed. The Colonel hummed a stately minuet tune, snatched a plate from the tea table to use as a pretend hat, bowed and flourished it while Molly dropped her deepest, most graceful curtsey.

Only Hetty sat glum and frowning in the corner.
“Have you no word of thanks for Mr. Warrington, child?” Theo asked her.
“I never cared much for dancing,” Hetty mumbled. “What is the point of standing opposite some stupid man and parading down a room with him?”
“Mercy, thank you for the compliment!” Harry said, confused.
“I did not say you were stupid—only, I meant country dances!” Hetty snapped, biting her lip when she caught Theo’s amused glance. She remembered she had just told herself Harry was stupid a few hours prior, and her sister’s gentle reminder made her bristle as if Theo had screamed a terrible rebuke.
“I hate dancing, there, I own it!” she tossed her head.
“But you loved it only last year!” her mother interposed.
“That was when I was a child! Clearly I have grown into an old crone now,” the Colonel joked. “Or perhaps Miss Hester has got the gout?”
“Fiddle!” Hetty snapped, stamping her small foot.
“What is a dance without a fiddle?” her unflappable papa grinned.

Harry’s face fell. He had come all the way over to make them happy, and the girl he liked best was telling him she hated dancing, and mocking every last guest and pastime at the Wells. He left that evening sore and confused, and when he found Molly alone for a moment, he asked what he could possibly have done to offend Hetty so. Molly’s heart softened for the honest lad even more, and she was sorely tempted to spill Hetty’s secret right then and there.

Theo cornered Hetty in their shared bedroom later, after their parents had said goodnight, to remonstrate with her sister for her rudeness. But Hetty would not hear a word of it, pacing the floor, cheeks flaming, as she poured out the soliloquy that churned in her heart:
“Suppose he hates me now? I fully expect he does. I hate myself. I scorn myself for being such an idiot. Why should he not hate me? I abused him, called him a goose, every cruel name I could think of, all the while knowing full well he is not stupid at all. I know I have sharper wits than he does. I only like him because he is tall, and has blue eyes, and a pretty nose. What an utter fool a girl must be to like a man just because he has a pretty face! I am a fool, and you cannot say a single word to the contrary, Theo. I said all those horrid things to him just to hurt myself, to punish myself the way I deserve. It made me glad for a moment to see him angry, because then he would think Hetty Lambert is a sour, ill-tempered little vixen, and that would prove to everyone that I am not chasing after Mr. Harry Warrington. Our papa is ten times better than he is. I will stay here by papa forever. Even if Harry asked me to run off to Virginia tomorrow, I would say no. You are worth more to me, my Theo, than every last Virginian that ever drew breath on this earth. If you liked him, I would never breathe a word of my own feelings. I would even get a rope ladder to help you elope with him, I would fetch the parson myself to marry you two, and then I would live alone forever. I would stay here and take care of papa and mamma, look after all the poor folk in the village, read all the tedious sermons I hate, and die without telling a single soul my secret. I know I will die young, anyway.”

The two sisters clung to each other and kissed, just as their mother knocked softly at the door, having overheard a snippet of their talk through the wainscot, to tell them it was long past time to sleep. Theo’s eyes closed almost at once, and she drifted off to rest. But poor Hetty tossed and turned for hours, wide awake, the new ache in her chest throbbing sharp every time she thought of how she had treated Harry. Only when the first pale streaks of dawn spilled over the window did she finally fall asleep, curled up tight against her sister’s side, a faint stain of dried tears glistening on her soft flushed cheek.

Most of us play with sharp, edged tools when we are young, and cut ourselves as a result. At first the cut stings so bad we drop the knife and wail like wounded babies. A very small, unlucky few stab themselves so deep the wound proves mortal, and they perish young. But heaven be thanked, most of us who get pricked by Love’s sharp arrows, scarred and tattooed all over with little heart wounds, heal in time, and go on to live full, lively lives. We too have tasted earthly joy, we too have lived, and gone on. By the time you are older, you will look back on a first sentimental disappointment and never once think you are at risk of an early grave. Let us trust there is no need for a sexton anywhere near Miss Hetty. But the very moment she wakes, that small sharp Care that pricked her last night will still be there, tearing gently at her little heart, softened just a little by her youth and her tears.

Flush with his easily won fortune, generous to a fault, and warmly hospitable to every soul he met, our young Virginian could not play the part of a gentleman of fashion without hosting a grand entertainment for all his fellow countrymen and fellow visitors to the Wells, according to the well-loved custom of the day. He booked the Assembly Rooms outright, sending invitations to nearly every remaining guest staying at the spa that season. Card tables were set up in the front parlour for all who could not bear to spend an evening without the pastime then ubiquitous across every drawing room in Europe; a supper chamber was heaped with crates of champagne and frothy spiced bowls of negus, while the great high-ceilinged main assembly hall was cleared entirely for dancing.

It was hardly a raucous affair, by our modern standards. The evening opened with minuets, reserved by unspoken rule for the highest ranking ladies in attendance. As the Earl's daughter, Lady Maria Esmond was the most noble guest present save for the lame Lady Augusta Crutchley, so Harry Warrington stepped out to dance the very first opening minuet with his cousin, acquitting himself so gracefully that the whole room broke into quiet applause, far outshining stiff, earnest Mr. Wolfe who had partnered Miss Lowther across the floor. The moment that dance ended, Harry turned next to blushing little Theo Lambert, asking for the honour of walking the following minuet with her. She glowed so bright with happiness as she moved through the stately steps that her parents could barely contain their delight, while Miss Humpleby, the vain daughter of Sir John Humpleby of Liphook, seethed on the sidelines, fully convinced she ought to have been the next partner called after an earl's daughter.

When the minuets drew to a close, the country dances began, their music played by a ragged trio of harp, fiddle and flageolet tucked high up in a dusty little balcony, plucking thin, melancholy tunes well into the small hours. Anyone who pulls out a tattered 18th century songbook today will marvel that anyone ever danced to such soft, plaintive strains. And yet the men and women of that era fell in love, frisked, laughed, and courted each other to those same sad notes, every air carrying a faint tang of amari aliquid, a hint of old forgotten sorrow. Perhaps it is the dust of the past clinging to them, their echoes drifting back to us from a limbo long abandoned. Perhaps they were bright and lively to the ears that first heard them; our own descendants, no doubt, will one day listen back to the chart-topping music of our time and exclaim, *Good heavens, was this what amused our forefathers?*

Harry's guest list boasted a true duchess that night: the famed, fiery Duchess of Queensberry, the muse of Pope and Prior herself. The old duchess pointedly turned her back on a certain other countess across the room, cackling loudly, glancing over her shoulder to jab her fan at the woman she snubbed. And yet nearly every other guest in the room bowed, scraped, cringed, and swarmed around that very countess, paying her far more deference than they gave Queensberry and all her sharp, witty airs. This was no other than the Countess of Yarmouth-Walmoden, the royal favourite whom King George II delighted to honour. She had met Harry on the promenade that morning, singled him out for great graciousness, and invited him to join her card table that night. Purblind old Colonel Blinkinsop, half deaf and half blind, had mistaken that invitation for his own and bowed so low he nearly toppled over, until she laughed and said, "Pooh, pooh, not you, old man! The young Firshinian!" and the whole crowd had clapped Harry on the back to congratulate him on his great good fortune.

Every respectable name in the room hovered around her that night: Lord Bamborough begged to take a seat at her quadrille party, the famously virtuous Lady Blanche Pendragon, the vaunted valiant Sir Lancelot Quintain, the pious Dean of Ealing, all the great generals, matrons, noblemen and high-born spinsters waited breathlessly for a smile from her, ready to leap up and fetch her a glass of negus at the flick of a finger. Lady Maria waited on her meekly as a lamb, and old Madame de Bernstein greeted the Hanoverian lady with profound, stately courtesy.

Harry had bowed to her no more than basic hospitality demanded, but Hetty Lambert chose to take fierce offence at the sight. She barely spoke a word to him all through the country dance they shared, and when he led her toward the supper chamber, she was no more communicative. To reach the refreshments they had to pass right by Lady Yarmouth's card table, and the countess called out good-naturedly to Harry, "Mr. Warrington, is your pretty little partner enjoying the dancing?"

"I thank your ladyship, I do not like dancing, and I do not like cards," Hetty snapped, tossing her head, dropping a stiff, block-like curtsey, and storming right past the table.

Harry was mortified, deeply stung. He was unfailingly courteous to every soul he met, and expected that same politeness in return, especially to an elder woman of rank. He saw the flash of indignation reddening his honest face as Hetty glanced sideways at him, well aware of the offence she had given, yet she still wore her artless, ingenuous little smile as she reached the sideboard.

"What a horrid, vulgar old woman that is, don't you think so?" she said brightly.

"What woman?" Harry asked, gruff.

"That German woman -- Lady Yarmouth -- that all these men are bowing and cringing to like dogs."

"Her ladyship has been very kind to me," Harry said, grim. "Won't you try some of this custard?"

"And you were bowing to her too, weren't you?" Hetty went on, unperturbed. "That negus you're drinking looks as if it has gone bad."

"It is very bad negus," Harry said, gulping it down anyway.

"And the custard is spoiled too!" Hetty cried. "I swear it's made with rotten eggs!"

"I am very sorry the entertainment and the company are not to your liking, Hester," poor Harry groaned.

"Oh, it's no fault of yours, I'm sure," she tossed back, flicking her curly little head. "You could not help it."

Harry clenched his fists, grinding his teeth, his whole frame tight with fury. "You look quite upset. Shall we go find your mother now?"

"Yes, let's go to your mother," he bit out, nearly stumbling over an unlucky waiter loitering in his path. "Curse you, get out of my way!"

"La, is that the way you speak to folks in Virginia?" Hetty teased.

"We are rough sometimes, there, madam," Harry said slowly, fire flashing from his eyes. "And it is hard not to be disturbed." Hetty could barely see straight the rest of the walk to her mother, never having seen him look so tall, so handsome, so noble in his anger. She told Mrs. Lambert she was just overheated, curtsied faintly to Harry, who bowed so deep his wig slipped an inch, and stormed off back to circulate among his other guests.

He was soon jolted out of his ill temper by a brewing altercation between his aunt Madame de Bernstein and the Duchess of Queensberry. As Lady Yarmouth passed the duchess's group, the old noblewoman gave her a withering stare out of eyes that had once set the whole ton ablaze, before breaking into peals of affected giggles, firing off a ceaseless stream of sneers and jabs at the royal favourite. Lady Yarmouth kept her eyes fixed on her cards, appearing not to notice the insult. The feud between the Duchess of Queensberry and the Hanoverian royal family stretched back decades.

"Look at all of you bowing down to that idol! Do not lie to me, you are as bad as the rest, my good Bernstein!" the Duchess cackled. "What a fine Christian country we live in! Your first husband the Bishop would have loved to see this sight!"

"Forgive me, your Grace, if I fail to follow your meaning," Bernstein said, playing demurely dumb.

"We are both old now, my dear, or else we pretend not to understand when we do not choose to," the Duchess laughed. "That is the way of us women. I was saying what fine Christians we are, because we are so wonderfully forgiving. Don't you remember the story in the scriptures, how the Pharisees wanted to stone the woman taken in sin? Far from stoning such a woman now, we all crawl on our knees for her! Any man in this room would go crawling around the whole floor on his hands and knees if yonder creature bade him!"

"Madam," Harry cut in, stepping forward with spirit, "I can name two or three men here who would do no such thing."

"Quick, bring them to me, and let me hug them to my heart!" the Duchess crowed. "Which are they, my dear Virginian? We shall make a party of four honest folk, if we can only find two more partners!"

"Here are three of us already," Bernstein said, with a forced laugh. "We can play a dummy hand."

"Where is the third?" the Duchess asked, looking around.

"Madam," Bernstein said, drawing herself up. "I will leave your Grace to boast of your own perfect honesty, but I will thank you not to cast doubts on mine before my own nephew and children!"

"See how she fires up at a mere jest!" the Duchess said, grinning. "I am sure you are as honest as the rest of the company, my dear creature."

"Which may not be good enough for your Grace of Queensberry and Dover, who might have chosen to stay away if you thought so poorly of us," Bernstein returned, with a stately curtsey. "But it is the very best my nephew could procure, and he has given you all that he has. He is not used to our tricky ways, madam."

"She is right to teach you, Harry," the Duchess said, rapping her fan against her palm. "To treat every guest, old or young, rich or poor, with equal welcome. That is the Virginian way, is it not? And we two old girls were friends long ago, when we were young, and there is no sense in quarrelling now that we are both grey." With that, the two dowagers exchanged a final grand curtsey, and the looming battle vanished entirely, before a single sharp word could spark an all-out war.

"Egad, that was like the standoff between Byng and Galissoniere!" Chaplain Sampson laughed the next morning, as Harry recounted every detail of the night's events to him. "I thought no power on earth could have kept those two seventy-four-gun warships from opening fire on each other!"

"And your Baroness Bernstein sailed clean out of the line of fire with the most perfect skill imaginable," Harry grinned. "Why should she be afraid? I have heard you say she is wittier than any woman alive, and has no reason to fear the tongue of any dowager in England."

Sampson hemmed, and hesitated. He knew very well why Bernstein had chosen to make peace, rather than join the Duchess in mocking Lady Yarmouth: her own long, scandal-ridden past meant every jibe levelled at the royal favourite would have landed squarely on her own reputation too.

"Sir," Harry cried, his face flushing bright with anger, "you do not mean to say there is any whisper against the character of my aunt, the Baroness de Bernstein!"

The chaplain stared at the young Virginian's perfect, unjaded innocence, and hesitated to speak further. "Stories much older than you or I, my boy. The sort of gossip that attaches to every soul in this wicked world, de me, de te. You yourself have had more than your fair share of slander since you arrived here, after all. No one escapes it. The best we can do is keep a clear conscience, and forgive."

"Forgive? That is your cloth, sir, but by George, I will not!" Harry thumped his fist down on the table. "Let any scoundrel say a single word against that dear old lady in my hearing, and I will pull his nose as sure as my name is Harry Esmond." It was at that exact moment that Colonel Lambert walked in, followed by his slow-moving servant Gumbo, just in time to see Harry's fist come down.

"Who is the poor fellow whose nose you are pulling now, Mr. Warrington?" the Colonel laughed.

Sampson winked at Lambert, signalling not to disillusion the boy about his aunt. "I was only telling Mr. Harry that every soul in this town is the victim of slander," the chaplain said, in his most unctuous clerical tone.

"True enough," Lambert nodded, playing along. "No one escapes it. Remember that silly story that went around about you and the dancing girl, Harry? The only soul in all our party who refused to believe a word of it was Hetty. She even stood up for you the other day, when someone came gossiping that you had been playing cards on a Sunday morning, when you ought to have been in church."

Harry stared, confused. "She scolded me half out of my wits last night," he said. "She snapped at everyone in the room, young and old, so that I told her in Virginia we do not suffer the young to speak so disrespectfully to their elders. We ended up having a regular quarrel, and I am very glad to hear she spoke up for me," he added, his voice softening, his cheeks flushing, his eyes growing misty.

Colonel Lambert looked at him, his warm, kind gaze softening. He saw at once that the honest, comely young Virginian was half head over heels in love with his sharp-tongued younger daughter. "You will never find a worse enemy than Hetty, Harry, you may be sure of that," he said, gravely.

The conversation turned to the Duchess, to Lady Yarmouth, who had been singing Harry's praises at the Pump Room that morning, declaring she had "a leedel boy in Hannover dat is wery like you, you sharming young mans," and who had won forty guineas off Harry at quadrille the night before. Before long, Lambert revealed that his funds were run out, and his whole family was leaving for their home at Oakhurst that very day. "You must come visit us, once our son Tom is home from the army," he told Harry. "My wife and I care for you very deeply, you know that -- and the girls do too, no matter how much they scold you. And if you ever get yourself into a scrape, as young men often do, you come straight to me, you understand? Count on me."

He dragged Harry out for a long walk across the common soon after, and Chaplain Sampson, looking out his upper window, saw the two men deep in earnest talk: first Lambert grinned and looked roguish, then he flung up both hands in shocked surprise. "The boy is asking for Hetty's hand," Sampson thought to himself.

Harry returned an hour later, his face grave and gloomy, flinging his hat down hard on the table and dropping into his armchair with a curse.

"The girls are leaving, and your heart is sore?" the chaplain teased, looking up from his half-written sermon.

"Heart!" Harry sneered. "That little termagant! What does she mean by treating me like a complete fool?"

By and by, Sampson asked after the little leather notebook Harry had lost a few nights before, the one stuffed full of bank notes and important private papers, which had vanished after a night of too much drinking. Harry admitted he had searched everywhere, and found no trace of it, kicking himself for getting so far gone that he had lost track of his own property.

"Confound all women, I say!" he growled at last, as Sampson joked about the charm of young country girls. It was a very cross, ungenerous sentiment, no doubt, and every right-thinking reader will surely rebuke the poor lovestruck boy for it.

It was plain the good Colonel had taken counsel with his wife, and the two had resolved to spirit their little Hetty away from Tunbridge Wells as swiftly as possible, to draw her clear of the charming young stranger who had unwittingly stolen her heart. For men, the old remedy of absence and distance often cures such passing infatuations easily enough, but I have long observed that the “alibi treatment” rarely works half so well on women. Many of them will travel leagues and stay away for months, and still that quiet, obstinate fondness clings to them, unshaken by climate or miles apart. You may rebuke them, neglect them, even use them roughly, and still these soft, deluded creatures will hold fast to their fidelity.

Nay, after long and wide observation of human nature, I will go so far as to say that there are few surer ways to secure the adoration and loyalty of a woman than a judicious dash of occasional neglect, a brisk dose of indifference as an alterative, and only doling out small sips of fondness and attention at long, sparing intervals. Too much love, too constant, quickly loses its flavour: the wives most indifferent to their husbands, the ones who yawn in their faces and prefer the company of fools to their adoring partners, are almost always the women cloyed to sickness on the sugarplums of overindulged devotion. But do not mistake me, dear ladies – I speak only in jest! I would never advocate anything approaching harshness towards your sex, and will say plainly that you are a hundred times more faithful and tender than our own rough, fickle kind.

Which brings us back: what, then, is the use of the Lamberts hurrying Hetty home, if the little maid will love Harry Warrington just as far away as she did when he was at hand? She will not make a scene at their parting, of course. She is far too ashamed of her secret to betray it, and Harry is far too preoccupied with his own affairs to guess it exists at all. He never sees the quiet grief lingering under her smiles, the sorrow hidden in every sidelong glance. He imagines her happy to get back to her music, her poultry, and her little rose garden, and does not even trouble to ride a mile along the road with their departing carriage. By the time he returns from his own afternoon engagements, the Lamberts are gone from Tunbridge Wells entirely: their windows stand open, and a card stuck in one of the panes announces the apartments are once more to let. A brief, passing twinge of sorrow at the empty rooms crosses his mind, but by four o’clock he is seated at dinner at the White Horse, calling loudly for his bottle.

That very same hour, when the Lamberts stop to sleep at their friend’s house in Westerham, poor little Hetty chokes on her tea. When she wakes the next morning, her cheeks are pale as wilted roses, and dark circles ring her eyes. It was the thunder, she tells her family. The night was so hot, she could not sleep. She will feel better, she swears, when they reach home the next day. When they do, she passes the gate where Harry fell from his horse, the bed he lay in while recovering, the chair he sat in by the parlour fire – and it feels like a hundred years have passed in the space of a few short weeks. She looks at the little girl who used to run through the garden calling her chickens and watering her flowers, and feels like a stranger to that old Hester Lambert. In one single night of quiet heartache, she has lived long, long years that no medicine of poppy or mandragora will ever wash into the soft, easy sleep she knew before Harry Warrington came into her life.

Down at the Tunbridge Wells assembly rooms, Maria Esmond watches the Lambert carriage roll away, and lets out a grim little sigh of relief. When Harry comes into his aunt’s card room later, flushed with good wine from the White Horse, he laughs gaily at Madame Bernstein’s teasing about which of the Lambert girls is his sweetheart, and says he loves them both like sisters. He cannot imagine a finer gentleman than the Colonel, and says the Duke is so fond of him he ought long ago to have been made a general. The Baroness teases him that he ought to make interest with the Countess of Yarmouth, the King’s favourite, to push for the promotion – the Countess is half German, and Madame Bernstein mimics her thick accent for Harry’s amusement, and crows that he carries off the hearts of all the old women in high society. “You do, don’t you, Harry?” she smirks, glancing at her niece Maria, who flinches as if stabbed by the remark. “You play cards like a grand seigneur, you never cheat – not that I blame anyone for a little cheating when they can get away with it, all of us do it, I and Maria included. But you might do very well to lose a few hundred to Lady Yarmouth gently, to win her favour. Why should Your Excellency not be made Governor of Virginia one day, eh?”

Harry asks why his aunt cannot introduce him at court herself, and the old lady’s rouged cheek flushes uncharacteristically. “I am not in favour at Kensington,” she says. “I may have been once, but there are no faces kings hate to see more than the ones they wish to forget. We all have little accounts we wish we could wipe off the slate, don’t we, Harry?” Both Harry and Maria turn bright red at that line, and the Baroness lets out one of her sharp, unpleasantly knowing laughs. Both of them have secrets they would rather keep hidden, secrets that would shock polite society if they were dragged to light.

Harry’s secret, for one, is heavy on his mind. For three days now, he has missed a little leather pocketbook he knows he had in his possession the night he got very drunk at the White Horse, and his servant Gumbo carried him up to bed. No one has seen it: his servants, the inn staff, none of them can find a trace. He dare not advertise for it, dare not make any public fuss, for the pocketbook is stuffed full of Lady Maria Esmond’s love letters. Pages and pages of giddy, overwrought professions of eternal fidelity, family secrets the Esmonds never dreamed of sharing, sharp, snide remarks about half the people they meet in society, her complaints of his attentions to other women – the whole foolish, tender farrago that every woman has written once in her life, before she married the man she eventually settled down with, and would die before letting anyone else read. Imagine if all your old love letters, the ones you wrote to your Edward before you broke off the engagement and married Mr. Jones, were laid out on the drawing room table for your husband to read? You would not like it one bit, no more than Lady Maria did. I have resolved, for my own part, never to write an unkind word about anyone ever again, lest my own old letters fall into the wrong hands. All my characters shall be perfect angels, every woman chaste and beautiful, every man wise and generous, when this book is done.

But for now, we are dealing with men and women who have not yet grown their angel wings, all of them with little failings of their own. Madame Bernstein has fallen asleep in her armchair after dinner, a little overstuffed with food and wine, Mr. Harry Warrington has wandered off to play billiards with Count Caramboli, and the chaplain Mr. Sampson is whispering softly to Lady Maria, careful not to wake the old Baroness. He remarks that Harry is wasting his youth in idleness, that a man of his fortune and station ought to find a place at court, take up a post in the service, and choose a wife of suitable rank. He mentions Harry’s distant Warrington cousins in Suffolk, the old knight Sir Miles, who has a daughter just about Harry’s age and reputed to be very beautiful, and Maria flushes bright red, and snaps that she sees no point in Harry mixing with those dull Suffolk country boobies who spend all their time drinking beer and hunting foxes.

Sampson leans in closer, his voice very soft. “I fear Mr. Warrington is in trouble, your ladyship. Six days ago, the night he dined at the White Horse and drank too freely, he lost a pocketbook full of letters.”

“Letters?” Maria gasps.

“Very private letters,” Sampson nods gravely. “He has been in a terrible state about it, making quiet inquiries. Gracious – your ladyship, are you unwell?”

Maria lets out three shrill, piercing screams, and tumbles straight off her chair in a dead faint.

The noise wakes Madame Bernstein from her nap, and she staggers to her feet on her tortoiseshell cane, flushed and wild-eyed from her dreams of old court days. “What have you done, sir?” she snarls at Sampson. He puts on a perfect look of innocent alarm, swears he did nothing but mention the lost pocketbook of letters, and the lady fainted. The Baroness dashes cold water on her niece’s face, until Maria lets out a feeble moan and begins to come around.

Her aunt glares down at her, grim and unforgiving. “You know exactly what has happened,” she says, her voice sharp as a knife. “The Esmond family curse, is it not? Letters lost, secrets out, the same old foolish story we have lived through a dozen times before! I thought you were wiser than to throw yourself away on a boy young enough to be your son. You will not rob Henry Esmond’s boy of his fortune and his youth, not while I am alive. I will not leave you a single shilling of my money if you ruin him.”

Maria, who has always been so meek and obedient to her aunt, suddenly flares up in defiance. “I do not care one penny for your paltry money! Harry Warrington has given me his word, and he has written me letters of his own. He will die before he breaks his promise to me.”

The old Baroness pleads with her, offers her five thousand pounds from her own personal fortune, right now, if she will only release Harry from his promise. Maria laughs in her face. She will not take it, she says. She has Harry, and she has ten times five thousand pounds to look forward to. She does not mind waiting – she is no silly young chit in a hurry for a husband, she can wait patiently, through whatever years it takes, for Harry to be hers. “If my letters are published to the world tomorrow, what of it?” she cries. “They hold secrets about the whole Esmond family, not just mine. I do not fear them. I have Harry’s word, and I trust it.” And she flings out of the room, just as Sampson comes back with the doctor, leaving Madame Bernstein shaking so badly she needs a full glass of cordial to steady herself, shocked to her very core by just how deep this entanglement runs.

Though Lady Maria had clearly come off the losing end of their sharp, pitched battle the day prior, the Baroness Bernstein greeted her niece the next morning without a flicker of anger or lingering rancour.

“Of course, my dear Lady Maria,” she purred, sipping her chocolate, “you cannot possibly imagine that I, as Harry Warrington’s near kin, would ever be pleased to see him tie himself to a woman as old as his own mother, with not a penny of her own fortune to bring to the match. That said, if the boy is fool enough to do such a ridiculous thing, it is no business of mine. I doubt I would ever have been taken seriously, anyway, on that foolish offer of five thousand pounds I flung out in the heat of our argument last night. So this little entanglement of yours was settled back at Castlewood, was it? Had I known how far things had gone, I would have spared myself all that unnecessary opposition. What use is railing over a broken pitcher, after all?”

“Madam!” Maria cut in, cheeks flushing.

“Pardon me, I mean no slight to your honour and character, which I am sure are perfectly unassailable. Harry says so, you say so—what more is there for anyone to ask?”

“You have spoken with Mr. Warrington then, madam?” Maria pressed.

“And he confessed he made you a promise at Castlewood, in writing, no less?”

“Most certainly he did,” Lady Maria replied, lifting her chin.

The older lady did not so much as flinch. “Ah. I will own I at first misread the tone of your letters to him. They hint at scandals touching other members of the family—”

“Who have spoken wickedly against me, and worked night and day to turn my dear Mr. Warrington against me!” Maria snapped. “Of course I wrote against them to defend my own name.”

“Naturally. You would be horrified, I am sure, to think any stray wretch might get hold of those family secrets and spread them as public gossip, hence all your disquiet earlier, I take it?”

“Exactly so,” Lady Maria agreed. “I hide nothing from Mr. Warrington, of course, but that is a very different matter from letting all the world know the petty quarrels of a noble house.”

“Upon my word, Maria, I admire you. I have done you an injustice these past twenty years, no less.”

“I am only glad you choose to do me justice at last,” the niece replied, cool as marble. “When I saw you last night opening the ball with my nephew, do you know what I thought of, dear?” Lady Maria added haughtily. “I have no notion what the Baroness de Bernstein chooses to think of.”

“I remembered you danced that very same tune with your dancing master, back in Kensington, years ago!” the Baroness laughed.

“It is a vile, infamous calumny!” Maria cried.

“Which got that poor dancing master cudgelled half to death for no fault of his own, too!”

“It is cruel and unkind of you to drag that up,” Maria flared, “and I shall not stay under the same roof as anyone who utters such slander against me. I mean to leave at once.”

“Leave? I can hardly blame you. Tunbridge will grow very unpleasant for you indeed, if those letters of yours ever turn up.”

“There is not a single word written against you in them, madam—you may set your mind entirely at ease on that count.”

“So Harry said, and he did you perfect justice, I must own. Well, my dear, we have grown tired of each other’s company, and we will both fare far better apart for a while.”

“That is precisely my own opinion,” Lady Maria said, dropping a frigid curtsey.

“Mr. Sampson may escort you back to Castlewood, if you like. You and your maid may take a postchaise for the journey.”

“We will take a postchaise, and Mr. Sampson may escort me,” Maria echoed. “You see, madam, I play the dutiful niece still.”

“Tell me, my dear— I have a very strong suspicion that Sampson has those letters in his keeping,” the Baroness said, quite openly.

“I will confess the very same thought crossed my own mind not long ago,” Maria admitted.

“And you mean to ride home in that chaise, and coax them right out of him, you little Delilah!” the Baroness cackled. “Well, they are no use to me, and I wish you all luck getting them back. You want to leave as soon as possible, I assume? We are women of the world, you and I. We only call each other names when we are in a temper. We don’t want each other’s company, so we part on perfectly good terms. Shall we go along to Lady Yarmouth’s tonight? It’s her at-home night. Nothing drives away the sour thoughts after one of those little nervous fainting fits you get, like cards and company, far better than any physician’s draught.”

Lady Maria agreed readily enough, and dressed for the party first, waiting in the drawing-room for her aunt to come down. The Baroness, descending the stairs, noticed Maria’s bedchamber door stood ajar. “She has those letters tucked in her stays, no doubt,” she thought to herself. The pair set off for their respective chairs to the party, displaying to each other all that charming, polished cordiality that only two women can muster even at the height of a bitter, hidden quarrel.

When they returned home late that night, the Baroness’s own maid, Mrs. Brett, answered Lady Maria’s bell, when the lady called for her lady’s maid to help her undress. Mrs. Brett hung her head in shame as she explained that Betty, Maria’s maid, was in no fit state to appear before her ladyship. Betty had gone off carousing with Harry’s black servant Gumbo, alongside Lord Bamborough’s valet and half a dozen other household staff from the neighbourhood, and the rum punch they had drunk had proven far too strong for the girl. Mrs. Brett offered to undress Lady Maria herself, but the lady waved her off, saying she could manage perfectly well on her own.

“Letters are in her stays for certain,” the Baroness thought to herself, as the two bade each other a sweet, amicable good-night on the staircase.

The next morning, a contrite Betty came to wait on her mistress, blue eyes swollen, to take her scolding for the night before. She admitted she could not resist the fine rum punch Gumbo brewed, which everyone said was the most delicate in all three counties. She meekly finished dressing her lady, then withdrew to her own room.

Betty was one of the Castlewood housemaids who had long been charmed by the good-humoured Gumbo, which had stirred no small jealousy in the breast of the Baroness’s head man, Mr. Case, who had long set his sights on the pretty blue-eyed lass. He had sworn more than once he would break Gumbo’s bones if he kept flirting with Betty, and the peaceable Gumbo had been doing his best to avoid him ever since.

But the night of the rum punch, Case had been the very soul of good nature. He had found Gumbo and Betty whispering in the cool doorway air, and instead of flying into a rage, he insisted that they all make a bowl of Gumbo’s famous punch in Betty’s room, drinking glass after glass until poor Betty was thoroughly intoxicated, and Case himself was so ill the next day he stayed in his bed the whole morning, not appearing to wait on his ladies until supper time.

“Case, I could have sworn I saw you galloping along the London road on horseback first thing this morning!” Harry said, as he sat supping with his aunt and the rest of the party that night.

“Me, sir? Bless your soul, I was in bed all day, sure my head was going to split clean in two!” Case protested. “I ate a little bread at six, drank a whole flagon of small beer, and I’m almost myself again now. But I’ll never touch Gumbo’s punch again, saving your honour’s presence.”

As they sat after supper, the Baroness was all sweetness to Lady Maria. She prescribed all sorts of fortifying cordials for the lady’s frequent fainting fits, and suggested Harry ride up to London on her behalf, to carry a note to her lawyer Mr. Draper and see that he added Harry as a main beneficiary to her will. He was also to carry her heavy trinket-box to the banker’s strong room for safekeeping, as there had been a rash of highwayman robberies on the roads of late.

Lady Maria paled at the news—she had been counting on Harry to escort her back to Castlewood. But the Baroness waved her off. “The boy has been tied to our apron strings long enough! He’ll ride up tomorrow, do the errand, and be back to Tunbridge by Saturday, well in time to see you off.”

Harry could not have been more pleased. The ill-considered promise he had made Maria at Castlewood, to marry a woman old enough to be his mother, had hung around his neck like a heavy millstone for weeks, and the thought of a rattling jaunt to London sounded like the sweetest relief in the world. He set out at dawn the next day, his pistols primed, Gumbo riding beside him on the box of the postchaise. No highwaymen stopped them on Blackheath. He caught his first glimpse of the gleaming domes of Greenwich through the trees, the Thames crowded thick with merchant ships, the ancient stone walls of the Tower of London. He pointed them out to Gumbo, giddy as a schoolboy, remembering how he and his dead brother George had read all about the Tower in their storybooks back in Virginia, and played at being prisoners in the Tower’s dungeons when they were small boys. They rattled over London Bridge, then through Southwark, and pulled up to Mr. Draper’s chambers in Middle Temple Lane.

The old lawyer, whose family had served the Esmonds of Castlewood for generations, took the trinket box and the Baroness’s letter, and locked them away in his strong closet. As they reached for their hats to go out, a young clerk stuck his head into the hall. “Beg pardon sir, those papers the Baroness asked for were given to Mr. Case two days ago!”

“Mind your own business, Mr. Brown,” Draper snapped at him, then steered Harry down the dark Temple stairs. Harry smiled to himself. So Case was the man he had seen galloping down the London road a couple days prior. Mischief was afoot, that was plain—but it was no business of his to pry.

He tipped his hat to the mouldering rebel heads nailed to Temple Bar as they walked past, startling the staid lawyer. “They were gentlemen who died for their rightful king,” Harry said, simply. “My brother George and I always swore we’d pay our respects when we saw them.” The rest of the day was pure delight to the young Virginian: he wandered the Strand, visited Leicester Field where his grandfather had fought a fatal duel decades before, caught a glimpse of the rough, shabby great author Mr. Johnson strolling in the gardens, bought a fine matched pair of bay geldings at the horse market in Hatton Garden, tramped through Westminster Abbey and the Tower and Kensington Palace, and ate and drank like a prince at his inn in Covent Garden.

The next morning, he read the Virginia dispatches in the newspaper, and his throat tightened. The leading gentlemen of the colony had formed a volunteer regiment to march against the French and their native allies, and he ached to be back in his home country, riding with them, instead of tangled up in all the silly, scheming mischief brewing back in Tunbridge Wells. The church bells of St. Paul’s, Covent Garden, began to ring for morning prayers, and Harry smiled to himself. He had not forgotten that the oily chaplain Mr. Sampson was scheduled to preach his great sermon for Lady Yarmouth that day. He had a shrewd suspicion that none of the tangled schemes the ladies back home were weaving would end quite as any of them hoped. The mischief was only just getting started.

At breakfast one morning, Mr. Harry Warrington flipped through his copy of the London Advertiser and spotted a public call to all lovers of manly British sport, inviting them to the Wooden House in Marybone Fields to witness a trial of skill between the legendary champion pugilists Sutton and Figg. The young Virginian, who had purchased a new matched pair of horses only the day before, resolved to attend the show immediately, hitching the team to his phaeton to drive himself out to the grounds.
He did not know the roads west of Covent Garden well, however, and veered and tacked far more than was strictly necessary on his journey, losing himself in the sun-dappled green lanes behind Mr. Whitfield’s round Tottenham Road Tabernacle, and the unfenced meadows that then stretched around the newly built Middlesex Hospital. He arrived at last, to find a vast crowd assembled to cheer on the two champions’ valorous feats.
A throng of ragged London roughs clustered around the doors of this temple of British sport, jostling for space alongside the gilded equipages of a handful of fashionable patrons who, like Warrington, had come to patronize the contest. Crippled beggars whined around the young gentleman’s heels, begging for alms; shoeblack boys tumbled over one another for the honour of polishing his boots; flower girls and itinerant fruiterers hounded Mr. Gumbo to buy their wares; piemen, pickpockets, tramps, and strollers of every sort hung about the perimeter of the battleground. A gaudy flag flapped atop the building, and a master of ceremonies repeatedly stepped out onto the front stage, accompanied by a drummer and a horn-blower, to announce to the restless crowd that the noble English sports were on the very brink of beginning.
Warrington paid his entry fee, and was shown to a gallery seat with an unobstructed perfect view of the combat stage. Gumbo settled himself in the cheap benches of the amphitheatre below, and whenever he grew bored, wandered out into the outer yard to drink a pot of ale or play cards with the other footmen and coachmen waiting by their masters’ carriages. The 18th century world was positively lousy with these liveried vassals, after all: no gentleman or lady could stir abroad without one, often two or three, trailing in their wake. Every theatre had a footman’s gallery of its own, an army of the uniformed throng clustered round every chapel door, they swarmed in anterooms, sprawled across landings and hallways, guzzled, cheated, bullied visitors for vails and lost whole fortunes at cards. That grand old race of footmen is all but gone now: only a handful linger still, tall, powdered, melancholy, in their plush livery and silver buckles, parading at royal levees, as rare a sight as the scattered camps of Red Indians you might still stumble across on the American frontier. The race is doomed: Uncas with his tomahawk and eagle plume, and Jeames the footman with his cocked hat and long cane, are both fading out of the world where they once walked in glory.
Before the headliners took the stage, a string of minor exhibition bouts were held. The first boxing match was a limp affair: neither man showed much spirit, neither landed a punishing blow, and the crowd grew quickly restless. Next came cudgel-play, but no competitor cracked a head memorable enough, no wound was severe enough to satisfy the bloodthirsty audience, who soon took to hissing, grumbling, and stamping their feet. “The masters! The masters!” they roared, until the two famous champions finally consented to make their entrance.
First up the stage steps strode the intrepid Sutton, sword in hand, saluting the crowd with his weapon and bowing very specifically to a private box where a stout, important-looking gentleman sat watching. Sutton was followed seconds later by the redoubtable Figg, to whom the stout man waved a hand of warm approval. Both fighters stripped to their shirts, their heads shaved clean to avoid any chance of an opponent grabbing their hair, their scalps crisscrossed with the old scars and cracks of dozens of former victorious bouts. Each wore a coloured silk ribbon, his “armiger,” tied around his burly sword arm. The two gladiators shook hands, and a roar went up from the crowd for the blunted combat swords.
The fight had barely commenced before Figg swung a blow so tremendous that, had it landed full on Sutton’s head, the comely young man’s skull would have been lopped off as clean as a carrot under a carving knife. But Sutton caught the full force of the blow on his own blade, and Figg’s sword snapped clean in his hand from the sheer weight of his strike. New blades were handed to the two men, and soon the first blood of the bout spouted from Figg’s heaving side, drawing a yell of triumph from Sutton’s supporters. The veteran called for a pause, however, appealing to the crowd and especially to the stout gentleman in the private box, to point out that the shard of his broken first sword had nicked him unfairly.
In the lull of the parley over the injury, Warrington spotted a gentleman in a riding frock and plain scratch-wig slip into the stout man’s private box, and recognised his old Tunbridge Wells acquaintance, the Earl of March and Ruglen. Lord March, who was notoriously sparing with politeness to most people, showed singular deference to the stout stranger, bowing very deeply as the other man pulled a handful of bank notes from his pocket-book and handed them over to him. As soon as their business was concluded, March spied Harry in his gallery, crossed over, and greeted his young friend warmly. They sat together to watch the rest of the fight, which raged with equal skill and valour on both sides for hours, until the two champions laid down their swords and took up quarter-staffs, whereupon the veteran Figg claimed the long-sought victory.
A heavy thunderstorm had broken over the building while the two men fought, and Warrington gladly accepted a seat in Lord March’s chariot for the ride back to Covent Garden, leaving his own phaeton to be driven home by his groom. Harry was utterly enraptured by the day’s entertainment, declaring it the finest sport he had witnessed since his arrival in England. True to his habit of wanting to share every pleasure he enjoyed with the companion of his boyhood, he sighed and began to say “I wish…” before he caught himself and fell silent.
“What do you wish, and what don’t you wish?” asked Lord March, lolling back against his carriage cushions and eyeing the young Virginian curiously.
“I was thinking of my elder brother, and wished he could have been here,” Harry explained. “We promised we’d share all sorts of sport back home, you see, talked of it a hundred times. Though he’d never have cared for this rough sort of fighting, even if he was the bravest lad alive. You should have seen him once, when he quarrelled with a gallant officer who was our friend – it was a foolish, trivial affair, but we could barely hold George back. I never saw a man so cool, or so savage and determined, God help me. Ah, for the credit of Virginia, I wish he could have come over here in my place, to show you what a real gentleman from the colony is like.”
“Nonsense, you’ll do very well on your own,” the amused nobleman replied. “What’s this I hear about Lady Yarmouth taking you into her favour, by the way?”
“I’ll do as well as any other man!” Harry laughed. “I can ride, and I daresay I shoot better than George, but my brother had the head, sir, the head!” he tapped his own honest skull for emphasis. “I give you my word, he’d read nearly every book ever printed, could play both fiddle and harpsichord, write the most elegant poetry and sermons. What can I do? I’m only good for riding, playing cards, and drinking Burgundy.” He hung his head for a moment in mock penitence, before grinning. “Though I’ll back myself to do all three of those better than most fellows you’ll meet.”
The jaded, world-weary Lord March found the young man’s unfeigned naivete as delicious as a perfectly cooked mutton chop to a man who has dined on every fancy dish in the world. “By Gad, Mr. Warrington,” he chuckled, “you ought to be taken straight to Exeter ‘Change and put on public display. A gentleman from Virginia who actually mourns the loss of his elder brother? The breed’s completely unknown in this country. Upon my honour, I do believe you’d actually like to have him back again.”
“Believe?” Harry cried, flushing bright red.
“Ah, you believe you believe you’d like him back,” March corrected, waving a careless hand. “But depend upon it you wouldn’t. It’s not in human nature, sir, not as I’ve ever read it. Look at these new houses we’re passing: that one on the corner is Sir Richard Littleton’s, that big empty one was Lord Bingley’s. It’s a crying shame they’ve left this great empty stretch of Cavendish Square fenced off with those ugly boards. By George, I don’t know where this town’s spreading to. Montagu House has been turned into a confounded Don Saltero’s museum, full of books and stuffed birds and rhinoceroses. They’ve cut that cursed New Road right behind Bedford House Gardens, spoiling the Duke’s privacy – though I suppose they’re lining his pockets for the trouble. Shall we go back via Tyburn Road and the Park, or cut through Swallow Street to the more habitable part of town? We can dine in Pall Mall, or go back to your rooms, and spend the evening however you like – with the Queen of Spades at the cards table, or…”
“With the Queen of Spades, if your lordship pleases,” Harry said, blushing.
The chariot accordingly pulled up at Warrington’s Covent Garden hotel, where the landlord hurried out to greet them, bowing so low at the sight of Lord March that his wig nearly brushed the nobleman’s shoes. The inn’s very best dinner was laid on for the two men, followed by more than enough wine, vintage good enough even for the famously epicurean earl. Over their glasses, they discussed heading to Vauxhall to watch the fireworks, or staying in to play cards. Harry had never seen any fireworks grander than a dozen squibs let off in Williamsburg on Guy Fawkes’ night, which he had thought a sublime display, but he yielded to his guest’s preference for piquet, and the two men were soon absorbed in the game.
Harry began winning, as was his usual luck, but after half an hour the tide turned, and favour ran entirely Lord March’s way. He was growing surly at an interruption when Mr. Draper, Warrington’s man of business, came bowing into the room. Harry, who was constitutionally generous to a fault, immediately invited him to sit and take a drink. If he had a crust, he shared it; a haunch of venison, he split it with his guest; a jug of water, he passed it around; a bottle of fine Burgundy, he drank it gaily with any thirsty friend who wandered by. It is a rare virtue, that unforced open-handedness, not the performative hospitality of the man who hosts six large dinners a year to show off to his acquaintances, but the genuine kind heart that does not wither away the moment it is transplanted to the stifling, selfish air of London.
Draper did not care much for wine, but he was utterly delighted to be in the company of a famous peer. He protested that nothing pleased him more than watching two consummate, fashionable players go at piquet, and he settled himself in a seat, unperturbed by Lord March’s sidelong scowls, to watch the game. Harry was nowhere near a match for the veteran London club player, and tonight March held far better cards to back up his skill. Their stakes were kept quiet, the two men agreed to play for shillings at the start, and counted their gains and losses in low undertones, perfectly polite and formal with one another, until a second interruption brought a vicious curse to Lord March’s lips.
First there was a scuffle outside the door, then whispering, then the sound of a woman sobbing, until at last a female figure burst headlong into the parlour, drawing that unseemly outburst from the earl.
“I wish your women would pick a better time to call, confound them!” March snapped, flinging his cards down on the table in a pet.
“What, Mrs. Betty?” Harry cried, astonished. It was indeed Lady Maria’s personal maid, and Gumbo stood right behind her, his face streaked with tears. “What’s the matter? Is the Baroness well?”
“Help! Help your honour!” Mrs. Betty shrieked, dropping straight down onto her knees.
Gumbo let out a loud wail from the doorway. “Gumbo, you scoundrel,” Harry said, half-amazed. “Have anything happened between you and Mrs. Betty?”
Gumbo stepped back with great dignity, laying his hand on his heart. “No, sir. Nothing hab happened 'twix dis lady and me.”
“It’s my mistress, sir!” Betty wailed. “Help, help! Here’s the letter she wrote me to give you, sir! They’ve taken her, sir!”
“Old Molly Esmond? Everyone knows she’s over head and ears in debt,” March said dismissively. “Dry your eyes in the next room, Mrs. Betty, and let’s get back to our game.”
“Help her! Mr. Harry, you won’t keep playing cards when my lady’s calling out to you for rescue!” Betty sobbed. “You used to come running fast enough when I fetched you over at Castlewood!”
“Confound you, hold your tongue!” March swore, more colourfully this time. But Betty would not stop weeping, and the fates had decreed that Lord March would not win another hand that night.
Harry pushed his chair back and reached for the bell pull. “My dear lord, the game is over for this evening. My relative writes to me in great distress, and I am bound to go to her aid.”
“Curse her! Couldn’t she wait until tomorrow?” March grumbled.
Harry ordered a postchaise brought round immediately, his own horses harnessed to take him as far as Bromley.
“Bet you don’t get there in an hour!” March crowed, already reaching for his pocket book. “Bet you don’t make it in five quarters of an hour! Four to one you get robbed on Blackheath! Bet you don’t reach Tunbridge Wells before midnight!”
“Done!” Harry laughed. March carefully scribbled all four wagers down in his notebook, before Harry unfolded the note the maid had brought him, scrawled in Lady Maria’s messy hand:
*MY DEAR COUSIN--I am fell into a trapp, the work of vile villains I can plainly see. I am a prisner. Betty will tell you all. Ah, my Henrico! come to the resque of your MOLLY.*
Half an hour after he received the note, Harry was settled in the postchaise, galloping across Westminster Bridge, the wheels kicking up spray from the rain-soaked road, on his way to succour his beleaguered kinswoman.

In my youth, a happy chance made me close acquaintance with a most garrulous gentleman hailing from that fabled “first gem of the ocean” island all impartial judges of maritime trinkets praise so highly. The stories he told of his kinsfolk there made my young blood curdle: every crime you can name, every line of the Ten Commandments shattered to splinters, rogueries no penny dreadful scribbler could dream up, murders and highway robberies even the notorious Thurtell or Turpin never dared pull off. He recounted every last one of them with perfect, unflinching accuracy, to any soul who would listen. It was a miracle the whole brood hadn’t been clapped in the prison hulks long before.

“Me brother Tim brought his fawther’s grey hairs to the grave,” he would say. “Me brother Mick robbed the parish church three times over. Me sister Annmarouia jilted the Captain, ran off with the Ensign, forged her grandmother’s will, and stole the family silver spoons—for which poor Larry the knife-boy got hanged in her place.” The cursed house of Atreus was nothing beside his clan, of course; not for all the world would I name the isle that spawned them.

What astonished my naïve young self most was that these parricides, forgers, and cutthroats wrote to one another as “my dearest brother” and “my dearest sister,” and lived for months at a stretch in perfect harmony. Tim, his hands still reeking of his father’s blood, would mix a spiced rum punch and pass his sister a glass without a second thought. Mick, his lips still black with the perjuries he’d sworn over the stolen will, would kiss his sister Julia’s cheek and weep with her over tales of their childhood “dear old castle,” and their sainted mother who had cheated them all out of the family estate. They embraced so warmly at meetings and partings you could forget all those little confessions that, if they told half the truth, every last one of them could hang the rest.

What finer gift than forgiveness? Is there anything more rational than screaming every insult under the sun at a man, then apologizing for your hasty words, pulling the decanter you hurled at his head out of the way, and making up? Some souls carry this angelic gift of forgiveness in their bones. The two ladies of Tunbridge Wells we followed last chapter were possessed of it in spades. Only yesterday they had screamed and snapped at each other over cards; today they laughed, teased, and played side by side, each taking a wing of the roast chicken, pulling the wishbone together, and tearing every other resident of the resort to shreds in conversation, while never so much as hinting at their own recent quarrel. They were like the Peninsular War soldiers who fraternized across truce lines, trading tobacco and wine, ready to grab their muskets and blow each other’s heads off the second the bugle blew to resume fighting.

The Baroness Bernstein’s threatened gout? All the twinges had vanished entirely, she said, and her niece Lady Maria was overjoyed to hear it. Maria’s frequent fainting fits? The Baroness clucked that they were quite gone, save for a tiny little recurrence the night before, and insisted Maria take iron tonics and fortify her constitution long after they left Tunbridge. She even offered to ship cases of the spa’s medicinal waters to Maria’s London lodgings. What kindness! Though we have no way of knowing what the Baroness whispered to her lady’s maid later that evening: “Fainting fits? Pah. Inherited epilepsy from that horrible scrofulous German mother of hers.” Nor can we be sure Maria did not order her own maid Betty to taste every glass of the Baroness’s offered spa water first, declaring her aunt was perfectly capable of slipping poison into it. These are merely precautions—those loaded muskets the truce-time soldiers keep cocked beside them, lying quiet in the grass for the moment.

With Harry Warrington’s signed bond tucked safe in her pocket, the wily Lady Maria had no intention of pressing for immediate payment. She knew the world far too well. She would give her young captive plenty of day-rule, plenty of leave to wander and amuse himself in London, no need to chafe or anger her pretty young mouse when the cat could wait purring by the wall, watching with sharp green eyes. Both ladies knew exactly what diversions a gentleman of Harry’s age sought in the capital, and spoke of them with the frank ease common to that unbuttoned era. Maria consoled herself readily enough during his absence, taking her amusement where she found it: she played cards for hours with the agreeable Mr. Jack Morris, who counted Lord March and Harry himself among his close friends, and who counted it almost a pleasure to lose small sums to an earl’s daughter. She wangled an invitation for him to the Countess of Yarmouth’s assembly, and everyone went home perfectly pleased.

The first two days after Harry’s departure passed very cheerfully indeed, until that Friday arrived—the day the Reverend Mr. Sampson had spent so long preparing his famous sermon for. The whole of Tunbridge Wells was ready to turn out. Sampson had a widespread reputation as a wildly entertaining, eloquent preacher, and when there were no breakfast parties, conjurors, or dancing bears performing, the spa’s visitors were happy enough to sit through a good sermon. Sampson knew full well the Countess of Yarmouth was the King’s dearest favourite, that she alone held the power to hand out fat church livings and even bishoprics, and that the King trusted her judgement on all spiritual matters far more than any bishop’s. So he spared no expense for the occasion: he bought a brand new flowered periwig on credit, and a crisp, rustling new cassock from a local mercer who was foolish enough to trust a popular chaplain’s promise to pay. He marched proudly from the Baroness’s pre-sermon breakfast to the church, his two patronesses walking at his side, their footmen trailing behind carrying their giant gilt-edged prayer books.

The Baroness looked radiant that day, laughing, greeting every acquaintance with a stately smile and a tap of her tortoiseshell cane. At the church door, all of Tunbridge’s fashion had assembled: the Countess of Yarmouth conspicuous in a flame-coloured taffeta gown and bright vermilion cheeks, a whole throng of lords and ladies chattering as they filed in. But there were odd visitors among the crowd too. Two shabby men in ragged coats slipped in just as the organ stopped, one with bright carroty hair sticking out under his ill-fitting scratch wig. He crossed himself unconsciously as he stepped over the threshold, and muttered to his friend: “Bedad, Tim, I forgot this was a Protestant church.” You could smell whisky rolling off them from ten feet away. Then two more men, sallow, hook-nosed, and very greasy, tried to push past the beadle. “We’re here to convert, governor,” one whispered in his ear, slipping a guinea into his palm, and the beadle stepped aside to let the two Jewish moneylenders enter.

The organ blared. The doors clanged shut. Sampson walked up the aisle ahead of the gold-laced beadle, rosy and jolly as any parson alive—until he lifted himself up over the pulpit cushion, glanced over the congregation, and turned as pale as death. There on either side of the west door stood the two Hebrew strangers. Slipping into a bench by the vestry door were the two whisky-scented Irishmen, their eyes meekly cast down to the floor, blocking every exit.

No one in the congregation noticed his terror. The sermon was hailed as the greatest any of them had ever heard. The Countess of Yarmouth declared it was “bewdiful, and made me tremble all over.” The Baroness called it excellent. Lady Maria waved her handkerchief up at the pulpit to congratulate their family chaplain on triumph. But Sampson barely saw her. His eyes were fixed on the four blocking his escape, long after the last “amen” was spoken.

The crowd streamed out, two by two, then one by one, until the church was almost empty. The Baroness and her niece lingered in the rector’s pew, chatting with the parson, until Maria stepped forward to make their exit. The two Irishmen stepped up to her at once. One, Mr. Costigan, pulled a long warrant from his pocket. “At the suit of Mrs. Pincott, mercer of Kensington, madam, I have the honour of arresting your ladyship,” he said, bowing very politely. “My name is Costigan, a poor gentleman from Oireland, forced by circumstances to follow this disagreeable profession. Will you walk, or shall my man fetch a sedan chair?”

Lady Maria shrieked three times, and fainted dead away on the stone floor. The Baroness’s eyes twinkled sharply as she ordered her maid to unlace her stays. As soon as the maid’s hands were busy, she snipped the thin hair chain around Maria’s neck that held a tiny sealed bag, stuffed it into her own pocket, and called for someone to dash cold water on her face. The debt, Costigan said, was one hundred and thirty-two pounds.

Meanwhile, Sampson had surrendered meekly to his own pursuer, the bailiff Simons. “At whose suit?” he sighed. “Buckleby the cordwainer,” Simons said. “Forty-eight pounds and charges, I know,” Sampson said. He had no money to pay. The two prisoners were carried off in waiting sedan chairs to the bailiff’s comfortable “spunging house” lodging, the two Philistines having captured their Sampson and his great patroness both.

That evening, the Baroness sent her servant Case with a gushing note to her niece, full of professions of ardent affection, but explaining that her own heavy losses at cards meant she could not possibly cover the debt. She said she had written post-haste to Mrs. Pincott to beg for more time. Maria and her maid could scrape together only eighteen shillings between them, so they decided Betty should pawn Maria’s gold chain to ride post haste to London, and find Harry Warrington, the champion they were certain would rush to pay their debts and rescue them. But when Betty brought the chain to the very toy shop where Harry had originally bought it as a gift for Maria, the shopkeeper thought she was a thief, and called for a constable. Betty had to confess the whole story: Lady Maria was arrested, locked up in a bailiff’s house. By dusk, every last soul in Tunbridge Wells knew the news.

But polite society pretended nothing had happened. That night at Lady Trumpington’s card assembly, the Baroness arrived looking perfectly cheerful. No one said a word about the arrest while she was in earshot. The Countess of Yarmouth asked after Maria, and the Baroness said she had fainted in church that morning and was keeping her room. Cards were dealt, fiddles played, the footmen waited for supper, the chairmen drank and swore outside, and the world went on spinning exactly as it would if no parson and no earl’s daughter were locked up in a spunging house. The Countess whispered to her servant Fuchs to find out exactly how much Maria’s debt was, she said—she might pay it herself, just to vex that cold old Baroness everyone knew was behind the whole arrest.

The Baroness went home at midnight, slept like a log, and did not wake until late the next morning, when her maid brought her tea laced with a little cordial, as was the custom for fine ladies of that era. She roused, and asked for the latest news.
“Someone’s here to give it you,” her maid said sullenly.
Before she could ask who, the bed curtains were drawn back.
It was Lady Maria, rosy cheeked, perfectly composed, dropping her aunt a low mocking curtsy. Harry Warrington had ridden into Tunbridge at midnight, paid all her debts and Sampson’s too, and sprung them both out of custody before the sun rose. With that little surprise, we may close our chapter.

“My dear Lord March” (wrote Mr. Warrington from Tunbridge Wells, on Saturday morning, the 25th August, 1756): “This is to inform you (with no small satisfaction) that I have won all three of our wagers. I pulled into Bromley two full minutes inside the agreed hour; my new pair of horses kept a capital pace the whole way. I drove them myself, with the postilion perched beside me to point out the turns, and my black servant inside the chaise with Mrs. Betty. I trust the pair found the journey no hardship. We were hailed by two highwaymen on Blackheath, but one look at our determined countenances sent them galloping off without daring to halt us, and we rolled into Tunbridge Wells, where I transacted all my urgent business, at forty-five minutes past eleven o’clock. This makes us quits, after yesterday’s piquet game, and I shall be delighted to give you your revenge whenever you please. I remain, Your most obliged and faithful servant, H. ESMOND WARRINGTON.”

That wild, breakneck dash across Kent is the very trick that freed Lady Maria Esmond from her unexpected debtors’ captivity. She had sent Mrs. Betty racing to London to beg Harry’s aid, never dreaming the woman could return the very same night of her departure. Midnight had fallen, and she and Parson Sampson were whiling away the hours over cards and a meagre supper the bailiff’s wife had scraped together, when the thunder of speeding carriage wheels came roaring up the lane. Maria dropped her trump cards mid-play, her heart hammering so loud she could scarce hear her own breath.

The chaise skidded to a halt right at the door. A few quick words passed at the gate, and in burst Mrs. Betty, cheeks streaming with happy tears, radiant as a sunrise. And behind her, tall, broad-shouldered, his riding boots caked with London mud, was Harry Warrington. The chaplain slapped his cards down with a wild huzzay, while Lady Maria turned white as a sheet, rose tottering to her feet, and with one hysterical little sob, flung herself straight into her cousin’s outstretched arms. What matter if he showered her with a thousand kisses, then a hundred, then a thousand more after the old Catullan fashion? No one shall call us to account for counting them. She knew he would come, her champion, to pluck her from the shame and ignominy of bondage. She wept so hard against his shoulder that her fine lace collar was soaked, and for once, every tear was genuine. She never looked more beautiful than she did in that moment, the author swears.

Harry was on cloud nine. “You are both free,” he told them, grinning. “Betty, fetch my lady’s hat and cardinal cloak. Chaplain, we’ll smoke a pipe back at my lodgings, that long ride has left me parched for refreshment.” Sampson, whose soft, impressionable nature was given to easy bursts of emotion, broke down entirely, seizing Harry’s hand to kiss it over and over, praying God to heap blessings on his generous young patron. Harry felt that warm, glowing thrill that comes only when you have the power to turn someone’s sorrow into joy, to lift the helpless out of trouble. He swaggered a little on the walk back to his lodgings, hat tilted jaunty over his eye, escorting his “rescued princess” like a conqueror fresh from a tournament, the world strung with laurel wreaths for him, trumpets blaring his praise. It was such a small thing he’d done, after all – only slipped the bailiff a handful of guineas to dispel the dragon guarding the door, send the tyrant of the house packing. A little vanity never hurt the good-natured lad; he bragged a little that night over their fine Burgundy, talked of London clubs, White’s and Almack’s, Lord March’s famous racehorses, like any fashionable young macaroni, and we can scarce hold it against him.

Sampson’s flattery knew no bounds that night. His whole life, as a wandering preaching parson, he’d trained his sensibilities to turn on a dime, to weep when a mourner wept, laugh when a tavern companion laughed, and this night his gratitude was so loud and fulsome it would have turned a wiser head than Harry’s. With every bumper he downed, he praised Harry as the noblest, finest gentleman alive, and Harry, simple soul, lapped every word up. “The younger branch of our family has used you scurvily,” he declared grandly, thumping the table. “But by Jove, Sampson, I’ll stand by you always! You’ve a little sister at boarding school, you said? Here’s a bank note to cover her fees, no thanks needed.”

Sampson froze, pushed the note back half an inch, and burst into fresh tears. “I don’t deserve your kindness, Mr. Warrington – no, by God, I don’t.”
“Pshaw,” Harry laughed. “I’ve plenty more. Only last week I lost that cursed pocket-book, had nary a farthing in it.”
“Ah – no, sir, there was no money in it,” Sampson mumbled, dropping his eyes.
Harry jolted upright. “How the devil would you know that, parson?”

It all spilled out then: Sampson had found the pocket-book the night Harry got too drunk at Barbeau’s tavern. He’d read all the letters inside, knew all the family secrets Harry had thought no soul but he and his brother George shared. He confirmed the ugly tales of Lady Fanny, and cousin Will’s reckless debts, all true. When Harry flew into a rage demanding to know if Sampson dared breathe a word against Lady Maria, the parson swore he never would, only added that in his humble opinion, Maria was far too old for a fine young gentleman like Harry, who deserved a wife his own age.

Harry ordered him to bring the pocket-book and remaining letters at once. But when Sampson returned from his chamber, he was as pale as a ghost. The pocket-book was there, he said – the one George had given Harry, with his name stitched on the cover – but the letters were gone. Someone had rummaged through his locked trunk while he was held at the bailiff’s house, and stolen them. The lodgings’ landlady swore no stranger had stepped foot in the rooms, Harry’s own things were untouched, no coin or clothing missing – only those few pieces of paper. Harry, still giddy from his successful wagers, his daring rescue, his fine vintage Burgundy, dismissed Sampson’s tearful pleas for forgiveness, waved off the whole mishap, pardoned the parson on the spot. By dawn they were both roaring drunk, toasting the Esmond family’s ancient glory, before they stumbled off to bed.

By noon the next day, a servant from Madame de Bernstein came to invite Harry over for chocolate. She greeted him with open arms, cooed over his new fine London-made clothes, thanked him profusely for rescuing dear Maria – then casually dropped that she’d had to send her steward Case galloping to London the very same day, to borrow three hundred pounds to cover her own card debts to Lady Yarmouth, she’d been stone broke. She laughed, and pressed a fifty-pound bank note on him, told him to go spend it on pleasure, that his mother the Virginian heiress would no doubt reimburse her. Then the mood shifted.
