She leaned across the table, sharp as a tack, and told him plainly he was a fool for getting himself betrothed to Maria – a woman of forty-two, as old as his own mother, who would gamble away every penny he had.

Harry’s face burned. “Who told you of my promise?”
The Baroness admitted the truth: when the bailiffs seized Maria, she fainted, and a little sachet holding Harry’s silly, flowery love letter slipped from her pocket. The Baroness had found it, read it – and burned it.

A jolt went through Harry. He ought to have been angry, but a wild, unplanned rush of relief flooded through him. His stupid letter, signed with oaths he’d written on his knees, gone. But his honour was too rooted in the Virginian code of chivalry to let him back out. “My word is given,” he said, standing firm. “Us gentlemen of Virginia do not break promises, not for all the gold in the Indies. If she holds me to it, I’ll marry her. If we end up wretched, I’ll take a musket and fight for the King of Prussia, and let a bullet end the trouble.”

The Baroness’s face crumpled. She curtsied stiffly, turned to leave – then her hand flew to her heart, and she sank back onto the sofa, weeping the first genuine, unselfish tears Beatrix Esmond had shed in more than fifty years. Harry knelt beside her, seized her cold hand, and kissed it, confessing how ashamed he was to admit he’d been glad when he heard she’d burned that foolish letter. The old worldly woman, whose hard heart had long been shielded from soft feelings, put her hands on his shoulders and kissed his forehead. “You will not tell Maria what I have done?” she whispered. He swore he never would, just as demure Mrs. Brett, her waiting woman, stepped through the door to find the two locked in that tender, sentimental moment.

By the end of the season, the little party from Tunbridge Wells was heartily sick of the spa’s quiet amusements and all too eager to strike out for new destinations. Madame de Bernstein had already set her sights on Bath for the autumn, where there were far more card tables, a busier crowd, and far more life to be found than the stagnant spa could offer, and she planned to stop off only at a handful of country house visits on the road there. Harry, with no great grace to hide his reluctance, agreed to ride with Lady Maria and Parson Sampson ahead of the main party, bound for the old Esmond family seat at Castlewood.

They passed the turn-off for Oakhurst village, and the warm, hospitable home where Harry had been treated like a favoured guest not long before. Lady Maria launched into a stream of sharp, cutting remarks about the two pretty Misses Oakhurst, their mother’s obvious determination to hook the wealthy young Virginian as a son-in-law, and how brazen the girls had been to set their caps at him the moment he stepped through the door. Stung and cross, Harry declared he would ride straight past his old friends’ gate rather than subject them to her ladyship’s unprovoked insults, and he stayed haughty and sullen for the rest of the day’s journey to the roadside inn where they stopped a few miles further on.

At supper, none of Lady Maria’s softest smiles could thaw his black mood, not even the ready, well-practised tears she summoned at will to try and soften him. To every one of her querulous, sentimental remarks, he growled out a surly, monosyllabic reply, and she was forced to retire to her chambers without ever getting the private tete-a-tete she had been craving: that stubborn old chaplain Sampson stayed planted in the parlour armchair as if he had received explicit orders to never leave the two of them alone. Harry bowed her out with stiff, perfect courtesy, called the landlady and her personal maid to see her up the stairs, and closed the door behind her.

Ten minutes later, a horse galloped out of the inn-yard at full tilt. An hour after Lady Maria had gone to bed, her maid Betty came back down to fetch her mistress’s bottle of smelling salts, and found Parson Sampson alone, puffing on a clay pipe. Where was Mr Warrington? He’d stepped out for a moonlight walk, Sampson said vaguely, as if no one could possibly be expected to keep track of where the young gentleman wandered. The next morning, Harry was back in his saddle beside Lady Maria’s carriage, his brow still dark, his black mood unbroken, barely speaking a dozen words for the whole rest of the journey. Lady Maria’s mind raced: *He must have found out I lied about stealing that little silken case*, she thought to herself.

The truth of it was, half a day earlier, as they climbed that steep hill three miles outside Oakhurst on the Westerham road, Lady Maria had been leaning heavily on Harry’s arm, pouring out her most overwrought sentimental vows, protests, and gushings of undying love. The more fawning and fond she grew, the colder Harry turned. Looking up into his face, the summer sun lit up hers, and for all its careful powder and preservative creams, the faint lines and wrinkles of forty years were plain to see. To Harry, the weight of her arm resting on his felt like a lead drag he would have to carry for the rest of his life, a dreary, suffocating prospect. He cursed the hot night, the spiced wine, and the stupid, reckless pledge he had made while half drunk, tying him irrevocably to this woman he did not love.

Maria chattered on, quoting scraps of sentimental plays, calling him over and over again her champion, her Henrico, her preserver, swearing her Molinda would be faithful to him until her dying day. She pulled a small silken case from the neck of her gown, holding it up to his face. “Have I not thy precious image, thy hair, thy loving note here?” she sighed. “It shall go with me to the grave – it will, sir, if my Henrico ever treats me unkindly.”

Harry jolted so hard he nearly wrenched his arm right out of her grasp. He had thought Madame de Bernstein had burned every last scrap of that stolen hair and that foolish old note, when she had destroyed the case right in front of him back at Tunbridge. That was the exact moment Lady Maria felt her first twinge of remorse: not that she had lied, but that she had been caught lying, a far more powerful spur to repentance than any pious instruction.

When they arrived at Castlewood, Harry’s bad mood did not lift. The Earl was away from home, the rest of the family out visiting, and the only member of the household they found on the grounds was Will Esmond, who trundled back up the drive from partridge shooting just as their party reached the gate. He went dead pale when he saw Harry, and Harry favoured him with nothing more than a surly, cold scowl of recognition.

Over supper that night, they made a show of civility at first, with Lady Maria sitting between them. Will made vague noises about how he’d done well at the recent local race meeting, until Harry leaned forward. “And you brought my horse back sound, I hope?” he asked, evenly.

“Your horse? What horse?” Will blustered.

“The brown thoroughbred I won from you at cards the night before you rode away from Tunbridge,” Harry said, stern and steady. “You remember that horse, Mr Esmond.”

“Mr Warrington, I perfectly well remember playing you for a horse, which my servant handed over to you the day you left the spa,” Will said.

“Mr Sampson, you were present at our game. Will you be umpire for us?” Harry said, turning to the chaplain with surprising gentleness.

“I must confirm that the wager was laid for the brown thoroughbred, sir,” Sampson said, looking away awkwardly.

“Well, he got the other one,” Will said, with a surly grin. “Sold it for thirty shillings! A broken-kneed old rip, that was more than it was worth.”

Harry kept up his perfect, polite smile for as long as Lady Maria remained in the room, pressing her to have more chicken, making small, easy conversation. When she rose to retire, he bowed her to the door with all the courtly grace he could muster, closed it behind her, and then called all the servants out of the supper parlour. He turned the heavy iron key in the lock, and pocketed it.

The click of the lock made Will jump. He was slouched over his punch, eyeing Harry askance, and swore out loud. “What the hell do you think you’re playing at?”

“I expect there’s going to be a quarrel,” Harry said, blandly. “No use making the servants stand gawking at a disagreement between gentlemen of quality.”

“Quarrel? What quarrel?” Will snapped, his hand closing around the big silver-handled carving knife on the table.

“Mr Sampson, you witnessed that I staked fifty guineas against Will’s brown horse, did you not?” Harry asked.

Will roared and denied it, but Harry cut him off. “Don’t take me for a fool just because I was raised in Virginia,” he said, stepping forward. “Hands off, chaplain, you stand back and see fair play!”

Harry never got the chance to finish his insult. Will hurled a full wine bottle straight at his head. Harry ducked just in time, and the heavy glass flew across the room, smashing straight through the face of a portrait of an ancient Esmond ancestor, before shattering against the wainscot and splashing a full pint of good port wine all over Sampson’s face and his neatly powdered wig. “Good heavens, gentlemen, I beg you to stop this madness!” the chaplain wailed, dripping red wine off his periwig.

Neither of the two men paid him any mind. Will dropped the empty bottle, seized the carving knife, and lunged straight at Harry’s chest. Harry had learned his boxing at the Marybone gardens, and he caught Will’s right wrist in his left hand, landing a sharp, heavy punch square on Will’s nose that sent him reeling backwards into the oak panelling. Will dropped the knife, which Harry kicked under the table out of reach.

Will had been to bare-knuckle fights at Hockley-in-the-Hole too, and he gasped for breath, then charged forward headfirst like a battering ram, aiming to drive his skull straight into Harry’s stomach. Harry had seen that trick before, both at the London fights and amongst the enslaved boxers on his mother’s Virginia estate. He skipped easily to the side, and landed a tremendous blow to Will’s right ear that sent him crumpling to the floor, his head cracking hard against the heavy oak table leg.

“Chaplain, you bear witness this was a fair fight,” Harry said, still quivering with the rush of combat, but striving to steady his voice. He pulled the key from his pocket and unlocked the parlour door, where half a dozen curious servants had clustered, listening to the crash of glass and the shouts. They burst in to find two men covered in red: the chaplain soaked in port wine, and the Honourable Will Esmond splayed unconscious on the floor in his own blood.

“Someone unlace his neckcloth – he may be dying,” Harry said. “Gumbo, fetch a fleam and bleed him. Wait, he’s coming round.” Will’s good eye fluttered open first, the other already swollen shut from the first punch. He gasped, then started swearing so loudly the parlour windows rattled.

“Looks like he’s on the mend,” Harry said dryly. The servants, who had never had a good word to say for the cruel, violent Will Esmond, laughed. “Gumbo, ask him if he’d like a second round?”

Will cursed them all, lashing out at Gumbo when he leaned over him. “Nobody here dares touch you, sir?” Harry said, straightening his lace ruffs. “That’s what I thought.” The servants murmured their agreement, none of them moving to interfere on Will’s behalf. Will staggered to his feet, wiping the blood off his face with a napkin, and skulked off to bed, trailing a string of curses after him.

The next morning, Harry sent Will a playful note, teasing him that if he was heading for London he could ride ahead and scare highwaymen on Hounslow Heath with his bruised, battered face. Then a maid brought a gushing, tear-stained letter from Lady Maria, begging her dearest Henrico never to be cruel to his Molinda again, declaring she had not slept a wink all night. Harry wrote a formal, carefully spelled letter to the Earl of Castlewood explaining the full circumstances of the fight, told Maria that he could not possibly stay under their roof after bruising and bloodying the master’s brother, and took his leave. The second he crossed Castlewood Bridge, his black mood vanished entirely. He put his horses to a gallop, singing to them as they flew ten miles an hour down the road, nodding at pretty girls standing by cottage gates, chucking roadside inn landladies under the chin. He was sick of Tunbridge’s petty gossip, silly sentimental games, and stuffy card parties. He was ready for London, for St James’s, for Newmarket, for all the amusements of a gentleman of quality.

By the time he rolled into London, the forty-four pounds he had left when he left Tunbridge was all but spent. He told himself it made perfect sense to sell five hundred pounds of his share of the family legacy stock: with a little luck at the tables, he would make it all back in no time. A gentleman of his rank, he reasoned, could not possibly keep the right company or appear properly in society on a paltry two hundred pounds a year. He moved out of the cheap Bedford Coffee House, took elegant, expensive lodgings in Bond Street, stabled his two horses at a nearby livery yard, and set tailors, mercers, and shoemakers to work making him a full new wardrobe. He laid aside his mourning, appeared in a laced waistcoat and a cocked hat trimmed with silver, had his hair powdered, and drove his fancy phaeton in the park Ring. Reports of his vast Virginian fortune had preceded him to the city, and every man of fashion was curious to meet the wealthy young colonial heir. Lord March had already written his name down for membership at White’s Chocolate House, even before he was old enough to be formally balloted in. At one-and-twenty, with a pocket full of cash, Harry was determined to drink deep of every pleasure London had to offer.

Among the unpublished papers of the late Lord Orford, one letter addressed to General Conway survives, copied out in Madam Esmond’s neat handwriting and marked *Mr. H. Walpole’s account of my son Henry at London*. It runs as follows:
> ARLINGTON STREET, Friday Night.
> My dear General,
> I have torn myself away from three weeks of devotion to our Lady of Strawberry, my old joints all wracked with rheumatism, to pay London a visit. Why shouldn’t an old man have his rattle, same as any other elderly baby? The Norfolk party was full of talk this week about some sort of young Virginian “savage” they met at Tunbridge, an offshoot of that disreputable Esmond family, where all the men are gamblers and spendthrifts, and all the women – well, your wife is reading over your shoulder right now, so I shan’t say the word. You know the old Baroness Bernstein, once Mrs Tusher, that notorious old beauty who flipped sides from the Pretender to the House of Hanover without a second thought? Her great-nephew is the young man in question.
> We ran into him at Vauxhall two nights ago, with that silly little busybody Jack Morris hanging off his arm. You never saw a creature so delighted by fireworks, or so ready to huzzay at a screaming singer on the stage! He’s the lad who won three hundred guineas off my nephew and Lord Rockingham at White’s the night before, and the whole gardens were buzzing about him. Jack introduced him to the singer after the show, and the big colonial boy blushed all the way up to the eyes and gave her a bow so formal you would have thought he was at St James’s court.
> Later, over our punch and chicken, I was regaling Tony Storer with a few of the old Esmond family scandals, including tales of that elderly beauty Lady Maria Esmond and her old flirtation with the late Prince of Wales, when the young “savage” himself stepped out from behind the next box, his face scarlet with rage, his hand on the hilt of his sword. He demanded to know which of us had dared malign his family, and I was forced to stammer out a full apology before he would even think of putting his blade away. What a creature! We shall see a great deal more of him, mark my words.

In Harry Warrington’s day, no one in learned or fashionable circles could stop bickering over the relative merits of the ancients and the moderns—and by and large, the verdict landed in favour of the former. The “moderns” of that 18th century are the distant ancients of our 1858 present, just as our grandchildren a hundred years from now will sit in judgment on the morals and wit of our own era. You respectable 1700s ancestors? For all your boasts of Gibbon, you must own yourselves beaten on book-learning: a pair of Cambridge and Glasgow professors today know more Greek than every university in Europe, Athens included, could scrape together in your time. Your science barely outstripped the heathen writers you deemed your inferiors. And as for public and private decency? Is 1858 really a match for 1758? Gentlemen of Disraeli’s Commons, does every last one of you have a price, as under Walpole or Newcastle? Or—far the more delicate question—have most of you already had yours? Ladies, I do not pretend you are a college of Vestal virgins, but the scandalous chronicles of a century back are so lurid you ought to thank heaven you did not live in those perilous times. On my conscience, I believe men and women both are better now: there are far more Susannas among us, and far fewer wicked Elders lurking about.

Have you ever read *Clarissa*, *Tom Jones*, *Roderick Random*, unexpurgated? Those are unvarnished portraits of the men, women, and seething society of that day. If we dared depict the unredacted exploits of a Lovelace, a Lady Bellaston, or that infamous “Lady of Quality” who laid her memoirs bare for the author of *Peregrine Pickle*, our pure, outraged 19th century would shriek, flee the room, yank all its young ladies out by the wrist, and order Mr. Mudie to ban every last book by that odious author forever. You, madam, at fifty-eight, are no doubt far too squeamish, crying out before you are hurt when no one ever intended to offend your ladyship. There is truth to the complaint that the novelist’s art is hobbled by these restraints, just as the fair limbs of many a harmless marble statue in St. Peter’s and the Vatican are spoiled by the frumpy tin draperies pious old churchmen swaddle them in. But that prudery is not entirely foolish, any more than state press censorship is entirely unfounded. If a page risks corrupting good morals, out come the censor’s scissors to snip the prurient line. Society the despot has issued its imperial decree, and we must submit. You have all seen those American pianos tricked out in frilled muslin trousers over their mahogany legs? Depend on it, that muslin muffled half the notes, muddling the music and slowing the player down.

What is this preamble leading us to? Harry Warrington, Esquire, in his Bond Street lodgings, and the wild life he and a thousand other young fashion-mad bucks led in those days—a life I can no more drag my gentlest young readers into than Lady Squeams can take her innocent daughter to an ordinary evening at Cremorne Gardens. My dear Miss Diana—pshaw, I know full well you are eight-and-thirty, however shy you pretend to be, however you try to convince everyone you have just outgrown pinafores and schoolroom dinners—when your grandfather was a young man about town, a member of White’s Club, dining at Pontac’s off feasts laid on by Braund and Lebeck, riding down to Newmarket with March and Rockingham, toasting “the best in England” alongside Gilly Williams and George Selwyn (who made jokes whose flavour has long evaporated since their first bottling), the old gentleman lived a life your noble aunt, author of *Legends of the Squeamses; or, Fair Fruits of a Family Tree*, has never breathed a word of to you. It was long before your grandmother adopted the severe piety for which she was celebrated in her final long residence at Bath, long after Colonel Tibbalt married rich soap-boiler’s heiress Miss Lye, that her ladyship sowed her own wild oats. She was as giddy as the rest of the gentry in her youth: ten card tables set out at her Hill Street house every Wednesday and Sunday evening, save for the short summer season when Ranelagh Gardens was open for Sunday entertainments. She gambled eight, nine, ten hours every single night of her life. Everyone else in society did the same. She won, she lost, she cheated, she pawned her jewels—and who knows what else she did not pledge, just to feed her ravenous hunger for play? What of that after-supper duel at the Shakespeare’s Head in Covent Garden between your grandfather and Colonel Tibbalt, where they drew swords and fought only in front of Sir John Screwby, who was passed out drunk under the table? They were interrupted by Mr. John Fielding’s constables, and your grandfather was carried home to Hill Street wounded in a sedan chair.

Those gentlemen in powder and ruffled cuffs, who turned the toes of their buckled pumps out so daintily, were terrible, ferocious fellows. Swords were perpetually being drawn, bottle after bottle drained dry, oaths roared unceasingly in conversation. Tavern drawers and watchmen were pinked and maimed, chairmen beaten, sober citizens insulted by reeling bands of pleasure-hunters. You have been to Cremorne with proper, vetted vouchers, of course? You remember our great London theatres of thirty years ago? You were too good a person ever to attend a play. Well, you have not the faintest idea what those playhouses, their notorious green boxes especially, were like when Garrick and Mrs. Pritchard trod the boards before them. For my children’s sake, I am grateful to that great retired actor who was the first to banish that shameful licence from the stage. No, madam, I do not plume myself on superior virtue. I do not claim you are naturally better than your rouged, gambling, loud, tearing 18th century ancestress, nor even than poor Polly Fogle just taken up for shoplifting, who would have been hanged for the same crime a hundred years prior. I am only heartily thankful my temptations are far slighter, for I have more than enough to contend with from the vices of our own century.

So if Harry Warrington rides down to Newmarket for the October races, and wins or loses whole sacks of gold there; if he carouses with a party of bucks at the Shakespeare or Bedford Head Tavern; if he dines at White’s ordinary and sits down afterward to macco and lansquenet; if he brawls with the watch and finds himself locked up in the Roundhouse for a night; if he lets himself go for a spell and turns into a wild, dissipated, harum-scarum young Harry, I, who know well the weakness of human nature, will not be shocked. Aware as I am of my own shortcomings, I have no interest in raining fire and brimstone on my neighbour. Mr. Sampson, the clergyman, did that for everyone else: in his Long Acre chapel he lashed vice unmercifully, gave sin no quarter, out-cursed blasphemy with thunderous anathemas, knocked drunkenness down and trampled the prostrate brute wallowing in the gutter, dragged conjugal infidelity out into the light and pelted her with endless stones of rhetoric—then, once service was over, he would turn up for dinner at the Star and Garter, mix a great bowl of punch for Harry and his friends at the Bedford Head, or take a hand at whist in Harry’s Bond Street lodgings, or Lord March’s, or wherever there was a good supper and cheerful company waiting for him.

Oftentimes I worry I may have taken my usual uncharitable, degrading view of Harry’s exploits during this period of his London residence—for I have not uttered a single word of virtuous indignation against his conduct, and if his actions were not actually reprehensible, then I have judged him cruelly indeed. O Truth, O Beauty, O Modesty, O Benevolence, O Pudor, O Ancient Decency, O Blushing Shame, O Namby-Pamby, each with your great honoured capital letters! O Niminy-Piminy! How dare I ever say a young man can be a young man? No doubt, dear young lady, I am slandering Mr. Warrington as my heartless custom dictates. For proof, here is a letter pulled straight from the Warrington family papers, written by Harry to his mother, that has not a single line to suggest he leads anything but a quiet, respectable life:

> **BOND STREET, LONDON, October 25, 1756**
>
>
> I take up my pen to acknowledge your esteemed favour of 10 July, per the *Lively Virginia* packet, which duly arrived forwarded by our Bristol agent, and I rejoice to hear your crops promise so well. ‘Tis Tully who says agriculture is the noblest of pursuits! How delightful when that pursuit is also profitable!
>
> Since my last letter from Tunbridge Wells, one or two incidents have occurred of which it is necessary [this word has been scraped at with a penknife but left uncorrected, no doubt to the writer’s satisfaction] I should advise my honoured mother. Our party there broke up at the end of August, right as partridge-shooting commenced. Baroness Bernstein, whose kindness to me has been unwavering, has departed for Bath, her usual winter retreat, and made me a most welcome present of a fifty-pound bill. I rode back in company with the Reverend Mr. Sampson, whose instruction I find most valuable, and my cousin Lady Maria, to Castlewood. [Could Parson Sampson have been dictating some of these remarks to Mr. Warrington?] On the way I paid a flying visit to my dear kind friends Colonel and Mrs. Lambert at Oakhurst House, who send my honoured mother their most affectionate remembrances. The youngest Miss Lambert, I grieve to say, is unwell, and her parents are some little anxious.
>
> At Castlewood I lament to say my stay was short, owing to a quarrel with my cousin William. He is a young man of violent passions, and alas, addicted to liquor, whereupon he has no control over himself. In a trifling dispute about a horse, high words arose between us, and he aimed a blow at me—or its equivalent—which my grandfather, my honoured mother’s father’s son, could not brook. I returned the blow, and felled him to the ground, whence he was carried almost senseless to bed. I sent to enquire after his health the next morning, but hearing no further news of him, set off for London, where I have remained save for brief intervals of absence.
>
> Knowing you would wish me to see my dear grandfather’s University of Cambridge, I rode thither lately in company with some friends, passing through part of Hertfordshire, and stopping overnight at the famous Bed of Ware. The October meeting was just beginning at Newmarket, near Cambridge, when I arrived. I saw the students in their gowns and caps, and rode over to the famous Heath, where races were being held—my friend Lord March’s horse Marrowbones, sired by Cleaver, won a great stake that day. It was a most amusing spectacle: the jockeys, horses, all very different to our poor races at home, and the betting something awful. The richest noblemen here mix right in with the jockeys, betting on every hand. Cambridge pleased me greatly, especially King’s College Chapel, a rich but elegant work of Gothic architecture.
>
> I have been introduced into the world, and made a member of White’s Club, where I meet gentlemen of the first fashion. My Lords Rockingham, Carlisle, Orford, Bolingbroke, and Coventry are my friends, all introduced by Lord March, of whom I have often written. Lady Coventry is a fine woman, but thin. Every lady paints here, old and young, so if you and Mountain and Fanny wish to be in fashion, I must send you out some rouge pots. Everybody plays cards: eight, ten tables at every house on every reception night. I am sorry to say all do not play fair, and some do not pay their debts. I have been obliged to sit down and do as Rome does, and have actually seen ladies I could name take my counters right out from under my nose!
>
> One day, his regiment the 20th being paraded in St. James’s Park, a friend of mine Mr. Wolfe did me the honour to present me to His Royal Highness the Captain-General, who was most gracious. A fat, jolly prince, if I may say so without disrespect, whose manners remind me of that unhappy General Braddock whom we knew to our sorrow last year. When he heard my name, and how dearest George served and fell in Braddock’s unfortunate campaign, he talked a great while with me, asked why a young fellow like me did not take up arms too, why I did not go to the King of Prussia, who is a great general, and see a campaign or two, and whether that would not be better than dawdling about at routs and card parties in London. I said I would go with all my heart, but was now an only son, on leave from my mother, and bound to tend to our estate in Virginia. His Royal Highness said Mr. Braddock had written home glowing accounts of Mrs. Esmond’s loyalty, and that he would gladly serve me. Mr. Wolfe and I have waited on him since at his house in Pall Mall. The latter, who is still quite a young man, served in the Scottish campaign with his Highness, whom Mr. Dempster so loves at home. Though he was too severe, if anything can be too severe against rebels in arms.
>
> Mr. Draper has had half the Stock, my late Papa’s property, transferred to my name. Until there can be no doubt of that painful loss in our family, which I would give my right hand to undo, the remaining stock must remain in the trustees’ name for the benefit of him who inherited it. Ah, dear mother! There is no day, scarce an hour, when I do not think of him. I wish he were by me often. I feel the better for thinking of him, and would for the honour of my family that he was representing it here instead of—
> Honoured madam, your dutiful and affectionate son,
>
> P.S. I am like your sex, who always, they say, put their best news in a postscript. I had something to tell you of a person to whom my heart is engaged. I shall write more of it later, there is no hurry. Suffice she is a nobleman’s daughter, and her family as good as our own.

Harry’s aunt, the Baroness de Bernstein, wrote separately to his mother in Virginia, her far sharper, more worldly missive penned two days prior to Harry’s own letter:
>
> My good sister, I think we have been all our lives a little more than kin and less than kind, to use the words of a poet whom your dear father loved well. When you were born in our Western Principality, my mother was not as old as Isaac’s wife was when he bore him his sons, but even then I was old enough to be your mother. Though she gave you all she could leave or give, including that small share of love that ought to have been my due, still, if we can hold goodwill toward one another we can do without affection. And you owe me a little kindness, for your son’s sake as well as your father’s, whom I loved and admired more than any man I ever knew in this world. He was greater than almost all, though he made no noise in it. I have seen hundreds of men who did make a noise, and believe me, I have found very few with such good heads and good hearts as Mr. Esmond.
>
> Had we been better acquainted, I might have given you some advice about introducing your young gentleman to Europe that you would have found wise in hindsight. You would have said afterwards, “What she counselled me was right, and had Harry done as Madam Beatrix wished, it had been better for him.” My good sister, it was not for you to know, nor for me to write to you of it when you never wrote to ask, but your boy, coming to England and Castlewood, found very few friends there—save one, his old aunt, of whom all manner of ill has been spoken for these fifty years past, and not without cause, perhaps.
>
> Now I must tell Harry’s mother what will doubtless astonish her: almost everyone who knows the boy loves him. He is prudent of his tongue, generous with his money, as bold as a lion, with an imperious, domineering way that sits very well on him. You know well enough if he is handsome or not. My dear, I like him none the less for not being over-witty or over-wise. I never cared for those “set the Thames afire” gentlemen who think themselves far cleverer than all their neighbours. Your father’s great friend Mr. Addison always struck me as a supercilious prig, and his follower Sir Dick Steele was no more pleasant in his cups than out of them. And returning to Harry, your Master Harry will certainly never set the Thames on fire with his wits. Of book-learning he is as ignorant as any lord in England, and for this I hold him none the worse. If Heaven did not give him a turn that way, there is no use trying to bend him to it.
>
> Considering the station he is to hold in his colony when he returns, and the stock he comes from, let me tell you he has not nearly enough allowance to support his station, and that narrowness of his income will make him all the more extravagant—sheer despair will make him break all bounds, even though extravagance is not natural to his character. He wants to live as well as the rest of his company, and between ourselves, he has fallen in with some of the rakes of the first rank in England. He thinks it a point of family honour not to back down, and many a time calls for ortolans and champagne when he would just as soon dine off a steak and a mug of beer. And I have no doubt, from the way he talks, naif as the French say

Though Harry Warrington clung stubbornly to the dismal promise his cousin had wrung from him, no benevolent reader could mistake the engagement for anything but a heavy millstone hung about the young Virginian’s neck. He had no taste for the match, and longed heartily to be free of it. It was very possible he had schemed to bring that very freedom about when he picked a fight and thrashed poor Will Esmond: a proper boxing match would surely spark a family feud, he reasoned. Maria might take her brother’s side in the quarrel, Harry would refuse all apology, Will would be forced to call him out to a duel, and Harry, certain he was the better man with both fists and a blade, would soon be released from his vow by either victory or honourable wounds. The ruse went off without a hitch—until the very end. The explosion of the brawl left no lasting damage beyond Will Esmond’s swollen nose and a black eye that lingered for a full week. He never summoned the courage to send his cousin a challenge, so neither man killed the other, and neither was killed. Will was knocked down, and he simply got up again: a course of action many a sensible gentleman would choose, could he settle a petty score in private, no one the wiser about who came off worse.

Far from rallying to her brother’s side, Maria declared wholeheartedly for Harry, as did Lord Castlewood himself once he heard the full tale. The chaplain confirmed it was Will who struck the first blow, dead drunk at that—he’d quarrelled in his cups a dozen times before, Castlewood pointed out, and Harry had only acted like a gentleman in resenting the injury. It was Will, not Harry, who ought to beg pardon. Harry refused all reconciliation, though, until his stolen horse was returned and the disputed bet paid. The chronicler has never found a single surviving letter or account that clarifies how that wager was finally settled, but it is certain the cousins soon met again across drawing rooms at half a dozen different friends’ houses, no blows exchanged between them.

At first, Castlewood had been perfectly content to see his sister marry the young Virginian. Maria had remained unmarried for decades, the hem of her long life’s gown snagged on brambles, caked in mud, frayed and stained by years of small misadventures, and any bridegroom who would take her was a blessing. A gentleman from the American colonies was even better: she could retire to his plantation “wigwam” across the Atlantic and be comfortably disposed of, and young Harry would surely outlive his elderly bride by decades, free to console himself however he pleased after she was gone. That all changed, though, the moment Castlewood paid a call on Aunt Bernstein in London. He came away not only trying to dissuade Maria from the match, but professing loud pity for the young man doomed to a lifetime of misery over a silly promise made at one-and-twenty!

Misery, indeed! Maria could not fathom why Harry ought to be miserable. Pity, forsooth! Her brother had never spared a thought for pity before he visited Bernstein. She saw right through the game: their aunt had dangled cold hard cash before Castlewood to break the match off. Harry was a man of honour, she declared, and she could trust him to keep his word.

Off Castlewood stormed then, heading for White’s and the other haunts he frequented, his mind seething with bitter self-reproach. “And so,” he thought, “all my fine ‘virtue’ has done is hand this rich young lamb over to every other wolf on the hunt. There is no earthly use in my sparing him now. That old schoolmaster’s adage runs, *Quem deus vult perdere*—whom the gods would destroy, they first make mad. If I do not fleece him myself, someone else will, that is plain. My brother Will has already taken a petty slice of his fortune, my sister means to swallow the whole of him bodily. Here I have been playing the righteous guardian, refusing to play for stakes higher than a sixpence, protecting his youth and innocence, and what for? I am a fool fattening a fine goose just for other people to carve! I have done very few good deeds in my life, and the only one I thought I had to my credit benefits nothing but strangers. Talk of remorse! By all the fires and furies, the only remorse I feel is for the wicked things I did not do, when I had the chance! Why did I spare Lucretia years ago? She hated me ever after, and her husband went straight to the ruin he was always predestined for. Why did I let this lad off easy? So that March and the rest of the rakes, who do not even care half as much about him as I do, can pluck him bare? Everyone calls me the wicked lord, points me out in the street, warns their sons to keep clear of me, and I am not a penny worse than any of my neighbours, only far unluckier. My cursed softhearted weakness has been my greatest enemy all my life.”

Of course, a chronicler who sets down a gentleman’s unspoken thoughts risks overdraughting the patience of his readers, who are not obliged to believe every word. But did not Livy, Thucydides, and a score of other ancient historians compose entire speeches for their heroes that those men never spoke aloud? With as much right, we transcribe the inner thoughts of Lord Castlewood, whose character we know as intimately as we know the lines of our own palms. A whole pack of wolves are hunting this lamb to make their meal of him—shall one hungry old hunter stand aside and not claim even a single cutlet? Who has not admired that famous speech of Lord Clive’s, when men reproached him on his return from India for seizing too many jaghires, lakhs, gold mohurs, diamonds and pearls? “Upon my life,” the hero of Plassy said, “when I think of all my opportunities, I am surprised I took so little!”

It pains a feeling mind to tell unkind tales about a gentleman until necessity compels it, and so the chronicler has held back much of the unpleasant truth about Lord Castlewood, letting the candid reader see only that he was a nobleman no good man ought to like. It is true that Lord March and the rest of the rakes Castlewood envied would have thought no more of stripping Harry Warrington of his last shilling at the gaming table than they would think of picking clean a chicken’s bones. They would take every advantage their superior skill at cards, at dice, or at the Newmarket races gave them, including private information about the horses running—after all, that was the accepted way of gentlemen in that era. But at least they played fair, and if they lost, they paid their debts.

Madame Bernstein had been loath to tell her favourite Virginian nephew all she knew of his family’s discredit. She had even been touched by Castlewood’s apparent forbearance when Harry first arrived in Europe, pleased that he had complied with her wishes to treat the boy gently. But during their conversation about Maria’s designs on Harry, Castlewood had spoken with his usual brutal cynicism, calling himself a fool for sparing a lad whom no amount of mercy could save from ruin anyway. He’d pointed to Harry’s reckless late nights at faro and hazard, his mad cross-country rides to Newmarket, his spendthrift companions, and demanded to know why he alone ought to keep his hands off the young man. Madame Bernstein’s protest that Harry was not actually as rich as he seemed was waved off with a snort. Bah! Harry was heir to a Virginian estate vast enough to be worth a fortune that could restore their whole ruined family, Castlewood declared, and there were a dozen money-lenders in London who would advance him thousands on post-obit bonds any day. Castlewood spoke from bitter experience: he had applied to those very sharks in his father’s lifetime, and the cursed crew had eaten up two-thirds of his already meagre income.

His desperate ill humour made Madame Bernstein thoroughly alarmed for Harry, and she determined to caution him at the very first opportunity. That very evening she picked up her pen to write him a note, but she had always been slow and clumsy with writing, and hated the task. “I never knew any good come of writing more than a short bon jour or a note of business,” she used to say. “What is the use of writing poorly, when so many clever people do it well? And even they would be wiser to leave the pen alone.” So instead she sent one of her footmen to Harry’s lodgings, bidding him come drink a dish of tea with her the next day, so she might give him her warning. But the next morning she was taken ill, and could not receive him when he called. She kept her chamber for two days more, then there was a great formal engagement she could not skip, and by the time she was free Harry had set off on some jaunt of his own. In the constant whirl of London society, how rarely does a man see his neighbour, a brother his sister, an old schoolfellow his long-lost friend? Weeks passed before Mr. Warrington and his aunt finally got the confidential conversation she had so long planned.

She began by scolding him gently for his extravagance and madcap frolics, though in truth she was secretly charmed by his bold, high-spirited ways. Harry laughed it off, saying young men will be young men, and it was his constant attendance on her that had introduced him to the set of wild companions he spent most of his time with these days. Then she prefaced her warning about Lord Castlewood with much hesitation, and Harry burst into a bitter laugh, saying the good-natured gossips of London had told him every wicked story there was to tell about his cousin already. “To say of a man of his lordship’s rank, or of any gentleman, ‘Do not play with him,’ is more than I like to do,” she continued, “but—”

“Oh, say on, aunt!” Harry exclaimed, almost swearing under his breath.
“Then you have already played cards with your cousin?” the old worldly monitress asked.
“And lost and won, madam!” Harry replied, gallant as ever. “It does not become me to say which. When we have a bout with a neighbour back in Virginia, over a bottle, a pack of cards, or a quarrel, we do not run home to our mothers to tattle. No offence intended, aunt!” Blushing, the handsome young fellow stepped forward and kissed her wrinkled cheek. He looked every inch the hero, draped in a new suit of velvet stitched with gold thread, his fair face glowing, his fine hair powdered, lace ruffs spilling over his wrists. On taking his leave, he pressed a generous handful of coins into the palms of every one of her servants who crowded to see him out.

It was a cold rainy winter’s day, and to spare his fine silk stockings from the mud, Harry called for a sedan chair. “To White’s!” he called to the chairmen, and off they carried him to the club where he spent more and more of his days. His well-wishers might have hoped he would have been a less constant frequenter of that gambling den, but to Harry’s credit, once he sat down at the tables he fought his battles like a true gentleman. He was never flustered by a run of good luck, and perfectly calm when the odds turned against him. Fortune is proverbially fickle to gamblers, but more gamblers are fickle to Fortune: they run away frightened the moment she favours them, deserting her for no reason but cowardice, so that she leaves them for good.

“By George, Mr. Warrington!” Mr. Selwyn cried one night, roused to rare enthusiasm. “You deserve to win! You treat your luck as a gentleman should, and as long as she stays with you, you behave to her with the most perfect politeness. *Si celeres quatit pennas*—you know the rest? No? Well, you are none the worse off for it. You will bow to her ladyship as she steps into her coach, and wave her off politely. Look at Lord Castlewood yonder, passing the dice box. Did you ever hear a man curse and rave so over losing five or six measly pieces of gold? Fortune must be a cruel jade indeed if she ever grants her favours for long to a niggardly cur like that!”

“We do not consider members of our own family to be canaille, sir,” Harry said sharply, “and Lord Castlewood is one of my blood.”

“I forgot, I forgot! I beg your pardon,” his neighbour at the hazard table said. “And let me offer you my compliments on that relation of yours, and his brother Will Esmond, too! The box is mine now. Five’s the main! Deuce-ace, there’s my usual cursed luck. *Virtute mea me involvo!*” he sighed, sinking back into his chair.

We cannot say for certain if it was on this very night that Harry threw the fifteen mains in a row that Horace Walpole mentioned in one of his surviving letters, but it is undeniable that in his first weeks at White’s, Harry enjoyed a run of prodigious luck that seemed to make him the very personification of the Fortunate Youth. The five hundred pounds he had withdrawn from his patrimonial estate in Virginia multiplied into thousands. He bought the finest broadcloth and velvet suits, purchased blooded racehorses, gave grand dinner parties, lavished handsome presents on his friends, and lived as if he were as rich as Sir James Lowther or the Duke of Bedford—and yet his pile of gold never seemed to shrink. No wonder he gave so freely, when giving was so easy, no wonder he carried a Fortunatus’s purse that never emptied. Other men who stumble on such endless luck tie the purse strings tight, drink small beer, and burn cheap tallow candles to save pennies—but that was never Harry’s nature.

In the middle of this golden run, he took the trouble to find out the full sum of Lady Maria’s debts, and paid every last shilling of them off. He even lavished magnificent gifts on Maria’s cold stepmother and half-sister, who had never liked her. “Had you not better get yourself arrested for debt, Will?” my lord said sardonically to his brother. “Even though you bit him for that paltry sum on the horse bet, the ‘Mohock’ will certainly bail you out of pawn.” It was then that Will Esmond felt a true, if far from humble, repentance. “Confound it,” he groaned, “to think I let this fellow slip away for no more than forty pounds! He was good for at least a thousand.”

As for Maria, that generous soul accepted the unexpected fortune with a grateful heart, and stood ready to accept as much more as Harry cared to give her. No sooner had he paid off all her old debts to milliners, modistes, and purveyors than she began running up new ones. Her lady’s maid Betty went the rounds of every shop in town, informing tradespeople that her mistress was about to marry a young gentleman of immense colonial fortune, so they might extend her unlimited credit. The tradesfolk had heard that same story two or three times before, so they did not give it full credit—but Harry was paying the old bills promptly, so they obliged her readily. She even ordered fresh supplies from Mrs. Pincott, of Kensington, the shopkeeper she had once quarrelled with, and when she drove from the mercer to the toy shop to the jeweller in her coach, with her maid and Harry sitting beside her, all London shopkeepers agreed she was a fortunate woman to have secured the Fortunate Youth—though most wondered at the young man’s strange taste in choosing a bride so far past her first bloom.

Mr. Sparks, the jeweller of Tavistock Street in Covent Garden, even waited on Harry at his Bond Street lodgings one morning, carrying the pearl necklace and gold etwee Harry had picked out for Maria the day before, asking if he ought to leave them there or send them to her ladyship with his compliments. Harry added a fine ring from the stock Sparks had brought along with him, bade the jeweller send him the full bill, and dismissed him with a majestic wave of the hand. Sparks bowed so low he nearly scraped the floor, even nodding respectfully to Harry’s Black servant Gumbo as he left.

Harry’s bounties did not end there. A few days later he drove up to Sparks’s shop in his new phaeton, and bought two fine trinkets for the two young ladies, Hetty and Theo, who had been so kind to him in his earlier days in England. “Ah,” he thought, “how I wish I had my poor brother George’s wit and talent for poetry! I would send these presents with pretty verses for them. If goodwill and real affection could make a poet of me, I should have no trouble at all finding rhymes.” So he called in Parson Sampson, and the two of them concocted the little accompanying billet together.

There was Mr. Harry Warrington of Virginia, settled in sun-faded Bond Street lodgings in London, eating of the land’s richest fat and quaffing bumper drafts of its finest claret, by the winter of 1756. The ton had universally dubbed him the Fortunate Youth: young, wealthy, broad-shouldered and handsome, easy of temper and quick to laugh, he was taken to the bosom of fashionable society as if he had been born to a London pewter and a coronet. Do not be too quick to cry out against the world’s selfish fondness for the fair and fortunate, my dear friends. If in my own club I may choose the company of a lively, well-bred young fellow who diverts me over that of a slouching, unwashed misanthrope or a ceaselessly prating coxcomb, may not all of society claim the same small liberty?

Harry was liked because he was eminently likeable. Over a bottle with roistering topers he would roar out a hunting song and drain his glass as deep as any man. With sporting gentlemen he would ride a twenty-mile chase after a fox or tramp through muddy fields after partridge as keenly as the oldest English squire. With ladies he carried a soft, blushing shyness that rendered him endlessly charming. To those of lower rank he was magnificently, unthinkingly liberal, slipping a guinea to a footman who fumbled a tray or sparing a poor groom a scolding for spooking his horse. He carried himself with the grand high air of a gentleman of rank, no different from any other man of quality in that day, when lines of hierarchy were drawn sharp and clear: the Secretary of State knelt to the King every morning with his despatches, and the Under-Secretary dared not sit down in his chief’s presence. Even I, for all my modern liberal notions, confess I bristle a little when a man whose only connection to letters is through the parish constable slaps my back and calls me “old boy” uninvited, so who are we to grudge Harry his proper dignity?

Every pleasure the 1750s London winter had to offer was his for the asking. He attended the Italian operas that all the wits pretended to decry as foolish, Popish, and unmanly – though every last one of them crowded the boxes night after night to gawk at the singers. He saw Garrick thunder through tragedy at Drury Lane, and Mrs. Clive steal the show in farce at Covent Garden. He drifted through masked masquerades and crowded ridottos, but found the private “drums” and card assemblies of the nobility tedious compared to White’s Club, where the play was higher, the stakes fairer, and no prattling old dowager tapped his wrist for betting too deep.

One day his kinsman Lord Castlewood dragged him to St James’s Palace, and presented him to King George II, newly come back from Kensington. The gruff little sovereign was in a black, ill humour, for he either disliked Castlewood or had heard tales of Harry’s gaming from his mistress Lady Yarmouth. “Oh, heard of you from Lady Yarmouth,” he grunted, and turned to Castlewood to snap a rebuke in rapid German that Harry could not follow. “Tell him he plays far too much!” And with that, the Defender of the Faith turned his royal back on the two of them.

Castlewood shrank back, pale as wax. “His Majesty thinks the play at White’s runs too high, and he is displeased,” he whispered.

Harry frowned. “If he does not want us here, we need not come again. For my part, I never thought that German fellow was a proper King of England.”

“Hush! For Heaven’s sake hold your cursed colonial tongue!” Castlewood hissed, clutching Harry’s arm. “The walls here have ears!”

Sure enough, every courtier who had been bowing and simpering at Harry ten minutes before was now shrinking away from him as if he carried the plague. But before Harry could laugh at the absurd spectacle, a broad, broad-shouldered man in a scarlet-laced waistcoat and a great old-fashioned full-bottomed wig stepped forward and clapped a heavy brown hand on his shoulder. “Shake hands, nephew. I heard every word you said. The walls may have ears, but so do I. If all the rest of them give you the cold shoulder, I’ll give you my hand.” He grinned. “You’ve got the very same eyes your father had, though I suppose you Virginians grow a little wiry out there on your plantations. I’m Sir Miles Warrington, your father’s brother. Castlewood knows me well enough.”

Castlewood looked positively yellow with fright. “Yes, my dear Harry, this is your paternal uncle, Sir Miles Warrington.”

“Might as well have come up to Norfolk to visit us instead of dangling about playing the fool at Tunbridge Wells, Mr. Warrington – or Mr. Esmond, whichever you choose to call yourself.” The baronet chuckled. “The old lady your mother still calls herself Madam Esmond, doesn’t she?”

Harry lifted his chin a little, proud. “My mother is not ashamed of her father’s name, nor am I, uncle.”

“Well said, lad. Come back to Hill Street with me at three o’clock, and eat a bit of roast mutton with Lady Warrington – that is, unless you cannot bear to go without your fancy White’s kickshaws.” He nodded at the still trembling Castlewood. “Don’t look so frightened, my lord. I shan’t go blabbing tales out of school.”

On their walk out to St James’s Street later, Castlewood begged Harry not to listen to any ill rumours Sir Miles might spread about him, explaining the two men had old family quarrels dating back years, and Harry ought to take all the baronet’s words with a very large grain of salt.

By the time Harry stepped into White’s an hour later, the story of the king’s snub had already spread far and wide. The tale had already warped past recognition: everyone was saying the king was jealous of Harry’s favour with Lady Yarmouth, that Harry was on the closest possible terms with the royal favourite, that his victories at the gaming table were the talk of every club in town. Half a dozen gentlemen clapped him on the back that night to congratulate him on his “conquest” of the court, and by dawn it was settled fact that the Fortunate Youth had added the royal household to his long list of triumphs.

Harry turned up at Sir Miles’s Hill Street house at three sharp, and found Lady Warrington stiff and stately, her two teenaged daughters curtseying so primly they barely spoke a word to him, and the little heir Master Miles propped up at the dinner table beside his tutor. Halfway through the meal, the small boy stared hard at Harry for a long minute and blurted out, “Are you wicked, cousin Harry? You don’t look very wicked!”

His tutor Mr. Walker turned bright red and tried to hush him, but the boy cried louder, “You said he was! And mamma said too that Lady Yarmouth is a wicked woman!”

Sir Miles roared with laughter. “We are all miserable sinners, Miley, haven’t you heard the parson say so every Sunday? He’s no more wicked than the rest of us. Run off with your tutor now, and you shall have a ride on your little pony in the park this afternoon.” He turned to Harry once the boy was gone, grinning. “My wife here has taken to Mr. Whitfield’s preaching these last few years, ever since our poor eldest son died, and that chaplain of theirs Ward that came over to Virginia brought back a whole sack full of wild tales about you and your brother George.”

Harry’s face flamed. “Say what you like of me, but if any man dares breathe a word against my brother George I will break his bones! That Ward was not fit to buckle my brother’s shoes, and if I ever catch him repeating the lies he told in our house I’ll cane him soundly.”

Sir Miles clapped him on the back so hard he nearly spilled his wine. “There’s the Warrington spirit! I always said you weren’t half as bad as you were painted.” That night Harry stopped off at a jeweller’s in Tavistock Street on his way to White’s, bought three pretty trinkets for his girl cousins, and told the shopkeeper to send them over with a note saying they were a gift from their aunt Madam Esmond in Virginia. The girls were overjoyed, and wrote a collective thank-you note that made its way across the Atlantic to Virginia that spring. Madam Esmond read it, smiled sadly, and knew full well the gifts were Harry’s, given in a fit of his usual generosity while his luck was still high. She immediately tightened the household purse strings, vowing to save every spare penny for when his luck turned – though the poor pinched servants on her estate began to steal and skirmish all the more to make up for their short rations.

A few weeks later Harry was lounging in his Bond Street lodgings in a brocade dressing gown, sipping chocolate, his face pale and haggard. His luck had turned sharply. Two nights running he had lost heavily at White’s, and owed Mackreth the club proprietor nearly a thousand pounds in counters. Parson Sampson crept in, fumbling with a crumpled piece of paper, and humbly begged Harry to settle the two hundred and forty three pounds of debts he had asked his patron to cover. Harry had laughed grimly, promised he would sell out a portion of his Virginia stock that afternoon to cover it, and sent Sampson away, his own head sinking into his hands as he prodded the coals in the fire with his poker, muttering oaths under his breath.

His old friend Colonel Lambert knocked not long after, fresh from the Captain-General’s levee, his military cloak still dusted with road grime from the country. Harry greeted him, and heard that the entire Lambert family was in London for a spell, staying with their old friend Lord Wrotham. But Harry’s face fell, for he knew well what was coming.

Sure enough, Lambert sighed and said, “Every man at the levee was gossiping about your great winnings at play. They say you have won six, eight thousand pounds in the last month alone. I did not undeceive them.” He pulled a small velvet packet out of his coat pocket, and held it out. “Harry, those pretty trinkets you sent my Hetty and Theo – they cannot be paid for with gaming house winnings. I cannot let my girls wear jewellery bought with money won off the turn of a card. Mrs Lambert kept the small locket you gave her, and sends you all her love and a God bless you. I would not bring these back to grieve you, lad, but I have no other choice.”

Pride, and the sharp sting of his recent losses, and the endless prying eyes of all London all came surging up in Harry’s breast. He stood up, bristling, and refused to take the older man’s outstretched hand. “I have had quite enough of unsolicited advice from you, sir. You make it your business to pry into my gains, my company, my amusements, when I never once asked for your counsel. I tried to show my gratitude for your past kindness by sending your family those small gifts, and you cast them back in my face. This is an insult I will bear from no man alive. My servants will show you to the door, sir!” And rustling in his brocade dressing gown, he turned on his heel and stormed off to his bedroom, leaving the good colonel standing alone in the empty parlour, the little velvet packet still in his hand.

When his carefully chosen peace offerings were turned away, our hot-headed young Virginian chief flew into a towering rage, not only with Colonel Lambert, but with every last member of that gentleman’s household. “He has humiliated me before the girls!” he fumed to himself. “He and that paragon Wolfe, forever lecturing me on morality and lording over me with their airs of superiority and protection—they’ve turned the whole family against me, painted me as nothing but a reckless scapegrace and ungrateful prodigal. So virtuous they won’t deign to shake my hand, and when I try to show them a little common gratitude for their kindness, they fling my gifts right back in my face!”
“Lord, sir, those trinkets you brought them must be worth a small fortune!” Parson Sampson murmured, his eyes glinting covetously as he leaned over the pair of morocco leather cases, where Mr. Sparks’ fine golden gewgaws rested plump on white satin cushions.
“They cost a pretty penny, Sampson,” Harry said. “Not that I’d grudge ten times the sum for folks who’d shown me half the kindness those Lamberts have.”
“Never a doubt of it, your honour!” Sampson cut in, ever ready to heap praise on his patron. “Not if I know your generous heart!”
“That repeater, they told me back in Paris, was a bargain at a hundred pounds. I remember little Miss Hetty chattering once that she’d give anything to own a repeating watch.”
“What a perfect treasure!” the chaplain cried. “A little circle of pearls set round the back, a tiny diamond knob for the stem! It would win any woman’s heart on the spot, sir!”
“There’s an apple-woman passing by in the street with her basket,” Harry snarled, half yanking the watch out of its case. “I’ve a mind to fling the whole thing down to her right now.”
When Harry set out an hour later on business that took him to the City and the Temple, his parasite didn’t dare follow him far past the Strand, turning off with a muttered excuse that he had a mortal terror of Chancery Lane and all its sharp-tongued lawyers and grim, narrow precincts. Harry met his broker, and the pair walked together to the Bank, where after a few short formalities and a quick signature or two, Harry left with a thick wad of crisp new banknotes tucked deep in his coat pocket. The broker treated him to dinner at one of the great, famous City dining houses, then walked him through the throng on the Exchange, where Harry hung his head in shame. What would his mother back at Castlewood on the Potomac say, he wondered, if she knew he was emptying most of his father’s patrimony straight into a gambler’s pocket? Every merchant on the floor, he was sure, was whispering about him: *That’s young Esmond, Madam Esmond’s son. He’s losing every last penny at the cards, selling off his estate bit by bit.*
His spirits only lifted once he’d passed under the grinning carved traitor heads above Temple Bar, and escaped the City’s noxious, prying streets. He wandered home through the Strand, glancing in at St James’s Street on his way, but the Chocolate Houses were still nearly empty, most of their patrons lingering over late dinners.
Back in his lodgings, Harry pulled out his bundle of banknotes, slipped three of them into a sheet of paper, and sealed it carefully, scrawling inside: *Much good may they do you. H. E. W.* He addressed the packet to the Reverend Mr. Sampson, left it propped on the chimney glass over the mantel, and told his servants to hand it to the parson the moment he returned.
His phaeton was drawn up at the door by then, and he climbed in, fully intending to drive round the park—until a sharp east wind bit at his cheeks, and he turned his horses’ heads straight down St James’s Street, pulling up at White’s a little after three o’clock. Hardly anyone else had arrived yet, the usual hour for dinner still dragging on. The only other soul in the coffee room was his cousin Lord Castlewood, lolling over a copy of the *Public Advertiser* fresh from his duties at St James’s Palace nearby.
Castlewood yawned and flipped a page idly. What to do with an hour to kill? A quick game of piquet? Harry had no objections. “Just an hour,” Castlewood said. “I dine over in Arlington Street at four.” “Just an hour,” Harry agreed, and the cards were called for.
“Shall we play upstairs, in the little back tea room?” Castlewood suggested. “Away from all this noise down here.”
“Certainly,” Harry said. “Out of the noise.”
By five o’clock, half a dozen gentlemen had drifted in after their dinners, loitering over coffee, cards, and gossip. Two of them leaned against the window frame, toothpicks stuck in the corners of their mouths, staring out at the street.
“Whose phaeton is that parked out front?” the first man asked.
“The Fortunate Youth’s,” his companion replied.
“Not so fortunate these last three nights, then. Luck’s turned dead against him. Lost thirteen hundred pounds to the table last night. John, has Mr. Warrington been in today?”
“Mr. Warrington is in the house right now, sir,” the footman answered. “He’s in the little back tea room with Lord Castlewood, been there since three, playing piquet.”
“Fine sport for Castlewood, that,” the first man sniffed, shrugging.
The second swore under his breath. “Curse the man. He never ought to be allowed in this club at all. He won’t pay a debt if he loses. No gentleman ought to play with him. Sir Miles Warrington told me at Court the other day Castlewood has owed him money on a bet these three years running.”
“Castlewood never loses when he plays one on one,” the first man grinned, showing his polished, clean teeth. “A big table flusters him, that’s why he never joins the big games down here.”
“Let’s go up and stop them,” the second man growled.
“Why bother?” the other said, nodding out the window. “Far better to watch the lamplighter climbing his ladder. Look at that old fool in the sedan chair down there—did you ever see such a droll old quiz?”
“Wait, who’s that just rushing out the door? It’s Fortunatus himself! Looks like he forgot his phaeton’s been waiting out here for hours. Two to one he’s lost every penny he had to Castlewood.”
“Jack, do you take me for a fool?” the first man scoffed. “Look at that fine pair of greys he’s got. My, how he’s flogging them!” They watched Harry gallop up St James’s Street, sedan chair men and coachmen scrambling out of his way, before Lord Castlewood slipped out a few minutes later, climbed into his own waiting chair, and vanished down the street.
Harry drove straight back to his lodgings, the horses’ hooves clattering on the wet pavement all the way. His servant Gumbo was lingering on the steps chatting to a country-looking maidservant, who dropped a quick curtsy and scurried off when she saw Harry. Gumbo was forever flirting with some pretty maid or other, wherever they went.
“Gumbo—did Mr. Sampson come by while I was out?” Harry called down from his driving seat.
“No, sar. Mr. Sampson ain’t been here!” Gumbo answered. Harry told him to run upstairs and fetch the sealed letter he’d left for the parson on the mantel.
“Letter for Mr. Sampson? Oh yes, sir,” Gumbo said, though he could not read a word of writing.
“The sealed one, you fool, in the glass above the chimney!” Harry snapped. Gumbo trundled slowly upstairs to fetch it. The moment Harry had the letter in his hand, he turned his horses’ heads back towards St James’s Street, and the two gossiping gentlemen still leaning out White’s window stared in surprise as the Fortunate Youth came galloping back past them.
When he and Castlewood had left the tea room, Harry had noticed a whole crowd of new patrons had gathered in the main gaming room, a new bank already set up. Several men had already donned their special gaming jackets, the heavy coats they kept stashed at the club for all-night sessions at the tables. Harry walked straight to the clerk’s desk, paid off his debt from the night before, and sat down at the table, calling for a stack of fresh counters. It had been a brutal unlucky week for the so-called Fortunate Youth, and this night was no different. He called for more counters, then more, his face pale and quiet, though he remained perfectly polite and affable to anyone who spoke to him. But he could not win, no matter how many hands he drew.
At last he stood up to leave. “Hang on, stay and turn your luck!” Lord March called, sitting beside him with a great heap of green and white counters stacked in front of him. “Take a hundred of mine, go on playing.”
“I’ve had enough for tonight, my lord,” Harry said. He trundled down to the coffee room, ate a broiled chop, and walked home to his lodgings a little after midnight.
A man often sleeps sound enough after a great, shaming catastrophe. It is the waking in the dark hours before dawn that is the cruel part. Last night you proposed to Miss Brown, you quarrelled and pulled Captain Jones’s nose over the wine, you sat down to cards with Colonel Robinson and left him a pile of IOU’s you can never hope to pay. All those memories come crowding in on you at dawn, throbbing behind your eyes along with your headache. What a vast, dreary gulf there stretches between today and yesterday! You feel like you have aged ten years in a single night. You yank your nightcap over your eyes, pull the blankets up over your nose, trying to sleep the whole disaster away. It was only a dream, you tell yourself. But sleep will not come. The watchman’s cry echoes up the street. Harry remembers the repeating watch he bought for Hetty, tucked under his pillow. Ting, ting, ting! It chimes six times in the darkness, then a little extra trill to mark the half hour. Poor little Hetty, bright and sweet and innocent, he thinks. He would have loved to see her face light up when he gave her that watch. What will Maria say? (Boring old Maria, he thinks suddenly, she has become such a drag.) What will his mother back at Virginia say when she learns he has lost every last penny of his ready money, five thousand pounds on top of all his former winnings, in just three nights? He tells himself Castlewood could not have cheated him—no, his cousin simply plays piquet far better than he does. Harry is even glad his kinsman, who so badly needed the money, walked away with it. And he had not played a penny more than he could afford to lose, at the very least. But the curse of his bad company, his foolish extravagance, the shame and remorse still burns hot in his chest. “Will my mother ever forgive me?” the young prodigal whispers to himself. “Oh, that I were home again, that I had never left the banks of the Potomac.”
At last the grey London dawn peeps through the shutters. The housemaid comes in to light the fire and let the thin pale morning light spill into the room, followed soon by Gumbo, who warms Harry’s dressing gown and sets out his shaving plate and clean linen. Then the hairdresser arrives to curl and powder his hair, while Harry sips his tea and reads his morning letters. By breakfast time, Parson Sampson shows up, eager-faced and smiling, his usual servile self. He explains he never made it to the lodgings the night before, some jolly fellows dragged him off to dinner at the St. Alban’s Tavern and they made a full night of drinking of it.
“Oh, Parson!” Harry groans. “That was the worst night you ever spent in your whole life! Look here, sir.”
“This torn open envelope with the words ‘Much good may it do you’ written inside?” Sampson says, glancing at the scrap of paper.
“Look at the address on the outside!” Harry cries. “That envelope was meant for you.” The parson’s face goes white with alarm. “Did someone break it open, sir?”
“Someone did, yes—me,” Harry says. “I broke it open myself, Sampson. If you had turned up yesterday afternoon as you said you would, you would have found that envelope stuffed full of banknotes. As it is, every last penny of it went last night, straight to the infernal macao table.”
“All of it?” Sampson gasps.
“All of it,” Harry says. “Along with all the money I drew from the City, every last penny of ready cash I had left in the world. Yesterday afternoon I played piquet with my cousin—with a gentleman at White’s—and he won every penny I had on me. When I remembered there was that money left here, unless you had fetched it, I drove back, grabbed it, and took it straight back to the tables, lost it along with every other shilling I owned. Great heavens, Sampson—what is the matter with you, man?”
“It’s my luck!” the poor chaplain wails, bursting into full, unashamed tears. “It’s always my cursed luck!”
“What, you are snivelling like a baby over the loss of a couple hundred pounds?” Harry snaps, angry and flustered. “Gumbo, get out of here! Confound you, why do you always poke your woolly head in at the door when you’re not wanted!”
“Some gentleman downstairs want to see master, with a little bill,” Gumbo mumbles.
“Tell him to go to Jericho!” Harry roars. “I’m not at home, sir, not to anyone at this hour of the morning!”
There’s a scuffle and a few muffled shouts out on the landing, then silence. Harry’s mood is no lighter after that altercation, and he rounds savagely on Sampson, who sits hunched over, his face buried in his hands.
“Why don’t you knock back a bumper of brandy to cheer yourself up, Mr. Sampson?” he sneers. “Hang it, man, don’t blubber like a silly woman!”
“It’s not for myself I’m crying!” Sampson snaps, lifting his head, wiping the tears off his face. “I’m used to bad luck, sir.”
“Not for you, then?” Harry blinks. “Are you weeping because someone else is hurt, pray?”
“Yes, sir,” the parson says, his voice cracking. “Because an honest family is going to be ruined, and it is all my fault. I’ve lodged for years above a bootmaker’s shop, a good hardworking man. A few days back, certain I could count on a friend to lend me the money I needed, I borrowed sixty pounds from him that he was supposed to pay his own landlord. Now I can’t get the money anywhere. The bailiff will be here tomorrow to seize all his goods, and his wife and his dear little children will be thrown out onto the street. All through my fault. But as you say, Mr. Warrington, I have no right to snivel like a woman. I thank you for all your past kindness, sir, and I will bid you good day.”
He grabs his broad-brimmed hat and walks straight out of the room.
Harry bursts out into a savage, bitter laugh, half mad with rage at himself, at his bad luck, at the whole world. Sampson hears the laugh from the stairs behind him, then Harry shouting after him: “Sampson! Hang you, come back! It was all a mistake, I beg your pardon!” But the parson is cut to the quick, and he keeps walking. Harry hears the street door slam behind him, and the sound thuds like a blow right against his own chest. He stumbles back into his room, sinks heavy into his plush armchair. He is the prodigal, wallowing knee-deep in the filth of his own bad choices: gambling, waste, drunken nights, dissolute companions, foolish choices that have trampled him flat.
But he is not quite beaten yet. He shoves all those ugly, gnawing remorses away from him, grabs the full glass of brandy he had offered Sampson a few minutes earlier, rips off his fine damask dressing gown, and rings for the trembling Gumbo. “Not that one!” he roars, when Gumbo hands him a bright green coat with plated buttons and a gold cord trim. “Give me a plain suit—the plainer the better. The old black mourning coat.” Gumbo brings out the heavy plain black suit Harry has not touched for months.
Harry lays all his valuables out on the table: first his new fine gold watch, then the pearl-backed repeater he had meant for Hetty, then the pearl necklace he had bought for Theo, his half dozen fancy rings (all save his grandfather’s old carved seal ring, which he kisses tenderly and tucks safely on his pincushion), his three gold snuff boxes, and last of all his old knit purse his mother had stitched back in Virginia, which holds only three shillings and sixpence and a worn old silver pocket piece he had carried with him across the ocean. He tucks all the trinkets under his arm, claps his hat on his head, and walks out the door.
On the landing he meets his landlord, Mr. Ruff, who bows and cringes, and holds out a bill a yard long. “I would be much obliged if Mr. Warrington could settle this today. My wife has a large account to pay off.” Ruff was one of the head waiters at White’s, close to the club’s owner Mr. Mackreth, and his demand only makes Harry’s temper worse.
“Of course I will settle the bill,” Harry says, glowering down at the man from the top of the stairs.
“Perhaps Mr. Warrington could settle it now?”
“No, sir, I will not settle it now!” Harry barks, bullying forward.
“I am very, very much in need of the money, sir,” Ruff pleads. “My wife—”
“Hang you, get out of my way!” Harry roars, shoving the man back hard against the wall, nearly tipping him head over heels down the landing. He tramps down the stairs and out into Bond Street.
The Guards

Long years moving through the world have put a vast parade of characters before my eyes, but I confess I have met scarcely one of that stock figure so common to plays and novels: the unalloyed religious hypocrite, who preaches piety from dawn till dusk and does not believe a single word of his own sermons—the infidel in broad brim and sable gown, exhorting, condemning, and blessing his neighbors without any real faith in heaven or fear of hell. Look at the procession trundling to Sunday evening services: the hobnail boots clumping down the lane, the rustling maidservants in new ribbons trailed by grinning young apprentices, the neat little lines of schoolboys, the trim young maidens and staid matrons clutching glistening prayer-books, all stepping to the chime of the chapel bell (even as the nearby Ebenezer congregation, a sea of great bonnets, pattens, and propped-up umbrellas, gathers under flaring gas-lamps). How many of those assembled are hypocrites, do you suppose? The maid is very likely thinking of her sweetheart; the grocer turns over in his head how to secure a much-needed shipment of sugar and whether the County Bank will accept his next note; the head schoolboy crams Latin verses he has not yet learned for Monday's exercise; the psalm clerk whose voice drones through the service is fretting over his daughter's secret trouble, scarcely aware of the words he recites; the very moment the parson bows his face to his prayer cushion, he may well be thinking of a bill that falls due on Monday. None of these people are heavenly-minded: they are of the world, worldly, their feet still planted firmly on its soil, but they are not hypocrites, not by half. Most people stow their religion away in a handy mental lock-up, a sort of valuable tonic they bring out only when life's ills strike. And everyone is eager to administer that tonic to their neighbor, same as the old 18th century country ladies, every one of whom kept a still-room and medicine chest stocked with pills, powders, and cordials to dose every villager round about.

My Lady Warrington, for her part, took full charge of both the consciences and the digestions of her husband's tenants and entire household, and tended to the spiritual and physical health of the servants' hall as a sacred personal duty.
