Heaven alone knows if her prescriptions, spiritual or medicinal, were always sound—but she dispensed both with unshakable faith in her own absolute authority, and all her household swallowed them down obediently. She was fully convinced she was one of the most virtuous, self-denying, wise, and learned women alive, and dinned that opinion so incessantly into the ears of everyone around her that a great many of them soon came to believe it too.

At Sir Miles Warrington's dinner table, the sideboard groaned under so much glittering silver plate, and so many liveried footmen circulated through the room, that it took a sharp observer to notice the ale poured from the massive silver tankards was thin, and the grandest silver serving dish on the table held nothing but a single plain joint of mutton. When Sir Miles toasted the King, smacking his lips over his glass, he eyed the wine and his assembled guests as if he were drinking ambrosia itself. He leaned over to ask Harry if Virginia ever produced port half so fine, and declared this vintage was nothing next to the cellars waiting for him in Norfolk. He praised the wine so lavishly that Harry almost convinced himself it was delicious, squinting into his own glass to try and spot all the wonderful qualities his uncle swore were hidden in the ruby liquid.

Just as so many well-to-do families of the era did, the Warringtons had their two celebrated paragons of young womanhood. The two grown daughters, Lady Warrington informed Harry in all confidence, were the finest creatures alive: the elder, Flora, was the realm's most renowned beauty, already betrothed to the kind, estimable Tom Claypool; the younger, Dora, was a genius and an angel, forever determined to refine Harry's wits and uplift his morals. She played the harpsichord for him for hours (though Harry privately thought her performance rather out of tune for a heavenly creature), and was never short of advice, instruction, and conversation—far too much of it, Harry thought, who would far rather have passed his time with his quiet little young cousin, who reminded him of Fanny Mountain back on the Virginia plantation. That small girl, though, was always sent off to the nursery as soon as the dinner ended. Flora drifted off to her own pursuits, Lady Warrington left to visit her poor tenants or scribble her lengthy, voluminous religious correspondence, and Sir Miles dozed off in his armchair, leaving Dora to keep their young cousin company. Harry found the calm, steady rhythm of the Warrington household a pleasant refuge from the raucous gambling halls and dissipated society he had been mixing with in London, and he could not have asked for a warmer welcome: the doors were thrown open to him at every hour of the day, and if Dora was not at home to greet him, Flora always was. Within days of his first visit, he and his little young cousin Miles had arranged to ride a galloping match in the park, and Harry, generous to a fault with everyone around him, was already planning to buy the boy a new horse far finer than the scraggy little beast he was currently riding—when disaster struck, and every last one of Harry's "coaches and horses" came to a sudden, crashing halt.

Though Sir Miles had once imagined Virginia was a tiny island somewhere far across the sea, the Warrington ladies were far better schooled in geography, and endlessly eager to hear every detail of Harry's home and native estate. Harry, for his part, was more than happy to talk. He described the sprawling bounds of his land, the long rivers that edged his property, the rich crops his fields bore. He had dabbled in surveying with a friend back in his boyhood, and he drew them a full map of his home county, dotting it here and there with fine, bustling towns that in truth were little more than rough log huts—though for the honor of his homeland, he saw no harm in making them look as handsome as possible. He marked the Potomac, the James River, the wharves where his mother's tobacco ships loaded their cargo to sail out to the sea. In truth, his whole estate was as large as an entire English county. He did not brag overmuch about his holdings, but to see the handsome young man in his velvet suit and silver lace, bent over his map, pointing out wooded hills and broad forests, anyone would have thought he was a traveling prince describing the vast dominions of his mother the queen. At moments, he almost fancied himself one. He owned miles of land for every single acre the average English gentleman could call his own.

Not just Dora hung on his every word—even the beautiful Flora bowed her fair head and listened with full attention. After all, what was young Tom Claypool, heir to a paltry five thousand Norfolk acres, loud and clumsy in his great mud boots, next to this charming American prince who spoke so easily of lords and macaronis, of March and Chesterfield, Selwyn and Bolingbroke? Even Dora, for all her supposed angelic temper, grew sharp and jealous, teasing Flora for shamelessly flirting with their handsome cousin. Tom Claypool in his gaudy red waistcoat would sit dumb and stammering before Harry in his fine ruffles and lace, spinning stories of London's highest society. Lady Warrington grew fonder of Harry by the day, treating him as her very own son. She fretted endlessly over the spiritual welfare of the native tribes and the enslaved people on his Virginia lands, desperate to help the sainted Madam Esmond (as she insisted Harry's mother must be) with her missionary work. Her pious butler and housekeeper were utterly charmed by Harry's servant Gumbo, gushing over his sweet singing and devout demeanor. "Ah Harry, Harry, you wild, dear boy!" Lady Warrington would exclaim, lifting her eyes to the ceiling in her usual pious pose. "Why did you not come to us sooner, and waste all those years running around with spendthrifts and vain, wicked company? But it is not too late! We must reclaim you, dear Harry! Mustn't we, Sir Miles? Mustn't we Dora? Mustn't we, Flora?" All three of the women nodded, eyes turned heavenward, all determined to rescue their dear prodigal—each competing to be the one to win him over first. Dora watched Flora jealously every time Harry spoke, and when the girls were out of the room, Lady Warrington spoke to him more tenderly and seriously still, promising to be a second mother to him in the absence of his own admirable parent. She pressed a new hymn-book into his hands, and kissed him gently on the forehead, every action motivated, she was certain, by nothing but pure, selfless love, tenderness, and religious devotion for her dear, wayward, amiable nephew.

While all these sentimentalities were unfolding within the Warrington walls, Harry's affairs out of doors had reached the direst of straits. The fortune that had favored him for so many weeks suddenly abandoned him entirely, and just a handful of days was all it took to kick down his entire heap of winnings. We would never dare insinuate that his own kinsman Lord Castlewood acted dishonorably over the green baize table, or stripped Harry of his fortune across a couple of private afternoon gaming sessions, out of respect for his lordship's good name—but there was no denying that every last legitimate penny Harry had owned was gone. Lord Castlewood would have gambled with him for his entire future inheritance too, if Harry had not finally thrown up his hands, too beaten to play another hand. Remembering that he still held one small remaining sum, set aside expressly for the poor clergyman Sampson, Harry risked that at the tables too. That last scrap of capital vanished along with all the rest, and Fortune fluttered off into the storm, leaving the luckless young adventurer almost stripped bare on the shore.

When a man is young, hearty, and generous as Harry was, the loss of money does not weigh on him overmuch. He would sell his horses and his carriage, scale back his entire household and expenses. If he needed quick cash, was not his wealthy Aunt Bernstein his willing banker? Or his kinsman Lord Castlewood who had won so heavily from him? Or his kind Uncle and Aunt Warrington, who talked endlessly of virtue and benevolence and swore they loved him as a son? He could call on any of them, whenever he pleased. For the moment, though, Sampson's tale of his landlord's desperate poverty weighed on his mind, and to raise a quick sum to help the clergyman, he gathered up all his trinkets and carried them to a pawnbroker's shop in St. Martin's Lane. That pawnbroker was a relative and business partner of the very Mr. Sparks of Tavistock Street from whom Harry had bought the diamond-handled enamelled repeater he had intended to give as a gift to his friends back at Oakhurst. When Mr. Sparks dropped by his partner's shop a short time after Harry had pawned his goods, he spotted the repeater at once, and burst into a stream of angry, unkind remarks about Harry that I will not repeat here, to avoid being accused of speaking far too plainly.

A man who counts a pawnbroker among his friends is sure to count a bailiff or two among his acquaintances, and those bailiffs' officers serve the law with perfect impartiality: they will lay hands as readily on the shoulder of the fiercest army captain with his epaulets glinting as on the finest dressed macaroni in all of London. The very same men who had arrested Lady Maria at Tunbridge Wells were soon set on Harry. They easily wheedled the information out of garrulous Gumbo, who was off courting the maid from the Lambert household next door, that his master was staying regularly at Sir Miles Warrington's house in Hill Street. The two bailiffs' men settled down to wait outside the door, while Harry sat inside blissfully enjoying the warm, loving family gathering around his aunt's dinner table. That evening had never been more pleasant: Sir Miles was more jovial than ever, Lady Warrington more gentle, gracious, and affectionate, Flora looked unusually lovely, and Dora was far more amiable than Harry had ever seen her. At parting, my lady pressed both his hands, and called down a shower of blessings on his head from the ceiling above them. "Hang it, nephew!" Sir Miles boomed in his heartiest tone. "When I was your age I would have stolen a kiss from two such pretty girls as Do and Flo, my own flesh and blood too! Don't look so bashful, oddsfish! It's the boy blushing, not the girls!" "Papa!" the two virgins cried out in unison. "Sir Miles!" his august wife chided him at the very same instant. But before anyone could protest further, the harmless little osculatory transaction was complete, and blushing Harry had pressed a chaste kiss to the damask cheek of Flora, then to that of Dora.

As Harry followed his uncle down the stairs, Lady Warrington turned to her daughters, staring fixedly up at the ceiling cornice as usual. "What precious qualities your dear cousin has!" she said. "What shrewdness mingled with his simple sweetness, what a fine, genteel manner—though of course I set very little store by mere worldly elegance. What a dreadful pity that such a fine soul should ever be lost! We must rescue him, my loves. We must draw him away from those wicked companions and those horrible Castlewoods—not that I would ever speak ill of my neighbors, of course. But I shall hope, I shall pray, that he may be pulled free from his evil courses!" She glowered at the cornice with such determined ferocity that the girls, their own eyes fixed wistfully on the door behind which their interesting young cousin had just vanished, did not dare speak.

His uncle walked Harry all the way to the street door, calling "God bless you, my boy!" with the utmost affection, squeezing Harry's hand and repeating his valuable benediction one more time at the threshold. The moment the door clicked shut behind Harry, and the light from the hall within had fully illuminated his face and figure, the two men who had been loitering on the opposite side of the street stepped forward rapidly. One pulled a scrap of legal paper from his pocket, clapped a hand firmly on Harry's shoulder, and declared him his prisoner. A hackney coach was waiting by the curb, and before he could even cry out in surprise, poor Harry was being carted off to Chancery Lane, to spend the night locked up in a squalid debtor's spunging-house on Cursitor Street. Only think of it: the son of Madam Esmond, the Virginian prince, his shoulder prodded by a ragged bailiff's follower, locked in a London jail. I do not envy our young prodigal his rest on that dismal night. My beloved young friends, let us not waste pity on him, now that he is down. Imagine the sharp stings of remorse keeping him awake on his dingy, scratchy pillow, the raucous jollifications of other hardened inmates ringing in his ears from the room next door where they sit carousing, the hot rage, shame, and utter discomfiture churning in his gut. After all, you good, honest young gentlemen have never indulged in extravagance or folly, or had to wake to pay the bitter reckoning of your own remorse, have you?

Harry Warrington felt sincere, hot remorse for his past follies and missteps the moment he found himself locked in that grim, cobwebbed Cursitor Street lock-up house, tangled up in equal parts rage and humiliation at the vulgar indignity of being arrested like some common debtor. Still, he assured himself the unpleasantness could not possibly last: he had at least twenty wealthy, loyal friends who would rush to spring him the second he sent word. The only question was, to whom should he appeal first?

There was Mr. Draper, the obsequious family man of business; his kind uncle Sir Miles, who had offered him a permanent home and loved him like a son; his cousin Castlewood, who had won such enormous sums from him at the card tables; his noble companions at the Chocolate-House; his sharp, warm-hearted old aunt Madame Bernstein. Any of them would surely come to his aid, he was certain, though the more prying relatives might dole out a well-deserved scolding for his imprudence. Most of all, Harry was desperate to keep the affair quiet: he could not bear the thought of the ton knowing a gentleman of his standing had been subjected to such a low, common process as arrest.

As if the world does not eventually learn every trivial thing it cares to pry out! As if the dinner I will eat tonight, or the hole in the stocking I am wearing as I write these words, could possibly stay a secret from some nosy enemy who has a mind to dig it up—even with my boots laced tight and my door fully locked when I dressed! I mention that hole in the stocking only as an example. There is no private detail of our lives the curious public cannot root out, if it cares to look. But there is a consolation, stubbornly rejected by every man caught in his own moment of shame, that the world simply does not care. Think of the centuries of scandal the public has been forced to sit through! It is jaded, blasé, utterly tired of that sort of gossip. Are you dragged off to prison and convinced you are irrevocably disgraced? Do you go bankrupt under suspicious circumstances? Do you get caught cheating a friend out of money and imagine all of society will turn its back on you? Psha! Your shame is nothing but vanity. Brush the mud off your coat, smile as if nothing happened, walk back into society as normal, and no one will bat an eye. Do you imagine the whole world will pull out its handkerchief and weep inconsolably when you die? Why on earth would it care whether you disgrace or distinguish yourself in life? The world will talk, dine, joke, yawn, and move on, just as it always has. Do not be so conceited as to imagine your private little affairs matter half as much as you think they do, my boy.

But Harry Warrington chafed and paced his cell as if every soul in London was already whispering about the heavy hand laid on his fine, noble shoulder.
“What a fine sensation my arrest must have made at the club!” he thought, glowering. “That man Selwyn will no doubt crack a dozen cruel jokes at my expense, plague take him! Everyone around the card table will have heard the news. March will be panicking over the bet I have with him, and faith, I shan’t be able to pay it if I lose, now. They’ll all hoot and cheer that the so-called Savage from Virginia has finally been clapped in irons. How am I ever to show my face in public again?”

After a moment’s thought, half sharp, half naive, he decided: he would not send word first to any of his relations, or any of his grand friends at White’s. He would call Sampson, the chaplain. The man had landed in exactly this kind of scrape a dozen times before, he would know exactly what to do. At the first faint streak of dawn—Harry was convinced the sun had deliberately forgotten to make the turn down Cursitor Street that morning, the hours dragging so slow they felt like days—he sent a messenger to Long Acre, begging the reverend gentleman to come at once to give him advice and comfort.

Harry had no idea that summoning Sampson to his side was the same as leaning over the edge of a lion pit and yelling down to your friend to come join you. He probably assumed Sampson’s own troubles were long behind him, or more likely, he was so wrapped up in his own distress he barely spared a thought for anyone else’s. Once the messenger was gone, he relaxed a little, and asked for breakfast. The attendant who brought him his tea and bread asked if he wanted to order dinner, or eat at Mrs. Bailiff’s common table with the other resident gentlemen.
“No,” Harry told him loftily. “I will be long gone from this place before dinner is served.” The turnkey smirked, having heard that exact line from a hundred panicked young gentlemen before. “Well, sir, if you do end up staying, there’s fine beef and carrots on the table at two o’clock,” he said, and shut the door on Harry and his brooding thoughts.

Ten o’clock came, then eleven, then noon, and still no sign of Sampson. Instead, around midday, Gumbo arrived, toting a portmanteau of his master’s fine clothes, and flung himself roaring and sobbing on the floor at Harry’s feet. He swore a thousand oaths of loyalty, declaring he would die for his master, sell himself back into slavery all over again, do anything at all to get Mr. Harry out of this terrible place. Harry was moved by the boy’s obvious affection, and told him to get up off his knees, where he was grovelling and clinging to Harry’s legs.
“All you need do now, lad, is hand me my clothes to dress, and hold your tongue about this whole business,” Harry said sternly. “Not a single word to anyone, you understand?”

“Oh no, sir! Never to nobody!” Gumbo vowed, his face deadly solemn, as he fussed over his master, dusting powder into his hair and dressing him in his finest silk coat and lace cravat, until Harry looked as polished and splendid as if he were just stepping into his sedan chair to attend a reception at St. James’s.

All the love and servility Gumbo felt for his beloved master could do nothing to undo what had already been done, though. He was utterly incapable of keeping such a juicy, dramatic secret. The language of the enslaved—black slaves, and white domestic slaves alike—is all lies. The oppressed creature slips away into half-truths and evasions like a hunted fox darting for its burrow the moment it spots its pursuer, the tyrant master. These strange, leftover relics of feudalism run through every part of our old social life. Our servants, who are men and brothers just as we are, are all forced to act as hypocrites in front of us. They never speak naturally, or tell the full unvarnished truth. We would fly into a rage, call them impudent, and kick them out of doors if they ever did.

The truth was, Gumbo’s tongue had been wagging nonstop since the moment he found out his master was arrested. He had already shared the woeful news with dozens of his fellow footmen, bragging, embellishing, and gasping out the story at the footmen’s club frequented by the staff of half the leading noble houses of London. He had stopped for a mug of ale in Sir Miles Warrington’s butler’s quarters and told the whole tale twice over. He had run to Madame Bernstein’s household to grieve with the servants there, and then trotted over to Lord Castlewood’s staff to spread the word further. When he laid his hand on his heart and swore he had told no one of his master’s misfortune, everyone who knew him could easily gauge exactly how much truth that statement held.

At last, shortly after noon, a letter arrived, not from Sampson in person, but scribbled in his messy hand, sealed with a still-damp wafer, the ink barely dry. The unlucky chaplain wrote:
“Oh sir, dear sir, I have done everything a man possibly can for my dearest patron! You did not know what peril you were drawing me into, or else if I was to go to prison, I would have happily shared yours, instead of being locked in a lock-up house three doors away from you this instant.
It is true! As I was hurrying to your side, ready to face any danger for the kindest benefactor I have ever known, two villains with a writ against me seized me, and dragged me to Naboth’s jail, so close to your rooms that we could almost shout to each other across our back garden walls.
I had so much important advice to give you that I dare not commit to paper. I hope your fortunes mend soon. I pray my own cursed luck turns around too,
Your honour’s afflicted Chaplain-in-Ordinary, J. S.”

Since Sampson refused to write down the full story, we may as well fill in the gaps he left. Gumbo’s gossip had not yet reached Long Acre the night before, so Sampson knew nothing of Harry’s arrest until his messenger arrived that morning. Burning with gratitude for the favour Harry had done him only days before, he ran straight to Lord Castlewood’s house to beg for his help: he knew full well how enormous a sum Castlewood had won from his cousin at cards, and was sure the man would not let his own kinsman rot in jail for lack of a few pounds. His passionate, sincere speech of appeal fell on entirely deaf ears.

Castlewood cut him off sharply. “Did I not tell you two days ago, when you came begging me for money, that I am as poor as any beggar on the street?” he snapped. “No one has left me a fortune since then! Every penny I won from my cousin was swallowed up by my own creditors. Not only can I not help Mr. Warrington, I swear to you I had no idea he was in trouble, and I wrote a letter to him this very morning begging him to lend me money.” That exact letter would arrive at Harry’s lodgings a few hours later, sent via penny post.
“I must get him money, my lord!” Sampson cried. “He barely had a shilling left in his pocket after he bailed me out. I will pawn my cassock and my clerical bands before I let him stay in there!”
“Amen to that,” Castlewood said, not looking up from his newspaper. “Go pawn your bands, your cassock, anything you like. Your enthusiasm does you great credit.”

Lady Maria had heard Sampson talking to her brother, and guessed exactly what the conversation was about. She caught the chaplain the moment he stormed out of the study, and dragged him into the dining room, her face streaked with real tears of sympathy. “Tell me what has happened to Mr. Warrington?” she asked.
“Your ladyship already knows?” Sampson exclaimed, shocked.
“Have I not been in mortal terror ever since his servant brought us the dreadful news last night?” Maria said. “We heard it coming home from the opera, in Lady Yarmouth’s box—my lord, my sister-in-law, and I.”
“So his lordship knew all along?” Sampson said, his temper snapping. He swore out loud, and spilled the whole story of how Castlewood had won thousands off Harry at cards, then refused to lift a finger to help him, and raved about Harry’s extraordinary generosity to him, the chaplain.

Maria then burst into a furious, unsparing tirade against her own family, the kind of unvarnished truths warring relatives will spill about one another with no filter. She shrieked curses, ranted about every single member of the Esmond clan, and then charged straight for her brother’s study door, screaming so loud the alarmed Sampson fled out into the street to avoid the coming scene.

Castlewood looked up from his paper, surprised at his sister’s red-faced fury, and threw out a sharp oath to try and stop her onslaught. But Maria, normally timid around her brother, was far too riled up to be frightened now.
“So, my lord!” she yelled. “You sit with that poor boy in private at cards, you fleece him dry! You take every last shilling he has, and you won’t even lend him a single guinea of his own winnings now he’s penniless and in jail!”
“That damned chaplain has been running his mouth, has he?” Castlewood said.
“Dismiss him! Pay his wages and send him off, he’ll be glad enough to go!” Maria shouted.
“I keep him around to marry one of my sisters off if we ever need it,” Castlewood said, glowering at her.
“What sort of women could we ever be, when our men are all as vile as you?” Maria cried.
“Very true,” Castlewood said, shrugging.
“We are bad enough, but you? You have no courage, no honour, no basic human decency! Your own equals refuse to play cards with you any more, so you go after this innocent boy from Virginia, your own cousin, and rob him blind! It’s a shame! A disgrace!”
“Everyone plays their own game in this world, don’t they?” Castlewood said. “Didn’t you play your own game and win, Maria? Where did this sudden squeamishness about the poor Virginia lad come from? Did Harry break off your arrangement, or did your ladyship land a better offer? If you won’t take him, I know the old Methodist aunt in Hill Street will give him a choice of her two granddaughters, mark my words. Are you a fool, Maria Esmond? Even more of a fool than usual?”
“I am a fool to expect any of my brothers could act like an honest man!” Maria snapped back. “A fool to think you would ever help a relative in distress, or pass up the chance to fleece any easy victim you find.”
“Fleece him? Psha! What nonsense are you talking? You saw what sort of life that lad was leading for months past. Somebody would have stripped him of every penny, sooner or later. If I hadn’t won his money, some other gambler at White’s would have. And I never stopped you from chasing your little plan for him, did I? Why are you throwing a fit now, just because I reached out and took the money he was throwing at every man he met? Don’t you see this whole mess is the best possible thing that could have happened for you? You were chasing a whole principality out in Virginia, weren’t you? A little misfortune like a stay in jail will make that boy far more likely to cling to the woman who bails him out, and far less likely to run off chasing some pretty 18 year old girl. That silly promise of marriage he all but gave you a Tunbridge Wells? He won’t dare back out of it now. You were raging like a lion a minute ago, and now you might just end up a princess.”

Maria, who had charged at her brother like a wild lioness, settled down meekly at his feet to listen to the rest of his scheme.

Over on Clarges Street, Madame de Bernstein had been furious when Gumbo brought her the news of Harry’s arrest the night before. She could not sleep a wink for thinking of him, and none of her household staff dared face her bad temper. She knew very well arrest was a common enough event in London society, but she fretted over how deep her favourite nephew had gotten himself in debt. He was the only person in decades that cold, tired old woman had ever felt genuine affection for, and she was ready to help him, as long as he had not landed himself in truly irreversible trouble. She sent a messenger at dawn to her lawyer Mr. Draper, ordering him to find out exactly what writs were holding Harry, and how much money was owed.

Draper’s men found Harry locked up only a few streets away. The only debts out against him that day were Mr. Sparks the jeweller’s bill for all the fancy presents he had bought, and his Bond Street lodging house bill. Draper pointed out that paying them off would be no trouble at all, and Harry could be out by midday, back home to dress and come dine with Madame Bernstein by two o’clock, ready to show his face at the clubs and laugh off the whole mess. But the Baroness shook her head.
“My good Mr. Draper,” she said, “that boy has sown far too many wild oats already. I want him to come out of prison when he is fully cured of his folly, with no lingering hidden debts hanging over his head. You know no gentleman ever tells anyone the full list of his debts, not even his own lawyer. Let him stay there a day or two longer. It will do him more good than any scolding I could ever give him.”

The gentle, loyal devotion of his servant Gumbo softened Harry Warrington’s wrathful, bitter spirit enough that his second night in the debtors’ sponging-house passed far more peacefully than the first. At least one soul in the whole cold, selfish world of London gentry cared enough to grieve for him, to tend to him, to share his misfortune. Even so, save for that one small spot of softness, Harry’s heart was still hardened with pride and resentment toward every other person he had once counted as a friend. All of them, he raged to himself, had proven selfish and unworthy: his pious Aunt Warrington back home, his haughty noble friend Lord March, his sharp, cynical cousin Castlewood. He would rot in prison for twenty years before he ever stooped to beg a favour from any of them again. What a fool he had been, to put his trust in their fine promises and their professed friendship! There was no true friendship anywhere in this cursed, cold English nation. He would leave it, that was certain. He would never trust an Englishman, high or low, ever again. He could ride to Germany and join the great King of Prussia’s army on campaign, or he could sail all the way back to Virginia, bury himself deep in the tobacco plantations, hunt from dawn till dusk, act as his mother’s land-steward, marry some steady local girl like Polly Broadbent or Fanny Mountain, and live out the rest of his days far away from these false, ungrateful fine gentlemen.

He rose the next morning with a forced cheerful expression, but a storm of angry pride still churning in his chest. Faithful Gumbo was already waiting outside his door at the first light, having walked all the way from their old lodgings on Bond Street, carrying Harry’s post. “I tried to bring more of your clothes, sir,” the honest man said, “but Mr. Ruff, the landlord there, wouldn’t let me take a single extra thing out of the house.” Harry had no appetite to look at the letters at first, but he slit the seals one by one anyway: every single one was a bill. The fourth letter came from the Bond Street landlord himself, informing Harry that no more of his property would leave the premises, that if his outstanding bill was not settled immediately he would sell all of Harry’s goods to pay himself, and that Gumbo would no longer be allowed to sleep on the property. Gumbo added that he had found a place to stay for the night, with some acquaintances at Lord Wrotham’s house. “With Colonel Lambert’s family, sir,” he said, peering hard at his master’s face. “And Miss Hetty, she fainted clean away when she heard the bailiffs had taken you up. Mr. Lambert, he’s a very good man, and he told me to tell you that the second you send for him, he’ll come running straight here.”

Harry’s heart twisted when he heard Hetty had been so distressed by his misfortune. He did not fully believe Gumbo’s story about the fainting fit, long accustomed to his servant’s tendency to exaggerate every dramatic detail, but when Gumbo spoke of Colonel Lambert his dark mood curdled again. *Me send for Lambert?* he thought, grinding his teeth until his jaw ached. The man who had insulted him to his face, who had flung all of Harry’s expensive gifts right back in his face? He would starve to death on a crust of bread in the gutter before he ever begged for a favour from Lambert.

Dressed at last, Harry called for his breakfast, and sent Gumbo off with a sharp, imperious note summoning Mr. Draper, the attorney in the Temple, to come attend him at once. “That note was so haughty, you’d think he was writing to one of his own enslaved field hands back in Virginia, not a freeborn English gentleman!” Draper later fumed to Madame de Bernstein. Harry had always treated the lawyer with unbearable condescension, of course. “It’s all very well for a fine gentleman to put on airs in his fine drawing rooms, but a fellow locked up in a sponging-house? Hang him, I half had a mind not to show up at all!”

For all his grumbling, Draper did go. He found Harry even more arrogant in the depths of his misfortune than he had ever been in the height of his wealthy, carefree days. Mr. Warrington was perched on the edge of the dingy iron bed in a magnificent brocade dressing-gown, his hair fully powdered and styled just as carefully as if he was dressing for a royal reception at St. James’s. He waved a hand at Gumbo, ordering him to pull a chair out for the lawyer.

“Excuse me, madam, but I have never been accustomed to such insufferable airs from a man in his position!” Draper ranted later to Madame de Bernstein, when he went to report back to her. She only smiled, highly amused at the lawyer’s wounded pride. She liked her nephew all the better for carrying himself like a great lord even when he was at his lowest ebb.

The plan for this interview had been carefully arranged between the Baroness and her attorney the day before. Draper was a sharp, capable man, who usually served his clients well, but he failed here that day because he was stung and angry, or more likely still, because he could never quite understand the proud, high-souled young gentleman he was dealing with. I think every reader who counts themselves a gentleman will have observed this odd, unspoken friction between people of different stations: you will offend a man who is not a gentleman without ever knowing how or why, and he will offend you a thousand times over, never guessing he has done anything amiss. He will say or do something that sparks your quiet scorn, he will spot that scorn instantly (always on edge, always overthinking his own manners) and fly into a rage. You will speak to him as naturally as you would to an equal, and he will be convinced you are sneering at him. You will feel nothing but indifference toward him, and he will hate you all the more for that indifference.

“Gumbo, pull a chair for Mr. Draper!” Harry said, folding his brocade dressing-gown tight around his legs as he settled on the bed. “Sit down, if you please, and let us discuss my business. Thank you for coming so promptly in answer to my note. Had you heard of this piece of ill luck before you arrived?”

Draper had, of course. “Bad news travels fast, Mr. Warrington,” he said. “I was eager to offer my humble services the moment you should require them. Your family will be greatly grieved that a gentleman of your rank should be confined in such a place.”

“I have been very imprudent, Mr. Draper. I lived far beyond my means.” Draper bowed. “I gambled with gentlemen who had ten times my fortune, and a run of terrible luck carried off all my ready cash, leaving me with liabilities of five hundred pounds and more.”

“Five hundred exactly is owed to the creditors who have you confined, sir,” Draper said.

“It is a mere trifle,” Harry said, staring at the lawyer in confusion. “I thought I could send a note round to a few friends yesterday, settle the debt, and walk straight home without any more fuss. I was mistaken. So I must ask you to arrange the sum for me as quickly as possible.”

Draper pulled a very long, grave face. “Why, sir, it can be done in time — but it will take a great deal of time. To touch the English property that comes to you only on the death of your brother George, we would need proof of his death, and the release of the trustees, and who can arrange for that? Your mother, Lady Esmond Warrington, in Virginia, would no doubt never let her son rot in prison, but it will take six full months at least to send a letter there and get a reply. Does your agent in Bristol hold any authority to honour your drafts for large sums?”

“He is only authorised to pay me two hundred pounds a year,” Harry said. “Then I suppose my only remaining option is to apply to my aunt, Madame de Bernstein. She will stand as my security.”

“Her ladyship would do anything for you, sir, she has told me so time and time again,” the lawyer said. “If she gives the word right now, you can walk out of this house this very minute.”

“Then go to her from me, Mr. Draper. I did not want to trouble my relations over this, but rather than waste more days in this pointless, horrible imprisonment, I will speak to her. Tell her exactly where I am, exactly what has happened, do not disguise a single detail. Tell her I trust in her kindness and affection for me to release me from this — this disgrace,” Harry’s voice shook a little, and he passed a hand over his eyes.

“Sir,” Draper said, eyeing the young man closely, “I was with her ladyship yesterday, going over every single most unpleasant detail of this business. I won’t call it disgraceful, like you do.”

“What do you mean? Madame de Bernstein already knows about my misfortune?” Harry cried.

“Every last circumstance, sir. Even about the watches you pawned, and all.”

Harry’s face burned bright scarlet. “It is a very unfortunate business, pawning those watches and trinkets you bought on credit and never paid for,” Draper went on. Harry shot up from the bed, his face so fierce the lawyer flinched back a little, alarmed. “It could lead to litigation, sir, very unpleasant remarks made in open court. Barristers respect nothing, and once they get a man in the witness box—”

“Great Heaven, sir, you do not think a gentleman of my rank would take a watch on credit with any intention of cheating the tradesman?” Harry shouted, shaking with agitation.

“Of course you meant everything honourable,” Draper said, winking slowly. “Only the law, you see, might not happen to see it that way. (Hang the supercilious beast, that hit him right where it hurts.) Your aunt says it is the most imprudent thing she has ever heard of, to put it no harsher name.”

“Are you putting no harsher name to it, Mr. Draper?” Harry said, speaking every word very slowly, visibly fighting to keep his temper under control. Draper did not like the look on his face.

“Heaven forbid I should say anything ungentlemanly between two gentlemen! But as your legal advisor, it is my duty to tell you, sir, you are in a very unpleasant scrape, just as a doctor must tell his patient he is gravely ill.”

“So you cannot help me pay this debt, and you have only come here to tell me I could be accused of common roguery?” Harry said.

“Of obtaining goods under false pretences? Most assuredly you could, sir. Don’t look at me like you are about to knock me down. (Curse him, I am making him squirm, anyway.) A young gentleman with only two hundred a year from his mother, ordering diamond buckles and gold watches, then taking them straight to the pawnbroker. You ask me what the world will think of that behaviour, and I am telling you honestly. Do not be angry with me, Mr. Warrington.”

“Go on, sir,” Harry groaned.

The lawyer thought he had won the argument entirely. “But you asked if I cannot help you pay the debt? And I say yes! I have the money right here in my pocket to settle every last penny this second, if you like — it is not mine, mark you, it is my honoured client’s, your aunt the Baroness’s. But she has every right to impose her own conditions, and I have brought them with me.”

“Tell them,” Harry said.

“They are not hard conditions at all! They are entirely for your own good. If you agree, we can call a hackney coach this instant and drive straight to her house in Clarges Street, which I promised her I would bring you to whether you agreed to the terms or not. I name no names, but you once made an imprudent promise of marriage to a certain party.”

“Ah!” Harry said, and his face lit up for the first time that day.

“To that marriage, my noble client the Baroness is utterly opposed. She has far better plans for you, and is convinced marrying that party will ruin you entirely — she is of noble birth and title, that is true, but if you will excuse me, she is not of the very best character, and far older than you are. You had given her that imprudent promise once, after all.”

“Yes, and she still has it,” Harry said.

“It has been recovered, sir,” Draper said. “She dropped it by accident at Tunbridge Wells, my client tells me. Her ladyship even showed it to me, it was written in bl—”

“Never mind what it was written in!” Harry cried, turning as red as the red ink he had scrawled that absurd, foolish promise in. He had regretted that mad, childish mistake a thousand times over.

“Along with it, a set of compromising letters you had written to her, that could bring great shame to that noble family, were also recovered,” the lawyer went on. “You had lost them, it was no fault of yours. You were out of the house when they were found. You must see that that noble family, and you yourself, have a friend few young men in this world are lucky enough to have. There is no earthly promise that can bind you now — nothing but idle words spoken over a bottle, that any gentleman can easily forget. All you have to do is say you will not go through with this marriage, give me your word of honour, and it is done. Cry off, I say, Mr. W! Do not be such a damned fool, saving your presence, as to marry an old woman who has jilted dozens of men in her time. Say the word, and I will go downstairs, pay every shilling you owe, and put you in my coach either at your aunt’s house or at White’s Club, if you prefer it, with two hundred guineas left over in your pocket to spend. Say yes, shake my hand! There is no sense sitting grinning behind these prison bars all day!”

Harry had longed to be free of that stupid engagement for months now. His old foolish infatuation for Maria Esmond had died out completely long ago. If he could be rid of it honestly, he would have thanked Draper a minute earlier — but the lawyer’s coarse, familiar manner disgusted him. He shrank back from Draper’s outstretched hand, scarcely even realising he did it, pulling his dressing gown tighter around himself.

“Give me just a little time to think this over, if you please, Mr. Draper,” he said. “Be so good as to return to me again in one hour.”

“Very good, sir, very good, sir!” the lawyer said, biting his lip, and seizing his hat, his face flushing bright red with anger. “Most people would not need an hour to consider such an offer as I have just made you, but I suppose my time must be yours. I will come back, and see whether you are leaving this place or not. Good morning, sir, good morning.” He stomped down the stairs, cursing under his breath the whole way. Won’t shake my hand, won’t he? Wants an hour to think it over? Hang his impudence! I will show him what an hour is!

Draper went back to his chambers in a towering huff, bullied all his clerks, sent a messenger off to Madame de Bernstein to tell her Harry had asked for a little time to consider, which he assured her was only a formality and he had no doubt he would agree. He attended to all his other clients, transacted all his other business, and then went out to a long, leisurely dinner, before finally making his slow way back to the sponging-house on Cursitor Street. “That haughty beast will still be waiting for me when I call,” Draper sneered to himself.

“Is the Fortunate Youth in his room?” Draper asked the bailiff’s assistant who opened the front double doors.

“Mr. Warrington is in his apartment,” the man said, winking and tapping the side of his nose.

“But what, Paddy from Cork?” Draper snapped.

“My name is Costigan! My family is noble, and my native city is Dublin, Mr. Six-and-Eightpence!” the janitor snarled, reeking of strong whiskey that saturated the small entryway between the double doors.

“Confound you, man, let me pass!” Draper bawled.

“I can hear you perfectly well, Six-and-Eightpence, except for your h’s, which you drop out of every sentence. I will thank you not to call names, me good friend, or me fingers and your nose will be getting very well acquainted. Walk in, sir! Be polite from now on to your superiors in birth and manners, even if they are your inferiors in temporary station. Confound the key! Walk in, I say! Madam, I have the honour to salute you most respectfully!”

A lady with her face hidden under a dark capuchin hood, and a handkerchief pressed to her mouth, gave a little startled cry as she hurried down the stairs that instant, rushing past the lawyer. Draper leaned forward to get a good look at her — he was always far too free with his manners toward women — but Costigan, the bailiff’s man, stuck his leg out between Draper and the retreating lady, crying, “Keep your own distance, if you please! This way, madam! I recognised your ladyship the moment I saw you—” He slammed the front door shut right on Draper’s nose, leaving the attorney to stumble his own way up the stairs to Harry’s room.

Back at Clarges Street, the old Baroness de Bernstein paced her drawing room for hours, stopping every few minutes to run to the window whenever she heard the rumble of a passing coach. She had delayed her dinner for hours at a time, though on ordinary occasions she would fly into a rage if her cook was even five minutes late with a meal. She had ordered two places set at her dining table, her finest silver plate laid out, and extra fancy dishes prepared, as if for a small celebration. Four o'clock passed, then five, and at six o'clock a coach finally stopped outside her front door.

“Mr. Draper,” her footman announced, and the attorney entered, bowing very low. The old lady trembled on her ivory cane. “Where is the boy?” she said sharply. “I told you to bring him here with you! How dare you come back without him?”

“It is not my fault, madam,” Draper said, “that Mr. War

When Mr. Draper stormed off in high dudgeon after his morning’s sharp exchange with Harry Warrington, he half fancied he heard the young prisoner call his name from behind him—and indeed, Harry had half risen from his cot, a cry half on his lips to summon the lawyer back. But his pride was raw, and Draper’s temper was already roused; Harry bit back the words before they could escape, and the attorney marched on without a pause. The sting of having to humble himself to a man of the law, forced to yield for no better reason than empty pockets and desperate need of coin, galled Harry so deeply he sank back sullenly onto his straw-stuffed mattress, resolving he could postpone the conversation an hour longer.

He told himself he did not care a farthing for Maria Esmond, that was plain enough. He burned with shame at the memory of how he had been tricked into their engagement: a wily, world-worn woman who had played upon his boyish, Virginian ardour, taking unfair advantage of him just as her brother had cheated him at the card table. They were his own blood, his kinsfolk, and they should have spared him. Instead, they had hunted him like prey, using him for every selfish end of their own. He raged inwardly at their betrayal of hospitality, at how they had turned the young trusting cousin who had walked so confidingly through their gates into a dupe. His heart ached so sore he let his head sink back into his pillow, and hot, bitter tears scalded his cheeks. “If ever they had come to my plantation in Virginia,” he thought, “I would have given them a welcome far kinder than this!”

He was dragged out of this dark despondency by the sight of Gumbo’s grinning face peeking around his cell door, announcing that a lady had come to call on Master Harry. No sooner had the little black servant stepped aside than the lady in the hooded capuchin cloak stepped over the threshold. Harry sat bolt upright on his bed, pale and gaunt, his cheeks still streaked with tears. The lady gave a soft sob, and before Gumbo had even slipped out and shut the door behind him, she ran to his side, flung her arms about his neck with a wild, genuine tenderness that was almost maternal, sobbing against his pale cheek, covering it with kisses as her own tears fell thick and fast.

“Oh, my Harry! Did I ever, ever think to find you here, of all places?”

Harry started back, half scared at the sudden rush of affection, but she sank to her knees beside his bed, clasping his feverish hand, wrapping her arms around his knees. There was no pretense in that regard, no artifice: the sight of his squalid cell, his haggard face, filled her with a pity and love she had never dared show before.

“I—I thought none of you would come,” Harry groaned out.

For a long minute, her only reply was more tears, more soft kisses pressed to his burning knuckles, more tight, clinging clasps of his hand. “Oh, my dear, my dear! I cannot bear to think of you suffering so,” she sobbed. Hardened though her old heart might have seemed, it was no block of marble, her dreary life no total desert. Harry’s own mother could not have spoken more softly, or clung to him more fondly, than his kinswoman kneeling at his feet.

“Some of these debts are my fault, I fear,” she admitted, and the words were true. “You bought trinkets and jewels to give me pleasure, and I hate every last one of them now! I never thought I could hate a gift from you. I have brought all of them here, and more besides—see! And every last shilling I own in the world!” She emptied the contents of her pockets into his lap: brooches set with paste, gold rings, an enameled watch, and a heap of nearly twenty guineas that glinted in the dim cell light. The sight moved Harry so deeply he could barely breathe.

“Dearest, kindest cousin!” he sobbed, and no other words would come, though his stammering gratitude and brimming eyes spoke louder than any speech. He grew light and gay not long after, smiling as he tucked away the trinkets he had once given her, recounting how he had fallen into this trap by buying goods on credit he could not pay back, and how the lawyer Draper had just insulted him over that very business not an hour before. He would not take her money, he swore—he had more than enough to get by for the present—but those twenty guineas were worth as much to him as twenty thousand. He would never forget her kindness, no, he swore by all that was sacred, he never would. He would write to his mother at once and tell her how good she had been to him, how she had cheered him when he was on the very edge of breaking under the shame and misery of his imprisonment. Heaven bless her for it, he cried.

The pair talked on, cheerfully and affectionately, no need to track every soft word they exchanged. After Maria’s visit, the dark gray day seemed far brighter to Harry; the narrow cell did not feel half so oppressive. The world was not all cold and selfish, he told himself. There was a dear, loyal soul here who truly loved him. Even Castlewood, her brother, had not been as unkind as he first seemed: he had been distraught he could not help his cousin, every shilling he had won from Harry at cards lost to other gamesters the very next day. He swore he would do anything he could, that he would come to visit Harry soon, stuck as he was at court on duty, as much a prisoner as Harry himself. They talked on until the light faded completely from the small barred window, and Maria sighed, bade him farewell, and slipped out the door.

The latch had barely clicked shut behind her before it opened again to admit Mr. Draper. “Your most humble servant, sir,” the attorney drawled. His voice grated on Harry’s ears, his presence an open insult.

“I expected you hours ago, sir,” Harry said curtly.

“A lawyer’s time is never his own, sir,” Draper replied, still reeking of the bottle of port he had just finished at the Grecian Coffee House. “But never mind, I am at your service now. I presume all is settled, Mr. Warrington? Got your trunk packed? Why, you’re still in your bedgown! Call your black man to help you tidy yourself, and I’ll go settle all the debts downstairs. I’ve got a coach waiting at the door, and we’ll go dine with the old Baroness.”

“Dine with the Baroness de Bernstein, are you invited to that, pray?” Harry said.

“Not me, no such honour. I ate my dinner long since. It’s you that’s to dine with your aunt, I thought.”

“Mr. Draper, you presume far more than you know,” Harry said, drawing his brocade dressing gown tight around his broad shoulders, standing tall and fierce.

“Good God, sir, what do you mean?” Draper spluttered.

“I mean, sir, that I have thought it over. I gave my word to an honourable, faithful lady, and it does not become a man of honour to break it.”

“Confound you, sir!” the lawyer shrieked. “I tell you she lost the paper! There’s nothing binding you, nothing at all! Why, she’s old enough to be—”

“Enough, sir!” Harry roared, stamping his foot hard on the stone floor. “You seem to mistake me for some other pettifogging knave you’re used to dealing with. I’ll have you know, Mr. Draper, you do not speak to a man who will break his given word for a handful of coin.”

“Pettifogger, indeed!” Draper yelled, flying into a rage. “Man of honour, indeed! I’d have you know I’m as honourable as you are, sir! I haven’t gambled away my whole patrimony, and lived like a lord on two hundred a year! I haven’t bought watches on credit and pawned them—don’t you dare lay a hand on me, sir!” He scrambled back toward the cell door.

“That is the way out, sir,” Harry said. “You can’t escape through the window, it’s barred. So your answer to your client is No, then, is it?”

Draper screamed the word back at him, white with fury. Harry stepped forward, fists clenched. “If you utter one more word—” he began, but the cell door slammed shut before he could finish the threat, and Draper was gone, storming straight back to Madame de Bernstein. Even though he told her his version of the story to make himself look as blameless as possible, she unleashed a far sharper, angrier torrent of abuse on him than Harry had ever spoken.

“What? Shall she trust me, and I desert her?” Harry paced back and forth across his cell, the heavy brocade of his gown rustling as he moved. “Dear, faithful, generous woman! If I lie in this prison for years, I will never break my word to her.”

The Baroness, left alone after throwing her lawyer out, sank down at the dinner table she had hoped to share with Harry. His place was laid out, the silver polished, the glasses glinting in the candlelight. One dish after another was set before her by her silent major-domo, who watched as she picked at each, then pushed it away untouched. At last he dared to speak. “It is eight o’clock, my lady. You have not eaten a bite all day. It will do you no good to go hungry.”

She could not eat. She sent for her coffee instead, told Case the footman to bring it at once. The servants cleared the plates from the table, leaving the old woman sitting alone, staring at the empty chair across from her. A few minutes later, Case came back into the parlour, no coffee in his hands, his face white and as scared as a man who had seen a ghost.

“Mr. Warrington,” he gasped.

The Baroness cried out, half rising from her armchair, only to sink back again, trembling all over. “So you have come at last, sir, have you?” she said, her voice soft and shaking with fondness. “Bring back the—ah!” She shrieked at the top of her lungs. “Gracious God! Who are you?”

Her eyes bulged wide, her white skin looked ghastly under the layer of rouge on her cheeks, and she clung hard to the arms of her chair to keep from fainting. The gentleman who stepped toward her had the exact face and figure of Harry Warrington, and when he spoke his voice had the same rich, familiar tone, but it was not Harry. He bowed politely to the Baroness.

“You expected my brother, madam, I think?” he said. “I only landed in London this very hour. I went first to his lodgings, and met his servant Gumbo at your door, who was carrying a letter for you. I thought I would bring it to you myself before I went to find him.” He laid the sealed letter on the table before her.

“Are you—” the Baroness gasped, “are you my nephew that we all thought was dead?”

“Killed in the French wilderness, and very much alive,” he said. “I am George Warrington, madam. And I ask you, his own kinsfolk: what have you done with my brother?”

“Look, George!” the old woman babbled, bewildered. “I expected him here tonight! That chair was set for him! I have waited for him till I am faint! I do not like being alone. Stay, and sup with me!”

“Pardon me, madam. Please God, I will sup with my brother Harry tonight,” George said.

“Bring him back here! Bring him back on any terms! It is but five hundred pounds! Here is the money, sir, if you need it, all of it!” she cried, fumbling for her purse.

“I have no need of your funds, madam,” George said. “I have coin of my own, and there is no better use for it than to rescue my brother.”

“And you will bring him to me, sir? Promise you will bring him to me!”

George gave her a stately, formal bow by way of answer, then turned and quit the parlour, walking past the gawking, amazed servants. He called to Gumbo in a sharp, commanding tone to follow him. Had Master Harry received no letters from home? Gumbo stammered that Harry had not even opened all his post the past few days, that no letter telling him his brother had escaped the French settlements and sailed home to Virginia had reached him yet.

Quick, horses! Quick down the Strand, across Temple Bar! Here is the house of captivity, and the Deliverer has arrived at last, to break the prisoner free.

Strain, hackney-coach steeds, and bear George Warrington as fast as your hooves will carry him through thronging Strand and rutted Fleet Street, bound for his brother’s prison and rescue! Any soul who has pored over Hogarth’s famous etching of a mid-18th century London hackney carriage and the mud-choked highway it navigates can picture how endless that short stretch of road felt to our young Virginian: scarce a public lamp to be seen, save for the guttering torches borne by ragged link-boys lurching through the dark, badly sprung coaches jolting over cracked uneven paving, gaping potholes that threatened to swallow a wheel whole, and winter quagmires of thick black mud that clung to the boots of every passerby. That three-mile drive from Piccadilly to the Temple felt longer to George than the entire cross-country journey he had completed that very morning, riding post-haste from Bristol where he had landed after eighteen months in French captivity.

He had written twice ahead to Harry: once to break the news that he was alive, not dead on the field of Braddock’s Defeat as all their family had believed, and a second note to say he had safely set foot in England. But the Channel swarmed with French privateers in those days, raiding British merchant craft within sight of the white cliffs, and the ship carrying George’s first letter had been seized mid-voyage. The second letter, mailed from Bristol, arrived at Harry’s London lodgings three days after Harry had been dragged off to the bailiff’s sponging-house, and the surly landlord Mr. Ruff had refused to hand over a single scrap of his former lodger’s post.

George went straight to Harry’s rooms first, on reaching London, to ask after his brother. The maid who opened the door screamed at the sight of his face, the exact mirror of the lodger she thought had simply run off, and bolted shrieking to her mistress. The landlady, not daring to admit she had allowed her husband to sue Harry for debt and throw him in prison, lied that Mr. Warrington had moved out and she knew not a single detail of his new whereabouts. George did not waste breath pressing her: he knew Aunt Bernstein’s house in Clarges Street was but a few steps away. He had read every one of Harry’s letters back to Virginia, gushing over the old Baroness’s uncommon kindness to the boy, a kindness that had even softened their stern mother Madam Esmond, who had never spoken a word of her disgraced sister Beatrix for decades. It was the Baroness’s own warm letter urging Harry’s welfare that had spurred George to set sail for Europe at once.

It was at his aunt’s door that he ran into old Gumbo, the family servant, who nearly fainted dead away at the sight of his long-dead master returned, and stammered out the whole story of Harry’s debt and imprisonment. George had arrived at the old lady’s parlour stiff with righteous anger, convinced their wealthy relations had abandoned Harry to ruin, but the sight of sharp, witty Aunt Bernstein breaking down in unfeigned tears for her favorite boy melted his sternness in an instant, and he chided himself for being far too hasty to judge, that old flaw of his that had gotten him into trouble more than once before in his young life.

The coach jolted and crept its way through the dark streets to the Temple, until at last they pulled up before the bailiff’s grim house. The Jewish porter unlatched the heavy outer door, locked it warily behind them, then led them down a narrow dim passage by the flaring light of a tallow torch, gawking at George’s face, which he mistook at first for the prisoner’s, risen from his bed upstairs. “You’ve come to see Mr. Warrington, sir? There’s two gentlemen already inside seeing to his release, step this way into Mr. Amos’s office for a moment,” he said, and led George into the tiny candle-lit room where the bailiff sat talking to a stout man in a laced hat and military cloak.

The stout officer rose to his feet, outstretching a friendly hand before he even looked properly at the new arrival. “No hard feelings left between us, Harry, my boy!” he called cheerily. “Thank the Almighty, Mr. Amos says there’s no trouble at all with me and James standing bail for you, you’ll be out of here by breakfast tomorrow.” Then he started back, shocked, as George grasped his hand. “Why—who in heaven’s name are you?”

“God bless you, sir,” George said, his voice faltering a little. “I know you at once. You must be Colonel Lambert, of whom my Harry wrote so many tales of kindness. I am his brother— the one left for dead on Braddock’s field, who spent eighteen months in French captivity, and has come home at last to thank you for all you have done for my brother.”

At that moment a second man in a red military tunic stepped through the door, and Colonel Lambert turned to him laughing. “James! James Wolfe, look here! The dead have come back to life! Harry the scapegrace’s brother has returned, whole and hale!” George bowed to the lean sharp-faced lieutenant-colonel, whom Harry had also written of many times. “I know your reputation, sir,” he said. “You helped my brother in his hour of need, and I shall count your friendship the greatest honour.”

Wolfe clapped him on the shoulder, half-smiling. “I’ll own I was cross with the hot-headed boy for speaking so unkindly to my good friend Lambert here, for no cause at all. But Lambert would not hear of leaving him to rot here over a foolish quarrel, and dragged me down to stand bail with him.” The bailiff Amos cut in, bowing, “Your honours’ security is as good as gold. If the young gentleman’s kin will have it, he can walk out of here this very night, no need to wait till morning for the lawyers.”

“The full debt is five hundred pounds odd, is it not?” George said, drawing a heavy purse from his coat. “I will pay the sum at once, and take the proper receipts. But no money will ever pay back what I owe you two gentlemen, for stepping forward to help my Harry when he had no one else to turn to. I thank you, in my own name and my mother’s back in Virginia, and may God bless you for your kindness.”

Upstairs, Harry sat moping over his pipe of home-grown Virginia tobacco, half heartsick even after a recent visit from his loyal sweetheart Maria, fretting a little that her devotion would tie him to a future he was not yet sure he wanted. The door flew open, and Gumbo burst in, eyes bulging, grinning so wide his cheeks stretched. “What is it, fool?” Harry laughed. “Hast thou found a new sweetheart to gape at?”

“No, master!” Gumbo cackled, his whole body trembling with delight. “I seen a ghost! A ghost that come all the way from Madame Bernstein’s house, in a hackney coach, and he’s downstairs in that office right now!”

Harry’s blood ran cold. “A ghost? Is—is my mother all the way from Virginia here?”

Gumbo shook his head so hard his ill-fitting wig slipped askew. “No, master! It’s your other master! The one we thought dead!”

Harry did not stop to button his coat properly, he tore out of the room and raced down the stairs, and paused at the office door to hear that familiar, long-lost voice say, “I thank you, gentlemen, in my mother’s name and mine.”

“Whose voice is that?” Harry cried out, his own voice cracking.

“It’s the ghost’s, mas’r!” Gumbo whooped behind him, and Harry burst through the office door.

Colonels Lambert and Wolfe turned their backs discreetly to give the boys space. The lost was found, the dead was alive. Harry flew straight into his brother’s outstretched arms, sobbing half apologies, half joy, as George held him tight. “Come away, James,” Lambert said softly, after a minute. “We are not needed here. The ladies back in Hill Street will never credit this tale, they will be up half the night gossiping over it. Will you two boys come back to sup with us, and tell the whole story?”

George and Harry shook their heads, smiling through their tears. They had a hundred private tales to tell each other, of captivity, of Virginia, of all the months they had spent apart, no other company needed. Half an hour later, they stepped out of the grim sponging-house door together, into the crisp London night, and for the first time in months, Harry’s heart was light.

When first I had the honour of being presented to Sir Miles Warrington in St. James’s Palace drawing room, I will own that—gazing at his ruddy round face, his broad padded waistcoat, and the unforced hearty bluster of his country manner—I fully believed I had stumbled upon the most agreeable acquaintance imaginable: that much-celebrated ideal of humanity, the good old English country gentleman.

To be that very figure, the world assures us, is to stand next to the gods, perched at the very peak of earthly happiness. You hold a vast rent-roll free of encumbrances, your farmers blessing the stars for a landlord as generous as your honour, their rents paid promptly without a grumble—save for one dilatory soul, of course, whose sole purpose is to give you occasion to show off your sublime Christian charity and universal benevolence. You hunt three days a week, live for the sport, and enjoy the robust health and ravenous appetite that comes of such exercise. You sit in your parish church, the very first man of the congregation, the village’s unchallenged benefactor, surrounded by a murmur of unspoken blessings, and join the rest in intoning “have mercy upon us miserable sinners” only for form’s sake, because the words are printed in the prayer book and it sets a fine example for the poorer folk. A good old country gentleman a miserable sinner? Ridiculous! So hale, so wealthy, so jovial, so revered by the vicar, so adored by his tenants, so worshipped by his family that his old gunroom story of the grouse that nearly shot the gamekeeper gets laughed at for three generations. You cannot make a man in such a position honestly believe he is miserable. Give any man five thousand a year, perfect health, a parish that bows to him, and a family that dotes on him, and you will never convince him he is a wretch worthy of pity. Were you a royal highness, arriving at church to see the entire congregation waiting for you to take your seat before the service began, would you think yourself miserable? You might, of course, if you were wracked with gout, all alone, staring death in the face, the doctor having forbidden you claret and ordered you nothing but arrowroot and a single glass of weak sherry. Then you might be humbled, admit your shortcomings, and acknowledge the vanity of earthly things. But in full health, under bright sunshine, in high spirits? That word miserable is no more than a turn of phrase. You cannot truly think you are to be pitied, not when Colin the ploughman lives with the ague, seven hungry children, eight shillings a week, and two pounds a year to pay for his tiny cottage. No: a rich, jolly, healthy country gentleman’s misery is very easy to bear, and there are barely a soul alive who will dare tell him he is a sinner. He may grow a little selfish, but he is perfectly satisfied with himself. For miles around, there is no one half so good or half so great—save my lord in the castle, of course. His excellent wife tends to his every want, and doles out small acts of charity to the parish; his children bow to his every word; the vicar treats him with deference; he carries weight at quarter sessions, makes poachers tremble, and every man doffs his hat to him at market. His great painted coach rumbles through the market town, his spotless daughters and sublime lady sitting on the cushions inside, and tradesmen cringe bareheaded to greet them, while farmers’ wives drop curtsies thick as blackberries. The ladies inside look down with beneficent smiles on the poor folk, buy a yard of ribbon with great affability, condescend to haggle over an ounce of salts or a packet of flower seeds, and deign to beat down the price of a fat goose at the stall. Their weekly drive is a royal progress, after all, the happy populace presumed to press around them and heap blessings on their heads.

But what if the market woman hid her fat goose when their coach drew near, for fear my lady would insist on buying it for a third of its worth? What if not a single copper ever came flying out of that grand coach window for the ragged boys cheering? What if Sir Miles served his tenants notoriously thin small beer at harvest feasts, and the poor of the parish nothing but watery broth that barely had a ghost of a meat flavour? Such fine old English gentlemen and ladies have existed by the dozen, you know. People who patronised the poor without ever relieving them, who shouted “Amen!” in church as loud as the parish clerk, who went through every form of piety and all the etiquette of the country gentleman’s life, and bought virtue for a bargain price, fully convinced they were honouring virtue by the purchase.

Poor Harry Warrington, stuck in debtors’ prison, sent a desperate plea for help to his relations. His aunt sent him a pious tract and her blessing. His uncle conveniently happened to be out of town on business, and of course could not find time to answer the poor boy’s petition. How much of this sort of behaviour passes every day in respectable society, do you suppose? You can picture Lord and Lady Macbeth huddling awkwardly after they have committed a murder, of course. But Lord and Lady Skinflint, the pair who lock themselves in their bedroom at night and agree to turn their luckless nephew away penniless, then go down to family prayers, discourse virtuously before their children and servants, then go back to whispering nose to nose about the kinsman fallen among thieves, groaning unheeded in his distress? What must they think of each other? How dare they keep up their virtuous airs? How dare they look each other in the face? Dare? Do you suppose they think they have done wrong? Do you imagine Skinflint lies awake tortured by remorse, thinking of the hunger he turned away empty? Not a bit of it. He is indignant at the prodigal for being a fool, never ashamed of himself for being a miser. What? A young man with such fine prospects squandered them on gamblers and tavern feasts? Horrible! Shocking! Take warning, children, that is what comes of extravagance! Per the great established church of the Pharisees, this is the perfect chance for a moral lecture.

“To think he deceived us so!” cries Lady Warrington.
“Very sad, very sad, my dear,” nods Sir Miles, wagging his jowly head.
“To think of such wild extravagance at his age!”
“Cards, bets, lavish feasts in the most wicked taverns, carriages and fine riding horses, the company of all the rich profligates of his own sex, and I fear, the most iniquitous persons of ours too!”
“Hush, my lady!” Sir Miles cuts her off, glancing at his daughters Dora and Flora, who have hung their heads, blushing bright red at the mention of those last naughty figures. “The children are in the room, for goodness sake.”
“No wonder my poor dears hide their faces!” their mother goes on. “I wish the very existence of such wicked people could be kept from you, my loves!”
“They can’t go to the opera or the park without seeing them, to be sure,” Sir Miles chuckles.
“To think we let that young serpent make himself at home in this family, that we left him in the company of our little guileless darling Miles!” She points to her small son, playing on the rug at her feet.
“Who’s a serpent, mamma?” the boy pipes up. “First you said Cousin Harry was good, then you said he was bad, now he’s a serpent. Which is he, Sir Miles?”
“He has faults like all of us, Miley dear. Your cousin has been wild, and you must take warning from him.”
“Wasn’t my older brother Hugh, the one who died, wild too? He was never kind to me when I was small, never gave me toys, never rode me on his shoulders, never—why are you crying, mamma? I remember you and Hugh were always fighting—”
“Silence, sir!” his father and sisters cry out at the same time. “You know you are never to speak that name!”
“I don’t care!” the sturdy little rebel declares. “I love Harry, and I never loved Hugh. If Cousin Harry is in prison, I’ll give him the half-guinea my godfather gave me, and everything I have—except my little pony, and my silver waistcoat, and Snowball the rabbit and Sweetlips the spaniel, and—my custard after dinner. But I’ll give him half the custard, anyway!”
“Shut thy mouth with that custard, child, and run along,” Sir Miles laughs. He had a good store of easy, good-natured humour.
“Who would ever have thought Harry would turn out so wild?” Lady Warrington resumes.
“Nay, youth is the time for sowing wild oats, my dear.”
“That we were so mistaken in him!” the two girls sigh in unison.
“To think he kissed both of you at the New Year party!” Sir Miles grins.
“Sir Miles Warrington! That sort of vulgar talk is unforgivable!” his wife huffs, drawing herself up to her full majestic height.
“Which of you was his favourite, girls?”
“Favourite indeed! I told him over and over again of my engagement to dear Tom, I did, Dora—why are you sneering, may I ask?” Flora tosses her pretty head.
“To do her justice, Dora turned him down too,” her father says.
“Flora was forever forgetting that engagement to Tom, if you ask me,” Dora remarks.
“I never! Never, never, never wanted to break things off with Tom! It’s wicked of you to say so, Dora! It’s you who are always sniping at him, always jealous because gentlemen happen to think I’m not ill-looking, and prefer me to people who are all full of their own ‘learning’ and witticisms!” Flora snaps, glancing at her reflection in the glass over the mantel.
“Why are you always staring at that glass, sister?” little Miley puts in. “Surely you know what your own face looks like by now!”
“Some people stare at that glass just as often who have far less reason to,” Sir Miles says gallantly.
“If you mean me, Sir Miles, I thank you,” Dora retorts. “My face is as Heaven made it, given to me by my father and mother. It is no fault of mine if I favour your side of the family. If my face is plain, at least there are brains inside my head. Me jealous of Flora, for capturing poor Tom Claypool? I might as well be proud of charming a ploughboy!”
“Pray miss, wasn’t your Mr. Harry from Virginia far cleverer than Tom Claypool? You would have had him at the asking, and you know it!” Flora fires back.
“And so would you, miss! You would have dumped Tom Claypool straight in the Thames if Harry had asked you!”
The bickering goes on, the shuttlecock of wrath batted briskly back and forth between the two sisters. “Oh my children! Is this how you dwell together in unity?” their mother cries, laying down her embroidery with a dramatic flourish. “What an example you are setting for this innocent little boy!”
“Go on, fight! I want to see!” Miley cheers, rubbing his small hands together. “At her, Flora! Worry her, Dora!”
“Good sport, isn’t it, Miley?” his father cackles.
“Oh Sir Miles! Oh my children! These disputes are unseemly, they tear a fond mother’s heart apart!” Lady Warrington moans, though she looks remarkably calm for a woman whose heart is supposedly lacerated. “How thankful we ought to be that our watchful care prevented any foolish engagements between you and your misguided cousin. If we were mistaken in him, is it not a mercy we found out in time? If either of you ever felt a fondness for him, your good sense will teach you to stamp out that silly, vain feeling. That we were kind to him can never be a regret—it only proves our good nature. The only thing we have to grieve over is that your cousin proved unworthy of our kindness, coming fresh from the company of gamblers and play-actors, and bringing contamination—almost pollution, I dare say—into this pure family!”
Flora snorts under her breath, “Oh bother mamma’s sermon.” Sir Miles has already tiptoed out of the room whistling softly, and little Miley is winding up his top, pegging it under the trailing hems of his sisters’ gowns. The top hums, staggers in drunken little circles, wobbles, and collapses long before Lady Warrington has finished her long pious harangue.
“Were you listening to me, my child?” she asks, resting her hand on Miley’s head.
“Yes mother,” he says, the whipcord from his top still in his mouth. “You were saying Harry is very poor now, and we ought not to help him. That’s what you were saying, isn’t it madam?”
“My poor child, you will understand me better when you are older!” his mother sighs, rolling her eyes up towards the ceiling, her favourite position for pious speeches.
“Get out, you little wretch!” Dora yelps, when the top nicks her toe. Miley cackles with glee at her discomfiture.
But what is this? Sir Miles comes hurrying back into the drawing room, his face as red as a holly berry, and Tom Claypool, his neighbour, trundles after him, breathless.
“Here’s a fine business, my lady!” Sir Miles cries. “The most wonderful wonder of wonders, girls!”
“For goodness sake, gentlemen, what is your news?” the virtuous matron demands.
“The whole town is talking of it!” Tom puffs, still out of breath. “I saw him last night at Ranelagh, Sir Miles, walking with a fellow who looks exactly like him. Same face, same height, one in a blue suit, one in a brown—suits Harry was wearing here in this very house, not a month back!”
“What suits? What fellow?” the girls cry, all in a breath.
“Why your fine young Virginian of a cousin, to be sure!” Sir Miles says. “Our precious heir to a whole Virginian principality.”
“Is my nephew released from his prison then?” Lady Warrington asks. “Is he plunged back into the vortex of dissipa—”
“Confound him!” Sir Miles roars, swearing far more loudly than his lady would approve of. “What would you think if that precious nephew of mine turned out to be an impostor? No better than a common adventurer!”
