“An inward monitor whispered me as much!” the lady gasps. “But I drove the unworthy suspicion from my mind. Speak Sir Miles, we are burning to hear your news!”
“I’ll speak when you’ve finished gasping, my love,” Sir Miles says. “What do you think of this fellow who waltzed into my house, ate my dinners, was treated like one of the family, kissed my wife’s hand, talked of his vast Virginian estates, and turns out to be nothing but a beggarly SECOND SON? A penniless nobody, my lady!”
“Sir Miles Warrington, no such violent language in front of the children! I sink to the earth, confounded by this unutterable hypocrisy. Did I leave you alone with that pretender, my innocent little boy?” the matron cries, hugging Miley tight.
“Who’s an impostor, mummy?” Miley asks.
“That confounded young scamp Harry Warrington!” his father bellows.
The boy stares for a second, puzzled, then bursts into full-throated howls, squirming out of his mother’s embrace. Just then the butler throws open the door, and announces, “Mr. George Warrington, Mr. Henry Warrington!”
Lady Warrington drops Miley straight onto the rug. Sir Miles’s face turns the colour of Tom Claypool’s scarlet waistcoat. The three ladies rise to their feet, dropping three of the frigidest curtsies ever seen, as the two young men walk into the room. Little Miley runs straight towards them, holding out one grubby hand.
“Oh Harry! No—wait, which is Harry? You’re my Harry!” He points straight at the right twin, throwing his arms around Harry’s legs. “Oh you dear Harry! I’m so glad you’re here! They’ve been saying all sorts of horrible things about you!”
“I came to pay my duty to my uncle,” the dark-haired twin, George, says, smiling. “And to thank him for all the kindness he showed my brother Henry while we were apart.”
“What, nephew George! The very spitting image of my brother! Both of you boys, I am delighted to see you!” Sir Miles cries, all his anger vanishing in a second, as he grabs a hand from each of them, his ruddy face glowing with unfeigned pleasure.
“This is truly a most mysterious and providential revelation,” Lady Warrington says, dropping another frosty curtsy. “Though I cannot help wondering why nephew Henry concealed the fact he was not the heir until now.”
“He did not know it himself, no more than your ladyship,” George says. The young ladies look at each other, their eyes cast down.
“Indeed! A most singular circumstance,” their aunt says. “We had heard the rumour, you see, and Mr. Claypool was just bringing us the news when you arrived. We were discussing it with my daughters only this very minute.”
“Yes!” Miley’s little voice pipes up. “And they said Harry was a imp—”
“Silence, child! Screwby, take Master Warrington up to his room at once!” his mother snaps. “These, nephew George, are your cousins Dora and Flora.”
The girls curtsy again, holding out their hands very coldly. George makes a deep, elegant bow that takes in all three ladies, hat pressed to his heart. “It is my duty, madam, to pay my respects to you and my uncle, and thank you for whatever hospitality you saw fit to extend to my brother.”
“It was not much, but it was our best!” Sir Miles roars, clapping George on the shoulder. “Ods bobs, it was our best!”
“And we both appreciate it greatly, sir,” George says, glancing around the room. “Give us thy hand, no more of this formality,” Sir Miles laughs. “What, do you think I’m some sort of ogre, that I won’t welcome my own dead brother’s sons to my house? What do you say lads,

Come step across the street with me, if you will, gracious reader, and you will find our young guests gathered at Lord Wrotham’s London house—one he has lent outright to his old friend General Lambert, that tight little household we first came to know at Oakhurst and later at Tunbridge Wells. James Wolfe promised to join them for dinner this evening, but the young lieutenant-colonel is loitering at Miss Lowther’s side, counting a single glance from her dear eyes far sweeter than the finest spiced kickshaw Wrotham’s celebrated French cook could turn out, or the lavish dessert laid out for tonight’s feast. You shall take his place at the table; rest assured he will not be coming. As for me, I shall linger at the sideboard, pen in hand, to jot down every word that passes.

Look first at the women’s faces, glowing bright as warm candlelight! When Harry Warrington was dragged away by bailiffs not long prior, I had half a mind to tell you how the good Mrs. Lambert flew straight to her husband the second she heard of the boy’s misfortune, begging, imploring, insisting that Martin do everything in his power to pull Harry out of the scrape. “Never mind his stubborn huff the other day,” she pleaded, “never mind that he was angry when we sent his presents back—of course a high-spirited lad like Harry would be cross! Never mind that our pockets are stretched thin, and every spare penny is earmarked for our own boys’ university fees. There must be some way to free him. Did you not pull Charles Watkins out of ruin two years ago? And did he not pay you back every last halfpenny? You made that whole family happy, blessed be God, and Mrs. Watkins prays for you to this very day. I swear every good thing that has happened to us since then has come of it—there is no doubt in my mind that your kindness is the very reason you made Major-General,” the fond wife finished, patting his arm.

Martin Lambert required barely any persuasion to do a good turn. He agreed at once to seek out his friend James Wolfe to stand bail for Harry, grabbed his hat and walking stick, squeezed Theo’s hand so gently she smiled and knew exactly what errand he was bound on (or perhaps her silly mamma had blabbed the whole plan already), kissed little Hetty’s flushed, excited cheek, and stepped out of the parlour—his wife following fast on his heels.

Alone with him in the hallway, the enthusiastic matron could not hold back her joy a moment longer. She threw her arms around his neck, kissed him a hundred times over in an instant, called down God’s blessing on his head, and wept freely on his shoulder. It was in this very sentimental embrace that old Mrs. Quiggett, Lord Wrotham’s bustling, long-tenured housekeeper, found them. The good woman stared a moment, utterly flabbergasted by the conjugal display.

“Had a little tiff, have you, and are making it up?” the General said, grinning, as he broke away. “Don’t go spreading tales out of school, Mrs. Quiggett!”

“La, I never!” Mrs. Quiggett cackled, her shrill laugh echoing through the hall, as sharp and lively as an ancient white cockatoo—an impression she bore no small resemblance to, with her hooked nose, snow-white head of hair, and decades of busy clattering around the great house. She laughed so hard her ring of jangling house keys bounced at her hip, and her old sides shook. “Well I never did!”

“Oh Quiggett!” Mrs. Lambert sobbed. “What a man that is!”

“Making up after a quarrel, are you, mum? That’s the right way of it,” the old housekeeper nodded.

“Quarrel with him? He never told a greater fib. My General is an angel, Quiggett. I could worship him, I could fall down and kiss his boots, I declare I could! There never was a man half so good as mine. What did I ever do to deserve such a husband? How dare I be so lucky?”

“My dear, I’d say the pair of you are matched perfectly,” the old cockatoo said. “Now what would you like for your supper later?”

When Lambert trundled in very late that night for that meal, and told them the whole tale: that Harry was free, and that his brother George, whom they had all mourned for months as dead, was alive and well and had rescued him himself—you can imagine the uproar of joy that shook that little parlour. If Mrs. Lambert had thought her General an angel before, he was a saint now. If she had wanted to kiss his boots that morning, what grander act of adoration might she have tried that evening? Little Hetty crept silent to her father’s side, nestled against his arm, and sipped a tiny sip of wine from his glass. Theo’s and her mother’s faces beamed like twin full moons, bright with uncomplicated happiness.

After supper, at a quiet little signal, all four of them sank to their knees, giving glad, reverent thanks—pure joy such as the angels are said to feel, for a lost sinner returned home. Just then there came a heavy, echoing knock at the front door. Who could it be? Lord Wrotham was miles away in the country, and it was past midnight, so long had they sat talking. Mrs. Lambert smiled, soft and knowing, before anyone else could speak.

A young man pushed through the door, leading his companion in. “This is George,” Harry said, breathless. “We’ve just come from Aunt Bernstein’s. We couldn’t go to bed, Aunt Lambert, without coming to thank you too. You dear, dear, good—” No more words came out audible. Mrs. Lambert was smothering Harry in kisses, Theo snatched up Hetty who had gone deathly pale with shock, and hugged her back to laughing, crying life. George Warrington stood with his hat off, then stepped forward once Harry had been released, and knelt a little to kiss Mrs. Lambert’s hand. The General passed his palm over his eyes. All of them looked soft and tender, bright with that special happy warmth generous hearts know so well: when a wrong is forgiven, when peace is restored, when a loved one everyone thought lost comes home at last.

“We saw your lights still on as we walked past from Aunt Bernstein’s,” Harry explained, grinning through his tears. “We simply could not sleep without saying good night. Could we, George?”

“‘Tis the finest nightcap any man could ask for, lads,” the General laughed. “When will you come and dine with us? Tomorrow?” No, they had to spend the next day at Madame Bernstein’s. The day after, then? Yes, they promised, they would come. And that day is this very day, this very dinner the reader has just been invited to take a seat at, in Lieutenant-Colonel Wolfe’s empty place.

It is no mere make-believe feast, let me assure you. We are all gathered here, not in Lord Wrotham’s grand formal dining hall, but in the snug little front parlour study. The tablecloth has been drawn away, the General has toasted the King, the servants have withdrawn to the kitchens, every soul around the table sits quiet, conticuere omnes—all silent, their full attention on their guest. George Esmond Warrington clears his throat, blushes a little, and begins.

“I remember, back at the General’s camp table in Virginia, that sharp little Philadelphia agent Benjamin Franklin made exactly the objections to our campaign that the disastrous end of Braddock’s march would prove to be perfectly right. ‘Of course, your Excellency,’ he said, ‘once your troops stand before Fort Duquesne, that tiny ramshackle place will never hold out against such a fine general, such a grand army, such fine artillery as you are bringing to bear. But have you calculated the difficulty of ever reaching the fort at all? Your march will cut through untrodden woods, over roads you will have to build yourselves, strung out across four miles of wilderness. That thin line, forcing its way through the forest, will be open to attack from front, rear, and both flanks by enemies you will never see, whose entire art of war is the laying of clever ambushes.’ ‘Pshaw, sir,’ Braddock scoffed. ‘Your raw American militia may be frightened of savages, but the Indians will never make any impression on His Majesty’s regular troops.’ ‘I heartily hope not, sir,’ Franklin sighed. The officers gathered around the general’s table all sneered at the postmaster, that pert civilian who had no business daring to give an opinion on matters far beyond his understanding.

“We despised the Indians on our own side, and our commander made light of their skill as fighters. Our officers drove away almost all the Indigenous scouts who had joined our expedition with their rude, insulting behaviour to the chiefs and their women. Only seven or eight of them remained with our force by the time we neared the fort. Had we had two hundred of those skilled forest fighters out in front of us on that fatal 9th of July, the whole course of the day would have turned out very different. They would have scattered the French and their raiding allies before they could spring their trap, and prevented the total panic that broke our lines. We know now that the French had already made plans to abandon Fort Duquesne, certain they could never hold it against our overwhelming numbers, and that their own Indigenous allies had argued against the audacity of attacking an army so much larger than theirs.

“I was with General Braddock and the main body of the troops when the first shots rang out ahead. One aide-de-camp after another galloped forward to carry orders. At first, our advance guard answered the enemy fire briskly, and our men cheered and shouted, full of fight. But soon our fire grew slack, while from behind every tree and every bush ringing us, single rifle shots cracked, laying man after man low. We had been marching in neat orderly line, skirmishers ahead, colours and two small field guns at the centre, baggage wagons guarded at the rear, moving across an open stretch of clear ground a mile long and half a mile wide—thick, tangled brushwood and forest hemming us in on both sides. Before long, the firing burst from both sides of the trees surrounding our whole column. Men dropped like flies, officers even faster than the rank and file. At first, as I said, we cheered and fired back, our guns blasting at the treeline and seeming to silence the ambushed French for a moment. But the hidden rifle fire picked up again. Our men halted, huddling together in a terrified mass, ignoring the shouts and orders of officers screaming for them to advance, firing wildly into the brush where they could see no enemy at all. No good that did, of course. Soldiers from the advance line came running back to the main body, pale and wounded, screaming that there were five thousand Frenchmen and a horde of howling Indian devils in front, scalping everyone who fell. We could hear their wild war cries ringing out from the woods, every time one of our own men crumpled to the ground. No force on earth could make our men step forward now. Aide-de-camp after aide-de-camp was sent out, and never came back. At last my turn came. I was sent forward with a message to Captain Fraser of Halkett’s regiment, a message he would never receive, and I would never deliver.

“I had not run thirty paces ahead when a rifle ball tore through my leg. I crumpled straight to the ground. I remember a rush of Indians and French soldiers surging past me, the first yelling their fiendish war cries, the latter just as wild and ferocious as their savage allies. I was stunned and mortified to see how few of the white-coated Frenchmen there were. Barely a score ran past me; in all, there were fewer than fifty French soldiers in that accursed battle that routed two of the finest regiments in the British army.

“One of them, half French, half Indian, dressed in moccasins, a tattered white uniform coat and a cockade, saw me lying wounded on the ground, turned back, and ran straight for me, his musket clubbed over his head to dash my brains out and rob me as I lay. My little fusil, the one Harry gave me before I left for the campaign, had fallen on the ground right by my side. I seized it, and the Frenchman dropped dead six yards before me. I was spared for that moment, but bleeding heavily from my leg wound, and growing very faint. I nearly fainted trying to reload my gun. It slipped from my hand, and my arm sank limp, useless, to the grass.

“I was barely conscious, the gunshots and yells ringing dim and far away in my ears, when I saw an Indian standing over me. He was busy rifling the pockets of the Frenchman I had just shot, but he glanced over at me, lying there bleeding. He stripped the dead man first, tearing open his coat and rooting through every pocket, then scalped him, his bloody knife glinting between his teeth as he turned to advance on me. I watched him coming as if through a film, as in a dream. I had no strength left to move, no strength to fight him off.

“He put his knee on my chest, his bloody hand seizing my long hair to yank my head up off the ground. As he lifted me, I saw a young French officer running fast towards us right behind him. Good God! It was Florac, the young man who had been my second in the duel at Quebec a year prior. ‘A moi, Florac!’ I cried out. ‘C’est Georges! Aide moi!’

“He started, ran straight to me at the sound of my voice, and clapped a hand on the Indian’s shoulder, yelling at him to stop. But the savage did not understand French, or chose not to. He gripped my hair even tighter, waving his dripping knife over my scalp, motioning for the young Frenchman to leave him to his prey. I could only cry out again, piteous, ‘A moi!’

“‘Ah, you brute, you want blood? Take this instead!’ Florac cursed, and the next moment the Indian fell dead across my chest, Florac’s sword run clean through his body.

“My old friend glanced around quickly. ‘Eh, what a pretty mess!’ he said. ‘Where are you wounded? The leg?’ He bound my thigh tight with his military sash to stop the bleeding. ‘The rest will kill you if they find you here. Here, take this white coat, this hat with the white cockade. If anyone passes by, yell out in French. They will take you for one of us. You are Brunet of the Quebec Volunteers. God keep you, Brunet! I have to go forward. The whole of your redcoats are running for their lives, my poor boy.’ It was an utter rout, a day of unmitigated disgrace for England.

“Florac’s rough bandage slowed the bleeding in my leg, and the kind creature helped me prop myself up against a thick oak tree, loaded my fusil for me and set it within easy reach to protect me from any other looters who might stumble by. He also gave me the gourd of the very French soldier I had shot earlier, the man who had meant to kill me. The water in that gourd revived me more than I can say. He marked the thick tree I was leaning against, noted every landmark around to make sure he could find me again, and hurried off to the fighting. ‘You see how much I love you, George,’ he said, ‘that I stopped behind for you at a moment like this.’ I do not think I ever told you, Harry, that Florac owed me a small kindness. I won money from him at cards in Quebec, only when he begged me to play, and when he could not pay the debt, I tore up his note of hand and lit my pipe with it. You see, sir, you are not the only reckless gambler in the Warrington family.

“When dusk fell, and the last of the brutal pursuit was over, that faithful lad came back for me, accompanied by two Indians with still-reeking scalps hanging from their belts. He told them I was his brother, a French soldier wounded early in the fight, who must be carried safely back to the fort. They laid me in a soft wool blanket and carried me, groaning in agony, all the way to Fort Duquesne, Florac walking right beside me the whole time to make sure they did not slip off the path to rob and murder me. He promised them a cask of brandy when we reached the fort if they brought me there unharmed. I barely remember the journey, the pain in my leg so fierce I fainted more than once. At last we arrived. I was carried straight to the officer’s log hut, and laid on Florac’s own bed.

“Thank God for my delirium. I had been smuggled into the fort as a wounded French soldier of their garrison. I learned later, during the worst of my fever, that the few British prisoners taken that day had been dragged under Fort Duquesne’s walls by their savage captors, and burned, tortured, and butchered to death, right in full view of the entire French garrison.”

A murmur of horror ripples through the little hush of listeners. Theo squeezes Hetty’s hand, and stares at George, eyes wide with alarm. Harry slams his fist down on the table, hard. “The bloody, murderous, red-skinned villains! There will never be peace in the colonies until every last one of them is hunted down!”

“They were offering a hundred and thirty dollars apiece for Indian men’s scalps in Pennsylvania when I left home,” George says, quiet and mild, “and fifty for the scalps of women.”

“Fifty for women, my love! Do you hear that, Mrs. Lambert?” the General laughs, lifting a handful of his wife’s soft curls.

“Murderous villains!” Harry snarls again. “Hunt them down, sir! Hunt every last one of them down!”

“I do not know how long I lay feverish and raving,” George resumes. “When I woke up clear headed, my dear Florac was gone. He and his company had been sent off on an expedition to attack an English fort in Pennsylvania that the French claimed as their own. When I was well enough to ask questions, I learned there were barely thirty European soldiers left in Fort Duquesne. The place could have been stormed a dozen times over, had any of our own men had the courage to come back after their terrible defeat.

“My old enemy, the malarial ague, settled over me again as I lay sick by the river banks. It is a miracle I ever survived. If it had not been for the kindness of a half-French, half

For months on end, our weary life dragged on within that rickety French frontier fort. Its commandant and I passed the days in a cycle of petty spats and quick, drink-mellowed reconciliations: greasy, smoke-hazed card games by tallow candlelight, discordant duets where he wheezed through his asthmatic old flute and I fumbled over chords on my cracked, warped guitar. The Seneca woman they called the Fawn took her lord’s blows and his jugs of raw liquor without complaint, tending her infant papoose, nursing the commandant through his worst gout flares, and tending me through bouts of chattering ague, and so the days drifted by until the start of last autumn, when a roving hunter rode in bearing news that set the tiny garrison buzzing with wild excitement.

The Marquis de Montcalm had dispatched a great body of troops to reinforce all French-held forts, and push new outposts deep into British territory. The regiments had left Quebec and Montreal, sailing up the St. Lawrence and inland across the lakes in bateaux, hauling artillery, rations, and piles of war stores. It meant our host Museau would be stripped of his independent command, superseded by a ranking officer who might choose to exchange me for a French prisoner, or hand me over to their native allies in reprisal for the cruelties British frontiersmen had visited on countless French soldiers captured on the border. The fort’s ragged rank and file were giddy at the prospect of reinforcements: they would march on Pennsylvania and New York, seize Albany and Philadelphia, drive the “Rosbif” redcoats into the sea, and claim all America for France from the Mississippi to Newfoundland.

For all that triumphant boasting, though, the coming of the reinforcements only soured old Museau’s mood.
“Eh, commandant!” I teased him. “Fort bien — but what of your farm in Normandy, your jugs of hard cider, and the tripes à la mode de Caen you rave about? Where will those be, stuck out here overseeing a garrison of a hundred rowdy regulars?”
“Ah, it all sounds very fine, my lad,” he grumbled back. “But where will you be, when honest old Museau is no longer here to watch out for you? Few men alive have my humanity. Once there’s a full garrison posted here, my successor will never grant you the leniencies I’ve let you enjoy. You’ll be locked in a sty like a pig fattened for slaughter. As sure as one of our officers falls into the hands of your frontier brigands and comes to harm, you will pay for it with your own skin. They’ll hand you over to our red allies — to the brethren of La Biche there behind you. Did you not see what they did to your countrymen we captured on Braddock’s field last year? Roasting was the mildest torment they meted, ma foi — was it not, La Biche?”

He went on to recount a string of gory, jocular descriptions of tortures: eyes burned out of their sockets, teeth and nails wrenched loose, limbs lacerated raw. I saw dear Miss Theo turn pale at the recital, and spared her the rest of the grisly details, out of pity. La Biche, for her part, was far less disturbed than the ladies in our parlor that night: she had witnessed such atrocities all her life, a Seneca woman whose home villages stood near the great cataract between Ontario and Erie, where tribes shifted their alliances between French and English as easily as the wind changed, and no man could say whether white or red skin bore the greater share of cruelty in that border war.
“They may chop me into cutlets and broil me for all I care, commandant,” I said coolly. “But you will never see that Normandy farm you dream of.”
“Go fetch the whisky bottle, La Biche,” he roared.
“And it is not too late, even now,” I pressed on. “I will pay any guide who sees me safe home a very large reward. On my honour as a gentleman, ten thousand livres — and I will give that sum to anyone who brings me a token to prove he has done it: my grandfather’s watch and seal, carved with our family arms, which I know sits locked away in a chest somewhere in this fort.”
“Ah, scoundrel!” he cackled, hoarse with laughter. “You have eyes everywhere, do you! All is prize in war, of course.”
“Think of the little house in your village,” I went on. “A fine field nearby, half a dozen cows grazing in it, an orchard heavy with fruit come harvest.”
“With Javotte at the door spinning at her wheel, and a pair of rascal children with cheeks as red as the apples! Oh, my country! Oh, my mother!” he whimpered, slamming his fist on the table. “Quick, La Biche, bring the whisky at once!”

That whole night the commandant sat turning the matter over in his head, and La Biche too sat silent and melancholy, huddled in a corner nursing her baby, her eyes fixed steadily on me every time I glanced her way. When the little papoose began to cry, Museau snarled a string of oaths and ordered her to take it off to her own hovel at the edge of the fort. Once she was gone, we spoke our minds freely, and I laid out every argument his greed could not resist.
“But how do I know that hunter you speak of will not betray us?” he asked.
“That is my secret,” I told him. And now, here among friends, I may confess it. The hunter Silverheels — that was his name — loved to linger in the fort for days at a time when he came in from the wilderness, drinking, gambling his furs against the garrison’s liquor, joining the rough concerts we held after tattoo, where I scraped away at my guitar and the men sang raucous chorus songs. At one of these gatherings, after we had run through all our French drinking songs, I announced I would sing an English ballad for them. To the tune of *Over the Hills and Far Away*, the same old air my grandfather used to hum in Marlborough’s camp, I strung together some rough verses:
“This long, long year, a prisoner drear;
Ah, me! I’m tired of lingering here:
I’ll give a hundred guineas gay,
To be over the hills and far away.”
The hunter pretended not to understand the words, but I caught the twinkle in his eye. The very next day, when no other men were within earshot, he slipped past me and hummed that exact refrain under his breath, in perfectly good English. “If you are ready,” he murmured, “I am ready. I know who your people are, and the way to reach them. Talk to the Fawn, and she will tell you what to do.” Then he switched to loud French as two soldiers rounded the corner, made a mocking bow, and wandered off to gamble elsewhere.

I knew then the escape was agreed, and the poor Fawn played her part with perfect, quiet deftness. No more words needed to pass between Museau and me. She had long been granted free access to my quarters, tending me through my wound and my fevers, bringing me food, helping keep my small log cabin tidy. She was permitted to leave the fort whenever she pleased, to gather vegetables from the garden plots by the riverside. Silverheels gathered up his store of flints, powder, and blankets once he had gambled away the last of his peltries, and rode off. Three days later, La Biche gave me the signal that the night of my escape had come.
My quarters were a small log cabin just behind the fort’s single small bastion gun, pointing west over the confluence of the Ohio and Monongahela, where the French Fort Duquesne stood on its little island. “You see those trees on the far shore?” she said to me in her rough French jargon, the day before. “He waits for you behind them.” That same afternoon, she came back from the fields with a pick slung over her arm and a basket of soup herbs, sat it down just inside my door, and whispered “Hide it. You will want it soon.” The next day, she stormed into my room pretending to be angry, yelling “My lord! My lord! Why do you not come to commandant’s dinner? He is in a very bad mood! Entendez-vous?” — and as she spoke, she tossed a coiled length of rope at my feet.
I hobbled after her on my crutch to the commandant’s quarters, and she breathed “Pour ce soir,” as I passed, and I knew the hour had come.

Museau played the fool perfectly. He snapped that the soup was cold, chatted idly of this and that, and settled in to play piquet with me as we smoked our pipes, while La Biche huddled in her usual corner. His whisky bottle ran dry, and he gave me a knowing little grin as he said he would fetch another bottle for both of us, stumping off to lock it away in his inner store room, out of La Biche’s reach. The moment his back turned, La Biche sprang to her feet, was at my knees in an instant, kissing my hand, pressing it to her heart, bursting into quiet tears. I had never guessed the depth of the poor creature’s silent, tender attachment to me before, and I was still flustered and off balance when Museau returned. He noticed nothing amiss, and we sat back to our cards, my mind so full of the coming escape I scarcely saw the faces on the cards before me.
“I am winning every hand from you to-night, milor,” he said, grinning grimly. “We play on parole, eh?”
“And you may count on mine,” I said.
“Ah, that is all you have left!” he laughed.
“Monsieur,” I replied, “my word is good for ten thousand livres,” and we played on.
At last he complained of a headache, and said it was time for bed. “Good night, my little milor,” he said, then paused, his eyes twinkling with sarcasm. “Wait — you will fall over if you leave your crutch behind.” I had been so caught up in my nerves I had forgotten my old limp, and was walking away as spry as a grenadier. “What a villainous night out there!” he added, glancing through the door. A great tempest was roaring over the fort, rain lashing down in sheets. “Bring a lanthorn, La Tulipe, and lock my lord comfortably into his quarters!” I caught a glimpse of poor La Biche peeking out behind him in the dark of the doorway.

The rain was so heavy the sentries huddled in their boxes, and no one heard me at work. The cabin was built of heavy logs set deep in the ground, and I dug at the earth under the base for hours, long past tattoo, long past midnight, until I lifted my hand up and felt the cold rain falling on it from the outside. I crept out through the hole, climbed up to the bastion, and slung my rope over the barrel of that small cannon, my heart thundering in my chest for fear the sentry pacing above would spot me and fire a musket ball into my back. The wall was only twelve feet high, and I dropped soft and silent into the ditch below. The moon broke through the storm clouds soon after, and I saw the silver sheen of the Monongahela stretching before me, the dark clump of trees waiting on the far shore. I ran for them as fast as my still-weak legs would carry me, and oh, what a rush of relief flooded through me when I heard a low voice humming, just under the trees, the exact refrain of that old ballad: *Over the hills and far away*.

As George spoke those last words, Miss Theo, who had been sitting at the harpsichord, turned around and dashed out the melody on the keys, and every soul in that little parlor broke into the merry, familiar chorus.
“Our route,” George went on once the singing died down, “lay along the right bank of the Monongahela, through flat, wild forest my guide knew like the back of his hand. By dawn we had reached a clearing we knew all too well: it was the fatal field where Braddock had fallen, the very ground I had been rescued from a year before, the trees now just beginning to blaze with the fiery crimson and gold of American autumn.”
“Ah, brother!” Harry cried out, seizing George’s hand tight in his own. “I was off gambling and making a fool of myself at Bath’s Wells and in London, while you were flying for your life through this very wilderness! What a miserable, selfish spendthrift I have been!”
“I think you are not unworthy to be called your mother’s son, dear boy,” Mrs. Lambert said softly, her eyes glistening with tears. To see Harry’s repentance, his unselfish joy at his brother’s safe return, was proof enough of the goodness still in that humbled, kind-hearted young sinner.
“We crossed the river soon after,” George resumed, “striking out along the western slopes of the Alleghenies, through grand old forests of oak, maple, and towering poplars that grew a hundred feet high without a single lower branch. We kept a careful watch for wandering Indian bands — their loyalty has never been certain, and they have turned far more hostile to us ever since we cheated and mistreated them, and the French routed Braddock’s force two years prior — and for roving French patrols.
I was still weak from my long illness, and our trek through the wilds lasted more than a fortnight. The nights grew sharp with frost, so we lit small fires at our feet and slept wrapped in our blankets as best we could. We passed multiple camps of mountain families, out in the woods at maple sugaring time, who welcomed us to their fires and shared their venison with us. We crossed the two ranges of the Laurel Hills, then the main Alleghenies, before descending the wild, breathtaking pass of Will’s Creek, a valley hemmed in by thousand-foot white cliffs that looked like the towers of some giant forgotten fortress, with eagles circling the crag tops to guard their nests.
And then we came down into Cumberland, where we had marched out a year before, now garrisoned with a full regiment of our own countrymen. You cannot imagine what a welcome sight it was, when I rounded the last bend of the trail and saw the English colours flying bright over the banks of our own native Potomac.”

George Warrington had recounted the full story we have just heard to Madame de Bernstein the evening before – at least, a partial telling of it, for the old lady nodded off in her velvet fireside chair half a dozen times mid-sentence, jolting awake the very second George paused to catch his breath, exclaiming it was “thrillingly interesting, dear nephew, do go on.” The young man stammered, hemmed, blushed, and stumbled through the tale very much against his will, nowhere near as eloquent as he had been in the warm, lamplit parlour of the Lamberts’ Hill Street house. There, Hetty’s wide wondering eyes, Theo’s soft sympathetic smile, Mrs Lambert’s gentle attentive face, and the General’s playful grins had made for an audience cheering enough to embolden even the shyest young man unused to public speaking. The General had joked afterwards that Mrs Lambert’s quiet sniffles as she listened were every bit as moving as the famous ill-fated trunk-maker scene from Mr. Addison’s tragedy, and she could make any flop of a play a West End hit all by herself, just sitting in a front box sobbing. That was exactly why the family had chosen Lord Wrotham’s house as the stage for George’s first full retelling of his adventures, so he could speak at his ease instead of pouring out two years of French captivity to a sleepy, sharp-eyed old cynic who could barely keep her head propped up.

“Most excellent and deeply fascinating, I am sure, my dear boy,” said Madame de Bernstein, lifting three lace-mittened little fingers to hide the twitch of amusement at George’s awkward stammering. “And your mother must have been overjoyed to see you home, no doubt.”
George gave the tiniest, almost imperceptible shrug, and bowed low, as his aunt’s keen old hawk eyes flicked up to pin him for a long, searching second. “Overjoyed to see you,” she repeated drily, “kill the fatted calf, all that sentimental nonsense. Though heaven knows why I say calf to you, nephew George – you never were the prodigal. That title belongs to my poor Harry, eh? You did go rooting among the swine, didn’t you, lad? Evil companions picked your pockets clean, stripped the very coat off your back.”
“He came to his own family in England, madam,” George said, flushing hot with annoyance. “The friends he fell in with were your ladyship’s set.”
“Then he could not have found worse advisers,” she snapped, tossing her silvered head, “and I would have told my sister that plain enough years ago, if she’d condescended to write to me by Harry when he sailed, same as she sent word by you.”
Later that night, as her maid Brett laced her stays for the high-stakes card rout she was bound for, she rambled on unprompted: “That boy George? I could see it in his face clear as day – his own mother is half sorry he turned up alive. Half sorry? I am perfectly furious! Why didn’t he stay laid out under that tree when he got shot at Braddock’s defeat? Why did that young rascal Florac have to drag him off to the French fort? I knew all those Floracs back in Paris in the Regent’s day, descendants of Henri IV’s favourite – heh heh, not just the favourite, the favourite’s lady, Brett, you hear me? Hand me my card purse. I don’t care for Monsieur George’s grand airs much, but he favours his grandfather Esmond strikingly – same eyes, same quiet slow tone sometimes. You heard me speak of Colonel Esmond when I was a girl? I liked his eyes, of course – he was the only man who ever loved me properly.”
She never missed a card party, not weekday not Sabbath, as long as she could hold a trump card or sit upright in a chair, so no sooner had George stammered through the last of his adventures than she dismissed both nephews. To George she gave two cool, outstretched fingers and a stately little curtsy, but to Harry she took both his hands, patted his cheek fondly. “My poor lamb, now that you’ve lost your inheritance, you’ll see how fast the rest of the world turns its back on you. There is only one wicked, heartless old woman in all London who will treat you just the same as before. Here, take this pocket-book – don’t gamble it away at Ranelagh tonight. That velvet coat of yours never half suited George as well as it fits you. Walk him round the gardens two full hours, introduce him to every curiosity, every pretty face there. Then off you go to the Chocolate House, play as if nothing’s changed at all. While you’re doing that, George can come back here with me, eat a bit of cold chicken – Lady Flint’s suppers are always abominable, and I want to go over his mother’s letter with him. Off you go, gentlemen!” Her chairmen and flaming link-boys’ torches were already waiting at the door, so off she sailed to her dressing chamber.

The two brothers headed straight for Ranelagh, where barely a handful of Harry’s usual acquaintances happened to be that night. They paced the circular promenade arm in arm, ran into Tom Claypool and his group of country squire friends, listened to the open-air orchestra, took tea in a private box, and Harry acted as master of ceremonies, introducing George to every notable oddity and fashionable belle on the grounds. George, who loved music far more than Harry ever had, was more giddy and excited than his brother had been on his own first visit to the pleasure gardens – it was the first time he had ever heard a full symphony, and a crisp, rousing performance of Mr. Handel’s work that brought tears to his eyes. Even at a time when fiddling was widely dismissed as effeminate, unmanly frivolity, when patriotic newspapers railed against foreign “fiddling foreigners” and all their silly accomplishments, Harry had nothing but respect for his brother’s delight in the music.
Nobody in Britain is proud of their ignorance these days, right? No conceit left, no dullness, no arrogance to be found anywhere… well, at the very least the arts have earned their full citizenship here now, treated almost as equals. If Mrs. Thrale chose to marry her music master today, I doubt her friends would shun her for it – if she had a good fortune and a good cook, folks would still turn up to dine, and treat Mr. Piozzi with full civility.

After Ranelagh, as Madame Bernstein had advised, George went back to her house, while Harry made his way to his club, where the gentlemen gathered nightly for supper and high-stakes gambling. No one so much as hinted at his recent spell in debtor’s prison, his old landlord Mr. Ruff waited on him with perfect grave civility, as if there had never been any disagreement between them. Harry had already moved all his trunks and clothes out of the Bond Street lodgings that morning, he and George now renting quiet rooms not far from Covent Garden.
But when the supper plates were cleared, and everyone moved to head upstairs to the macco gaming tables, Harry spoke up: he wasn’t playing tonight. He’d already burned his fingers too badly, couldn’t afford any more wild spending.
“Come now,” said Jack Morris flippantly, “you must have won far more than you lost, Warrington, all things considered.”
“Ah, so I don’t know my own affairs better than you, do I, Morris?” Harry said sharply, he’d never forgotten how the man had sneered at him when he was locked up. “But there’s more to it. A few months back I was heir to a great estate, could afford to lose a little at cards. Now, thank God, I’m heir to nothing.” He looked round at the group of gaming men lounging at the tables or clustered by the fire, his face flushing hot.
“What the devil do you mean, Warrington?” Lord March called out, “Have you lost Virginia too? Who won it? I’ve half a mind to play you for that stake myself, breed a better strain of slaves out there on the plantations.”
“The rightful owner has it back,” Harry said. “You all heard me talk of my twin elder brother, who was supposed to have died in Braddock’s defeat two years back.”
“Good God, man,” someone gasped, “he hasn’t come back to life, has he?”
“He landed in London two days ago. He was held prisoner in a French fort for eighteen months, only escaped a few months back, and sailed for England almost immediately after he got home to Virginia.”
“Dear me, I suppose you haven’t had time to order mourning for yourself, eh Warrington?” Selwyn said good-naturedly, and simple Harry didn’t get the dry joke until George explained it to him later.

When Harry had taken his leave, the men fell to gossiping behind his back.
“Damned if I don’t think the lout is actually glad his brother’s turned up alive!” Lord March laughed. “American savages still cling to those simple silly virtues of family affection, barely civilised at all.”
“They love their kin, and scalp their enemies,” Walpole simpered, yawning. “Hardly Christian, but very natural. Wouldn’t you love to see a scalping match, March, watch a man skinned alive?”
“An elder brother is a man’s natural enemy, obviously,” Selwyn said placidly, counting out his piles of counters. “Get used to a little torture, broiled bones and pepper, and plain hanging will seem boring after, right?”
“I’m hanged if there’s a man in all England who’d be happy to see his elder brother turn up alive,” Lord March agreed.
“Or his father, neither!” Jack Morris cackled.
“First time I ever heard you had one, Jack,” March tossed back. “Give me five hundred pounds worth of counters.”
“All this talk about dead brothers rising from the grave is mighty suspicious,” Jack went on. “Who’s to say this isn’t a scheme the two of them cooked up together? This lad turns up calling himself the Virginian Prince, the Fortunate Youth, gets invited into our society-“ the whole room burst out laughing at his lofty phrase “our society” “-Who’s to say this isn’t a con? The younger brother comes first, marries a great heiress, gets hold of her fortune, then the elder pops up out of nowhere! And when did this elder brother turn up? Why, exactly when Harry’s schemes went bust, when all his money was gone! Who’s to say this George hasn’t been hiding in a garret in Seven Dials, eating tripe and cow heel in a cellar this whole time, waiting for Harry to get settled? Dammy, as gentlemen we ought to protest this! That Warrington lad has taken a most outrageous liberty with this entire club!”
“Who sponsored him in here, anyway? Wasn’t it you, March?” a bystander called.
“Aye, and I thought I was sponsoring a proper heir to a thirty thousand a year estate, didn’t I?” March snapped. “Shut your damned mouth and play your cards.”
But Jack Morris’s lies found plenty of listeners all over town. Everyone agreed it was shockingly improper of Harry to have ever thought his brother dead, that his arrival in England in the first place was deeply suspicious, that all these foreign colonials and adventurers ought to be treated with the utmost caution.

Harry, meanwhile, was sitting alone smoking his Virginia pipe, waiting for George to come back from Madame Bernstein’s. He was free of prison, free of debt thanks to his aunt’s generous gift, his beloved brother was restored to him, and Maria Esmond had stood by him through all his worst troubles – but he was far from happy. It wasn’t the loss of the great estate that grieved him, he never cared a farthing for that, he knew George would share every penny with him just as he would have shared with George. The weight on his chest was that he was now poor, and irrevocably bound to marry his elderly cousin Maria. There was no getting around it, she was old – that day she’d come to see him in that horrid Cursitor Street debtor’s den, the tears had streaked her rouge clean off, and she’d looked as wrinkled and yellow as his own mother. He thought of the terrible fights there would be between her and his mother when he brought her home to Virginia, and shuddered. He’d take her out to the farthest, most isolated plantation, he decided, live there with a handful of negro hands, farm the land as best he could, hunt every day to keep busy. But Maria, who was used to London court balls, card parties, assemblies every single night – what kind of life would that be for her? He’d be honest, he’d work as overseer for George’s estates, make up for all his wild, wasteful spending over the last six months, the five thousand pounds of his own patrimony he’d gambled away in half a year. He was a beggar now, except for George’s kindness, and the only thing he had left in life was that old wife to be. A fine figure he’d cut in Europe, all dressed up in velvet and silver lace, a pretty end to all his grand dreams! He hadn’t been happy a single day since he sailed for England, not really – except those four perfect days he’d spent with the Lamberts in Hill Street, kind Mrs. Lambert, sweet Hetty and Theo, the brave good General who’d scolded him for his follies and still worked tirelessly to get him out of prison. God bless all of them, he thought, puffing slowly on his pipe, as he listened for the sound of his brother’s footsteps on the stairs.

The maternal grandfather of our two Virginian brothers, Colonel Esmond, who had long since quit the crowded streets of old London to settle in the broad, sunlit expanses of the New World, had whiled away many quiet decades of his American leisure writing down the memoirs of his stormy, passionate youth. His manuscript pages gave a great and vivid part to Madame de Bernstein, the former Beatrice Esmond, who for half a century had been one of the most celebrated belles of English high society. George had pored over those tattered, ink-stained volumes a dozen times over on quiet evenings at the Virginia plantation, so he knew his kinswoman long before he ever crossed the Atlantic to meet her: knew the bright, wilful, dark-eyed girl of fifty years prior, before he ever sat across the fire from the old, rouged, diamond-draped dowager she had grown to be.

As his aunt stumbled in after a long rout, paint smudged a little at the jaw and her silk train trailing behind her cane, George wondered, with a quiet melancholy, how it must feel to be a beauty no more: to have faded cheeks and dimmed eyes, and still carry the memory of your own bloom sharp in your head. When the heart is withered, does it ache to remember the days it beat warm and fast with first love? When the spirits are languid and worn thin, do you like to look back on how bright they once were, how buoyant your hope, how eager your taste for every small pleasure life had to offer? All those first buds of youth, all the roses of beauty, all the lush summer harvests fall and wither in the end, after all, leaving nothing but bare branches to shiver in the winter wind.

“And that was a beauty once,” George thinks to himself, staring at her. “That ruin was once a splendid palace. Crowds of men sighed before those decrepit feet once, and were dizzy with the light of those eyes.” It reminds him of the King’s Birthday fireworks he watched back home in Williamsburg once, after the last sparks had fizzled out: nothing left of the grand display but the charred skeleton of the firework wheel, and the empty, blackened sockets of the spent Roman candles. All the dazzle and chaos of Aunt Beatrice’s early life unfurled in his mind as he turned over the pages of his grandfather’s memoirs in his head.
Honest Harry had flipped through the manuscript too, of course, but he was no bookish man, and had not paid it much mind. Even if he had, he would never have stopped to moralize over the vanity of youth the way his quiet, melancholy older brother did. George decided there was no use telling his aunt how well he knew every detail of her early life from the old memoirs, and held his peace on the subject.

When their supper was cleared away, the old lady pointed her cane at her escritoire, and bade her maid fetch the letter tucked under the inkstand there. George recognized the superscription at once: it was the very letter he had carried across the Atlantic from their mother’s plantation home.
“It would appear by this letter,” the old lady said, staring hard at him through a great pair of heavy spectacles, “that ever since your return to Virginia, there have been some disagreements between you and my sister.”
“Indeed? I did not know Madam Esmond had spoken of them to you,” George replied.
The Baroness slid those spectacles over the eyes that once had shot fire, and kindled a hundred passions in a hundred young men half a century before, then scanned the letter once more and handed it over to George to read. It was dated Richmond, Virginia, December 26th, 1756:

> I have received, and thankfully acknowledge, your ladyship’s favour sent by the Rose packet, dated October 23rd last, and I write back straightaway at this season that should be one of goodwill and peace to all men – though Heaven has seen fit that we still must bear our share of earthly sorrow and trouble. My reply is brought to you by my eldest son, Mr. Esmond Warrington, who returned to us so miraculously out of the Valley of the Shadow of Death (as our earlier letters have already told my poor Harry), and who has my full consent to visit Europe, though he has scarcely been home with us for any time at all.
> I grieve to think that my dearest Harry first arrived in England under false colours, as it were: that he was presented to his Majesty, to our family, and to everyone, as his father’s heir, while my dear son George was still alive, though lost to us. Ah, madam! For those eighteen months he was held captive by the French and their Indian allies, what anguish his mother’s heart, his brother’s heart, have borne! Harry’s is the tenderest heart of any man alive today. In the joy of seeing Mr. Esmond Warrington return from the dead, he will forget the worldly fortune he lost. He will take up a younger brother’s comparative poverty without a single pang. The most generous, the most obedient of all sons, he will gladly give up to his elder brother that inheritance that would have been his own but for the accident of birth, and the providential return of my son George.
> Your kind intentions towards dearest Harry are more welcome than ever now he is reduced to a younger brother’s slender portion! Many years ago, there was an excellent opportunity to buy him a fine estate in this province, and by now he would be master of a great stretch of land and a full household of negroes, and cut a very respectable figure here, if my wishes had been followed, and his father’s small portion, which sits earning paltry interest in the British funds, had been invested in that purchase. But the quirks of the law, and I grieve to own it, my elder son’s foolish scruples, prevailed, and that fine opportunity was lost to us! Harry will find all the savings from his late income have been carefully stored away – long, long may he live to enjoy them! May Heaven bless you, dear sister, for whatever you add to his little store! I gather from your letter that the allowance he received was not enough to cover his expenses in the fine company he has been keeping – and the grandson of the Marquis of Esmond, who nearly was his lordship’s heir, may surely claim equality with any nobleman in Great Britain! I have a sum set aside that I always intended for the poor child to set him up, and I entrust it to my eldest son, who to do him justice has a most sincere affection for his brother, to lay it out for Harry’s best advantage.

“It took him out of prison yesterday, madam. I think that was the best possible use we could put it to,” George interposed at this point.
“Nonsense, sir! I don’t know that at all!” the old lady cried. “Why not have kept it to buy him a pair of colours in the army, or to put towards another estate and a few negroes, if he fancies coming back to Virginia? Besides, I wanted to pay that debt myself.”
“I beg you to let his brother do that,” George said. “I ask leave to be my brother’s banker in this matter, and consider I have borrowed that sum from my mother, to be paid back every penny to my dear Harry.”
“Do you say so, sir? Fetch me a glass of wine! You are a very extravagant young man! Read on, and you will see your mother thinks the very same. I drink to your health, nephew George! This is fine Burgundy, you know. Your grandfather never cared for Burgundy. He preferred claret, the little that he drank.”

George picked up the letter and continued:
> This remittance will, I trust, amply cover any expenses dearest Harry may have incurred, owing to the silly mistake over his status as heir. I wish I could trust his elder brother’s prudence as confidently as I trust Harry’s! But I fear that even in his captivity, Mr. Esmond Warrington learned little of that humility that becomes all good Christians, and which I have ever striven to teach to both my boys. If by chance you show him these lines, when the great ocean divides us, he will know that a fond mother’s blessing and prayers follow both her children, and that no act I have ever done, no wish I have ever expressed (however little he may have cared to obey it!) was anything but the fondest possible wish for my dearest boys’ welfare.

“There’s a scratch from a penknife there, and a great blot on the page like a drop of water fell on it,” the old lady noted, not unkindly. “Your mother writes a fine hand, George. I suppose you and she had your falling out?”
“Yes, ma’am, many,” George answered, sadly. “The last was over money – the ransom I promised the old French lieutenant at the fort who helped me escape. I told you he had a mistress, a poor Indian woman, who helped me, and was very kind to me. Six weeks after I got home to Virginia, the poor creature turned up at Richmond, having found her way through the woods by almost the exact same trail I took when I fled. She brought me the token Museau had promised to send me when he helped me run. A new commanding officer and a huge garrison of reinforcements had arrived at Fort Duquesne, and charges of embezzlement – I don’t know the full details, her English was very bad – were brought against Museau. He was arrested, and tried to escape, but less lucky than me, he was shot dead on the ramparts. He sent the Indian woman to me with my grandfather’s old watch, and a scrawled note he wrote in his prison cell on his deathbed, begging me to send whatever money I could to a notary at Havre de Grace in France, to forward to his relatives at Caen in Normandy. Our friend Silverheels the hunter helped my poor Indian messenger on her way – I don’t know how she would have avoided being scalped otherwise. But at home, they received her very coldly. They hardly gave her a welcome at all. I will not speak of the silly, cruel suspicions they threw on her and on me. The poor wretch took to drinking whenever she could find liquor. I ordered that she be given food and shelter, but she became the joke of our negroes, and the subject of every bit of tittle-tattle from all the old gossips of our little town. Luckily, our Governor was a sensible man, and I got a pass for her to travel back to her own people. Her very grief at parting with me only confirmed all the stupid rumours against her. I do believe a local preacher even denounced me from the pulpit over it, and I had to cane another busybody who spread slander. I had a terrible fight with Madam Esmond – a rift that is not healed to this day – because I insisted on paying the sum I promised Museau’s heirs for my deliverance. Scandal flourishes right on the edge of the wilderness, you know, just as much here in the Old World.”
“I’ve suffered from scandal myself, my dear!” Madame Bernstein said demurely. “Fill your glass, child! A little sip of cherry-brandy! It will do you all the good in the world.”

Madam Esmond’s letter continued:
> As for my poor Harry’s marriage, though I know full well from sad experience the dangers youth is exposed to, and would keep my boy far from imprudent matches at any cost, and though I would wish him to marry a woman of rank that befits his birth, Lady Maria Esmond is utterly out of the question. Her age is almost the same as mine, and I know my brother Castlewood left his two daughters with barely a penny between them. My Harry is so obedient that I know one word from me will be enough to make him give up this silly, ill-suited match. Some foolish people once supposed I myself thought of a second marriage once, to a man of rank far above our station. No! I knew what duty I owed to my children. As Mr. Esmond Warrington will inherit the Virginia estate after me, he is amply provided for. My task now must be to save for his less fortunate younger brother, and as I do not care to live entirely alone, let Harry come home to his fond and loving mother without delay.
> The account your ladyship gives of my Harry fills my heart with the warmest gratitude. He is all a mother could ever wish. A year in Europe will have given him a polish and refinement he could never gain in our homely, rough Virginia. Mr. Stack, one of our valued ministers in Richmond, has a letter from Mr. Ward – my darlings’ old childhood tutor – who knows Lady Warrington and her excellent family, and says my Harry has been spending a great deal of time with his cousins lately. I am so grateful to think my boy gets to stay with his good aunt. May he follow her good counsel, and listen to those who will guide him to his best welfare! Adieu, dear madam and sister! Accept the grateful thanks of a mother’s heart for all your kindness to my boy. Though we have been distant until now, may these kind ties draw us closer and closer. I am thankful you speak so kindly of my dearest father. He was, indeed, one of the best of men! He, too, I know, thanks you for the love you have borne to one of his children; and his daughter subscribes herself,
> With sincere thanks, your ladyship’s most dutiful and grateful sister and servant,

> *P.S.* – I have already written to Lady Maria myself, but there is no need to tell her or dear Harry that his mother or your ladyship hope to be able to increase his small fortune. The match is entirely unsuitable.

“So far as I am concerned, madam,” George said, laying the letter down on the table, “my mother’s letter tells me nothing new. I always knew Harry was the favourite son with Madam Esmond, and he deserves to be. He has a hundred good qualities I have never had. He is handsomer, for one–”
“Nay, that is not your fault,” the old lady said, slyly glancing up at him. “And if it were not for him being fair and you dark, one could almost pass the two of you for twins.” George bowed, and a faint pink flush rose up his pale cheek.
“His disposition is bright, and mine is sombre,” he went on. “Harry is cheerful, and I never have been, I suppose. He knows how to make everyone love him, but I have never had much luck finding friends.”
“My sister and you have your pretty little quarrels, then. We had the same sort of things in our family in the old days,” the Baroness said. “And if Madam Esmond takes after our mother–”
“My mother has always described hers as an angel upon earth,” George interjected.
“Ah! Dead people so often get to be angels, don’t they?” the Baroness cried. “And Rachel Castlewood was an angel, if you like – at least your grandfather thought she was. But let me tell you, sir, angels are often very inconvenient to live with. Maybe they are too good for the rest of us sinners, and the air down here on earth doesn’t agree with them. My poor mother was so perfect she could never forgive me for being anything other than perfect myself. Mon Dieu! How she used to oppress me with those angelical airs!”
George cast his eyes down, and thought of his own quiet, melancholy youth back at the plantation. He had no wish to lay more of his family’s private secrets before this cynical old woman of the world, though she seemed to understand him perfectly even when he said nothing.
“I see you perfectly, sir, even if you won’t speak,” the Baroness went on. “A sermon in the morning, a sermon at night, two or three on Sundays. That’s what people call being good. Every pleasure is a sin, all worldly people are excommunicated, a ball is an abomination, a play is forbidden, a hand of cards is straight to perdition! What a life! Mon dieu, what a life!”
“We played cards every night if we wanted to at home,” George said, smiling, “and my grandfather loved Shakespeare so much my mother never dared say a word against her own father’s favourite author.”
“I remember! He could recite whole pages by heart – though for my part I far prefer Mr. Congreve,” the old lady said, tapping her fan. “And that dreadful, dreary Milton, that he and Mr. Addison both pretended to adore!”
“If your ladyship does not care for Shakespeare, you will not quarrel with my mother for being indifferent to him, either,” George said. “And truly, I think you do not do her justice. Wherever there are poor people, she relieves them. Wherever there are sick people, she–”
“She doses them all with her horrible purges and boluses!” the Baroness laughed. “Exactly the same as my own mother did!”
“She does her very best to cure them! She acts for the best, and does her duty as far as she knows how to.”
“I do not blame you, sir, for doing your own duty, and keeping quiet about Madam Esmond,” the old lady said. “But at least the three of us are all of one mind on one thing: this absurd marriage must be stopped. Do you know how old that woman really is? I can tell you, though she tore the first page with her birth date out of the family Bible at Castlewood.”
“My mother has not forgotten her cousin’s age, and is shocked at the huge difference between her and my poor brother,” George said. “A town-bred lady of that time of life, used to all the gaiety and luxury of London, would find our Virginia plantation a very dismal home. Besides, the estate, such as it is, is not Harry’s. He is welcome there, Heaven knows – more welcome, perhaps, than I, who will inherit the property in the natural course of things. But as I told Harry, I doubt very much how his wife would like our colony.”
The old lady cackled shrilly. “He he! Nephew Warrington! You need not scruple to speak your mind. I will not tell tales to your mother: it is no news to me that she has a sharp temper, and will have her own way. Harry never said a word, but you do not need a conjuror to see who was mistress of that house, and what sort of life my sister led you. I love my niece Lady Maria so much that I would gladly see her spend two or three years in Virginia, with your mother ruling over the

For days after Harry’s arrival in London, the two Esmond brothers huddled behind the closed door of their lodgings, trading the lost years apart like boys sorting through a hoard of stolen trinkets, no detail too small to merit skipping. First came all the quiet, beloved trivialities of home: were Harry’s favourite staghounds still roaming the estate? Had little Dempster the stable boy finally stopped stealing apples off Madam Esmond’s table? Good old Nathan, the family butler of thirty years, still as gruff and loyal as ever? Mrs. Mountain the governess keeping well, and her niece Fanny grown into a proper pretty young lady at last?
They laughed till their sides ached when they recalled Parson Broadbent’s daughter, the girl Harry had once been so smitten with that he’d lingered three nights a week at the parsonage, losing shillings at cards to the old parson and downing mug after mug of spiced rum punch just to have an excuse to loiter on the off-chance of passing her on the staircase. Heaven knew Harry had been half ready to propose, too—till Madam Esmond had sniffed, raised one perfectly arched eyebrow, and made it unmistakeably clear that no daughter of a country parson, however sweet-faced, was good enough to marry one of her boys.
Next came the story of Colonel George Washington’s new wife, the pleasant, good-humoured lady of great fortune he’d brought to call on Madam Esmond at the Castlewood Virginia estate. George recounted the absurd, stilted state visit with such droll humour that Harry rolled on the sofa cackling: the two proud, formidable women trading three layers of excessive curtsy and over-polished civility, neither willing to concede an inch of dignity. “Never you mind, Georgy dear!” Mountain had cackled afterwards, winking broadly. “The Colonel’s gone and taken himself another wife now, but I’ll swear to it—once upon a time, you two lads came this close to getting yourselves a stepfather six feet two tall in his boots.” The silly old governess was forever matchmaking, after all: let two people sit beside each other at a card table or share a dish of tea, and she’d immediately be plotting out their wedding banns. It was that same harmless, tattling old woman who’d let loose the first silly rumour about the poor Indian woman Biche. When Parson Stack had brought the gossip to Madam Esmond’s ear, she’d dismissed it with such sharp scorn it had made the parson flinch: “I’d as soon believe one of my boys stole the silver spoons from the pantry, or ran off to marry a negro scullery maid, as believe that nonsense.” But for all she refused to brand Biche guilty, Madam Esmond treated the poor young woman with such frigid, unapproachable hauteur that Biche soon slipped away to the servants’ quarters, and took to drinking rough cider brandy to drown the quiet hurt.
The picture George painted of his two months back in Virginia after his release from French captivity was far from cheerful. “The birthright is mine, Harry,” he said, his voice soft and half bitter, “but you are the favourite. God help me, I do believe our mother almost grudges it to me. Why did I have to be the one born first? Had you been the elder, you’d have inherited the best cellar, ridden the finest stallion on the plantation, and been the most popular man in the whole colony. I’d have been the second son—set up as a lawyer in Williamsburg, or shipped off to university in England to take orders, saying grace at your grand dinner table every Sunday. The time is out of joint, lad. O cursed spite, that ever I was born to set it right!”
“Georgy, you’re quoting poetry at me, I swear you are!” Harry laughed, then flushed when George smiled and said the lines belonged to a playwright far more famous than him. “I know! I saw those two authors you’re always going on about at Tunbridge Wells, you know! Tipped my hat to both of them, even if I never could keep up with their clever books. I did it for you, old man—just thinking of how you’d ramble on about their work for hours when we were lads.” His voice thickened, and he swiped at his eye with the back of his hand. “It’s like a dream, having you back. Thinking of that bloody Indian with a knife at your head over in the woods! I wish I had something grand to give Monsieur de Florac for saving your life—all I’ve got left is these little gold knee buckles, and they’re not worth two guineas.”
“You have half of every penny I own,” George told him. “The moment I’ve paid the ransom money to Museau’s heirs, we split the rest, no questions asked.” Harry burst out in such a roar of grateful blessings and loud, emphatic oaths that the neighbours banged on the wall in complaint. For days afterwards, his eyes followed George everywhere: he’d drop his knife and fork mid-bite at dinner, or set aside the newspaper he was pretending to read, and grin to himself like he’d just stumbled on the greatest secret in the world. When they walked the Mall or through Hyde Park, he’d glance around at all the fine lords and ladies parading by, his chest puffed out, as if to announce to every last one of them: Look here. This is my brother. The one who was dead and is alive again. Can any man in Christendom show off a brother half as fine?
Harry was unshakable in his opinion that George must keep his word and pay the full ransom sum to Museau’s heirs, just as he’d promised the dying Frenchman. That very question had been the source of weeks of bitter strife between George and his mother back in Virginia. Museau was dead, Madam Esmond had argued, sharp with rage, so the bargain was void. The man had been a rogue from the start, trying to extort money from a prisoner of war—why reward his iniquity? George was of age, he controlled the small independent fortune left to him by his father, but she would be party to no such folly: throwing twelve thousand livres at a parcel of Norman peasants, at a time England and France were at war, money that would no doubt end up in the pockets of priests and the Pope himself. If he was determined to squander that money, she’d cried, why not give it to his own flesh and blood, to poor Harry who’d been robbed of his inheritance, rather than a pack of papist, priest-ridden foreigners? The fight had raged till the morning of George’s departure, when Madam Esmond had come to his bedside after a sleepless night, pale and hollow-eyed, and asked if he still intended to throw his father’s property away. “My word is passed,” he’d told her, grief heavy in his chest, “and I must do as my honour bids me.” She’d answered that she would pray Heaven would soften his proud heart, and give her strength to bear such a heavy trial. The last sight he had of her was her standing by his bedside, tearless and rigid, before she turned and walked slowly out of his room.
“Harry, how do you do it?” George went on. “How do you make every soul you meet like you within five minutes? Teach me your tricks of popularity—though on second thought, I don’t think I want them. When I find people hate me, I’m more amused than angry. When I first got back to Virginia, everyone thought I was some sort of hero: the only man who escaped Braddock’s massacre, fresh off months of captivity and illness. The parson preached a whole sermon about my escape, all the neighbours called on us, people smiled wherever I went. The girls even started setting their caps at me—till our mother scared every last one of them off with her icy grandeur. My popularity was already fading fast by then, anyway. The army officers thought I was a dull stick because I wouldn’t join their drinking bouts, or throw dice all night, or roar oaths at the top of my lungs. The ladies thought I was too sharp-tongued, and their endless gossiping over tea left me so stupefied I could barely speak. I was lonelier there than I ever was in the French prison, believe me. Half the time I caught myself pining for the quiet, uncomplicated days I spent in Duquesne, no one breathing down my neck or spreading stories behind my back.”
“Then that cursed gossip about poor Biche started, didn’t it?” George’s voice rose, hot with old rage. “The boys hooted at her in the street if she so much as stepped out of the servants’ wing. The ladies dropped me half a curtsy and crossed the road to the other side when they saw me coming. That Parson Stack went from tea table to tea table preaching about the horrors of seduction, and the loose morals young men picked up in papist countries. Everyone agreed her turning up in Richmond weeks after my return was a secret plan between us, that she’d hidden on the other side of the river waiting for my signal to come join me. The officers cracked their clumsy, vulgar jokes about me at the coffee house. I was so enraged I nearly moved out to old abandoned Castlewood to live alone in utter solitude—till the news came of your troubles over here in England, and gave me the perfect excuse to leave. I left home, Harry, with the worst reputation any young gentleman in the colony ever had.”
Harry jumped to his feet, red-faced, and strode up and down the room, fists clenched. “I’ll break the bones of every last one of those lying scoundrels! I already did for Bob Clubber, the little sneaking backbiter who hangs around my lord at Greenway Court, sponging off every gentleman he meets!”
The narrator here cannot resist a brief, wry aside: what a marvellous, harrowing book the world would read, if every man wrote down every false rumor that had ever been spread about him since he came of age. The public does not merely know all your business, you see—it makes up a hundred times more of it, and swears it is the truth.
When George had finished telling his side of the story, it was Harry’s turn to unburden himself of all his own troubles over in England. He spoke fairly of Lord Castlewood, admitting he had no hard feelings over losing to him at cards—sportsmen paid their losses, after all—but he thought the man a cold-hearted wretch for refusing to help his chaplain when the poor man was in desperate need, dismissing him with thin, lying excuses. He had settled matters with Will Esmond after the crooked horse-dealing incident, too: had given him such a punch right to the face that his nose swelled black and blue for a fortnight. He thought the Countess a selfish, card-obsessed old cat, and Lady Fanny a frivolous, shameless flirt—all stories he’d heard, of course, from Lady Maria, who knew them better than anyone.
And on the subject of Maria, Harry was unshakable, his face flushing bright red as he spoke. “I know it’s imprudent. I know Madam will raise holy hell when she finds out, and fight Maria tooth and nail. But I won’t leave her. She’s been too good to me. You remember, when I was dead broke? She brought every last jewel she owned, and all her saved-up guineas, and dumped the whole lot in my lap. I’d sooner be made Governor of the whole of Virginia tomorrow than turn my back on her. I’ve given her my word, George. What’s said is said. I’ve made my bed, and I’ll lie in it.”
George sighed. “I was sent here by our mother to break that engagement, if I can. I can’t imagine a marriage more unhappy for you. But I will never, ever tell you to break your word to a woman who has stood by you.”
The two brothers had struck that quiet, loyal bargain between them the very first night they met. But after George’s long, sharp chat with Aunt Bernstein, that worldly old woman who knew every secret of the Esmond family, he had begun to doubt. He could not urge Harry to break his promise—but he was already turning over plans in his head, thinking of a way to put Lady Maria’s affection to the test, to see if she truly loved Harry for himself, or only for the Esmond fortune waiting for him back in Virginia.

A hundred years past, Kensington Square sat a long, lonesome carriage ride out from London’s bustling heart—far enough that footpads lurked in the hedgerows along the lane, far enough that George Selwyn swore he dared not travel there after dark, for fear of being robbed twice over: once by masked highwaymen on the road, and once by rouged ladies at the quadrille table within the house of his neighbour, Lord Castlewood. The nobleman’s Kensington dwelling was spacious enough to house his entire family, and perfectly convenient for their frequent attendances at the royal palace just a stone’s throw away, whenever the King was in residence there. His lady wife held regular evening card-parties for all the court circle who cared to make the journey, though attendance had always been thin for the reason Selwyn joked of.

On the noon the day after Harry Warrington had reappeared at White’s, the whole of the virtuous Castlewood clan gathered for breakfast around the table, even Will, who was due to present himself for court duties that afternoon. The ladies came first, sipping their chocolate, then Will trundled in in his full formal court suit, and last of all the lord of the house wandered languidly in, still wrapped in his bedgown and nightcap, not yet having donned his periwig for the day. It was Will who brought the gossip, fresh from the Star and Garter tavern the night before, where he’d supped with men who’d just returned from Ranelagh and heard the story straight from White’s:
“Heard what? Seen what?” Lord Castlewood asked, flipping open his *Daily Advertiser*.
“Ask Maria,” Lady Fanny snickered. My lord turned to his elder sister, who sat with a face of utter, portentous woe, pale as a starched linen tablecloth.
“Tis nothing but one of Will’s usual coarse, silly fabrications,” Maria said sharply.
“Fabrication my arse,” swore Will, with his favourite string of oaths. “Tom Claypool from Norfolk saw them both at Ranelagh last night, plain as day. Jack Morris rode straight back from there to White’s, where Harry Warrington told the whole story himself. Curse the fellow, I’m bloody glad of it!” He slapped the table hard enough to rattle the chocolate cups. “What d’you make of your precious Fortunate Youth, your Virginian prince that you all fawned over? Turns out he’s nothing but a second son!”
“The elder brother isn’t dead?” my lord asked, sitting up a little.
“Never was. Not a day. I’ll bet they swapped places or pulled some cross trick from the very start.”
“Mr. Warrington is far too honourable for such duplicity!” Maria cried, her voice shaking.
“I’m sure no one can say I ever encouraged the fellow,” Lady Castlewood put in quickly. “Nor Fanny, either. We paid him no special attention at all, indeed!”
“Nor we, indeed!” Lady Fanny echoed at once.
“The man’s nothing but a beggar now, I’ll wager he hasn’t a penny to pay for the coat on his back,” Will went on sneering. “I’m glad of it. Hang him, I’ve always hated him.”
