“You’ve never liked him, not since he blacked your eye at the stables, Will,” my lord grinned. “So the poor lad found his brother alive, and lost his whole estate in one go?” He glanced over at Maria, who looked the very picture of misery, and the sight struck his warped sense of humour so sharply he burst into a shrill, high laugh. The poor lady’s face flamed bright red, and the next moment she was sobbing into her handkerchief. “It’s a shame! A cruel shame!” she gasped.
Lady Castlewood and her daughter exchanged a look. “We never do quite follow your lordship’s particular brand of humour,” the former said, stiff and grave.
“I don’t see the least reason you should,” my lord replied coolly. “Maria, my dear, forgive me if I said or did anything to hurt your feelings.”
“Anything? You fleeced him for every penny he had when he was prosperous, and now you laugh at him when he’s ruined!” Maria shot to her feet, glaring at every face around the table.
“Excuse me, my dear sister, I was not laughing at him,” my lord said gently.
“Oh, never mind who or what you laughed at!” she cried. “You took every last thing he had to lose. All the world points at you, says you feed on your own flesh and blood. Now you’ve stripped him bare, you make merry over his misfortune!” And she rustled out of the room, flinging looks of open defiance at every member of the family left behind her.
“Tell us the whole story, Will, at length. My sister’s grief won’t interrupt us now,” my lord said. Will recounted every juicy detail of the gossip buzzing through London that day, cackling with unbridled glee at Harry’s downfall, while Lord Castlewood listened with a faint frown. Harry was a good, brave lad, he thought—he liked him well enough, as much as any worldly peer likes his handsome, rich young cousin. Of course he’d played piquet with Harry, and taken every advantage he could to win his money—but why shouldn’t he? Any other man would have plucked that ripe peach just the same, so why shouldn’t he eat it himself? If that was the worst sin on his conscience, he’d never lie awake a night uneasy over it, he thought. “Where is Mr. George Warrington lodging these days?”
Will grumbled that he’d rather be damned than know or care where the man stayed.
“Then we shall invite both of them here, and treat them with every possible mark of respect,” my lord declared.
“Full of piquet tables, I suppose,” Will growled.
“Or do you plan to drag him out to the stables and sell him one of your overpriced broken nags, Will?” my lord retorted. “You’d have won all Harry’s money fast enough if you hadn’t cheated so clumsily he thrashed you with a cudgel. I tell you, I want every attention paid to our cousin Warrington.”
“Meaning no one is to disturb you when you sit down to the card table with him, of course, my lord,” Lady Castlewood said.
“Madam, I desire fair play—for Mr. Warrington, for myself, and for every member of this amiable family,” my lord snapped back.
“Then Heaven help the poor gentleman if your lordship intends to be so very kind to him,” his stepmother replied, dropping a sarcastic curtsy. The quarrel would no doubt have dragged on far longer, if a phaeton had not just that moment driven up to the front door, with both of the young Virginian cousins seated inside.

It was the same carriage Harry had bought in the height of his fortune, and he still drove it—George sat at his side, their two negro servants perched on the seat behind them. Harry had begged to hand the reins and full ownership of the whole equipage over to his brother the moment they’d met. “What business has a poor devil like me with horses and carriages, Georgy?” he’d said humbly. “I’ve nothing in the world but the coat on my back and the purse my aunt gave me. You take the driving seat, brother. It’ll ease my mind to see you behind the horses.” George had laughed him off, saying he did not know the London roads half as well as Harry did, and that as for the carriage, he would only claim half of it, just as he’d already claimed half of Harry’s fine new wardrobe. “A bargain’s a bargain,” he’d grinned. “If I share your coats, you must share my breeches pocket, Harry. That’s only fair!” Harry swore a dozen times over there was no better brother alive in all the world. He rattled his horses down the Kensington road at a fine pace, glowing with pride to have his older brother beside him, and their servant Gumbo thundered on the Castlewood front door with a knock loud enough to rival the grandest footman in all St. James’s.

Only Lady Castlewood and Lady Fanny were in the drawing-room to greet them. Will had no wish to face Harry after their old quarrel, my lord was still not dressed, and Maria had her own reasons for staying out of sight until the swell of tears in her eyes had dried. It is a strange, universal little comedy of society, is it not? How often we walk in on our friends unannounced, grinning and simpering, stepping over the still-smouldering ashes of a domestic row that raged only minutes before we arrived? The very second a servant calls out your name, the entire family rearranges themselves into a pretty tableau: the daughter pretending to arrange flowers in a vase, the son leaning over a devotional book, mamma shoving the unpaid butcher’s bill under the sofa cushion and picking up a piece of fancy work, even the grumpy pater sticking out a warm hand and exclaiming over how delighted he is you’ve dropped by for lunch. We are all of us the victims of these little deceptions, and we ought to be grateful for them. That polite hypocrisy is not vice—it is the kindest self-denial imaginable. What a dreadful, unbearable world it would be if every man said exactly what was on his mind the moment you walked through the door!

Lady Castlewood advanced to greet the young men with perfect ease and good humour, no trace of the earlier quarrel on her face. “Harry, we have heard this most extraordinary news!” she said, laying a soft hand on his arm. “Lord Castlewood said at breakfast he meant to call on you both this very day. Cousin Harry, we promise you we shall not love you one bit the less now you are poor.”
“Now we can prove we never liked you for your acres at all!” Lady Fanny chimed in, following her lead.
“And what of the acres that have fallen to me, then?” George asked, with a smile and a polite bow.
“Oh cousin, we shall like you for being just as good and kind as Harry!” the lively Lady Fanny replied.
The two ladies turned almost all their attention to Harry from that moment, barely more than civil to the new heir George. They were soft and familiar with Harry, gently affectionate, playfully reproachful for not coming to call on them for days at a time. “It would have done you far more good to sit and drink tea and play a quiet game of piquet with us than to gamble with all those unsavoury characters at White’s,” Lady Castlewood told him. “If we had won enough off you to buy a paper of pins we would have been perfectly content. Young gentlemen never know what is good for them.”
“Now you have no more money to play away, you can come and visit us every day, cousin!” Lady Fanny added, lifting a playful finger. “Your misfortune has turned to good luck for us!”
George was puzzled. The welcome given to his penniless younger brother was far warmer than any he had expected, even from this family of sharp fortune-hunters. Perhaps, he thought, they were not quite so bad as Harry had painted them?

After twenty minutes of this gushing affectionate chatter, Lord Castlewood made his entrance, fully wigged, his sword buckled at his side. He greeted both brothers with equal, easy politeness. “If only you had come to us a few months earlier, Mr. George,” he sighed, shaking George’s hand. “That fateful evening of piquet would never have happened then. A younger son would surely have been more prudent.”
“Or an older kinsman more compassionate,” Harry put in.
“Alas, the love of play runs in all our blood, I fear,” my lord said, spreading his hands. “I inherited it from my father, and it has made me the poorest peer in all England. Those two ladies before you are not immune to it, my brother Will is a martyr to it, and what I win one night I lose the very next day. It is a shocking plague, this rage for gambling that has seized all of England. And as for your banknotes, Harry—every last one of them was gambled away by me within twenty-four hours of winning them. Not a penny of it left.”
“I play like any other gentleman, but I never cared overmuch for the sport,” George remarked.
“We scolded him so thoroughly when we heard he’d played against you, Harry!” Lady Castlewood cried.
“And even if I had not won that money, you know very well some other stranger would have fleeced you of every penny,” my lord went on. “It is a poor consolation, but better that your own friends, who wish you well, take your money than some random crook who would not care if you starved in the gutter afterwards.”
“An aching tooth still hurts the same, even if your own brother is the one pulling it out, my lord,” George laughed. “Harry must bear the penalty of his faults, and pay his debts like any other man.”
“I am not the sort of Englishman who sulks when he’s fairly beaten,” Harry said, holding out his hand to my lord.
“Spoken like a true man!” my lord exclaimed, shaking it warmly. The ladies exchanged pleased little smiles.
“Our cousin in Virginia has raised her sons perfectly, like proper gentlemen!” Lady Castlewood gushed.
“You must not turn so very amiable now you are poor, cousin Harry!” Lady Fanny teased. “We never noticed half your good qualities back when you were just the Fortunate Youth, Prince of Virginia! You look exactly like him, cousin George, but I vow you cannot be half as amiable as your brother.”
“I may be the Prince of Virginia now, but I fear I am not the Fortunate Youth,” George said gravely.
Harry was about to blurt out that George was the best man alive on earth, when the jangle of a harpsichord drifted down from the upstairs drawing-room. Harry blushed bright red, and the two ladies smiled knowingly.
“That is Maria, up there,” Lady Castlewood said. “Shall we all go up and join her?”
The ladies rose and made for the door, Harry trailing after them, his face still flushed. George was about to follow too, but Lord Castlewood held him back.
“Nay, if all the ladies are going after your brother, let me have the pleasure of your company to myself for a little while,” he said. “I have been dying to hear the full story of your time in captivity and your rescue, cousin George!”
“Oh, we all want to hear that story too!” one of the ladies called back, lingering by the door.
“I am greedy, and I wish to hear it first hand, all to myself,” my lord said, staring at her so sternly she scurried out after the rest of the party. He bowed them out, and closed the drawing-room door softly behind them.
“Your brother has no doubt told you everything that has befallen him in this house, cousin George?” he asked, turning back to their guest.
“Yes, including his quarrel with Mr. Will, and his engagement to my Lady Maria,” George replied, bowing politely. “I think I may be forgiven for saying he has met with nothing but ill fortune here, my lord.”
“No one on earth deplores that more than I do,” my lord said earnestly. “My brother Will keeps company with jockeys, boxers, and the wildest young rakes in town, and we have barely a scrap of sympathy between us. We would never all live under the same roof if we were not all so dreadfully poor. This very house belonged to our grandmother, before she left for America to marry Colonel Esmond. Half the wainscoting and furniture here was hers.” George glanced around the panelled parlour with faint interest. “Our family has not thrived these last twenty years, though we did manage to secure a promotion in our rank at court some years back, thanks to a bit of influence we had there. But the mania for gambling has ruined us all. I am its most miserable victim. I am far too proud to sell my title and marry a common rich tradesman’s daughter, as so many less scrupulous noblemen have done. Pride is my great fault, cousin. I never forget the blood that runs in my veins!” He laid his hand on his ruffled shirt front, stuck out his toe, and looked George nobly in the face.
George was naturally inclined to trust everyone he met— but once he saw through a man’s pretences, he was completely, dryly sceptical. He hid his sardonic amusement well, keeping his face perfectly grave.
“We all have our faults, my lord. A love of cards is widely forgiven amongst gentlemen of our rank. Having already forgiven my brother for all his follies, I am hardly fit to sit in judgement over you. Instead of both of you playing and losing, I only wish both of you had played and won!”
“So do I, with all my heart!” my lord sighed. “I can tell you are a good man, with far more sense and knowledge of the world than most young men of your age. Poor Harry has the kindest heart in the world, but I fear his wits are not the strongest.”
“They are not, indeed. But he has a knack for making friends everywhere he goes, and most people love him in spite of all his imprudences.”
“We all love him, as if he were our own brother!” my lord cried.
“He wrote to our mother constantly, describing what a warm welcome he received here. She has kept every one of his letters. Harry’s style is not very learned, but his heart is so good, reading his notes is better than any witty book.”
“I think you have a kind heart and plenty of wit too, cousin,” my lord said, still forcing graciousness.
“I am what Heaven made me, with a little more experience and sorrow than most young men my age,” George said. “This great good fortune of mine, my sudden reappearance—has it left Harry with no resources at all?” Lord Castlewood asked, very gently.
“Nothing but whatever small sums our mother chooses to leave him, or whatever little I can spare him after her death. What is the usual portion for a younger brother here in England, my lord?”
“Ah, a younger brother is… well, everyone knows what a younger brother’s lot is,” my lord said, shrugging his shoulders, and meeting George’s eye.
George went on smoothly: “We are the best of brothers, but we are flesh and blood, and I have no intention of spoiling him by giving him large sums of money he will only squander away at cards or on horse races. We have gamblers and jockeys in Virginia too, and poor Harry distinguished himself in exactly the same way

Madame de Bernstein was scarcely less delighted than her two Virginian nephews when the final interview between Harry and Lady Maria drew to its close. George sent her a brief billet recounting every detail of the meeting that very same evening, and before long Lord Castlewood—whose visits to his aunt were notoriously rare—arrived at her door to pay his respects, and spoke openly of all that had transpired. No man was better than his lordship at striking a frank, unguarded tone when it suited his purpose, and now that the match between Maria and Harry was well and truly ended, there was no need for pretense or hypocrisy. The game was played, the final move made: he saw no harm in recalling its stratagems, finesses, and small, clever schemes.
“She is my own sister,” he declared, with a show of warm affection. “She will not get many more chances as good as this to marry and settle her future. I may not have approved of the match in every particular, and I may have pitied your ladyship’s young Virginian favourite, but such a stroke of good fortune was not to be thrown away, and I was bound to stand by my own flesh and blood.”
“Your candour does your lordship infinite honour,” Madame de Bernstein replied dryly, “and your devotion to your sister is positively edifying!”
“Nay, we have lost the game, and I speak with no rancour in my heart. It is you, who won, that have no cause to bear malice,” Lord Castlewood said, bowing with easy grace.
The Baroness protested she had never been in better humour in her life. “Confess it now, Eugene: that visit Maria paid Harry at the spunging-house, that dramatic, tender little scene where she gave back all his gifts—was that stroke of genius yours?”
“Pity for the young man, and a sense of what was due from an affianced lady to her lover in misfortune—sure those are motives sufficient to explain her conduct,” Lord Castlewood replied, affecting a demure innocence before he shrugged, and owned he had indeed advised his sister to call on Mr. Henry Warrington. “And we should have won, in spite of all your ladyship’s interference,” he added, “had not the elder brother risen from the grave to make his appearance. I have been doing my best to console my poor Maria, in fact, by pointing out how very lucky it is, on the whole, that we lost.”
“Suppose she had married Harry, and then your cousin George had turned up alive after all?” the Baroness pointed out.
“Effectivement!” cried Eugene, taking a pinch of scented snuff. “As the grave chose to give up its dead, let us be thankful it disgorged them in the nick of time! I must own that Mr. George Warrington seems a man of sound sense, no more selfish than any other eldest son and man of the world. My poor Molly had fancied he might be a greenhorn, like his younger brother, you see. She fondly hoped he would be inclined to share and share alike with Twin junior, and she was so infatuated with the young man, I do believe she would have taken him even then. ‘Harry Warrington with half a loaf might do very well,’ I told her, ‘but Harry Warrington with no bread at all, my dear!’”
“No bread?” the Baroness asked.
“No bread but a spot at his elder brother’s side table. The man said as much to me, plain as day.”
“What a hard-hearted wretch!” Madame de Bernstein exclaimed.
“Ah, bah! I show you my cards, aunt, cartes sur table! Mr. George only did what every other man in his position would have done, and we have no right to be angry with him, not really. Molly acknowledged as much herself, after her first burst of tears was over, and I had brought her to listen to reason. The silly creature! To be so wild about a young lad half her age!”
“‘Twas a real passion, I almost do believe,” said Madame de Bernstein. “You should have heard her take leave of him. C'etait touchant, ma parole d'honneur! I cried, right there before George, I could not help myself. The young fellow with muddy stockings, his hair falling over his eyes, flings himself into our dinner party, makes his offer to Molly in a frank, noble manner, in very fine language too, and then she replies. Begad, it put me in mind of Mrs. Woffington in that new Scotch play Lord Bute’s man wrote—Douglas, what d’ye call it? She clings round the lad, bids him adieu in heartrending accents, steps out of the room in stately despair, no more chocolate for her, thank you. If she had made a mauvais pas, no woman alive could have retreated from it with more dignity. ‘Twas a masterly defeat, we were starved out of our position, but we retired with all the honours of war.”
“Molly will not die of this disappointment,” my lord’s aunt observed, sipping her spiced tea. My lord grinned, showing his yellow teeth. “He, he! She has had this very malady very severely two or three times before, and recovered perfectly. It does not kill, as your ladyship well knows, not at Molly’s time of life.”
How should her ladyship know? She had not married Doctor Tusher until she was well advanced in years, nor become Madame de Bernstein until even later. Old Dido, the poet remarks, was no stranger to misfortune, and so learned to have compassion on the wretched.
Folk in the small world brawl and feud, and keep up their quarrels for years, refusing to make peace. But the people of the great world are surely wiser in their generation. They fall out, they cease calling on each other, then they make amends and meet again, no awkward questions asked. A stray prodigal, or even a stray puppy-dog, is welcomed back under the terms of an unspoken amnesty, no matter where he has been roaming. For six whole months, ever since the Castlewoods and Madame de Bernstein began their battle for possession of poor Harry Warrington, the two branches of the Esmond family had kept entirely apart. Now, that the quarrel was settled, they were free to meet again as if no difference had ever divided them: Madame de Bernstein drove her great gilded coach to Lady Castlewood’s rout, the Esmond ladies appeared smiling at the Baroness’s weekly drums, and they all professed to love each other every bit as dearly as they had done before the feud began.
“So, sir, I hear you have acted like a hard-hearted monster to your poor brother Harry!” the Baroness cried, delighted, tapping George playfully with her ivory cane.
“I only acted on your ladyship’s hint, to see whether our kinsfolk wanted Harry for himself, or for the fortune everyone thought he had,” George replied, flushing bright red.
“Nay, Maria could not marry a penniless fellow who had nothing at all, when his own elder brother declared he would not give him a penny!”
“I did it for the best, madam,” George insisted, still blushing.
“And thou didst, thou little hypocrite!” the old lady cackled in delight.
“Hypocrite, madam! And what makes you say that?” Mr. Warrington asked, drawing himself up with great offended dignity.
“I know all, my infant!” the Baroness switched to French. “Thou art the very image of thy grandfather. Come, that I embrace thee! Harry has told me everything, how thou hast divided thy little patrimony evenly with him!”
“It was but natural, madam. We have shared hearts and purses since the day we were born. I only feigned that hard-heartedness to call those people’s bluff,” George said, his eyes glistening.
“And thou wilt divide the great Virginia estate with him too?” the Baroness pressed.
“I do not say that. It would not be just,” Mr. Warrington replied. “The land must pass to the eldest born, and Harry would not have it otherwise. It may be I die young, or our mother outlives us both. But half of everything that is mine is his, and it must be remembered he only fell into debt because he was misled to believe he was the heir.”
“Ah! It is a knight of old, it is Bayard, it is the old grandfather come back to life!” Madame de Bernstein declared to her waiting-woman as she retired for the night. That evening, when the two lads took their leave, she only offered Harry two fingers in polite parting, but pressed her rouged painted cheek to George’s, who blushed as deep as that well-dyed rose for very bashfulness at the favour.
Harry Warrington was the least envious soul alive, and had always honoured his brother as his chief, his guide, and his better, so it was no surprise that a heavy sense of humiliation and disappointment weighed on him after he was deposed from his lofty position as the Fortunate Youth, heir to boundless Virginian territories. His friends at Kensington might vow over and over that they would love him all the better after his fall; Harry bowed low and thanked them earnestly, but he could not fail to notice, when he accompanied George to the grand state dinner Lord Castlewood threw for his newly-found kinsman, that George was the centre of everyone’s attention. All the compliments, all the small, tender little attentions, were lavished on him, while no one paid Harry any mind at all—save poor Maria, who followed him all evening with wistful, heavy eyes, that seemed to carry dismal, silent reproach, blaming him for the very thing she had done.
“Ah!” those eyes seemed to say. “It is all very well for you, Harry, to accept the freedom I gave you, but I never, sir, intended for you to be quite so pleased to be let off.” She had set him free, and yet she could not forgive him for taking her at her word. She would not marry him, and yet she would have liked to keep him pining after her. Oh, my young friends, how delightful is the beginning of a love affair, and how undignified, sometimes, the end! What a romantic vista opens before young Damon and young Phillis, or middle-aged lovers of the same, when they declare their artless affections to each other, twine their arms around each other’s waists, and survey that charming pays du tendre stretching out before their feet! Linked together, they will wander down its paths until extreme old age. There may be rough rocks and roaring rivers in the way, but will not Damon’s strong true love carry his sweetheart safely over them? There may be dragons and dangers in the path, but shall not his courageous sword cut them all down? Then at evening, they will rest cuddled together like two pretty babes in the wood, moss for their couch, stars for their canopy, their arms for each other’s pillows! That is the wise, perfect plan young folk draw up when they set out on the journey of love—and, alas, they have not walked a mile before they come to a great solid wall, and find they must turn back. They are squabbling with the post-boy at Barnet, the very first stage on the road to Gretna Green, and suddenly Strephon has no money in his pocket, or there is papa waving a great whacking horsewhip, who drags the young lady back, locks her up in the schoolroom to cry her eyes out. The parting is heart-breaking at the time, but years later, when she has married the banker and borne him eight children, and he has become either a prosperous barrister or a seedy scapegrace who has gone bankrupt two or three times, when they meet again by chance, is not the whole situation faintly ridiculous? Nevertheless, I hope no young man ever falls in love while doubting the eternity of his passion. It is only when a man has had a second or third amorous attack that he begins to grow doubtful. Some women are romantic to the very end, and from eighteen to eight-and-fifty, for all I know to the contrary, are always half expecting their hearts to break. In short, when you have been in love and are in love no longer, when the King of France, with twenty thousand men, colours flying and music playing, all the pomp of war, marches up the hill and then proceeds to march right back down again, he and you are in a very absurd position.
That was exactly what Harry Warrington felt, no doubt, when he went to Kensington and met those melancholy, reproachful eyes of his cousin Maria. Yes, it is a foolish position to be in. But it is also melancholy to look up at a house you once lived in, and see black empty casements where once the welcome fires blazed. Melancholy? Yes, but ha! how bitter, how absurd, to pass by that number 13 and look up sentimentally, only to see somebody else grinning out of the window, on the best possible terms with the landlady. I always feel a little aggrieved, even at an inn I frequent, when I see other people’s trunks and boots lined up outside the rooms that were once mine. Did those muddy vulgar highlongs rest their feet on the sofa where I once reclined? Kick you out of my sight, you clumsy things!
So, considering his tenancy of Maria’s affections was well and truly over, and if her heart was not let to a new tenant yet, it was at any rate up for let, Harry never felt easy in his cousin’s company, nor she in his. He found they had nothing to say to each other that was worth hearing, and Maria’s softest accents and most melancholy pouts were far less agreeable to him now than the red lip of a well-loved white clay pipe filled with his own Virginia tobacco. So when George went to call at Kensington, Harry rarely cared to tag along, and made excuses of other engagements.
At his uncle’s house in Hill Street, the poor lad fared no better, and the virtuous folk who lived there barely paid him any attention at all. The ladies did not scruple to tell their servants to deny themselves when he called. He could scarcely believe such insincerity was possible, after all their former caresses, their warm welcomes, their repeated vows of undying affection—until one day, sitting with the Lamberts for an hour after he had called on his aunt, he saw her chairmen arrive with the empty sedan, and his aunt step out of it to go inside, not even blushing when he bowed to her from the opposite window. To be denied by his own father’s brother’s wife! To find that door which once had opened so wide to welcome him now slammed in his face! He would never have believed such coldness possible, simple honest Harry declared. He might have thought the door-knocker had a tender heart, and was not made of brass. My Lady Warrington’s virtuous, unsmiling face was no more changed than the polished brass head of that very knocker when she passed him by.
“Oh, Aunt Lambert, Aunt Lambert!” he cried, with his usual impetuosity. “Did you ever see such heartless behaviour? What have I done to offend her?”
“Do we treat you any differently, my dear Harry?” Aunt Lambert asked, glancing sideways at her youngest daughter. “The rest of the world may turn cold, but we do not belong to it. You may come to us whenever you please, in perfect safety.”
“This house is different from every other house I go to,” Harry replied. “I do not know how to say it, but I always feel quiet, and happy somehow, the moment I step over your threshold.”
“Quis me uno vivit felicior? aut magis hac est Optandum vita dicere quis potuit?” General Lambert called out, turning to his eldest son, the college student home for Easter holidays. “Do you know where I got those lines, Mr. Gownsman?”
“From Catullus, sir,” the scholar replied.
“Got no such thing, sir,” the General laughed. “I got them from my favourite Democritus Junior—old Robert Burton, who has supplied hundreds of indifferent scholars with far more learning than they would ever dig up on their own.” Burton and Montaigne, indeed, were the good General’s two favourite authors in all the world.

It has already been noted that our two Virginian brothers, with that peculiar brand of earnest, ill-informed wisdom common to spirited youth, had adopted staunch Jacobite opinions and professed an almost absurd devotion to the exiled Stuart royal line. The banished prince had formally recognized Madam Esmond’s father as the rightful Marquis of Esmond, and she could not bring herself to bear ill will toward an unfortunate royal house that had been so eager to acknowledge the merits of her own family. As for the petty, scurrilous gossip linking her sister Madame de Bernstein to the Old Chevalier, she tossed the memory of that odious tale aside with complete scorn, asserting quite truthfully that the first two Hanoverian monarchs were no more moral in their private lives than any Stuart king that ever sat on the British throne.

That said, the reigning de facto king was still the king, duly anointed and crowned in church, and the man who had soundly defeated the Stuart claimant outright when the two factions met on the battlefield to fight for the crown. Madam’s unshakable opinion was, then, that her sons owed it to themselves as well as to their sovereign to make their proper appearance at his royal court. If His Majesty saw fit to bestow a well-paid sinecure, or a red or blue ribbon of honour on either of the lads, she would not have been the least bit surprised. She had full faith the King knew the Virginian Esmond name as well as he knew the names of half the oldest peers of his realm. So the boys received strict orders to present themselves at court, and one can only imagine how cross their mother would have been to learn that George had borrowed Harry’s finest laced embroidered coat the very day he went to make his bow to the sovereign.

A hundred years ago, the King’s drawing room was open almost every day to the nobility and gentry of the realm, and loyal subjects – especially now that war was raging across the colonies and the high seas – could indulge their eagerness to glimpse the august sovereign a dozen times a month. The king’s council had wisely decided that risking the royal person to capture by French warships while crossing the Channel to visit his beloved native Hanover would be an inestimable loss to the British Isles, so the monarch was obliged to forgo those long-dreamed-of trips to Herrenhausen and remain, very reluctantly, among his adoring British subjects. A Hanoverian countess whose tender friendship had endeared her to the prince did her best to console him for the forced separation from his home, and from the lips of the Countess of Walmoden (whom the Crown had graciously raised to high British peerage) the Defender of the Faith could still hear the soft accents of his native German.

To this beloved sovereign, George Warrington asked his assiduous courtier uncle Sir Miles to present him. As General Lambert also had business at Kensington that day, to thank the King for his recent promotion, the two men made the journey together in a hired hackney-coach, now that Lord Wrotham had returned to his London townhouse and reclaimed the use of his own private carriage. They alighted at Kensington Palace Gate, where the sentries on duty knew and saluted the old general, and proceeded on foot at a modest pace toward the summer residence of the King.

Walking under the palace’s grand stone portico, they entered the long gallery that led to the famous black marble staircase, richly decorated and frescoed by the artist Mr. Kent, then passed through a succession of chambers hung with fine tapestries, lined with master paintings and marble busts, until they reached the King’s great drawing room. Here hung Titian’s famous *Venus*, and other works including Rubens’ *St. Francis Adoring the Infant Saviour*. Along with the rest of the waiting courtiers, the two gentlemen lingered there until His Majesty emerged from his private apartments, where he had been in conference with what the newspapers of the day referred to discreetly as his M-j-ty’s M-n-st-rs.

George Warrington, who had never stepped foot in a royal palace before, had plenty of time to admire the grand surroundings and observe the crowds around him. He saw great works of fine art for the first time in his life, lingering delightedly over Van Dyck’s magnificent portrait of King Charles the First, his queen and their children, and Tintoret’s grand canvas of Esther before Ahasuerus, where all the figures were clad in sumptuous period Venetian dress. He was so enraptured by the paintings that he barely heard General Lambert whispering the names of the notables scattered around the room in his ear.

“Yonder are two lords of the Admiralty,” Lambert murmured. “Mr. Gilbert Elliot, and Admiral Boscawen – the man whose fleet fired the first shot in your Virginia waters two years back. That stout gentleman fairly plastered in gold lace is Mr. Fox, who was once Minister, and is now content to serve as Paymaster with a princely salary.”
“His waistcoat is stitched like it was mined straight from Potosi,” George laughed.
“Aye, he loves to gather wealth and spend it freely,” Lambert went on. “Yonder is my Lord Chief Justice Willes, talking to my Lord of Salisbury, Doctor Headley – if he serves God half as faithfully as he serves the King, he’ll rise to very high honours in Heaven. He dates back to your grandfather’s time, loved by Dick Steele and hated by Dean Swift. With them is the Bishop of London, the learned Doctor Sherlock. The lawn-sleeved lords of the church don’t get half the deference they used to these days. I can remember when I was a little boy, my mother made me kneel down to the Bishop of Rochester – the one who fled over the water to serve that unnamed Stuart pretender, that Perkin Warbeck of a bishop. That handsome fair-haired man is Admiral Tom Smith, they call him Tom of Ten Thousand in the fleet. He presided over poor Byng’s court martial, and fought in vain to save him from the firing squad. The French ambassador had him broken of his rank as a lieutenant for daring to make a French man-o’-war lower its topsails to him – and our King made him a full captain the very next day. That tall, haughty man is Lord George Sackville. Now that I’m a Major-General myself, I’ll see he treats me better than a footman. I wish our stout old Blakeney was here – he’s the darling of every common soldier, and as kind and brave as that poker of a nobleman is arrogant and – Your lordship, your very humble servant. This is a young gentleman just fresh from America, who was there at that sad Braddock expedition two years ago.”
“Oh indeed?” drawled the haughty lord, looking down his nose. “I have the honour of addressing Mr. —?”
“Major-General Lambert, at your lordship’s service, who served in His Majesty’s forces long before you held your commission. Mr. Warrington, that man over yonder is Mr. Speaker Onslow, the first commoner in all of England. Where is your uncle? If Sir Miles delays much longer, I shall present you to the King myself.”
As he spoke, the old general turned his full attention back to George, paying the arrogant noble no further notice, and the man stalked off looking stunned, as if he could not believe anyone would dare treat him with such lack of deference – for a hundred years ago, a lord was a lord, and expected universal awe as a matter of right.

Presently Sir Miles’s scarlet waistcoat came bobbing through the crowd, and the three men greeted each other warmly. The general had quit Lord Wrotham’s house now that his lordship had returned to town, and Sir Miles gushed that all the neighbourhood missed him terribly. “My daughters were quite half in love with your two lovely girls, upon my word they were,” he cried. “My Lady Warrington and the girls have been scheming for weeks to find a proper way to make your acquaintance. We feel like we are old friends already! We love you, sir, for all your kindness to our dear nephews – my own flesh and blood, my poor dear brother’s boys. I confess we were a little jealous, watching them trudge off to your house so often. I’ve said to my Lady Warrington a dozen times, ‘My dear, why do we not invite the General and his family over for a plain family dinner, no fuss at all?’ Pray carry my sincerest respects to Mrs. Lambert, and thank her for all she has done for our lads.” He brushed a hand over his eyes, quite overcome with affectionate emotion, and George had to struggle mightily to keep a straight face.

Just then the doors to the King’s private apartments swung open, and the pages stepped out, preceding His Majesty. He was followed by his burly, corpulent son the Duke of Cumberland, all clad in blazing scarlet coat and matching scarlet face, and behind them came a train of officers and ministers – among whom George immediately spotted the famous Secretary Pitt, tall as a colossus, with his eagle beak of a nose and his grave, majestic bearing. Even at a distance of a hundred years, the writer feels a genuine awe looking back at that solemn figure, and an urge to doff his hat. We do not tremble at the sight of George the Second, nor are our eyes dazzled by the Duke of Culloden and Fontenoy’s portentous bulk – but the Great Commoner, the terrible Cornet of Horse, strides across the narrow map of 18th century Britain like a Colossus, and we fall quiet as he passes by in his gouty shoes, his thunderbolt hand wrapped in soft flannel. No doubt he has just come from a long, stormy interview with his royal master, boring the sharp little old king for hours with grand, thunderous speeches full of noble rhetoric even on the most trivial topics, rhetoric the thrifty, plain-spoken king heartily detests. The sublime minister passes solemnly through the crowd, and every courtier lines up respectfully against the walls.

The King walks the circle of guests, his royal son lingering a little behind to chat with favoured individuals. He is a small, sharp, bright-complexioned old man with very prominent eyes, dressed in plain old-fashioned snuff-coloured coat and brown stockings, his only ornament the blue sash of the Order of the Garter. He speaks English with a thick German accent, but with great shrewdness and simplicity, stopping to speak to those he wishes to notice, and passing others with a brief nod. He knew General Lambert very well, who had served under him at Dettingen and fought for his son in the Scottish rebellion, and he congratulated him heartily on his promotion.
“It is not always easy to do as one likes,” the King said kindly, “but I was very glad to grant that favour in your case, General – there is no better officer in my entire army.” The old veteran blushed bright red and bowed, completely gratified.

Meanwhile the King’s eyes fell on Sir Miles Warrington, whom he knew perfectly as the man who begged every minister for every available favour, and then on the young man standing at his side. “Who is this?” he asked, pointing directly at George, who stood clad in poor Harry’s best embroidered coat, holding himself in a respectful attitude. Sir Miles bowed so low he nearly bent double, and informed His Majesty that this was his Virginian nephew, Mr. George Warrington, who had come to pay his humble duty to the crown.
“Ah, so this is the other brother?” the King said dryly. “Good thing he made it over in time, or the first brother would have spent all the family fortune. My Lord Bishop of Salisbury, what are you doing out in this bitter weather? You ought to be at home in your warm bed!” With that, the little king wandered on to greet the rest of the courtiers.

Sir Miles was almost beside himself with delight at the royal condescension. He clapped George on the shoulder. “God bless you, my boy!” he cried. “Did I not tell you you would see the greatest monarch and finest gentleman alive? Is he not the very pattern of a king, my Lord Bishop?”
“That he is!” the bishop cried, clasping his hands and rolling his eyes up to the ceiling. “The best of princes and of men!”
“Yonder young man surrounded by the crowd is Master Louis, Lady Yarmouth’s favourite nephew,” Lambert pointed out to George, and before long the stout Duke of Cumberland made his way over to their little group. He clapped Lambert on the hand. “Congratulate you on your promotion, Lambert,” he said.
“Sir, I owe it entirely to your Royal Highness’s good offices,” the general said gratefully.
“Not at all – you deserved it long ago. Always been a good officer. No doubt we’ll find some active work for you soon. Is this the young gentleman James Wolfe wrote to me about?”
“His brother, sir.”
“Ah, the famous Fortunate Youth! You were with poor Ned Braddock in America, were you? Taken prisoner, and lucky enough to escape. Come and see me at my house in Pall Mall, lad. Bring him to my next levee, Lambert.” And with that, the broad back of the royal prince turned away.

“It’s pouring rain!” Sir Miles cried. “You two came on foot? No, no, you will ride home with me in my coach. I will hear no denial!” he insisted, and bundled George and Lambert back to his Hill Street townhouse. He presented the general to Lady Warrington and his two daughters Flora and Dora, and insisted they stay for a light collation, as they must be cold and hungry after their time at court.
“What, only cold mutton? An old soldier can eat cold mutton well enough,” Lambert laughed.
“And a glass of my Lady Warrington’s own spiced cordial, made by her own hand, to chase that cold palace chill away,” Sir Miles added heartily. “Capital mutton, six years old, straight off our country estate! The Warringtons have loved good mutton ever since the Conquest, you know. We live very plainly here – can’t afford to feed our rascally servants on seven-year-old mutton, ha!”

Sir Miles proceeded to tell his wife and daughters a wildly exaggerated, glowing account of George’s reception at court, so full of fulsome praise that George could barely recognize the quiet half-snub he had actually gotten from the king, and could not bring himself to contradict his uncle in front of his whole family. General Lambert sat by staring in complete disbelief – he had been at the same court that day, and seen none of the grand, flattering audiences Sir Miles described.
“We are all so proud of you, dear George,” the whole family chorused. “We love you not for your great estates or your ancient name, but for the courage you showed fighting for your country and your king.”
A little piping voice came from small Master Miles, the youngest child: “I still like Harry best.”
Sir Miles shooed the little boy off to his tutor, then turned back to Lambert, insisting he and his wife and daughters must come for a proper formal dinner at their house very soon, no refusals allowed. The ladies dragged George off to their drawing room, insisting he stay and tell them every last gory detail of the Braddock battle and his dramatic escape from the Indians, and Tom Claypool wandered in to hear the end of the tale, while Flora dabbed at her eyes with her handkerchief over the story.

When General Lambert finally got home, he could not help regaling his wife with a full account of the absurd new family they had met. The new fashionable slang word “humbug” had just come into vogue, and that was exactly the word he used to describe the entire Warrington household. He told her of the father’s over-the-top forced hospitality, the mother’s pompous flattery, the girls’ obvious coquetry, the mutton so tough it nearly broke his teeth, and the cordial that tasted like spiced turpentine. Mrs. Lambert of course contrasted their current fawning over rich, newly respectable George with the way they had snubbed poor Harry when he was visiting them earlier, before he had any fortune to make them polite.
“Is that Miss Warrington really so handsome?” Mrs. Lambert asked.
“Extremely handsome,” Lambert laughed, “and the most shameless little flirt I have ever set eyes on in my life.”
“The horrible hypocrites! I have no patience for people like that!” Mrs. Lambert huffed.
To that, her husband only answered with a silly monosyllable: “Bo!”
“Why on earth did you say ‘Bo!’ Martin?” his wife asked, confused.
“I say ‘Bo!’ to a goose, my dear,” he grinned.
Mrs. Lambert protested that she had no idea what he was talking about, what silly secret thought he was hiding, and Lambert only smiled wider and said: “Of course you don’t.”

The earnest, humdrum business of ordinary life, I think, makes up very little of a novelist’s stock-in-trade. We may turn to tales of military service, where courage and cowardice, devotion and sacrifice, heroic death and narrow escape, naturally lend themselves to high, stirring narrative; but the rest of daily toil scarcely belongs between the pages of a story. What use is there in lingering over Ficulnus haggling over sacks of sugar, spices, and cheese at his wharf? Or Causidicus poring for twelve hours straight over mildewed black-letter law volumes? Or Sartorius cross-legged on his workbench, chalk in hand, taking the measure of a gentleman for a new pair of breeches? Would anyone sit through a tedious, blow-by-blow chronicle of a farm labourer’s hobnail boots tramping mud, his wages of eighteen pence a day? Even the poets of our own time dress their shepherds in pink silk breeches and chintz waistcoats, dancing before their flocks and playing a flageolet tied up with blue satin ribbon, rather than show them mucking out pens and threshing barley. I say this in reply to the gentle, potent critics who chide me for skipping over the finer details of professional life: saving for the theatre of war, there is no room for full descriptions of stockbroking, polemical theology, linen-drapery, or the daily grind of the apothecary’s shop. All a writer can do is depict his characters out of their working hours—ruled by their passions, their loves, their laughs, their hatreds—taking their daily labour for granted, leaving it as a quiet, unspoken background to the moments we share with them.

So it is that we only ever find our friends lingering in theatre lobbies, coffee houses, ridotto halls, fair booths, and feasting rooms, while the rest of the world plods on unseen in counting houses, weaves at looms, and tends to its endless, uncelebrated labours. Corydon the shepherd does not only make love to Phillis; he carts manure and stacks hay too. Ancillula the maid scrubs the nursery, waits at breakfast, and drags fractious children out for walks before she can snatch her five minutes of stolen courtship behind the area railings with her policeman sweetheart. We only ever stumble across our characters in the small, precious gaps between their work—and that is where we meet our equally disengaged readers, too.

The macaronis and fine gentlemen who haunted White’s and Arthur’s had turned so cold a shoulder to poor Harry Warrington that he soon stopped seeking their company at all. The Ring, the Mall, and the gaming tables knew his face no more. His aunt Madame de Bernstein bade him defy the town’s indifference, vowing that the world would soon relent if he only faced its snubs with a bold front. But Harry was far too honest to wear a false smile when he was stung, to hide his mortification under a mask of impudent wit, or flatter his way back into favour as so many men and women of fashion learned to do to get ahead.

“Fiddlededee, child!” the old lady snapped at him when he pulled a long face and complained of his treatment. “Everyone eats impertinence in this world. If you get a box on the ear when you are poor and fallen, you bite your lip, smile it off, and if you are clever, pay the insult back ten years later. Do you suppose I never had to swallow humble pie in my time? All of us do, when our luck runs out. Now that you are no longer the Fortunate Youth, be the Clever Youth, and win back the place you lost to bad luck. Go out more than ever. Attend every rout and party you are invited to, and seek out more still. Be civil to everyone, especially every woman you meet—only never forget to show the spirit you have in plenty. With economy, and your brother George’s admirable generosity, you can still cut a genteel figure. With that handsome face and frame of yours, you cannot fail to catch a rich heiress. Tenez! Go down to the City and mingle with the merchants there. They will never have heard that you are out of fashion at the Court end of town. A little management, and you can build a fine position for yourself again. And when last did you wait on Lady Yarmouth? She took a great fancy to you, you fool. I order you to attend her evenings regularly, and lose no opportunity of paying court to her.”

The old woman who had doted on Harry when he first stepped off the ship from Virginia, who had hung on his artless stories and lavished him with kisses and favours, was now siding with the world against him. She greeted him with coldness now, grew peevish and patronising, and would cast gibes and cutting jests at him in front of her guests until his honest face burned bright with humiliation, a dull ache of bewildered grief settling heavy in his manly, gentle heart. Even her servants, who had once fawned on him and bowed so deep their wigs nearly touched the floor, scarcely paid him any mind. More than once the footman told him her ladyship was indisposed or engaged when he called; no one pressed him to wait, no one invited him to stay for dinner as they had done in the days when he was the wealthy Fortunate Youth, companion to dukes and earls.

Harry brought all his woes to the Lamberts’ little Soho parlour, and poured out his heart to Mrs. Lambert in a passion of sorrow, reeling from the shock of how quickly the whole world could turn heartless on a man the moment his luck failed. While the kind ladies of the house bustled about their domestic chores, poor Harry would sit glum in the window seat, heart-sick and silent.

“I know you are the best, kindest people alive,” he would say to them. “And I know I must be the dullest company in all the world—yes, that I am.”

“Well, you are not very lively just now, Harry,” said Hetty, who had begun to take a sort of gentle command over him, and who secretly wondered, for a moment, was this the dashing hero she had once dreamed him to be?

“Why should he be lively when he is hurt?” Theo asked softly. “He has a good heart, and it pains him to see friends desert him. There is no harm in that at all.”

“I would have too much spirit to show I was hurt, no matter what they did to me!” Hetty cried, clenching her little fists. “I would smile even if that horrible old painted woman boxed my ears. She is dreadful, mamma. You think so too, don’t you, Theo? You said so last night, and mimicked her hobbling in on her crutch, grinning round at all her guests!”

“I may not like her,” Theo said, blushing bright red. “But there is no call to speak rude names of Harry’s own aunt right to his face.”

“You provoking thing, you are always right!” Hetty laughed. “And that is what makes me so cross. Harry, I beg your pardon, truly, for speaking ill of your relation.”

“I do not care about the rest,” Harry said. “But it is hard that she of all people should turn on me. I grew very fond of her. And somehow, it makes me mad when people I care for deeply turn away and treat me unkindly.”

“Suppose George were to do that?” Hetty asked, teasing. The little quiet web of affection was already being spun between them: George and Hetty, Theo and Harry, all tangled together in the soft, unspoken way of young people.

“You are clever and lively, Hetty, and you may fancy all sorts of things—but not that!” Harry cried, standing up straight, his face flushing dark. “You do not know my brother as I do. You would never dare to suppose my George could do anything unkind or unworthy.” He looked so fierce and loyal, his eyes bright, that Hetty turned pale as a sheet. She looked up at him, and said not a single word.

A little later, before he took his leave, Harry said in his simple, earnest way, “I am very sorry, Hetty, I beg your pardon if I spoke too roughly. But I will always fight anyone who says a word against my brother George.”

Hetty said nothing at all, just gave him her hand and dropped a tiny, prim curtsey. That night, when she and Theo were sitting up late, twisting their hair into curl papers and whispering all their secrets, Hetty sighed. “I thought it would be such pure happiness to see him every day, and I was so glad when papa said we would stay in London. But now I do see him, I keep offending him, over and over. I know he is not clever, Theo. But oh! is he not so good, and kind, and brave? Did he not look perfectly handsome when he was angry just now?”

“Silly little thing,” Theo laughed. “You are always making him out to be handsome, no matter what he does.”

General Lambert, for his part, had long ago taken to calling his wife “Bo” as a gentle rebuke for that all-consuming love of sentiment and match-making that lives in every good woman whose heart is worth a fig. He teased her that she was a fool if she fancied the two Virginian twins would fall in love with his girls. “Little Hetty may have her little fancies,” he said, “and little girls do, but they get over them. You know perfectly well, Molly, you fancied a dozen other young men before you set eyes on me,” he said, and his soft-hearted wife could not deny it. Harry, after all, was no great catch now: penniless, overshadowed by his elder returned brother, not a single acre he could call his own.

“Oh, of course, now he is poor we will turn him out just like all the rest of the world, I suppose!” Mrs. Lambert protested, wiping her eyes with her pocket handkerchief.

“Do I ever turn my back on a friend in distress, Molly?” the General asked, gently.

“No, my dear, I am a perfect goose, I own it!” she laughed.

“Then let the poor boy come to us whenever he likes, and welcome. This selfish town has scarcely another house that will take him in. He is unhappy, and being with us eases his mind. For God’s sake, let him stay as long as he likes!” the kind officer said. And so Harry always had a place at their dinner table, a chair by their fire whenever he wanted it. George, too, was welcome. At first he did not come with the easy, warm affection Harry felt for the Lamberts, for he was colder by nature, more mistrustful of himself and other people. But the family’s unfeigned kindness soon won him over, and he learned to love them for their own sake, as well as for their tender care of his brother. He could not help but see how low-spirited Harry was, and pity his brother’s quiet despair. He would joke dryly with him over their pipes, saying, “My dear Harry, I am George the Unlucky, now that you have ceased to be Harry the Fortunate. That rogue Florac would have done far better to leave that Indian brave to take my scalp in the forest, instead of killing him. Then everyone at White’s would still treat you like a prince. Our mother would be weeping over me as a poor defunct angel, instead of being angry that I have come back to supplant her favourite. You are her favourite, and you deserve to be. The whole world’s favourite—though if I had stayed dead, your cousin Maria would have insisted on marrying you, and that is how the gods would have revenged themselves on you for all your good luck.”

“I never can tell if you are laughing at me, or at yourself, George,” Harry said. “I never know when you are jesting and when you are serious.”

“Precisely my own situation, my dear Harry!” George laughed.

“But this I know: there never was a better brother in the world, nor better people than the Lamberts.”

“Never a truer word was spoken!” George said, squeezing his brother’s hand.

“If I am miserable, it is not your fault, nor their fault, nor even mine, perhaps,” Harry went on, in a low voice. “It is fate, you see. It is having nothing to do. I must work, but how, George? That is the question.”

“We will wait to hear what our mother writes us. We will plan once we have her letter,” George said.

“George?” Harry said, quiet and a little alarmed. “Do you know, I do not think I could bear to go back to Virginia.”

“What! Are you in love with one of the lasses here?”

“I love them like my own sisters, every bit! The dearest, best girls that ever lived!” Harry said quickly. “That is not why. After all that happened, and you saved me, I do not want to go back to that life of hunting, duck-shooting, planting tobacco, playing whist, and sitting through three hour sermons, over and over again, for the rest of my days, George. What else is there for me there? What is there for me to do at all? That is what makes me miserable. You could make your way anywhere, you are so clever. But for a poor fool like me, what chance is there? Until I find something worthwhile to do, I will never be happy.”

“Have I not always said the same thing? Are you finally coming round to my way of thinking?”

“What way of thinking, George? You know I always agree with whatever you think, you know that!” Harry said, the dutiful younger twin.

“That Florac should have let that Indian take my scalp, my dear!”

Harry burst out in an angry exclamation, and then the two lapsed into quiet, friendly silence, puffing on their pipes side by side.

They lived together, following their own separate routines, bound only by their deep, abiding affection for each other. Harry would never so much as touch one of George’s books, and would sit as quiet as a mouse in their lodgings while his brother pored over his studies. Soon they moved out of the Court end of town, much to Madame de Bernstein’s disgust, who fussed and pshawed at their “low” new address. George had taken a great liking to Sir Hans Sloane’s new reading room and museum at Montagu House, so they rented cheerful lodgings in Southampton Row, Bloomsbury, overlooking the green fields that stretched all the way to Hampstead, behind the Duke of Bedford’s gardens. Soon after, Lord Wrotham’s family returned to their Mayfair house, and General Lambert, whose work kept him in London, moved his household into furnished apartments in Soho, scarcely a ten minute walk from the twins’ new home. Night after night, Harry found refuge in their little parlour.

George was there often, too. As their acquaintance ripened, he visited more and more frequently, finding the Lamberts’ company far more pleasant than his aunt’s gambling circle, or Sir Miles Warrington’s heavy port and overdone mutton, or the noisy chatter of the coffee houses. Since the Warrington twins and the Lambert ladies were all relative strangers to London’s pleasures, they began to explore them together, visiting Vauxhall and Ranelagh Gardens, Marylebone Pleasure Grounds, the Tower of London, and, of course, the playhouse. General Lambert loved nothing more than to give his girls every innocent amusement he could afford, and George, who was open-handed and generous by nature, loved nothing better than to treat the friends who had been so kind to his brother.

George Warrington loved the theatre with every fibre of his heart. He had never once seen a proper stage play in Virginia, and had only enjoyed a handful of performances in Quebec, when he had visited Canada. Now that he was in London, with both Drury Lane and Covent Garden operating at their full glory, he thought he could never see enough plays to sate his appetite. Everything he loved he wanted to share with his friends, so it was no surprise he was eager to arrange a party to the theatre. “Drury Lane, ladies?” he asked. “You can see Garrick himself playing Shakespeare there.” But much to his surprise, the ladies declared they wanted to see the famous new tragedy showing at Covent Garden, written by a celebrated new Scottish author.

A brilliant new star had blazed across London’s theatrical sky: the great Mr. John Home, a Scottish Presbyterian clergyman, had written a tragedy called Douglas that everyone agreed was more classic, more elegant than anything written since the days of ancient Greece. The wits in the coffee houses all asked why on earth Mr. Garrick had refused to stage such a masterpiece at Drury Lane. Everyone said that while Shakespeare was great (and had grown far more popular lately, ever since Monsieur Voltaire had dared to criticise him), his plays were full of rough barbarisms that would shock a polite modern audience. Mr. Home, by contrast, knew how to be graceful even in the midst of grief and passion, how to depict death not just as awful, but delicate and pathetic, and he never degraded the Tragic Muse by larding it with crude buffoonery and cheap puns, as the old Elizabethan playwright had done. No less a person than the poet Mr. Gray of Cambridge declared there had not been dramatic dialogue of such true, noble style for a hundred years, and back in Edinburgh, where the play had first been staged, the triumphant Scots had shouted out from the pit in their broad dialect, “Where’s Wully Shakespeare noo?”

“I should like to meet the man who could beat Willy Shakespeare!” the General laughed.

“Pure national prejudice, no doubt,” George said.

“Beat Shakespeare indeed!” Mrs. Lambert huffed.

“Pooh, pooh, Molly!” the General teased. “You have cried far more over Mr. Richardson’s novels than you ever did over Shakespeare. Very few women truly love reading Shakespeare, no matter how much they claim to.”

“Oh, papa!” all three of the Lambert ladies cried, throwing their three pairs of hands up in protest.

“Well, then, why do all three of you insist we go see Douglas? And you two young Tories—will you go watch a play written by a Whig Scots minister who was actually captured fighting for the rebels at Falkirk?”

“*Relicta non bene parmula*,” George quoted, the scholar.

“Nay, it was *relicta bene parmula*!” the General corrected. “It was the Highlanders who flung their targes down and cut our redcoats to pieces that day. If they had won all their battles like that, and the Young Pretender

The theatre curtain had barely fallen for the final time that night before our whole party bundled into hired coaches bound for Mr. Warrington’s London lodgings, where the two Virginian brothers had laid out a lavish, warmly welcomed supper spread. George was determined to play the host to his guests in the most generous style he could manage, and General Lambert and his wife accepted the invitation of the two bachelors with unfeigned pleasure, glad to return the kindness that had made their young new friends feel so at home in the city.

The full company sat down soon after: the General and Mrs. Lambert, their college-aged son Jack, their two bright blooming daughters Theo and Hetty, and Mr. Spencer of the Temple, the new friend George had struck up a conversation with over a dish of coffee only a few days prior. They laughed and dug into the landlady’s best cooking with hearty good cheer. I cannot swear to the exact order of every chair at the table, but somehow Miss Theo found herself settled snugly between the platter of roasted spring chickens and George Warrington, while Hetty divided her attention and her wit equally between a honey-glazed ham and Harry. Mrs. Lambert sat to George’s right hand, leaving only three spots to account for: the General, young Jack, and the Templar, which hardly leaves room for any great mystery over who sat where.

Mr. Spencer had been at the Drury Lane theatre on a prior night, and had even escorted George backstage to the green room once before, so the conversation turned naturally back to the tragedy they had all watched that evening, half the party swearing the piece was utterly sublime.
“As for what those two men at the far end are muttering,” Mrs. Lambert declared directly to Mr. Spencer, “do not believe a word of it. It is a perfectly lovely play, and my husband and Mr. George behaved shockingly badly through the whole of it.”
“We laughed at the wrong bits, when we ought to have been dabbing at our eyes with our handkerchiefs,” the General confessed, grinning. “That is the plain truth.”
“You made every person in the surrounding boxes turn around and hiss ‘Hush!’ at you! You set the pit calling out for silence in the boxes up there! I never saw such outrageous conduct in all my days, I was quite ready to hide my face for shame, Mr. Lambert!”
“Your mamma thought it was a tragedy, you see, and we thought it was a great bit of fun,” the General said. “George and I behaved perfectly well, did we not, Theo?”
“Not when I was looking your way, papa!” Theo shot back at once.
“Did anyone ever see such a saucy little baggage?” the General laughed.
“I did not speak until I was spoken to, you know, sir,” Theo added, with a modest little tilt of her chin. “I own I was very much moved by the play, and by Mrs. Woffington’s beauty and acting. My heart ached so for that poor mother who found her long-lost child only to lose him again. I am sorry if I ought not to have been sorry!”
“Women are not half so clever as men, you know, Theo,” Hetty called from her end of the table, throwing a sly look across at Harry. “Next time we go to the play, brother Jack, do pinch my arm when it is time to cry, and nudge my elbow when it is proper to laugh, will you?”
“I wish they had added the fight scene,” General Lambert put in. “The brawl between little Norval and the giant Norwegian – that would have been rare sport. Jack, you ought to write to Mr. Rich the manager and suggest it at once.”
“I have not seen that play, but I did see Slack and Broughton box at Marybone Gardens once,” Harry said gravely, and blinked in surprise when the whole table burst out laughing. “It would not take any giant at all to knock over that little fellow in the red boots,” he added. “For my part, I could throw him right over my shoulder.”
“Mr. Garrick is a small man in height, but there are moments when he looks every inch a giant,” Mr. Spencer said. “How grand he was in *Macbeth*, Mr. Warrington! That dagger scene was so awful it made your hair stand on end. You should have seen our host here, ladies! When I brought him back to the green room, I introduced him to both Mr. Garrick and Mrs. Pritchard, and the actress playing Lady Macbeth did him the very great honor of taking a pinch of rappee straight out of his snuff box.”
“Did the Thane of Cawdor’s lady sneeze after?” the General boomed out in a deep, tragic voice.
“She thanked Mr. Warrington in tones so hollow and dramatic that he stumbled back in shock, and must have spilled half the rest of his snuff over the green room floor – for Macbeth sneezed three times right after!”
“Macbeth! Macbeth! Macbeth!” the General chanted, thumping the table lightly. “And that great philosopher Mr. Johnson who was standing close by called out, ‘Mind your nose, Davy, lest your sneeze wake Duncan!’ – who, by the way, was leaning against the wall chatting with the three witches while they waited for their next scene.”
“Oh! I would give worlds to go behind the scenes at a play!” Theo cried out, her eyes sparkling.
“And see the stagehands yank the ropes, smell the thick tallow candle smoke, peer at the pasteboard gold crowns and tinsel jewels and the painted old actresses? No, do not look too close,” George said, the playful scepticism soft in his voice as he sipped his glass of hock. “You were cross with your papa and me, you know.”
“Nay, George!” the girl protested.
“Nay? I say yes! You were angry with us for laughing when you were all ready to weep. If I may speak for both of us, sir,” he added, bowing to the General, “I think we could not bring ourselves to grieve like the ladies, because we had already peeked behind the scenes of that kind of performance, as it were. We stood close enough to the tragic young hero to see half his grand speeches were just rant and tinsel; and that the pale grieving mother’s deathly pallor was nothing but white chalk, and all her great sobbing was just for show, done with her handkerchief. Own it now, Theo, you thought me quite unfeeling last night, did you not?”
“If you have already worked that out without me confessing, what use is there in me saying so?” Theo smiled back.
“Suppose I were to die,” George went on, “and you saw Harry grieving for me – that would be real affliction, a true tragedy, and you would grieve too. But you would not feel any of that real grief if you saw the undertaker parading around in his weepers and long black cloak, would you?”
“Indeed I would, sir!” Mrs. Lambert declared. “And so would any daughter of mine, I promise you.”
“Perhaps we would find weepers of our own, Mr. Warrington,” Theo said softly, and at that George’s cheeks flushed bright red, and hers did too, for both of them noticed Hetty’s bright curious eyes fixed on the pair of them from across the table.
“Our older writers understood very little of true pathos,” Mr. Spencer, the Temple wit, remarked.
“What of Sophocles and Antigone?” Jack Lambert called out.
“Faith, most of us wits about town trouble ourselves very little about him, unless an Oxford gentleman comes along to remind us he exists! I did not mean to go back further than Mr. Shakespeare, who I think we can all agree does not understand elegant pathos half as well as our modern playwrights. Has he ever written anything that comes close to Belvidera, or Monimia, or Jane Shore? Can you find any of his comic heroines with the elegance of Congreve?” The Templar held out his snuff box to the guests on either side of him.
“I wager Mr. Spencer has tried his own hand at a play, has he not?” someone asked.
“Many a gentleman of leisure has. I will own Mr. Garrick had a copy of one of mine a while back, though he saw fit to send it back to me.”
“And I confess I have four full acts of a tragedy tucked away in a box somewhere,” George added.
“I will wager it is better than any of those modern things,” Harry whispered to Hetty, his neighbour.
“Is it a tragedy or a comedy?” Mrs. Lambert asked.
“Oh, a tragedy, with at least two or three dreadful murders, I promise you,” George laughed.
“The tragedy! Fetch the tragedy at once, we shall read it aloud!” Mrs. Lambert called to Gumbo, George’s Black servant. Gumbo bowed low. “Tragedy? Yes, madam.”
“It is in the great cowskin trunk, Gumbo,” George said, deadpan. Gumbo bowed again, perfectly grave. “Yes, sir.”
“But that trunk is at our agent’s warehouse all the way in Bristol, stacked at the bottom under piles of linen, books, boots and trinkets,” George went on. “Gumbo would have to hire post-horses, ride all the way down there, and we could keep our supper going until he comes back the day after tomorrow.”
The ladies all groaned a comical disappointed “Oh!” and the General, more practical, spoke up. “Let us all be thankful for our escape. It is high time we made for home too. Our young gentlemen have treated us nobly tonight – let us drink a parting bumper to Madam Esmond Warrington of Castlewood, Virginia. Tell me, boys, what if you came home to find a tall handsome new stepfather waiting for you? Women of her years have been known to marry again, after all.”
“To Madam Esmond Warrington, my old schoolfellow!” Mrs. Lambert toasted. “I shall write to her straight away to tell her what a lovely supper her sons have given us. And Mr. George, I shall not breathe a word about how shockingly he behaved at the play last night!”
With that final toast, the whole company took their leave, the General’s coach waiting outside with a footman holding a blazing flambeau to light their path home.

After such a pleasant gathering, what could be more natural than George paying a call the very next day, to inquire after whether the Lamberts had made it home safe and slept well? Their coach could have taken the dark unfenced road behind Montague House towards Oxford Road, and been set upon by footpads in the fields. The ladies could have caught a chill after the excitement of the play, or tossed and turned all night. There was no excuse he needed to make to himself for turning his steps towards Dean Street, so he shut his books early at the Sloane Museum, and found he could not for the life of him recall a single word he had read that day.
What young man who has ever been in love does not recognise that giddy eagerness, that foolish hesitation, that huffing “psha, what nonsense” to himself as he fumbles with his gloves, and his heart hammers so hard he can hear it as he raps at the door of the house he is half afraid to enter? Every old man who ever was young remembers that throbbing in the chest, long after the years have worn the spring out of his steps. We old worn chargers turned out to grass, if we hear a trumpet blow over the hedge, we still kick up our heels and gallop a little way across the paddock, before we remember our old bones are not made for running any more.
We follow the footman up the stairs to the General’s apartments, and enter right behind George Esmond Warrington, who makes a very grand formal bow the moment he steps over the threshold. There is only one lady in the room, seated by the window – there is seldom much bright sunshine in Dean Street, but the light gilds Theo’s cheeks like a fresh bloom of rose, and her eyes shine as soft as violets. A hundred years ago, poets in the old magazines would have written acrostics about her, called her Lambertella, praised her neck as lily-white and her form as nymph-like, and printed the verses right between a map of Prague and a chart of the Delaware counties.
Theo blushes exactly like that rose when she sees him. Mrs. Lambert had insisted only an hour earlier that her daughter was pale and tired, and ought not to come out with the rest of the party that morning, when they went to pay their respects to Lord Wrotham’s family to thank them for the use of their house. Papa is at the Horse Guards, in wonderful spirits, for he expects a new military command soon, though Mrs. Lambert is in a constant fret lest he be ordered to serve overseas again.
“Harry and my brother Jack have gone off to visit my little brother at his school at the Chartreux,” Theo told him, her head bent over the little boy’s shirt she was busy hemming. “They say my two older brothers are bound for the clergy, I think. Harry comes over almost every day now,” she added, looking up at him. “Poor fellow, he likes our company far better than the fine society folks who do not care for him now that he is no longer rich and fashionable himself. Why have you not set up for the ton yourself, Mr. Warrington? You never frequent the chocolate houses or the racecourses.”
“Has Harry gotten so much good out of all those haunts and grand friends that I ought to go and follow his example?”
“You might at least visit Sir Miles Warrington, your uncle – I am sure his doors are wide open to receive you. Her ladyship called on us this morning in her chair, and did nothing but sing your praises! She declares you are certain to rise fast in the world now. Says his Royal Highness the Duke spoke very highly of you at court. When you are a great man, will you forget all of us, Mr. Warrington?”
“Yes, when I am a great man I will, Miss Lambert.”
“Well then, Mr. George –”
“Mr. George? When papa and mamma are not even in the room, you surely do not need to stand on ceremony with a ‘mister’,” Theo said, looking out the window, a little flustered. “What have you been up to all day? Reading books, or writing more of your tragedy? Is it going to be the kind that makes us cry, the kind we like, or just the scary full of murders kind you favour?”
“There is plenty of killing, I fear, but very little of the soft pathos. I have not spent much time around women, you see. I am told I have a sharp, sarcastic way about me that displeases most of them.”
“Perhaps you never much cared to try to please them?” Theo said, blushing.
“I displeased you last night, did I not?”
“Yes, but it was not really displeasure. Afterwards, I thought you and papa were quite right.”
“Did you think about me at all when we went our separate ways last night, Theo?”
“Yes, George – that is, Mr. – well, George! I thought you were right about the play, that all the great grief we were weeping over was nothing but show and affectation. I wonder if it is a blessing or a curse to be able to see the tricks behind the show so clearly? Hetty and I agreed we would be far more careful from now on about how we let ourselves get swept up by staged tragedies. So be careful when yours is finished! What is its name?”
“It has not been christened yet. Will you be its godmother? The name of the main character is –”
But just at that very moment, Mrs. Lambert and Hetty walked in the door from their walk, and Mrs. Lambert broke into a flutter of exclamations, saying she never expected to see Mr. Warrington that day – well, that she had half thought he might come, that it was so very good of him to call, and the play and the supper had all been perfectly charming, only Theo had a little headache that morning.
“I am sure it is all better now, mamma,” Hetty said, with a little grin.
“Indeed it was never anything to fuss over,” Theo added, tossing her head.
Then they got to talking about Harry, and how low he had been of late. He needed something to occupy him, some purpose. He hung around the Military Coffee-House from dawn to dusk, poring over every map of Frederick the Great’s campaigns he could get his hands on. It was cruel to keep him lingering in London after he had squandered his own fortune, living off his brother. He never complained, but everyone could see how ashamed he was of his old useless life, and how he avoided all his former rakish haunts and companions. Only the other day, walking past the guard post at St James’s with Jack Lambert, he had leaned over and said, “Why may I not be a soldier too? I am as tall as that sentry over there, and I can shoot a fowling-piece as well as any man alive. But I cannot earn sixpence a day. I wasted all my own money, and now I am eating half my brother’s bread. He is the best of brothers, but that makes it all the more shameful for me to live on him. Do not tell him I said that, Jack Lambert.”
