“And my boy Jack promised he would not breathe a word,” Mrs. Lambert said. The girls had stepped out of the room a few minutes before she spoke, to give the two of them privacy. George told her he had already written home to his mother, that half his own patrimony was at Harry’s disposal, and the other half too if he needed it, to buy an army commission, or fund any project that might give him occupation and advancement.
“He has the best brother in the world, that is for certain. Let us hope good times come for him soon,” Mrs. Lambert sighed.
“Good things come to those who wait, madam,” George said softly.
“Ah, George! My Theo is – well, never mind what Theo is, George Warrington!” the lady cried, her eyes brimming over with happy tears. “Foolish of me, I know, I am going to make a silly gaby of myself, just as I did at the tragedy last night.”
George had been turning over a clever little private plan in his head for weeks now, one he thought would secure Harry’s future. After he had been presented to his Royal Highness the Duke of Cumberland at Kensington Palace, General Lambert and several other friends had told him the Duke had asked after him specifically, and wondered why the young Virginian did not come to his public levee. It would have

Every loyal Briton of spirit, we may safely say, burns with righteous indignation when they hear the tale of George Warrington’s conduct towards that gallant, gracious Prince—beloved son of the best of monarchs, and Captain-General of all His Majesty’s armies. What inestimable favour the young man spurned! What golden path to rank and distinction he cast underfoot!

Will Esmond, whose coarse tongue was never short of the most blistering oaths, poured out his strongest curses on his cousin’s head, crowing with delight that the accursed young Virginian Mohock was busy cutting his own throat. His cousin Castlewood merely shrugged and drawled that a savage gentleman had every right to scalp himself if he pleased; then added, with a touch of reluctant charity, that no doubt George had heard more than enough of war-whoops and slaughter in Braddock’s disastrous campaign, and had no stomach left for fighting.

Will rejoiced that the younger Warrington brother had long since gone to the dogs, and was chuffed to see the elder following close on his heels. The next time he met George, he swore, he would tell him exactly what every man of sense in London thought of his craven folly.
“If you dare to insult George, you had best make very sure his brother Harry is out of earshot first!” Lady Maria snapped— a retort that earned her a fresh volley of oaths from Will, directed at both the Warrington twins.
“Tut, tut, tut!” my Lord Castlewood cut in, flapping a languid hand. “No more of this squabbling. We cannot all be warriors in the family, after all.”
“I never heard your lordship lay any claim to the title!” Maria shot back.
“Never, my dear, quite the contrary!” he smiled. “Will is our household champion, and one fighting fool is more than enough for the house. I dare say the two Mohocks follow the same rule: George is the bookish one, and Harry is the man born for battle. What a pity it was, Will, that when you were set on picking a quarrel, you did not have George in your grip instead of the other brother!”
“Your lordship’s hand is famous enough—at piquet,” Will’s mother put in dryly.
“It is a very pretty hand,” my lord agreed, holding up his slim fingers to admire them with a simper. “My glove was the exact size of my Lord Hervey’s, if you will credit it. Yes, as you say, mine is far fitter for cards than for war. Yours, my Lady Castlewood, is deuced deft with a scandal too. How I bless the day you bestowed that hand on my lamented father!” He was never loath to indulge in this cut and thrust of sarcasm, his cool head letting him outwit every last member of his family with ease.

When Madame de Bernstein heard of her nephew’s blunder, she flew into a towering rage, stormed through her household scolding every servant within earshot, and would have given George a piece of her mind too—only she found she no longer had the fire of her younger days. What was more, she had grown a little afraid of her steady, quiet nephew, and treated him with a deference she never showed anyone else.
“You will never make your fortune at court now, nephew!” she groaned, when George came to wait on her soon after the incident.
“It was never my wish to do so, madam,” George replied, with a quiet, stately courtesy.
“Your wish was to help Harry? You might have done him a world of good, years from now, if you had accepted the Duke’s offer. Princes do not love to have their favours thrown back in their faces, and I do not wonder his Royal Highness was offended.”
“General Lambert said the very same thing,” George admitted, turning a little red. “I see now I was in the wrong. But you must remember, I had never stepped inside a court before, and I was never likely to shine there.”
“Very likely not, my good nephew,” the old lady said, taking a pinch of snuff. “And what then?”
“I never craved that sort of glory. I can be perfectly happy without it. When his Royal Highness spoke to me—most kindly, I own—all I could think was that I should make a very poor soldier, and Harry would make an excellent one. He has a hundred qualities for the profession I lack entirely, and would serve his commanding officer a thousand times better than I ever could. Suppose the Duke was in battle, and his horse was shot, as my poor colonel’s was on our Virginian frontier: would he not fare far better with a beast bold and strong enough to carry him anywhere, than one too faint-hearted to bear his weight?”
“Faith, his Royal Highness’s charger must be a very strong one, my dear!” the Baroness chuckled.
“Expende Hannibalem,” George muttered with a shrug. “Our Hannibal weighs no trifling amount.”
“I do not follow you and your Hannibal, sir,” she said.
“When Mr. Wolfe and General Lambert remonstrated with me just as you have done, madam,” George laughed, “I gave them the very same defence. I told them I had offered the Prince the best soldier in our family, and they both allowed my absurd blunder had at least some small excuse. Who knows but they may set me right with his Royal Highness? The little taste of battle I saw was enough to show me my genius never runs that way. We all went to see that new Scottish play everyone is raving about the other night, and when young Norval declared he ached to follow some warlike lord to the field, I thought to myself: that is my Harry to the life—except Harry never brags. He is pining for a red coat so badly he will soon enlist for a shilling if we do not watch him. He keeps a map of Germany spread out on his table everywhere he goes, and follows every move the King of Prussia makes. He fears neither man nor devil. As for me, I love my books and my quiet best, and would far rather read of battles in Homer or Lucan than fight them.”
“Then what ever made you turn soldier at all, my dear? Why did you not send Harry with Braddock, instead of going yourself?”
“My mother loved her younger son best,” George said, his face darkening a little. “Besides, with the enemy marching on our borders, it was my duty, as head of the family, to go on campaign. If I had been a Scotsman twelve years ago, I should have been—”
“Hush, sir!” the old lady cut in, feigning fury while her face lit up with perfect pleasure.

George’s explanation might appease Madame de Bernstein, whose principles we fear were never particularly strict, but to the loyal, rigid hearts of Sir Miles Warrington and his lady, the young man’s conduct was a severe shock indeed.
“I should have thought,” Lady Warrington huffed, “from my sister Esmond Warrington’s letters, that my brother’s widow was a woman of sound sense, and had raised her sons to behave as proper gentlemen should. But what, Sir Miles, what, my dear Thomas Claypool, are we to make of an education that has ended in such a lamentable failure for both boys?”
“The elder seems to know a power of Latin, though, and speaks French and German too,” Mr. Claypool put in. “I heard him chatting with the Hanover Envoy at the Baroness’s rout last week. He jabbered French as easy as you please, and when he stumbled over High Dutch, the pair switched to Latin and talked away so fast the whole room stared at them.”
“It is not languages we care about, it is principles, Thomas Claypool!” the virtuous matron exclaimed. “What sort of principles can Mr. Warrington have, when he can reject an offer made him by his own Prince? If he can speak High Dutch, all the more reason he should have accepted his Royal Highness’s condescension and made himself useful in the campaign! Look at our son, look at little Miles!”
“Hold up thy head, Miley, my boy!” Sir Miles prodded his son.
“I trust, Sir Miles, that as a member of the House of Commons, and an English gentleman, you will wait on his Royal Highness’s levee tomorrow, and tell him plainly that if such an offer had been made to us for that child, we would have accepted it at once—though our boy is barely ten years old!”
“Faith, Miley, thou wouldst make a fine little drummer boy, wouldst thou not?” Sir Miles laughed. “Wouldst like to be a little soldier, Miley?”
“Anything, sir, anything! A Warrington ought to be ready at any moment to be cut to pieces for his sovereign!” the matron cried, pointing dramatically at the boy—who, as soon as he grasped what his mother was proposing, set up such a loud, wailing roar that he had to be carried off kicking by his nurse Screwby.

True to his wife’s orders, Sir Miles attended the Prince’s levee the next day, and poured out such a fulsome declaration of his loyalty and devotion that the Prince deigned to smile and reply: “No one ever doubted that Sir Miles Warrington would refuse any place offered to him.” It was a gracious compliment indeed, and Lady Warrington repeated it to every acquaintance she met for months, as proof of how implicitly the royal family trusted the loyalty of the Warrington line.

Accordingly, when the worthy couple next saw George, they greeted him with a ghastly, pitying kindness of the sort that one reserves for friends and relatives who have just committed some fatal public blunder: when they have lost a lawsuit, or walked in on a whole room full of people abusing them, or had their banker go bankrupt, or been forced to appear in the commercial pages of the London Gazette under the list of unfortunate debtors. Who does not know that faint, commiserating smile? Whose dear relations have not deplored him as good as dead, while he is still very much alive? If you have never scraped through such a scrape, if you never sowed a handful of wild oats, if you have always been perfectly fortunate, perfectly good, perfectly careful, and never let an imprudent word slip your lips—then you are a stuffy old wiseacre who would never waste your time on an idle novel, and this tale was never written for you.

It was hardly just of Sir Miles to turn on George for rejecting the Prince’s offer, for he had heartily approved of George’s plan to avoid a military career entirely. It was for that very purpose that Madam Esmond had written to him from Virginia: George had announced his intention of entering the Temple to study the law, and qualify himself for the magisterial and public duties that would fall to him in time as head of his family. No one applauded the resolution more than Sir Miles, who introduced George to a leading barrister of good reputation, under whose guidance the young man settled down to read at a leisurely, steady pace. Madam Esmond wrote back from Virginia to voice her full approval, agreeing wholeheartedly that the British Constitution was the envy of the whole world, and the proper object of every English gentleman’s study. The only part of the plan she objected to was the idea that George would have to sit down to dinner in the Temple’s great hall, carving shoulder of mutton and drinking small beer out of tin pannikins, side by side with rough, shabbily dressed students who wore gowns no better than a parish clerk’s.

Harry shared every bit of that indignation. Anything was good enough for him, he declared: he was a younger son, and prepared to rough it anywhere. But George, togged out in a student’s gown, eating off dirty pewter alongside three nobodies of no family or fortune! Harry could not bear the thought of his brother condescending so far, and fretted that George should never sit anywhere but at the highest table of the hall. He was even disappointed that a plan his mother hinted at in her letters was not feasible: to petition the Master of the Temple, and inform him that Mr. George Warrington was a gentleman of noble birth and vast property in the Virginia colonies, and ought only to be seated alongside the very best company in the hall. When he laid this proposal before their new coffee-house friend Mr. Spencer, the man burst into such roars of laughter that he could barely breathe; no record in the Warrington papers survives of any application ever being made to the Master on that absurd subject.

Alongside his beloved literary and historical studies, George pored over English law, attended the courts at Westminster where he heard great orators like Henley, Pratt, and Murray hold forth, and haunted the public galleries of the two Houses of Parliament, that great school of eloquence and patriotism. Gradually he made the acquaintance of many members of Parliament and distinguished barristers, who came to know him and speak of him as a young man of excellent parts and gentle breeding. Their kind reports were so complimentary that his good uncle’s heart softened towards him, and his cousins Dora and Flora began to smile on him again.

This full reconciliation dated from the news that his Royal Highness the Duke of Cumberland had been defeated by the French at the battle of Hastenbeck, and had signed the notorious convention of Kloster-Zeven, a capitulation King George II flatly refused to ratify. As all the world knows, the Prince flung down his commission in disgrace, laid aside the commander’s baton (which he had never wielded with much luck or skill, it must be said), and never again appeared at the head of an army, or in public life. He would not suffer a single word of complaint against his father and sovereign to pass his lips, but as he retired with his honour smarting, and no longer had any interest or authority, or places to dole out to favourites, Sir Miles’s anger against his nephew faded right along with his respect for the disgraced Prince.

One day, as George and Harry were walking through St. James’s Park with their friend General Lambert, they came across the Prince in plain civilian clothes, no star pinned to his coat, and bowed low. The Prince stopped to speak to them.
He asked Lambert how he liked serving under my Lord Ligonier, his new commanding officer at the Horse Guards, and how he found his new duties. Then, with that remarkable memory for faces that runs in the royal family, he turned to George.
“You did well, sir, not to come with me when I asked you last spring.”
“I was sorry then, sir,” George replied, bowing very low. “And I am far sorrier now.”
“Thank you, sir,” the Prince said, touched his hat, and walked away.

Harry wrote the whole story down in a letter to his mother in Virginia, and the anecdote made such an impression on Madam Esmond Warrington that she repeated it hundreds of times over the rest of her life, until every last one of her friends and acquaintances knew the tale by heart, and no doubt grew heartily tired of hearing it.

The three friends walked on through the park, heading towards the Strand where they had business to attend to. Lambert pointed up at the great stone lion perched on the roof of the Earl of Northumberland’s new house at Charing Cross.
“Harry Warrington!” he called out. “Your brother there is just like that lion.”
“Because he is as brave as one!” Harry grinned at once.
“Because I respect virgins?” George laughed.
“Because he is a stupid old lion,” Lambert went on, chuckling. “He turns his back on the East, and faces the setting sun. What earthly good do you think you will get by being polite to a man in utter, hopeless disgrace? Your uncle will be more angry with you than ever—and so am I, sir.” But his face was crinkled with his usual waggish grin, and he did not look the least bit angry.

If Harry Warrington harboured even a spark of passion for all things military, the roar of war echoing across 1750s Europe, and the endless din of campaign gossip in every London drawing room and coffee house he frequented, was more than enough to fan that spark into a roaring blaze. Our own gracious Hanoverian monarch might have met defeat on the continent, but that Protestant hero, the King of Prussia, was filling every corner of the known world with the thunder of his astonishing victories—for which I count myself singularly lucky that poor Harry played no part. Were he to have ridden to battle beside Frederick, this veracious little biography of mine would have been forced to describe great slaughters already claimed by far greater storytellers. I count it a mercy that Harry Warrington was not at Rossbach, that famous Gunpowder Fete-day on the 5th of November 1757, nor at the dreadful, blood-soaked field of Leuthen a month later. Those prodigious actions are destined for far grander volumes, which all the world—myself included—waits with bated breath to behold.

Would you have my humble story compete with that epic? Could my jaunty yellow park phaeton jostle for space against that grim, thundering war chariot? Could my meek little jog-trot Pegasus hope to stand against that foaming, fiery-eyed steed of battle? Dear, kind reader, with whom I love to step aside and chat from time to time, even as our characters go about their business in the dress and speech of a hundred years past—believe me, it is a blessing for both of us that Harry never followed the King of the Borussians as he once ached to do. I should hate for you to draw odious comparisons between my quiet little tale and the masterwork Carlyle is soon to paint of those wars.

Harry not only failed to join the Prussian ranks, he chafed and pined miserably at being kept from them. The truth is, he fell into a sullen, useless rut. He hung about every military coffee house in the city, and cared to read nothing but the daily papers. He was never a man of literary tastes; he thought popular novels ridiculous, and could not for the life of him understand what made fine ladies cry their eyes out over Mr. Richardson’s tales of sentiment. He laughed loud and hearty, to be sure, but always a beat or two after the joke had landed. And why should every gentleman be expected to turn a couplet, or pore over folios? Do we think less of our friends who never penned a line of verse in their lives? Ruined, forced into idleness, dependent on his brother for every shilling, falling asleep the second he opened any book not full of battle dispatches, with no worthy work for his great strong hands to do—what a miracle it is that he did not stumble into far worse mischief! Think of Achilles, spirited away by his mother to a faraway court to keep him out of harm’s way, left to idle his days among a house full of women spinning at their distaffs: look what came of that, when Pyrrhus was born. A hot-blooded, strong young Achilles is not meant to be led around by women’s apron strings, fawning over coffee cups and dawdling by the spinning wheel. When he cannot fight, depend on it, he will soon stumble into far greater trouble.

The two elder Misses Lambert, and their mother, with whom Harry spent most of his time, lavished on him that soft, tireless, tender kindness that only women—and very few of them at that—know how to give. Who cheers the grieving, consoles the troubled, soothes the wrathful? Who doubles your joy in times of happiness, rejoices unfeignedly in your prosperity, and stands by you against the whole world in your disgrace, dressing the rankling wounds Fortune dealt you with gentle unguents and warm compresses? Who but woman, I ask you? If you, worn and battered by Fate’s blows, count one or two of these sweet physicians among your friends, return thanks to the gods for that greatest of consolations. What gentleman is not a little bit Prometheus? Who has not his rock, his unbreakable chains, and his liver gnawed raw by trouble? But the sea nymphs come—gentle, sympathetic, unshaken: they kiss our writhing feet, they moisten our parched lips with their tears, they do their blessed utmost to console us Titans, and never turn their backs on us after our fall.

Mrs. Lambert and Theo were full of nothing but pity for Harry, but Hetty’s heart seemed curiously hard, almost savage, towards him. She chafed at his unremarkable, idle state. The whole world was in arms, and could he not carry a musket? It was harvest time for glory, with hundreds of thousands of reapers out swinging their flashing sickles—could he not lift his own, and cut down at least one small sheaf of renown?

“Whatever has gotten into that little thing, to be so sharp with him?” Mr. Lambert laughed one evening, after Hetty had spent an hour firing tiny stinging shots at Harry, who sat uncomplaining on their drawing room sofa.

“Her behaviour is perfectly abominable!” cried Mrs. Lambert. “She deserves to be sent straight to bed and whipped.”

“Perhaps, mother, she cares for him more than any of the rest of us do,” Theo said softly. “That’s why she’s angry. If I were fond of someone, I would want to admire and respect him always—think everything he did was right, and believe my gentleman better than every other man alive in the world.”

“The truth is, my dear,” Mrs. Lambert smiled, “that your father is so much better than all the rest of the world, he has spoiled us all. Did you ever see anyone to compare with him?”

“Very few indeed,” Theo admitted, blushing.

“Very few. Who is as even-tempered?”

“Nobody, mamma, I think.”

“Or as brave?”

“Well, I’m sure Mr. Wolfe, or Harry, or Mr. George are very brave.”

“Or as learned and witty?”

“Oh, Mr. George is wonderfully learned, and witty too, in his way,” Theo said eagerly. “And his manners are so fine—you must admit that. Madame de Bernstein, who has seen all the world, says so too. He has this lofty, noble way about him I never see in other men. And even though he is so fond of satire, he only ever directs it at mean, petty people and acts. No gentleman could have a tenderer heart. Just yesterday, after he’d been speaking so sharply about greedy people, I looked out the window and saw him stop to buy a whole crowd of ragged children apples from the corner stall. The day before that, he brought me a new copy of Moliere, and stopped on the steps to give a whole handful of coins to a beggar. And he reads French so beautifully! Though I do agree with him about Tartuffe: clever and lively as the play is, it seems such a waste to make a low hypocrite the main character of a great work. He said Iago is just as terrible a villain, but he is not the lead of *Othello*—that honour goes to the noble Othello, undone by his own great, trusting nature. And the verses he read us—oh, I daren’t repeat them properly!”

“But you know them by heart, my dear?” Mrs. Lambert teased.

Theo blushed brighter. “Oh yes, mamma! I know them by—nonsense!”

I do believe there were soft kisses, a few palpitations, and a very flustered Miss Theo fleeing the room then, cheeks flushed as a rose at midsummer. Why had she stumbled over her words? Because her mother was looking at her so very knowingly. And why did she always peer out the window looking for George when he was due to call? Why do cheeks blush? Why do roses bloom? Old Time still flies by, carrying spring and buds, summer and bloom, autumn and seed, and winter when the bare treetops are shivering under snow.

Whenever George knocked at the door, Theo would come tripping down the stairs minutes later, heart fluttering, cheeks flushed like a fresh-picked nosegay made just in his honour. And if Harry was the one at the door? She would stay in her own room, working at her embroidery or pretending to read, and send Hetty down to greet him, or one of her little brothers if they were home from school. Her eyes were sharp enough to tell the difference between Harry’s golden curls and George’s dark locks, even from halfway across the street—no one else could tell the twins apart half the time, but Theo never once mistook one for the other. And Hetty? She was never pert, never sharp, never rude, when the dark-haired Mr. Warrington walked into the drawing room.

The Warringtons could come and go to the Lamberts’ house as they pleased, and stay as long as they liked. One afternoon, Harry sprawled on the drawing room couch looking more idle and dejected than usual, when who but Hetty came tripping down the stairs to keep him company. It was a most curious little arrangement, that the sisters would never, ever admit to any collusion: Harry called, Hetty answered. George arrived, Theo came down. It was as natural as breathing, no scheming needed.

“Pray tell me, sir,” Hetty said, dropping into a chair opposite him, “what makes your honour look so very glum this morning?”

“Ah, Hetty!” he sighed. “I’ve nothing at all to do but look glum. I remember when we were boys, and I was the laziest scapegrace alive, I was always begging my tutor for a holiday. I’d spend the whole day swinging on a gate, or skipping stones across the pond, and those empty do-nothing days were always the most melancholy of all. Now what have I got to fill my time from dawn till dark?”

“Breakfast, a walk—dinner, another walk—tea, supper, and a pipe of your fine Virginia tobacco, I suppose,” Hetty said, tossing her head.

“Only the other night, I walked Charley back to his school at the Chartreux,” Harry went on, “and I almost turned to the master and said, ‘Sir, teach me. That boy at thirteen knows more Latin and Greek than I do, ten years his elder. I’ve nothing to do all day—why not let me go back to my books, make up for all that idleness when I was a lad?’ Why are you laughing at me, Hetty?”

“I can just picture you standing at the front of the class waiting for the master to call on you!” she giggled.

“I’d never be top of any class,” Harry said humbly. “George could be top of any class in the world, but I’m no scholar. I neglected all my studies when I was young, and I never had a head for books. Our tutors hardly ever got to cane us back home at Virginia, but if they’d laid the strap on me more, it might have done me a world of good.”

Hetty drummed her little foot on the floor, and looked at the big, strong, melancholy young man slouched across the couch. “Upon my word, it might do you a world of good even now!” she nearly said out loud. “Does Charley’s stories of school canings make you long to go back to the classroom, pray?” she asked instead.

“His stories just made me see how much time I wasted when I should have been working,” Harry said simply. “I’ve no gift for books. So what am I good for? To spend my patrimony the second I step off the boat in London? Lounge around coffee houses and racecourses? Gallop after fox hounds back home? I’m good for nothing at all.”

“What? A great brave strong fellow like you, good for nothing?” Hetty cried. “I’d never admit I was useless to any woman, not if I was twice as idle as you!”

“What am I supposed to do? I’ve written to ask my mother for leave to join the army, and Madam Esmond never writes back. It’s the only thing I’m fit for. I’ve no money left to buy a commission. I spent every penny of my own, and so much of George’s already— I can’t, I won’t, ask him for more. If only my mother would send me off to fight, you know I’d jump at the chance.”

“Pshaw! A gentleman of spirit doesn’t wait for a woman to buckle his sword on for him or clean his musket for him!” Hetty huffed. “Didn’t Papa tell us about that young courtier yesterday? Sir John Armytage—”

“Sir John Armytage? I knew him well at White’s, back when I was going to the clubs. Fine noble young man, has a great estate up north.”

“And he’s engaged to the famous beauty Miss Howe, Lord Howe’s sister! But I suppose that’s no obstacle to a man who wants glory?”

“An obstacle to what?” Harry blinked, confused.

“To glory!” Hetty declared. “No woman of spirit would say ‘stay’ to her lover, no matter how much she adored him, the second his country says ‘go.’ Sir John volunteered for that new expedition being readied at court, and when the King asked him when he would be ready to sail, he said ‘Tomorrow, please your Majesty.’ The King said that was a proper soldier’s answer. Even Papa is longing to go, though he has Mamma and all us brats at home. Oh, dear! Why wasn’t I born a man? Both my brothers are going into the Church, but I know I would have made a famous little soldier!” She strode around the room as she spoke, chin held high, looking as bold and fierce as Joan of Arc herself.

Harry watched her with soft, tender admiration. “I think I’d hate to see a musket slung over that tiny shoulder of yours, or a scar on that pretty face, Hetty.”

“Wounds? Who fears wounds?” the little maid cried. “Muskets? If I could carry one, I’d use it. You all think women are only good for making puddings and stitching samplers. Why wasn’t I a man, I say? George was reading us out of Tasso yesterday—look, here’s the book, we left a mark at the verse that made me think it was written just for me.”

“Marked in the book?” Harry said dutifully, leaning forward.

“Yes! It’s about a woman furious that her brother refuses to go to war, and she says:
‘Alas! why did not Heaven these members frail
With lively force and vigour strengthen, so
That I this silken gown and slender veil
Might for a breastplate and a helm forgo;
Then should not heat, nor cold, nor rain, nor hail,
Nor storms that fall, nor blust’ring winds that blow,
Withhold me; but I would, both day and night,
In pitched field or private combat, fight—’
Fight? Yes, that I would! Why are both Papa’s boys set to be parsons? One of his children should be a soldier!”

Harry laughed a gentle, kind laugh, looking down at her small frame. He could not imagine ever lifting a hand to hurt such a tiny, fierce little warrior. “Look here,” he said, holding out his own thick finger, “this finger is almost as big around as your whole arm. How do you think you’d stand against a great big soldier? But I’d love to see any scoundrel dare lay a hand on you. I should just like to catch some rogue Frenchman daring to be rude to Miss Hester Lambert!” He started pacing up and down the room himself, chafing at the very thought of anyone hurting her.

It was this quiet, unshakable courage of his that had won Hetty’s heart, the strength she had always dreamed of in a man. She was no virago, no fierce Amazon—else by the rules of nature and contrast she would have fallen for some soft, bookish young gentleman who could play the flute. Everyone knows the old truth: great strong men have an affinity for tiny tender women, and little sharp-witted women are drawn to big honest strong men, and your burliest war heroes are almost always the ones who end up happily henpecked. It was easy to see where this pair would end up, if they kept on this path.

For a while, Harry barely felt Hetty’s little stinging jabs, letting her shoot them off without bothering to pluck the tiny arrows out of his skin. She meant to rouse him to action, of course, but his simple, generous heart was too big to pick up on small hints. She meant to shame him by saying that even a weak woman would don a breastplate and fight—but Harry either melted at the thought of her in danger, or laughed soft and warm.

“Pray what is the use of that great strong hand of yours, if you only use it to hold a skein of silk for my mother?” Hetty went on. “What good is all that strength in a drawing room? No one’s asking you to throw a man out the window, Harry! A great strong man, indeed! You could find a stronger man than you wrestling at Bartholomew Fair any day. James Wolfe isn’t a strong man at all. He looks pale and sickly, was coughing the whole time he visited last month, as if he’d just seen a ghost.”

“I never could understand why anyone would be frightened of a ghost,” Harry said.

“Pray have you ever seen one, sir?” Hetty teased.

“No. Once back home when we were boys, I thought I did—but it was only old Nathan the butler wandering around in his nightgown. I wasn’t scared even when I thought he was a ghost. There’s no such things. Nurses just tell a pack of lies about them.” Harry said gravely. “George was a little frightened, but he’s different from me. Our mother is the boldest woman you ever met, but she screams at the sight of a mouse—can’t help it, it’s just her nature. So maybe George can’t bear ghosts, and I don’t mind them.”

“George always says you’d make a far better soldier than he ever would.”

“So I think I would, if anyone had ever let me try. But he can do a thousand things better than me, or any other man alive. Why didn’t he let me volunteer on Braddock’s expedition? I could have got knocked on the head then, and I’d be just as useless as I am now—only I wouldn’t have ruined myself, and made people point at me and say I disgraced the Warrington name. Why

George Warrington never allowed his legal studies to cramp his small pleasures, disrupt his easy comfort, or put his precious health at risk. In her letters, Madam Esmond had reminded him that while he might wear a student’s gown and sit to hall-commons among a crowd of unnamed strangers, he bore an old, distinguished name he was bound to uphold, and could take equal rank with any gentleman of quality at home or across the Atlantic. She bade him study as a gentleman, not a drudging professional hack, and George obeyed her well enough. He never ranked among the law’s rank-and-file pupils, but served rather as a volunteer in her retinue, much like other young men of independent fortune we have encountered before.

A hundred years prior, the law was far less exacting than it is today: it granted its disciples far more leisure, far more merrymaking over punch, far more hours lingering in coffee-houses and away from dreary chambers, than the modern jealous mistress allows her votaries, who are scarcely left time for amusement, instruction, sleep, or a decent dinner. Even then, though, she demanded a good deal of a man’s attention. We are told Murray might have made a name as a second Ovid, but he chose instead to become Lord Chief Justice, wrapping himself in ermine rather than poet’s laurel. Doubtless George Warrington might have risen to a peerage and the Woolsack himself, had he studied long and relentlessly, had he mastered the arts of a dexterous courtier and made himself a favourite of every petty attorney. In short, he might have reached that height had he been anyone other than himself. He treated Themis with decent respect and punctuality, but he loved letters far more than law: the black-letter pages of Chaucer were infinitely sweeter to him than the dense, Gothic tomes of Hale and Coke.

In those quaint old times, letters were deeply cherished, and authors were treated as living authorities. Gentlemen would cite Virgil or Lucan in open court or on the floor of the House of Commons, debating what Statius, Juvenal, not to mention Tully or Tacitus, had said on some point of law or politics. Those good old heathens’ reign is long over now: the worship of Jupiter and Juno is no more out of fashion than the study of Pagan poetry and ethics. We live in an age of economists and calculators, and Tooke’s Pantheon sits deserted, a ridiculous relic of the past. Now and then, a Stanley might sacrifice a kid to the Olympians, a Gladstone might weave them a wreath, a Lytton might burn a little incense in their honour—but what do the crowds of Lambeth, Birmingham, or Tower Hamlets care for those ancient rites and forgotten divinities? Who on earth are the Muses, and what use is all that Greek and Latin rubbish? Where is Helicon, and who cares? Who was Thalia, pray, and how many letters are in her name? Is Melpomene pronounced in three syllables or four? And do you know whose design I stole for that little figure of Tragedy that adorns the initial G at the head of this chapter?

It has been noted before how Mr. George whiled away the long idle hours of his youth at home, and during his long imprisonment in the French fort on the banks of the Monongahela, by paying court to Melpomene, the Tragic Muse. The fruit of their union was a full five-act tragedy, omitted from Bell’s Theatre collections though I dare say it is no worse than half the plays printed in those volumes. Most young literary men pay their first homage to Tragedy first, just as they fall in love with women far older and grander than themselves. Let every candid reader who ever dabbled in writing own the truth: his earliest ambition reached the very highest peaks. In his green unknowing youth, he aimed only at tragedy and epic, and no prize but the very greatest was fit for his hand. Only in riper years did he scale back his pretensions, and decide that translating an ode of Horace, or adapting a song of Waller or Prior into decent alcaics or sapphics, was the full extent of his small talents.

Once settled in London, George attended performances at both patent playhouses, haunted the theatrical coffee-houses to hear the regular critics hold forth, and could be found loitering in the Bedford between the acts, or supping at the Cecil Tavern with wits and actors long after the curtain fell. Gradually he made the acquaintance of every well-known player and popular playwright of the day. The gruff, tough old Macklin, the frolicsome Foote, the vivacious Hippisley, and the sparkling, incomparable Mr. Garrick himself, were all regular faces at those supper tables. George won immense popularity in these circles for his wit, his modesty, and the widely circulated rumour of his large independent fortune: actors would happily share a bowl of punch with him, and critics would sup at his expense with the greatest affability. Many a young man has dreamed of such intimacy with celebrated authors and performers: to hob and nob face to face with the actor who plays Bobadil or Henry the Fifth, to take a pinch of snuff straight from Aristarchus the critic’s own box, to hand Juliet to her coach, or Monimia to her sedan chair—no wonder George Warrington fell so deeply in love with the theatre. It was all the more delightful for being forbidden fruit at home, where Madam Esmond only half approved of playhouses and their raucous denizens. He threw more than one lavish feast for the players, and it was whispered that more than one celebrated genius had condescended to borrow small sums from him.

As he polished his tragic masterpiece, adding new flourishes and tightening scenes, it is no surprise he sought the advice of his theatrical acquaintances, who plied him with no end of lavish praise and friendly counsel. His new Temple acquaintance Mr. Spencer hosted a breakfast in his Fig Tree Court chambers, where George read large portions of his play aloud to a room of guests, who all agreed it held uncommon merit. Even the learned Mr. Johnson, who had been invited as a special guest, was good enough to declare the piece showed remarkable talent. To be sure, he noted, it violated all the classical unities—but many great authors before him had broken those same rules, and Mr. Warrington was fully welcome to follow their example. There was something in the tragedy, he said, that strongly reminded him of both *Coriolanus* and *Othello*. “Two very great works, sir!” George protested, delighted. “No doubt of that,” Mr. Spencer put in, “and your catastrophe is terrible, perfectly just, and drawn in part from real history, making it all the more awful.”

The plot of Mr. Warrington’s tragedy was stuffed full of battle, betrayal, and bloody murder. His grandfather’s favourite old book had been the life of George Frundsberg of Mindelheim, the famous Imperial landsknecht colonel who fought at the Battle of Pavia and served under the Constable de Bourbon. One of Frundsberg’s close military companions, a mercenary named Carpzow or Carpezan, became George’s tragic hero. The first act, as it survives in Sir George Warrington’s original manuscript, opens before a walled convent on the banks of the Rhine, besieged by Lutheran troops under Carpezan’s command. These Lutherans are a rough, godless gang: they have plucked the beards of Roman friars and torn the veils from hundreds of religious women. Two dozen nuns tremble behind the convent walls, and the small garrison has sworn to surrender if no expected reinforcements arrive by midday. A temporary armistice is in place, and the sentries on the walls look down with hungry eyes as the mercenary soldiers and camp followers gamble on the grass outside the gate. Then the convent bell peals twelve: ding, ding, dong. No reinforcements have come. The gate swings open, and the famous Protestant hero, the terror of the Turks on the Danube and Papal troops in the Lombard plains, Colonel Gaspar Carpezan, marches in. He is clad head to toe in polished steel, his massive battle hammer slung over his shoulder—the same hammer he has used to shatter so many fortress sconces and sacred images. His banners fly, his trumpets blare. “No rudeness, men,” he orders. “The wine, larder, and cellar are yours to plunder. The church plate will be melted down. Any of the garrison who wish to take service with me will be welcomed, and paid handsomely. But no insult to the religious ladies! I have promised them all safe conduct, and the man who lays a finger on any of them hangs on the spot. See to that, Provost Marshal!” The giant Provost Marshal, dressed all in a vivid red doublet, nods his assent.

“We shall see a good deal more of that Provost Marshal, who doubles as our on-field executioner,” Mr. Spencer explained to his guests.

“A very agreeable acquaintance, I am sure! I shall be delighted to meet the gentleman again,” Mr. Johnson rumbled, wagging his head over his teacup. “This scene of the mercenaries, the camp followers, and their wild sports is novel and stirring, Mr. Warrington, and I give you my full compliments on it. The Colonel has gone inside the convent, I think? Now let us hear what he does there.”

The Abbess, and two of her oldest senior nuns, step forward to face the conqueror. Fierce as he is on the battlefield, they confront him in their sacred halls, well aware of his reputation for vandalising every convent he has ever sacked. That same battle hammer of his has smashed hundreds of sacred images across Germany, and pounds upon pounds of stolen convent plate are known to have passed through his hands. It is no wonder the Abbess-Princess of St. Mary’s, a lady of noble birth, fierce prejudices, and a sharp, uncurbed tongue, takes an instant dislike to this lowborn heretic who lords it over her house, and proceeds to give Carpezan a full piece of her mind. The scene, where the elderly noblewoman at first gets the better of the rough soldier, was much admired by George’s audience. For all his warlike ferocity, Carpezan is initially shaken by her brisk verbal assault, and for a moment, the great conqueror seems to be vanquished by his own prisoner. But an old veteran like him would never be bested permanently by a woman. “Pray tell me, madam,” he says, “how many ladies live in your convent, so that my men may arrange proper transport for them all?” The Abbess, her face dark with trouble and anger, replies that besides herself, there are twenty-three noble sisters of St. Mary’s. She had been about to say twenty-four, and corrects herself mid-sentence. “Ha! Why that hesitation?” asks Captain Ulric, one of Carpezan’s roguish, lighthearted young officers.

The dark-faced mercenary chief pulls a crumpled letter from his coat pocket. “I demand from you, madam,” he says sternly to the Abbess, “the person of the noble Lady Sybilla of Hoya. Her brother was my favourite captain, slain fighting beside me in the Milanese campaigns. On his death, she became heiress to all his vast lands. We have received word that a greedy uncle tricked her here, and immured her in this convent against her will. The damsel herself shall choose her fate: she may stay here as a cloistered nun of St. Mary’s, or return to the world as a free woman, the Baroness of her brother’s estates.” The Abbess is visibly shaken by this demand, but replies haughtily that there is no Lady Sybilla in the house: every inmate is a professed nun, and all their lands and wealth belong by law to the Order. “Give me the Lady Sybilla of Hoya at once!” Carpezan roars in great wrath. “If you refuse, I will signal my reiters, and give your convent over to full sack.”

“Faith, if I lead the storm, I won’t waste time on the old Abbess,” Captain Ulric jokes, “I’d choose some plump, smiling, red-lipped young nun like—like—” As he leans forward, trying to peer under the veils of the two attendants standing behind the Abbess, the old woman snaps at him: “Silence, fellow, with your ribald talk! The lady you ask for has passed beyond sin, temptation, and vanity. Three days ago, our Sister Agnes died.”

At this announcement, Carpezan is visibly staggered. The Abbess calls on the convent chaplain to confirm her statement, and the ghastly pale old man admits that yes, Sister Agnes was buried three days prior. This is too much. From within the lining of his steel coat, Carpezan pulls out the letter Sybilla herself snuck out to him, in which she wrote that she was soon to be “buried” not in hallowed ground, but in a sealed oubliette beneath the convent floors, to be kept on bread and water or starved to death entirely. He seizes the unflinching Abbess by the arm, while Captain Ulric grabs the chaplain by the throat. He blows a sharp blast on his horn, and his furious landsknechts pour into the convent from outside. Walls are smashed, doors are kicked in, and in the chaos of flames, screaming nuns, and clashing steel, Carpezan himself carries the fainting Sybilla out of her dungeon, slung over his shoulder. It was that same pretty, red-lipped young nun Ulric had been staring at who had shown them the way to the oubliette, and passed Sybilla’s letter to Carpezan in the first place.

“The convent is suppressed with a vengeance,” George smiles. “We end the first act with the whole building in flames, the soldiers roaring in triumph, and the nuns screaming for mercy. They had best change their costumes at once, because in the next act, most of them will be appearing as court ladies.” His guests break into discussion immediately: if the play were staged at Drury Lane, Mrs. Pritchard might not like playing the Abbess, who only appears in the first act, but her daughter Miss Pritchard would make a lovely Sybilla, and Miss Gates a perfect mischievous attendant nun. Mr. Garrick, they note, is not particularly tall, but no one ever thinks of him as anything less than as big as a grenadier when he is performing, so he would make a magnificent Carpezan. Mr. Johnson agrees that the comic actor Woodward would play the roguish Ulric perfectly, as he already excels at Mercutio-style mischievous roles. By the end of the discussion, the whole company has cast every part in the imaginary production.

In Act the Second, Carpezan has married Sybilla. He has grown enormously wealthy from years of plunder in the wars, has been ennobled by the Emperor, and lives in great state and splendour in his castle on the banks of the Danube. For all his wealth, title, and new bride, though, the newly made Lord Carpezan is not happy. Perhaps his long years as a mercenary fighting for every side have left him haunted by the memory of his crimes. Perhaps his rough, unpolished soldier manners clash terribly with the imperious temper of his highborn wife. She makes his life a misery, taunting him endlessly about his low birth, mocking his old war comrades that the veteran still loves to gather around him, until more than once he wishes he had never fished this lovely, quarrelsome, wayward shrew out of that oubliette. After the chaos of the first act, this act is far quieter, consisting mostly of bitter quarrels between the Baron and Baroness, until hunting horns sound, and messengers announce that the young King of Bohemia and Hungary is riding that way on a progress.

Act III unfolds in Prague, where his Majesty has invited Lord and Lady Carpezan to his court, with great promises of promotion for the Baron. He is to be raised from Colonel to General-in-Chief, and made a Count. Sybilla immediately becomes one of the most brilliant, sought-after ladies in the entire court. “Oh, wait a minute—I recognise this story now, sir!” Mr. Johnson interrupts. “It’s in Meteranus’ *Theatrum Universum*. I read it when I was a boy at Oxford. Carpezanus, or Carpzoff—”

“That takes us straight to Act Four,” George says. In the fourth act, the young King’s attentions to Sybilla grow more and more unmistakeable. Her husband struggles against his jealousy, refusing to believe the worst of his wife for as long as he can, until her infidelity is placed beyond all possible doubt. The act closes on the terrible event that actually happened in the real history he drew from: convinced of his wife’s guilt, Carpezan orders his regimental executioner to slay her in her own palace chambers. The curtain falls moments after the murder, in a room lit only by moonlight streaming through a great oriel window, just as the young King arrives outside her door with his lute, strumming the secret tryst song that they agreed on as a signal between them. That very same song, written in the style of Mr. Waller, was sung earlier in Act III at a great royal court festival, and Mr. Johnson praised it as an excellent imitation of the old poet’s manner. The way the bright, cheerful melody echoes right outside the chamber where Sybilla’s corpse lies, deepens the tragic horror of the moment perfectly.

“But what happened to him afterwards?” Johnson asked. “I remember in Meteranus’ account, Carpezan was taken back into favour by Count Mansfeld, and doubtless went on to murder plenty more people on the Protestant side.”

George had deliberately departed from historical fact for his fifth act. King Louis of Hungary and Bohemia, still reeling from the violent end of his affair with Sybilla, receives word that the Emperor Solyman the Magnificent is invading his Hungarian dominions. Two noblemen enter, and report that during the King’s war council, the enraged Carpezan burst into the royal chamber, shattered his sword before the King’s feet, and flung down a glove he dared the King to wear, swearing he would one day come back to claim it. After making that wild challenge, the rebel fled Prague and has not been seen since. Rumour says he has joined the Turkish invader, converted to Islam, and is now in the Sultan’s camp, whose white tents gleam across the river, right in the path of the King’s advancing army. Then the King enters his tent with his generals, draws up his battle lines, and sends all his officers to their posts, keeping only his old, faithful master of the horse at his side.

The faithful Gumbo was inconsolable for his master’s departure: judging by the wails and torrents of tears he shed the moment he learned Harry had enlisted as a soldier, any onlooker would have sworn the poor man’s heart was fit to shatter at the separation. It was no wonder he fled to find comfort among the maids at Mr. Lambert’s lodgings; wherever that dusky young man went, he sought solace in the company of women. Their soft, tender hearts knew exactly how to pity the sad African, and the depth of his complexion was no more repulsive to them than Othello’s was to Desdemona. I do believe 18th-century Europe has never grown so squeamish about people of African descent as certain other corners of the world have since. Many Black men—take the celebrated fencer and favourite of the Parisian salons, the Chevalier de Saint-Georges, for example—have long been darlings of the fair sex, and in his own humbler station, Gumbo was no different. The Lambert household servants wept right alongside him, the maids treating him not just as Mr. Harry’s personal man, but as a beloved brother.

Hetty could not help but huff a small, fond laugh when she found Gumbo howling that her master had run off to be a “volumteer” and left him behind. He swore up and down he’d split himself into twenty thousand pieces to save Harry’s life, any day of the week, and he meant every word. All the same, the poor fellow had to keep his strength up, so he snuck large tankards of beer and plates of cold roast beef from the kitchen larder. That he was greedy, idle, and prone to stretching the truth, no one could deny—but Hetty slipped him a half-crown all the same, and treated him with a gentleness no one had ever seen from her before. Her tongue, once famously sharp and full of pert little jokes, turned soft and quiet these days. She moved about the house meek as a lamb, humble to her mother, grateful to the footmen and maids for even the smallest favour, patient when her little sister Polly tugged at her hair while combing it, long-suffering when schoolboy Charley trod on her toes or knocked her workbox askew, and silent as a church mouse in her father’s presence. It was a transmogrified little Hetty no one had ever met before. If her father had ordered her to roast a whole leg of mutton for dinner, or walk to church arm-in-arm with Gumbo, she would have bobbed a perfect curtsy and said, “Yes, if you please, dear papa!”

Leg of mutton, indeed! What kind of meals were the poor volunteers eating right now, with cannonballs whistling over their heads? Church! When the parson read the war prayer aloud at Sunday service, her knees knocked so hard together under the pew she thought they’d crack, and she buried her face in her hands. When he read out the commandment *Thou shalt do no murder* from the communion rail, she was convinced he was staring straight at her. She fussed over every traveller on land or sea, ran for the morning post the second it was delivered to hunt for any scrap of news about the expedition, and hung by the front door every evening to read the news on her father’s face the second he came home from the Ordnance Office. Was Harry well? Had he been made a general already? Was he wounded? A prisoner? Oh, mercy, what if a single shot tore both his legs clean off, like the old Chelsea pensioner they’d seen hobbling on wooden stumps in the gardens not a week prior? She swore she’d walk on wooden legs her whole life if it meant Harry came home safe, and that she’d never get up off her knees until he did. “Haven’t you heard of people whose hair turned completely grey in a single night, Theo?” she’d ask her sister, wide-eyed. “I shouldn’t wonder if mine does. Not one little bit.” She’d dash to the looking glass every hour to check for the first silver strand.
“Hetty dear,” Theo would murmur, “you were never half this nervous when Papa was off on his posting to Minorca, years ago.”
“Ah, Theo!” Hetty would shoot back, cheeks flushing. “It’s very easy to be calm when the man you care about isn’t off fighting the French, but safe right here at home.” Theo blushed bright red, and fell quiet, for they both knew she spoke of George, safe under their very roof.

We won’t drag out the family’s anxiety any longer: for the moment, Harry was as safe as any Life Guard trooper quartered at Regent’s Park barracks. His first expedition as a volunteer could be called technically successful, but never glorious. The British lion, like any other, cannot always find a worthy foe to fight or a grand royal battle to win. Suppose he sets off to hunt a tiger who refuses to show, and winds up pouncing on a stray goose to gobble down? Lions, after all, have to eat. But then, suppose he marches roaring through the forest in search of that tiger, only to find six tigers coming straight for him? That is clearly not a fight he wants to pick. He tucks his tail between his royal legs and trots straight home to his warm den as fast as he can. If he tried to fight six tigers, no one would call him a lion, they’d call him an ass.

That was exactly the nature of Harry’s first taste of war. Thirteen thousand fighting men sailed from the Isle of Wight on the first of June, and at dawn on the fifth, the fleet slipped into Cancale Bay on the coast of Brittany. Harry and his fellow gentlemen volunteers spent hours peering at the strange French coast from the decks, while the commander-in-chief and the Commodore snuck close in a small cutter to reconnoitre. They spotted cattle grazing on the cliffs, and a handful of dragoons who trotted off over the hills the second they saw the ship. A tiny, rickety fort mounting only two guns had the audacity to fire a volley at the Duke of Marlborough and the Commodore as they passed. By two o’clock the whole British fleet was anchored, and the order went out for all the grenadier companies from eleven regiments to pile into flat-bottomed boats and gather around the Commodore’s ship, the *Essex*. Commodore Howe hoisted his flag on the frigate *Success* and sailed as close to shore as he could, the rest of the frigates trailing behind him to shell any defences before the landing. With Lord George Sackville and General Dury leading the charge, the volunteers, the grenadiers, and three battalions of Guards rowed for the beach.

The gentlemen volunteers never got the chance to do any heroic deeds that day, because the Frenchmen who should have stayed to fight them had all run for their lives. The frigates silenced the tiny fort’s paltry two guns, the landing party stormed in, and took the entire garrison prisoner. The whole garrison, as it turned out, was one single old man, who had bravely fired both guns. He told his captors, quite proudly, that if every Frenchman fought as he did, the British would never have landed at Cancale at all. The vanguard of invaders took possession of the small village of Cancale, and lay on their arms all night. Harry’s new comrades teased him mercilessly for bragging he’d go out on the “war path” and bring back two French scalps with his Virginian tomahawk, but no Frenchmen came within a mile of him to make that possible. The only man killed all day was a French gentleman out riding with his servant, who stumbled straight into Lord Downe leading the front rank of Kingsley’s regiment. Lord Downe offered him quarter, which the fool refused, and so he, his servant, and both their horses were shot dead on the spot.

The next day the whole force landed, and marched from Cancale to St. Malo. Every village on the road was completely empty, many of the lanes were so narrow the men had to march single file, and they could have been picked off one by one from behind the thick, leafy hedges if any enemy had cared to ambush them. They reached the walls of St. Malo at dusk, and took a few random, useless cannon shots from the town that did no harm in the dark. Under cover of that fire, the British set every ship, every wooden storehouse, every pile of pitch and tar in the harbour alight, and a great roiling fire burned bright all night long. The French never once came out of the town to harass the raiders. Rumours flew that a huge garrison was hidden inside St. Malo, waiting for them to storm the walls, so the Duke of Marlborough and Lord George Sackville decided there was no point trying to take the town, marched their men all the way back to Cancale, and loaded everyone back onto the ships.

If this were not a strictly true history, I could easily have sent our Virginian off on a far more glorious campaign. Exactly four weeks after he left England, Harry stepped back onto Portsmouth’s docks, and wrote a letter straight to his brother George. George ran off to the Lamberts’ Dean Street lodging the second he tore the seal open, and burst in on the whole family at breakfast.
“Glorious news, ladies!” he shouted. “Our champion is home safe! He survived every danger, and even swears he saw dragons, upon my word!”
“Dragons?” Hetty yelped, half jumping out of her chair. “What on earth do you mean, Mr. Warrington?”
“Great long-tailed monsters with steel scales on their backs that spit fire and gobble up one virgin a day,” Mr. Lambert put in, teasing gently. “He must have seen the Seven Champions of Christendom, of course. They saw St. George’s flag flying and ran for the hills.”
“I’ve read about them!” little Charley, home from his school in Chartreux, put in very solemnly. “They love to eat women. There was one that was going to eat Andromeda, you know, and Jason killed another one that guarded the golden apple tree.”
George laughed, and started reading the letter aloud:
> I think you’ll be glad to hear I am returned, still with no commission, no wounds, and no great glory to brag of—but at the very least, alive and hearty. On our ship we were crammed in so tight it felt like poor Mr. Holwell and his friends stuck in the Black Hole of Calcutta. We had rough weather, and a lot of the fancy London volunteers who are used to calm waters grumbled nonstop. Their stomachs are too dainty for plain sailor’s rum and hard biscuit, not after the fancy dinners they get at White’s Club. But I’ve been to sea before, so I ate my rations and sipped my spiced flip very contentedly, determined to show those foppish English macaronis that a Virginia gentleman is as good as the best of them.
> For the honour of old Virginia I wish I had more to brag about, but all I can say for certain is we went to France and came right back. I don’t think even your dramatic, tragedy-writing pen could make something grand out of this campaign. We landed at Cancale Bay on the sixth, saw a few dragons on a hill that galloped away without stopping to fight. We slept under canvas, marched to St Malo, and burned a whole fleet of privateers in the harbour. Then we got back on the ships without crossing swords with a single enemy, save a few poor local devils the troops plundered. Better luck next time! It wasn’t grand or glorious, but I loved it. I’ve smelled gunpowder, and a whole lot of rosin and pitch from the fires we lit. I’ve seen the enemy, slept rough under canvas, been dreadfully crowded and seasick, and I’m ready to go again. My best to dear Aunt Lambert, and tell Miss Hetty I wasn’t the least bit frightened when I saw the French horses.
> Your most affectionate brother,

Hetty’s knees went weak with relief. A little while later, Mr. Lambert went on official business to inspect the troops camped at Portsmouth and the Isle of Wight, and George came with him. They found Harry tanned, bright-eyed, and bursting with health, his mood lightened entirely by the thrill of the little campaign. He was eager to learn every detail of his new military duties, active, cheerful, and nothing at all like the listless, moping young man who had dawdled around London coffee houses and the Lamberts’ drawing room only a few months prior. The whole camp was under canvas, the weather was bright and warm, and George found his brother thriving in the brisk, open-air school of war. Strolling arm in arm with him through the streets of Portsmouth, George recalled his own short, disastrous military experience two years prior, and marveled at how massive this force was, compared to the tiny, ill-fated army he had once marched with.

The raid, unimpressive as it was to anyone who could see the full picture, sent the whole nation into a frenzy of excitement. The papers declared they had humiliated the proud Gaul, and would have routed the French entirely if only they’d dared to show their faces. What valour on earth could match British valour, the crowds cheered? The whole country demanded more victories, and the enthusiastic army set sail on a new expedition, this time with a very distinguished volunteer on board: the King’s own son, Prince Edward, who was ferried to the *Essex* in the ship’s twelve-oared barge, the standard of England flying from the bow, the Admiral’s flag barge following behind, all the other captains trailing after in strict order of seniority. The whole fleet weighed anchor, and Harry waved his hat wildly to his friends cheering from the shore. George was sure Harry would earn his commission soon, no need to buy an ensigncy if he kept impressing his superiors the way he was. His colonel already sang his praises, officers and men alike loved him, and it was clear he was a young man of great promise and spirit.

Ten days after the fleet sailed, the most glorious news imaginable arrived in London. On the 7th and 8th of August, the King’s troops had landed in the Bay des Marais, two leagues west of Cherbourg, right in the face of a large force of French defenders. The French had scattered the second they saw the British advance. Cherbourg had surrendered unconditionally, and the Union Jack flew over all three of its outer forts. Twenty-seven enemy ships had been burned in the harbour, and hundreds of fine brass cannons had been seized. The rest of the old iron guns had been spiked and tossed in the water, and the famous French harbour basin the people of Paris had bragged about for decades, as well as the two stone piers at the harbour entrance, had been blown to smithereens.

London exploded in celebration. The captured colours from the great British victory at Louisbourg paraded from Kensington to St Paul’s, escorted by eighty Life Guards and eighty Horse Grenadiers, with their standards, kettledrums, and trumpets blaring. The Dean and Chapter met them at the west door of the cathedral, and the Tower and Royal Park guns boomed out a deafening salute at exactly that moment. The next day, the captured Cherbourg cannons were dragged through the streets, their sides carved with fleurs-de-lis, royal crowns, and grand boastful mottos: *Tonnere*, *Malfaisant*, *Le Vainqueur*—“The Victor”, indeed, that piece of French bragging, captured by the British! The crowds screamed so loud the windows rattled. Hetty and Mrs Lambert were fully convinced Harry had dragged every single one of those cannons out of the French battery himself, and thrown every last French artilleryman into the sea. Even the haughty old Madame de Bernstein was asking after him, and his cousin Lady Maria had begged George to come visit her and give her any news of Harry he could find. George, who had once been the undisputed favourite of the household, found himself completely deposed, barely noticed by Hetty at all. His fancy wit, his learning, his dramatic plays, all were very well—but what could any of that compare to great victories and captured brass cannons? He accepted his demotion meekly. The Lamberts and their friends daydreamed that the 15,000 British soldiers would march straight to Paris next, and could not wait to brag to Harry’s snobbish great-aunt Lady Warrington, back in the country, and ask her what she thought of her unruly Virginia nephew now. Every house in London lit up with candles for the victory illuminations, and the Lamberts lit up every window in their own home, grinning from ear to ear.

But the bright fair weather did not last. The commanders, drunk on the acclaim of the Cherbourg victory, decided they would go back and finish the job they had abandoned at St Malo. They landed near the little coastal town of Saint-Cast, but the Governor of Brittany had gathered a far larger French army to defend the coast, and the planned surprise raid was impossible. The British commanders ordered an immediate retreat back to the fleet anchored in Saint-Cast Bay. Hide your faces, all the bards of military glory, for the terrible day of Saint-Cast was about to dawn. Two-thirds of the British troops, and all the artillery, had already been loaded onto the longboats, when a French army sent from Brest came pouring down the heights surrounding the bay. Four companies of the First Regiment of Guards, and all the elite grenadier companies of the raiding force, were left as a rearguard on the beach, 1100 men in total, facing ten times their number of French troops. The guardsmen made a fatal mistake: they left the high, thick stone dyke on the shore, a perfect defensive position they could have held for hours, to charge the advancing Frenchmen on the open sand. The small rearguard was quickly overwhelmed, and broke and ran for the boats in a sauve qui peut panic. Seven hundred of the 1100 were killed, drowned in the surf, or taken prisoner, their commanding officer shot dead on the beach.

I am a man of peace, who knows very little of the finer points of war, and I will not dwell on the fight itself. What weighs on my mind far more than two soldiers stabbing at each other, one English one French, is the people they left waiting back home. The girl on Tower Hill who clung to her guardsman’s neck the morning he sailed, the lass in Brittany who gave her French soldier his favourite tobacco box the day he marched off to war

You may marvel at the endless, vainglorious posturing of great powers, and of the French in particular: would you believe that after the skirmish at St. Cas – little more than a small rearguard action, by all accounts – they wasted whole casks of gunfire in celebration at Paris’s Les Invalides, blustering and bragging over our misfortune? Is there any shred of magnanimity in cheering because five or six hundred brave souls were trapped by ten thousand foes on a tidal shore, and met the fate that ever threatens the hindmost of a retreat?

I had half a mind to paint a merry picture of London’s rejoicings for our earlier glorious success at St. Malo: polished captured guns dragged in procession by grinning tars, stout horse-grenadiers prancing past, the mob waving hats, roaring cheers, and picking pockets all the while, while our dear friends looked down on the triumph from a Fleet Street balcony. But now that the French have copied the Tower of London’s displays and set their trivial St. Cas victory up against our St. Malo win, I scorn to waste words on the stale affair. *Nolo, non Malo* – I want no part of that foolish one-upmanship. All I care for is that Harry returned from the whole sorry business with a whole skin. Have I ever said he was so much as bruised? Have I not, for fear of distressing my tender young readers, insisted he was in finer fettle than he had ever been in his life?

The sea air had tanned his cheek, the musket ball that whistled past his temple had only singed the curl at his side. The ocean soaked his gaiters and his uniform through to the skin, but never swallowed him. It is true he showed his coat lapels to the enemy for a little while – but only for as short a time as possible, slipping out of their line of sight as quick as his legs could carry him. And what are lapels, after all, but reverses? Coats wear them just as men do, and our only duty is to bear small setbacks with courage and good humour.

“I can tell you,” Harry recounted to his gathered friends, “we all ran for it when our line broke. The luckiest man was he who reached the boats first. French horse and foot were hard on our heels all the way down the beach, cutting down stragglers and bayoneting the wounded on the sand. Poor Armytage was shot no more than three paces ahead of me, and fell. I hoisted him up over my shoulder and staggered through the surf to our boat. The sailors in our craft didn’t flinch an inch, even though shot was whistling past their ears, shattering their oar blades, and riddling their ensign through and through. The officer in command was as cool as if he’d been sipping punch in a Portsmouth tavern – and you may be sure we drank a full bowl of that very punch the moment we set foot back on English soil. Poor Sir John was less fortunate than me. He never lived to reach the ship. The service has lost a fine soldier, and Miss Howe a true gentleman for a husband. These casualties are inevitable, you see. His younger brother inherits the baronetcy.”

“It is the poor lady I am thinking of,” Miss Hetty cut in, the story half-told. “And the King! Why did the King encourage Sir John to go? No gentleman could refuse a command from his sovereign. And now the poor man is dead! Oh, what a state his Majesty must be in!”

“I have no doubt his Majesty is in a very deep state of grief,” said Papa Lambert, wagging his head with a dry little smile.

Hetty flushed. “You are laughing! Do you mean to say, sir, that when a gentleman dies almost in his service, the King of England would not feel for him? If I thought that, I vow I would turn for the Pretender this very day!”

“That saucy tongue of yours would make a very pretty ornament for Temple Bar’s spiked heads,” the General teased, for he saw the turmoil under Hetty’s sharp words: the remorse, the consternation, the gush of gratitude that Harry had come home unharmed, sending her small heart beating fast under her stays. “No, my dear. If kings wept for every private soldier lost in battle, what a life of misery we would condemn them to. I think better of his Majesty than to imagine him so weak. And if little Miss Hester Lambert got her Pretender on the throne, I doubt she would be any happier. That Stuart family was never famed for being overburdened with tender feelings.”

“But if the King sent Harry – that is, Sir John Armytage – off to the war where he lost his life, oughtn’t his Majesty to repent very deeply?” the young lady pressed.

“If Harry had fallen, no doubt the court would have gone into full mourning. As it is, the ladies and gentlemen were all in bright coloured gowns and coats only yesterday,” remarked the General.

“Why not light bonfires to celebrate our defeats, and put on sackcloth and ashes to mark our victories?” George put in, dry as ever. “I protest I have no desire to thank Heaven for helping us burn a handful of fishing ships at Cherbourg.”

“Ah, but you do, George!” Harry said, earnest, even though he acknowledged his brother’s wit was far sharper than his own. “When your country wins a fight, you’re glad – I know I am. And when I had to run before the French, I was ashamed. I couldn’t help it, even though I did it. It doesn’t seem right, somehow, that an Englishman should ever have to turn his back to the foe.” He paused, and grew grave. George smiled, but did not ask his brother what the average French private might think of the matter.

“’Twas a bad business,” Harry went on, “but lucky it was no worse. Word from prisoners we exchanged says the French commander, the Duke of Aiguillon, was what you’d call a soft, moistened chicken. Our whole retreat could have been cut off to a man, only we happened to be in a very great hurry to get away ourselves. The French local militia fought famously, I will say that – dozens of their gentry volunteers marched right in the front line, as men of station ought to do. They say the Chevalier of Tour d’Auvergne charged after us despite the Duke’s explicit orders to hold back. The officers who brought over our lists of prisoners and wounded to General Bligh and Lord Howe told us all that. By the by, George – that young Howe is a lord now, since word came home his elder brother was killed fighting in America. He’s a brave fellow, no matter if he’s a commoner or a peer.”

“And his sister, who was to have married poor Sir John Armytage – only think what a state of grief she must be in!” Hetty sighed, who had grown far more tender and sentimental these past weeks.

“And his mother!” added Mrs. Lambert. “Have you seen her advertisement in the newspapers, appealing to the electors of Nottingham? ‘Lord Howe being now absent upon the public service, and Lieutenant-Colonel Howe with his regiment at Louisbourg, it rests upon me to beg the favour of your votes and interests that Lieutenant-Colonel Howe may supply the place of his late brother as your representative in Parliament.’ Is that not a gallant woman?”

“A perfectly Laconic woman,” George agreed. “What son could fail to be brave, raised by a mother like that?” the General added.

The two Warrington brothers glanced at each other, unspoken understanding between them. “If one of us were to fall in defence of his country, we have a Spartan mother back in Virginia who would write just that same notice,” George said.

“If Sparta lies anywhere south of the Potomac, I reckon we do,” Harry put in, grinning. He fell quiet again, pensive. “And to think we two have both faced the enemy now, and both been whipped by him, brother.”

Hetty looked at him, and her heart ached. She saw him in her mind’s eye, staggering through the surf towards the boats, his wounded comrade heavy on his shoulder, the French closing in behind, shot flying all around him. It was her words that had goaded him to volunteer for the expedition, to prove he was no idle fop. And now he was home, and he never once reproached her for it. Unless directly asked, he barely spoke of his adventures at all. He was gentle, grave, and unfailingly courteous to Hetty, and open and tender to every other member of the Lambert household. But those taunts she had flung at him had cut deep. His whole bearing seemed to say to her, Little hand, you never ought to have been lifted against me! It is cruel to scorn any man, much less one who has been so devoted to you and yours. I may not be quick of wit, but where the heart is concerned, I am the equal of the best of men, and the very best of my heart has always belonged to your family.

Harry’s quiet endurance of the wrong she had done him restored his place in Hetty’s esteem, a place he had lost in those months of idle, aimless drifting before the expedition. She gave him the respect that all brave men are owed: she no longer snapped at him with pert answers, no longer made cutting, sarcastic remarks about his conduct. In a word, Hetty was humiliated, and altered, and greatly improved.

The whole world seemed to change its mind about Harry, just as he had changed himself. He was no longer sulky and indolent, no longer moping over his own unworthiness or defying his neighbours to find good in him. The colonel of his regiment wrote an official report praising his conduct as exemplary, and recommended him for one of the vacant ensign’s commissions left open by the men who fell at St. Cas. Unlucky as the expedition’s end had been, it had turned out a stroke of fortune for him. When the rest of the volunteers trickled back to St. James’s Street, they all sang his praises. The volunteers and their exploits were the toast of every drawing room in town. Even if he had been a commanding general struck down mid-victory, Sir John Armytage could scarcely have earned half the public sympathy the nation lavished on the survivors and dead of the failed Brittany raid. The newspapers brimmed with letters eulogising him, wits and men of feeling vying to write the most beautiful epitaph in his honour, and the whole country bewailed the fate of his affianced bride.

Lord Howe himself spoke of Mr. Henry Warrington’s courage in the highest terms, and so Harry received his full share of the favour and admiration the city lavished on all the returning volunteers. No doubt thousands of common soldiers who had fought alongside them were every bit as brave – but the English nation has always loved its gentlemen to distinguish themselves in battle, and the young volunteers were unanimously hailed as modern Paladins and heroes.
