White’s and Almack’s put on illuminations for their homecoming, and all of St. James’s welcomed the young knights back with open arms. Even Harry’s distant relations wrote to congratulate him. A letter arrived from Castlewood, where Aunt Bernstein had lately taken up residence, full of praise for his valour and tucked with a generous little bank bill as a token of her affectionate approval. It came enclosed under Lord Castlewood’s frank, who sent his kind regards to both the Warrington brothers, and an open invitation to come and stay at his country house whenever they pleased.

Along with that, a private letter arrived for Harry, spelt very badly but in a handwriting that made him smile the moment he saw it. His affectionate cousin Maria Esmond wrote that she had been hearing nothing but his praises everywhere, and shared fully in all his good and bad fortune, and that whatever happened to him, she begged he would keep a small little place for her in his heart. Parson Sampson, she added, had preached a wonderful sermon that very week on the horrors of war and the noble courage of gentlemen who volunteered to face battle for their country. The chaplain soon wrote to Harry himself, a gushing, overheated letter hailing him as his friend, his benefactor, his glorious hero. Even stuffy old Sir Miles Warrington sent a hamper of game all the way from Norfolk: one small bird, shot sitting, had a string and note tied round its leg, sent with Harry’s love, as the very first victim of young Miles’s new fowling-piece.

And before long, Mr. Lambert came trundling over to their Southampton Row lodgings, his face bright with unmistakeable joy, to announce that Mr. Henry Warrington was to be gazetted forthwith as Ensign in the Second Battalion of Kingsley’s, the 20th Regiment of Foot, which had seen heavy fighting in the Brittany campaign and was now being reorganized as the distinct new 67th Regiment. Its colonel had not been with the men on the St. Cas expedition: he was off at Cape Breton, even then leading the capture of those guns at Louisbourg whose triumphant arrival in England had sparked such national celebration just weeks before.

Many of my gentle readers will no doubt know the famous menagerie in Regent’s Park, where our finned, feathered, and four-footed fellow creatures are boarded and lodged, and show themselves off for our amusement and instruction. There I wandered one day, my private thoughts clinging to me even as I stopped before the aquarium glass, and to my surprise, found my mind still turning to our old friends the Warrington brothers of Virginia. The most graceful creature gliding through the green water was none other than our homely, familiar friend the flounder—every curve of his body smooth and harmonious, now turning his glossy black back to the light, now baring his soft pale underbelly in a motion so quick and elegant one would never guess he was the same fish we devour unthinkingly in water souchy at Greenwich, never suspecting he could be so beautiful.

As the race of man goes, so too does the race of flounders. See the creature in his proper element, and he is agile, strong, comely. Drag him out onto dry land, and all that grace vanishes: he flaps absurdly against the unforgiving ground, gasping out his weak life before your very eyes. Tenderly lift him before it is too late, and cast him back into the Thames, and he is himself once more—though I need not belabor the old proverb of a fish out of water, I daresay other naturalists have noted the same truth long before me.

Harry Warrington, for many months past, had been floundering far outside his natural element. The moment he stepped back into a life that suited him, health, spirits, strength, and all his old energy flooded back. The tap of an epaulet on his shoulder transformed him entirely. He fell utterly in love with his new army profession, devoured every detail of drill and protocol, and mastered them with the eager quickness of a boy who has found his calling. Had I half the wit of my friend Lorrequer, I would follow Harry into camp, watch him on the march, at the regimental mess, striding the parade ground, share a dozen roistering evenings with his brother officers, camp with him under canvas, and explain every nuance of war’s maneuvers and the life of a soldier. As it is, the reader must fill in the bright colors of the picture themselves, drawing on their own imagination and experience, and picture Mr. Harry Warrington in his smart new red coat trimmed with yellow facings, happier than he has ever been in his life, proud to bear the King’s colors and eager to learn and perform every duty of his post.

George Warrington, we may be sure, was bursting with pride at his brother’s success. The two young men admired each other unreservedly, and recognized one another’s finest qualities without a hint of jealousy. George penned a warm, affectionate letter home to their mother in Virginia, recounting all the praise he had heard of Harry’s gallantry—praise Harry’s own modesty would never have repeated aloud. He described how Harry had won his first commission by his own courage, and asked Madam Esmond’s permission to split the cost of purchasing him a higher rank, as a small recompense for the fact that George’s unexpected return from the dead had stripped Harry of the entire inheritance he had long considered rightfully his. George noted that Harry had run up far more debts than he ever would have dared as a mere younger son, on the false assumption he stood to inherit the whole Esmond estate, and he counted it a joy, a thank-offering for his own narrow escape from captivity, to contribute generously to secure his brother’s future.

Having finished his account of Harry’s affairs, George turned to his own, and broached a subject close to his heart. He reminded his mother that the kindest, truest friends the boys had found in England were Mr. and Mrs. Lambert, the latter an old schoolfellow of Madam Esmond’s youth. Where their own blood relations had been cold and calculating, the Lamberts had opened their hearts and their home to the pair, unreserved and generous. General Lambert was respected by the entire army and beloved by everyone who knew him, and Mrs. Lambert had doted on both boys as if they were her own sons. Now, George wrote, he had formed an attachment to the General’s eldest daughter Theo, on which he believed the whole of his future happiness depended, and he begged his mother’s leave and approval for the match. He had not yet made a formal proposal to the young lady or her parents, but he had made no secret of his feelings, and he was certain both Theo and her family looked on his suit favorably. Theo, he wrote, was the most dutiful, gentle, pious creature alive, and he had no doubt she would prove a loving, devoted daughter to his mother as well. In page after page, he painted her as a paragon of perfection, and swore that his entire future joy hung on winning her hand.

The sentimental reader may ask why I do not reproduce this letter here, given that the full Warrington correspondence sits in my hands. The answer is simple: it would be cruel to lay bare the secrets of a young man’s first love, to record his incoherent vows, his wild raptures, the soft foolish fancies of his passion in cold black and white. Shall we play eavesdropper at twilight window embrasures, count every sigh and hand-shake, bottle hot tears, press a stethoscope to the delicate young breast of a girl in love to track its every throb? I protest, love is a sacred thing. Wherever you see it in the world—flaring sudden between two pairs of eyes, softening a mother’s gaze as she looks down at the baby in her lap, lighting a father’s face as his daughter whirls across the dance floor with her captain, glinting in the tired old eyes of a couple who have walked life’s path together for half a century—do not pry. It is a sin not just to kiss and tell, but to tell of kisses. Anyone admitted to that sweet mystery should hush about it. Woe to the man who would vulgarize the sacred secrets of love: you cannot dine with him without him printing every word of your private conversation, cannot sail with him without him throwing you over to the public eye.

While Harry has been off smelling gunpowder, charging enemy lines, and carrying wounded comrades out of the line of fire, George has been far more peacefully occupied: perhaps penning sonnets to the curve of Theo’s eyebrow, pacing the dark street under her window late at night to watch the small lamp glimmer through her chamber curtains, inventing a hundred trivial excuses to send tiny notes that never quite need a reply, and somehow always get one, culling lines from his favorite poets and fresh Covent Garden flowers for her delight. He walks to St. James’s Church with her, sits side by side in the same pew sharing the same Prayer-book, and never hears a single word of the sermon, so entirely is his mind full of her. He is unfailingly affectionate to every member of Theo’s family: dotes on her little schoolboy brother and sister, teases her sharp-witted younger sister Hetty, and is so warm and attentive to Mrs. Lambert that General Lambert jokes that the matron is half in love with George herself. It is a known truth, after all, that while fathers sometimes glower at the arrival of their future son-in-law, mothers turn sentimental, and live their own young courtship all over again through their daughter’s.

Gumbo and Sady, the Warrington boys’ enslaved servants, are forever trotting back and forth between Southampton Row, where the Lamberts live, and Dean Street, where George has his lodgings. All summer long, the group plans endless outings: trips to Ranelagh, strolls on Hampstead Heath, evenings at Vauxhall, concerts at Marylebone Gardens, and a hundred other small pleasures. George insists the famous tragedy he has been writing needs to be copied out fair for the stage, and who has a more delicate, beautiful Italian hand than Miss Theo? The sheets pass back and forth between them, every bundle wrapped in tiny notes of thanks, teasing questions, and soft, unspoken admiration. I hold the very packet of her letters in my hands, marked in George’s neat, precise script: “T’s letters, 1758-9.” Shall we pry them open and lay their tender secrets before the public eye? Those gentle, blushing lines were written for one pair of eyes alone. Years later, no doubt, George read them over with sweet pangs of remembrance, long after they were man and wife. It would be a sacrilege to expose them to strangers. Take my word for it: the young lady’s letters are modest, pure, and full of quiet warmth, the gentleman’s full of respect and soft devotion.

Theo is not, perhaps, the most beautiful woman in London. A hundred other girls, from Coelia to Ardelia to their own cousin Flora, are far more striking to look at. But her sweet face pleases George better than any other in the whole world. She is not the wittiest, or the most learned, but her voice is the dearest sound he knows, and in her company he finds himself sharper, more eloquent, more generous and clever than he ever is anywhere else—so of course he delights in being with her. And as thank Heaven I have never thought so poorly of women as to believe them entirely fair, I need not tell you that Theo endows her George with every virtue, wit, and grace under the sun.

When George’s letter arrived at Castlewood in Virginia, it sparked no small commotion around Madam Esmond’s fireside. The boy was in love, and wished to marry! It was only natural, and would keep him out of mischief. So long as he chose a well-bred, Christian young woman, Madam Esmond saw no harm in it.

“I knew every unmarried woman in England would be setting their caps at him,” sniffed Mrs. Mountain, her lifelong companion. “They all fancy his wealth is as vast as his estate. He never says if the girl has a penny of her own. I fear she has nothing at all.”

“I have no doubt plenty of people here at home would set their caps at him too,” Madam Esmond replied, fixing her dependent with a sharp grim look. “They would all try to catch Mr. Esmond Warrington for their own daughters, girls no richer than this Miss Lambert may be.”

“I suppose you are pointing at me!” Mrs. Mountain cried, stung. “My Fanny is poor, as you say, and it is very kind of you to remind me of her poverty!”

“I said people would set their caps at him. If the cap fits you, tant pis, as my old father used to say.”

“You think I am scheming to marry Fanny to George? After all these years we have lived together, you have a very low opinion of us!”

“My dear Mountain, I know you far too well to imagine you could ever fancy your daughter would be a suitable match for a gentleman of Mr. Esmond’s rank and station,” Madam replied, drawing herself up with great dignity.

“Fanny Parker was every bit as good as Molly Benson at school! My Mountain’s daughter is as good as any Lambert’s daughter in England!” Mrs. Mountain exclaimed.

“Then you did indeed plan to marry her to my son! I shall write to George at once and tell him how sorry I am to have disappointed you.” We may well suspect Mrs. Mountain had long harbored ambitious hopes for her daughter, for nothing else would explain the rage she flew into at the news of George’s intended match.

In her reply to her son, Madam Esmond wrote that she was delighted by the fraternal affection George showed, and entirely agreed that some compensation was due to Harry for the debts he had run up under the false impression he would inherit the whole estate. She would gladly split the cost of purchasing Harry’s higher commission, she said, and thanked Heaven that Harry’s own gallantry had won him his first step. This generosity to his brother, she added pointedly, was far more satisfactory than other foolish extravagances she would not name. The extravagance she alluded to, of course, was the ransom George had paid to the French captain’s poor family after his release from captivity—a sum Madam Esmond had flatly refused to reimburse. Her will was as stubborn as her son’s own, and George’s persistence in paying the sum she dismissed as foolish pride and obstinacy.

After paying his own ransom, settling all Harry’s gambling debts, and putting aside half the sum for his brother’s new commission, George found a large chunk of his personal patrimony was already spent. But he made the sacrifice cheerfully. His mother never ceased reminding him in every letter that he was descended from the noble old Esmond line, and must uphold the dignity of his family at all costs. She sent him endless commissions to buy goods in England, and though she had sent him barely a penny in remittances so far, she constantly exhorted him to move in the highest circles of London society, attend court as his ancestors had done, and live in a style befitting his rank. George took her at her word, assuming his mother would send the funds as soon as his own ran short, and obeyed her injunctions to the letter. The surviving Esmond papers from that period are full of bills for elegant dinner parties, tailor’s receipts for court suits, payments for fine liveries for his servants and chairmen, and horse-dealer’s bills for his fine team of carriage horses. George was no wild spendthrift like his brother: he gambled never, kept no racehorses, but his household was generous, his equipages handsome, and his purse always open. Everyone knew he was the heir to a vast Virginia estate, and no one doubted he was rolling in wealth.

The honest Lamberts were not mercenary people by any means, but they could not help but be pleased to see their eldest daughter growing attached to a young man of such sterling character, fine wit, noble family, and boundless expectations. George was a true gentleman: a little cold and reserved towards strangers, especially the lords and ladies of high society, but never supercilious, unfailingly courteous to all women, and unfailingly tender, lively, and warm to the small circle of people he loved. No wonder Theo had come to think him the best man in the whole wide world—even better than her dear papa. Great love transforms a man, making him kinder, sharper, sweeter, in the eyes of the woman who holds his heart, than every other man alive. We will not linger over their soft private whispers any longer. Those words were never meant to be written down for strangers. Lay down the book for a moment, if you are of a sentimental turn, and think back on your own first love. It may be decades dead and buried, but for a moment it rises from the grave, smiles, whispers, just as it did when it clung to your arm, and dropped hot fresh tears on your heart. It is long gone now, of course. The vase still sits on your shelf, but the roses within are dust. The shore is still there, but the ship that once moored there raised its anchors long ago, and sailed over the horizon forever.

But that is idle sentiment, and has nothing to do with George and Theo. The whole Lambert family was perfectly satisfied with the state of affairs between the two, and though George had not yet popped the formal decisive question, everyone in the house already knew exactly what Theo’s answer would be. Mrs. Lambert thought the question was taking far too long to come.

“Psha, my dear,” General Lambert laughed at her. “There is time enough. Theo is barely seventeen. George is not yet forty, for goodness sake, and he has to wait to get his mother’s approval from Virginia first. What is the rush?”

“But what if Madam Esmond refuses?” his wife fretted.

“That will be a sad day for all of us,” the General replied. “But let us imagine she will consent. I cannot fancy anyone in the whole world refusing Theo anything she has set her heart on—and I am certain her heart is entirely set on this match.”

So the whole household waited with bated breath for Madam Esmond’s reply, trembling daily for fear that French privateers patrolling the Atlantic might seize the packet ship carrying the precious, long-awaited letter.

A few weeks after Harry Warrington, our Virginian, joined his new regiment, his commanding officer landed fresh from America: none other than James Wolfe, the man whose gallantry at Cape Breton had won him a promotion to lead the regiment’s newly formed second battalion. Harry went to call on his new commander with unfeigned respect and open good will, for all of England was already turning its eyes to this rising young soldier. After a string of humiliating failures by once-celebrated officers—from the 2nd Duke of Marlborough, who proved no worthy heir to his great ancestor’s fame, to Lord George Sackville, whose cowardice at Minden had thrown away a certain victory—the nation hungered for military glory, and the crown’s ministers were desperate for a general who could deliver it. Both Wolfe and General Lambert, Harry’s old mentor, had business keeping them in London, and their old easy friendship was renewed at once: no one rejoiced more than Lambert to see his young protégé Harry’s fortunes rise.
Whenever he was off duty, Harry could listen to Wolfe recounting last year’s campaigns for hours. The general spoke with a frank, generous simplicity that would later mark Nelson: he hid no part of his thoughts, owned to every feat and every misstep openly. Some of the fine powdered dandies loitering about St. James’s might sneer at his unpolished eagerness, but in our small circle of friends, we drank in every word he said. For all his military fire, there was a boyish romance to him: he loved music and poetry, and would later say on the very eve of his death that he would rather have written Gray’s *Elegy* than won a great battle. It was inevitable that George Warrington, the bookish elder Virginian brother, should grow close to a man of such literary tastes. Both were already betrothed, both eager to lay laurels at their beloveds’ feet, and no doubt their many sentimental conversations together would make for wonderful reading, could we transcribe them word for word. George wrote of the friendship years later:
> “I had the honour of seeing a great deal of the famous General Wolfe during his last stay in London. We shared an interest that never failed to hold our attention, and I could not but marvel at his simplicity, his candour, and that singular, glorious bravery that defined him. He was deep in love, and hungry for heaps of laurels to lay at his mistress’s feet. ‘If it be a sin to covet honour,’ he would cry, quoting his beloved Henry V, ‘I am the most offending soul alive.’ He got his fill of glory on that last day of his life, sure enough. He did not seem merely a resolute soldier doing his duty, but a medieval knight riding out in search of dragons. I have had the honour to know another great chief from my own Virginia, of a very different, far sterner temper, and I scarce know which I admire more: the Briton’s chivalrous fire, or our Virginian’s more than Roman constancy.”
With General Lambert’s official duties keeping him tied to London, his whole family settled contentedly in town, and George was perfectly happy in the quiet of Southampton Row, wandering the leafy green walks of Bedford Gardens with no urge to travel far. He made one short pilgrimage out to Castlewood, where he stayed a few days in the old chamber his grandfather Esmond had occupied as a boy, received politely by the members of the family in residence. But he would far rather have been back in London, by the side of the young lady whose company pleased him far more than Lord Castlewood’s circle—though the ladies of the house were all gracious, especially Lady Maria, who was utterly charmed when George and Parson Sampson read his new tragedy aloud to them. The chaplain had fallen so in love with the play that it was all down to his influence, not Samuel Johnson’s, that the work ever made it to the stage. Johnson had indeed pressed the tragedy on his friend David Garrick for Drury Lane, but Garrick had just struck a deal to stage a new play by John Home, author of the hit *Douglas*, so George’s *Carpezan* was taken over to John Rich at Covent Garden, who accepted it at once.
On opening night, George threw an elegant supper for his friends at the Bedford Head tavern just steps from the theatre, after which the whole party traipsed over to Covent Garden to claim their box. George himself stayed behind at the coffee house with a small handful of companions, where messengers ran back and forth throughout the performance to bring him updates. The great Barry played the title role of Carpezan, Shuter took the part of the aged nobleman, Reddish made a perfect Ulric, and the King of Bohemia was played by a talented young Dublin actor named Hagan, who looked and performed the part to universal acclaim. Peggy Woffington as the heroine Sybilla looked a touch too old in the first act, but her much-doubted on-stage murder in the fourth act played out to the audience’s terrified delight, and Miss Wayn sang the plaintive ballad the page sings just as Sybilla is led to execution. The whole house agreed Barry was breathtakingly terrible and tender in that final scene, and the young actor Hagan won nothing but cheers for his grace and charm. Rich had spared no expense staging the play, though some whispered he had no business wheeling out the famous pantomime elephant, borrowed from a former harlequin show, to lead the procession of Janissaries in the final act—perched on the elephant’s back in full Turkish livery was one of George’s two black footmen, Gumbo, while the other sat whooping and applauding uproariously from the footmen’s gallery at all the right moments.
Sybilla’s execution was the turning point of the play: once her head fell, George’s friends breathed easy, and one messenger after another burst into the coffee house to tell him his tragedy was a full, unqualified success. Barry stepped forward at the final curtain to announce the play would run for a second night, and revealed to roaring applause that it was the first dramatic work of a young gentleman from Virginia.
We would have given anything to sit in the Lamberts’ box that night, to watch Theo’s anxious flutters turn to bright, tearful smiles as the audience’s cheers grew louder. Harry, sat next to her, had gone deadly pale during the tense fourth act—paler, Mrs. Lambert swore, than Barry caked in stage chalk. Once the final curtain fell, he clapped so hard he could scarcely feel his hands, as if Briareus’s hundred hands were not enough to make the noise he wanted. Wolfe and General Lambert cheered themselves hoarse; Mrs. Lambert of course was sobbing through the final scene, and even Hetty, who’d teased all week that the characters got exactly what they deserved, was bouncing in her seat with glee, little Charley on leave from his boarding school and Miss Lucy brought home especially from her own school both screaming with the rest of the crowd. Lord Castlewood and Lady Maria were in a box of their own; the Earl trotted backstage to congratulate Barry and the other actors, while Parson Sampson led the cheering in the pit, having signaled to Gumbo in the gallery earlier to follow his lead and make as much noise as he did.
The celebrations did not end at the theatre. There were suppers, and more suppers, that night. Gumbo threw a feast for all his fellow footmen in fine livery who’d turned out to cheer for his master’s play; Harry hosted a raucous dinner for ten of his new brother officers at the Star and Garter in Pall Mall, who had all come up from camp expressly to back *Carpezan*. The grandest supper of all, though, was hosted by George, with the lead actors of the play, the entire Lambert party, Samuel Johnson, the painter Joshua Reynolds, Lord Castlewood and Lady Maria, and a handful of other guests. Lady Maria happened to sit right beside young Hagan, the actor who had played the King of Bohemia. George, of course, found himself sat next to Theo, and passed a very pleasant evening indeed. The mood grew more boisterous as the punch was passed around, and Lady Maria laughed gaily when her turn came to toast “The King of Hungary.” The young actor, full of fire and eloquence both on and off the stage, swore that he had “died” once already that night on the stage, and would gladly die a hundred more times on the same field; dead or alive, he vowed, he was her ladyship’s most humble servant. If only he had a real crown instead of his pasteboard stage diadem, he cried, he would lay it at her feet that very instant. Lord Castlewood and Esmond were not at all pleased by the young man’s excessive gallantry, which they rightly put down to his having taken far more than his share of the punch bowl. Theo and Hetty, new to the wild ways of theatre folk, were a little startled by his outburst, but the far more experienced Lady Maria took it all in excellent good part. When the hour grew late, the gentlemen escorted the ladies out to their waiting coaches, and many of the party drifted back to the supper room for more drink. By the end of the night, Carpezan (Barry) had to be carried home in a sedan chair, the King of Bohemia woke the next morning with a brutal headache, and the playwright himself, though he recalled making a dozen grand speeches, was utterly shocked when half a dozen of his guests showed up on his doorstep the next day for the second round of supper he’d drunkenly invited them to the night before.
George had walked Mrs. Lambert and her daughters to their coach the night before, all three ladies flurried, over-excited, and glowing with joy, and of course George was round at their Soho house the very next day, going over every detail of the play, the audience, the actors, over and over again. Mrs. Lambert, who had heard endless warnings that theatre people were dangerous company for young men, fretted a little that George would spend too much time lingering in the green room.
George smiled. “I have a perfect amulet against all green room temptations that I do not fear in the least,” he said, and looked right into Theo’s eyes, as if her gaze was all the protection he would ever need.
“Why should he be afraid, mamma?” Theo asked simply, with no thought of guile or danger in her head.
“No, my darling, I don’t think he need be afraid,” Mrs. Lambert said, kissing her forehead.
“Pray tell me, who would fall in love with that painted old creature who played the lead heroine?” Hetty tossed her head. “She must be old enough to be his mother.”
“And pray who says no woman can have a heart once she passes a certain age?” Mrs. Lambert snapped back, suddenly sharp. “I should hope your father does not think me past caring for him, miss. He does not sneer at age, whatever silly little girls just out of the schoolroom may do. You would do well to remember the fifth commandment, Hetty!”
“I did not think I was breaking it by saying an actress was old enough to be George’s mother,” Hetty protested.
“George’s own mother is exactly my age, miss! We were at school together, for heaven’s sake! I will not have our age made a mock of by our own children, and I would thank you to spare us that, if you please. Do you think I am too old to care for you, George?”
“I am only too glad that my own mother is as kind and dear as you are, Aunt Lambert,” George said warmly, and no man who has ever been newly engaged will think it strange that he was perfectly, genuinely fond of his future mother-in-law. General Lambert, for his part, joked that he was jealous: Mrs. Lambert doted on George more than any other person in the house. She fussed over him if he so much as sneezed, sent him her own special health recipes, dressed Theo in her very finest gowns to meet him, and then always found some excuse to slip out of the room and leave the two of them alone, pretending she had to tend to the younger children or give an order to the servants, lingering just outside the door for a few minutes before coming back to sit, perfectly artless, at her worktable, as if she had no idea the two young people had been blushing and stammering at each other in her absence.
At last the long-awaited letter arrived from Virginia, in Madam Esmond’s sharp, neat handwriting. George trembled and blushed before he broke the seal. It was his mother’s reply to the letter he had sent months before, telling her of Harry’s commission and his own engagement to Theo. She fully approved of Harry’s advancement, and wrote that she had no great objection to early marriages: she would take George’s glowing portrait of Theo with the appropriate allowance for lovers’ bias, and hope for his sake that the girl was all he claimed. It was a pity, she wrote, that the young lady appeared to have no fortune of her own, for though the Esmonds were wealthy in land, they had little ready cash to spare. But Heaven had blessed them with more than enough to provide for their children, and their sons’ wives would be welcomed as her own. She asked only to hear more from Mr. and Mrs. Lambert before she gave a full, formal reply, and admitted freely that she had once held higher hopes for George, who as a Warrington might have courted the greatest heiress in the kingdom—but since Heaven had seen fit for him to choose her old friend’s daughter, she would acquiesce. The letter was being brought over by a Mr. Van den Bosch, a wealthy Albany landowner who had just bought a vast estate bordering the Esmonds’ Virginian property, and was sailing to England to place his young granddaughter in a boarding school. Madam Esmond wrote that she was no mercenary woman, and did not urge her sons to pay the girl attention merely because she was one of the richest heiresses in the colonies—but if Harry could find a good, suitable companion for life in her, then Madam Esmond would have the joy of both her sons settled near her in her declining years.
The letter was not warm, and it was clear Madam Esmond was far from fully satisfied, but it held her formal consent to the engagement. George ran all the way to Soho to share the news, and the Lamberts read the joy on his face before he even opened his mouth. Mrs. Lambert took Theo’s hand and kissed her, her eyes bright, and George, pale and trembling a little, turned to General Lambert and said: “Madam Esmond has given her blessing to our attachment, sir. I can only hope you will be as kind to me as she has been.”
“God bless you, my dear boy!” the General said, laying his hand on George’s head. “I could not ask for a better son. No need for kneeling, you two—though you may thank the good Lord for giving you the best little wife in all England. You never once gave me a moment’s heartache, my dear,” he said to Theo, “and happy is the man who wins you.”
No doubt the young couple knelt before them after the custom of the day, and Mrs. Lambert kissed both of them and soaked her handkerchief through with happy tears. Hetty was not present for the soft, sentimental scene, and when she heard the news at first she tossed her head and laughed sharply, saying “Is that all? I have known the two of them were in love for months. Do you think I have no eyes to see, no ears to hear?”—but later, in private, she flung her arms around Theo’s neck and hugged her so tight it hurt, vowing no one would ever love her sister half as much as she did. She teased George mercilessly after that, but he was too happy to care, and too generous to miss that her sharp jokes were only a mask for a quiet, unspoken jealousy.
When they all re-read Madam Esmond’s letter a few days later, they noticed how vague it was: there was no promise of a marriage settlement, only a note that the young couple would be welcome to live at the Virginia estate. General Lambert shook his head over it, his face grave.
“Bah!” George laughed. “The play will earn me three hundred pounds. I can write a new tragedy every year if I put my mind to it. We can live very comfortably on that.”
“On that, and your patrimony,” the General said.
George hesitated, and then admitted the truth: what with paying off his mother’s old debts, covering Harry’s commission and his former gambling debts, and the ransom he had paid to get himself back after he was kidnapped months before, his patrimony was almost entirely spent.
The General’s face grew even graver, but when he saw Theo’s eyes fill with tears of alarm, he pulled her into his arms and swore no poverty on earth would stop his little girl from getting the happiness she wanted. George frankly admitted he had no desire at all to sail back to Virginia and live entirely dependent on his mother’s sharp, domineering temper. Why should he not stay in England, write more plays, study for the bar, and carve out a name for himself here? He set to work planning a second tragedy at once, bringing pages of his new work to Theo and Hetty to read. Hetty yawned over the verses, but Theo swore every line was even more perfect than the last.
The engagement was formally announced to the rest of the Warrington family, and George sent a ceremonious letter to his great-uncle Sir Miles Warrington. For a little while Sir Miles saw no great harm in the match, though he huffed that George, with his name and connections, could have “looked higher” than a penniless girl with no fortune of her own. The truth was, Sir Miles assumed Madam Esmond had settled a vast sum of money on her elder son, and that George was very well off indeed. When he found out the truth: that George’s patrimony was gone, that he was penniless and entirely dependent on his mother’s good will, his rage knew no bounds. He wrote off to Madam Esmond in Virginia fulminating against her two profligate, irresponsible sons, and declaring that the Lamberts were no more than scheming fortune hunters who had inveigled his foolish nephew into a ruinous match. He would barely give George half a finger to shake when his nephew called at his London house, and never once invited him in to share the famous family home-brewed small beer. He was a little softer on Harry, who had seen active service and been named in dispatches for gallantry: Harry had sown his wild oats, he said, and was trying to make amends, but George was a young prodigal rushing headlong to ruin, whose name was only spoken in the Warrington household with

Our soft, tender human hearts shrink from lingering on the sharp ache of parting, so I will waste no time dwelling on every raw, tangled feeling Harry Warrington carried with him as he said goodbye to his brother and all the friends who had grown dear to him across his years in England. His plight was no singular one: thousands of men stood exactly where he did that day, bound for the western military campaigns. Had not the brave General Wolfe paused before his own embarkation to kiss his mother goodbye—his gallant father had already passed away while Wolfe was off fighting the glorious Louisbourg campaign—and wrap his betrothed in one last tight, lingering embrace? Had not stout Admiral Holmes, before weighing anchor with his squadron of the Somerset, the Terrible, the Northumberland, the Royal William, the Trident, the Diana, and the Seahorse (his own flag flying from the Dublin), said his goodbyes to Mrs. Holmes and his daughters? Even Admiral Saunders, who set sail the very day after Holmes, was not exempt from the soft tug of human affection that ties men to the homes they leave behind.

Away the ships go, their crews of jovial, weathered sailors ploughing through tumbling grey waves, while poor Black-eyed Susan lingering on the shore watches the last vessel shrink to a speck against the sunset. It dwindles westward, and the darkling night falls soft over the ocean. The men are gone, but their hearts linger back home for a little while yet. In the quiet of that first night at sea, every man’s heart swells with an unutterable softness, thinking of the loved ones left behind. A chorus of tender, pleading prayers rises up to the Father both at sea and on shore: from the wife kneeling in tears beside her now-empty bedside, from the mother huddled with her children around the home fire pouring out their supplications, and from the seaman leaning on the ship’s rail, gazing up at the unblinking stars as the vessel cuts through roaring midnight waters. By the next dawn, the sun rises on ordinary life once more, and everyone returns to their daily toil and duty.

George Warrington travels with his brother, lingering for some days at Portsmouth waiting for a favourable wind to blow the fleet out of harbour. He shakes Wolfe’s pale hand one last time, looks on his gaunt, determined face, and watches the vessels depart amid the clangour of church bells and the thunder of cannon salutes booming from the shore. The very next day he is back at his London home, throwing himself into the absorbing, self-focused work that nearly every man of thirty years has long since apprenticed himself to. He feels a sharp little twinge of sadness when he pauses by Harry’s old lodgings and glances through the window to the small bedroom his brother once occupied, seeing half-burned scraps of Harry’s notes still scattered in the cold grate. But within minutes he is hurrying on to Dean Street, whispering soft nothings by the fitful firelight to his clinging, adoring sweetheart. Theo is so overjoyed to have him home that she is almost ashamed of it. Is it not heartless to be this giddy, when poor Hetty is still sunk in melancholy? “Don’t, sir!” she murmurs, flushing, when he teases her for it. “Well, I ought to be wretched, and it is very, very wicked of me if I’m not.” No one could blame the soft-hearted girl for that little rush of guilty joy, of course. The dim room fills with light the second the servants enter bearing supper and lamps, the rest of the Lambert family file in, and conversation turns general.
Everyone in town now knows the fleet’s destination: its force is more than large enough to rout every French soldier in Canada, and under an officer as fiery and determined as Wolfe, it will surely undo every blunder and disaster of earlier campaigns. Wolfe looks dreadfully ill, it is true, but a great soul burns bright in that frail body, and both the ministers and the whole country hold their breath in hope of victory. After supper, Mr. Lambert leads his modest household in their regular evening prayers, George counted fully as one of the family, and as they all kneel together to pray for the safety of all travellers by land and sea, Theo and Hetty huddle side by side on the rug.

As the weeks slip by, the ships speed farther and farther west, carrying Harry ever further from home. George’s first tragedy *Carpezan* has now run a successful thirty to forty performances, and the theatre has moved on to new productions. Some loyal fans grumble at how fickle the town is, to tire of such a masterpiece so soon, but the sceptical George takes the fate of his play with perfect philosophy. He pockets the hundred pounds the bookseller Dodsley pays him for the printed edition, and the two hundred plus guineas the theatre manager hands over for its run, all glowing reviews ringing in his ears as he sets straight to work on a new play he hopes will outshine his first.
These studies, and the sweet, all-consuming new happiness of his courtship of Theo, make the months slip past unnoticed. It is the happiest time of youth and life: when love is first spoken and returned, when the dearest eyes greet you every day, and the fondest lips never tire of whispering their sweet secrets, when the parting goodnight look carries a delicious promise of tomorrow, when your heart overflows so full of joy you have kindness left to spare for the whole world, when doubt feels like cowardice, misfortune seems impossible, and poverty feels like no more than a sweet little trial of constancy. Theo’s parents, who remember their own prime all too well, sit soft and quiet by, watching the young people play out their pretty little gentle comedy. On one of the few occasions George is temporarily away from home, he dutifully writes to Theo to note that he paused to look up at the windows of their old happy house in Dean Street, wondering who now sits in the little chamber where the two of them spent so many sweet hours.

We can trace the course of these months, and keep track of all their friends, through a long, lively letter George writes to Harry, dated 20th August 1759, from his old window opposite Bedford Gardens:
> “Why are you gone tramping over rugged rocks, bleak northern shores, sweltering summer heat and nipping winter cold out in the colonies, when you could have been in Germany reaping heaps of military laurels with the rest of the King’s regiments? They come back from Minden strung with honours as covered as a Jack-in-the-Green on May-day. Our six regiments fought absolute wonders, and our cavalry would have wiped the French off the field entirely if that fool Lord George Sackville had just obeyed orders. When Prince Ferdinand shouted ‘Charge!’ he claimed he could not hear, or could not translate the German word for ‘Forward’, so we only beat the French instead of annihilating them, as we surely would have done if Lord Granby or even your humble brother had been in command. My lord is back in town now, shouting for a court martial to clear his name. He held his head high enough in prosperity, and in disgrace he carries on with such unshakable arrogance that one almost finds oneself admiring the man. He looks half like he envies poor Admiral Byng, as if the government refusing to shoot him is a sheer lack of respect.
> “The Duke of Cumberland has had notice he ought to make ready to leave this world of grandeur, victory, and bitter disappointment. A mild palsy attack struck his royal highness, and pale Death popped his head in at the door, as it were, and said ‘I shall be back another day’. Tyrant as he was in his prime, this prince has behaved with noble dignity in disgrace, and no king ever had a truer servant than our late king found in his son. I always do find myself rooting for the losing side, don’t I, and bridling against the men who win all the glory? I have gone to hear that famous Mr. P——, your general’s great patron, speak in the House of Commons two or three times now, and I cannot stand his grandiloquent posturing. I wish some little David would come along and topple that strutting giant over. Every thought and every line he speaks is deliberately posed for effect. I much prefer Barry the actor’s plain, natural manner, even if Mr. P.’s delivery is far more thunderous and imposing.
> “My new play *Pocahontas* is coming on famously. Barry is delighted with his part as Captain John Smith, though he insists Smith ought to wear a red coat with blue facings and an epaulet. I am fighting him tooth and nail to dress the part exactly like the portraits of Queen Elizabeth’s gentlemen up at Hampton Court: a crisp ruff, a neat square beard, square-toed leather shoes. ‘And what of Pocahontas? Are you planning to have her tattooed?’ Uncle Lambert teases me. Hagan has the part of the native warrior who loves her, and who sees her partiality for Captain Smith, then nobly risks his own life to rescue Smith from execution. I am sure his performance will be a great hit. Hagan is a strange old fish: his mouth is forever full of play lines and dramatic rant, but he is good, honest, and brave, if I do not miss my guess. He is furious he has been cast as Sir O’Brallaghan in Mr. Macklin’s new farce *Love A-la-mode*, saying he ‘will not de-grace his tongue with imitations of that rascal brogue’. As if he needs to fake a brogue, when his own natural Irish twang is thick enough to cut with a knife!
> “Shall I tell you a secret? Shall I keep it from you? Shall I hurt your feelings, rouse you to a fit of jealous rage, and make you beg your commanding officer for immediate leave to sail home to Europe? Know then, that though our *Carpezan* closed long ago, cousin Maria Esmond haunts the playhouse every night. Tom Spencer has spotted her again and again in the gallery, always turning up on the nights Hagan is performing. Quick! Burroughs, fetch Mr. Warrington’s boots and portmanteau! Order a chaise and four to Portsmouth at once! That letter I burned that morning when we were both at breakfast, that I told you never to ask about? I may as well spill the cat out of the bag now, when you are thousands of miles away: it was a note from cousin M., begging me not to breathe a word about her little theatre visits to anyone. But I cannot resist whispering just to you that Maria is at this very moment consoling herself for her old heartbreak as fast as she possibly can. Should I spoil her sport? Should I tell her brother? Is this affair any business of ours? What have the Esmonds ever done for you and me but win all our money at the card tables? Yet I still like our noble cousin. It seems to me he would be a good man if he could—at least, he would have been, once, before he was set on a path of vice it is probably far too late to drag him back from now. Oh happy farmers! Our old Virginia plantation was dull, but thank heaven we were raised there. We were kept a little sheltered, but we were never made slaves to gambling, or to the wicked, cruel company of the sort of men who waylaid my poor Harry on the high roads of England and stripped him of all he had. I do not think you are a bit the worse for that robbery, you silly thing. Now you are off to make a great name for yourself, kill more French dragons, and become a famous commander. Our mother will soon be bragging about her son the Captain, then the Colonel, then the General, and have his portrait painted all decked out with stars and epaulets, while poor dawdling old me will be no more than a scribbling poet, or if luck turns my way, a snug government clerk with a little cottage at Richmond or Kew, and half a dozen little picaninnies bobbing curtsies at the garden gate every time their uncle the General rides up on his great war charger, his aide-de-camp’s pockets stuffed full of gingerbread for all his nephews and nieces. You are the one meant to brandish Mars’s great sword. As for me, I look forward to a quiet life: a little home of my own, a little library stuffed full of books, and a little someone dulce ridentem, dulce loquentem sitting on the other side of the fire, smiling and chattering, as I scribble away at my plays. I am so perfectly happy with this prospect, that I catch myself afraid it might slip away from me, and even to my dearest Hal I am almost shy of speaking of how bright my future looks. What do I care for grand ambition, when this happiness is almost within my grasp? What do I care for wars, with this soft, beatific peace waiting right around the corner?
> “Our mother’s old friend Mynheer Van den Bosch has been off on a tour back to Holland to track down his long-lost family, and much to everyone’s surprise he found them. That daughter of his, the one our mother once hoped would make you a perfect wife, has spent the last six months at Kensington School, and is coming out into society with a hundred pretty accomplishments that are supposed to turn her into the perfect fine lady. Her papa brought her to Dean Street to make a curtsy the other day, and it was the most elegant curtsy I ever saw. Though she is barely seventeen, no sixty year old Mayfair dowager could carry herself with more ease. She conversed with Aunt Lambert as if they were equals, treated the girls like silly little chits—to Hetty’s great fury and Theo’s huge amusement—chatted politics with the General, and gossiped about the last routs, new gowns, operas, fashions, and scandals with such perfect poise that, barring one or two small blunders, you would swear Miss Lydia was born and bred in the heart of Mayfair. She says she means to live in the court end of town, and has no patience at all for her father’s choice of lodging in Monument Yard. For anyone who favours a pretty dark beauty, there is no sweeter little mignonne creature alive. But my taste, dearest brother, you know full well…”

The rest of the letter dissolves into a page of rapturous, flowery praise for Theo, full of the sort of poetic quotations and gushings no editor could possibly reprint in polite company. Gentlemen and ladies of a certain age will no doubt remember when they indulged in exactly the same kind of rhapsodic foolishness in their own youth, when they could not stop singing the praises of their beloved, when all the flowers of life were in full bloom and every spring bird was singing loud in their chest. The twigs may be bare now, the leaves long fallen, but we have no reason not to look back soft and fond on that bright vernal time. And for you young people, whose May (or perhaps April?) of life has not even begun yet, you do not need to linger over other people’s love rhapsodies. Rest assured, when your own spring comes, kind Nature will warm all your flowers into full bloom, and rouse your glad young hearts to pour out their own full, happy song.

As George Warrington noted in the letter quoted just prior, for all the messy gambling disputes Lord Castlewood had once had with his younger brother Harry, the two kinsmen remained on easy, friendly terms, meeting with all the warmth of long acquainted relations. Should George need a frank to skip the exorbitant postage fees for a letter home, an introduction to gain admittance at St James’s, or a reserved spot in the House of Lords gallery to catch a fiery debate, his cousin was never anything but happy to oblige. He was a sharp, witty companion, and would bend over backwards to advance any of George’s interests—so long as his own were never put at risk.

At this point, he went so far as to promise he would pull every string he had with the current administration to secure George a steady, respectable government post. George had grown more averse by the day to sailing back to Virginia, and placing himself once more under the iron, unyielding rule of his mother Madam Esmond. It was no mere sentiment keeping him in England: London’s wide world of coffee house debates, theatre nights, and clever, congenial company suited him far better than any life he could carve out back on the plantation. A planter’s idle, quiet life might have suited him well enough, if he could have enjoyed true independence there. But in Virginia, he was nothing but the first, and as he saw it the worst treated, of his mother’s subjects. The very thought of returning home with his young bride Theo made his stomach turn: he could not bear the dull, rigid routine, the constant petty squabbles over household management, the endless jealousies and clashing opinions that would define their days the second they stepped off the ship. It was far better to scrape by on quiet freedom and a small income in England, surrounded by people who understood them, with the faint bright hope of future distinction, than to drag his soft, gentle wife into a life of unending subordination to Madam Esmond’s will.

So George accepted Castlewood’s promise of patronage with wholehearted eagerness. His lordship, to be fair, had never done much to provide even for his own younger brother, and for all his title of peer, his own position in society was far from secure. But we always believe what we wish to be true, and George chose to set great store by his kinsman’s offer of help. Unlike the rest of the Warrington family, Castlewood was unfailingly gracious when he learned of George’s engagement to Miss Theo Lambert. He called on her parents at their home in Soho, sang George’s praises to them, and praised Theo to George, and made himself so unfailingly charming that the kind, unworldly Lamberts forgot all the unsavoury rumours that clung to his name, and decided the gossips of the town must be the wicked, scandalous ones, not him. He swore he was a better man for spending time in their company—any man would be, he said. He left all his rakish worldliness and vice hanging up with his coat in the hall, and only put it back on when he climbed back into his coach to return to his usual circles. What weary worldling sailing through life’s storms has not found some quiet, calm harbour like that, to dock at for a little rest? It is very possible Castlewood was genuinely a better man for the hours he spent with the Lamberts, no hypocrite at all for that little stretch of time.

The Lambert elders certainly did not think any worse of his lordship when he openly confessed his quiet admiration for Theo. The fondness was perfectly genuine, and he never pretended it ran very deep.

“It won’t keep me up at night, and I am not going to break my heart that Miss Lambert prefers someone else,” he told Mrs Lambert, once. “I only wish that when I was a young man, I’d had the good fortune to meet someone as innocent and good as your daughter. I might have avoided so much harm. But innocent, good young women never crossed my path back then, or they would surely have made a better man of me.”

“Surely, my lord, it is not too late,” Mrs Lambert said softly.

Castlewood started back, misunderstanding her at first. “Not too late, madam?” he asked, confused.

She blushed. “Too late to court my dear daughter, my lord, yes—but never too late to repent. We read no man is turned away at the eleventh hour, so there is no reason you should give up hope.”

“Perhaps I know my own heart better than you,” he said, his tone quiet and plaintive. “I speak French and German fluently, you know why? I learned both in the nursery. A man who learns those languages later in life can never get the perfect accent on his tongue. It is the same with goodness. I cannot learn it at my age. I can only watch others live it, and admire them. When I find myself on the side opposite Lazarus, will Miss Theo toss me a drop of water? Do not frown! I know I am bound for there, Mrs Lambert. Some folks are fated that way, and I think a good number of my own family are among them. Some people are wishy-washy, you can never tell which way their moral scales will tip. But others are predestined angels, flying straight to heaven naturally, doing good without even trying.”

“Oh, my lord, why should you not be counted among the predestined?” the fond matron cried. “While there is still a day left, still an hour, there is hope!”

“I know what you are thinking, my dear madam—nay, I can see your prayers in your very face. But what good can they do?” Castlewood asked sadly. “You do not know the half of our worldly lives, how early they begin, how selfish nature, then necessity, then education have made us. It is Fate holding the reins of the chariot, and we cannot escape our doom. I know better. I see better people than I am, and I still go my own way. My way? No, not mine—Fate’s. And Fate is not entirely unkind to us, for it lets us stumble across good souls like yours every now and then.” He took her hand, bowed to her with melancholy grace, and looked her full in the face. Every word he said was true. There is no greater mistake than to assume weak, bad men are strangers to soft feelings, or lack all sensibility. The only catch is that the good feeling never lasts—those moments of sentiment are a kind of debauch for old libertines, as if the very softness and grief of good people adds a new, sharp flavour to their pleasures. Mrs Lambert, of course, knew nothing of the inner workings of his mind. To her, he was a deeply interesting, much maligned man, far better than his reputation made him out to be. Of course there was still hope for him.

Only time would tell which of the two of them had the right measure of his character. For now, even if the lady’s endless, fond prayers for the rake’s repentance never managed to reform him, they certainly did no harm. Kind-souled women—and what good woman is not a born physician of souls?—dote over a reprobate the way doctors hover over a dangerous, high-stakes case. The second their patient recovers their health, their interest drifts to the next sick man to tend to.

While his “malady” was still under treatment, Mrs Lambert could never get enough of her interesting new friend. A fast friendship bloomed between Castlewood and the entire Lambert household. It would be unfair to pretend that no small worldly motive crept in alongside her spiritual hopes for his soul, of course—even the purest Eden guarded by flaming angels finds some little crack for worldliness to slip through. Her own son Jack was soon to take holy orders, after all. Castlewood had already hinted that his current chaplain, the dissolute heterodox Mr Sampson, would likely soon leave his post, and the small, quiet, well-paid church living attached to the family estate would be vacant, perfect for a young clergyman of good principles and gentle manners, happy with a modest stipend and a small, friendly congregation.

So the two families grew close. The female members of the Castlewood household, ever on their best behaviour, came calling at the Lamberts’ drawing room more than once, curtsying politely to the parents and complimenting the two young ladies. Lady Castlewood’s weekly card assemblies were now open to Mrs Lambert and her girls. It was true everyone played cards there—everybody in London gambled these days: the King himself did, all the bishops, every peer and peeress in the land. No one was forced to play if they did not wish to, and there was no reason to feel guilty about the practice when such august, respected figures indulged in it every day. Mrs Lambert attended her ladyship’s routs more than once, and was grateful for the warm welcome she received, and delighted to see how much her daughters’ beauty was admired by all the guests.

As readers will recall from earlier letters, there was a family of Dutch-American extraction, neighbours of Madam Esmond’s in Virginia, who had come to England with a very strong, explicit letter of recommendation from her to her two sons. The match-making matron’s intentions were so clear that Mrs Lambert could not miss them at all. George was already engaged to Theo, and poor Harry, who had once been the target of the plan, was away on military service in Canada—something Hetty Lambert’s mother was secretly a little relieved by. She teased George openly, telling him he ought to obey his mother’s commands, break off his engagement to Theo, and court Miss Lydia Van den Bosch, who was ten times, no, a hundred times richer than her own poor daughter, and far more beautiful to boot.

“That much I will own,” George laughed. “She is prettier, richer, and very possibly even cleverer than my Theo. Mr Samuel Johnson is far cleverer than I am, too—Mr Hagan the actor is far taller and handsomer, Sir James Lowther far richer. But you do not suppose I am jealous of any of those three men, or that Theo would jilt me for any of them, do you? So why should I not admit Lydia is prettier, richer, livelier, better bred? Call her an angel if you like. My Theo is not afraid. Are you, child?”

“Never, George,” Theo said, her eyes so bright and honest they could shame any jealousy out of even the most sceptical man. And after that little exchange, if Mrs Lambert suddenly remembered she had left her scissors, or her thimble, or even her handkerchief in the parlour a few rooms away, and ducked out for two minutes, you would not catch me the least bit surprised to find George stood very close to Theo when she returned, his hand just slipping away from hers, her cheeks flushed bright pink. You would not catch me pretending I have any idea what they got up to in those two short minutes. Would you, dear reader? Do you not remember what you got up to when your own sweetheart came calling? If you were not there in that room with them, there is no sense crying shame and scandal. Shame on you, Mrs Grundy, you busybody.

With Harry off fighting in Canada, and George irrevocably engaged to Theo, Madam Esmond’s little scheme to marry one of her sons to the rich Lydia was dead in the water. So why should Mrs Lambert not have a new scheme of her own? Now that Lydia was free, surely her son Jack, home from Oxford, would make a perfect match for the beautiful, wealthy little heiress? That was the plan she chattered on about to General Lambert, who as usual laughed and called her a silly old goose for her pains. No harm in it, she protested. Madam Esmond had explicitly asked them to welcome the Van den Bosches to London, and it was not her fault Harry was off risking his life for the crown. Would he rather Harry abandon his regiment, throw away his reputation, sail back to England just to marry Lydia and break Hetty’s heart? We need not go into the rest of her very unconvincing arguments, nor be rude enough to point out that General Lambert was perfectly right to tease his fond, meddlesome wife.

Back then, there was a sharp divide between the lofty court set and the respectable merchant class of the City of London. When Mr Van den Bosch first arrived in London, he and his granddaughter barely mixed outside of City circles. He lodged near his merchant agent, and when Lydia came home from her boarding school for holidays, he took her on day trips out to Islington or Highgate, or an occasional walk in the Artillery Ground at Bunhill Fields. They attended the Baptist meeting house in Finsbury Fields, and snuck off a few times to see Mr Garrick perform, or the funny, roguish Mr Foote at the Little Theatre. An invitation to a Lord Mayor’s feast was the highest possible treat for the old merchant, and dancing with a young mercer’s son at the Hampstead assembly gave Lydia more joy than any grand ball could have. When George first called on his mother’s friends, he found their old acquaintance from the Temple, Mr Draper, hovering around Lydia, paying her endless attentions. The married lawyer warned George to watch his back, that the girl came with a very large fortune attached to her. A young Quaker gentleman named Mr Drabshaw, nephew of Madam Esmond’s Bristol agent Mr Trail, was also constantly at Lydia’s side, and flew into a jealous panic the second George made his first appearance.

Wishing to do honour to his mother’s neighbours, George invited the Van den Bosches to a dinner at his own apartments. Naturally, he invited his own friends the Lamberts to join them, and every last one of them had to admit Lydia was a little marvel of beauty. She had the tiny, light foot of a fairy, the arms and neck and flashing dark eyes of a little brown huntress of Diana, fresh from the woods. She carried a soft, plaintive Virginian lilt to her speech—an accent that all the rude Londoners loved to mock in bad Cockney impressions, but that I say, for my part, is utterly charming when it comes from a pretty girl’s lips. What right has anyone to sneer at Miss Whittington for dropping her h’s, or the bonnie Miss Nicol Jarvie for her Scottish burr, or the lovely Miss Molony for her Dublin lilt? All accents sound sweet on pretty lips, no matter if they come from a rose, a thistle, a shamrock, or the new star-spangled flag across the ocean. Lydia’s accent was nothing but pleasant the second she stepped on English soil, you may be sure of it—her schoolmistress in Kensington would never have done a poor job polishing her speech.

After six months at Kensington Academy, where according to her grandfather’s calculations she was supposed to learn every possible ladylike accomplishment, Lydia returned home happy, and ready to step out into society. At first her world was small, but she was a determined little thing, set on expanding her social circle, and her doting old grandfather followed wherever she led. He had been treated very harshly as a young man, he said, and it had done no one any good. He had been strict with his own son, and the boy had turned out badly. As for little Lyddy, he was determined to give her every bit of happiness he could. Did not George think he was right? It was rumoured in Virginia, he said, that the young Warrington boys at Castlewood would have been far happier if Madam Esmond had let them make a few more of their own choices as children. George could not disagree, nor bring himself to talk the kind old man out of spoiling his granddaughter. And the Lamberts, of course, could not help but welcome the gentle, generous old man—Madam Esmond’s old friend—with open arms.

The second Lydia came home from school, Grandfather Van den Bosch moved them out of their old lodgings in Monument Yard to an elegant, fashionable house in Bloomsbury. At first all their old City friends followed them: merchants from Virginia Walk, the worthy tradesmen the old man did business with, their wives and sons and daughters, all of them fawning over the beautiful Miss Lyddy. But one by one, the old familiar outings stopped. No more day trips to Belsize House, no more jaunts to Deputy Higgs’ villa in Highbury, no more country dances at honest Mr Lutestring’s house in Hackney. Even their Sunday routine changed: oh, the horror of it! Old Mr Van den Bosch left Bethesda Chapel in Bunhill Row, and took a new pew at Queen Square Church.

Queen Square Church, of course, was just a short walk from George’s own lodgings in Southampton Row. Everyone could see exactly who Lydia was setting her cap for. Mr Draper, who had sung the old merchant’s praises to the skies just a few months prior, now took George aside to warn him, and told him all kinds of ugly new rumours about the Van den Bosches: that for all his bragging about noble Dutch ancestry, the old man had been born a nobody in Albany, that he had made his fortune through shady land speculation, privateering that was barely distinguishable from piracy, and the Guinea slave trade. His son, he said, had run off with a servant girl in a union that barely counted as marriage, been disowned, and died young, lucky to die peacefully in his own bed.

“Mr Draper has been telling you bad tales about me, I expect,” the placid old man said to George, when they met for tea one afternoon. “Well, we are all sinners. There is a little bit of truth to the bad things people say about all of us, and far more that is completely made up. Did he tell you my son and I fell out? I already told you that myself. Did he spin wicked stories about my family? The rascal liked my family well enough that he wanted me to marry Lyddy off to his own brother. Heaven bless her, I have had dozens of offers for her hand. And you, young sir, are the one I would have chosen for her. I don’t even mind that you prefer someone else—though begging your pardon, I cannot for the life of me see what you find in your Miss Lambert next to my Lyddy.”

“There is no accounting for taste, my good sir,” George replied, with his usual easy, charming smile.

“No, sir, it is a wonder of nature, that happens every day. Back when I kept a little store in Albany, there was a top-of-the-line gentleman who could have married my daughter, Lyddy’s mother, when she was young. She had a good fortune back then—back when her father and I had quarrelled, little Lyddy here would have been left a pauper, you see. But instead of my beautiful Bella, the fool chose a plain little girl no prettier than your Theo, who had

Before we follow Miss Lydia Van den Bosch’s adventures any further, we owe readers an explanation for that puzzling line in Mr. Warrington’s letter to his brother, referencing Lady Maria Esmond—a secret no properly respectable person could ever be expected to guess at first glance. How could innocent, well-bred young folks possibly imagine that a noblewoman of ancient line, long acquaintance with the world, the same lady we saw so deeply smitten with her young cousin Harry Warrington a mere dozen months prior, would throw all decorum to the wind? My very fingertips flush as I write it: she did not only fall in love with a man of far humbler birth, years her junior, but she married him, half in secret, behind the gossips’ backs, no less, with Parson Sampson tying the indissoluble knot at his little Mayfair chapel.

Do not condemn her out of hand, I beg you. Because Lady Maria once indulged, and then outgrew, a foolish partiality for her young cousin, must she never be allowed to love anyone else ever again? Are men the only souls granted the privilege of changing their hearts, and women to be shrieked at for daring to snatch a small share of comfort when it comes their way? Few invectives are ruder, less logical, than Hamlet’s rages against his mother over her second marriage. The truth of it is, tender, clinging creatures crave something to twine themselves around: when Hamlet Senior was gone, she wrapped herself round Claudius. We have known women so determined to attach their affections somewhere that they can twine round two gentlemen at once, if need be. Why should there be no new marriage feasts after the funeral baked meats are eaten? If you said grace over your dinner yesterday, is that any reason to go hungry today? The healthy appetite that relishes tonight’s supper is proof you will no doubt be ready for your dinner again at eight tomorrow evening. For my own part, whenever I have been the object of a fine lady’s favour (you may picture them as ravishing beauties of the highest rank, if you please), I have always reminded myself that a day will come when they will be fond of someone else. We are served à la Russe in this world, eaten one course at a time, just like the captives in Polyphemus’s cave: today me, tomorrow you. Some of these love devourers will consume dozens of us, young and old, tender and tough, plump and lean, fair and plain, with no discrimination, and one by one we slip down their omnivorous maws. Look at Lady Ogresham! We all remember how she gobbled up poor Tom Kydd last year, picked his bones clean, and tossed him aside. Now she has Ned Suckling trapped in her den, quivering and transfixed under her great predatory eyes. She creeps closer, he draws nearer, and soon there will be a few feeble pleas for mercy, and hobblegobble—he will vanish. Ah, it is a pity, too. I knew Maria Esmond had lost her heart many times before Harry Warrington ever stumbled on it, and I had fondly imagined he would be the last to hold it, that she would mourn her ill-fated love and cherish it in decent, quiet celibacy for the rest of her days. If I, in some foolish moment of dotage, were to fall in love tomorrow, I should still delude myself I owned the full fee simple of my beloved’s heart, not that I was merely a short-term tenant of a shabby old furnished apartment, where the dingy wine glasses have been clouded by a hundred pairs of lips, and the lumpy sofas are still mud-stained from the last lodger’s boots.

But this Maria, living a century ago, was a woman of no steady mind. You, dear reader who knows the world (and do not pretend you have no experience, for you have heard your mother tell the tales), know that an old flirt, when she tires of one passion, will inevitably run headlong into another. Flirting is just like drinking: when the brandy bottle is empty, the confirmed drinker will fall to gin. So if Maria Esmond found a successor for Harry Warrington, and set a new sultan on the throne of her heart, what else could anyone possibly have expected? That realm was like the Low Countries, long used to conquest, forever open to new invasions.

And the man who had won her was none other than Mr. Hagan, the young Irish actor who had played the lead in George Warrington’s tragedy. His voice was thrilling, his eye bright, his bearing noble; he looked so impossibly handsome in his gilt leather armour and great buckled periwig, speaking the poet’s glowing lines, that the lady surrendered her whole heart to him as Ariadne did to Bacchus, the moment her affair with Theseus was well and truly over. The young actor was both flattered and elated by the highborn lady’s attachment. He might have preferred a Lady Maria Hagan a few years younger, but no woman alive could have been more tenderly devoted to him. She clung to him so closely that when their secret marriage finally leaked out, and her furious noble family disowned her entirely, she retired with him to his humble little lodgings in Westminster without a second thought.

General Lambert brought the news home to his family from his office in Whitehall one day, and made merry over the tale with his wife and girls. Those were homely times, and a joke was none the worse for being a little broad: a fine lady would laugh over a raucous page of Fielding and weep over a letter in *Clarissa* that would make any modern lady’s eyes start from her head in horror. The merry General cracked every witticism he could think of: he joked about George accidentally having a hand in the match, about how furious Barry Lyndon would be when he heard the news, swore it was a shame cousin Hagan had not asked George to be his groomsman, that their first child ought to be named Carpezan or Sybilla after the tragedy, that they could never afford a full coach but might beg a chariot with pasteboard dragons from the manager of Rich’s Theatre, that the baby could be christened in Macbeth’s cauldron, with Harry Warrington and Harlequin as godfathers.

“Why shouldn’t she marry him if she likes him?” little Hetty piped up. “Why shouldn’t he love her just because she is a little older? Mamma is a little older than you, and you love her no less. You told me yourself, sir, that you were very poor when you married my mamma, and you were perfectly happy, and no one laughed at you!” The innocent child spoke out of pure unworldliness, with no knowledge of Lady Maria’s long history of follies.

“So her whole family has deserted her?” Miss Hett continued, after George confirmed how wild with rage all the Esomonds were: Lady Castlewood had gone into full formal mourning, Mr. Will swore he would cut the rascal actor’s ears off, and Madame de Bernstein was the most furious of all, half mad with mortification. “It is an insult to the family, of course, to have a relative of their rank marry a man of Mr. Hagan’s station, and I can imagine how indignant those fine ladies must be. But to desert her entirely? That is quite another matter.”

“Indeed, my dear child,” Mrs. Lambert intervened, “you do not understand what you are talking about. After Lady Maria’s conduct, no respectable person can possibly pay her a visit.”

“What conduct, mamma?”

“Never you mind,” her mother said, brushing the question away. “Little girls cannot be expected to know, and ought not to be curious to ask about, the sort of behaviour that has brought her ladyship to this pass. Suffice it to say I am shocked she was ever received in this house, and no honest person ought to associate with her now.”

“Then Aunt Lambert, I must be whipped and sent to bed!” George declared with mock gravity. “I will own, though I did not confess it before, while the affair was still private, that I have already been to visit my cousin the player and his lady wife. I found them in very shabby lodgings in Westminster, where that good fellow has the modesty to shelter not just his noble wife, but his old widowed mother, and a little brother he is putting through school. I came away quite liking the man, almost respecting him, even if I own his marriage was wildly improvident. But then, people are endlessly improvident when it comes to marriage, aren’t they, Theo?”

“Improvident, yes, when they marry spendthrifts like you,” the General laughed. “Master George went off to visit his long-lost relations, and I will wager he left his purse behind with them.”

“Not the purse itself, sir,” George said, smiling soft and tender at Theo. “Theo made that purse, after all. But I will own it came home perfectly empty. Mr. Rich, the theatre manager, is in a fine fury. He says he hardly dares put Hagan on the stage now, for fear of a riot, just like the trouble Garrick had over the foreign dancers. This would be a riot of fine gentlemen: the macaronis are all furious, and swear they will pelt Hagan off the boards and cudgel him afterwards. My cousin Will took a public oath at Arthur’s Club that he will tear the actor’s ears off. Hagan has not dared perform, so they have cut his salary off entirely, and now that luckless pair of lovers have no way at all to buy their daily bread and cheese.”

“And you took supplies to them? That is just like you, George!” Theo breathed, gazing at him with adoration in her eyes.

“Your purse took the supplies, dear Theo,” George corrected her.

“Mamma, you must go and visit them tomorrow!” Theo begged her mother.

“If she doesn’t, I shall divorce you, my dear!” the General laughed. “Come here and kiss me, you little pet—with your new husband’s permission, of course.”

“Monsieur mon beau fiddlestick, papa!” Miss Lambert retorted, and I have no doubt she complied with her father’s affectionate demand at once. It was the first time George Esmond Warrington, Esquire, had ever been called a fiddlestick.

Any man who has made an imprudent marriage, even in our modern day, knows well the gauntlet of family abuse, scorn, wrath, and misplaced pity he must run afterwards. If your respectable relatives shriek at you for marrying a poor curate’s charming daughter, or agreeing to wed a young barrister whose only income comes from writing court reports, who will have to pay off his Oxford debts out of your small fortune—if they rage at those comparatively sensible matches, you can imagine the wild uproar that followed the news of Lady Maria Hagan’s marriage, among both her noble family and the actor’s own kin.

Take old Mrs. Hagan, for a start. Her son had dutifully kept her in quiet comfort ever since he left Trinity College after his father’s death, and made his debut as Romeo at Dublin’s Crow Street Theatre.
