His salary had long been enough to send his little brother to school, help his sister who worked as a lady’s companion, and keep the old clergyman’s widow in warm fire, soft tea, and plenty of plain dinners. Now all at once, a fine noble lady with every extravagant habit in the world had moved into their little home, taken a seat at their small table, and claimed the cream off the milk, the wings off every chicken, the best half of every meal, where there had only ever been just enough for three before. If Hagan had not been such a fierce, high-spirited fellow, and the old mother not so very afraid of crossing him, I doubt Lady Maria’s life in those Westminster lodgings would have been very comfortable at all. But love, when it takes a passionate, romantic hold of a person, never stops to count consequences or measure available space. Who has not known that reckless mood? What thrifty wife has not seen her husband come home, cheeks flushed, with a devil-may-care grin, and announce he has invited twenty people to dinner next Saturday, even though he knows the dining table only seats sixteen? Never mind, he will say, two of the pretty girls can sit on the young gentlemen’s knees, some of the guests will not show up, there will surely be enough food. Drunk on love, people throw themselves into that kind of reckless housekeeping, never calculating the monthly butcher’s and fishmonger’s bills that will land on the poor housekeeper’s doorstep all too soon.

Old Mrs. Hagan’s quiet grumbling was nothing next to the deafening clamour in Lady Maria’s noble circle at Kensington. Think of all the tittering whispers between the ladies in waiting at the Princess’s court, where Lady Fanny held a post; the crude jokes from Will’s brother officers at the usher’s table; the waggeries printed in the daily newspapers and magazines; the huffs of outraged prudes, the laughter in the gentlemen’s clubs, the sneers of the ungodly! The second she got the news, Madame de Bernstein had hysterical fits and fled to the solitude of her beloved Tunbridge Wells rocks, where she claimed she never saw more than forty people a night at cards. Lord Castlewood refused to see his sister ever again, and his countess, dressed in full mourning, called on her royal patroness, who very graciously condoled with her on the terrible disgrace that had fallen on their house. For three whole days the entire town was amused and absorbed by the scandal—until fresh news came: a great victory in Germany, uncertain dispatches from the American colonies, a general officer recalled home to face a court martial, a ravishing new Italian soprano, and the public entirely forgot Lady Maria huddled in her garret, eating the hard-earned meals of the actor’s family.

Below is an extract from the long letter George Warrington wrote to his brother Harry, then campaigning abroad, describing his visit to the newlywed pair and other recent events:
> “My dearest Harry, our Theo was wild to come with her mother on this errand of charity, but I thought Aunt Lambert’s first visit would be far more appropriate without her young spinster aide-de-camp tagging along. Cousin Hagan was out at the theatre trying to arrange a minor part when we called. We found her ladyship in a loose undress wrapper, her hair half-done in messy papers, playing cribbage with the neighbour from the second floor, while good old Mrs. Hagan sat on the other side of the fire sipping a glass of punch, her well-thumbed copy of *The Whole Duty of Man* open in her lap.
> “Maria, your Maria once, burst into tears the moment she saw us, and Aunt Lambert was ready with all the softest sympathy imaginable. While she comforted the lady, I paid every polite compliment I could think of to the old mother, and between the two of us we managed to turn what would have been a very dreary, awkward interview into something almost pleasant. We talked of you, of General Wolfe, of the war, and you must be face to face with the Frenchmen by this time, Harry dear. God send you safe home, victorious. We follow every dispatch, hang maps of the St. Lawrence on the wall, pore over charts of Cape Breton every evening. I shall never forget the joy on your face the day I came home safe from that little skirmish with the French raiding party, and I know I will see that same joyful look on your face when you return from Quebec. I feel so certain of your safety, so elated by the hope of your success, that everyone here has caught my good humour. We talk already of the campaign being over, and Captain Warrington’s promotion being a settled fact. May Heaven grant all those hopes come true, very soon.
> “Is it not ridiculous that you, the hot-headed, mettlesome brother, have gotten through all this time without a single quarrel, while I, the peaceable fellow who wishes no man any harm, have somehow had duels thrust on my hands? What do you think? I have just had another near miss, and with no less a person than your old enemy, our kinsman Will Esmond.
> “I cannot imagine who or what put him up to picking a fight with me. Spencer, who acted as my second (do not be alarmed, it is all over now, no one has a scratch on him) thinks someone prompted him, but I cannot guess who. His behaviour has been unbearable lately. We have met very often at good Mr. Van den Bosch’s house, where our dear mother entrusted her pretty little granddaughter Lydia to both of our care. Oh, dearest mother! Did you know that sweet little girl would turn out to be a cause for war, making men draw swords and threaten each other’s lives? But that is exactly what has happened. Will hangs about that house constantly, and I suspect he is paying court to Miss Lydia, with her grandfather’s ships, his hundreds of negroes on the Jamaican plantations, and her forty thousand pound fortune as his end goal. The old gentleman never stops talking about his money, adores his granddaughter, and half the fine gentlemen in London are lining up to adore her too. Will was fool enough to imagine I would give up my Theo for a million guineas, a plantation of slaves, and Venus herself, all at once. He has gone out of his way to be rudely insolent to me, contradicting me again and again in front of the whole family, until I had to draw on reserves of patience I did not even know I had. Our little Miss Lydia unknowingly poured fuel on the fire just yesterday, when we were all gathered over dessert.
> “‘Ah!’ the heedless little thing said, ‘tis lucky for you, Mr. Esmond, that Captain Harry is not here.’
> “‘Why, miss?’ Will growled, swearing a blue streak, as he always does. He must have offended a fairy in his cradle, who cursed him to spit curses out of his mouth for ever after, just as that old tale cursed a girl to spit out toads and serpents whenever she spoke. The petty falling-out between George Warrington and his cousin Will Esmond led George to all but abandon his visits to Bloomsbury Square. Will had grown assiduous in his attendance on Lydia Van den Bosch, and now that the pair were formally bound over to keep the peace after their aborted duel, his behaviour grew so outrageously provoking that George had to clamp down hard on his temper every time they met to keep from pummelling him on the spot.

Artless little Lydia had a most peculiar way of receiving her friends. Only six weeks prior, she had been wild with jealousy over rumours that George favoured Theo Lambert over her, but now she took every chance to sing Theo’s praises in conversation, declaring the quiet, gentle girl was perfectly matched to George, her ideal wife. How lucky, she would laugh, that the constables had arrived just in time to stop their duel! It was perfectly ridiculous to recall how Mr. Esmond had raged and sworn at being cheated out of his fight. “Those officers saved your precious life, dear Mr. George,” she would say with a soft, demure smile, “and I am certain Miss Theo ought to bless them for it forever. You won’t stay to dine with us today and meet Mr. Esmond? You needn’t shrink from his company, you know – he can do you no harm, and I am sure you would never harm him.”

These kindly-sounding little speeches, dropped casually in front of other visiting gentlemen and ladies, did no favours for George’s reputation, and soon made him loath to seek out Miss Lydia’s society. Their near-duel had been kept secret from the Lamberts in Dean Street for days, George not wishing to disturb their peaceful household with his quarrels, but when the ladies finally learned of it, the whole home erupted in a flurry of consternation.
“Oh George!” Theo cried, horrified. “You very nearly went and took another man’s life, and you came to visit us all the while and never breathed a word of it! It is shocking!”
“He insulted me and my twin brother,” George argued. “Was I to sit idle and hear us both called cowards, and thank him for the privilege?”

General Lambert sat by the fire, looking very grave. “You know it is a wicked, un-Christian practice, George. I have said a hundred times I wish more gentlemen had the courage to refuse a duel.”
“Refuse?” echoed Jack Lambert, the General’s young clergyman son, his face just as glum as his father’s. “That must take a prodigious strength of will. I think if any man called me a coward, I should be very likely to forget my holy orders and fly at him.”
“See, brother Jack is on my side!” George exclaimed.
“I cannot very well side against you, Mr. Warrington,” Jack said stiffly.
“Mr. Warrington?” George sputtered, flushing bright red.
“Would you have George break the Sixth Commandment and commit murder, John?” Theo gasped, aghast.
“I am a soldier’s son before I am a parson, sister,” Jack replied drily. “Besides, Mr. Warrington committed no murder at all. We shall hear news from Canada soon, no doubt – the great fight for supremacy between the British and French out there is bound to come to a head before long.” He turned his back to George as he spoke, and George stared at him in bewilderment. Hetty had gone pale at her brother’s odd remark, and Theo tugged her out of the room on some thin pretext. George started up to follow the retreating girls to the door, then spun back to face the two men.
“Great heavens!” he burst out. “On my honour, I believe you two think I shirked that duel with Esmond!”
The General and his son exchanged a long look. “A man’s nearest and dearest are always the first to insult him,” George flared, stung.
“Not guilty, my boy?” the General cried, his eyes misting over. “Thank God for that! I told you so, Jack.” He scrubbed a hand over his face, blushed, and wrung George’s hand so hard his knuckles whitened.
“Not guilty of what?” George asked, utterly confused.
“Nay, let Jack tell you,” the General said. “It was his story first, and I believe it’s a downright lie, with all my heart.” With that uncharacteristically rough utterance, he walked straight out of the room.

The Reverend Jack Lambert looked absurdly sheepish. “And what is this damned lie that someone has been spreading about me?” George asked, grinning despite his anger.
“To question a man’s courage is always a grave offence, and I rejoice to find yours has been slandered,” Jack said.
“Who told you that falsehood?” George roared. “I demand his name.”
“You forget you are bound over to keep the peace,” Jack reminded him.
“Curse the peace!” George yelled. “We could take a boat to Holland and fight there, no one would be the wiser. Tell me his name, I say!”
“Softly, Mr. Warrington,” the parson said, holding up a hand. “My hearing is perfectly good. It was no man who told me the story I – I confess I repeated to my father.”
The truth dawned on George all at once. “That artful, wicked little vixen in Bloomsbury Square?”
“Vixen is no name to call any young lady, George Warrington!” Jack exclaimed, outraged. “Far less the charming Miss Lydia! Artful? She is the most innocent creature Heaven ever made. Wicked? She is a perfect angel! She spoke with such unfeigned delight that the quarrel was over, such devout gratitude that no kin’s blood would be spilled, singing your praises for being so considerate as to avoid bloodshed by turning the two of you over to the constables before any harm could be done.”
“Laying an information?” George shouted, stamping his foot. The curses he unleashed on Miss Lydia then are far too violent and ungentlemanly to repeat.
“Do not dare utter such words!” Jack snapped, turning angry himself. “Do not insult the most innocent, charming creature of the sex to my face! If she was misinformed about you, and thought you chose a peaceful path rather than a sinful duel, you have no right to blacken that sweet girl’s name with foul language. Are you to be my brother, after all?”
“I hope for that honour,” George said, smiling now, the pieces clicking into place.
“Then what – though it is far more bliss than a sinful man like me deserves – what if one day she was to be my sister? Who could look on her beauty and not fall in love? I confess I am her utter slave. Those Latin Sapphics published in the September issue of the *Gentleman’s Magazine*, the ones beginning *Lydicae quondam cecinit venustae*? They were mine. I have told my mother all about us, and she thinks Miss Lydia looks very favourably on me too. I have written a formal proposal letter, and my mother was all ready to call on her grandfather this very day to ask for his blessing, to bring me an answer that will make me the happiest or most miserable man alive. It slipped out in our family talk, I suppose – that comment about your courage. Heaven knows I never doubted it, not for a second! I think jealousy has been gnawing at my heart, that horrible suspicion that my future brother-in-law was winning too much of her favour, favour I wanted all for myself. Ah George, who knows all his own flaws? I am half distracted with passion. What right have you to laugh at me, anyway?”

George’s roar of laughter drew the General back into the room. “Have you two boys made your peace at last?” he asked.
“I was just remonstrating with Mr. Warrington for that rude, ill-timed laughter,” Jack huffed, red-faced.
“George is bound over to keep the peace for two years, Jack, you can’t fight him till that runs out,” the General chuckled. “Till then, let’s hope you’ll sort out your quarrels like gentlemen. Dinner’s on the table, lads – we’ll drink to absent friends, to an end of the war across the sea, and no fighting outside the army.”

George pleaded a prior engagement to slip away early from the table, and Jack was not far behind him. When George stopped by his own lodgings to scribble a sharp note to Miss Lydia calling out the slander about his duel, he turned up at the Bloomsbury Square house to find Jack already on the steps, deep in conversation with the footman there.
“Master and the whole household left town yesterday,” the servant told them.
“Poor Jack!” George whispered, when the footman had turned away. “You had that proposal letter in your pocket, didn’t you?”
Jack nodded, miserable. “My mother was in her sedan chair halfway here, I think, to call on her.” George had his own sharp note for Lydia tucked in his coat too, which he had not yet mentioned to Jack, and he had no intention of leaving it now the household was gone.
“Will they be back soon?” he asked the footman politely.
“They’re gone to stay with quality,” the man replied, handing over a scrap of paper with an address scrawled in Lydia’s neat hand: *The box from Madam Hocquet’s to go by the Farnham Flying Coach, addressed to Miss Van den Bosch, at the Right Honourable the Earl of Castlewood’s, Castlewood, Hants.*
“Where?” Jack gasped, aghast. “I thought she’d only visited Lady Castlewood once!”
“His lordship and the family have called here many times,” the footman said, preening. “We’re very intimate.”
“Miss Lydia took a power of boxes and gowns with her,” he added. “They’re bound to stay a good long while.”

The two young men walked away, each crumpling his unused letter in his pocket. “What was that exclamation you just made?” George asked.
“Distraction!” Jack groaned. “I am beside myself, George. I barely know what I’m saying. She’s gone to Hampshire, and Mr. Esmond is gone there with her!”
“Othello could not have spoken better,” George said. “And she has a very fine scoundrel for company down there.” Just then they spotted Mrs. Lambert’s sedan chair swinging down Great Russell Street, preceded by her footman.
“No use going further, Aunt Lambert!” George called out. “Our little bird has flown.”
“What little bird?”
“The bird Jack hoped to wed: our Lyddy bird. Fie, Jack! You swore this morning you wanted to break the Sixth Commandment, and now here you are swearing again!”
“Confound it, leave me alone, Mr. Warrington!” Jack snarled, striding far ahead out of reach of the chair’s bearers.
“What is the matter with him, George?” Mrs. Lambert asked, bewildered from inside the chair.
“Jack has no patience today, aunt,” George said. “He tells everyone I am a coward, then flies into a rage when I take offence. Then he finds his ladylove has vanished to the country, and he stamps and swears like a common trooper. O fie! Beware of jealousy, aunt – did the General ever make you jealous?”
“You will make me very angry if you speak to me in that tone,” Mrs. Lambert said, huffily. George bowed low. “I am respectfully dumb,” he said. “Good day.” He turned away towards Holborn, his soul burning with wrath. He was ready to quarrel with anyone that night. If he had run into cousin Will, he would have forgotten his peace bonds entirely. He hunted Will down at Arthur’s, then at his lodgings, and finally at the Castlewood London house, where the servants told him Mr. Esmond had already left to join the party in Hampshire.

George sat down and wrote two sharp, polite letters that night. The first to Will: *My dear kind cousin William, you know I am bound over to keep the peace, and would never quarrel with a dear kinsman – much less one my own brother once caned for his insolence. But if you ever meet anyone who claims I prevented our duel by laying an information to the constables, do tell your informant that it is not I, but he, who is the coward.* The second went to old Mr. Van den Bosch, warning him that a rogue was spreading slanderous lies about his character, and begging him to be wary of such company. He sent them off by post, then dressed for the theatre, enjoyed the play, and ate a hearty, cheerful supper at the Bedford tavern to settle his temper.

A few days later, a letter franked with the Castlewood seal sat on his breakfast table, written in the Earl of Castlewood’s own hand:
> Dear Cousin,
> There has been far too much strife in our family of late, and it is high time all quarrels ended. Two days ago my brother William brought me a very angry letter signed G. Warrington, and told me of the fracas between you two, where I must say your conduct was uncommonly violent. It is a poor use for good wine to fling it in an old man’s face, after all – you ought to have shown more respect to good Mr. Van den Bosch. I will not pretend Will’s behaviour is not often provoking; he has tried my own temper within these very 24 hours.
> Why should we not all live in peace and harmony? You know I have long held a sincere regard for you, and admire the excellent young lady you are engaged to with all my heart – give her my most cordial greetings. I hope soon to introduce a new Countess of Castlewood to the family. At my mature age, it is no uncommon thing for a man to take a young wife. My Lydia – you will guess by now I am happy to call the elegant Miss Van den Bosch my own – will naturally survive me. She will soothe my declining years, and I shall not grudge her choosing a happier, younger man to succeed me when I am gone, though I shall envy him the possession of so much beauty and perfection. Though she comes of an illustrious Dutch family, the dear girl says her rank is not equal to mine, and she is delighted to share the Castlewood name. I, in turn, shall be overjoyed to see heirs to my house, and to restore our estates to the splendour they enjoyed before two or three improvident predecessors ran them deep into debt. Lydia, who is sitting beside me now, sends you and all the Lambert family her warmest remembrances.
> The wedding will take place here at Castlewood very soon. May I hope to see you in the church? My brother William will not be there to quarrel with you. When we told him of the match yesterday, he flew into a terrible passion, uttered words he will surely regret one day, and has gone off to stay with neighbours in the village. The Dowager Lady Castlewood will keep the Kensington house, and we will set up our own household, where you will always be welcome, dear cousin.
> Your affectionate humble servant,

And sure enough, the November 1759 issue of the *London Magazine* carried the short announcement:
> Saturday, October 13th: Married, at his seat Castlewood in Hampshire, the Right Honourable Eugene, Earl of Castlewood, to the beautiful Miss Van den Bosch of Virginia. Fortune: £70,000.

As I sit gazing across my hearth at the familiar armchair where the partner of my last fifty years of life rests, I find myself repeating the same old question again and again — a privilege no middle-aged man can be fairly denied, after all, for we hoard our jokes, our anecdotes, and our favourite little queries as carefully as we hoard our old port. “Did any two young fools ever make a rasher, more imprudent choice than we did,” I ask her, “when we married the very year the old King breathed his last?”

My son Miles, that most fearless of fox-hunters, answers the same way when he is home from the chase: he says that when he stops to look back at the gaps and flooded rivers he cleared at full gallop, his blood runs cold at the thought of the risk he ran, and he cannot believe his own foolhardiness. Yet there is no keener sportsman across the whole two counties. He will break his collarbone, tumble ten times in a day (to his mother’s constant terror), and be back in the saddle by sunrise next morning. I have had my own share of tumbles, too: thrown head-first over my old mare Sultana’s head when she slipped on a park path stone, both of us half-asleep while my mind wandered off to a new verse or a speech I was to give at Quarter Sessions. Miles’s reckless hunting has been the joy of his life, and my reckless marriage has been the blessing of mine — and I never think of it without giving thanks to Heaven.

Mind you, I do not hold our example up to all the young folk of the parish. If I stood up in vestry meeting and bade every lad marry on twopence a year, the faces round the table would turn black enough to sour the ale. But my wife is a desperate match-maker, Heaven bless her: when Hodge and Susan trudge into my justice room, shyly mentioning they have a half-crown a week saved to set up house, we add a little purse of our own money to their store, send for the vicar, and make a wedding of it.

I know the answer I will get when I tease my dear oracle, of course — that is half the fun of asking. If I say, “My dear, did not the moon look exactly like cream cheese tonight?” she will smile back and say, “Well, papa, it did, to be sure — there is no one alive with such droll similes as you.” If I grumble that Mr. Pitt’s speech was fine enough, but never half as grand as what I remember his father Lord Chatham delivering, she will agree at once that no man ever lived to match the old Earl. Then one of the girls will cry out, “But papa has said a hundred times Chatham was nothing but a charlatan!” and mamma will only laugh and say the girl takes after her wild Aunt Hetty.

As for Miles, none of this matters a whit to him. He only reads the hunting notices in the Norwich paper, and cares no more for politics than he does for Greek. The rascal has never read a line of my poems, much less my tragedies — when I mentioned Pocahontas to him the other day, he thought it was a tributary of the James River in Virginia. He cannot construe a line of Corderius, so how could he possibly understand my Latin verses? My little memoir notebook sits on the corner of the fireside table, with my spectacles resting on the cover, for anyone to lift and read if they please — and Miles has never touched it. I fill its loose pages with caricatures of him, little jokes at his expense, and he never notices a thing. Only once, I came back to find my fine China-ink sketch of Miles snoring after dinner (a drawing my friend Bunbury himself would have been proud of) crossed out, and a rude scrawl of a picture of me flying over Sultana’s head, titled *The Squire on Horseback, or A Fish Out of Water*. Miles roared so loud with laughter that the girls all tittered in corners, and my wife swore she thought I would fly into a passion when I opened the book. But I can take a joke against myself, even if — strange to say, for a man who has counted many of the great wits of the age as his friends — I have never heard a truly good original witticism in my whole life. No matter, Miles, I love you none the worse for being no wit. There never was any friendship between two wits under one family roof, after all. His mother swears he is as handsome as Apollo, or as the Prince of Wales, who was born the very same year he was. She has a print of the Prince by Coates hanging in her dressing room to this day, and will point out the resemblance to anyone who will listen. [Note in a neat, slanted female hand: “My son is no spendthrift, no breaker of ladies’ hearts, as some young gentlemen are. But that he was the very image of His Royal Highness when both were babes is past all doubt: the Duchess of Ancaster herself said so, when Gumbo and my poor Molly used to wheel him round St. James’s Park for his daily airing. Th. W.”]

What different prospects lay before the other boy born that very same year: Lord Esmond, the son of the Earl of Castlewood. Even then, my lord and I had already settled into a cool, distant acquaintance, and Heaven knows no fairy godmother laid gold christening cups in honest Miles’s cradle when he was born. But things have mended since then — Laus Deo, indeed! — for I suspect neither Miles nor his father would ever have gotten half so far in the world relying only on their own wits.

Castlewood House bears a very different face now than the venerable, weathered old place I knew in my youth. Back then, its walls were lined with the wrinkles of hundreds of years, the scars of old civil wars, the cracks and blemishes time had marked on its hoary stone features. I love best to remember it as it was when young George Warrington (that is, your humble narrator, writing these lines) was invited down by its owner, to attend his lordship’s wedding to Miss Lydia Van den Bosch, “an American lady of noble Dutch family,” as the county papers announced her. The towers stood just as my grandfather Colonel Esmond — the Marquis, as Madam Esmond will insist on calling him — had seen them. The old woods had been thinned a little, to be sure, but many of the same rooks that cawed over the Colonel’s head threescore years before still wheeled and cawed above the treetops. His portrait hung in the hall, the same house that would have been his, had he not chosen love and loyalty over wealth and a noble title. As I paced the long corridors, the dew-damp terraces, and the cool, dark avenues, I half fancied myself one of Mr. Walpole’s cavaliers, ruff at my throat, rapier at my hip, buff coat and gorget on my back, ready at any moment to spot a Jacobite spy slipping out from behind an oak tree, or a Roundhead raider peering from a carved oak cupboard. I dreamed up a hundred old-world romances there: secret intrigues, serenades under balcony windows, scaling ladders, Oliver’s men battering at the gates, bluff King Hal’s beefeaters pricking across the plain before the castle walls.

I was courting my dear wife at the time, of course — your eyes had no need of spectacles back then, my love, and not a single wrinkle or silver thread marked your brow. I wrote ream upon ream of flowery, romantic descriptions of the old house to her, all franked under Lord Castlewood’s name, and she never tired of reading a single line. Now she teases me that when I go up to London, I only send her three lines of note. That is not out of laziness, my dear — it is only that I will not fatigue your old eyes.

I spared no expense on a new, fine suit of clothes for the wedding, and arrived at Castlewood a few days before the ceremony, attended by my faithful servant Gumbo. I ought to mention that we had sent Sady, our other lad, home to Virginia on a merchant ship not long before. A vicious inflammation of the throat and lungs, which killed hundreds of people the year of General Wolfe’s expedition to Quebec, had nearly carried him off, and the doctors swore only the air of his native colony would cure him. We parted in floods of tears, though Gumbo had shed just as many when I myself left for the army at Quebec. But he had made too many friends in England to care for a military life, so he stayed on in my service.

Castlewood House was packed full of guests, relations, and well-wishers. sulky Lady Fanny was there, dragged there against her will to act as a bridesmaid, along with a bevy of other young ladies from the neighbouring county families. The Baroness Beatrix, that sharp old bishop’s widow, had brought her brother-in-law, a London bishop, down to Hampshire to officiate at the wedding of Eugene, Earl of Castlewood, and Lydia Van den Bosch, spinster. For weeks before and after the ceremony, the old house hummed with a gaiety it had not known for generations. The county gentry flocked over to pay their respects to the new couple. Everyone gossiped endlessly about the lady’s fortune, of course, and no two versions of the sum ever agreed. The naughty rumours that had spread through London, of her jilting half a dozen disappointed suitors, took months to drift down to Hampshire — and when they did, no one cared to listen. The Hampshire folk were far too glad to see Castlewood House open again, beer flowing in the cellars, horses stabled in the stalls, and spits turning over the kitchen fires to be overly curious about her behaviour in town. If she had laughed at a few suitors and turned them away? So had half the heiresses in England, and she was no more mercenary than the rest of them. Her marriage settlement was advertised as seventy thousand pounds, and the county folks whispered that was but a small fraction of her wealth — when her rich old grandfather died, they said, the plums would fall thick from the tree.

That sharp, quiet old grandfather of hers set to work at once untangling Castlewood’s accounts, which decades of neglect, poverty, and careless extravagance had left in total ruin. Every hour of his days, for months and years afterwards, was spent patching up Lord Castlewood’s finances: raising rents where it was fair to do so, paring down the household expenses to the bone, so that he could track every yard of worsted lace on the footmen’s coats, and every pound of beef sent up to their tables. His old sharp eye counted every flagon of beer drawn from the buttery, and made sure no food went to waste in the larder. The household staff was smaller, but every soul was paid on the dot, no more overdue wages; the footmen’s liveries were neat and new, and no tailor was ever left to dun for his money. The gardeners and grooms grumbled a little, even as their pay came on time — but the horses grew fat on less corn, and the fruit and vegetable harvests were larger than they had been in living memory, all overseen by that old man from his tiny chamber in the house turret.

These improvements took years, not days, to come to pass. Slowly, with steady thrift and careful spending, the estate and its household grew prosperous again. No one could deny how well the house ran — not even the old dowager Countess and her two children, who now rarely set foot inside Castlewood’s gates. The new young Countess had declared war on them the moment she took possession, and routed them completely. Though she had been raised in the colonies, and knew nothing of the fine nuances of noble London society in her youth, Lydia had a sharp tongue and an iron will that no one who quarrelled with her could stand against. The dowager and Lady Fanny fled all the way back to their jointure house in Kensington, and no one missed them — least of all Lord Castlewood, who was never one to grieve over the absence of anyone who had left his household.

As for me, who had known my lord for years, I never for a moment imagined he would grieve if I fell ill, or met with an accident, or died. He was too well-bred, too witty, too polished, to show any of that petty sentiment. I rather enjoyed watching his peculiar ways, even if he had no courage and no heart at all. What are those things, after all, for a man of the world? You do not demand that every gentleman be brave and loyal, any more than you demand he have half a million pounds in the funds. All society asks is that he be pleasant company, keep a decent household, and pay his way. My grandfather, Colonel Esmond, who had turned down the very title and estate my lord now owned, my lord once tapped his own placid, high forehead and said, “That old fellow must have been a little touched here.” There are some acts of unselfishness that selfish men can never understand, which they dismiss as outright madness or lies. “I do you the justice to say, cousin,” I told him once, “that you would never give up even the smallest advantage for any friend alive.” He shrugged his shoulders in the French fashion, pinched a pinch of snuff from his box, and laughed. “Eh! I am selfish, but am I any more selfish than the rest of the world?”

Once, when we were walking the fields, my lord was wearing a fine scarlet coat, and a cow took a sudden run at him. The ordinarily languid, slow-moving nobleman cleared a five-barred stile faster than any schoolboy I ever saw. He did not even try to pretend he was not trembling afterwards, or hide that he was no brave man. “I dare say you respect me no more than I respect myself, George,” he said, candid as ever, and then launched into a very witty, sardonic little speech about the fall of man, and all our faults and shortcomings, and wondered aloud why Heaven had not made every one of us tall, handsome, brave, and rich. I could not help but like him, for all his weaknesses. There was something in his look that reminded me of the poor ass in Mr. Sterne’s famous story: *Do not beat me, he seemed to say, but if you must, you may*. No man who is not a bully and a coward himself will ever be cruel to a creature that makes no pretence of spirit at all.

From the well-loved fairytales we read as children, we all know that no christening or wedding ever passes without at least one guest nursing a grudge, swearing vengeance for the slight they have suffered. So no one need be surprised to learn that cousin Will Esmond raged and cursed with unbridled fury the second he learned his older brother had secured a formal engagement to the wealthy colonial heiress. In the first flush of his wrath, Will stormed out of the house swearing he would never set foot in Castlewood again. But no one, not even Will himself, put much stock in his dramatic oaths. The unrepentant prodigal drifted back home after only two days: the promise of the lavish wedding feasts spread out across Castlewood’s tables was too great a temptation for him to resist. He returned to eat and drink his fill, framing every mouthful as a petty act of revenge. He raised a brimming bumper to the newly married couple, muttering a curse of perdition on the bride under his breath. As the earl spoke his vows to love, honour, and cherish his new wife in the castle chapel, Will’s responses to the service were all smothered maledictions.

He was far from the only disgruntled party to the match, as George Warrington soon discovered. In the months that followed, he heard an endless litany of abuse directed at the new countess and her grandfather. The old merchant’s City friends, his legal advisor, the Dissenting minister whose chapel they had attended on their first arrival in England, and even gentle Jack Lambert, the earnest young orthodox divine who had cherished hopes of winning her hand, all seethed at what they called the young American’s treachery. Every one of them had a tale to tell of being charmed, led on, then cast aside by the heiress. The lawyer, who had once compiled a meticulous inventory of all her properties, estates, ships, enslaved people, and future fortunes, now swore the entire list was a fabrication: he claimed New York and Virginia were hardly real places, that the Guinea trade was a myth, and that the old planter Van den Bosch had invented every last “black falsehood” about his Virginian holdings. The Dissenting pastor moaned over his stray lamb – if such a wily, mischievous creature could ever be called a lamb at all. Poor Jack Lambert wrote to his mother to confess he still kept a lock of the heiress’s black hair, which he soaked with tears and addressed in language far too unclerical for a man of his calling.

As for Will Esmond, he howled and cursed so loudly the walls almost shook – even within earshot of his new sister-in-law – calling on Acheron itself to bear witness that no such artful young devil as Miss Lydia existed anywhere above ground. He swore she was an infernal female Cerberus, and rained down every curse he could conjure on his swindling rascal of a brother, who he claimed had cajoled him with fair words only to steal his fortune right out from under his nose.

“Why,” George said dryly, when Will ranted to him at length on the subject, “if the girl is half the she-devil you describe her to be, you should count yourself lucky to have missed her. If you’re right and she means to deceive her husband and slip him a dose of poison, you escaped a terrible fate! You ought to thank the gods, Will, for robbing you of that fury. The best revenge you could possibly get on my lord is letting him keep her all to himself.”

“That’s all very well,” Will snarled back, “but that doesn’t make my brother any less of a scoundrel, cheating me out of the fortune I risked my very life to win.”

George blinked, hardly able to fathom how Will had ever risked his precious life (which, George privately thought, a whipping at the end of a rope would have suited perfectly). Will, never one for false modesty, spilled the whole story: how the little Cerberus herself had arranged that duel between the two of them, the one broken up by Sir John Fielding’s men; how she had constantly taunted George for sneering at Will, and taunted Will in turn for being too much of a poltroon to retaliate to George’s jibes. She’d even spread tales that George had run screaming from Braddock’s battlefield, nearly dead of fright. “Deuce take me,” Will said, “I never was more surprised in my life than when you stood your ground that coolly in Tottenham Court Fields. My second and I had already wagered half a guinea you’d never even turn up to the meeting!”

George laughed out loud, and thanked Will for that flattering estimation of his courage. “Though it’s lucky for me the constables turned up when they did,” he added. “Another minute and you’d have run your sword right through my waistcoat. Didn’t you see how clumsy I was standing there before you? You were so angry you turned white all over and shook like a leaf!”

“Curse me, that’s just my way of showing rage,” Will grumbled, flushing bright red this time. “I was confoundedly angry with you, cousin! But now the only man I hate is my brother, and that little devil of a countess – a countess, indeed! A pretty countess she makes!” He punctuated the remark with another thunderous volley of oaths.

“Well, cousin,” George said, looking him dead in the eye, “you let me off remarkably easy. I dare say I owe you my life, or at the very least an undamaged waistcoat. I admire your forbearance and your spirit. What a waste it is for a man with your courage to be stuck as a mere court usher! The king’s army is missing out on a fine officer there, you truly are.”

“I never can tell if you’re joking or being serious, Mr. Warrington,” Will growled.

“Very few gentlemen would dare joke with you, cousin, if they valued their own ears or their hides,” George laughed. He loved teasing his grand kinsman in that deadpan way, watching with droll amusement as Will choked back curses, ground his teeth too cowardly to lash out, and smothered his seething, petty anger. “And you really ought to moderate your language when you speak of the dear countess and my lord your brother,” he went on. “They both speak of you with nothing but the greatest tenderness. Her ladyship has told me every last detail.”

“Every last detail?” Will yelped, taken aback.

“As much detail as any woman ever tells, cousin. She confessed she thought you were more than a little in love with her. What woman could possibly resist liking a man who adores her?”

“Why, she hates you,” Will blurted out, “says you were wild about her, Mr. Warrington!”

*Spretae injuria formae*, cousin!” George quoted.

“For me? What’s for me?” Will asked, confused.

“I never cared for her at all, which is probably why she dislikes me. Don’t you remember that old story of the captain of the guard’s wife?”

“Which guard?” Will frowned. “Lord Falmouth is Captain of the Yeomen of the Guard, Lord Berkeley of the Pensioners. Before that it was Lord Hobart. I suppose you haven’t been in England long enough to know who’s who, cousin.”

George explained he was talking about the captain of the guard for the King of Egypt, whose wife hounded the young man Joseph for rejecting her advances. Will waved the story off, saying Egypt must be a confoundedly long way away, and if that lord’s wife was telling lies about people, that was just the way of women the whole world over.

The truth was, when George paid his first post-wedding visit to Castlewood, the new countess had told him her own version of the falling out between herself and Will. It differed wildly from Will’s account – though George would not say for certain which of them was telling the full truth. The little countess grieved to think how sadly she had been deceived in her brother-in-law. She feared his years hanging around court and the town had eroded the noble, high principles all Esmonds were born with. She claimed Will’s word could never be trusted, that his loose lifestyle and endless money troubles had made him mercenary, blunted his honour, and even eaten away at the chivalrous courage “that we Esmonds,” she tossed her pretty little head as she spoke, “that we Esmonds must all possess – at least, you and me, my lord, and my cousin Harry have it, I know! Oh, cousin George! I must confess I was even led to doubt your courage for a moment, and no man of our ancient and noble family is worthy of the name if he lacks that! As a Christian lady, and the head of one of the very first families in all the kingdom and the whole world, I shall try to forgive my brother William for speaking ill of a member of our family, even if you are a younger branch through the female line, and for making me doubt you, however briefly. That’s exactly what he did. I daresay he told you a hundred wicked lies about the things you supposedly said about me.”

“I, my dear lady?” George cried, astonished.

“Things he claimed you said about me, cousin. I hope you never did, and I pray heartily that you didn’t. I can afford to despise any such stories. It is true he paid me court, of course – so have plenty of others, I’m quite used to it. He might even have fared better than he did, back before I met my dear lord and realised how great and eminent his qualities are, out of the fullness of my grateful heart now! But oh! I soon found William was completely lacking in courage. No man without a spark of it can ever earn the esteem of Lydia, Countess of Castlewood, never! He claimed it was you who lacked spirit, cousin, and made me so angry by telling me you were always abusing me. But I forgive you, George, truly I do! And when I tell you that he was the coward – the mean skunk! – who actually sent for those constables to break up that duel between you and him, you won’t wonder I don’t value a fellow like that even a single pinch of snuff.” She snapped her little fingers for emphasis. “Noblesse oblige, and an Esmond without courage is worth nothing to me. Look at our ancestors on these walls! The Esmonds have always fought for their king and their country. Not a single one of us would shrink back when the moment comes to prove he is an Esmond and a nobleman! If my eldest son ever showed the white feather, I would say to him ‘My Lord Esmond – that’s our family’s second title, you know – I disown you right now!’” As she spoke, she glanced around the drawing room at the stately portraits of her new forebears, painted by Lely and Kneller, lining every wall.

Very quickly, the new Countess had total dominion over the whole apartment, the entire house, the surrounding estate, and the neighbouring village. It was astonishing how fast she learned to command. She did not follow the usual unspoken rules of precedence that great English ladies abided by, but invented her own regulations, issued them as law, and made everyone around her submit. She had been raised a Dissenter, and was not overly familiar with the services of the Established Church – George noticed she made a few blunders in her first few attendances at chapel, for instance, forgetting when to turn to face east, a custom unknown in the other Reformed churches. But by George’s second visit to Castlewood after the wedding, she had mastered every part of her duties to perfection. She sailed into the chapel on George’s arm, her two footmen trailing behind her carrying her massive prayer book, as demure as the pious old devotee accompanied by her lackey in Hogarth’s famous *Morning* print, as if she had kept a personal chaplain her entire life. She patronised not just the new chaplain, but the whole service and the church itself, as if she had never once in her life sat through a ranting sermon in a barn back in the colonies.

She made all the most established county families – grave baronets and their wives, worthy squires who could trace their line back twenty generations – who rode over to Castlewood to pay their respects to the newlyweds, know their proper place, and give her precedence. She hunted down an old heraldry book, and tracked down a sharp old maiden lady from Winchester who was a walking encyclopedia of court etiquette and genealogy, who had learned the rules back in the days of Queen Anne. Before long she was chattering volubly about gules and sables, bends and saltires, not always correctly, but with unshakable confidence. She made grand excursions to the neighbouring towns in her gilded coach and six, or through the village in her sedan chair, claiming a near-royal right to homage from every tenant and labourer on the estate. She lectured the parson on his theology, the bailiff on best farming practices, instructed the astonished housekeeper on how to preserve fruit and pickle vegetables, and even tried to teach the fancy London footmen how to leap up behind the carriage, though it was too high for her little ladyship to climb up and demonstrate. She gave the village wives detailed instructions on how to nurse their children long before she had any of her own, and when it came to dosing the household with physic, she was every bit as stubborn and dictatorial as Madam Esmond was back in Virginia. It was hard not to think of the Fisherman and the Genie from the Arabian Nights: how had such a prodigious, forceful spirit ever been corked up inside such a tiny little bottle of a body?

When George headed back to London after that first post-wedding visit, she pressed him to carry small gifts back for his young friends in Dean Street, the Lamothes: a trinket for one, a book for the other. George swore to himself that Theo’s present was a fine wax doll, and Hetty’s a nursery primer full of single-syllable words. As for Will, her younger brother-in-law, she treated him with a kind of maternal gravity and tender protectiveness that struck George as endlessly diverting, even if it made Will’s usual cursing and blasphemy twice as loud as before.

Lydia had very little respect for old age as a general rule. As soon as the marriage settlements were signed and settled in her favour, she treated old Mr. Van den Bosch and his enormous periwig with no more ceremony than she treated Dinah, her personal Black attendant. She would pinch Dinah’s great ears and yank at her woolly hair without a second thought when the woman annoyed her – or so Dinah told Gumbo, who passed the tale on to his master. Every last soul in the household trembled before the new countess: the old housekeeper, who even the late dowager and the previous earl had treated with deference; the pampered London footmen, who used to grumble if they were disturbed mid-card game while they swilled endless tankards of beer, now scurried to obey the second they heard her ladyship’s voice. Even old Lockwood, the gate porter who had held his post for more than half a century, tried to rally his foggy old wits when she marched into his lodge to throw open his window, inspect his wood store, and chase his mangy old hounds out into the cold. Lockwood bared his bald old head, cast a pleading look at his niece, and trembled before the tiny new mistress’s authority.

Gumbo, dressing his master for dinner that evening, babbled about the prophet Elisha that the chaplain had read of that very morning, “with his bald head, and the bad boys who called him names, and the bears that ate ’em all up – served them right, too,” Gumbo said. But when George brought up old Lockwood to the countess later, she waved the old man off dismissively. “Pooh, pooh! Stupid old man! Past all his work, and his dirty old dogs! They’re as old and ugly as those mouldy old carp in the castle pond!” She pointed to the two legendary monster carp that local tradition claimed had lived in the Castlewood garden ponds for centuries, their backs crusted over with thick grey slime. “Lockwood has to go. The workhouse is the place for him. I’ll put a smart, tall, good-looking fellow in that lodge, who’ll do our livery credit.”

“He was my grandfather’s own man, and served him through all the Queen Anne wars,” George protested.

“O Lord, Queen Anne’s dead, isn’t she?” the countess snapped back petulantly. “We aren’t going to go into mourning for her, are we?”

The matter of Lockwood was brought up at the family dinner that night, when the countess formally announced her intention of dismissing the old porter.

“I’ve heard,” old Mr. Van den Bosch said demurely, “that the laws here in England take excellent care of poor old servants and all kinds of elderly poor folks. I do wish we had such asylums back home in the colonies – it would save us all the trouble and expense of keeping our old labourers on when they can’t work no more.”

“If a man can’t work, he ought to go!” the countess cried.

“Yes, indeed, that’s a fact!” her grandfather agreed.

“What? An old servant who’s served the family for fifty years?” the earl asked, frowning.

“Mr. Van den Bosch must have been very independent of servants back in his youth,” George remarked.

“Greased my own boots, opened my own shutters, sanded and watered my own – ” the old man began.

“Sugar, sir?” the earl teased.

“Not sugar, my son-in-law, the floor!” the old man laughed. “Though there’s plenty of that sort of trickery in the grocery stores, begging your ladyship’s pardon.”

“La, pa, what do I know about grocery stores?” Lydia cried, flustered.

“Hey, don’t you remember stealing the sugar as a boy, and the trouble it got you in, my dear ladyship?” her grandfather chortled.

“At any rate, a fine tall man in our livery will look far better than that shrivelled old porter creature!” the countess insisted.

“No livery is half as becoming as a head of silver hairs, madam,” George said, “and no lace as fine. What will the rest of the county say if you banish old Lockwood?”

“Oh, very well, if you’re determined to plead for him, I suppose he can stay next to the carp pond. Should I drag a couch out of my drawing room for him

Our Castlewood kin hosted us right up to the turn of the new year, and no sooner had a fortnight of separation passed than the infatuated, foolish young Harry Warrington came rushing back to the side of his charmer, those two weeks stretching for him as long as a lifetime. Madame de Bernstein, for her part, was in no hurry to linger in the home of her father, and grew far more unguarded in her conversation the further we traveled from the old house. She never breathed a word of what passed during the dramatic showdown between her and her new young niece, the Countess, but she set aside all her earlier talk of moulding *cette petite* to her will. When she did allude to the girl, it was with a nervous, half-amused laugh, no trace of ill will at all. Her nephew Eugene, she declared, was clearly doomed to be henpecked for the rest of his days, and a little firm order brought to the Castlewood household would do it a world of good. That plain, unvarnished old American gentleman Van den Bosch struck her as a sharp, capable man, who would make an excellent steward for the estate. She had heard rumor that the Countess’s mother was a convict transported from England, no doubt having beaten hemp in half the kingdom’s gaols, but there was no need to carry that news to the town crier. After all, for folks of that station, what did their birth matter? The girl was clever, she would pick up fluent English soon enough, and the noble name she bore was grand enough to win her entry into any society drawing room. What did it matter if Mr. Van den Bosch had once been a grocer, a smuggler, or even a slave trader? The Countess of Castlewood could afford to be any man’s daughter, and the moment her nephew Eugene brings her to town, she said, it is the whole family’s clear duty to stand by her.

With Madame de Bernstein’s temper so softened towards the new Countess, Mr. Warrington dared hope she might extend that same goodwill to his sister-in-law Lady Maria, and spoke of his visits to Mr. Hagan and his wife, begging his aunt to look kindly on the couple. But the old lady was immovable on the subject of Maria, begging that her name never be mentioned in her hearing, then immediately proceeded to chatter for two whole hours of nothing but anecdotes about her niece, tales far too unseemly to set down in this family story, written for the edification of the young and innocent of our line. This much I will say of the poor creature: if she sinned, she was far from the only sinner in our family, and if she repented, many others would do well to follow her example. Hagan, as all know, lived an exemplary life after he left the stage, growing famous for his elegant, fiery eloquence in the pulpit. His wife embraced strict dissenting views, and was greatly respected by the sect she joined, though the last time I saw her she spoke to me of a peculiar spiritual illumination I strongly suspected came more from a too free use of strong drink than from heaven. I still remember, though, how good the two of them were to me and mine at a time when we needed kindness sorely, and many a pious Pharisee turned his back on us.

I have written before of how fickle our aunt’s favor could be, of how each of us brothers was in turn the golden child of the household, then cast aside. My own turn in the sun came after the success of my play. I was introduced to all the London wits, held my own in their company well enough, was declared tolerably well-bred by the macaronis and the leaders of fashion, and might have risen far in that world if only my purse had been long enough, if I had chosen to chase that sort of life, if I had not already loved a pair of soft, kind eyes far better than the brightest orbs of the Gunnings or the Chudleighs, or all the painted beauties who paraded the Ranelagh ring. Would you believe it, children? Just because I was fond of your mother, my genteel family declared my tastes to be low, and lamented my way of life. My pious Lady Warrington mother and my worldly Aunt Bernstein put their elderly heads together to grieve over it. “Why, with his name, he might marry any woman he pleased!” meek Religion declared, keeping one eye fixed firmly on heaven and the other on the main chance. “I meddle in no man’s affairs, and I admire genius,” said my uncle, “but it is a great pity you consort with poets and scribblers and that low sort of company, when you might have married a lovely creature with a hundred thousand pounds, but you let her slip and run after a penniless country girl.”

“But I gave her my promise, uncle,” I said.

“Promise? Promises are matters of prudence and careful arrangement! When you first made that engagement to little Miss Lambert, you had not yet seen that lovely American heiress your good mother naturally wanted you to wed. Your duty to your mother, nephew — your duty to the Fifth Commandment — would have fully warranted your breaking with Miss L., to fulfil your excellent mother’s intentions regarding that rich Countess, what’s her silly Dutch name? Never mind the name, but a plumb, Master George, is something well worth chasing! Why, I have my dear little Miley at dancing school with Miss Barwell, Nabob Barwell’s daughter, and I make no secret of my hope the children will form an attachment that lasts their whole lives. I told the Nabob so. We left the House of Commons early one dancing day to watch them, and it was beautiful to see the two young things walking a minuet together! It brought tears to my eyes, for I have a tender heart, George, and I love my boy!”

“But if I prefer Miss Lambert, with her twopence to her name, to any Countess with a hundred thousand pounds?” I said.

“Why then, sir, you have a very singular taste, that is all,” the old man huffed, turning on his heel and leaving me. I could perfectly understand his vexation that I could not see the world as plainly as he did.

Aunt Bernstein liked my engagement no better, nor the quiet, unpretending Lambert household I spent so much of my time in. Their simple, unworldly ways wearied, and perhaps annoyed, this old creature who had spent her whole life moving in high society, and she no more relished their company than a certain gentleman who is not quite so black as he is painted relishes holy water. She chafed at my hanging around my sweetheart’s side every chance I got. Having risen high in her favor after my play, I began to fall out of it once more, and Harry became the household’s new favorite — a turn I did not begrudge him in the least. He was our family hero now, writing us brief, plain letters from the war front, that at first not even Madame de Bernstein bothered to read closely, for his accounts were simple, the facts he narrated far from sensational.

Early in London, we got the news of the glorious action at Minden on the first of August, where Wolfe’s old regiment was one of the six British lines that won that famous day of victory. At that very hour, the young General lay fever-stricken in his camp outside Quebec, no doubt burning with rage and disappointment at the recent repulse his troops had suffered. The fleet carrying Wolfe and his army had sailed up the St. Lawrence in June, and landed the men on the last day of the month on the Island of Orleans, directly across from the towering cliff that Quebec stands upon. After the great battle where the General met his death, my brother Harry wrote me one of his simple letters, describing his own small, modest part in that glorious September 13th, adding nothing new to the dozens of accounts already written of the fight, save one detail: he swore, on the testimony of a fellow aide-de-camp who stood at Wolfe’s side the moment he was struck, that the General never spoke a single word after receiving his mortal wound, so all the famous dying lines attributed to him are no more authentic than a grand made-up speech by Livy or Thucydides.

From his post on the Island of Orleans, Wolfe watched hungrily for any chance to meet the enemy on even ground. He landed men above Quebec, he landed them below, shifting from spot to spot, determined to attack the moment he saw an opening. It was surely a terrible blunder on the part of the Marquis de Montcalm to accept a pitched battle on equal terms with Wolfe, for the British General had no heavy artillery, and after that famous scalade of the heights that put us on the Plains of Abraham, we were certainly closer to the city, but still as far as ever from being inside its walls. The game of cat and mouse those two brave commanders played from July until Wolfe won his final, high-stakes wager in September must have been as fascinating a contest as any two competing players ever engaged in.

My brother narrated how the sport began on the very first night after landing: at midnight, the French sent a whole squadron of flaming fire ships drifting down upon the British vessels that were unloading stores at Orleans. Our sailors thought it a fine game to tow the fire ships clear of the fleet and beach them on the shore, where they burned out harmlessly. The moment the French commander learned the British fleet had entered the river, he marched his men to Beauport, just ahead of the city, and took up a nearly unassailable fortified position. Once Wolfe’s stores and hospitals were properly established on Orleans, he crossed the river to the left shore, drawing nearer to his enemy, but every mile of land before him was up in arms. Indians lurking in the forests seized any of our advanced parties that strayed in to clear the trees, and murdered them with unspeakable tortures. The French themselves were as savage as their native allies. The broad, rushing Montmorenci River stood between Wolfe and the French camp, and he could not attack them there, nor force a way into the city behind them. Determined to find some other point where the enemy might be vulnerable, Wolfe sailed past Quebec and skirted the far left bank of the river, but every foot of the shoreline was heavily guarded, and after braving fire from every battery along the banks, he returned to his post at Montmorenci.

On the far right of the French position, across the mouth of the Montmorenci that was fordable at low tide, stood a small enemy redoubt. Wolfe determined to seize it, hoping that Montcalm would be forced to march his men out of their fortified lines to defend it, and give him the pitched battle he craved. On the last day of July, he played this desperate hand. He and his second-in-command General Monckton, who occupied Point Levi across the river, crossed the St. Lawrence from their respective posts, braving a storm of artillery shot as their men rowed for the shore. No sooner had the troops landed than they charged at the French redoubt in wild disorder, were cut down in great numbers before its walls, and were forced to retreat in disarray. The second wave of British troops, who were meant to cross the Montmorenci at low tide, advanced across the river in perfect order, and the enemy even evacuated the redoubt and fell back to their main lines — but from those entrenchments, they poured in such a murderous fire that any hope of breaking their line was hopeless, and the General was forced to call a full retreat.

That disastrous Battle of Montmorenci, which Harry and I have fought over again a hundred times over our wine glasses, formed the heavy, dismal news in the first dispatch from Wolfe that reached England, plunging all of us into deep gloom. What more could anyone expect from a commander so rash? What other disasters were bound to follow? Was there ever a scheme so wild, as to send three separate bodies of men across wide, fast rivers, in the face of murderous batteries, on nothing more than the chance of luring a heavily entrenched enemy out of his defenses to fight you? It was the talk of every drawing room and every coffee house in London. Grave men shook their heads, and prophesied fresh ruin. The General, who took to his bed shuddering with fever right after that failure, had barely six weeks left to live, and to die immortal. How is greatness ever achieved, anyway? By merit? By madness? By frolic? By fortune? Is fate that doles out our victories and defeats? Does the just cause always win? How did the French steal Canada from the savages, and we steal it from the French, and after which of those conquests was it right to sing Te Deum? We are always so ready to drag heaven into our petty quarrels, and call on the gods to side with us no matter the dispute. Does the prizefighter Broughton, after pummeling Slack black and blue, lift his swollen, blackened eye to Jove and thank him for his victory? If ten thousand boxers are entitled to that grace, why not one? And if Broughton deserves to be grateful, what on earth is poor Slack supposed to be?

“By the list of disabled officers, many of whom are of rank, you may perceive, sir, that the army is much weakened. By the nature of this river the most formidable part of the armament is deprived of the power of acting, yet we have almost the whole force of Canada to oppose. In this situation there is such a choice of difficulties, that I own myself at a loss how to determine. The affairs of Great Britain, I know, require the most vigorous measures; but then the courage of a handful of brave men should be exerted only where there is some hope of a favourable event. The admiral and I have examined the town with a view to a general assault: and he would readily join in this or any other measure for the public service; but I cannot propose to him an undertaking of so dangerous a nature, and promising so little success…. I found myself so ill, and am still so weak, that I begged the general officers to consult together for the public utility. They are of opinion that they should try by conveying up a corps of 4000 or 5000 men (which is nearly the whole strength of the army, after the points of Levi and Orleans are put in a proper state of defence) to draw the enemy from their present position, and bring them to an action. I have acquiesced in their proposal, and we are preparing to put it into execution.”

So wrote the General, of whose noble, moving letters it is plain our dear Harry was not the author or secretary, from his headquarters at Montmorenci Falls on the 2nd of September. And on the 14th of October following, the Rodney cutter arrived in England with that sad, worrying news. The attack at Montmorenci had failed, the commander was deathly ill, the army was dwindling away, and the city they meant to take was so strongly fortified a direct assault was next to impossible. The only remaining chance was to fight the Marquis de Montcalm on far better terms than storming his entrenchments, and lure him out of his current stronghold. Would the French commander, whose great military genius was famous across all Europe, fall into such a trap? No wonder there were pale, anxious faces in the City that day, and doubt and gloom spread everywhere the news traveled.

Three days after that first melancholy dispatch arrived, the famous letters came bearing word of that miraculous, triumphant turn of fortune that crowned Mr. Wolfe’s brilliant career. If no man can be called happy until he has met his death, what are we to make of this one? His end was so glorious that I swear not even his own mother or his sweetheart ought to have mourned it, or wished him alive again. I know we speak of a hero here, and yet I vow I scarcely know if I admire more the result of his genius, his invention, and his daring, or the boldness of a gambler winning impossible odds. Suppose his men’s ascent up the cliffs had been discovered half an hour sooner, and his troops beaten back as they most assuredly would have been? Suppose the Marquis de Montcalm had never left his fortified entrenchments to accept that strange challenge? Change those two points, neither of which Wolfe had any control over at all, and what becomes of the glory of the young hero, of the great minister who discovered him, of the whole intoxicated nation that rose up frantic with self-congratulation at the victory? What strange fate is it that shapes our ends, or the ends of great nations? In all the high-stakes games my Lord Chatham played, he won this one prodigious gamble, and even as the greedy British hand seized all of Canada, it loosened its grip on the American colonies, which would soon slip away entirely.

Of course that kind of hindsight wisdom is easy, thirty years after the event. We wonder now at the rashness of that plan, now that the deed is done, and marvel at Montcalm’s blunder. What brilliant generals we all are on paper! What witty retorts come to us long after the conversation is over! How clearly we see how the game should have been played, once the final move is made! But at the time when we first heard the news of Wolfe’s glorious deeds on the Plains of Abraham, of the army marshaled in the dark and rowed silently up the midnight river, of those cliffs scaled by the fearless leader and his troops, of the miraculous surprise that caught the enemy completely unawares, of Montcalm’s willingness to meet our challenge on the open plain, and his total defeat there by the sheer valour of our men — all of England was drunk with joy. The whole nation rose up, and felt itself made stronger by Wolfe’s victory. Not merely every man who fought in that battle, but even those of us at home who had once condemned the whole campaign as reckless, felt ourselves heroes. Our spirits soared as the enemy’s faltered. Friends embraced each other when they met in the streets. Coffee houses and public squares were thronged with people all eager to talk the news. Courtiers rushed to pay their respects to the King, and to the great minister whose wisdom had set the campaign in motion. When Lord Chatham stepped out in public, the people followed him down the streets with shouts and blessings. No one mourned the dead warrior — they marveled at his noble, perfect end. Should James Wolfe’s friends weep and wear mourning, because a chariot of fire had come down from heaven to carry him away? They should watch with wonder, and see him depart, radiant, rising far above all of us. To have a friend who had been near Wolfe was a mark of distinction. Every soldier who fought under him was a hero. In our own little circle, I swear it felt like a great distinction to be Harry’s brother. We did not doubt for a moment that he, who knew the ground from earlier scouting expeditions, had found that secret path up the heights and pointed it out to his General. His promotion was a certainty, of course. Even our stuff

Had your father, dear young folks, possessed even the smallest modicum of common prudence, not only would this chapter of his history never have been written—you yourselves would never have drawn breath in the world to plague him a hundred ways. You would never come thundering and shouting through the passages when he wants quiet to pore over his books; never rouse him from that doze every healthy country gentleman earns after dinner; never mislay his spectacles right when he needs them, or steal away his newspaper before he’s finished the leading piece. You would never have run him ragged over tailor’s bills, mantua-maker’s bills, and tutor’s fees, never broken his rest mid-night when you took it into your heads to fall ill, sending your silly mother into such a tizzy that she never sat still for half an hour. What use is there in Darby pulling on his nightcap when Joan won’t rest? Every trifling ailment any one of you ever caught scared her half out of her wits, and I protest I never knew a moment’s peace. Were I not the most long-suffering man alive, I’d have been glad to pack the whole rambunctious brood off to boarding school for good.

Now that you’ve outgrown childhood—long petticoats, chickenpox, smallpox, whooping cough, scarlet fever, all the other charming mishaps of juvenile life—your unconscionable mother has gone and proposed turning the whole south wing of the house into a nursery for hypothetical grandchildren. She’s determined to marry off your brother Captain Miles early, just as we were, fretting that he spends too much time loitering at Brookes’s and Goosetree’s when he’s up in London. She has the perversity to hint that while an invitation to Carlton House may sound very grand, it’s far too dangerous for a young man, and that Miles ought to live somewhere far from temptation, sow his few wild oats, and settle down just as we did.

Marry? My dear creature, we never ought to have married at all! By every rule of prudence and duty, I ought to have wriggled out of my little engagement to Miss Theo (who would have found some other perfectly good husband), and wedded a wealthy heiress. Your Uncle John was a parson and could not duel, poor Charley was still a boy at school, and your grandfather was far too old a man to call me out with sword and pistol. There never was a more foolish match in all the world than ours, and all our relations were perfectly right to fly into a rage over it. What are relations made for, after all, if not to be angry and find fault? When Hester marries, mind you, Master George: quarrel with her if she does not pick a husband of your exact choosing. And when George gets his church living, after making senior wrangler and fellow of his college, Miss Hester, toss that pretty little nose of yours right up at whatever young lady he fancies for himself. As for you, my little Theo, I will not part with you. You must never leave your old father: he likes you to play Haydn for him after dinner, and peel his walnuts when the meal is done.

[On the blank leaf opposite this paragraph, a large, girlish hand scrawls: “I never intend to go. — THEODOSIA.” “Nor I. — HESTER.” The family Bible, however, tells us they both married in the end: Theodosia Warrington wed Joseph Clinton, son of the Rev. Joseph Blake, who later became Master of Rodwell Regis Grammar School; Hester Mary married Captain F. Handyman of the Royal Navy, in 1804. — ED.]

While they had the great “blessing” of meeting and billing and cooing every single day, your two parents drifted through a fool’s paradise, barely heeding the world around them, all its tattle and meddling. Rinaldo was as brave a warrior as ever slew a Turk, but you know he could not resist lingering in Armida’s enchanted garden. Pray, my Lady Armida, what spell did you cast over me in youth, so that glory, fashion, the gaming tables, and the company of every witty man I ever met could not keep me long from your apron strings, or out of reach of your dear, simple prattle? What did we even talk about, through all those endless hours we spent together? I never napped after dinner back then. Which of us was the witty one? Was it me, or was it you? And how on earth did every conversation feel so perfectly delightful?

I remember that year I did not even bother to go gawk at the Earl of Ferrers’s trial and hanging, when all the rest of London was crowding to see the spectacle. The King of Prussia’s capital had fallen; if the Austrians and Russians had camped right outside the Tower of London, the city could not have buzzed more. But Miss Theo and her young gentleman felt no great rush of pity or indignation over the news. What was the fate of Leipzig or Berlin to us? The plain truth is, that dear little old house on Dean Street was a garden of delights all its own. I have been idle in the years since, but never half so happy. Shall we order the postchaise tomorrow, my dear, leave the children to keep house, and drive all the way back to London to see if those old lodgings are still to let? You shall sit in your old spot in the window, and wave a little handkerchief as I walk up the street. Call what we did imprudent all you like. We would do it all over again, would we not? My good friends, if Venus herself had walked into the room to claim the golden apple, I was so infatuated I would have handed it straight to your mother. And had she been the one choosing, she would have picked me, in my threadbare old coat, over Lord Clive with every single diamond he brought back from India.

Once, for a terrible little stretch of that year, I half-went mad. I daydreamed of turning highwayman just to get caught and hanged like Lord Ferrers, or enlisting in the Prussian army and begging one of his enemies to knock my brains out, or signing up for the India service to perform some reckless exploit that would end in my utter destruction. Ah me! That was a dreadful time. Your mother scarce dares speak of it now save in a whisper of terror, and even thinking of it makes her flinch—such cruel, sharp pain it was. She was unhappy years later on that same anniversary, until one of you was born on that exact date. Suppose we had been parted? What would have become of us? What would my lot have been without her? When I let myself dwell on that possibility, the whole world goes blank. I do not speak of a parting now, after thirty happy years of union God has granted us. We are in the autumn of our days, our successors are grown and ready, and whichever of us is called away first knows the other will follow before long. But we were actually parted once, in our youth, and I tremble still to think what ruin might have fallen on us if a dearest friend had not stepped in to bring us back together.

All unknown to me, my relatives in England—very likely thinking they were acting for my own good—chose to write to Madam Esmond in Virginia, and lay out what they called the utter folly of the engagement I had entered into. Every last one of them sang the exact same song. I saw all those letters years later, when my mother showed them to me at home in Virginia, and burned the whole cursed stack to ash. Aunt Bernstein was first in line with her advice: a young person with no remarkable good looks, no grand family, no money? No match could be more imprudent, it was their duty to break it off for dear George’s sake. She had a dozen eligible heiresses lined up for me, what a shame to throw myself away on this girl, her sister ought to step in at once.

Lady Warrington had to write too, in her own peculiar style. Her ladyship’s letter was crammed full of scripture texts, dressing all her worldly disapproval in fancy phylacteries. She pointed out that I was keeping low company, running about with actors and other such people who, she would not say were absolutely ungodly (Heaven forbid!), but who were deplorably worldly. She would not say outright that some artful woman had inveigled me for her daughter, after having failed to capture my younger brother Harry first. She was far from speaking ill of the young woman I had chosen, but it was undeniable that Miss Lambert had no fortune, no expectations, and her parents were clearly eager to compromise me. Sir Miles, that wise judge of worldly affairs, fully agreed with her, even begged her to write and entreat Madam Esmond to interfere before the ill-advised match could go forward.

And then the new Countess of Castlewood had to stick her finger in the pie too, writing a majestic letter to Madam Esmond stating that as Providence had placed her at the head of the Esmond family, it was her sacred duty to warn her kinswoman to put a stop to this marriage.
