I am certain the three women laid their heads together beforehand, sending packet after packet of warnings across the Atlantic to the Virginian lady.

One raw April morning, I set off as usual to pay my call on my dearest girl, expecting to find her waiting with that familiar soft smile to welcome me. Instead I found Mrs. Lambert, her eyes bright red with crying, and the General as pale as death. “Read this, George Warrington!” he said, as his wife dropped her head in her hands. I recognised the handwriting at once. Even to this day, the sound of fire irons clattering against a hearth in a room overhead gives me a tremor—for I heard exactly that noise that day, coming from the girls’ bedchamber where they were sobbing together. Poor, gentle child! Poor Theo!

“What can I do after this, George, my poor boy?” the General asked, pacing the room in desperation. I did not even finish reading all of Madam Esmond’s letter, for a faint, sick dread washed over me, though I fear I could recite great chunks of it by heart to this day. Its tone was polite enough, its words temperate, but every line implied that Mr. and Mrs. Lambert had inveigled me into the marriage, that they knew full well such a union was unworthy of me. Madam Esmond wrote that, as she understood it, they had first wanted the exact same match for her younger son Harry, a plan they had only abandoned when they learned Harry would not be the heir to the Virginian estate. If Mr. Lambert was a man of spirit and honour, as he was said to be, she could scarcely imagine he would persist in pushing for the match after her warning. She would not lay commands on her son, whose temper she knew well, but for the sake of Miss Lambert’s own reputation and comfort, she insisted the dissolution of the engagement must come from her family, not from the just unwillingness of Rachel Esmond Warrington of Virginia.

“God help us, George!” the General said, “and give us all strength to bear this grief, these cruel charges your mother has seen fit to bring! They are hard, but they do not matter half so much as sparing my poor girl all the pain we possibly can. She has never given a soul a moment’s unhappiness since the day she was born, and it is wicked that she should be made to suffer.” He passed his hand over his own dry, glistening eyes.

“It was my fault, Martin! My fault!” poor Mrs. Lambert wept.

“Your mother spoke fairly to us once, and gave her promise,” the General said.

“And do you think I will withdraw mine?” I cried, swearing a thousand frantic oaths that I was bound to Theo before Heaven, that nothing on earth would ever part me from her.

“She herself will demand the parting,” the General said. “She is a good, dutiful girl. She will not have her father and mother called schemers, and treated with public scorn. Your mother most likely did not realise what harm she was doing, but the harm is done. You may see the child, and she will tell you the same. Of course, George, you will give me your word of honour not to try and see her afterwards. As soon as my military business allows, we will leave London, and all be together somewhere quiet. It is you, perhaps, who ought to leave first. But give me your word, at any rate, that you will not seek her out. We must spare her pain, sir! We must spare her pain!” The good man sat down, so deep in his own anguish that I, still not yet crushed fully under the weight of my own grief, felt his suffering, and pitied it.

It could not be that the dear lips I had kissed only yesterday would speak to me but once more. We were all in that familiar room, the one we met in every day, my own sketchbook sitting on the table next to her little workbox. She was in the chamber upstairs, and she would have to come down soon. The door creaked open, and I saw her sweet face, pale as our little Mary’s was when we thought she would die of her fever. There was even a faint, brave smile on her lips. She came up to me, and kissed my cheek. “Good-bye, dear George!” she said.

Great Heaven! I sit here now, an old man, with my wife’s old workbox across the table from me, and she is but five minutes away in the kitchen serving out tea to her pensioners, and my eyes grow so dim and full I can not see the words on the page before me. I am three and twenty years old again, reliving every step of that agony. Who dared sully her sweet, innocent love with suspicion? Who had any right to stab such a soft, gentle bosom? You can see those three ladies sharpening their knives, and that poor child baring her breast to the blade.

“What makes you look so angry, papa?” my wife says, stepping into the room.

“My love,” I tell her, “it is the thirteenth of April.” A flash of old pain shoots across her face, then melts into a soft, tender smile. She bore that martyrdom, and out of the old pang comes a halo of forgiveness. I can not forgive, not until I grow so doting in old age I can no longer remember a single thing. “Hal will be home for Easter,” she says, “he will bring two or three of his Cambridge friends with him.” And straight away she starts chattering of plans for little parties, treats, walks to amuse the boys. When is she ever doing anything but plotting to make everyone around her happy?

An old man in spectacles scribbling down his own pitiful old miseries over his ledger is a quaint, ridiculous sight, I will own. My corns ache, I know, but I suspect every man’s neighbour has his own pinching shoes. I will not howl over my old grief for too long. Many a man, I dare say, has had the light of his day snuffed out suddenly, the joy of his life extinguished, left to wander in dark, vague torment. To this day, when I pick up Howel’s Letters and stumble on the passage about Prince Charles in Spain, that whole old tragedy comes leaping back to life. I fled to Brighthelmstone then, took a room facing east, and watched the sun rise every morning for weeks after nights of total wakefulness, smoking my pipe of Virginian tobacco right in his face. If I happen to see that same sun rise there now, I shake my fist at him, remembering what horrible grief and savage wrath he once watched me suffer. Even though my wife is mine for good now, I am still cross about it. Who dared make us hurt so?

I kept my promise. I never set foot inside the General’s house after that last, terrible parting. But at night I would creep past, and stare up at her window, watching the lamp burn long into the dark. I would visit her little brother at the Chartreux school, stuff him full of cakes and hand him half-crowns. I would invite her elder brother to dine with me, and almost kiss him goodbye when he left. I breakfasted every morning at a little coffee house in Whitehall just to see General Lambert walk to his office, and we would nod at each other sadly, and pass on without a word. The women never came out. They were with her, trying to talk her into forgetting me. Oh, the weary, weary days! Oh, the maddening, endless stretch of time!

At last I saw a doctor’s chariot drawing up outside the General’s door every single day. Was she ill? I am half ashamed to own that I was almost glad she was ill. My own suffering was so infernal, that I greedily wanted her to share my pain. And of course she would—what gentle, compassionate heart like hers would not feel every last pang of my own grief, what pain would she not bear to spare me even a single twinge?

I hunted that doctor down. I poured my whole story out to him, laid my heart bare with such passionate sincerity that he won his sympathy. My confession let him understand his young patient’s malady, the one no dose of his physic could cure. I told him everything: that I would marry her no matter what risks I had to brave, that without her I was utterly wrecked and ruined, and cared not a farthing what became of me. My mother had once given her consent, and to take it back now, when the bond between us was drawn so tight it outstripped any duty I owed her, was nothing less than cruelty.

That good man must have been unhappy in love himself once, so gently did he know how to succour the miserable. He would not act as a secret messenger between two forbidden lovers outright, but he said he could safely tell Miss Lambert that he had seen me, and was prescribing for my broken heart as well as hers. He said he had never seen anyone bear suffering with such angelical sweetness as Theo. He prescribed Jesuit’s bark for her, he told me, but he suspected hearing news of me did her more good than all his medicine put together. I had a little ring set with a cameo of Hercules, too small for his finger, and the good old man never wore trinkets anyway, but I made him hang it to his watch chain, in the hopes that Theo would see it, and know the token came from me.

I clung to my friend Spencer in those days, the man from the Temple who had also made his own ill-fated love match, and we would walk for miles, back and forth between my lodgings and his chambers, our conversation never straying far from the women we loved. I dare say I told every stranger who would listen my grief. My landlady and Betty the housemaid both pitied me

The flurry of the first shock and greeting had barely settled when the sharp little maiden launched straight into her rebuke. “So you have finally come round to ask after Theo? And you deign to feel sorry that your cruel neglect has laid her low these past six weeks, while you never sent so much as a single word of inquiry? Very fine behaviour indeed, Mr. George, I am sure!”
“Kind?” I gasped, my own pale, fever-worn hands trembling where I clutched the half-empty vial of lavender cordial the doctor had left on my mantel that morning. “Do you call it kind to sit at her side every hour of every day for a full year, then vanish without a single farewell?”
“My dear girl, you know full well I gave your father my solemn promise—”
“Promise!” Miss Hetty tossed her head, shrugging her small shoulders so hard the mob cap perched on her curls slid askew. “A very grand sort of promise, that, to make my darling waste away, then out of the blue bid her ‘good-bye’ and walk off for ever. I do suppose gentlemen keep those promises only when it suits them. If I were a man, I would never trifle with a poor girl’s heart then abandon her. What harm did Theo ever do you, but be foolish enough to love you far too well? By what right do you steal her away from all the quiet happiness we had before you ever stepped through our door, then cast her off just because some old lady across the Atlantic does not think her good enough for her precious son? She was the sun of our whole house before you came! I was the whole world to her, until you turned her head. And now, forsooth, because your mamma fancies you might catch a richer bride, you desert her!”
“Great heavens, child!” I cried, stung to exasperation by her warped, unseeing version of the truth. “It was not I who drew back! It is not I who am forbidden your threshold! Your father demanded my honour on the spot that I would never attempt to see her again—”
“Honour!” she laughed, bitter as winter frost, flinging the half-embroidered handkerchief stitched with Theo’s initials onto my table. “You men preen yourselves as our superiors, and expect us to bow down and admire you! Upon my word, George Warrington, you ought to be sent back to your Virginia schoolroom, let your black nurse tuck you up in bed, and beg your mamma’s permission before you dare step out for a walk. Oh George, little did I think my sister would give her whole heart to a man with no more spirit than to flee at the very first sign of trouble! When Dr. Heberden told me he was attending you these past weeks, I resolved to come and see you myself—and you do look wretched, thank goodness, so I know you are not quite as hard-hearted as you seem. I will not tell Theo you are ill, though. She has not forgotten you, you see. She cannot simply walk out of a room, break every solemn vow she ever made, and step gaily back into society the next day as if nothing ever happened. That privilege is reserved for men, our betters in courage and wisdom—men who will desert an angel, yes, an angel ten thousand times too good for you, the angel who was the blessing of all our lives until she laid eyes on you! That is what you call honour? I despise the lot of you! Your clever plays, your verses, your fine wit—half the time they are dreadfully stupid. I will not stay up half the night copying your manuscripts, nor loiter for hours at the window wasting my time just to catch a glimpse of your worship strutting down the street with your hat tilted at that absurd cock. If you are set on running off, then give me back my sister! Give me back the old Theo who loved every one of us, before you stole her away and left her to die here alone while your mother hunts you a wealthier wife. O brave, fine gentleman! Go marry whoever your mother picks out for you, and leave my dearest to waste away!”
“Hetty, for the love of all that is good!” I cried, reeling under the force of her passion. “It is not I who wish to leave her! I offered to keep my promise to marry her, and your father turned me away, and bound me on my honour never to seek her out. What have I in this world, but my word and my good name?”
“Good name, indeed! You keep your word to him, and break it to her! A very pretty sort of honour, that! If I were a man, I would soon show you what I think of your fine honour—oh, George, George! Do you not see how distracted I am? I hardly know what words I am saying, I am so distraught. They do not guess the truth back at our lodgings. They do not see what I see, that she will surely die if you leave her. Say you will not leave her! Have pity on me, Mr. Warrington, and give me back my dearest!”
The warm-hearted, overwrought creature careened from blazing anger to wild entreaty, from sharp scorn to scalding tears, her whole small frame shaking with sobs. Was my fiery little self-appointed doctor right about her patient’s case? Was there no other cure but the one she begged for? Have not thousands of other souls endured that same cruel amputation of a heart, wasted away through the same fever and despair, lain convinced there was no life left worth living, only to recover after all, and limp on through the rest of their days? Once, Theo and I had sat snug by our fireside, listening to Hetty grieve over her own long-ago hopeless attachment, and we had smiled complacently, wrapped in our own perfect happiness, as you might huddle warm indoors and hear the winter wind howl outside the panes, or stand safe on the shore and watch a ship toss through a storm at sea. But in that moment, I did not care a farthing for that old proof that hearts could heal after separation. I was all too ready to share Hetty’s terrors, and fully convinced that the life I held dearest on earth would be snuffed out if we were kept apart.
I was half ready to pour all this out to Dr. Heberden when the good little man clamped a hand over my mouth, his round eyes wide with fright. “Hush! Not a word of this to me, sir! If two people who happen to be acquainted chance to meet and talk in my patient’s rooms, that is no fault of mine. But match-making? Love plots? I will have no part of it! General Lambert will challenge me to a duel behind Montagu House the second he returns to London, that I swear, and I am far too fond of my own skin to meet him there!” He grabbed his gold-headed cane, his wig askew and his silk stockings rolled down at the ankle, and scurried out to his waiting chariot before I could protest. “And no more secret meetings with Miss Hetty, mind you!” he called over his shoulder as the footman shut the carriage door.
Oh, of course! We were men of honour, after all, our word our bond. I had been granted that one precious, unexpected glimpse of Hetty, and I told myself I could be content to hold out for weeks more. I walked with her all the way to the edge of Soho, never once dreaming of arranging another meeting—but the clever little emissary had thought of that for me.
“Still go up to the British Museum to read your old histories, don’t you?” she asked, not looking at me.
“Oh yes, sometimes,” I said. “Though I am far too wretched to read now. The words blur right off the page. Even my beloved Pocahontas manuscript feels wearisome to me these days. I—”
“Nonsense!” she stamped her tiny kid slipper on the cobblestones. “You are more stupid than Harry, I do declare! You leave the Museum at three o’clock. You cut across the road to Tottenham Court, walk through the village, and come back down that Green Lane that runs north of the new Foundling Hospital. You know you do! Walk there for a week, it will do you no harm at all. Good day, sir!” She dropped me a sharp little curtsey, pulled her veil down over her face, and vanished down the street.
That Green Lane is all built over with neat brick terraces now, but back in the days of good old King George the Second, it was a rough, half-rural track skirting London’s outskirts, so dangerous that parties of folk out for junkets in Hampstead and Highgate would only return after dark escorted by tavern waiters bearing lanthorns, to ward off the footpads that lurked in the hedgerows. The two hilltop churches of Hampstead and Highgate rose clear against the blue sky at the end of the lane, and for three days straight I walked that path, lingering to look out over the open fields toward the hills. Halfway down the lane there was a little roadside alehouse with a sign for The Protestant Hero, selling spiced cake and cool bitter beer. On my third pass by, the landlady, a plump decent woman in a clean starched apron, smiled and curtseyed at me over her threshold. “The lady has not come by yet, sir,” she called out. “You are welcome to step in and take a can of my best cool beer while you wait.”
At last, on the 25th of May—a day I will mark with the whitest stone of my memory for as long as I live—just past Mr. Whitefield’s Tabernacle on Tottenham Road, I spied a landau bobbing toward me. Perched on the box-seat beside the driver was young Charley Lambert, who waved his hat wildly and shouted my name. I ran to the carriage so fast my knees knocked together, I thought I would stumble and fall under the wheel. Inside, behind the open window, sat Hetty—and beside her, propped up on a stitched linen pillow, was my Theo.
The little hand that slipped into mine was so thin and light it felt like holding a sparrow. Her cheeks were flushed and hollow, her eyes bright with that strange, burning light illness brings, and the thrill of her soft voice as she spoke my name wrapped around me so tight I could not tell if the pain in my chest was grief or joy, the two tangled up so close.
“I am taking her out for an airing to Hampstead,” Hetty said, demure as a lamb, though I caught the wicked little twitch at the corner of her mouth. “The doctor says the open country air will do her a world of good.”
“I have been ill, but I am better now, George,” Theo whispered.
Just then, a great swell of psalm music burst from the congregation pouring out of the Tabernacle beside us. I held her hand fast in mine, and her eyes met mine, and it felt as if we had never been parted at all. I have heard that psalm a thousand times since then: my wife has played it on her harpsichord, our little ones have warbled it at the nursery fire. Do you understand now, my dears, why I have always loved it so? It was the music that played when our love was given back to us, the music that sang hope to me in the very darkest, most miserable stretch of my whole life. Even the long harsh confinement at Fort Duquesne had its soft little memories, after all: kind old Biche, my drunken jailor, the trill of the forest birds at reveille, the distant military bugles of the garrison.
Young Charley leaned down from his perch on the box, grinning at the sight of Theo and I lost in our own little world, Hetty half smiling beside us listening to the psalm. “I say, I think I would like to go inside and hear Mr. Whitefield preach right now! Come along with me, Charley,” Hetty said, tugging at his coat sleeve. “George can drive on ahead for half an hour with Theo, up toward Hampstead and back, and we will meet them here when the service is done.”
Charley made a face, no great desire to sit through a two-hour sermon, and suggested George might go into the chapel with him instead—but Hetty was not to be swayed. “I will never help you sneak out to cock-fights or horse races ever again, sir, if you do not come along this instant!” she threatened, and the poor boy was forced to clamber down off the box, and the two of them vanished through the chapel doors together.
Let any priggish moralist, who remembers all my old promises to General Lambert, judge me now. Could any man alive blame me for climbing straight up into that landau and sitting down beside my dearest Theo? Suppose I did break my word? You are welcome to your fine, spotless virtue, reverend sir, if you would have done any different. I do not suppose any of my own children would ever be so bold as to follow their own hearts and choose the person they love, after all. No no, my dears, you will all let papa pick your spouses for you, be hungry exactly when I tell you to be, and arrange your own children’s marriages just as soon as you are grown.
I looked over at the sweet lady beside me now, her needles plying soft wool by the fireside, and laughed. “There we are, my dear. I have reached that part of the story at last.”
“Which part is that?” Theo said, lifting her head, her cheeks flushing pink. “Do skip all that silly love nonsense, and get on to the grand battles, and your heroic defence of—”
“Of Fort Fiddlededee in 1778!” I teased. “When I pulled General Washington’s epaulet right off his shoulder, gouged General Gates’s eye, cut off Charles Lee’s head and pasted it back on again!”
“Tell us the fighting bits, papa!” the boys clamoured, and even our old friend the Captain, home on leave, nodded gravely and said he would deign to listen to any military details, even from a militia officer.
“Softly now, young gentlemen, everything in its proper turn. I have not reached the war yet. I am still just a foolish young fellow, climbing into a landau beside the girl I swore I would never speak to again, holding her small, hot hand that was thumping a hundred and twenty beats a minute, do you remember that, my love? And as the carriage trotted slowly up the Hampstead road, I said to Miss Lambert—”
“Ah! Ah! Now we listen!” the two little girls cried in unison, and their French governess Mademoiselle Eleonore laughed, shrugging her pretty shoulders. “La parole est a vous, Monsieur le Chevalier!”
We were all circled round the fire that night: Theo in her usual chair on one side, me on the other, Mademoiselle de Blois over in the corner (the Captain was looking very sweet at her, and I suspected our friend the Chevalier de Florac had a hand in bringing her to us), the two girls listening as attentively as little nymphs learning song from Apollo, and John and Thomas trundling in the tea tray and the silver urn. I pulled my crumpled manuscript from my pocket and waved it at them all. “Very well. Now I shall tell you all your mother’s secrets, and mine.”
“There is nothing there to be ashamed of, papa,” my sweet wife said, the blush rising all the way over her kind old face.
“But before I begin, young folks, allow me two or three little questions.”
“Allons! Always questions!” Mademoiselle laughed, and tossed her head.

You, Captain Miles Warrington, have the honour of winning the good graces of a lady—of ever so many ladies—of the Duchess of Devonshire, let us say, of Mrs. Crew, of Mrs. Fitzherbert, of the Queen of Prussia, of the Goddess Venus, of Mademoiselle Hillisberg of the Opera—never mind of whom, in fine. If you win a lady’s good graces, do you always return to the mess to blab every detail of what passed between you?
“Not such a fool, Squire!” says the Captain, preening his side curl in the mantel glass.
“Have you, Miss Theo, told your mother every word you said to Mr. Joe Blake, junior, in the shrubbery this morning?”
“Joe Blake, indeed!” cries Theo, stamping her little foot.
“And you, mademoiselle? That scented billet which came to you under Sir Thomas’s frank, have you told us all the letter contains? Look how she blushes! As red as the stage curtain, on my word! No, mademoiselle, we all have our secrets” (says the Squire, here executing his most elegant French bow). “No, Theo, there was nothing in the shrubbery but nuts, my child! No, Miles, my son, we don’t tell all, even to the most indulgent of fathers—and if I tell what happened in a landau on the Hampstead Road, on the 25th of May, 1760, may the Chevalier Ruspini pull out every tooth in my head!”
“Pray tell, papa!” cries his wife. “Or, as Jobson, who drove us that day, is still in your service, perhaps you will call him in from the stables! I insist upon your telling!”
“What is then this mystery?” asks the French governess, in her pretty accent, leaning over to my wife.
“Eh, ma fille!” whispers the lady. “Thou wouldst ask me what I said? I said ‘Yes!’—behold all I said.”
And so ‘tis my wife peached, not I; that was the sum of our conversation, as the carriage, all too swiftly as I thought, galloped towards Hampstead and flew back again. Theo had not agreed to flout her honoured parents—no such thing. But she would marry no other person; no, not if she lived to be as old as Methuselah; no, not the Prince of Wales himself would she take. Her heart she had given away with her papa’s consent—nay, order—and it was not hers to resume. So kind a father must relent one of these days; and if George would keep his promise—were it now, or were it in twenty years, or were it in another world, she knew she should never break hers.
Hetty’s face beamed with delight when, my little interview over, she saw Theo’s countenance wearing a sweet, unruffled tranquillity. All the doctor’s physic had not done her half so much good, the fond sister declared. The girls went home after their small act of disobedience. I gave up the place I had held for that brief, shining spell at my dear invalid’s side. Hetty skipped back into her seat, and little Charley scrambled up onto his box. He told me in after days that it had been a very dull, stupid sermon he’d heard; the little chap was far too loyal to the established church to love dissenting preachers’ rambling discourses.
Hetty was not the only one of the family who remarked her sister’s brightened looks and improved spirits. On the girls’ return home, their mother embraced both of them, especially the invalid, with more than common ardour of affection. “There was nothing like a country ride,” Aunt Lambert said, “for doing her dear Theo good. She had been on the road to Hampstead, had she? She must have another ride to-morrow. Heaven be blessed, my Lord Wrotham’s horses were at their orders three or four times a week, and the sweet child might have the advantage of them!”
As for the idea that Mr. Warrington might have happened to meet the children on their drive, Aunt Lambert never once entertained it—at least, she never spoke of it. I leave anybody interested in the matter to guess whether Mrs. Lambert could by any possibility have supposed that her daughter and her sweetheart could ever have come together again. Do women help each other in love perplexities? Do women scheme, intrigue, make little plans, tell little white fibs, provide little amorous opportunities, hang up the rope-ladder, coax, wheedle, mystify the guardian or Abigail, and turn their attention away while Strephon and Chloe are billing and cooing in the twilight, or whisking off in the postchaise to Gretna Green?
My dear young folks, some people there are of this nature; and some kind souls who have loved tenderly and truly in their own time, continue ever after to be kindly and tenderly disposed towards their young successors, when they begin to play the same pretty game. Miss Prim does not. If she hears of two young persons attached to each other, it is to snarl at them for fools, or to imagine of them all conceivable evil. Because she has a hump-back herself, she is for biting everybody else. I believe if she saw a pair of turtles cooing in a wood, she would turn her eyes down, or fling a stone to frighten them; but I am speaking, you see, young ladies, of your grandmother, Aunt Lambert, who was one great syllabub of human kindness; and, besides, about the affair at present under discussion, how am I ever to tell whether she knew anything regarding it or not?
So all she says to Theo on her return home is, “My child, the country air has done you all the good in the world, and I hope you will take another drive to-morrow, and another, and another, and so on.”
“Don’t you think, papa, the ride has done the child most wonderful good, and must not she be made to go out in the air?” Aunt Lambert asks of the General, when he comes in for supper.
“Yes, sure, if a coach-and-six will do his little Theo good, she shall have it,” Lambert says, “or he will drag the landau up Hampstead Hill himself, if there are no horses;” and so the good man would have spent, freely, his guineas, or his breath, or his blood, to give his child pleasure. He was charmed at his girl’s altered countenance; she picked at a bit of chicken with appetite, drank a little negus which he mixed for her himself: indeed it did seem to be better than the kind doctor’s best medicine, which hitherto, God wot, had been of little benefit. Mamma was gracious and happy. Hetty was radiant and laughing. It was quite like an evening at home at Oakhurst. Never for months past, never since that fatal, cruel day that no one spoke of, had they spent an evening so delightful.
But if the other women chose to coax and cajole the good, simple father, Theo herself was too honest to continue for long even that sweet and fond delusion. When, for the third or fourth time, he comes back to the delightful theme of his daughter’s improved health, and asks, “What has done it? Is it the country air? is it the Jesuit’s bark? is it the new medicine?”
“Can’t you think, dear, what it is?” she says, laying a hand upon her father’s, with a tremor in her voice, perhaps, but eyes that are quite open and bright.
“And what is it, my child?” asks the General.
“It is because I have seen him again, papa!” she says.
The other two women turned pale, and Theo’s heart too begins to palpitate, and her cheek to whiten, as she continues to look in her father’s scared face. “It was not wrong to see him,” she continues, more quickly; “it would have been wrong not to tell you.”
“Great God!” groans the father, drawing his hand back, and with such a dreadful grief in his countenance that Hetty runs to her almost swooning sister, clasps her to her heart, and cries out, rapidly, “Theo knew nothing of it, sir! It was my doing—it was all my doing!”
Theo lies on her sister’s neck, and kisses it twenty, fifty times.
“Women, women! are you playing with my honour?” cries the father, bursting out with a fierce exclamation.
Aunt Lambert sobs wildly, “Martin! Martin! Don’t say a word to her!”
Again Hetty calls out, then staggers back towards the wall, for Theo has fainted dead away on her shoulder.
I was taking my breakfast next morning, with what appetite I might, when my door opens, and my faithful black announces, “General Lambert.” At once I saw, by the General’s face, that the yesterday’s transaction was known to him.
“Your accomplices did not confess,” the General said, as soon as my servant had left us, “but sided with you against their father—a proof how desirable clandestine meetings are. It was from Theo herself I heard that she had seen you.”
“Accomplices, sir!” I said (perhaps not unwilling to turn the conversation from the real point at issue). “You know how fondly and dutifully your young people regard their father. If they side against you in this instance, it must be because justice is against you. A man like you is not going to set up sic volo sic jubeo as the sole law in his family!”
“Psha, George!” cries the General. “For though we are parted, God forbid I should desire that we should cease to love each other. I had your promise that you would not seek to see her.”
“Nor did I go to her, sir,” I said, turning red, no doubt; for though this was the strict letter of truth, I own it was evasive.
“You mean she was brought to you?” says Theo’s father, in great agitation. “Is it behind Hester’s petticoat that you will shelter yourself? What a fine defence for a gentleman!”
“Well, I won’t screen myself behind the poor child,” I replied. “To speak as I did was to make an attempt at evasion, and I am ill-accustomed to dissemble. I did not infringe the letter of my agreement, but I acted against the spirit of it. From this moment I annul it altogether.”
“You break your word given to me!” cries Mr. Lambert.
“I recall a hasty promise made on a sudden at a moment of extreme excitement and perturbation. No man can be for ever bound by words uttered at such a time; and, what is more, no man of honour or humanity, Mr. Lambert, would try to bind him.”
“Dishonour to me! sir,” exclaims the General.
“Yes, if the phrase is to be shuttlecocked between us!” I answered, hotly. “There can be no question about love, or mutual regard, or difference of age, when that word is used: and were you my own father—and I love you better than a father, Uncle Lambert,—I would not bear it! What have I done? I have seen the woman whom I consider my wife before God and man, and if she calls me I will see her again. If she comes to me, here is my home for her, and the half of the little I have. ‘Tis you, who have no right, having made me the gift, to resume it. Because my mother taunts you unjustly, are you to visit Mrs. Esmond's wrong upon this tender, innocent creature? You profess to love your daughter, and you can’t bear a little wounded pride for her sake. Better she should perish away in misery, than an old woman in Virginia should say that Mr. Lambert had schemed to marry one of his daughters. Say that to satisfy what you call honour and I call selfishness, we part, we break our hearts well nigh, we rally, we try to forget each other, we marry elsewhere? Can any man be to my dear as I have been? God forbid! Can any woman be to me what she is? You shall marry her to the Prince of Wales to-morrow, and it is a cowardice and treason. How can we, how can you, undo the promises we have made to each other before Heaven? You may part us: and she will die as surely as if she were Jephthah's daughter. Have you made any vow to Heaven to compass her murder? Kill her if you conceive your promise so binds you: but this I swear, that I am glad you have come, so that I may here formally recall a hasty pledge which I gave, and that, call me when she will, I will come to her!”
No doubt this speech was made with all the flurry and agitation belonging to Mr. Warrington’s youth, and with the firm conviction that death would infallibly carry off one or both of the parties, in case their worldly separation was inevitably decreed. Who does not believe his first passion eternal? Having watched the world since, and seen the rise, progress, and—alas, that I must say it!—decay of other amours, I may smile now as I think of my own youthful errors and ardours; but, if it be a superstition, I had rather hold it; I had rather think that neither of us could have lived with any other mate, and that, of all its innumerable creatures, Heaven decreed these special two should be joined together.
“We must come, then, to what I had fain have spared myself,” says the General, in reply to my outbreak; “to an unfriendly separation. When I meet you, Mr. Warrington, I must know you no more. I must order—and they will not do other than obey me—my family and children not to recognise you when they see you, since you will not recognise in your intercourse with me the respect due to my age, the courtesy of gentlemen. I had hoped so far from your sense of honour, and the idea I had formed of you, that, in my present great grief and perplexity, I should have found you willing to soothe and help me as far as you might—for, God knows, I have need of everybody's sympathy. But, instead of help, you fling obstacles in my way. Instead of a friend—a gracious Heaven pardon me!—I find in you an enemy! An enemy to the peace of my home and the honour of my children, sir! And as such I shall treat you, and know how to deal with you, when you molest me!” And, waving his hand to me, and putting on his hat, Mr. Lambert hastily quitted my apartment.
I was confounded, and believed, indeed, there was war between us. The brief happiness of yesterday was clouded over and gone, and I thought that never since the day of the first separation had I felt so exquisitely unhappy as now, when the bitterness of quarrel was added to the pangs of parting, and I stood not only alone but friendless. In the course of one year's constant intimacy I had come to regard Lambert with a reverence and affection which I had never before felt for any mortal man except my dearest Harry. That his face should be turned from me in anger was as if the sun had gone out of my sphere, and all was dark around me. And yet I felt sure that in withdrawing the hasty promise I had made not to see Theo, I was acting rightly—that my fidelity to her, as hers now to me, was paramount to all other ties of duty or obedience, and that, ceremony or none, I was hers, first and before all. Promises were passed between us, from which no parent could absolve either; and all the priests in Christendom could no more than attest and confirm the sacred contract which had tacitly been ratified between us.
I saw Jack Lambert by chance that day, as I went mechanically to my not unusual haunt, the library of the new Museum; and with the impetuousness of youth, and eager to impart my sorrow to some one, I took him out of the room and led him about the gardens, and poured out my grief to him. I did not much care for Jack (who in truth was somewhat of a prig, and not a little pompous and wearisome with his Latin quotations) except in the time of my own sorrow, when I would fasten upon him or any one; and having suffered himself in his affair with the little American, being haud ignarus mali (as I knew he would say), I found the college gentleman ready to compassionate another's misery. I told him, what has here been represented at greater length, of my yesterday's meeting with his sister; of my interview with his father in the morning; of my determination at all hazards never to part with Theo. When I found from the various quotations from the Greek and Latin authors which he uttered that he leaned to my side in the dispute, I thought him a man of great sense, clung eagerly to his elbow, and bestowed upon him much more affection than he was accustomed at other times to have from me. I walked with him up to his father's lodgings in Dean Street; saw him enter at the dear door; surveyed the house from without with a sickening desire to know from its exterior appearance how my beloved fared within; and called for a bottle at the coffee-house where I waited Jack's return. I called him Brother when I sent him away. I fondled him as the condemned wretch at Newgate hangs about the jailor or the parson, or any one who is kind to him in his misery. I drank a whole bottle of wine at the coffee-house—by the way, Jack's Coffee-House was its name—called another. I thought Jack would never come back.
He appeared at length with rather a scared face; and, coming to my box, poured out for himself two or three bumpers from my second bottle, and then fell to his story, which, to me at least, was not a little interesting. My poor Theo was keeping her room, it appeared, being much agitated by the occurrences of yesterday; and Jack had come home in time to find dinner on table; after which his good father held forth upon the occurrences of the morning, being anxious and able to speak more freely, he said, because his eldest son was present and Theodosia was not in the room. The General stated what had happened at my lodgings between me and him. He bade Hester be silent, who indeed was as dumb as a mouse, poor thing! he told Aunt Lambert (who was indulging in that madefaction of pocket-handkerchiefs which I have before described), and with something like an imprecation, that the women were all against him, and pimps (he called them) for one another; and frantically turning round to Jack, asked what was his view

Years later, when I sorted through the stack of old family papers at home, I came across a sheet docketed in my mother’s neat, familiar handwriting: “From London, April 1760. My son's dreadful letter.” When it fell into my hands I burned the whole document at once. I would not have that record of domestic strife and grief left in our family annals for future Warringtons to gawk at, nor for disobedient sons yet unborn to hold up as proof that rebellions against parental authority had happened before them. For the exact same reason, I destroyed the angry, unyielding reply my mother sent me back in that season of tyranny, revolt, petty irritation, and raw hurt.

Maddened to my wits’ end by the pain of separation from the woman I loved, and rightly holding Mrs. Esmond to be the sole cause of the worst misery I had ever suffered, I wrote home to Virginia a letter that might, in truth, have been far more temperate—though I did my best to keep it as respectful and guarded as I could. I told her I did not know what motives had driven her to act as she did, but that I held her accountable for ruining the rest of my life, a ruin she had willfully chosen to inflict. She had torn me away from a virtuous, innocent young creature whose own hopes, health, and happiness had been shattered forever by her interference. The deed was done, I wrote, as I feared it was, and I would waste no breath judging the person who had committed it, for she would answer for it to God alone. But I did not hide from my mother that the harm she had done me was so deep and permanent that neither her life nor mine could ever mend it: the old bond of filial obedience was broken, and I would never again be the dutiful, respectful son I had been to her before.

Madam Esmond replied with a letter of immense dignity—her style and correspondence were extraordinarily elegant and refined, you must know. She did not utter a single reproach or harsh word, but coldly made clear that it was to that awful tribunal of God she had brought our quarrel, to ask for guidance, and that as far as her own conduct as a mother went, she was ready to face that judgement in all humility. Might I, as a son, she wrote, be equally able to answer for myself when the Great Judge called on me to account for whether I had honoured my father and mother? Ah, me! My grandfather quoted a line of Homer in his memoir once, remarking how we are forever dragging the gods into our petty troubles and griefs. When pride, avarice, self-interest, or the urge to dominate stokes our anger, do we not pester Heaven unceasingly to side with our cause? In our great American quarrel, did not both sides appeal to the skies for justice, sing Te Deum after every victory, and boldly declare their confidence that right would prevail? Was America right because she won? Then I suppose Poland was wrong, just because she was defeated? How do I wander off into digressions about Poland, America, and all the rest, when all the while I am thinking of a little woman long dead, who appealed straight to Heaven and backed her case with a thousand Bible texts, all because her son wanted to make a marriage that did not suit her? We appeal, we swear oaths, we fall to our knees, we demand blessings, we shriek out for judgement according to law—all the while the great world keeps turning unheeded. We pant, we strive, we struggle, we hate, we rage, we weep passionate tears, we reconcile, we run the race and win, we run the race and lose, then we pass away and other little strugglers take our place. Our days run out, our night falls, and another sun rises that shines on us no more.

I did not keep my angry letter to Madam Esmond hidden. I showed a duplicate copy to Mr. Lambert, for I wanted him to understand exactly what my relations with my mother were, and how determined I was that no future threat or quarrel would ever make me consider my separation from Theo anything but temporary. The moment I could see her again, I would. My promise to her was for all eternity, or at least binding as long as I drew breath. I made clear that she was equally bound to me, and her good father knew that much for a fact. He could separate us if he wished—just as he could slip her a dose of poison, and that gentle, obedient creature would take it and die—but any such death or separation would be his doing, for him to answer for. He was so tender to his children it verged on weakness, and he could never bring himself to subject one of them—least of all Theo—to deliberate torture. We had tried to part, and we could not. He had tried to separate us, and it was more than he had the power to do. The bars were up, but the young couple, the maid on one side and the knight on the other, loved each other just the same. The wall was built between us, but Pyramus and Thisbe whispered to each other through the cracks in the plaster. For all his grief and perplexity, Uncle Lambert had a sharp sense of humour, and he could not help but see what a sorry role he was playing. Light was already seeping through that lime and roughcast wall; the lovers were getting their hands through the gaps, then their heads. It was high time for that wall to crumble and retreat.

I do not remember the exact day-to-day, step-by-step sequence of events, nor does it matter much for the instruction of future ages. When my descendants get tangled in their own love scrapes, they will find their own way out of them. I never went back to Dean Street to live, but the doctors prescribed open-air carriage drives as the most healthful remedy for Miss Lambert’s lingering complaint. I bought a fine new horse, and rode along beside her carriage every time she went out. The old woman who kept the roadside cottage up Tottenham Court Road got to know us both very well, and nodded and winked at us in the friendliest way every time we passed. I fancy that old goody was no stranger to playing chaperone to young couples, and had hosted many a pair of star-crossed lovers under her roof before us.

Doctor Heberden and the country air worked a miraculous cure on Miss Lambert. Hetty always came along as duenna, and sometimes, on his school holidays, little Charley would ride my horse while I climbed into the carriage to sit with the girls. What a world of love-making Miss Hetty overheard! And with what exemplary patience she listened to every word! I will not say she went back to Methodist sermons after that, but it is certain that whenever we had a closed carriage, she would very kindly and considerately press her face to the window to watch the scenery. Then there were piles and piles of secret notes! Gumbo’s bandy little legs were forever trotting between my lodgings and Dean Street, and Molly, the girls’ maid, was for ever hurrying back to Bloomsbury with replies to my letters, for my sake and for her own sweetheart Gumbo’s. By the time autumn leaves started turning pale on the trees, Theo’s cheeks were flushed with the roses of perfect health again, and Doctor Heberden declared his cure was complete.

What else happened in that blessed, happy stretch of time? Mr. Warrington finished his great tragedy of *Pocahontas*. This time, the play was not just accepted by Mr. Garrick—our friend Dr. Johnson had spoken well of the work, after all—but my cousin Hagan was engaged by the manager to play the hero, Captain Smith. Hagan’s new engagement could not have come at a better time. I had been helping him and his family with sums of money that were disproportionate to my means, especially given my running feud with Madam Esmond. It was towards autumn that I got her reply to my angry April letter: she wrote back from Virginia answering war with war, restriction with restriction. But her threats hardly frightened me at all. My poor mother’s thunder could not reach me all the way across the Atlantic, and my conscience, or my own convenient casuistry, supplied me with counterarguments to all her biblical texts, so that her oracles had no power to scare me away from my purpose. I did not write to tell her, or any other of my relatives on either side of the family who had raged against my marriage, of my new happiness. What use was wrangling with them? Far better to seize the day and its sweet loves and pleasures, and leave the gossips to grumble, and the elders to dispense their unwanted advice, at their leisure.

I must own that back in the mad, angry days of our temporary separation, I had written notes of searing sarcasm to my Uncle Warrington, to my Aunt Madame de Bernstein, and to the Lord or Lady of Castlewood (I forget which exactly), thanking them for all the trouble they had taken to ruin the dearest happiness of my life, and promising them the eternal gratitude of their obliged relative. Business brought the jovial Baronet and his family to London that year earlier than usual, and Madame de Bernstein was never sorry to get back to Clarges Street and her card tables. I met all of them, and they found me perfectly well and cheerful. They concluded my match was entirely broken off, and I did not choose to undeceive them. The Baroness took heart seeing how content I was, and made many sly jokes about my philosophical, worldly-wise behaviour as a man about town. She was still dead set on finding me a rich wife, and I fear I paid no end of elaborate, teasing compliments in her drawing room to a wealthy young soap-boiler’s daughter from Mile End, whom the good Baroness was determined to marry off to me.

“You court her with infinite wit and esprit, my dear,” my pleased kinswoman said to me once, “but she does not understand half of what you say, and the other half, I think, frightens her. That tone of playful irony works very well in our circle, but you must spare it, my dear nephew, when you are talking to these common folk.”

That Miss Badge eventually married a young gentleman of royal descent but shattered fortune from a neighbouring island, and I trust Mrs. Mackshane has long since forgiven my levity towards her. There was another person at my aunt’s house who understood my ironic teasing no better than the young lady herself: that was a dowager who could remember the reign of James II, who was still alive and as worldly as ever in King George II’s time. I loved spending time with her, and if my own little children were not going to read this volume, I could fill a hundred pages with stories of the great old figures she had known in the bygone days—of George I and his mistresses, of St. John and Marlborough, of the late king and the old Prince of Wales, and the causes of their famous quarrel. But my modest muse pipes only for boys and virgins. My son Miles cares nothing for old court gossip, and if he did, he has a whole new budget of scandal from Carlton House just as naughty as any tale the old Baroness could tell. No, my dear wife, you need not shake your powdered curls at me! Papa will not scandalise our nursery with old world tittle-tattle, nor bring a blush to our innocent children’s bread-and-butter faces.

But this one piece of gossip I cannot resist telling. My aunt used to recount it with immense gusto; for to do her justice, she hated people who paraded their “goodness” in public, and sniggered at the faults of the self-righteous with uncommon satisfaction. In her later days she had no use for hypocrisy at all, which made her better than some of the whitewashed pretenders we all know. Well, to the story. My Lady Warrington was one of the tallest, most pious women of her sex, who had goodness forever on her lips and “Heaven in her eye,” like the heroine in Mr. Addison’s tedious overlong tragedy that somehow still holds the stage while far better plays have been forgotten. But she kept the whole rest of the worldly right in her other eye, and a very sharp, eager desire to climb the social ladder. When everyone supposed my marriage to Theo was broken off, what did she do but try to play on me the same arts she had used on my poor Harry, with exactly the same lack of success? It was not the beauty Flora she threw at me—Flora was reserved for a far grander match, I take off my hat at the very thought of that illustrious connection! It was Dora, the supposed “muse” of the family, that she set after me, to languish at me, pity my broken heart, read my godless tragedy, applaud it, and console me.

Meanwhile, what was the beauty Flora doing? Would you believe that my severe aunt threw a grand entertainment for the notorious Lady Yarmouth, presented her little son Miles to the royal favourite, and placed the poor boy under her august protection? That part is certain enough, but could it be true that she sent her daughter Flora to stay at Lady Yarmouth’s house, which the old King visited every day, with the exact matchmaking aims old Aunt Bernstein attributed to her? “If it hadn’t been for that fit of apoplexy, my dear,” Bernstein said, “that aunt of yours intended there to be a Countess in her own right in the Warrington family!” My neighbour and kinswoman Lady Claypole has long been dead and buried. Grow white over Flora’s grave, ye daisies! I can see my pretty Miles, dressed in the smart little uniform of the Norfolk Militia, being led up by his mother to the lady the old King delighted to honour, and that good-natured old royal favourite laying her hand on the boy’s curly head. I am often accused of being a lukewarm royalist, but I can well contrast those corrupt old times with our own, and acknowledge the difference between the late sovereign and the current one, who was born a Briton, and set an example of decorum and virtuous life for every family in the empire. [The Warrington manuscript is dated 1793. —Ed.]

And so my life passed in the pleasantest possible occupation. Being so happy myself, I could afford to feel kindly towards all those relatives who, after all, had done me no lasting harm, but only made my final happiness all the sweeter by putting small obstacles in my way. We had made no specific formal plans, but Theo and I both knew the day would come when we would never have to say goodbye again. If that day came a year from then, or ten years from then, we were ready to wait. Day after day we pored over our little plans, with Hetty as our trusted confidante. On our drives we spied out tiny cottages that we thought would suit a young couple of small means, and dreamed up all sorts of delightful, childish little economies. We were Strephon and Chloe, no less! A cottage and a brown loaf would content us, we vowed. Gumbo and Molly would wait on us, as indeed they have done from that day to this. At twenty, who is afraid of being poor? Our small hardships would only make our love stronger. The “sweet sorrow” of every day’s parting only made the next day’s meeting more delicious, and when we separated we ran home to write each other those precious, overwrought letters that all young men and women write when they are in love. Though my wife has kept them all in a great tin sugar box in her bedroom closet, and I own I have looked at them once, and even thought some of them quite pretty, I hereby order my heirs and executors to burn all of those letters unread after our deaths. I specifically request my son the Captain, who I know has no patience for reading old manuscripts, to perform that duty. Those secrets we whispered to the penny post, or passed between Gumbo and Molly, were meant only for us, and no ears of our descendants shall ever overhear them.

We got short letters one after another telling us that our dear Harry was still with the army, serving as General Amherst’s aide-de-camp after the death of his own glorious general. By mid-October, news came of the Capitulation of Montreal, and the surrender of all Canada. Harry added a short postscript saying he would ask for leave now, and return home to see the old lady in Virginia, who was writing letters as sulky as a bear, Captain Warrington dryly remarked. I could guess exactly why she was in such a temper, though her claws could not reach me across the Atlantic. I had written to my brother fairly fully about how matters stood with me in England.

Then, on the 25th of October, news broke that his Majesty George II had dropped dead at Kensington Palace, and that George III now reigned over us. I fear we grieved very little for the old king. What do two people whose hearts are full of nothing but each other care for the faraway royal family? We gladly accepted the common report that the new young prince was endowed with every possible virtue, and joined the loyal crowd crying huzzay at his accession. We simple young sweethearts, whispering our little love stories in our quiet corner, thought it could make no difference to us at all.

But who can say how great events will touch even the humblest of us? Did not our little Charley, at his school in Chartreux, impiously wish for a new king the moment he heard the news, all because the strict headmaster Doctor Crusius gave all the boys a holiday to celebrate the new king’s accession? Charley, Hetty, Theo, and I—Theo was strong enough now to walk many a delightful mile—went to watch the Heralds proclaim the new Majesty before Savile House in Leicester Fields, and a pickpocket stole a gentleman’s watch and chain right next to us, got caught immediately, and was dragged off to Bridewell for a whipping, all on account of the royal accession. If the old king had not died, the gentleman would never have been in that crowd, his chain would never have been stolen, and the thief would never have been caught. In that small, roundabout way, many of us lowly folk were connected to the great change of reign, and we would soon find ourselves directly affected by it.

It happened this way. Lord Wrotham was a great friend to the Savile House family, who knew and deeply respected his many virtues. Of all men alive, Lord Wrotham loved and esteemed his old neighbour and fellow-soldier Martin Lambert best, declaring there was no finer gentleman alive in the whole world. And Lord Bute, who was all-powerful in the new king’s first days, a nobleman who was very eager at the start of his brief, ill-fated time in office to reward merit wherever he found it, had been led to think very highly of Mr. Lambert by his old, constant friend Lord Wrotham.

Our old acquaintance Parson Sampson, who had been in and

We, who had all a hand in the furtive, ill-judged scheme to secure Theo and I a union behind good General Lambert’s back, felt thrice over guilty when we saw what a blow we had dealt the man we loved and honoured beyond all others. He was the kindest soul that ever breathed: his own cherished child had deceived him, his entire household had banded together to keep a secret from him. Looking back now, my dearest, I swear neither of us would ever have found the heart to do it again. To wound that gentle creature, who never spoke a harsh word to any of us, was no better than striking a child or laying a blow on a woman who has nursed you at her breast. When all the deceit came out, we grovelled in shame before him before he, ever ready to pardon, pulled us to his breast, forgave us freely, joined our hands in blessing, and then sailed away for his new colonial governorship, leaving Theo and me standing hand in hand on the shore, silent, flushing hot with guilt, as though we had sent him to his grave before his time.

Our “wedding trip” to Winchester and Hampton was no giddy, laughing affair. For weeks we moved like ghosts, quiet and subdued, half-convinced we had committed a sin so black no amount of General Lambert’s kindness could ever wash it away. We settled into my old Bloomsbury lodgings, quiet, modest, with no fine wedding feast, no parade of guests. I sent a letter back to my mother’s estate in Virginia, laying the news out plainly: I had made an honourable promise to Theo, and when General Lambert departed for his post, I had kept my word, and meant to finish my law studies to earn our keep, no matter if at home or across the Atlantic. Mrs. Mountain wrote back at Madam Esmond’s bidding—my mother would not so much as put pen to paper to acknowledge my marriage, so great was her fury.

That fury spread to every branch of our London relations, and it was almost comical to watch. The butler at my uncle Sir Miles Warrington’s Hill Street door looked as though he were about to drop dead of shock when I presented myself on his threshold with Theo on my arm, stammering “Sir is not at home, madam, sir” before he slammed the door in our faces. We were laughing at that absurd performance, tripping down the street, when we came upon Lady Warrington’s sedan chair stuck fast in a traffic jam. I swept off my hat and bowed as low as I knew how. “I wonder you dare look me in the face!” she gasped. “Nay, your ladyship, do not rob me of that precious privilege!” I teased. She screamed at her chairmen to move on, but the crowd was too thick. “You would not impale your own husband’s flesh and blood on that spiteful glance of yours, surely?” I called. She rattled the glass shut with a snap, and I bowed again, so elaborately that Theo had to bury her face in my shoulder to smother her giggles.

A few days later in Hyde Park, we spotted her little son, my cousin Miles, trotting along on his pony with a groom trailing behind him. The moment he saw us, he dug his heels into his horse’s sides and galloped full tilt over, the groom yelling “Stop, Master Miles, stop!” at the top of his lungs. “Mama says I am not to speak to you,” he panted, grinning at us, “but sending Harry my love isn’t speaking, is it? And you—” he nodded at Theo, “you’re my new cousin! Nobody said I couldn’t talk to you. You’re very pretty!” The groom caught up to him, apologising to us, and the boy trotted off, waving over his shoulder.

“See how all my grand relations have set their faces against me,” I laughed to Theo. She looked up at me, eyes shining brighter than any diamond in a court lady’s jewellery box. “As if I cared a straw for your relations, when I have you!” she said. Oh, those first quiet months of our marriage! That brisk, cozy winter, the kettle singing on the hearth, the rum punch poor Mr. Sampson would stumble in to make of an evening, the trips to the playhouse where we daydreamed that my new tragedy *Pocahontas* would outstrip every hit ever staged at Drury Lane.

Old Madame de Bernstein, that wicked sharp old aunt of mine, loved the story of Lady Warrington and the stuck sedan chair so much I had to act it out for her over tea. The Clarges Street aunt who had first received us with nothing but scorn, once she saw how sweet and unassuming Theo was, fell utterly in love with her, insisting we come for supper every night, even making us use the back stairs so none of her grand company could spy on us—“You are no longer fit for polite society now you’re married for love, dears,” she would say, as if that were the silliest crime in the world.

The Dowager Countess of Castlewood invited us to her card parties in Kensington, but we quickly found that losing half our small fortune at cards and paying for a hackney coach all the way across London was more than our slender budget could bear. We stopped going, and no one missed us a bit, no more than any other poor relation who slips out of the fashionable world. Theo never regretted it for a moment—she looked far lovelier in her simple white gown, her only ornaments the little bits of jewellery her own mother had left her, than all the wrinkled old duchesses blazing in rubies and diamonds at those parties. Only one fool, that silly fop Beau Lothair, bothered her, sending a silly love note to our lodgings. I ran into him in Covent Garden a week later, and promised I’d break his nose if he ever showed his face near Bloomsbury again, and we never heard a peep from him after.

The only guests we had at our little dinners were Hagan the actor and his wife, poor dear Maria, who’d run off and married him for love, and my old friend Spencer from the Temple, who would sigh over his own unlucky love affairs as he sipped our home-made punch. Even great Dr. Johnson would drop by unannounced of an evening, begging for a dish of Theo’s famous tea—though Gumbo would grumble after he left that he drank enough to fill a pail, and ate half the larder. The gruff old doctor would sputter and argue, fling his bread crumbs across the table, and tell Theo every time he saw her: “Madam, you do not love me. I see it in your face. But you are far prettier than any portrait Sir Joshua Reynolds ever painted, and I would have him paint you, if you would let him.” I never dared, for I knew Sir Joshua’s fee was far out of our reach, and I wish now I had—so our grown children might see just how bright Theo’s face was, all those years ago.

The silliest quarrel we ever had that winter was when Hagan offered to read scenes from my new tragedy after tea. Dr. Johnson huffed and refused, saying he would far rather hear Theo chat about her household than listen to any declaimed verses. He ate so much of Theo’s famous butter sauce that he stuffed a whole big dollop of it into the bosom of his dirty dingy shirt, which Hagan teased him about, and the old man flew into a towering rage, yelling that Hagan was rude and uneducated, before he realised he was being ridiculous, laughed, and blew the anger away like a gust of cold wind. Maria, meanwhile, was gazing adoringly at Hagan, as though he were a prince from a play, reciting lines from her favourite tragedy under her breath, lamenting that he would have to play the unromantic Captain Smith in my *Pocahontas*.

Ah, that tragedy—all our hopes were pinned to it. By that point, my small patrimony was almost gone: I had paid off my brother Harry’s old debts, honoured all my mother’s drafts from Virginia, and spent nearly three hundred pounds keeping us fed and housed. I had no other income, save what the play might earn. Foolish youth, to count your fortune on a theatrical hit, to think a single tragedy would keep us housed, fed, and set up for life! But General Lambert had left for his post convinced I had plenty of funds set aside, his wife Aunt Lambert was certain Providence would never let a good, kind couple starve, and Theo believed every word I said, so we threw all our hopes on those five acts of verse, and our three hundred pounds of ready cash.

Opening night drew near. I went with Theo to call on Lord Wrotham, an old friend of General Lambert’s, who gave us his blessing, bought a whole box of seats for his friends, and promised to drum up support. The Baroness said she would send two of her servants, dressed in their finest, to take a front box. The Dowager Countess sent word she was having a card party that night and could not attend. My uncle and Lady Warrington would not have stepped foot in Drury Lane to save my life. Poor Sampson, who had helped negotiate the play’s production, had bragged to the manager that Lords Bute and even the King himself would attend—and now Garrick, the manager, was in a fine fury, taking snuff so fast he sneezed three times in a row. At the final rehearsal that afternoon, he handed me a letter, his face dark as thunder.

I read it. It was from one of Lord Bute’s secretaries. His lordship, the letter said, was a great patron of the arts, but he could not possibly attend the performance of a play whose lead actor, Mr. Hagan, had contracted a clandestine marriage with the daughter of a peer of the realm—far less could he ask his Majesty the King to grace such a performance.

I walked home to Bloomsbury, my face pale as a sheet. Theo had a hot dinner all set out on the table, waiting for me. I told her I was only tired from the long rehearsal. I did not dare tell her that all our hopes, all our plans for our new life, had just shattered at my feet.

We Virginians, who still hold dear the memory of that gentle, unassuming, warm-hearted Indian princess, know far more of the story of Pocahontas than the average London theater-goer. At the urging of his friends, Mr. George Warrington penned a short ballad honoring her, printed in several popular magazines only a few days before his full tragedy on the same subject was set to premiere.

The enthusiastic Parson Sampson called the trick nothing short of genius. “It is ground-bait, sir!” he cried, bouncing in to wave the magazine under Warrington’s nose. “You will see the fish rise in swarms on opening night!” He and young Spencer swore up and down they’d heard the poem debated and praised in half the coffee houses they frequented, where patrons misattributed it to Mr. Mason, to Mr. Cowper of the Temple, and even to the revered, reclusive Mr. Gray. Warrington suspects honest Sampson himself spread those false rumors. He is half-convinced that if someone had claimed the full tragedy was a lost work of Shakespeare, Sampson would have sworn Pocahontas was among the Bard’s very finest performances.

George first fell in love with the story of brave Captain John Smith as a small boy, curled up in his grandfather’s library back in Virginia, his favorite tattered volume spread across his knees, while the old man sat beside him spelling out the Virginian hero’s adventures. He pored over tales of Smith’s travels, captures, and daring escapes across Europe no less than in the American wilderness, and even now, pulling that same well-worn book from the shelf of his London study, he feels himself shrink back to that small boy again, all the soft, warm memories of his early home crowding back unbidden. His grandfather used to draw him pictures of Smith battling the Turks on the Danube, or being led out by Virginia’s native peoples to face execution. He still thrills to think of that legendary fight with the three Turkish champions, and his childish delight over the final, most terrifying of the three, the giant Bonny Molgro. What a name it was! What enormous turbans, curling whiskers, and glinting scimitars the pair of them drew for that great brute! After Smith had struck off the heads of his first two foes, he and Molgro met in a ferocious axe fight, so fierce that the pair of them were left barely able to stay on horseback, until Smith lost his own battle axe, drawing a roar of triumph from the Turkish ramparts. But using his fine steed’s speed and his own sharp wit, he dodged every blow, drew his falchion, and ran Molgro clean through back and body beneath his armor. The Turk toppled from his horse, and lost his head just as his two compatriots had. For that feat, Duke Segismundus granted Smith a coat of arms bearing three Turkish heads, and a yearly pension of three hundred ducats.

As a poet, Warrington took the small liberty of shifting that same dashing, daredevil combat energy to the banks of the Potomac and James River for his play, unbound by the strict rules of timeline that ordinary historians follow. The little ballad he penned as preamble ran thus:
> Wearied arm and broken sword
> Wage in vain the desperate fight
> Round him press the countless horde,
> He is but a single knight.
> Hark! a cry of triumph shrill
> Through the wilderness resounds,
> As, with twenty bleeding wounds,
> Sinks the warrior, fighting still.
>
> Now they heap the fatal pyre,
> And the torch of death they light
> Ah! 'tis hard to die of fire!
> Who will shield the captive knight?
> Round the stake with fiendish cry
> Wheel and dance the savage crowd,
> Cold the victim's mien and proud,
> And his breast is bared to die.
>
> Who will shield the fearless heart?
> Who avert the murderous blade?
> From the throng, with sudden start,
> See, there springs an Indian maid.
> Quick she stands before the knight,
> 'Loose the chain, unbind the ring,
> I am daughter of the king,
> And I claim the Indian right!'
>
> Dauntlessly aside she flings
> Lifted axe and thirsty knife;
> Fondly to his heart she clings,
> And her bosom guards his life!
> In the woods of Powhattan,
> Still 'tis told by Indian fires,
> How a daughter of their sires
> Saved the captive Englishman.

There is no need to recount the full plot of the tragedy here, for Warrington’s own children can pull the small octavo edition, or the later splendid quarto of his collected original and translated works, from any shelf and read it for themselves. He will not be volunteering to read it aloud to his household any time soon, though – last Christmas, at his wife Theo’s request, he read two acts over supper, and both Captain Miles and Parson Sampson fell fast asleep before the end of the second. Any reader familiar with plays and novels could easily fill out the rest of the cast and story for themselves: a noble Indian king, the brave princess and her handmaiden who falls in love with Smith’s bumbling English servant, a traitor hidden inside the Jamestown fort, a valiant Indian warrior pining unhappily for Pocahontas, and a scheming, cruel medicine man (played masterfully by the actor Palmer) determined to torture Smith and chase all English settlers from the land. Throw in the wild war cries Gumbo had learned to mimic perfectly from Virginia’s native peoples, the dramatic arrival of the English fleet, and rousing references to the recent glorious British victories in Canada and the nation’s resolve to rule and thrive across the American colonies, and Warrington and his friends had every reasonable right to believe their play would be a runaway triumph.

But he has already spoken of the ill omens that hounded the production all the way to opening night: the peevish, jealous, skittish theater management throwing obstacle after obstacle in their path, and the violent prejudice against the piece that had already sprung up in powerful, high society circles. Was it any surprise Pocahontas did not turn out to be the grand victory they hoped for? He scoffs at the petty, malicious critics who panned his work, who had the audacity to call the shoddy play *Carpezan* a masterpiece while sneering at his far more carefully crafted, heartfelt tragedy. Hagan, the actor playing John Smith, was so magnificent in the role that the theater’s own manager could not help but be jealous of his skill, and but for the deliberate cabal to sabotage the performance, the play would have been a smash hit. Sampson swore the theater had been deliberately filled with the manager’s stooges, “the house swarming with Macs by George, so thick you could wash the galleries with brimstone!” He was fully convinced Mr. Garrick himself had vowed the play would never succeed, and that even during the thunderously heartfelt scene in the second act where Pocahontas leaps to save Smith from the stake, when the whole genuine audience was cheering and weeping with sympathy, the hired saboteurs did their utmost to drown out the applause.

Any curious reader can pull up the published tragedy themselves to judge: the verses are elegant, the language rich and noble, and that famous rescue scene far from unmerited praise. One of the only reasons for its failure was Warrington’s stubborn devotion to historical accuracy. He had gone to the British Museum to copy and carefully tint a portrait of Sir Walter Raleigh, and Theo had donated some of her own mother’s finest vintage lace to make an exact, perfect ruff for Hagan’s costume – no man could have looked more like the real Raleigh. He had dressed Miss Pritchard as Pocahontas exactly as he had seen native princesses dressed in his Virginia home, and when she first stepped onto the stage, half the pit erupted in stifled tittering. The audience grew used to her soon enough, but just as they were fully swept up in the emotional moment where Pocahontas throws herself into Smith’s arms, a wag in the pit bawled out “Bedad! Here’s the Belle Savage kissing the Saracen’s Head!” A roar of foolish laughter burst across the pit, and sputtered out in little fits and snickers for the rest of the performance. That same idiot repeated the tavern joke ad nauseam for the rest of the night, greeting every new character to the stage with the name of a public house sign: the bearded English governor he called the Goat and Boots, the broad-faced Lieutenant Barker he dubbed the Bull and Mouth, on and on. The curtain finally fell to a shrill storm of whistles and hisses that targeted poor Hagan every time he so much as opened his mouth. Sampson spotted the treacherous scoundrel Will up in the green boxes with a group of his racy acquaintances, and is fully certain he was one of the ringleaders of the sabotage. “I would have flung him straight into the pit,” honest Sampson swears, “but I spotted a pair of Mr. Garrick’s bruisers loitering in the lobby and had to sheer off.” All the eggs they had carefully counted on selling at market were smashed to bits before they ever got there.

Warrington had peeked out from backstage before the curtain rose, and saw the house was nearly full. He spotted Dr. Johnson in the front boxes, wearing his laced waistcoat, with his deaf friend Mr. Reynolds the painter beside him – the one man nearly blind, the other nearly deaf, the pair of them good-naturedly turning up together to judge his poor tragedy. He recognized Lady Maria in the lower gallery, wrapped in the familiar hood she always wore, delighted for the chance to watch her beloved Hagan play a leading role. As for Theo, she had confessed she could not bear to come and watch, and he had not pressed her – he knew that if things went wrong, seeing her suffer would be far more painful than any jeer from the audience, and he let her stay home without argument.

He had always prided himself on his even temper, his ability to bear good and bad fortune without losing his composure, but even he could see the day was fated for disaster. The air backstage felt gloomy, charged with bad luck. Miss Pritchard had a splitting headache. The barber who had delivered Hagan’s wig had powdered it so lopsided it looked a deliberate insult. Every face in the green room was doubtful, tight with anxiety. The flippant, rude theater manager even had the audacity to snap at him, “For Heaven’s sake, Mr. Warrington, go get a glass of punch at the Bedford and stop frightening us all half to death with your dismal face!” “Sir,” Warrington shot back, “I might pay five shillings for a seat to comment on your face, but I never gave you permission to make remarks on mine.” “Sir,” the manager huffed back, “I wish from the bottom of my heart I had never seen your face at all!” “Yours, sir,” Warrington laughed, “has entertained me greatly for years, and when you are painted up for the role of Abel Drugger you are the funniest man alive.” He bowed, turned on his heel, and walked back out to the coffee house, where he did not speak a single word to the manager for five full years, until they met by chance at a nobleman’s party, and the man apologized. Warrington brushed the whole incident off, saying he had completely forgotten the silly argument, adding “After all, there is no shame in being unsuited to writing plays. Mr. Garrick – you, sir, were born to act.” The compliment landed perfectly, and the quarrel was mended.
