Sampson, his faithful ever-loyal companion, came running over after the first act to say things were going mostly well, save for that silly titter at Miss Pritchard’s entrance. “I cannot help it if Indians dress so!” Warrington laughed, pouring him a bumper of fine punch. “Why then,” Sampson argued, “would you paint Caractacus blue like an ancient Briton, or dress Boudica in nothing but a cowhide? No one mocks those plays for historical accuracy!” Warrington still half-believes that strict devotion to real history was the very thing that brought ridicule down on his tragedy – and if that is the case, he is not in the least ashamed his play failed.

After the second act, Sampson came rushing over, his face as white as a sheet, bearing terrible news. Oddly enough, though he had been nervous before the performance, Warrington found himself perfectly calm in the face of disaster. He paid his bill, put on his hat, and marched back to the theater as unhurried as if he was heading to a quiet dinner at the Temple, with Sampson prancing at his side, shoving stray link-boys out of his path and shouting “By George, Mr. Warrington, you are a man of spirit – a true Trojan, sir!” There were men of great spirit in Troy, after all – but fate was still too strong for them. No man could say Warrington did not bear his misfortune with perfect steadiness. He could no more stop the hisses and jeers of the sabotaging crowd than a ship’s captain can still a hurricane that sinks his vessel, but he stood firm in the wings for the rest of the performance, unshaken by the noise. Sampson later told Theo that not even Regulus stepping into his torture barrel could have been calmer than her husband that night. He always insisted that men of the “parasite” class like himself are never unfaithful in hard times, and Sampson proved that true – rich or poor, he was as loyal a friend as ever lived, happy to share a meager crust at the Warringtons’ table just as eagerly as he had ever feasted with them in better days.

When Warrington finally walked home after the curtain fell, he saw Theo waiting for him in the doorway, her face pale as a lily. She had already heard the news of their defeat. The supper table was decorated with the best flowers the gardener of Bedford House had given her that day, little bright tokens of welcome she had laid out for her “hero” to celebrate his triumph, and the battle had been lost entirely. He had held strong all through the performance, but the second he looked at his wife’s soft, sad face, his courage crumbled, and his heart ached sharper than it had ever ached before. The supper was quiet, mournful, though they did their best to make light conversation. They talked of old Mrs. Hagan’s lingering illness, the rumors of the King’s upcoming marriage, and the recent death of beloved Mr. Richardson, the author of *Pamela* and *Clarissa*, whose works they all adored. As they spoke of Clarissa’s tragic end, Theo wiped her eyes a time or two, and said softly how much she missed her own dear mother, who she wished could be there to comfort her. They mixed a bowl of punch spiced with Jamaica limes, drank a toast to the Governor of Virginia, and then Warrington filled his glass, smiled, and raised it for a second toast: “To better luck next time.”

That was the breaking point. Theo and Lady Maria flew into each other’s arms, sobbing all over each other’s neck handkerchiefs. “Oh Maria! Is not my George so good and kind?” Theo wept. “And my Hagan!” Lady Maria gasped, “How godlike he was in that role! It was that vile cabal that ruined him – I could plunge a knife straight into Mr. Garrick’s black little heart, the odious wretch!” She grabbed a knife from the table for a moment, then threw it aside and rushed to wrap her arms around Hagan, hugging him tight in front of all their little company. Everyone in the room was wild with shared grief and affection, and even in the middle of the disaster, the love wrapped around them was so warm and sweet Warrington almost did not regret the failed play at all.

Two or three days later, on their shared wedding birthday, a letter was brought to Warrington in his study, scrawled in his wife’s familiar handwriting:
> Returning from the cruel fight
> How pale and faint appears my knight!
> He sees me anxious at his side;
> 'Why seek, my love, your wounds to hide?
> Or deem your English girl afraid
> To emulate the Indian maid?'
>
> Be mine my husband's grief to cheer,
> In peril to be ever near;
> Whate'er of ill or woe betide,
> To bear it clinging at his side;
> The poisoned stroke of fate to ward,
> His bosom with my own to guard;
> Ah! could it spare a pang to his,
> It could not know a purer bliss!
> 'Twould gladden as it felt the smart,
> And thank the hand that flung the dart!

He will not argue that the verses are masterpieces of poetic craft, but he loves them as dearly as if they were the finest lines ever written. When he walked into the drawing room a few moments later, he found Theo blushing there, waiting for him, and her sweet young face seemed more beautiful to him than any angel’s face he could ever have imagined.

Seated in my easy-chair in the soft glow of a winter’s evening, I have often looked back on that rash, headlong jump into matrimony that I persuaded my dear partner to take with me, when we were both scarcely more than lanky, foolish teenagers. As a man, a father, with a proper sense of how critical a well-cooked mutton chop is to household peace, and how dangerous it is to fall behind on the baker’s bill—with a brood of impulsive children clustering around us who threaten to run off for Scotland at any moment, citing the example of their own father and mother as excuse for their impertinence—I know full well I ought to tread softly when narrating this early stretch of George Warrington and his Theo’s wedded life. I ought to beat my breast, cry mea culpa, assume a demure, penitent air, and sit here swaddled in a metaphorical white sheet perched on the repentance stool, holding myself up as a warning to all hot-headed, imprudent young folk who would dare marry before their pockets are full.

But truth be told, that married life, which every one of our prudent, respectable relatives prophesied would end in ruin and starvation, disappointed every last one of their gloomy expectations. It had its trials, to be sure—bitter passionate griefs that God in His mercy softened with the passage of years, days of straitened poverty that we bore so lightly that even our sympathizing onlooking relatives stared in wonder, precious, tender blessings and rewards so great I scarce dare whisper them across the page, too sacred for any ear but His to whom all men lift their prayers and thanks. No one can deny that marrying without a settled competence is wrong, dangerous, a transgression of our social codes—but do not tens of thousands of our fellow men commit that “crime” every year, trusting to nothing but Heaven, their own health, and the labour of their own two hands? Are young couples to never dare set up house until their cottage is fully furnished, their larder and cellar are stocked, their cupboards brim with silver plate, and their strongbox bulges with coin? If the rules our gentry live by were made universal, the human race would soon cease to multiply. Our gentlefolk stand trembling on the bank of matrimony in their silk stockings and polished pumps, waiting years and years for a fancy bridge or gilded barge to carry them across, while the poor do not fear wetting their bare feet, planting them firm in the brook, and trusting to fate and their own strength to carry them over. Who would wish to see his daughter consigned to poverty? Who would counsel his son to drag the woman he loves away from comfort and security, subject her to debt, privation, friendlessness, sickness, and all the hundred grim consequences of a straitened household? I look at my own dear wife and ask her forgiveness for ever imposing such a pain-filled, dangerous lot on one so gentle. I think of all the trials she bore, and I am thankful for them, and for that unfailing love and constancy with which God blessed her, and strengthened her to bear every last one. I am no fair judge of marriage, you see: mine was the rashest match imaginable, and it brought me more happiness than I ever dared hope for, so I have no right to offer young people advice. I lived in poverty, and rarely found it more than tolerable: had I not endured it, I never would have known the unexpected kindness of friends, the quiet thrill of gratitude, the small, surprising joys that creep in beside a scanty meal and a narrow fireside, that lighten the drudgery of a long day’s work. Of one thing I am certain: far too much superfluous pity is lavished on the decent poor. Good-natured wealthy folk who step out of the sunshine of their fortunes into our dim little lodgings are almost blinded by the gloom at first, while we saw everything clear and cheerful; they stumbled over obstacles that did not exist for us, and marveled that we could drink small beer with a smile, and say heartfelt grace over a plate of cold mutton.

My good father-in-law General Lambert had married his Molly when he was no more than a humble foot regiment subaltern, his purse nearly as empty as my own. They had weathered all the ups and downs of fortune together. I suspect—though my wife will never admit it—that they eloped, as young folks sometimes did in those days, without asking their parents’ leave first. [The Editor has pored over Burns’ Registers of Fleet Marriages and found no record of Martin Lambert and Mary Benson’s union, for the curious.] At any rate, they were so well pleased with their own happy match that they bore no grudge against their children for following suit, and were not at all frightened at the thought of any small hardships we might face in our wedded life. When I laid out my pecuniary situation for Mr. Lambert before he sailed for Jamaica, I was so eager to reassure us both that I counted a very doubtful sum as good debt, and he left for the islands fully believing I had two thousand pounds at my disposal, enough to keep his darling daughter comfortable for years at the very least. After paying for his family’s outfit, the good man sailed away scarcely richer than his new son-in-law; and Theo’s whole marriage portion was a handful of trinkets, some fine lace that had belonged to Aunt Lambert, and a purse stitched by her mother and sisters holding twenty bright new guineas.

The sum I had counted as good debt was one my honoured mother never once acknowledged, not even on the day the resolute old lady was called to pay her own final debt. The money I had disbursed on her behalf, she argued, had all been spent to improve and maintain the Virginia estate that would be mine upon her death. Any spare money she had, she declared, was to go to my poor brother Harry, who had nothing—who never would have spent his own means imagining himself sole heir to the Virginian property, as he had every right to suppose, the good lady repeatedly emphasized in her letters, but for that half-hour’s accident of my birth before him. Harry was now distinguishing himself nobly in the King’s service, she insisted, and it was my duty as his older brother to buy him the promotions he deserved. Long before news of my marriage reached her, Madam Esmond had written to me through our housekeeper Mountain more than once to say I was welcome to return home once I finished my legal studies in the Temple and my silly theatrical amusements, to take my rightful place in the colony.

You may imagine the full flood of maternal indignation that poured forth when she learned what I had done. When Canada was pacified after the fall of Quebec, my dear Harry applied for leave and dutifully sailed back to Virginia. His letters described his reception at home: Castlewood, which my mother had not stepped foot in since we sailed for Europe, was thrown wide open to all our old colonial friends, and Wolfe’s comrade, the veteran of Quebec, was greeted with every honour our acquaintances could heap upon him. Naturally, there were frequent stormy quarrels: Harry stubbornly refused to stop singing the praises of his dear friend Colonel Washington of Mount Vernon, whom I hold to be a man of every virtue—one whose glorious constancy and success in the struggle that ended so fatally for England a few years back I can admire as much as his warmest adherents do.

As I read Harry’s accounts of these frequent domestic battles, I could not help wondering why he chose to stay on at home. One obvious reason suggested itself that I scarcely dared mention to my Theo: we had both long discussed our little Hetty’s quiet, romantic attachment for my brother, and wondered how Harry could never have seen it. It was plain, of course, that my gentleman had found some young lady back home far more to his taste than our dear Hester, and that was the reason he lingered on in Virginia.

Presently a letter arrived from him that did not fully confess the fact, but clearly hinted at it: some unnamed being, all perfect beauty and grace, just as smitten young men describe their beloveds. My wife asked to see the letter, and I handed it to her with a very heavy heart, fully expecting to see her grieve for poor Hetty’s disappointment. To my great surprise, she read it without a shadow of sorrow crossing her face.

“I thought of this long ago, my love,” I said. “My heart aches for you over poor Hetty’s disappointment.”

“Ah, poor Hetty,” Theo murmured, her eyes fixed on the carpet.

“It never would have worked out between them,” I said.

“No—they never would have been happy together,” she sighed.

“How strange that Harry never once guessed her secret!” I went on.

She looked full at me with a very odd little expression on her face. “What does that look mean, my love?” I asked.

“Nothing at all, my dear—nothing! I am only not surprised,” she said, blushing bright pink.

“What?” I asked, a strange flutter in my chest. “Do you mean to tell me, Theo, that you ever cared for anyone before me?”

“Oh George!” she whimpered, “When I was at school, there was—there was a boy at Doctor Backhouse’s boys’ school, the one whose loft looked out over ours, and I thought he had the most lovely eyes in the world! Then I went to Mr. Grigg the mercer’s shop to buy a cloak for baby, and there he was, standing behind the counter. I was so mortified I never knew how to tell you!”

I snuck off later to see this wonder with the lovely eyes, after Theo described his clothes to me, and found a little bandy-legged wretch in a blue camlet coat, his foxy red hair tied back with a dirty ribbon. I was too generous to ever reproach my wife over it, and she will never know I laid eyes on the poor fellow until she reads this very page. I thought to myself, if our wives saw us exactly as we are, would they love us half as well? Do we misjudge them as much as they sometimes misjudge us? I look up at my wife’s candid, open face, and know full well it never once deceived me.

Lest I encourage my own children to copy my imprudent example, I will not tell you how tiny the capital was that Theo and I started our wedded life on. My tragedy never earned us a penny, though the critics have since spoken kindly of its merits, and Mr. Kemble himself did me the honour to praise it. Our good friend Lord Wrotham wanted to have it published by subscription, sent me a banknote, and asked for a hundred copies for all his friends, but I never cared for that way of extracting money from acquaintances. I chose to keep my poverty unburdened by favours, and locked the manuscript away, with Theo’s own verses tucked into the very first page. I never could understand why the play gave such offense at court, unless it was because the actor who had run off with an earl’s daughter played the lead role; but I was told that the speeches I put in the mouths of my Indian characters, declaiming against ambition and the greed for British rule, were declared dangerous and unconstitutional, and so any faint hope of royal favour I might have held was entirely extinguished.

What was I to do? A few months after the play failed, I sat down to count the remains of our fortune—an arithmetic that took no time at all—and came to the conclusion I must leave our pretty Bloomsbury apartments. I gave our kind landlady notice, telling her my wife’s health required us to take lodgings in the country. We did not go farther than Lambeth, though, where our faithful servants Gumbo and Molly followed us, so that we lived as people of condition ought, waited on by a footman and maid both in proper livery. You may be sure our kind relatives cried out at our “extravagance”; indeed, is it not always our relatives who are quickest to find fault with our faults, and proclaim them to all the rest of the world?

One day I came back from a trip into London to visit the booksellers, and spotted our family arms and livery blazoned on a grand gilt coach drawn up outside a public house near our lodgings. A crowd of local loiterers had gathered around the splendid vehicle, staring in awe at the footmen standing resplendent in the sun, quaffing foaming tankards of beer. I walked up the stairs to our little apartment to find Lady Castlewood sitting opposite my wife, their sitting room looking out over a bright, pleasant stretch of the Thames dotted with barges and wherries, and the ancient towers and trees of the Archbishop’s palace and gardens beyond. Theo, who has a droll, vivid way of describing people and scenes, told me every detail of the Countess’s conversation after her ladyship left.

“I’ve been gossiping here with cousin Theo this ever-so-long,” the Countess had said, “while you’ve been off at the coffee house, no doubt, making merry with your friends, drinking punch and coffee. I expect she finds it lonely here, nothing to do but sew little baby caps and hem frocks. Never mind, dear, you’ll soon have a little companion to amuse you when cousin George is off at his coffee house! What a nice lodging you have here, I do declare. Our new house we’ve taken is twenty times the size, gilded from top to bottom, but I like this just as well. Bless you, being rich is no better than being poor. When we lived at Albany, I did all the work myself, scrubbed the rooms, boiled the kettle, helped with the wash, and I was just as happy as I am now. We only had one old negro to tend the store. Why don’t you sell Gumbo, cousin George? He’s no use here lazing about and making love to the servant girl! Fogh, these English folks don’t care much for proprieties, do they?” She rattled on in perfect good humour until it was time for her to leave, pulling out a fine repeating watch to say she must pay a call on the Queen at Buckingham House. “And mind you come visit us, George,” she called, waving a gloved hand out of the coach door. “Theo and I have settled all about it.”

“There, at least, is someone who is not afraid of our poverty, nor ashamed to remember her own humble beginnings,” I said, as the laced footmen clambered up behind the carriage and our magnificent little patroness drove away.

“Ashamed!” Theo said, picking up her tiny, fine needlework. “To do her justice, she would make herself at home in any kitchen or any palace in the whole world. She gave me and Molly twenty whole lessons in housekeeping while she was here. She says when she lived in Albany, she roasted, baked, swept the house, and milked the cow.” Theo pronounced the word “cow” in our droll American way, mimicking the Countess’s broad accent so perfectly I laughed out loud.

“And she has no pride at all,” I added. “It was good-natured of her to ask us to dine with her and my lord. When will Uncle Warrington ever think to offer us a crust of bread, or a glass of that famous beer of his?”

“Yes, it was not unkind of her to invite us,” Theo said slyly. “But my dear, you don’t know all the conditions!” Still mimicking the Countess’s manner, she laughingly laid them out for me. “She pulled out her pocketbook and told me exactly what days she was busy,” Theo said. “On Mondays she receives a Duke and Duchess, and half a dozen other members of my lord’s family and their ladies. On Tuesdays there are more earls, two bishops, and an ambassador. ‘Of course you won’t come on those days?’ she said. ‘Now you are so poor, fine company ain’t no good for you. Lord bless you! father never dines on our company days, he don’t like it, he just takes a bit of cold meat in his room.’ I told her Mr. Warrington only cared for the best of company, Theo laughed, “and suggested she invite us on a day when the Archbishop of Canterbury was dining with her, so his Grace could give us a lift home in his coach to Lambeth. She’s a very economical little soul, too, Theo went on. “‘I thought of bringing some of my baby’s old caps and clothes that his lordship has outgrown, but they might be wanted again, you know, my dear,’ she said. So we lost that gift, Theo smiled, “and Molly and I will have to make do without her ladyship’s charity. ‘When people are poor, they are poor,’ she said, plain as day, ‘and must get on the best they can. What we are to do for that poor Maria, goodness only knows! We can’t have her to visit us like we can you, even though you are poor: an earl’s daughter to marry a common play-actor! La, my dear, it’s dreadful! The King and the Princess have both spoken of it! Every noble family in the kingdom who’s heard the story pities us, though I have a plan to help those poor unhappy people, and sent Simons, my groom of the chambers, down to tell them all about it.’ Her plan was that Hagan, who had nearly finished his terms at Dublin College, should go back there to take his degree and enter holy orders, ‘and then we will give him a chaplaincy in our own household, you know,’ Lady Castlewood added.” I may note here that this kind plan was carried out a couple of years later, and I myself was able to do a small service for Mr. Hagan, who was one of the kindest, truest friends we had in our own days of want. Lord Castlewood kept his promise loyally enough, got Hagan ordained and a colonial posting, where he distinguished himself both as a soldier and a preacher, as you shall hear later—though not a single guinea did his lordship ever spare to help either his sister or his kinsman in their trouble. I never once asked him for aid, thank Heaven, though to do him justice, no man ever expressed more genuine, unfeigned joy than he did when my days of poverty finally came to an end.

As for my Uncle Warrington, his pious wife, and their daughters, I will do them the justice to say that their sorrow over my poverty was perfectly consistent and unwavering throughout my whole period of trial. I still had acquaintances who ran into them from time to time, and of course—as friends always will—they brought me back reports of their opinions and conversations. I never once heard that my relatives uttered a single good word on my behalf or my wife’s. They spoke of my tragedy as a positive crime, and of its author as a miserable reprobate who staggered around Grub Street day and night in rags and squalor

Our little Miles drew his first breath scarce a handful of days after the royal Prince George, who would one day hold command over the regiment the boy would one day join. Across London, the birth of the royal heir was marked by blazing street illuminations and thundering cannon volleys, while crowds of gawkers thronged St James’s Palace to peek at the princely infant laid behind gilded railings, dandled under the watch of high-born court nurses.

No crowds, no bowing courtiers lined the threshold of our small Lambeth lodgings to greet our own little prince. The only faithful retainers who doted on him were our devoted servant Gumbo and sharp, warm-hearted Molly, who loved and admired the tiny heir to our straitened household with a loyalty no court flatterer could equal.

We might have named him George, for the new royal paragon and for his own father, as was custom. But we chose instead Miles, for a small, scapegrace member of our Warrington line: the single distant cousin of my father’s blood who had shown me true kindness at a time when every other kinsman had turned their back. Theo and I had agreed the moment we knew we were expecting that our son would bear that name, in tribute to that long-forgotten act of gentle generosity. We sent word of the birth to my family across the Atlantic, and boldly printed his notice in the *Daily Advertiser*, marking our small home in Church Street plain for every London gossip to see.

Aunt Bernstein’s reply came swift, sharp-edged as ever but warm under its briskness: “My dear boy, whatever possessed you to broadcast to all the world that you are tucked away in such a hovel, where you have chosen to bury yourself? I kiss the little new mother, and send a keepsake for the child.” That keepsake was a fine silk coverlet edged with lace so delicate it might have graced a royal cradle. The gold spent on that lace would have fed our household for a full month, but Theo and Molly clapped their hands over the gift, and our son’s cradle was draped as fine as any nobleman’s babe in Mayfair.

Good Dr. Heberden called often to check on Theo, and recommended a skilled local surgeon in the neighbourhood to tend her lying-in, though she needed very little extra care beyond the attention our landlady and Molly lavished on her. Soon after, the gilded, gleaming chariot of Lady Castlewood rolled up our rickety lane, drawing stares from every passing street vendor. She brought a pot of jellied sweetmeat, she said, certain Theo would crave it — no doubt leftover from one of her own grand banquets, served to dozens of fine guests the week before. She chattered nonstop about court ceremonies, the feasts and masquerades thrown to celebrate the royal heir’s birth, all the glittering splendour that surrounded that other little prince across the city.

Mr. Samuel Johnson happened to pay me a call that very same hour, just as Lady Castlewood was stepping down from her chariot. He bowed to her with that heavy, lumbering courtesy of his, far more earnest than graceful. She greeted me as “cousin” with great affability, and even helped spoon the jelly out of her polished silver serving dish into our chipped earthen pan. The good Doctor took a full spoonful, smacked his lips, and pronounced it excellent. “The great of the world are fortunate in all things,” he rumbled. “They can hire the most skilful cooks, just as they gather the wittiest men around their tables. If this sweetmeat, as its well-worn dish suggests, has already done service at my lord’s table, it has kept fine company. It has trembled under the gaze of celebrated beauties, been sipped by ruby lips, divided the attention of a whole room of distinguished guests alongside tarts, creams, and fruits that were no doubt as delicious as itself.” He proceeded to eat a good half of the pot before anyone could stop him. I am bound to add, though, that Theo took one small taste later and pushed the dish away, declaring it not at all to her liking, and Molly tossed her head and announced plainly that the jelly had turned mouldy sitting unused on a nobleman’s shelf for three days.

Our little Miles had the rare honour of an earl’s daughter for his godmother: kind Lady Maria, who had long lost her own solitary chance at motherhood. Her attention to Theo and the new infant was beyond all praise; she yearned over our small boy so tenderly that it brought tears to even Gumbo’s eyes, and many of the fine little linen garments he wore in his earliest days had been stitched and laid aside for the child she would never hold. Years later, when Captain Miles rode with the Prince’s Hussars in a uniform blazing with gold braid, as fine a fashion plate as any in the regiment, I hope he remembers that quiet, gentle kindness that surrounded his cradle.

Sampson Hagan christened him in the very same Southwark chapel where Theo and I had been wed. No man ever read the words of the Prayer Book more beautifully or more movingly than he that day — until he reached the final blessing, and his voice cracked, and every last one of us in that tiny congregation was dabbing at our eyes. “Mr. Garrick himself could not have read those words half so nobly,” Hagan said afterwards. “No innocent babe ever entered the world carried on more tender, sincere wishes than our little Miles.”

I have not yet told how Miles came by his name, when we had fully intended, two days before the christening, to name him George for his father. We heard the patter of tiny pony hooves clattering up our cobbled lane, our gate bell jangled, and there was young Cousin Miles, dusty from the long ride, who I suspect had snuck off from his parents’ house that day in open disobedience. “You know Cousin Harry gave me my little pony,” he panted, red-cheeked and breathless, “and I can’t help but love you — you look so much like Harry, and they are always saying unkind things about you at home, and it’s not fair. I brought my whistle and coral that my godmother Lady Suckling gave me, for your little boy. And if you are really as poor as they say, Cousin George, here is my gold moidore. It is worth a great deal, and it’s no use to me anyway, since I am never allowed to spend it.”

We carried the boy up to Theo’s bedchamber, his scuffed little riding boots (of which he was inordinately proud) thumping on every stair. Theo kissed his grubby cheek and thanked him, and that same gold moidore has rested in her purse from that day to this.

My mother Madam Esmond wrote to me soon after, full of royal surprise and displeasure that I had dared christen my son Miles — a name unheard of in the proud, ancient Esmond line. I did not explain the reason at the time, but when, in after years, I told her the story of that small boy galloping all the way to Lambeth on his pony to give our babe his most precious treasure, I saw a tear roll down her wrinkled old cheek. I heard afterwards that she sent for Gumbo half a dozen times, to ask every last detail about the little cousin who gave his name to our Miles — our Miles Gloriosus, the future toast of Pall Mall, Valenciennes, Almack’s, and Brighton.

When Harry and I were larking through our boyhood days on the Virginian plantation, forever playing pranks on our poor long-suffering tutor, who on earth would have guessed that Mr. Esmond Warrington would end up as a “bearleader” himself, paid to chaperone and tutor another man’s son? When my mother and I were reconciled at last, she never could bring herself to name that stretch of my life outright, only ever referring to it as “that terrible time, my love, which I can scarce bear to look back on,” “those dreadful years when there was strife between us,” and so on. And though my former pupil, a most worthy and grateful soul, shipped barrels of the famed ale that built his family’s vast fortune all the way out to Jamestown as gifts for me, Madam Esmond always spoke of him only as “your friend in England,” “your wealthy Lambeth acquaintance,” never so much as breathing his name, and never once sipped a drop of his beer. We brew our own ale down at Warrington Manor, of course, but the good Mr. Foker never fails to send two full butts of his unadulterated strongest brew every year out to Ipswich for us. His son is now a fine dandy of the ton, wed to an earl’s daughter, while the old brewer himself remains as kind and generous a gentleman as one could hope to meet. It was the happy luck of making his acquaintance that put the most welcome guineas I ever earned into my own empty pockets.

It was never the size of the stipend he paid me, mind, that made the post so precious to me in those dark days, but the steady work, the small daily purpose, the glimmer of hope it gave our little household. Mr. Foker’s brewery, later moved to a larger site, stood back then near Pedlar’s Acre in Lambeth, and the surgeon who attended my wife through our first confinement also tended to the brewer’s large family. He was a Bavarian man born, named Voelker, and our shared acquaintance Mr. Lance the surgeon must have told him my name and my ruined fortunes. The good doctor would smoke pipe after pipe of our homegrown Virginia leaf in our tiny back garden, and grew very fond of me and my family. He brought his patron Mr. Foker round to call one afternoon, and when the brewer learned I could speak a smattering of his native tongue, and could even sing that old ballad “Prinz Eugen the Noble Ritter” — a song my own grandfather had brought home with him after Marlborough’s wars on the Continent — he conceived an immediate great affection for me. His lady put her own sedan chair and family chariot at my wife’s full disposal; his young daughter grew utterly besotted with our baby (and to do the boy justice, though he is now as rough a plain-looking fellow as any man who ever wore a pigtail queue, he was as beautiful as a cherub in those days) [The very image of the Squire at thirty, every soul on the plantation swears so. M.W. — Note in the original manuscript]; and his heir, young Master Foker, was being hounded and tormented mercilessly at Westminster School by his peers for the low trade his father made his fortune in, so his parents came to ask if I would take charge of his education, and paid me a sum that kept our household comfortable without the need for begging favors from distant noble relatives.

Mr. Foker was a shrewd man of business, and since he and his family had grown to care for us genuinely, I laid out all my tangled, straitened pecuniary affairs before him with almost no reserve. He said my honesty only deepened the respect and kindness he felt for me. He laughed outright when I told him of the paltry “charity” my noble kin had doled out to us: my aunt’s moth-eaten old coverlid, Lady Castlewood’s mouldy pot of jelly, the haughty cold shoulder Lady Warrington had turned on us when we called. But he cried real tears when I told him the story of poor little Miles’s lost moidore, and as for our friends Parson Sampson and the actor Hagan, “I vow,” he said in his thick rolling accent, “they shall have as much beer as they can ever drink, for nothing.” He sent his own wife to call on Lady Maria, and treated her with the utmost deference and respect whenever she visited his house. It was at the Fokers’ home that Lady Maria stayed when Hagan went off to Dublin to finish his university degrees, and the brewer’s generous purse supplied all his outfit and living costs while he was away.

Once Mr. Foker knew the full extent of my circumstances, he began to speak of me in the most enthusiastic terms, as if my small conduct had been some act of extraordinary virtue. I have written before of how my mother saved all her profits for Harry, and how both she and my brother were deep in my debt. But Harry never once thought of the money he spent as anything but his own, and Madam Esmond could never be made to see she had treated me unfairly — once the coin was spent, as far as she was concerned, the matter was closed for good. Then at the end of 1762, I remember, Harry sent a very considerable sum across the Atlantic to purchase his army promotion, writing in the same letter to remind me I was welcome to draw on his agents at any time if I found myself in need. He had no idea how small my own little remaining capital had already been eaten through.

Of course, I could not touch that money meant for his advancement — that would have delayed his promotion for months, even years — and though I own I was sorely tempted at times, I never drew on him. Nor did I dare ask our good General Lambert for funds, knowing as I did how small his own pension was, how little he had to spare. These simple acts of forbearance my worthy brewer insisted on treating as marks of almost saintly virtue. And what did the man do but write privately to my brother out in Virginia, praising me and my wife as the most perfect couple alive, then call unannounced on Madame de Bernstein — who never once told me of his visit, though I soon noticed she began treating us with a singular gentleness and respect that astonished me, for I had always thought her nothing but a selfish, worldly old woman. Years later I asked him how he had ever talked his way into the Baroness’s front door. He laughed loud and long. “De Baroness!” he said. “I knew her husband de Baron when he was no more than a walet in Munich, and I was a poor brewer’s apprentice.” It seemed best not to dig too deep into that particular branch of our family tree, after that.

And so the stretch of my life that ought to have been the most miserable of all was softened by a host of good friends, small happy moments, and strokes of unexpected luck. The “bear” I was hired to lead was a gentle, docile little cub, who danced to my tutelage without complaint. Far better to guide that boy about his lessons, I thought, than hang about the lobbies of booksellers waiting for a publisher to glance at my manuscripts, or dance attendance on theatre managers who might deign to give my play a reading. My wife and I, in what we jokingly called our “Lambeth exile,” spent dozens of warm, pleasant evenings with these kind benefactors. We were not short of small intellectual joys, either: Mrs. Foker and Theo had both fine singing voices, and would perform duets by the hour together. On nights when I felt in good humour, I would read my unperformed play *Pocahontas* aloud to our small circle, and Mr. Foker swore I gave a better performance even than the tragedian Hagan himself.

I saw almost nothing of my namesake young Miles Warrington after that little scrape of his, and heard very little news of my father’s side of the family for months on end. Sir Miles was assiduous in his attendance at court — I do believe he would have fawned as diligently on Nero himself — and I laughed out loud one day when Mr. Foker told me he had heard rumor on the Exchange that “they are going to make your uncle a Beer.” “A Beer?” I said, confused. “Can’t you make out the word, man?” the testy old brewer huffed. “Well then, a Lort!” Sir Miles was indeed the most obedient, humble servant of whatever minister held power at the time. I half expected him to start speaking with a thick Highland accent during the short reign of Lord Bute, the Scottish favorite. I ran into him and his wife once, just after Mrs. Claypool had been presented to the Queen as Lady Warrington, stepping out of their gilded gilt coach. I had our little boy perched on my shoulder. My uncle and aunt stared resolutely straight through me through the coach window, as if I were no more than a paving stone. The footmen holding their nosegays stared blankly ahead. If I had worn the fairy’s magic cap and turned invisible, my father’s own brother could not have passed me by with less notice.

We rarely took up Lady Castlewood’s odd, casual invitation to come take tea and sup at her house when no other company was present. Old Mr. Van den Bosch, shrewd as he was and brilliant at making a fortune, had no gift for small talk — save with his own daughter, who would rattle on for hours about household accounts, stocks and shares, the ups and downs of the city market, buying and selling farm stock, every bit as sharply as her father. My Lord Castlewood was almost never at home, and his wife did not seem to miss him when he was gone, nor was he ever very comfortable in his father-in-law’s company. The Countess told all this to my wife plainly, in her simple, forthright way. “Guess my lord and my father don’t get on together at all, nohow,” she said. “My lord is forever begging for money, and father keeps the key to the strongbox — and quite right too. If he could get his hands on all our fortune, he’d gamble it all away before the month was out, and then what would become of our fine noble family? We pay every last bill, my dear — except play debts, and those we won’t settle for him, not ever. We pay the cooks, the grooms, the wine merchants, the tailors, everyone — and they’re lucky to get their money, for my lord would never have paid them a farthing! And we always make sure he has a guinea or two in his pocket, so he can go about looking like a proper gentleman. Goodness only knows what he owed, and what he was up to, before we came along! My father and I do our best to make him respectable, but it’s no easy job, let me tell you. Law! He’d melt down every piece of family silver if father didn’t keep the key to the strong room, and when we go down to Castlewood House in the country, father travels with me, and he’s armed, too, along with all the servants.”

“Good heavens!” my wife cried. “Your ladyship does not mean to say you suspect your own husband of wanting to —”

“To what? Oh, nothing, of course! And I’d trust our brother Will with untold sums of money, wouldn’t I? Just as much as I’d trust a cat left guarding a cream pan! I tell you, my dear, being a great lady of rank isn’t all fun and games. If I bought myself a countess’s coronet, I paid a pretty dear price for it — that I did, sure enough.”

And my Lord Castlewood had paid a steep price, too, to have his family estate cleared of every last debt and encumbrance, his houses and stables newly furnished, all his old gambling bills wiped clean. He was the complete slave of his little wife and her shrewd old father. No wonder he could not bear the old man’s company, and snuck away from his own grand fine house as often as he could, to drink and feast at his club if he had the coin, or seek out any company at all rather than the stifling dependence he found at home. To work as a bearleader, as I did, was no grand position, I will own. To cool my heels in a bookseller’s antechamber waiting for the man to finish his dinner and deign to give me audience was often a bitter pill for a man of my name, with all my old Virginian pride. But would I have traded my small, honest poverty for Lord Castlewood’s public ignominy? Would I have chosen his miserable bought dependence over my own? Never. At least I earned every penny of my wages. No man can say I ever flattered my patrons, or groveled before them, or was anything but stiff-necked and proud in all my dealings.

And Fate had given me a life partner who bore all our small privations with such sweet, uncomplaining grace that even niggardly Fortune herself seemed to soften before her, like the wild ogre in the old fairy tales who melts at the kindness of a gentle soul. Poor as we were, every soul who knew my wife saw that she was a true fine lady through and through. The little tradespeople, our landlady, all the humble folk round our Lambeth cottage treated her with far more respect than they showed many of the grandest folks in the parish. “My dear,” good-natured Mrs. Foker said once, when they rode out in her chariot, “you look for all the world like the mistress of the carriage, and I only like your maid.” Our landladies adored her. The shopkeepers ran to fill her small orders as eagerly as if a duchess had placed them, as if waiting on her would make their fortunes. I thought often of the Lady in Comus, moving serene and untainted through all the ruck and rabble of the world around her.

As often as we asked, the kind Fokers would lend us their chariot to drive out into the country or call on the few friends we had. To tell the truth, we drove out once to the Protestant Hero tavern and had a syllabub in their gardens, and the landlady insisted on calling my wife “your ladyship” the entire afternoon. We took tea once with Mr. Samuel Johnson, too, and the clever Mr. Oliver Goldsmith was there in the company, and the good doctor escorted my wife all the way out to our carriage when it was time to leave. But our most frequent visits were to Aunt Bernstein, and I was never in the least jealous that she soon developed a great, adoring fondness for Theo.

That fondness grew so fierce that she would send for her three or four days a week, begging her to stay for days at a time, and complained endlessly that Theo’s husband and baby were nothing but pests, keeping her favorite away from her. Not that my wife was not worthy of all anyone’s affection, of course, but the constant small difficulty of getting away from our cottage to visit the old baroness only fanned her affection into something near a passion. She poured out notes to Theo that read like love letters, and her servants were forever knocking at our kitchen door at odd hours of the day. If my wife did not go to her, she would send heartbreaking appeals, and scold me roundly whenever I called on her for keeping Theo away. Once our little boy fell ill — Fate has seen fit to spare that Captain to be a considerable trial to our tempers these many years — and Madame Bernstein turned up at our cottage three days running, vowing there was nothing at all wrong with the baby, that we were only pretending he was sick to vex her.

The current Countess of Castlewood was just as brash and unceremonious with her old aunt as she was with everyone else, high or low. “What are you all scraping and bowing to that old woman for, I can’t make heads nor tails of it!” she would say. “Her a fine lady! Nonsense! She ain’t no finer than any other lady walking this earth, and I’m just as good as any of them with their high heels and their grand airs! Her a beauty once? Take away her wig, her rouge, her false teeth — and what’s left of that beauty, I’d like to know? You could tuck the whole lot in a bandbox, and all you’d find left is a shrivelled up old woman!” And the plain-spoken little Countess spoke nothing but the truth. All beauty must fade at last, wither on the vine or rot underground. Here was old age with no reverence left to it, grey hairs hidden under wigs and painted over, the old Baroness still clinging to the world with her crutch at fourscore years old. She had had beauty, pleasure, flattery in her time — but what secret rages, disappointments, humiliations she must have suffered! What thorns hidden under all those roses! What stinging bees tucked inside the sweetest fruit! “You are no beauty, my dear,” she would say to my wife, “and you may thank your stars for it. Don’t tell me your husband adores your face and you care for no other man’s admiration! Every woman in the world would rather be beautiful than anything else — richer than Croesus, perfectly good, gifted with every fairy blessing, it matters not! Look at that portrait yonder — it’s a poor enough painting, that vain fool Kneller never could capture my eyes, my hair, my skin. What a figure I had then! And look at me now, this wrinkled old neck! Why must our time of beauty be so short? I remember seeing Mademoiselle de l’Enclos when she was far older than me, still fresh and lovely. We can’t hide our ages. They are written down in the parish books for all to see. I was born the very last year of King James’s reign. I am not old, not really — only seventy-six. But what a wreck I am, my dear — isn’t it cruel that our time should run out so fast?”

My wife would reply with the soft, gentle truth that the time of every living soul on this earth is short, no matter how high or low their station.

“Ah!” the Baroness would cry. “Did not Adam live nigh on a thousand years, and was not Eve beautiful every single day of it? I used to puzzle that poor creature Mr. Tusher with that argument, years ago! What have we done since then, that our lives are shrunk so small, I ask you?”

“Has your life been so very happy, then, that you would want to stretch it out for many more years?” Theo asked her once. “Do you who love wit so much not remember Dean Swift’s famous story of the immortals in Gulliver? My father and my husband say it is one of the finest, most awful sermons ever written. It would be far better not to live at all than to live without love — and I

When my mother learned I had taken a paid post here in England rather than surrender to her demands that I bring my whole family back to Virginia to live dependent on her bounty, I do not think she was best pleased. It seems she meant to starve me into submission, cutting off my allowance entirely to force my hand. We never once, not on the very day of her death, spoke openly of that bitter pecuniary rift between us. She withdrew all support; I said not a word of complaint, and contrived to keep my household going without a penny from her. I never heard she owned her injustice outright, save for a private confession Harry passed on to me years later. When we met at last, long after our years of estrangement, Madam Esmond showed me unusual gentleness, and lavished uncustomary respect and affection on my wife, no doubt intending I should read in that behaviour her silent admission she had been in the wrong. But she spoke no formal apology, and I never asked for one.

Harry was well provided for, and I could not grudge his good fortune, so all my mother’s thrifty, carefully hoarded savings fell to me as her heir in time. Once, a few guineas would have served me far better than the hundreds that came to me long after I had any need for them, but by the time Madam Esmond and I met again, my days of scraping by were far behind. I no longer had to scheme over mean little economies, or haggle to pay the doctor’s bill: I had more than enough, and all her fortune could do was add to what I already possessed. I do not doubt her pride gnawed at her to think my children had gone hungry once, and she had turned away from their need to let strangers relieve them. Proud? But was I prouder still? A single soft word of explanation would have healed our rift years earlier, but I would not speak first, and no more would she. When I do a wrong and recognise it afterwards, I love to ask pardon not out of pure humility, but to salve my own pride, to prove to myself I have not fallen short of my own standards of honour. That stubborn regard for my own ego, I think, is what kept me from ever stooping to a mean or underhand act. What must it be like to live a whole life made up of lies, schemes, and petty subterfuges? What company do men keep when they are alone, every smile a ruse and every wink an act of hypocrisy? Do they wear their masks even in private, before their own consciences? When I choose to overlook an injury, I fear it is rarely out of Christian forgiveness: it is only because I can well afford to write the debt off, and disdain to hound the offender for settlement. I have known one or two rare, sweet souls for whom forgiveness comes as naturally as a flower blooms, but I myself only know how to remit a wrong – not truly forgive it. I wonder if we proud men are secretly proud of being proud?

For years I gave her no sign of submission at all, and we stayed estranged, only brief, cold notes passing between my wife and her, to announce a child’s birth or some other trivial piece of family news. Our troubles after the Stamp Act riots in America were soon followed by new misfortunes for me in London. Though I had stood on the Tory side of the colonial quarrel, fully believing the Imperial government held every right to levy taxes across the colonies, I could not resist publishing a sharp, public letter to a member of the Virginia House of Burgesses that roundly criticised the mother country’s habitual overbearing treatment of the colonies. The sentiments I voiced were so offensive to men in power that I was stripped of my post as hackney-coach licenser, to my uncle’s unutterable horror – he never could abide anyone who fell out of favour at court. He had grown very fond of my wife and little boy, of course, but to me he extended a sort of pitying, quiet contempt that never failed to amuse me. He had a natural scorn for poverty, and a corresponding devotion to luck and worldly success. Any opinion that strayed even an inch from the common accepted track shocked and terrified him, and any plain speaking of truth would turn him pale with fright. He must have had some genuine warmth of heart left in him, for all his snobbery: even after the shocks my imprudence gave him, he still called to see Theo and the child, and nodded a mournful greeting to me when we met, regarding me as a pitiable lost soul past all hope of worldly advancement. No matter. I set about casting about for new work, and the unexpected repayment of an old debt Harry owed me kept my household afloat for months, even years. Oh, the foolish fatuity of youth! I still marvel at how we dared to be so poor, and yet so little cast down by it.

It was at this time that His Majesty’s uncle, the Duke of Cumberland, dropped dead of a sudden fit. Strangely enough, his death was the turning point that changed all my fortunes. My poor uncle Sir Miles Warrington never missed a single court ceremony he could finagle his way into: he was present at every drawing-room, royal christening, court ball, and state funeral. If any prince or princess fell ill, his coach would be parked outside their door before most folk had heard the news. Now nothing would do but he must attend the stout duke’s funeral, standing bareheaded for hours in the pouring rain. He caught a savage cold that turned to inflammation of the throat, and before I had even heard he was taken ill, a lawyer turned up at my Bloomsbury lodgings, and saluted me by the name of Sir George Warrington.

The party quarrels, the fear of tomorrow, all were over now. We laid the poor old gentleman to rest beside his little son in the family churchyard, where so many generations of his kin slept. Little Miles and I walked as chief mourners behind the coffin. Obsequious tenants bowed and curtseyed before us, falling over themselves to win favour with the new master of the estate. The dowager Lady Warrington and her daughter soon withdrew to Bath, and my family and I took possession of the manor house that I have now called home for thirty years. Be not in too much haste, my son, I tell the boy who will one day inherit it: wait but a little while, and I too shall sleep under those yew trees at the churchyard edge, and the villagers will toss their caps in the air for you, Sir Miles.

The records of a quiet, prosperous country life are easily told. The steward’s ledgers note what rents were paid and what forgiven, what crops were sown and in what rotation. The visitor books record who came to stay, and how long they remained; what pensioners my wife supported, who tended their ills, and who passed peacefully away. I was made sheriff one year, the hounds met on our lands a dozen times over – all these trivial details are written down in our house journals, for any heir of mine who cares to take the trouble to read them. We could not afford the grand Hill Street mansion my uncle had once occupied, so we took a smaller London house, where we spent our money far more freely than he ever did. We kept none of the ostentatious show he was famous for, with liveried footmen, gilded equipages, and endless silver plate, but our home-brewed ale was stronger, and my wife’s charities cost far more than the dowager’s had ever done. I have no doubt the old lady thought there was no sin in fleecing the new owners: she charged us unconscionable prices for every stick of furniture she left behind at the country house, and I bore all her extortions with unending good humour. What a fancy price she put on the potted plants in her greenhouse! What a fortune she demanded for that dreadful old spinet she left gathering dust in the drawing room! And those framed bits of worsted work stitched by the accomplished Dora and lovely Flora – why, they could not have fetched higher prices even if they were masterpieces by Titian or Vandyck.

Yet for all our generosity, for all that our care for the local poor far outstripped the dowager’s, we had the worst reputation in the shire for years, all sorts of ugly stories circulated about my supposed dangerous opinions. I had hoped I might step into my uncle’s seat in Parliament alongside his landed property, but I soon found no such luck was coming my way. I would not bribe voters, and I would not force my own tenants to cast their ballots for me at the 1768 election. A gentleman came down from Whitehall with a pocketbook stuffed full of banknotes, and I stood no chance against my government-backed competitor.

Good heavens! Now that we were free of all worldly worry, now that tenants bowed and curtseyed as we walked to church, now that we drove to call on neighbours in the great old family coach pulled by four plump, well-fed horses – did we not often find ourselves longing for the days of our poverty, for that tiny dear cottage in Lambeth where Want was always prowling at the door? Did I not catch myself pining for the old days when I trundled foreign authors around London, swearing that translating books for publishers was not such terrible drudgery after all? When we went up to London, we made sentimental pilgrimages to every old haunt we had once known. I dare say my wife hugged every former landlady we ran across. We invited every old friend from our days of hardship to come and share the comfort of our new home. The Reverend Mr. Hagan and his wife visited us more than once, and when he preached in our local parish church his fine, fiery oratory caused a grand scandal through the whole neighbourhood. Sampson came too, that other unlucky clergyman, and we made him welcome for as long as he cared to stay. Mr. Johnson talked of coming down to see us, but put us off again and again. I dare say our country house was very dull. I know I myself would fall silent for days at a time, and I fear my moodiness tried the patience of the sweetest-tempered woman in the world who ever lived as my wife. I did not care for field sports. The act of killing one partridge was so like killing another that I never could understand how men could spend whole days chasing after that sort of pointless slaughter. Their fox-hunting stories would start the moment the dinner cloth was removed, and run right on till supper time. I would sit silent and listen, and doze off day after day. No wonder I was never popular with the local gentry who called on us.

What confession is this I am making? The storm had passed, I had avoided all the sharp rocks, the ship was safely in port – and the sailor was not even especially content? Was the Susan I had dreamed of all through the long voyage not half the beauty I had expected to find waiting for me on the shore? Well, Susan and all the family will read these pages, so I shall not set down all my secrets here. No, Susan, I never had any secrets from thee. I have seen far more beautiful women than you, but none who ever suited me half so well. I have met Mrs. Carter and Miss Mulso, Mrs. Thrale and Madame Kauffmann, the angelical Gunnings, the Duchess of Devonshire, and a whole host of great beauties who were not a bit angelic, and none of them ever dazzled me. Do not think, young folks, that though I may have led your mother a weary life, and been a great testy Bluebeard to her, that I ever hid another woman’s head in my closet. But once the first joy of taking possession of our new home wore off, I own I quickly tired of my crown. When you boys inherit it, you will be far better princes than I ever was. You can ride to hounds five days a week and find the sport endlessly diverting. I dare say you could sit through the same dull parish sermon fifty times and not yawn half as much as I did the first time I heard it. But my sweet Joan, my beloved Baucis! Thy faithful husband, thy true lover always, thy old Darby is ashamed of how often he was testy with you. Arrived at the very peak of supposed perfect happiness, thy Philemon begs pardon for dozing off so often after dinner. There came a stretch of my life where I had climbed to the very top of the mountain of felicity, and found the view from the summit terribly dull. I yawned in Eden, and said, “Is this all? What, no lions to bite? No rain to drench you? No thorns on the rose bush to prick your finger when you sit down? Nothing but Eve, for ever sweet and tender, and figs for breakfast, dinner, supper, week in week out?” Shall I make a clean breast of it? Listen then.

* * * * * *

Three entire pages are torn out of Sir George Warrington’s manuscript here, for which the editor can only offer sincere regret.

I know the theory and practice of the Roman Church, but raised as I was in another faith (and sceptical enough of my own creed at that), I cannot help doubting whether Catholics ever truly confess all their sins. Do we Protestants ever do so? Has education ever made those fellow men of ours so fundamentally different from ourselves? I do not think we ever imagine Catholic priests or laymen are any more frank and open than we are. Which brings me back to my question: does any man confess all? Does that dear woman who has shared my life for thirty years know every last corner of it? The one who has always been ready to soothe any sorrow I told her of, who has sat silent beside me when I would not speak, or worn a bright, easy smile out of that charming womanly hypocrisy, so that I would not feel pressed to share a secret I wished to keep private? Oh, that dear hypocrite! Have I not watched her hide the boys’ small misdeeds from my anger? Have I not known her scrape money out of the housekeeping accounts to pay off their little wild extravagances, then talk to me with the most artless face in the world, pretending she did not know that our eldest son, the captain, had been borrowing money from the moneylenders in Duke’s Place, and our younger son, the university student, had very pressing reasons to bar his door against tradesmen come for payment? From the very earliest days, that wise woman of mine was forever hiding little things from me: this one stealing jam from the larder, that one getting into trouble at school, that naughty rebel (put on the caps, young folks, whichever fits you best) flinging an inkstand at his mother in a rage, while I was told the stained gown and carpet had been ruined by a complete accident. We all hide little things from one another. We all have our secrets. We are all alone in the end. We sin alone, and let us hope we repent alone too. That dear woman would gladly break her own foot to spare me a twinge of the gout, but when the pain does come, the ache is only in my own slipper.

At the end of a novel or a play, the hero and heroine marry or die, and the poet cheers them on till their postchaise rounds the corner, or calls for the hearse and plumes, and shovels them underground, and the story is done. But when Mr. Random and Mr. Thomas Jones go home to their brides, is all the excitement over? Are there no quarrels behind closed doors? No Lady Bellastons waiting out in the world? No constables to outrun, no temptations that may conquer you or that you must conquer? The Sirens sang long after Ulysses was married, and suitors whispered in Penelope’s ear. They both had many a long, weary day of doubt and care, just as we all do. My inheritance freed me from all worry about money, but does not black care sit behind the baronet just as surely as it sits behind the poorest common knight? My friends in London all congratulated me on my perfect happiness. Who would not want to be master of a fine house and a fat estate? But can Gumbo, my butler, shut the front door on the blue devils, or drown them forever in a red sea of claret? Does a man sleep better for having twenty-four whole hours a day to doze in? Do his wits brighten after a sermon from the dull old local vicar, ten minutes of sycophantic chattering from the village apothecary, or the company of Sir John and Sir Thomas and their ladies, who ride ten miles through mud and moonlight to eat a haunch of venison and play a hand of whist? All those little indulgences are very well: tradesmen bowing to your carriage door, a place of honour reserved for you at quarter sessions, your wife being led in to dinner second or third in order of precedence. But those pleasures fade fast, and bring their own irritations. For seven years after we moved into Warrington Manor, our two best neighbours in the shire were my Lord Tutbury and Sir John Mudbrook. Our family was older than the Mudbrooks, so when we dined at their house, Lady Tutbury – who was deaf, and fell asleep half way through dinner – always fell to me as my dinner companion. If I was paired with Lady Mudbrook instead, she chattered with such unending, empty folly that even my wife, consummate hypocrite that she is, could barely keep her polite smile pasted on her face, even as she watched me fuming inwardly at the woman’s endless clatter.

I went up to London one season, showed my tongue to Dr. Heberden, and poured out my whole long list of complaints. “Pshaw, my dear Sir George!” the unfeeling physician said. “Headaches, languor, bad sleep, bad temper—” “Not bad temper,” my wife cut in. “Sir George has the sweetest temper in the world, only he is sometimes a little melancholy.” “Bad sleep, bad temper,” the doctor went on, ignoring her. “My dear lady, his inheritance has been his ruin. A little poverty and a great deal of hard work would do him more good than all the physic in my apothecary’s shop.”

It is true. My brother Harry ought to have been the squire of Warrington Manor, with the estate to pass on later to my son Miles, of course. Harry’s letters from Virginia were full of nothing but high spirits and good cheer. His estate throve, his enslaved people multiplied, his tobacco crops were bountiful, he had been elected a member of the House of Burgesses, he doted on his wife, and wrote that if only they had a child his happiness would be entirely complete. If Hal had stood in my place as master of Warrington Manor, he would have been adored by the whole shire. He would have been the steward of every local race meet, the merriest of all the

An appeal from our mother such as that we had received would have softened hearts far sterner than ours, and we at once began spinning plans for a swift return to Virginia, even arranging to book every last cabin berth aboard the *Young Rachel* for the crossing. But fate intervened: our youngest child fell ill, and no one could dream of risking a long ocean voyage for a feverish little one, nor could the mother bear to part from her, so the *Young Rachel* sailed that year without us. The next brought a new obstacle: my first sharp, humbling attack of the gout, which kept me hobbling by the fireside for weeks, though it later did much to clear my wits and stir my lagging spirits. Then came a far sadder, heavier reason to delay, in the grim news that reached us from Jamaica.

Some two years after we had settled ourselves at our English Manor, dear General Lambert returned home from his colonial governorship. He came a little richer in worldly coin than he had set out, but bearing a loss no fortune on earth could repair; indeed, no sooner had he stepped ashore than he declared he never meant to return to the West Indies. My Theo’s beloved mother – the tenderest, truest friend (save one) I have ever known – had died out there of the island fever. Her last spoken regret was that she would not live to see our household thriving, and hold our little ones on her knee.

“She sees us still, though we cannot see her,” her husband said, quiet and steady, pressing Theo’s hand. “And she thanks you, George, for being good to her girls.”
We all thought he would not linger long before joining her. His love for his wife had been the whole business and joy of his life; to be parted from her felt to him like no life at all. It was pitiable to watch the good man sitting with us of an evening. My wife, in the tilt of her head, the lilt of her laugh, a hundred tiny unthinking gestures, would constantly bring his lost wife back to his heart, sharp and sudden as a knife twist. All the comfort we could offer him we gave freely, but little Hetty, under Heaven, soon became his chief stay and consolation. The General told us she had turned down no fewer than three advantageous matches while in Jamaica; and no sooner had they landed back in England than the heir to Lord Wrotham had laid his coronet and fortune at her feet. But Hetty only smiled and said she would rather stay with her father. As long as he did not tire of her company, she wanted no husband.

“Nonsense,” we told them, when the Wrotham match was first proposed. “Let the General spend six months here at our Manor, and the other six with you at Oakhurst. You will have all the time together you could wish.”
But Hetty declared her father could never bear to live at Oakhurst now, with no beloved wife there to fill the empty spaces, and she would never marry a man for his title or his gold, not she. The General, when we spoke of it later, said gravely that Hetty’s refusal to marry likely stemmed from some early heartbreak she never spoke of, and we, respecting her silence, never pressed her on the matter.

By this time, my brother Jack Lambert held a small college living near Winchester, and of course had a wife to grace his parsonage. We bore no ill will to the woman, but never pretended to more than lukewarm liking for her, though we made her welcome when she came to stay. Her theory for Hetty’s determined celibacy was far more foolish than my own. This Mrs. Jack was a chatterbox, proud as anything of speaking her “unvarnished mind” – which was, in fact, only a habit of saying cruel things to her friends and calling it honesty.

“My dear Sir George,” she would prattle at any who would listen, “I have told our dear Theo over and over that I would never suffer a pretty sister living under my roof, making tea for my husband Jack while I was upstairs with the children, all neat and trim in her best gown while I am fussing over pies and puddings in the kitchen. Oh, I trust Jack! To be sure I do! I should like to see him so much as glance at another woman! But that does not mean I will leave them alone together when my back is turned – no, that I promise you! And so I warned Theo, before Hetty ever came to stay.”

“Am I to understand, madam,” the General said to her, very grave, “that you have done my Lady Warrington the favour of warning her against my own daughter, Miss Hester?”
“To be sure I have, sir!” she cried. “Duty is duty, and a woman is a woman, and a man is a man, as I know very well. Do not tell me otherwise! Every man alive is flesh and blood, even with all his parson’s sanctified airs!”
“Ah, and you yourself have a married sister, I think?” the General went on. “It was at her house that your husband Jack first had the honour of making your acquaintance, was it not?”
“Of course I do! Everyone knows that, and I have been a second mother to her children, that I have!”
“Then am I to gather from your words that your own attractions proved a powerful temptation to your sister’s husband?”
Mrs. Jack went scarlet as a berry, voluble and indignant. “Law, General! I never said any such thing! How can you go and put words in my mouth like that?”
“Do you not see, my good woman, that it is you yourself who have insinuated as much – not only about yourself, but about my two own daughters, and Theo as well?”
“Never, never, never, as I am a Christian!” she shrieked. “It is most cruel of you to say so, sir! All I said was that a sister is best kept out of the house, and that with Theo lying in soon, I was doing my duty to warn her!”
“Have you happened to notice, madam,” the General said, still quiet, “if my poor Hetty has stolen any of our silver spoons? I came down to breakfast this morning, and she was all alone at the table, with no less than twenty pieces of silver laid out before her.”
“Law, sir! Who ever said a word about spoons? I never accused the dear girl of anything! May I drop dead on this very hearthrug if I did! I am not used to being spoken to in such a way! Jack and I both remarked on it, and I was only doing my duty!” With that, she flounced out of the room, tears streaming down her face.

The General turned to Theo, who had come in to join them at the tea table, looking a little pale and delicate as her time drew near. “Has that woman really had the impudence to say all this to you, my child?”
“She has told me every single day since she arrived,” Theo said, with a dry little laugh. “She comes bursting into my dressing room to tell me, and stands in my nursery wringing her hands and crying, ‘Ah, I would never have a sister prowling about my nursery, that I wouldn’t!’ Oh, what a blessing it is to have such amiable, well-bred relatives, is it not?”
“Thank Heaven your poor mother was spared that woman,” the General groaned.
“Our mother would have taught her better, papa,” Theo said, leaning up to kiss his cheek, and I saw that both of their eyes were glistening, half in amusement, half in sorrow.

It must be owned that loving one’s relatives is not always the easiest of tasks, and living beside one’s neighbours is far from a constant amusement. The next day, I could see from Jack Lambert’s sullen demeanour that his wife had given him her own lopsided version of the argument. He was sulky, but not dignified; angry, but not so angry that he lost his appetite, and he preached us a sermon that Sunday so perfectly dull and stupid I nearly fell asleep in the pew. Little Miles, all in his small mourning sables, sat perched on his grandfather’s knee, his tiny hand curled tight around the old man’s palm.

We proposed that the General and Hetty should stay and keep house for us during our Virginia trip. The housekeeper would be entirely under Hetty’s direction, and the General should hold all the butler’s keys, for Gumbo – who had married our Molly some years prior, and filled a neat cottage on our park grounds with a whole brood of little tawny Gumbos – had agreed to sail with us, though not, I thought, with any great show of good grace. So we left our English Manor in the care of the two people we trusted most in all the world, travelled to London, and then on to Bristol, where our obsequious local agent bowed and scraped before us, vowing he would offer up constant prayers for our safe voyage, and declaring he had never seen two children as beautiful as our Miles and our new baby daughter, little Theo, who came aboard with us for the crossing.

We had a perfectly uneventful sail, and the feeling that washed over me as we stepped ashore at Richmond was stranger than any I had ever known. A coach stood waiting for us, surrounded by a whole host of grinning negro servants in our livery, and nearby a gentleman on horseback, also attended by our own people, who sprang from his saddle and came rushing over to embrace us. It was my dearest Hal! We were both half beside ourselves with joy to see him. He rode beside our coach all the way to our mother’s door, and there she stood, waiting on the steps to welcome us, and Theo knelt down on the path to beg her blessing.

Harry got back into the coach with us for a short way, but said he would not spoil the moment by coming in with us at once. “She sees me often enough,” he said, “and we are on pretty good terms, but Fanny and she are best kept apart, I can promise you there is no love lost between them. Come and meet me at the tavern when you are free, George. Tomorrow I will bring Fanny over to pay her respects to your wife. I only chanced to ride into town yesterday, heard the ship had been signalled, and waited for you to land. I sent a negro boy home ahead to tell Fanny the news.” With that, he jumped down from the moving carriage and left us to meet our mother alone.

Since I had last parted from her, I had dined with kings and queens, and paid our formal respects to King George and Queen Charlotte at St. James’s, but I had never seen a more stately, graceful person than the woman who welcomed us now. She raised Theo from her knee, embraced her, and led us into the house. It was a plain, wood-built Virginian manor, with a wide gallery running all around it, but if it had been a royal palace with an empress on the throne, we could not have been received with more courtesy and warmth. Old Nathan was still there, as major-domo, and a score of familiar black faces all grinning to welcome us. Some I remembered as small children were now grown tall, strapping young lads and lasses; some I had left with jet black hair now had snowy white pates; and new little ones born long after my departure peered round doorways with great round eyes and bare little feet, piping out their names to us. “I’m little Sip, Master George!” “I’m Dinah, Sir George!” “I’m Master Miles’s own boy!” squeaked a tiny urchin in a brand new livery, his boots polished only by the dirt of the earth. Before the day was out, every single soul on the plantation had found some excuse to pass before us, bowing and grinning and making us welcome. I do not know how many feasts were laid before us that first day. That evening, Theo received every gentleman and lady of the little town, and carried it off with such perfect grace and good humour that everyone sang her praises afterwards. I shook hands with a dozen old acquaintances – old enemies, I almost said, but I had come into my fortune now, and was no longer the naughty prodigal son returning home. A whole drove of fatted calves was slaughtered in our honour. Poor Hal was there at the entertainment, but he looked gloomy and crestfallen. His mother spoke to him, but it was as a queen might speak to a rebellious prince who has not yet earned full pardon.

Later that night, we slipped away from the crowd and went up to the rooms that had been set aside for me, ready to talk freely at last, but before long our mother appeared at the door, taper in hand, her face soft and pale. Did I want for anything? Was everything to my liking? She had peeped in at the children, she said, and they were sleeping like little cherubs. She cooed over them, stroked their curls, delighted in Miles’s bossy little airs and baby Theo’s dimpled smiles. “Supper is just coming to the table, Sir George. And if you prefer our home cookery to the tavern, Henry, you may stay and join us.” The difference in the warmth of her tone to each of us was so plain even a blind man could see it. Hal hung his head, and followed her down to the parlour. The local clergyman asked a blessing over the meal, speaking with great eloquence of our safe passage across the stormy Atlantic, and of the love and forgiveness that would await all of us in our Heavenly Father’s house when the storms of mortal life were done.

This new clergyman was nothing like the lazy, drunken parsons I remembered from my boyhood, and I praised him to my mother, but Madam Esmond shook her head. She feared his principles were very dangerous, she said, and feared a great many other leading men in the colony shared those dangerous opinions. Had I not seen the petition signed by the burgesses and merchants at Williamsburg the year before – the Lees, the Randolphs, the Washingtons, the Bassets, and oh, my dear, it pained her to say it, even our own name, your brother Harry’s, and that very Mr. Belman who had said the blessing over supper the night before?

If there had been petty quarrels in colonial society when I left home, they were nothing to the raging feuds I found on my return. We in England had passed the Stamp Act, then been forced to repeal it. Then we tried a new set of duties on glass, paper, and other goods, and were forced to repeal almost all of that too – save for a small duty on tea. From Boston to Charleston, every shipment of tea was seized and poured into the harbour.
