Even my mother, loyalist as she was, gave up drinking her favourite tea rather than pay the tax, and my poor Theo would have had to forgo hers too, if we had not brought a private cask of it over on the ship, for which we had already paid four times the duty at home. For my own part, I would never have hesitated to pay the lawful tax: the home government must have some source of revenue, or all its claims to authority are nothing but empty air. People say the colonies were tyrannised over, but I say the home government was tyrannised and tried beyond endurance. It is no more than a matter of history now; we fought the quarrel, and we lost, and the matter is as settled as the Norman Conquest of Britain. But from honest conviction, I have always sided with the British side of the dispute. In my own short, unhappy experience of warfare in my youth, every man in the army, every loyal subject, knew full well that Braddock’s expedition had failed, and disaster had fallen on all of us, because of the selfishness, the rapacity, and the utter remissness of the very colonists we had come to defend against the French. The colonists wanted every favour done for them, and would do nothing in return. They haggled for exorbitant prices with the soldiers who had crossed the Atlantic to protect them; they broke contracts, gave out supplies in niggardly dribbles, and dragged their feet with endless delays until the hour for action was long past, and the disaster came that need never have happened but for their ill will. When the news came of the conquest of Canada, there were shouts of joy across every colony, and ovations for the great British statesman who had planned and won that victory. Monsieur de Vaudreuil was right when he said that the fall of Canada was the very signal for the North American colonies to throw off their allegiance to Great Britain. Lord Chatham, who had done more than any man to win Canada, then turned around and did more than any man in England to encourage the colonies to rebel. Scores of thousands of waverers must have taken heart to resist, because the great Chatham cheered on their mutiny. It was as if a general stood before a rioting regiment and cried “God save the King! Men, you are perfectly right to mutiny!” No wonder one town put up a statue to him, another hung his portrait, and a third hanged the King’s ministers in effigy. The wiseacres of Williamsburg even subscribed to buy a grand portrait of Chatham, painted as a Roman orator speaking in the Forum, his hand pointing directly at the window of Whitehall Palace where Charles I had been beheaded! A very neat little allegory, that, and a charming compliment to a British statesman! Though I hear the portrait was copied from a bust, and Chatham himself never even knew the controversial detail was there.

My home was England, not America or Virginia, and I took – I take still – the English side of that old dispute. My loyalties were always to the old country, where I was now a squire and a citizen of long standing. But I know full well that if my lot had been to plant tobacco and live on the banks of the James River, my opinions would no doubt have been very different. When I visited Harry at his new plantation house, I found him and his wife Fanny as staunch American patriots as we were loyal British. We had our share of words over the dispute, as everyone did in those troubled times, but our arguments were never bitter. Even my new sister-in-law, for all her efforts to stir up strife, could not make us quarrel, though I have no doubt she lectured Harry by the hour behind closed curtains. But we trusted each other far too deeply for Harry’s wifely duty ever to turn him against his own brother. He loved me from the old days when my word was law to him, and he still swore that he and every other Virginian gentleman of his party had no ill will to the Crown. The war had not yet broken out, and men of opposing views still treated each other with courtesy. At public dinners and festivals, everyone ostentatiously drank the health of the King. Every colonial assembly, even as

What perverse quirk of Fate is it that always lands me in the minority? If a bill were tabled to hand this realm over to the Pretender of Rome, or the Grand Turk, and submit all of us to his new faith, it would no doubt pass—for I would be the only soul voting nay.

Back home in Virginia, I found myself out of step with everyone as usual. The Patriots branded me a Tory, as I had never troubled to hide my loyalties; the Tories before long declared me a dangerous Republican. The times were utterly out of joint, cursed spite to match the bard’s old grumble. Ere I had been twelve months on Virginian soil, I ached to return to the banks of the Waveney, but the air hummed with such trouble that I could not leave my mother, a lone widow lady, to face looming war and chaos alone. Nor would she quit the colony in such a hour, and no man of spirit could abandon it either. At Governor Dunmore’s table, over brimming flagons of his plentiful claret, that vow was sworn by dozens of the loyalist gentry, repeated across countless bumpers. *Statue signum, signifer!*—Raise the standard, standard-bearer! We Cavaliers would rally round it, and in those days, the Governor talked like the boldest of brave men.

Of all my Virginian acquaintance, Madam Esmond alone was unshakably consistent. Our local gentry had flocked to Williamsburg for the season, and a great number of them planned to host a grand ball for the Governor’s lady, Lady Dunmore—until news of the Boston Port Bill landed on our shores. Straightway the House of Burgesses passed an indignant protest against Parliament’s measure, and decreed a solemn public fast and humiliation across the colony, with prayers to Heaven to fend off the calamity of civil war. But the invitation to Lady Dunmore had already been extended and accepted, so the stewards agreed the ball would go forward on its appointed night, and they would don sackcloth and ashes three days thereafter for the fast.

“A ball?” scoffed Madam Esmond, when she heard the plan. “I will not attend a feast thrown by rebels who mean to publicly insult his Majesty a week later! I would die first!” She wrote the ball stewards to say that, given the dangerous state of the country, she for one could not in conscience join their entertainment.

What was her surprise, then, when next she ventured out in her sedan chair, to be greeted by cheers from a hundred souls, white and black alike, shouting “Huzzah, Madam!” “Heaven bless your ladyship!” The crowd had mistaken her refusal to attend the ball for a patriotic stand against the Crown. To leave no room for misinterpretation, Madam stuck her head out of the sedan window and cried “God save the King” as loud as her sharp old voice could carry. The crowd took up the cry, shouting it back. *Everybody* cried “God save the King” in those days, no matter what plots they were hatching behind closed doors.

On the night of the ball, my poor Harry, a Burgess and one of the feast’s hosts, donned his old scarlet uniform from General Wolfe’s campaign—the coat he would soon trade for a very different colour—and set off with his wife Fanny. My Lady Warrington and I, being counted as strangers and near-English in the colony, were permitted by Madam to attend the assembly, which she of course absented herself from. I had the honour of dancing a country-dance with the lady of Mount Vernon, whom I found a lively, pretty, and most amiable partner; but when Theo returned home and sang Mrs. Washington’s praises, my mother received her account with the grimmest of scowls. Could not Sir George Warrington have danced with Lady Dunmore or her daughters, or anyone else, she huffed, rather than Mrs. Washington? To be sure, the Colonel thought so well of himself that he no doubt deemed his wife the grandest lady in the room—she remembered him when he was nothing but a road-surveyor earning a guinea a day! There was no measuring the pride of these provincial upstarts, she declared, and no doubt Lord Dunmore’s favour had turned the man’s head entirely. I do not pretend to judge Mr. Washington’s pride; I only know my good mother never could abide him, nor anything that belonged to him.

She was no more pleased with him three days later, when the appointed fast and humiliation came, and he attended the solemn service our new clergyman conducted. She had invited the Reverend Mr. Belman to dinner that day, along with several colonial officials, but the parson excused himself to join the public fast. Madam Esmond tossed her head and said he might do as he liked. She put on a full parade of a feast, lit every window in her house that night when all the rest of Williamsburg was wrapped in darkness and gloom, and begged Mr. Hardy, one of the Governor’s young aides fresh from England, to sing “God Save the King.” The crowd gathered outside in the street listened quietly, thinking it some devotional rite Madam was holding, until she called for “Britons, Strike Home!” The simple young gentleman had barely struck up the tune when a great roar burst from the street, and a large stone, flung from some rebellious hand, plumped straight into the punch-bowl set before me, scattering rum, citrus, and spiced sugar all over our dining room carpets.

My mother did not flinch an inch. I can see her rigid little figure now, standing framed in the open window, head tossed high, frilled arms outstretched against the twinkling starlight, singing in full chorus at the top of her lungs: “Britons, strike home! strike home!” The crowd at the palings hooted and roared, but other voices began to call out: “Silence! For shame! Go back, you rascals!” “Fling more stones, if you dare!” the brave little lady shouted down at them. More missiles might have come, but a party of gentlemen issued from the Raleigh Tavern and pushed through the crowd. “You will not insult a lady,” said a voice I knew well. “Huzza, Colonel! Hurrah, Captain! God bless your honour!” the crowd shouted back, and the disturbance died away.

My mother, protesting the whole ruckus was over, would have made Mr. Hardy sing another song, but he gave a sickly grin and said he really did not care to perform to such accompaniments, and the impromptu concert ended for the night. I am bound to add, though, that some scoundrels returned long after dark, frightened my poor wife nearly out of her wits, and broke every single pane of glass in the front of our house. “Britons, Strike Home!” was a step too far; Madam ought to have contented herself with “God Save the King.”

All across the colony, militia drilled, bullets were cast, ammunition stores were stashed, and clever schemes to thwart royal ordinances were devised and carried out—but still every patriot swore loyalty to the Crown. When I protested, “You are scheming for separation! You are calling down the inevitable wrath of the greatest power on earth!” they always made the same retort: “We mean no separation at all! No man surpasses us in loyalty! We glory in the name of Britons!” The gunpowder was stacked in cellars, the fuse was laid, but Mr. Fawkes still dutifully petitioned King and Parliament, and swore he meant no harm at all.

It is easy now, after we have lost, to look over the map of that great empire we tore ourselves from, and point out all the ways we ought never to have lost it. Long Island ought to have wiped Washington’s ragged army out of existence; he ought never to have emerged from Valley Forge except as a prisoner. The South was ours after the battle of Camden, but for the unthinkable meddling of the Commander-in-Chief in New York, who paralysed the only capable British general to appear all war, and sent him stumbling into that miserable cul-de-sac at Yorktown, from which he could only emerge defeated and a prisoner. Oh, for a week more! a day more, an hour more! When I read over our American campaigns, from their unhappy start to their inglorious end, now that we can see the enemy’s movements and straits as clearly as our own, I fancy a single well-timed advance, a single swift march, would have put men who had no means to withstand us in our power, and turned the whole tide of the struggle. But Heaven willed it so, for the good of both empires, that the great Western Republic should split away from us. And the gallant soldiers who fought on its side, their indomitable chief above all, earned the glory of facing and overcoming not only well-supplied veteran troops hardened to war, but cold, hunger, wretchedness, mutiny, and treason in their own ranks—where all would have fallen to ruin, but for that pure unquenchable flame of patriotism burning in their leader’s breast. What constancy, what magnanimity, what stubborn persistence against the worst fortune! Washington in battle was no better nor braver than hundreds who fought beside or against him—who has not heard the sneers at “Fabius” his factious captains were forever spouting? But Washington as the chief of a nation in arms, navigating clashing parties, calm in the middle of conspiracy, serene against the open foe before him and the darker enemies at his back; Washington breathing order and spirit into troops hungry and in rags, stung by ingratitude but showing no anger, ever ready to forgive; invincible in defeat, magnanimous in victory, and never more sublime than on the day he laid down his victorious sword and retired quietly to his Mount Vernon estate—there is a character to admire and revere, a life without a stain, a fame without a flaw. *Quando invenies parem?* In that larger work on the great war I have planned and partly written, I hope I have done full justice to the character of its greatest leader. [And I trust my recorded opinions of him prove I too can be just and magnanimous to those who bear me no personal favour. For my brother Hal, ever eager to make peace between me and his beloved chief, showed his Excellency some early sheets of my history. General Washington, who read few books and made no pretensions to literary taste, remarked: “If you want my honest opinion, my dear General, Sir George’s projected work, from the sample I have seen, is certain to offend every single party on both sides.” — G. E. W.]

That respect was earned purely by the force of his eminent virtues. In my young days I had little sympathy for the young Mr. Washington, though my brother, far more frank and affectionate than I, was his fast friend from the days they were equals, to later years when the General, as I freely own, stood above most of mankind.

I have spoken of that contrariness in our dispositions which somehow landed Hal and I on the wrong sides of the quarrel that raged for five years, until the mother country was forced to acknowledge her defeat. Hal should have been the Tory, and I the Whig. My theoretical opinions were far more liberal than his; after his marriage especially, he grew what our Indian nabobs call a *Bahadoor*—stately, ceremonious, and quick to demand respect. When Lord Dunmore talked of freeing all enslaved people to draw them to the King’s standard, Hal flew into a rage, swearing he would hang the Governor and all the “Black Guards” he had crimped. “If you gentlemen are fighting for freedom,” I pointed out, “sure the negroes may fight for it too.” Hal roared, shaking his fist: “Infernal villains, if I meet any of them, they shall die by this hand!” My mother agreed the idea of a negro insurrection was the most abominable, parricidal notion ever to spring up in her unhappy country. She was at least more consistent than Hal: she would have all souls, black and white, obedient to the ruling powers, whereas Hal insisted freedom was a right reserved only for white men.

As proof of her argument, Madam Esmond and Hal both pointed to Gumbo, our old family servant. I had freed him years before, as a reward for his unfaltering fidelity to me in our darkest hours, and when he returned to Virginia he was far from a welcome guest in our household. He was free, and the rest of the servants were not: he was a walking centre of unrest. He gave himself no end of airs, bragging of his friends and adventures in “home” (as he called London), and for a while drew all the household staff around him to listen to his tales, like the monkey who had seen the world. Hal’s personal servant Sady, who had visited England of his own will, was not free, and soon grew deeply jealous of Gumbo. The two fought repeated brawls, practicing the boxing and butting tricks they had learned at Marybone Gardens and Hockley-in-the-Hole. Nor was Sady the only jealous one: almost all of my mother’s servants hated Gumbo for his strutting ways, and I am sorry to say his own wife Molly was as resentful as the rest. The other black women would not pardon her for marrying a man who was free; she got no respect, could wield no authority, and came to her mistress with endless complaints of the idleness, knavery, lies, and thefts of the other servants, before finally working herself into a jealous fury over a girl named Dinah, who I heartily hope was as innocent as her namesake, the moonlit visitant of Endymion.

On the matter of morality, Madam Esmond was a very Draconess: an accused person was a guilty person, as far as she was concerned. She laid charges against Gumbo, and he replied to them with asperity, forgetting he was a free gentleman. My mother ordered him to be whipped, and at that the fiery Molly flew at her ladyship, all her wrath over her husband’s supposed infidelity vanishing at the thought of the indignity done him. A full rebellion broke out at Castlewood. I took Gumbo’s side against my mother, and Hal and Fanny sided with her, a rift that did some small good by drawing Madam closer to her younger son and his family. Our little disagreement was soon healed, but it was clear the “Standard of Insurrection” had to be removed from our house, so we determined Gumbo and his lady would sail back to Europe.

God knows my wife and I would gladly have gone with them. Our little boy had sickened and wasted away, laid low by the deadly swamp fever of the low country, and Theo was now great with child, soon to lie in of our son Henry. She would not hear of leaving me, though: her father and Hetty back in England would care for our elder children, and she would not leave my side. I see her still, sitting silent at her worktable, stitching piles of little linen shirts for the voyage, stealing soft, stealthy visits to the children’s bedrooms while they slept, the terrible morning of the parting when the barge carrying the servants and little ones rowed out to the waiting ship, and she stood on the shore with silent tears running down her face. If the Prince of Wales himself had sailed on that voyage, he could not have been better provided for. Where, my lad, is the Tompion watch your grandmother gave you? And how did you survive all the boxes of sweet cakes she stowed away in your cabin?

The same ship that carried our children away returned bearing the Reverend Mr. Hagan and my Lady Maria, who had meekly resigned her rank, and was known in the colony (which would not be a colony very long) only as plain Mrs. Hagan. When I was in favour with Lord Dunmore, a parish living fell vacant in Westmoreland County, and he gave it to our kinsman. They arrived in Virginia just in time to christen our baby boy Henry, and to preach sermons on the gloomy state of the times that Madam Esmond pronounced to be prodigiously fine. My Lady Maria won Madam’s heart entirely by refusing to walk ahead of her at any doorway. “My father, your brother, was an earl, ‘tis true,” she said, “but you know your ladyship is a marquis’s daughter, and I never could dream of taking precedence of you!” Madam grew so fond of her niece that she even allowed Hagan to read plays aloud—including my own humble compositions—and was fairly forced to own there was merit in my tragedy of *Pocahontas*, which our parson delivered with uncommon energy and fire.

Hal and Fanny rarely came to Castlewood or Richmond while the chaplain and his wife were staying with us. Fanny was curt and rude to Maria, giggling strangely in her company, and repeatedly reminding her of her advanced age, to my mother’s vast astonishment. She often asked if there was some hidden quarrel between her niece and her daughter-in-law, but I held my tongue. My heart ached for the meek way the elder lady bore Fanny’s petty persecutions. Fanny loved to torment her in her husband’s presence, and the poor elder woman winced as little as she could under the lash. Once I remonstrated with Madam Harry, and asked her if she had been raised by Red Indians, that she tortured her victims so. “Have I not had enough torture in my own time?” the young lady snapped back, her eyes sharp. “The blows that wound worst are the ones that never are aimed. The people who hate us are rarely the people we have injured.” I thought of little quiet Fanny in our early days, ever smiling, ever eager to run and do all our biddings, and my heart grieved for my poor brother Hal, who had taken this sly, bitter creature into his bosom.

In the days of old British dominion across the Atlantic, one of the quiet uses we made of our American colonies was as a holding ground for all the sinners we had no place for at home. Beyond the convicts and assigned labourers we shipped across the ocean, we unloaded whole droves of scapegraces and disgraced younger sons whose debt, dissipation, and bad behaviour had made England far too hot for them to dwell in. Just as Captain Cook used to hand the native inhabitants of his newly discovered islands stray English livestock and other odd specimens of European civilization, we made a point of sending over all our finest black sheep to browse the colonial pastures as best they could, and propagate their rare, precious breed.

I must own I bore a little guilt for this practice myself, having gone out of my way to secure a living in America for the worthy Hagan, husband to my kinswoman Maria. At the very least I was guilty in that, for we could find no employment for him in England, we were glad to pack him off to Virginia and hand him a colonial pulpit-cushion to thump from the height of a parish. To his credit, he bore himself there as a brave, honest gentleman, doing his full duty by his congregation and his king, and doing no small credit to my small act of patronage. My wife Theo would always urge this fact whenever I confessed my scruples on the matter, proving as was her wont that my conduct on this, as on all other subjects, sprang from the highest possible moral principle. But would I ever have granted Hagan the family living at home, and selected him and his wife to minister to our own parish? I fear not. I never once doubted our cousin Maria’s sincere repentance, but I will admit I was secretly glad when she went to work it out far from polite society in the wilderness. I say this openly, acknowledging my own foolish pride and error. Twice when I needed them most, that kind Maria aided me with steady sympathy and unwavering friendship. She bore her own hardships bravely, and soothed the distresses of others with a devotion no one could fault. And yet I, and some of my family (though never Theo), would look down on her. Shame, shame on our foolish, cruel pride!

Poor Lady Maria was far from the only member of our family we packed off to the American wilderness to be rid of them. After borrowing, lying, and cheating every last person he could reach at home until no one would lend him a penny, or let him run a scam, the Honourable William Esmond, Esquire, was granted a cushioned sinecure in New York. His noble elder brother and his royal master alike heartily hoped they would never set eyes on him again. When the first troubles broke out across the colonies, we began to hear tales of the man and his misdeeds in his new home. Lies and mischief ran ahead of him wherever he travelled. My Lord Dunmore sent word to me that Will was declaring publicly all across New York that the Castlewood estate was only held by our family at his brother’s pleasure: that his father, out of some faint regard for Madam Esmond, his lordship’s half-sister, had granted her the property only for her lifetime, and that he, William, was currently in negotiations with the present Lord Castlewood to buy the full reversion of the estate!

We held the full original deed of gift locked in our strongroom at Castlewood, and it had been properly registered in due legal form at Williamsburg, so we had no fear of losing our home over the lie. But the very audacity of the claim spoke volumes, and Hal and I swore that the first time we ever met Mr. William face to face, we would force him to retract that pretty story outright. I need scarcely describe the full force of Madam Esmond’s fury when she heard the tale. “What? My father, the Marquis of Esmond, was a liar, and I am a cheat, am I?” my mother cried. “He will steal my son’s property the moment I am dead, will he?” She was for writing not just to Lord Castlewood in England, but to his Majesty himself at St James’s, and I only dissuaded her by assuring her that Will’s lies were notorious to every single person who knew him, and no one could possibly expect him to be inconsistent enough, in our case, to tell the truth.

Not long after, we heard he had become one of the loudest Loyalist firebrands in New York, first serving as Captain and then as Major of a volunteer corps that sent glowing addresses out to all the well-disposed gentlemen across the colonies, announcing their full readiness to die for the mother country.

Back in Williamsburg, we found we could not stay in our rented house for all the broken windows left by rioters, so we nailed up the shutters of that ill-starred mansion, and Madam Esmond left the little colonial capital behind, my whole family returning to Richmond, which had been emptied of the members of the recently dissolved Assembly. Captain Hal and his wife returned early to their plantation, and I, not a little vexed by the direction events were taking, split my days between my own household and that of the Governor, who made a great show of being eager for my advice and company. Strong political divides ran through every circle, but there was still no open personal quarrel between the opposing sides. Even after the Assembly was dissolved and its members adjourned to a tavern, where they held that famous meeting where I believe the very idea of a unified congress of all the colonies was first floated, the most vocal opposition leaders remained on friendly terms with his Excellency, dined at his table, and joined him on pleasure rides and excursions. When the session ended, the gentry all rode home to their respective counties and held local meetings; as the assemblies of nearly every other colony had also been abruptly dissolved, it was agreed across the board that a general continental congress must be called. Philadelphia, the largest and most important city on the continent, was chosen as the meeting place, and those famous conferences began: the angry, tense preface to a full-scale war. We were still singing *God Save the King*, still sending humble petitions to the throne, but the air hummed with danger.

I rode out one day to visit my brother Harry at Fanny’s Mount, his new plantation that lay not far from our own Castlewood, with the Rappahannock River running between the two properties, close to the banks of the Mattaponey. Harry rode out on business early that morning, so in the afternoon I decided to take a ride myself, and one of his grooms told me his master had headed towards Willis’s Ordinary. Thinking no harm at all, I set off in that direction to find him. I had just ridden out of the trees into a wide, sunlit clearing not far from Willis’s when I came across Captain Hal on horseback, surrounded by some three-and-thirty countrymen, armed with every sort of weapon you could imagine: pikes, scythe blades lashed to wooden poles, old fowling pieces, and worn muskets. Hal, with two spry young fellows acting as junior officers under him, was putting the whole ragtag group through drill.

A confused, guilty look crossed Hal’s face the moment he saw me. “Present arms!” he barked, and the whole makeshift regiment stumbled through the salute as best they could. “Captain Cade, this is my brother, Sir George Warrington.”

“As a relation of yours, Colonel, the gentleman is more than welcome,” the man addressed as Captain said, holding out a calloused hand to shake mine.

“And — and a true friend to Virginia,” Hal added, his face flushing bright red.

“Thank you for that, gentlemen, please God it is true,” I said, at which the whole ragged little regiment gave a hearty cheer for the Colonel and his brother.

When drill was over, the officers and the men were all eager to adjourn to Willis’s Ordinary for drinks, but Colonel Hal told them he could not stop for refreshment that afternoon, and we trotted away together towards his house.

“So Hal, the cat’s well and truly out of the bag,” I said.

He gave me a hard, determined look. “I’d say there are far wilder cats still waiting to claw their way out. This was always bound to happen, George. And — don’t tell Madam, will you?”

“Good God!” I cried. “Do you truly mean that you and these fellows I saw out there are going to make war against the greatest nation on earth, with the finest, best-trained army in the world?”

“I reckon we’re going to get one awful whipping, that’s the plain truth,” Hal said. “But then, George,” he added, with that sweet, kind smile of his, “we’re young. A whipping or two never hurt any lad, did it? Isn’t that right, old Dolly?” He gave his shaggy old hunting hound, trotting at his horse’s heels, a playful tap of his whip.

I did not try to press our British Loyalist arguments on him then — I had made that case dozens of times before, to no avail. He always brushed my reasons aside, saying, “It’s all very well for you, brother. You speak as an Englishman, and you cast your lot with your country. I cast mine with mine.” There was no arguing that point, I admitted. All two sides could do then was fight it out, and the side that won got to say what was right. Who was right in the old civil wars a century before? King or Parliament? The side that came out on top was right, and the Parliamentary victory was far more humane than the Cavalier triumph would ever have been. Nay, even as a Loyalist, I could not help the strange feeling that if we Tories won the day in America, the triumph would be so bloody and terrible, strung full of gallows ropes and scaffolds and noble heads laid low, that I secretly wanted the Whigs to win.

My brother Hal, who would soon distinguish himself greatly in command of his regiment, never allowed an unkind word to be spoken against the enemy he fought. “The officers of the British army are gentlemen,” he would say. “At least, they have not changed much since the days I served under them. You may find scoundrels and ruffians amongst the King’s troops — I daresay we could find just as many amongst our own lot. Our business is to beat his Majesty’s forces, not to slander them. Any rascal can call names.” From a nickname Mr. Lee gave him that many of his rough backcountry troopers did not fully understand, Harry would soon be known across the Continental Army as “Chevaleer Baird,” a knight truly without fear and without reproach.

When I pressed him how his ragtag militia could ever hope to beat regulars, Hal had a steady answer. “They will beat them, Mr. George. That is exactly what they will do.”

“Great heavens!” I cried. “If you had your old company of the 67th Foot regulars under your command, would you not charge straight at five hundred such men and cut them to pieces without a second thought?”

“With my old company of the 67th, I would go anywhere,” Hal said. “And I agree with you, at this moment I know far more about soldiering than any of these lads. But you put me on that open clearing you just found us on, give me half a dozen of my men with rifles posted in the woods all around the edge of it — who do you think wins, George? You were Aide-de-Camp to General Braddock. You know the answer better than any man alive.”

There was no arguing with that level of quiet determination. “You know exactly where my loyalties lie, Hal,” I said. “And now that I have stumbled across you drilling your militia, I have a duty to report what I saw to the Governor.”

“Of course you must,” he said, easily. “You saw the local county militia out for drill. You will see just the same sight in every colony from here to the St Lawrence River, all the way down to Georgia. Since I’m an old regular soldier, they elected me their Colonel. What could be more natural? Come on, brother, let us trot on. Dinner will be on the table soon, and Mrs. Fanny hates to be kept waiting.”

We rode up to his house, which stood open as all Virginian gentlemen’s houses did in those days, where every friend, neighbour, stranger and traveller was guaranteed a warm welcome.

“So, Mrs. Fanny,” I said, when we walked in. “I have found out what game my brother has been playing out of doors.”

“I trust the Colonel will have all the sport he deserves before long,” she said, tossing her head with a bright, defiant smile. My own wife still thought Harry had been out hunting all afternoon, and I did not have the heart to undeceive her, even as the heavy shadow of coming war settled soft and dark over all of us.

When my visit to my brother Harry drew to its close, and my wife Theo and our young child had returned to our maternal home outside Richmond, I made haste to ride out to the Royal Governor’s country seat a few miles from Williamsburg, to confer with him on the open war preparations spreading not just across Virginia, but every colony we had word from.

Men whose names would soon be known the world over as founding figures of a new nation had just been named Virginia’s delegates to the upcoming General Congress in Philadelphia. In Massachusetts, Royal troops and colonial militiamen stood face to face, almost on the brink of open fighting; Maryland and Pennsylvania still held a reputation for far greater loyalty to the Crown, while the Carolinas and Georgia, it was said, counted staunch adherents to the mother country in the vast majority of their populations. No one imagined Virginia, proud of its ancient Cavalier lineage, would ever abandon its long tradition of loyalty. We had barely a handful of regular troops in the province, but crowds of loud, confident Loyalists swarmed the Governor’s household, all eager for the moment they could draw their swords and scatter the rascally rebels before them.

In every one of these assemblies, I was forced to hear endless harsh condemnations of my poor Harry. All agreed, not entirely without reason, that his wife Fanny had led him to adopt the strident anti-British opinions he had begun to declare openly of late. Worse, they claimed he was hopelessly infatuated with the gentleman of Mount Vernon, whose views Harry had always followed, and who was daily committing himself further to the desperate, dreadful path of resistance. “This is the man your Excellency favoured!” the Governor’s courtiers would cry. “The man you trusted, who enjoyed your hospitality over and over again!”
It was impossible to deny much of this was true, though what the hot-headed Loyalists called treachery was in fact proof of Mr. Washington and his compatriots’ long, earnest desire not to cast off their allegiance to the Crown, but to exhaust every last possible chance for reconciliation before risking the terrible alternative of full revolt and separation.
Let traitors arm, let villains draw the parricidal sword, they cried: they would stay faithful. England’s unconquerable power would crush the misguided, ungrateful provinces and drag them back to obedience. How loudly we cheered King George’s health after our banquets! We would die defending his rights, they vowed: we would invite a prince of his royal house to cross the Atlantic and rule his ancient Virginian dominions.

In recognition of my own and my excellent mother’s long record of loyalty, they insisted Harry’s delinquent conduct ought to be forgiven. Was it not still possible to win him over with the offer of a fine command? Would I not intercede with him, who everyone knew held such great influence over his choices?
Our Williamsburg councils swung wildly between extremes: one hour exalted and triumphant, the next seething with rage at the rebels, full of anxious hope for reinforcements from home, then sinking into doubt, distrust, and gloomy dread.
I promised I would speak to Harry. I wrote to him, I admit, with very little hope of success, repeating and reinforcing the same arguments I had laid out to him in our many long talks before. My mother also threw the full weight of her authority behind the cause, though I expected very little good to come of that. She assailed Harry, as was her habit, with carefully selected Scripture texts she believed backed her position, threatening him with divine punishment for disobeying the powers ordained by God. She pointed to my example as the elder son, and repeatedly hinted that he was entirely under his wife’s thumb — the very worst possible argument she could have chosen for that sort of debate. She never showed me the letter she sent him, likely knowing I would protest the ferocity of some of her phrasing, but she did let me read his reply, from which I could easily guess the full tenor of her case. To my great surprise, Harry had countered every one of her Biblical citations with a dozen of his own, in a neat, temperate, even elegant letter I had believed only his wife Fanny was capable of writing. It turned out he had enlisted the help of Mr. Belman, the New Richmond clergyman who had taken a firm Whig stance, and who was busy preaching and publishing anti-Tory sermons that routinely out-argued our own chaplain, Hagan.

My exhortations to Harry fared no better than our mother’s. He never replied to my letters. Badgered further by the Governor’s loyal circle, I made the imprudent mistake of writing to say I would visit him at Fanny’s Mount at the end of the week. When I arrived, however, only Fanny was at home. She greeted me with perfect cordiality, but informed me Harry had ridden far out towards the Blue Mountains to inspect a herd of fine horses, and would be gone indefinitely — she could not say when he would return.
I knew then there was no hope left.
“My dear,” I said to her, “as far as I can read the signs of the times, the powder train that has been laid these past years will soon have a match set to it. Harry is riding far away, and God alone knows what end he rides towards.”
“The Lord prosper the righteous cause, Sir George,” she said.
“Amen, with all my heart. You and he speak as Americans. I speak as an Englishman. Tell him from me that when anything in the course of nature befalls our mother, I have more than enough for myself and my family in England, and I shall cede every inch of our Virginian land to him entirely.”
“You do not mean that, George?” she cried, her eyes brightening. “Of course it is only right and fair — why should you, who are only older by an hour, have everything? A palace and lands in England, the plantation here, the family title, and children, and poor Harry nothing? But it is generous of you, all the same — handsome and proper, and I never expected it of you. You do not take after your mother in this, Sir George, not a bit. Give my love to sister Theo!” She turned her cheek to me to kiss, before I mounted my horse to ride away from her door. With a woman like Fanny at his side, how could I ever have hoped to turn my brother back to our side?

I returned to the Governor to report my total failure, and we agreed it was high time to arm in earnest, to prepare for the shock that was surely coming. His Excellency and his whole circle of officials were far more agitated than I thought necessary, savagely abusing the wicked Whigs at every turn and roaring “Old England for ever!” at the top of their lungs, all equally eager for the day they could meet their adversaries face to face and ride the rebel forces straight into the dust.
I left his lordship with the formal thanks of the Council, and a commission to do my utmost to raise a company of men in defence of the Crown. This was the origin of the corps later known as the Westmoreland Defenders, of which I had the honour to be named Colonel, tasked to lead them when they took the field. We announced the formation in the Government Gazette, and filled our officer ranks without difficulty — but the recruits, it must be said, were slow to enlist, and even quicker to desert. Our chaplain Hagan volunteered for the post at once. My mother sewed and presented our regimental colours, and travelled around the countryside drumming up volunteers, but the most zealous recruiter of all was my old tutor, little Mr. Dempster, who had fought on the Jacobite side in Scotland as a boy. He travelled south specifically to the Carolinas, to recruit among the descendants of his banished comrades who had worn the white cockade of Prince Charlie, and who still remained the most fiercely loyal to the Crown of all the colonies’ inhabitants.

Harry’s “horse buying expedition” did not stop at the Blue Mountains. He travelled on to Annapolis, then Baltimore, and then to Philadelphia, where the Second General Congress was in session, attended by the same Virginian delegates we had sent the year before. Meanwhile, every almanac of the time records what happened next: Lexington, the first shots of the war that would end in the colonies’ independence. The colonists still protested their loyalty to King George, but declared their determination to die free rather than submit. Twenty thousand armed militiamen assembled outside Boston, carrying arms and artillery they had seized from government stores. Mr. Arnold began the famous, doomed career for which he would be remembered, by staging a daring, almost burglar’s raid to capture two undefended royal forts. Three generals fresh out of London, with a huge reinforcement of regular troops, were sailing to lift General Gage out of his precarious position in Boston.
The two armies soon clashed, and the British high command launched their campaign of “conquest and pacification” in the colonies with the glorious blunder of Breed’s Hill. They fortified their position afterwards, too weakened to press for more “victories” over the rebels, and the two armies settled down to watch each other while Congress deliberated in Philadelphia over who should take command of the combined colonial forces. We all know now who that fortunate choice fell on. One of the Virginian regiments that marched north to join the new Commander-in-Chief was led by Henry Esmond Warrington, late a Captain in his Majesty’s service, and riding at his side was his brave little wife, whose courage we would hear many stories of in the years that followed. For my part, I was glad Fanny had left Virginia: if she had stayed after Harry’s departure, my mother would inevitably have marched over to her house to pick a fight, and I was thankful that particular terrible domestic clash of civil war was spared our family.

Nearly all the farmers and country folk around us flocked to join the new northern rebel army, and the whole colony was flattered that a Virginian gentleman had been chosen for the highest military post. The news of bloodshed at Lexington sent a thrill of wrath and fury through every province, and the colonists shouted denunciations of the cruel, wanton brutality of the British invaders. The invaders, of course, were only doing their duty, trying to recover government property seized by armed rebels — but no one stopped to weigh their words once they had made up their minds to be angry. The colonists had picked their side, and with a natural, fiery ardour, they were determined to test their strength against the braggart, domineering mother country. Breed’s Hill became a mythic mountain, visible to every man on the North American continent, with Liberty, Victory, and Glory blazing on its summit. The red-coated regulars, everyone saw, could be resisted by farmers and ploughmen. The famous British officers could be outgeneralled by doctors, lawyers, and ordinary civilians! Granted that Britons could conquer the whole world, their children across the Atlantic were just as capable of conquering Britons!
I do not know which of the two sides deserves the greater prize for bravery, or for vainglory. We laugh at our French neighbours for their boasting and gasconading, but for steady self-esteem and indomitable confidence in their own courage, greatness, and magnanimity, no one can match the Britons — except their children across the Atlantic.

The vast majority of people in our neighbourhood threw their lot in with the rebel cause, and the ranks of Sir George Warrington’s Westmoreland Defenders dwindled away to almost nothing, not just after the news of the northern battles, but because of the behaviour of our Royal Governor, whose conduct enraged none so much as his own loyal partisans across the colony. Everyone had agreed, over countless meetings and thousands of bumper toasts, that he would plant the King’s standard and summon every loyal gentleman to rally around it. I could name dozens of gentlemen now serving as smug officers of the United States government, whom I have heard hiccup out prayers that they might die wrapped in the folds of the royal flag, or roar challenges to the absent traitors who had run off to join the rebel army. But let bygones be bygones.
This much is public history, however: his lordship, our Scottish peer, the Sovereign’s representative in the Old Dominion, who had loudly invited every loyal subject to rally to the King’s standard, was the first man to stuff the flag in his pocket and flee to his ships, out of all reach of danger. He would not leave the safety of their decks, save to act like a pirate under cover of midnight to burn and destroy colonial property.
All us loyal gentlemen were left stranded on shore, fully committed to the royal cause, and placed in far greater danger than ever before, all thanks to the cowardice and cruelty of the man who should have been our leader.

It was the start of June, our orchards and gardens all blooming thick with summer blossoms. A week earlier, I had been in Williamsburg, exchanging compliments with his Excellency, devising plans for future moves to push back the rebellion, shaking his hand heartily at parting, with vincere aut mori — conquer or die — the last words on all our lips. Our little family was gathered at our Richmond house, talking daily over the latest news from the north, and the constant bickering between the colonial Assembly and his Excellency, when our chaplain Hagan came rushing into the parlour.
“Have you heard the news of the Governor?” he gasped.
“Has he dissolved the Assembly again? Put that scoundrel Patrick Henry in irons?” my mother asked.
“No such thing! His lordship, his lady, and all their family snuck out of the Palace in the dead of night. They are on board a man-of-war anchored off York, from which he sent a dispatch to the Assembly begging them to keep sitting, and announcing he only left Government House out of fear of the people’s fury.”

What was to become of the sheep, when their shepherd had run away? No entreaties were more pathetic than those from the members of the House of Assembly, who guaranteed the Governor full personal safety if he would only come ashore, and implored him to appear before them even just to pass routine bills and conduct necessary business. He refused. The man-of-war was now his seat of government, and he ordered the Assembly to come out to the ship to wait on him. That was “planting the King’s standard”, in very deed. The Governor had abandoned us, and the Assembly was forced to take over governing in his stead. Crowds of people, including dozens of enslaved people who had run away from local plantations, flocked out to join the fugitive Viceroy on his ships. He and his new raiding parties landed under cover of darkness to burn and seize property, matching the most lawless of the rebels in their eagerness for plunder. He not only invited runaway enslaved people to join his ranks, but sent envoys to Indigenous communities to beg them to take up arms on the Crown’s behalf. Whenever he did land, it was only to burn and destroy: and when the colonists resisted, as they did at Norfolk and Hampton, he would retreat straight back to the safety of his ships.

Even my mother, after this miserable flight of our supposed leader, was shocked by the state of affairs, and began to doubt the rebellion would be crushed quickly. Arming the enslaved population was, in her view, the most cowardly blow of all. Many of the loyal gentry were ruined, robbed of their only livelihoods. A score of our own enslaved hands from Richmond and Castlewood deserted to join the Governor’s fleet; not all of them, though some, were killed, and a couple were hanged by rebel forces for plunder they committed while serving in his lordship’s precious army.
But though her property was wantonly damaged, and the King’s chief representative in the colony had proven a complete imbecile, Madam Esmond had no intention of abandoning the cause of Royalty and Honour. My good mother was never more grandly dignified, loudly and enthusiastically loyal, than after she heard of the Governor’s lamentable defection. The local population, most of whom disagreed fiercely with her politics, listened to her speeches without unkindness. Her oddities were well known across the whole province, and I fear many young wags were in the habit of teasing her, drawing out her long stories about the Marquis, her father, and the splendours of the Esmond family. But along with her oddities, everyone remembered her charity and kindness, and many a “rebel”, as she called them, held a quiet soft spot for the pompous little Tory lady.

As for me, the Colonel of the Westmoreland Defenders, my command vanished entirely after our chief’s outrageous conduct — but I escaped very serious danger that would have befallen me and my family because I had the courage to confront Lord Dunmore on his own ship, after he had burned the stores at Hampton and issued his proclamation inviting the enslaved to rally to his standard. I remonstrated with him sharply over both decisions, begging him to return to Williamsburg, where hundreds, thousands of us, would defend him to the very last. I spoke so freely, and my behaviour made my contempt for his conduct so obvious, that his lordship flew into a rage, called me a rebel just like all the rest of them, and ordered me arrested on the spot. In my capacity as a militia officer, I demanded an immediate court martial, and turned to the two other officers who had witnessed our altercation, asking them to record every word that had passed between his lordship and me. These gentlemen shared my low opinion of the Governor’s conduct, and our interview ended with me walking back ashore entirely unguarded.
The story leaked out among the Whig gentry, and grew in the telling. I had spoken my mind manfully to the tyrannical Governor, it was said — no Whig could have spoken more bold, liberal sentiments. When riots broke out in Richmond, and most remaining Loyalists fled to the ships for fear for their lives, my mother’s property and house were never endangered, nor any member of our family insulted. We were still in that early stage of the conflict where many still fondly hoped reconciliation with England might be possible. “Ah! If all Tories were like you,” one leading Whig gentleman once said to me, “we and the government at home would soon come to terms again.”
This was all before the famous Fourth of July, and the Declaration that made any reconciliation impossible. Once parties grew far more rancorous, far less creditable motives were assigned to my conduct, and it was said I was a cunning old fox who had chosen to be a moderate liberal Tory only to hold onto my family estates no matter who won the war. That, I must say, remains the prevailing opinion of my humble conduct in very high circles back in England, where everyone has long assumed my actions through the unhappy conflict were guided purely by my profound regard for my own interests.
Only two or three people in the world knew I had no mercenary motives for the path I chose — I had never told my mother of my resolution to cede all my life interest in our Virginian property

What use was there in being a Colonel without a regiment? The Governor and Council who had paraded so much pomp and ceremony to thank me for my commission, to endow me with that empty honour, were long gone from sight: skulking aboard their ships offshore, making occasional forays to commit piracy and arson on the undefended shore. My Lord Dunmore’s black allies had turned the very people he claimed to protect against him, and worse still, we had word he had sent envoys south to court the Indigenous nations of the interior, promising them plunder if they swept down on our settlements and tomahawked us all back into “good behaviour.” “And these are the allies we choose to fight our own kinsmen!” I said to my mother one evening, our faces grim as we exchanged looks, and my mind darted back to that ghastly, sharp memory from Braddock’s Field: the painted warrior whose glare had been inches from my own, his knife pressed to my throat before Florac struck him down mid-strike.
We fortified Castlewood as best we could, stacking furniture against lower windows, posting nightly watches, but the truth was we feared the raiding parties of Natives and freed enslaved fighters far more than the local rebel militia. I never saw my mother lose her courage but once before that night: she had broken down recounting the details of my father’s death in an Indigenous raid more than forty years prior. So when a group of travelers stumbled past the house after dark one evening, no amount of reasoning could convince her they were not raiders. She sank straight to her knees, hands clasped, crying out “Lord have mercy on us! The Indians— the Indians!”
In the end, Lord Dunmore’s Black allies scattered back to his ships or vanished to find pay and plunder elsewhere, and the fearsome painted war parties from the South never materialized. Even so, I could not look at my mother’s grey head, my wife’s soft brown hair, or our little boy’s bright golden ringlets without a cold, sharp pang of dread, thinking they might fall victim to this brutal, unregulated ruffian’s war. And we of the Royal cause were the ones who had unleashed these horrors, who had enlisted these cruel allies! If I did not hate the silliness of men who claim to read the direct finger of Providence in every small event, I would say our choice to hire German mercenaries and rouse Indigenous nations to fight for us brought its own retribution. The Provincials cut the mercenaries down easily whenever they met them, and the triumph of beating those brutal foreign troops lifted the Continental army’s spirit higher than any victory over regular British soldiers could have. Worse still, the murder of a single young woman, Miss McCrea, by half a dozen drunken Natives did more to turn public sympathy against the Crown than the loss of a dozen pitched battles or the destruction of whole regiments.
Once the Native panic passed, Madam Esmond’s courage returned in full, and she grew justly, seriously uneasy at the danger my presence at Castlewood put my family in.
“What harm can they do me, a poor old woman living alone?” she would argue. “I have one son a colonel with no regiment, and another with two hundred Continentals at his back in Mr. Washington’s camp. If the Royalists ride through, they will spare me for your sake. If the rebels come, Harry’s name will be my passport. I will not have your delicate wife and this sweet little baby here, adding risk to all of us. You must send them away to Boston or New York. Do not talk of staying to defend me! No one would dream of hurting a harmless old widow. If the rebels break in, I will hide behind Fanny’s petticoats, and I will be far safer with no able-bodied Loyalist gentlemen loitering about the house making trouble.”
She spoke partly out of practical good sense, but far more out of a quiet determination to send me and my family out of harm’s way. For all the danger, she would never leave the land where her father was buried, the ground she herself had been born on. She lived, you might say, looking backwards. She had welcomed the new generation, blessed them, and bid them safe farewell. She belonged entirely to the past, to old days and half-forgotten memories no one else could touch.
We were still debating the journey to Boston when the news arrived: the British had evacuated that unlucky city entirely. They had never once dared to storm Mr. Washington’s camp at Cambridge, even when he lay there for months with almost no gunpowder, completely at their mercy. They had waited, instead, until he procured enough ammunition to seize and fortify Dorchester Heights, the high ground that overlooked the entire town, forcing the whole British army and every loyalist resident to beat a hasty retreat to their ships. That the King’s troops won the battle of Bunker’s Hill is as certain as the fact that we beat the French at Blenheim—but after that day, our commanders seemed perpetually terrified of storming entrenched Continentals. Why else would they hesitate for six months, from July to March, to strike an enemy almost completely defenceless? Why the dithering at Long Island, when the whole Continental army was well within our grasp? Why that absurd timorousness of General Howe’s before Valley Forge, where the ragged, starving, sick remnants of the Continental force could barely man their lines, while a great, fresh, fully provisioned British army sat just out of striking distance?
As the hopes and fears of both sides rose and fell, the shifting tone of the partisans around us was impossible to miss. When news of the Boston evacuation reached the Virginia countryside, every small local Whig stopped by Madam Esmond’s door to bow politely and advise her to submit quickly to the new government. She did not flaunt her Loyalist flag in public faces as openly as she once had, but she never wavered from her loyalty. Poor brave Parson Hagan prayed for the Royal Family every morning and night at our private household services, and on Sundays any neighbor was welcome to attend, where my mother acted as a boisterous, emphatic clerk, and the prayer for the High Court of Parliament under our most religious and gracious King was delivered with ringing, unmistakeable defiance.
Hagan was a parson without a living, just as I was a Militia Colonel without a regiment. He had kept praying loudly for King George in Williamsburg long after Governor Dunmore had run away to his ships—until one Sunday he arrived at his church to find a corporal’s guard posted at the door. They told him the Committee of Safety had installed a new minister in his place, and he would do well to keep his tongue quiet. Hagan, ever fond of grand tragic speeches, told them to lead him before their chiefs, and so he was marched all the way through the streets to the Capitol, a jeering mob of white and Black idlers tugging at the hem of his gown the whole way. He got his audience with Patrick Henry and the new state officers, who he called “the robbers in their den.” He was all ready to deliver a grand heroic martyr’s speech, the sort of speech that would sound far better to a crowd watching him be dragged off to jail, but Mr. Henry had no intention of giving him that satisfaction. He kept Hagan waiting in an antechamber for three hours with a crowd of enslaved servants, and when Hagan finally marched into his office with his chin held high and began “Sir, by what authority am I, a minister of the—” Henry cut him off short. “Mr. Hagan, I am too busy to listen to speeches. And as for King George, he has no more authority in this country than King Nebuchadnezzar. Mind that, and hold your tongue if you please! Stick to King John and King Macbeth, sir, and if you send round benefit tickets, the whole Assembly will come and hear you. Did you ever see Mr. Hagan perform on the London stage when you were there, General?” He turned to General Lee, Washington’s second in command, who had come to Virginia on state business, and before Hagan could protest, he was bustled out of the room, red-faced and near tears with humiliation. After that, we thought it best to move the worthy parson out of the city and keep his ministrations confined to our small private congregation at Castlewood.
The new revolutionary government had flattered and bribed many of our leading Virginia gentry with the highest civil and military posts, men who might well have stayed loyal to the Crown if the British government had not behaved so outrageously foolishly, and made a real stand against the rising rebellion. Even so, though we Loyalists were gagged and muzzled, though the Capitol was in Whig hands, and most of our vaunted loyalist recruit regiments were no more real than Falstaff’s ragtag band, the faithful kept in secret communication across the whole colony. We did not rise up, many of us did run away, and many more of our people, when dragged before Committees of Safety or local justices, put on a great show of being Republican, vowing perdition to kings and nobles if it would keep them safe. But we all knew each other, perfectly well. As the tides of war shifted, we hid our loyalties, showed them, half-showed them, or even apostatised for a little while and shouted “Down with King George!” when we had to. Our enslaved servants carried messages and tokens from house to house, and endless quiet underhand plots were hatched in the dark where no prying Whig eyes could see. When the fighting is done, the neutrals all rush to join the winning side, shouting their support as loud as the most ardent patriots. No one counts the runaways. Will any man tell me that the signers and ardent supporters of the Declaration of Independence were not a minority of the nation, and that that minority did not win?
We had word that a part of the British army defeated at Boston was about to launch a major southern expedition, and the Loyalists of Virginia rested all their greatest hopes on its success. I, for one, was eager to move as soon as there was a chance for real action, so I made contact with ex-Governor Martin of North Carolina, and arranged to meet him with three or four other Virginia gentlemen—all officers of that fine Loyalist corps we were still waiting to recruit privates for. We made no particular secret of our departure from Castlewood. The new Congress government was still not strong enough to tyrannize over gentry of doubtful loyalties, and in our southern fashion, it was perfectly normal for a gentleman and his family to visit friends for months at a time. My wife, our infant, and a small retinue of servants took our leave of Madam Esmond, ostensibly to pay visits to neighboring plantations. We moved from friend’s house to friend’s house, leisurely, until we reached Wilmington, North Carolina, the port where we were supposed to meet the coming British relief force.
Before we arrived, the Loyalist Carolinians had already risen in arms, but their clashes with the Whig militia had gone badly. The poor Highlanders who fought for King George now were no luckier than the Highlanders who had drawn their swords against him on their own native soil, decades prior. We reached Wilmington at the end of May, to find Admiral Parker’s whole squadron anchored there, with General Clinton and five full British regiments aboard, bound for a landing at Charleston.
I presented myself to the General immediately, and when he saw that my “regiment” consisted of Lady Warrington, our nursing infant, and three Black servants, he gave me a very grim welcome indeed. But Captain Horner of the frigate *Sphinx*, who had served on the Jamaica station and had received many kindnesses from my father-in-law General Lambert, heard that my wife was the General’s daughter, and welcomed her aboard at once, giving up his own best cabin for our use. So we were refugees, just like my Lord Dunmore—we had waved our flag proudly, then tucked it away in our pockets and slipped out the back door. We sailed quickly from Wilmington for Charleston, and during the voyage and our long wait in the harbor before the assault, I got to know Mr. Clinton far better, and the acquaintance grew into a lasting friendship. It was the King’s birthday when we sailed into the river, and we all agreed it was a glorious day to launch our expedition.
The attack did not commence for several days after, and I will spare you all the overwrought scenes of parting between my Penelope and her Hector, before I climbed down the ship’s side into the landing boats. For one thing, Hector was perfectly well, a little gouty but unharmed, and no rascal of a Pyrrhus was there to carry his wife off. And in times of war and chaos, scenes of grief, terror, and parting play out every single hour. I can still see my wife’s gentle face peeking over the bulwark as we pulled away, and the little smile of our baby in her arms. Old memories, yes! Captain Miles, my boy, you have no taste for poetry, so you have forgotten the verses in Mr. Pope’s Homer that describe a young son waving his father off to battle, but your mother read them to you a hundred times as a boy, and she still keeps the steel gorget I wore that day tucked in the back of her dressing box.
My second attempt at fighting was no luckier than my first. We came back to our ships that evening thoroughly beaten. That madcap Charles Lee, the same man who had faced Clinton at Boston, now met him at Charleston, and he and his gallant garrison put up a brilliant, completely successful defence. The fort on Sullivan’s Island we attacked was a nut we could not crack. The fire from all our frigates could not pound through its soft palmetto walls, and the shallow creek we had planned to wade through to storm the fort was far deeper than our maps had told us, as Sir Henry and his leading officers found out when they waded in, chest-deep in the cold water, the first to charge. I had braved death by gunshot, by drowning, by the risk of catching my death of cold, many times before I stumbled back to the boats and returned to my wife. Our frigate ran aground for a time, and while we struggled to free it, the enemy cannonaded us mercilessly until we floated free of the bank.
A small incident in the middle of that disastrous battle sparked the close friendship that bound me to Sir Harry Clinton for all the rest of the war I spent with the Royal army. Men may argue all they like about his abilities as a commanding officer, and I will not speak ill of a man I respect and admire with all my heart. But of his personal courage and bearing there can be no doubt. He was always the first to charge, whether at Bunker’s Hill leading the rallied troops to carry the Continental lines, here outside Sullivan’s Fort, or a year later at Fort Washington, where he charged up the hillside with the regimental standard in his hand, the first man through the fort’s gates.
We were pushing off in our boats to force a path to the fort, hoping our own gunfire had deepened the channel enough to let us wade through, when a well-aimed shot struck the boat right beside ours. It knocked three quarters of its crew out of action instantly, killing the officer steering and tearing the flag right out of his hands. I could not help crying out “Bravo! Well aimed!” for no set of ninepins ever went down as helplessly as those poor fellows did before that round shot. The General turned to me, his face grim. “Sir! The behaviour of the enemy seems to please you!” “I am pleased, sir,” I answered, “that my countrymen over there fight as well as any Englishman should.” We floundered on towards the fort under constant fire from small arms and cannon, until we found the water rising higher and higher, up to our breasts, and had no choice but to turn our boats back and pull out of harm’s way. Afterwards, Sir Henry came aboard the *Sphinx* to call on my Lady Warrington, and was most gracious to her, joking endlessly about the author of this memoir, whom he teasingly described as a rebel at heart.
I pray my children will never live to see, or take part in, a great revolution like the one currently tearing apart our poor neighbors in France. Save for a very few people, the actors in these grand tragedies do not bear close scrutiny. Their great leaders are often no better than ranting quacks, their heroes no more than ignoble puppets, their heroines far from pure. The prize does not always go to the bravest man. In our revolution, for once and by some miracle, it fell to the most deserving. His great triumphs were never the rare small battles where he won a trifling upper hand—they were his triumph over Congress, over hunger and disease, over lukewarm friends and smiling enemies in his own camp, whose petty jealousies he had to meet and master with his great, steady spirit. When the war ended, our own Royal commanders spent all their time squabbling and making excuses before Parliament, pointing fingers, claiming their fleets arrived too late, their regiments misread their orders, their cannonballs would not fit their guns. But Washington beat us all, often with no shot, no powder, no money at all. He never once considered surrender. Through all the doubt and darkness, the danger and long tempest of the war, I think only his indomitable soul stayed entirely steady.
Of course, the enemy made the most of our failed Charleston expedition, declaring it a prodigious, history-making victory. Mr. Lee rushed back to New York, trumpeting himself as the conqueror of conquerors, and no man received him with more eager delight than the Commander-in-Chief of the American Army. It was “my dear Lee” and “my dear General” between them, and it always touches me to read that simple, unfeigned confidence Washington had for officers under him who had once served in the King’s army. The old Mexicans looked on in the same awed wonder when they first saw an armed Spanish horseman galloping towards them. That vain, flashy braggart Lee, and other Continental generals whose names and luck became notorious later, took shameless advantage of Washington’s modesty, blustering, sneering, and disobeying his orders, piling up new obstacles in his path every single day, obstacles only his astonishing endurance could have allowed him to overcome.
While we were away on the South Carolina expedition, the famous Fourth of July had come and gone, and we and the thirteen United States were parted forever. My own native state of Virginia had also made its grand declaration: that all men are born equally free, that all power rests with the people, who have the unalienable right to alter, reform, or abolish their government whenever they please, and that the idea of a hereditary ruler is unnatural and absurd. Our General handed me that brand new document fresh from Williamsburg as we sailed north past the Virginia capes, laughing as

It has always struck me—speaking with all deference to men who have made war their lifelong trade—that the earthen ramparts thrown up on Breed’s Hill shaped the entire course of our American conflict for the British Crown. The carnage those ragged colonists dealt us from behind those rough defences was so brutal, their stand so stubbornly unyielding, that every British general who came after moved through the rest of the war with a lingering, unnecessary awe of any rebel barricade. By the time of the White Plains engagement, when Mr. Washington’s half-starved army lay completely at the mercy of our victorious troops, we learned later that our advance halted dead in its tracks before a makeshift fortification built of nothing but cornstalks and loose straw.

Another chance to crush the rebellion slipped through our fingers entirely: the whole long winter that the dwindling, demoralized Continental force huddled freezing and unarmed at Valley Forge, under the very nose of Sir William Howe’s perfectly provisioned, grandly quartered army in Philadelphia. Our men feasted, gambled, danced to fiddle tunes, and threw mock medieval tournaments where fine ladies wove wreaths for the “clement” general, inscribing their favors with absurd verses promising his laurels would never fade. I have always wondered why the grateful rebels never erected a statue to him: no officer in their whole army served their cause half so well, fumbling every chance we had to strike a decisive blow, wrapping our defeats in soft cotton so the rebels barely felt the hurt of them, helping their broken, outnumbered forces back to their feet again and again.

Think of Wolfe, eighteen years prior, the fiery young warrior England sent to seize Quebec: pacing his lines day and night, sleepless, eaten up with eagerness, prowling midnight forests, climbing craggy precipices before dawn, watching until his great heart was worn thin before he struck, and died victorious on the Plains of Abraham. Compare him now to Howe, laughing mid-dance at a Philadelphia ball, his fiddles sawing out tunes while the rebel army he should have crushed froze to death in their huts a few dozen miles away.

The grand scheme hatched by ministers in London and our top generals in New York was simple: drive a military corridor from Canada down the Hudson to New York City, split New England off from the rest of the colonies, and crush the rebellion piecemeal. Gentleman Johnny Burgoyne was given command of the expedition, and set out from Quebec with all the pomp of a conquering hero, firing off grand proclamations threatening the colonists with England’s full might, summoning the “misguided rebels” to lay down their arms. He brought with him a fearsome regular British force, a corps of hardened German veterans, a savage band of Indian auxiliaries, and a full park of heavy artillery. Everyone assumed the Loyalist populace along his march would flock to the royal standard. The Continental force opposing him was small at first, and Washington’s main army was weakened by the thousands of men he was forced to rush north to block Burgoyne’s advance. A second British detachment was supposed to fight its way up the Hudson from New York, clear the river of all rebel resistance, and meet Burgoyne at Albany. At that point, Washington’s depleted army could have been crushed once and for all— but Providence willed it otherwise, and I for one do not regret how the war ended.

Looking back across the board now, every blunder our side made is plain as day. We were perpetually too late. Supplies and reinforcements from home arrived too late. Succor to our beleaguered outposts reached them too late. Our fleet hove into view off Yorktown only hours after Cornwallis had already struck his colors. When an escape route opened for Burgoyne, he delayed retreating until it was already gone. I have heard disgraced old officers argue for hours over wine, proving that a single favorable wind would have kept America in the empire, that one unseasonable tempest alone stopped us from destroying the entire French fleet, that nightfall alone snatched Washington and his whole army out of our grasp no less than three separate times. Who that loves history has not speculated on all the “what ifs” that change the course of the world? I pull my tattered old war map from the shelf sometimes, stare down at the battleground, and marvel at the string of silly, trivial turns of luck that lost us a game we held all the best cards to win.

I cannot deny the old fight still stirs my languid, aging blood. My brother Hal, settled safe on his Virginia plantation, is perfectly content with his quiet lot: the company of his neighboring planter friends, tending his tobacco crops and his enslaved laborers, fishing the creeks, shooting ducks, hunting the hardwood forests, then settling in for a rubber of cards and a hearty supper by his fireside. Happy Hal, dozing on his porch surrounded by hounds at his feet, his sharp little wife running the whole household and her easygoing husband, who obeyed her every word when she lived and grieved her only a short while before he found his peace. His lot would have felt like prison to me, but how lucky the man whose foot fits the exact shoe fortune gives him!

My own income is five times Hal’s, my English house built of fine brick faced with freestone, my wife— I would not trade her for any other woman alive, my children all healthy and bright. But for all the plums and peaches that spill out of Plenty’s horn into my lap, I fear I have been something of an ingrate. My gatekeeper Hodge, sharing his crust of bread and scrap of bacon with a family as large as my own, seems to enjoy his simple meal far more than I enjoy Mrs. Molly’s finest sweetmeats and Mr. Gumbo’s choicest claret from the cellar. Sweetmeats have lost their savor for me, and the scent of old wine palls on an old man’s nose. Our parson Joe Blake has preached many a sermon at me over the years, though I confess I did not always listen closely when he first delivered them. You remember that October evening, honest Joe? (He does, for he has told the story over a bottle as many times as he has preached his sermons, and my Lady Warrington pretends she has never heard it a hundred times.) The night we scrambled through an embrasure at Fort Clinton, and a rebel soldier lifted his musket to dash my brains out with the clubbed end, and your sword ran him through before he could strike. Back then you wore the red coat of the brave 63rd Foot, where your captain Sill died pierced through with a dozen wounds beside you. Now you wear black, and preach in my pulpit, your sermons short, your doctrine sound, and your belly so round I doubt your old 63rd uniform could ever button shut again across it. The other day we read the papers together over our wine: of old friend Howe’s glorious naval victory on the first of June, of our old comrade Lord Rawdon joining the Duke of York’s force, of the duke’s full retreat before Pichegru, and my son Miles helping to take Valenciennes with barely a fight. Oh, Joe, would you not give a year of your quiet parson’s life to be young again, to leave this gouty toe of mine at home, saddle my old mare, and ride back out to feel your blood pound with the thrill of the game once more?

The last engagement I saw played out was a gallant little victory for our side, though it came far too late to change the war’s outcome, and could not stop the catastrophe that was about to swallow Burgoyne’s whole army. At the end of September 1777, after weeks of frustrating delays that weakened the blow we were meant to strike, an expedition finally sailed out of New York harbor. Had it set sail a fortnight earlier, it could have saved Burgoyne’s doomed force— but the fates willed otherwise. The delay was no fault of Sir Henry Clinton’s, who dared not leave New York City unprotected; contrary winds simply held up the long-awaited reinforcements sailing from England. Those ships brought us our first letters from home in months, full of news of our children safe with their Aunt Hetty and their grandfather.
